This was truly unavoidable. In ancient times, the sūtras and their commentaries circulated separately;

thus, regarding the profound depths of the sūtra’s meaning, the commentaries were developed with exhaustive detail and precision, while for the explicit portions of the sūtra text, they merely provided structural divisions and key points.
Later generations insistently sought to merge the commentary with the sūtra, which resulted in the fragmentation of the sūtra’s phrasing and punctuation.
Now, as I wish to expound the meaning according to the text, yet without damaging the structural integrity of the sūtra, how could the topical divisions (ke-ʼan) not be slightly revised?
Although Master Zhìzhě’s eloquence was vast and his expositions were extensive, and although Zhān’ān only began to study them after the Master’s passing—
much like Ānanda compiling the teachings after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa— while they fully accord with the Master’s intended meaning, they are not necessarily entirely definitive in every detail.
The writings of the Great Master (Zhiyi) are thus characterized by a forceful and archaic style that eschews ornate artifice; it is only through long-term study that their subtlety becomes apparent.

For practitioners at the initial stage of the path, these scrolls may seem bewildering—how could the text not be made somewhat more accessible? As for the Venerable Jingxi (Zhanran), his work is like refined gold tempered a hundred times;
both its literary expression and its doctrinal meaning are profound, yet it still bears a slight trace of the Six Dynasties aesthetic, which might cause some slight friction [to modern readers].
The time has come for the revelation of the Great Master’s intent beyond the literal words;

this is not something that those who merely follow the traces of the written characters can understand—would it not be tantamount to inserting one's own personal opinions? The treasury of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is profound, solid, and remote;
since the Great Master Zhiyi was able to harmonize with its source, how could he have failed to fully proclaim its detailed implications? —Thus said Zhizhe Dashi, and Chang’an [Zhanran] [concurs].

If the Venerable One could record its general outline, how could he have recorded every detail? And even if the Venerable Jingxi could expound its essentials, how could he have fully analyzed every nuance?
Here, taking one insight from a thousand deliberations of an ordinary person, I employ it to suit the needs of the times.
How could I fear the reproach of contradicting the ancients and thus fail to exhaust my meager clarity to offer this humble contribution?
This is a categorization according to their essential meanings. Thus, those who understand me will surely do so by meeting these meanings;
those who criticize me will likewise do so by meeting these meanings. This preface was written on the fifth day of the middle winter month of the year Geng-You (1511).

△ This commentary on the main text of the sutra is divided into two parts: first, the title; second, the entry into the text. The title has two sections: first, the title of the sutra; second, the titles of the chapters.
The title of the sutra is explained in detail as in the *Xuanyi Shiqian* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning) and briefly as in the *Miaoxuan Jiyao* (Essentials of the Profound Meaning);
it will not be discussed further here. Now, I shall first explain the chapter title and then enter the text. There are two [sections] to the chapter title.

18. First, I shall now explain the "Introductory Chapter" (*nidāna-parivarta*); the remaining chapters will be explained as we reach their respective texts. Regarding the first chapter, the "Introductory":
the term *xiùxù* (庠序) signifies orderly sequence; it means that the stages, the host and guest, and the questions and answers are all conducted with orderly propriety. Furthermore, it follows from...

The exposition of these three meanings and so forth constitutes the five matters that serve as the preface to the beginning of the sutra. The six auspicious omens in the *Prabhāsa* [chapter] represent the introductory origin of the incitement.
The questions and answers that resolve doubts constitute the formal exposition (*nirdeśa*), while the preceding narrative serves as the prologue (*upodghāta*).

Because it possesses these three meanings, it is called the "Preface Chapter" (*nidāna-parivarta*). In Sanskrit, this is called *varga*, which is translated here as "chapter" (*pin*); its meaning refers to a category or class.

A "chapter" (*varga*) is so named because similar topics are gathered into a single section. Alternatively, a chapter may be proclaimed by the Buddha himself, as in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* or the *Cittabhūmi*;
or it may be established by the compilers, as described in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, where the original *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* consisted of only three chapters (1.
Introduction, 2. Māra’s Deeds, 3. Entrustment). Or, chapters may have been added by translators, such as when Kumārajīva translated the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* into nine chapters.

Regarding the ten chapters: the current "Chapter on the Original Acts of Bhaiṣajyarāja" is the Buddha’s own discourse, while those concerning "Sughoṣa," "Avalokiteśvara," and so forth, were added by the compilers.
In the Sanskrit original, these chapters were already complete; they were not appended by the translators. Since this marks the beginning of the chapters, it is called the "First."
△ Entering the text, there are three sections: first, a general exposition of the two gates of the Trace and the Origin; second, a specific explanation of the two gates of the Trace and the Origin;
third, the circulation of the two gates of the Trace and the Origin. This is further divided into four parts: first, the causes and conditions;

second, the application of the teachings; third, the Origin and the Trace; fourth, the contemplation of the mind. From the beginning with "Thus have I heard" until the end with "and departed," the text is interpreted through these four meanings.
I have now briefly recorded [the four explanations], whether three, two, or one; what is valued is simply grasping the essential meaning. As for why I employ four explanations:
an extensive treatment causes the intellect to retreat, while a concise one fails to encompass the full meaning. I now teach by taking a middle path so that the principles may be easily understood.

Furthermore, "causes and conditions" (nidāna) is also termed "stimulus and response" (ganying). Although sentient beings lack the capacity [to respond], they do not perceive [the Buddha's presence] even when he is near; yet through the power of his roots of goodness, he is far-reaching.

Because they communicate with one another through the mutual intersection of the Way, this is explained by means of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*). Indeed, the sentient beings who seek liberation are numerous;
the sages who arise to respond to them are likewise numerous. This principle is even more extensive. Wherein does it reside? A Great Sūtra states:
"The power of the roots of goodness of loving-kindness and compassion has immeasurable gates; briefly stated, these are the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). These supernormal powers are precisely...

"Response" (*ying*) is another name for "correspondence" (*shi*); when contrasted with "stimulus" (*gan*), it is termed "resonance" (*ganying*). Although responses may be manifold, they do not exceed compassion;
although stimuli may be numerous, they do not go beyond the quest for liberation. Thus, the two characters "stimulus" and "response" are clearly situated at the center.

Now, if the stimuli and responses throughout the ten directions are as vast as empty space and the teachings are even more expansive, how can one speak of being "situated at the center"? This present treatise concerns the Sahā world.

The Buddha-work of the sounds of the land opens the gate of ambrosia; interpreting these according to the teachings based on sound, one takes the Golden Mouth as the foundation—neither more nor less than what is clarified therein.
Now, in establishing teachings to respond to capacities, there are differences in provisional and real, shallow and deep.
When looking from the fundamental to the traces, the capacities are many and the teachings differ; since those traces must be extensive, how can they be said to have a fixed location?

Now, by placing the finger in the middle, one preserves the moon while letting go of its traces. Although the discussion of both the fundamental (the moon) and the traces (the finger) is extensive, it is clarified that the fundamental resides in a single place.
Indeed, seeking the traces leads to vastness and only results in self-exhaustion; seeking the fundamental leads to height that cannot be reached.
It is like counting another's treasures while possessing not even half a coin oneself; one should simply observe the height and breadth of one’s own mind, which is as inexhaustible as empty space.
The Sage responds to capacities and achieves the ultimate goal; having attained his own benefit, he employs the contemplation of the mind as the method of interpretation.
Regarding the proof by means of causes and conditions, the "Expedient Means" chapter states: "The Buddhas of the ten directions appear in the world for the sake of the one great causal condition.
Regarding the proof by means of the provisional teachings, the "Expedient Means" chapter states: "He proclaims and reveals the Buddha through various Dharma gates."

The *Mahāvaipulya-mahāsannipāta-sūtra* states: "Both harsh words and gentle speech ultimately converge upon the primary meaning. Regarding the proof of the fundamental and the provisional (the original and the manifested), the *Ayuṣpramāṇa-parivarta* says:
"Today, gods, humans, and asuras all say that I left home at a young age and attained *samyak-saṃbodhi* not far from the city of Gayā;
yet, in truth, since I first attained Buddhahood, it has been immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) kalpas."
Throughout kalpas, he has used these skillful means to guide and benefit sentient beings. As stated in the "Chapter on Receiving Prophecy":

"Internally he keeps secret his bodhisattva practices, while externally he manifests as a śrāvaka; in reality, he purifies his own buddha-field, yet he shows himself to the assembly as possessing the three poisons and even manifests the appearance of false views.
My disciples employ such skillful means to deliver sentient beings. Thus, both master and disciple are enlightened.
Regarding the realization of the mind through the fundamental and the trace, the *Parable* chapter states:

"If a person believes what you have said, they shall see me, as well as you and the assembly of bhikṣus, along with all the bodhisattvas. You should know that according to whatever they hear, they observe it with a discerning mind;
within their mind of faith, they attain the vision of the Triple Gem. Hearing this Dharma being preached, they truly see me."
This Buddha-treasure beholds you as the Sangha-treasure. Now, for the time being, I shall demonstrate the characteristics of causes and conditions through three stages:
first, sentient beings have long since received the Buddha’s skillful means, which caused them to plant the seeds for the causes and conditions of the Buddha-way;

second, meeting [the Buddha] in the interim, he further employed various expedient means to assist in revealing the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) and brought them to maturity; and third, today, flowers rain down and the earth trembles.

They are brought to liberation through the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata. Furthermore, planting the seeds in the distant past, ripening them in the past, and attaining liberation in the recent present—this refers to those who emerged from the earth and others.

Furthermore, planting the seeds in the interim, ripening them through the four flavors, and attaining liberation at the royal city—this refers to those currently undergoing the stages of opening, showing, awakening, and entering. Furthermore, planting the seeds in this present life...
That which ripens in the next life and brings liberation in subsequent lives refers to those who will attain deliverance in the future; this is explained by taking the general meaning.
Within this, each successive stage is treated as the three periods of time—the nine periods consisting of planting the seed, ripening, and liberation.

For such reasons and conditions, there is the introductory section (*nidāna*). The assembly beheld these rare and auspicious omens and, with eager anticipation, yearned to hear the full teaching in its entirety.

Because it suffices to explain that the Buddha established his transformative teachings by responding to capacities through the vehicle of the Buddhas, thereby revealing, awakening, and entering into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, there is the "Section on the Correct Teaching.

Because not only did those present at that time obtain great benefit, but even during the distant period of the final five hundred years, the wondrous Way would still reach them, there is the "Section on Circulation.
Next, regarding these three sections, I shall demonstrate their characteristics according to the provisional teachings; this introduction is not intended for the sake of humans or devas.
Qingsheng’s preface is not written for the minor path of the Two Vehicles; it is not written for those who take emptiness as their immediate goal while penetrating the Three Vehicles;

nor is it written for the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas alone. Rather, it is written as a preface for that which is upright and straightforward, which abandons expedient means and speaks only of the unsurpassed Buddha-way.
This "uprightness" does not refer to the mundane world, nor does it refer to the light of a firefly. It analyzes [the nature of reality].
Wisdom is what is correct; it does not point to the substance of lamps or torches. Dharma-knowledge is what is correct; it does not point to the stars or the moon.
Path-knowledge is what is correct; it points to the sunlight. All-encompassing knowledge is what is correct.

This circulation [of the teaching] is not for the sake of spreading the leaves of trees, nor for wooden oxen or wooden horses; it is not a circulation of the "half-words," nor a circulation of the "shared words."
This is not the circulation of separate characters, but rather the circulation of the *pūrṇa* (full) dharma of the *sūtra* of perfect fulfillment.

Next, regarding the three sections to demonstrate the fundamental and the trace: when [the Buddha] was practicing the bodhisattva path for a long duration, he proclaimed the *Lotus Sūtra* of the former Buddhas;
this also has three parts—superior, middling, and inferior—and its words likewise possess both the fundamental and the trace, though these are relative when comparing one Buddha to another.

This would then lead to an infinite regress. Now, we shall separately take the words of the first, middle, and last parts of the *Lotus Sūtra* preached by Śākyamuni at the time of his initial attainment of Buddhahood, and designate them specifically as "the Superior" and name them "the Root. Why?

Because it was the very first teaching he gave upon his initial attainment of Buddhahood; furthermore, his intermediate activities of conversion assisted Buddhas such as Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū and Dīpaṃkara in proclaiming the Dharma.
Regarding the three divisions of the *Lotus Sūtra*, they are designated only as "Middle" and only as "Trace. Why is this?
Because there was that which preceded them—the "Superior" and the "Root"—the three divisions taught today at the Royal City (Rājagṛha) are designated only as "Inferior" and only as "Trace.
Furthermore, even the three divisions taught eternally in the future are likewise pointed back to the very beginning as being "Superior."
To take a fundamental analogy, it is like a great tree: although it has thousands of branches and ten thousand leaves, when one considers its root, they all share the same single trunk;

thus, one cannot point from one to another in a chain of transmission. Next, regarding the demonstration of the characteristics of contemplation (*citta-bhāvanā*) by means of three stages, one should discuss precept (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*) in relation to one’s own mind as three divisions of practice: namely, precept at the beginning, concentration in the middle, and wisdom at the end.
In the Dharma-gate, wisdom is the root, while concentration and precepts are the traces. Furthermore, each of these—precepts, concentration, and wisdom—is divided into three parts.
Regarding the three parts of the precepts: first, the preliminary preparation; second, the formal *jñapti-caturtha-karman*; and third, the conclusion. Regarding the three parts of concentration:

first, right contemplation during the twenty-five conditions; second, traversing the conditions; and third, skillfully entering, abiding in, and emerging from concentration. These constitute the three [aspects] of concentration.

Regarding the division of the wisdom [of the sūtra] into three parts: the "Emptiness" section constitutes the Prologue (*nidāna*), while the "Correct" and "Provisional" sections constitute the Circulation (*pravartana*).

Having thus demonstrated the four kinds of correspondence (*saṃprayukta*) by means of these three parts, one should employ this principle from the beginning with "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) until the conclusion with "having paid homage, he departed.

A practitioner should skillfully contemplate this as a method for interpreting the text through the four intentions (*catur-abhiprāya*). Indeed, if there were no explanation of the initial causes and conditions, it would not even be possible to... [proceed].

Unlike external heterodox views, these four *siddhāntas* (purposes) of the causal discourse apply universally throughout the single transformation; one must know that this is now the Great Matter. These four *siddhāntas* are not for other [teachings].

Through the opening and manifestation of response and stimulus, the four *siddhāntas* constitute the One Way, leaving nothing outside them. The four *siddhāntas* of the long distant past are not found in other sutras.
The four *siddhāntas* of contemplating the mind encompass all within a single contemplation. By means of these four *siddhāntas*, which apply from beginning to end, they are categorized accordingly.

The three [categories] beginning with "Teaching" (jiao) must also be explained exhaustively; for if they were not explained according to the teachings, one would fail to distinguish between the partial (pian) and the complete (xiao).

By means of the four [categories] and eight [categories], one distinguishes and clarifies the provisional, the opening, the sublation, and so forth. In contrast to the previous teachings and divisions, only now is it truly real, as there is no longer any other designation for any of the expressive vehicles (qian).
Therefore, these must be clarified to manifest the wondrous scripture. If there were no explanation of the three aspects of "Original" (ben) and "Trace" (ji), who would know?

Transcending all that is discussed regarding the bodies and lands within the teachings of a single period, everything today is nothing other than a provisional manifestation pointing toward that Great Universal [Dharma].

It is like first dispelling ignorance through the "two-night" [teachings] of the *Shinmitsu* (Secret Mandala), yet remaining deluded regarding the provisional body; it is only now that this is finally cleared away.

If one still clings to the stump [of old views] and remains muddled, how can one discern the merit of the expressive teachings without the interpretation of the four contemplations of mind? How could the function of the teachings be realized?
Why is this? Because it serves as the fundamental basis for long-term cultivation of practice, every single phrase enters the mind to form contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).

When contemplation accords with the sūtra, one realizes that this is not like "counting another's treasures. Only then does one know that the entire work on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* is the raft for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*.

Only by synthesizing these four meanings can the essential purport of the entire work be briefly revealed. One should know that even the [previous] two or three [sections] were still brief; how much more so the first!
Because they are capable of attaining this, each and every phrase realizes these four meanings; thus, every phrase differs from all other teachings.

First is a general exposition of the two gates of the traces and the source. Second, the first [section] concerns the time and place where the Dharma was heard; second, the companions who heard and upheld it.
The place where the Dharma was first heard:
"Thus have I heard at one time the Buddha was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha.

Here, "thus" (*evam*) refers to the essence of the Dharma as it was heard; "I heard" (*śrutam mayā*) refers to the person who was able to retain it; and "at one time" (*ekasmin samaye*) [refers to the occasion].
"Those who hear and uphold" refers to the harmony [of the assembly] at a time other than that [of the Buddha's presence]; "the Buddha" refers to hearing from the Buddha at that time;
"the royal city and Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa" are the places where they hear and uphold; and "together with the great bhikṣus and others" refers to their companions in hearing and upholding.

Therefore, these five matters are placed at the beginning of the sūtra. Regarding the causal explanation, the phrase "Thus" (evam) appears at the beginning of the sūtras of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
"All are at peace" refers to the *loka-siddhānta*, wherein the path of these Buddhas is identical and does not contend with the world.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "To raise up time and direction so as to inspire faith in people is the *pudgala-siddhānta*.

Furthermore, the refutation of the non-Buddhist [view] through the two characters "A" and "O"—meaning "not like" and "not so"—is the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta*. (In all non-Buddhist scriptures, the two characters "A" and "O" are used...)

First, regarding what he calculates as these two [the teacher and the teaching], they are both elucidated within his own school and do not transcend what he has calculated. Furthermore, "thus" (*evam*) is a term signifying faith and compliance:
faith means that the principles one has heard are integrated, and compliance means that the way between teacher and disciple is established; this is the *paramārtha-siddhānta*.
As for the explanation according to the teachings (*yōkyō-shaku*), since the various sūtras differ, "thus" likewise differs; one should not attempt to open all [sūtras] with a single spoon.
Furthermore, the two texts—the *Hu* and the Buddha’s words to Ānanda—are not different; they function as the expressive means (*vyañjana*) that express the expressed meaning (*artha*).

Now, what text did Ānanda transmit from the Buddha, and what was the meaning expressed? It is impossible to transmit the Sudden through gradual texts; therefore, it is with partial texts that the Perfect is expressed.
If this transmission and expression are erroneous, then the text does not accord with the text; and if the text does not accord [with itself], then the principle [is lost].
This meaning is not difficult to clarify provided one examines it with careful scrutiny. If it is said that the Buddha clearly taught that while conventional (saṃvṛti) letters exist,
ultimate (paramārtha) letters do not, and that Ānanda transmitted the Buddha’s conventional letters such that they did not differ from what the Buddha spoke—

and thus they are called "thus" (tathā)— and that because these conventional letters accord with the principle of ultimate truth, they are called "is" (satya), then this is precisely what is clarified at the beginning of the Tripiṭaka sūtras.

It is thus: if one says that the Buddha’s clarity is "form is emptiness and emptiness is form," that "form and emptiness are non-dual and without distinction" and "form and emptiness are not different," and that this is "the suchness of reality as it is" (ji-shi-er-zhen), then this is the *Ānanda* transmission of the Buddha’s text.
To say that the signifier is identical to the signified is "suchness"; this constitutes the beginning of the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*) scriptures.

This clarifies it as such. If one says that the Buddha clarified that birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) has limits while nirvāṇa is limitless—emerging from the limits of birth-and-death and entering the limitlessness of nirvāṇa, or emerging from the limitlessness of nirvāṇa and entering the Middle Way—then Ānanda’s transmission of "emerging from existence and entering non-existence" and "emerging from non-existence and entering the middle" does not differ from the Buddha’s teaching; it is thus. From... [the source].
From the shallow to the profound, everything is said to be "this"; such is the beginning of the Separate Teaching (prthaktva-naya) sūtras.
If it is said that the Buddha clarifies that birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is itself *nirvāṇa* and also the Middle Way, how much more so must *nirvāṇa* itself not be the Middle Way?

True Suchness (*tathatā*), the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the true nature (*bhūtadhātu*), and the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) pervade all places; there is nothing that is not the Buddha-dharma. Ānanda transmitted this.

This is the "Thus" at the beginning of the Perfect Sūtra. What is the fundamental source? What is the trace? To explain by way of the Buddha’s initial attainment of enlightenment: the opening words of the sūtras stating "Thus have I heard" at that time constitute the fundamental source.
The subsequent teachings given while acting as a Buddha throughout his life, including the opening words "Thus have I heard" of the sūtras spoken on this day, are all traces.
Furthermore, the "Thus have I heard" transmitted by Ānanda refers to the traces; the "Thus have I heard" spoken by the Buddha himself refers to the fundamental source.
Furthermore, that teacher and disciple have attained such realization is neither a beginning from today nor something occurring midway;

these are the "essence" (hon), while "midway" and "today" are the "traces" (shaku). As for the "Exegesis of Contemplating the Mind," it means to contemplate all such meanings as the various traces of the *siddhānta* teachings mentioned above;
since they are all phenomena produced by causes and conditions, the very fact of their being dependently originated is itself emptiness—that is, it is the contemplation of penetration (*tongguan*).
That "causes and conditions are themselves emptiness and themselves the provisional" refers to the distinct contemplation (*bīe guān*).

That "the two contemplations serve as the path of skillful means to enter the Middle Way of the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*) while simultaneously illuminating the two truths" refers to both the universal and the distinct contemplation.

That "all of the above is the Middle Way" refers to the contemplation that is neither universal nor distinct. The text says: "If a person believes what you have said, they shall immediately attain [it]."
"To see me is also to see you, as well as the community of bhikṣus and all the bodhisattvas"—this is the clear exposition of contemplative practice (*guanxing*).
"Faith" refers to the capacity of the recipient (*jī*), while "seeing" refers to the response of the Buddha; this is the principle of causes and conditions (*yīnyuán*).

Furthermore, there are various distinctions such as the shallowness or depth of faith and the provisional or ultimate nature of seeing; this is explained according to the teachings (*jiàojiào*). Moreover, regarding the faith in the *Lotus Sūtra*...
If one sees the transformation of Śāriputra, one sees the original state of Nāgadatta (the *Tattvasaṃgraha* states that Subhūti is the Buddha Nāgadatta of the East;
some cite the *Mahāratnakūṭa-sūtra*, which says Śāriputra will become a Buddha named Suvarṇanāgadatta, though this has not yet been verified).
If one sees the newly attained Śākyamuni Buddha, one also sees the primordially attained Buddhas of the past. If one sees the twelve hundred bhikṣus and eighty thousand bodhisattvas...

This also reveals its fundamental source. Furthermore, having heard the sutra and believing it in one’s heart without doubt, when this faith is perceived as luminous and pure, this is seeing the Buddha.
When the various categories are clearly distinguished, this is seeing Śāriputra. When the various categories are clearly distinguished, this is seeing the bhikṣus.
When the mind of compassion is pure, this is seeing the bodhisattvas. These four sections of the explanation are thus concluded. [The Section on] Causes and Conditions.

Regarding the phrase "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*), some say it means "I have heard thus. This is because the original texts of the sūtras differ; these two expressions are raised interchangeably at the beginning and end [of different versions].

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Because the faculty of hearing is unimpaired, the sound is within the range of audibility, and the mind is intent on hearing—through the convergence of these various conditions—it is said, 'I have heard.
Question: One should say "the ear hears"; why then do you say "I have heard"? Answer: "I" is the master of the ear.

Regarding the statement "I [Śāriputra] gathered the assembly" as a condition for this world, it is explained that when Ānanda ascended the seat, he proclaimed "Thus have I heard," and the great assembly all wailed with grief;
having just seen the Tathāgata, they now proclaimed "Thus have I heard. Furthermore, when Mañjuśrī compiled the teachings, he first chanted the title and then proclaimed "Thus have I heard";
at that time, the assembly wailed with grief. Both instances arose from the production of longing and attachment; this is well-suited for human beings.
This is an explanation. Ānanda’s body resembled that of the Buddha, being only three finger-widths (one finger-width being two cun) shorter than the Buddha.

The assembly doubted whether it was the World-Honored One Śākyamuni appearing again, or a Buddha from another direction who had come, or whether Ānanda had attained Buddhahood. Now, by chanting "I have heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*), these three doubts are all dispelled.

This is the explanation for the purpose of counteracting [these doubts]. For a learner such as Ānanda, following worldly convention, one says "I have heard"; yet in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there is no self.
Within this [teaching], there is no self and no hearing; from antiquity, all the various exegeses have agreed that these are merely one principle: dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

Within the context of dependent origination, even the first three [of the four truths] are themselves not yet complete, let alone the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and how much less so when considering the three [categories] such as the "teaching according to the doctrine" (*yathāśāsana*)? Next, regarding the teaching according to the doctrine:

the *Śāstra* explains that ordinary beings possess three kinds of what they call "self"—namely, the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), the conceit of self (*asmimāna*), and worldly convention (*loka-vyavahāra*).
The Master Buddhabhadra explains that among those who study, there is no view of self (*anātman-dṛṣṭi*) except for two types;

and among those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), there is no sense of "I" (*asmimāna*) except for one type. Now, when Ānanda hears the Dharma, he is a student with the view of non-self who is able to subdue the conceit of "I";

it is merely to conform to worldly convention that he is called by the name "I," which is without fault. This interpretation of "self" is based on the intent of the Tripiṭaka. [From] the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*.

The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "To assert 'self' through any of the four propositions is to fall into false views. Within the Buddha’s True Dharma, there is no self; who, then, hears this?

This employs the meaning of the Shared Teaching (*p’ung-chiao*). The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "The learned Ānanda knows that 'self' and 'no-self' are non-dual, yet he discriminates between them as both 'self' and 'no-self.

This employs the meaning of the Distinct Teaching (*pieh-chiao*)—where "non-duality" refers to those who have attained the stages (*bhūmi*), and "simultaneous illumination" refers to those prior to the stages.
Furthermore, Ānanda knows both "self" and "non-self" as non-dual; as an attendant, he upholds the Tathāgata’s unimpeded wisdom.
By means of his sovereign voice, he transmits the provisional and the ultimate—what could be improper in this?

This is explained through the perspective of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). Moreover, the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* clarifies that there were three Ānandas; "Ānanda" is translated here as...
Ānanda Bhadra, translated as "Joyful Sage," joyfully upheld the Śrāvaka Piṭaka; Ānanda Sāgara, translated as "Joyful Ocean," received and upheld the Kṣudraka Piṭaka;
and Ānanda Garbha, translated as "Treasury," upheld the Buddha-piṭaka and the Āgama-sūtras.
Thus, it refers to a single individual endowed with four virtues who transmitted and maintained these four dharma-gates; this is the meaning.
Regarding the manifestation of the three aspects of origin and trace: if one has not yet realized their convergence, one may say that Ānanda followed worldly convention by being called "I.

However, if one reveals the trace to manifest the origin, he was simultaneously resolved upon the mind at the time of the Buddha Śūnyarāja; as a skillful means, he manifested as a transmitter of the Dharma—what could he not accomplish?
Fourth, regarding the contemplation of the mind: one contemplates that phenomena produced through causes and conditions are simultaneously empty and provisional.
That which is the Middle is emptiness, meaning there is no self; that which is the Provisional is the discrimination between self and non-self;
that which is the Middle is the true, wondrous self. Having completed these fourfold explanations of "self," next, regarding the listener Ānanda:
he was born on the night the Buddha attained the Way and attended the Buddha for barely more than twenty years. Before attending the Buddha, he presumably had not heard [the Dharma].
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: When Ānanda was compiling the Dharma, he said himself, "When the Buddha first turned the wheel of the Dharma, I did not see it at that time.

From this successive hearing, one should know that he did not hear everything in its entirety. Because there is a distinction between what is heard from others and what is heard by oneself, there is a difference between what has not been heard and what has already been heard.
Those who have not yet heard it desire to hear it, while those who have already heard it give rise to joy; this is the worldly [perspective].

Regarding "Xiye" (悉也), the ancient commentaries explain it as follows: Ānanda was able to hear [the teachings] through the power of the Buddha’s *bodhi-samādhi* and subsequently reported them to others.
The *Ren'en jing* (Sūtra on Repaying Kindness) states that Ānanda sought four vows, among which was the vow that the Buddha would re-explain sūtras he had not yet heard.
It further states that the Buddha spoke them secretly from his own mouth. The *Taijing* (Womb Sūtra) states that the Buddha extended his golden arm from within the golden coffin to speak again.

Regarding Ānanda manifesting the signs of entering the womb, this is heard in all the sūtras; how much more so when it is explained in other places? This is the *prātipakṣika-saṃvṛti* (remedial conventional truth).
This sūtra states that upon receiving his prediction, Ānanda recalled his original vows and maintained the teachings of the former Buddhas exactly as they were before;
this is the *paramārtha-saṃvṛti* (ultimate conventional truth). If we consider this according to the [four] teachings (*yāna*), Ānanda was filled with joy, his face like the pure full moon.
With eyes like blue lotuses, he personally received the Buddha’s instructions as one holds a perfect vessel; he transmitted them to transform others as if pouring from one vessel into another.

This is the transmission of hearing the Dharma that has already been heard. Ānanda, dwelling in the stage of training with joy, attained the eyes of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, such that his faculties of eye, ear, nose, and tongue were not leaking; this is the upholding of the Dharma both heard and unheard. He is the Treasury Keeper, Ānanda.
Capable of receiving and retaining much, like a great cloud that holds rain—this refers to the preservation of what was not previously heard and the hearing of the Dharma.
Ānanda, this ocean of the learned is one who can naturally understand and comprehend both the permanent and the impermanent.

If one knows that the Tathāgata is permanent yet does not preach the Dharma, this is called a bodhisattva being fully endowed with much learning; the great waters of the ocean of the Buddha-Dharma flow into them.

Ānanda’s mind maintains this transmission, yet it is not a matter of hearing what has not been heard. Now, this Sūtra is the ocean; Ānanda maintains the wondrous Dharma of that which has not been heard and is not heard.
Regarding the three aspects of origin and trace: as mentioned above, the four instances of "hearing" are all traces.

They are drawn forth from the original ground, which is inconceivable. This is because the original substance is lofty and difficult to measure, and the principle of the original is profound and difficult to contemplate.

Because the fundamental reality (*honji*), its manifestations (*jakuji*), and its transformations (*ke*) are unfathomable, there are four ways of explaining the "Hearing" (*mon*) through the contemplation of the mind (*kan-shin*): 1. Contemplating the dharma of causes and conditions (*innen-hō*) is the contemplation of hearing-hearing;
2. Contemplating emptiness (*kū*) is the contemplation of hearing-not-hearing; 3. Contemplating the provisional (*ke*) is the contemplation of not-hearing-hearing; 4.

Contemplating the Middle (*chū*) is the contemplation of not-hearing-not-hearing (and so forth). The contemplation of a single thought-moment (*ichinen-kan*) is the wondrous contemplation (*myō-kan*) (and so forth). These are the fourfold explanations of "I have heard."
[End. Regarding the explanation of the term "at one time" (*ekasamaya*): Master Zhaò says that this refers to the occasion when the Dharma King inaugurates his mandate, a time of auspicious assembly;

this is the perspective of the world at large. The *Śāstra* states that *kāla* is the actual time, intended for internal disciples—referring to those who eat at the proper time and put on their robes;
whereas *samaya* is the conventional time, intended to refute the false views of external paths, and is used in contrast [to the former].
Regarding "governing" (*zhi*): if one is in accord with the Way at this time, it is the "First Meaning" (*paramārtha*). Regarding the "classification of teachings":

from the realization of the Truths (*satyadarśana*) upward and down to the stage of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa*), it is called the "Lower Single Time. If three types of persons enter the First Meaning together, it is called the "Middle Single Time.
If one has ascended to the stages (*bhūmi*) and above, it is called the "Upper Single Time. If one is from the first dwelling (*prathamavihāra*) and above, it is called the "Highest Single Time."
"An occasion" (*ekasamaya*) refers here to the supreme "occasion. Regarding "original and trace": the various preceding "occasions" are the trace;

the "occasion" of the eternally distant, true attainment is the original. Regarding "contemplating the mind": contemplating the mind first as empty, then as provisional, and finally as the Middle is the sequential contemplation of the mind;
contemplating the mind as simultaneously empty, provisional, and middle is the perfect and wondrous contemplation of the mind.

These [levels of] coarse and subtle each have their respective contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) and object; when these are unified, it is called "simultaneity" (*yugapat*), and this refers to the contemplation of the present sutra.
The fourfold explanation of "simultaneity" is hereby concluded. Regarding the explanation of the Buddha by way of causes and conditions (*nidāna*):

at the beginning of the eon there was no illness; as the eon drew to a close, illnesses became frequent. During times of long life there was happiness, while during times of short life there was suffering. In the eastern continent (Pūrvavideha), there is abundance and longevity.
In the western continent, there are many jewels, cattle, and sheep; in the northern continent, there is no sense of "mine" and no subjects.

In such times and places, the Buddha does not appear. From the time when the human lifespan was eighty thousand years down to the time it was one hundred years, the Buddha appeared in the southern continent, for it is there that people cultivate the causes before seeing the fruits. The true Dharma-joy is like eating milk gruel, after which nothing more is required. It is sustained by the Middle Way and the Śīla-pāramitā that accompanies it;

it gathers in sentient beings through the precepts and subdues the realm of Māra, such that the Buddha-realm is realized. Having long since perfected the merits of the fundamental stage, one is capable of riding the vehicle.
To tame sentient beings, one manifests traces in the form of the five flavors. Thus it was transmitted and cited by the Bhikṣu.
Sentient beings are as previously explained. One who contemplates the mind observes that a single thought-moment is pure like empty space, unimpeded by the shackles of the two extremes.
This great wisdom of equality—non-abiding and non-attachment—is called "leaving home.

Sustaining oneself through the Middle Way and naming the wisdom of the Dharma-body as one's livelihood makes one a "beggar for the Dharma" (*dharmabhikṣu*). To contemplate the afflictions of the five abodes is precisely this.
"Bodhi" (Enlightenment) refers to the destruction of all extremes, perversions, and non-illuminations; it is precisely the Middle Way, which is the "terrifying of Māras.

(As for the Middle Way, its aspects of emptiness, the provisional, and their sequential or non-sequential arrangements can be seen through the various teachings. "Assembly" (*saṃgha*) is a Sanskrit term translated here as "harmonious assembly.
One person, two persons, or three persons do not constitute a *saṃgha*; only from four persons upward is it called a *saṃgha*. This is because [the *saṃgha*] performs communal affairs.

There is no distinction between harmony and the dharma of not being separated from the assembly; there is no distinction between harmony and the principle of not being separated from the Buddha, who is always accompanied by one thousand two hundred and fifty people.

While the number of followers in various sutras may be indefinite—more or less—the *Śāstra* explains four kinds of Saṃghas: those who do not rely on the name of purity are called the "precept-breaking Saṃgha";

those who do not understand the laws and regulations are called the "deluded Saṃgha"; those who possess the five expedient means are called the "ashamed Saṃgha"; and those who practice the dharma of suffering... [text fragment].

"Endurance" (kṣānti) refers to the name of the true Saṃgha; herein, there is only the true Saṃgha. (The four foundations of mindfulness and the four roots of goodness are called the five expedient means and the assembly of harmony in the world.

The Buddha constantly associates with them because he produces goodness in sentient beings. The *Śāstra* [below] discusses "counteraction" to exclude evil people. "In this context" [refers to] the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), for it exists within the reality.

If one relies on the Four Teachings, this Saṃgha passes through the partial and perfect [teachings], the five flavors, and the seats, acting as co-hearers. Now, this is precisely the Perfect [Teaching].

Within the teachings, this refers to the "Certainty of Faith. Regarding the "Original and Traces" (*honjaku*): the Original is in harmony with the principle of the True Aspect (*shinjitsu sōri*), and it is also in harmony with the capacities and conditions of sentient beings within the Dharma-realm.

As for the Trace, it consists of the monastic community of both provisional and ultimate phenomena and principles throughout the five flavors, which guides various sentient beings to contemplate the mind.

Among those who first study the Middle Way (*chūgan*), having entered the stage of semblance (*sōji i*), they have not yet manifested true awakening; thus, they feel a sense of shame regarding their [limited] rank.
First, regarding the meaning: those who feel shame before the various sages are the Sangha with a sense of shame; if contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-prajñā*) arises, they are the true Sangha.
If they differ from this, the former two types of Sangha do not rely on contemplative practice and are thus called the "precept-breaking Sangha";
they do not understand the characteristics of contemplation and are thus called the "deluded Sangha. Having finished citing these categories, to clarify their number: they are twelve thousand people.

[The number refers to different worlds; hearing [the Dharma] many times leads to becoming a person of goodness, destroying evil, and entering the truth—this can be seen by applying the same principle. As for those who do not discuss it in terms of the teachings, although the specific teachings differ, the numbers are the same, so there is no difference in the explanation. If one follows the numbers to generate understanding, then the teachings are distinct. Question:

Why is it that whenever the assembly is enumerated or those who have attained the Way are counted, their number is invariably complete without any deficiency? Answer: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Dàlùn), in its commentary on the "Great Number" (*mahāsāhasra*) section of five thousand, states:

"Whether exceeding or falling short, they all remain within the 'great number'. Regarding the fundamental and the manifested (*benji*): the fundamental is twelve thousand bodhisattvas, while the manifested are twelve thousand śrāvakas.]
Furthermore, regarding the contemplation of the mind: one contemplates the twelve *āyatanas*. Within a single *āyatana*, there are the ten dharma-realms;
each realm further contains ten realms, thus making one hundred realms. Each realm possesses the ten suchnesses (*daśa-tathatā*), thus making one thousand suchnesses.
Since a single *āyatana* already comprises one thousand suchnesses, the twelve *āyatanas* comprise twelve thousand dharma-gates. △ Second, clarifying the stages and extolling the virtues.
All are arhats whose outflows are exhausted, who no longer possess afflictions, who have attained their own benefit, who have ended the fetters of existence, and who have attained mastery of mind.
"Arhat" refers to the stage of illumination; "whose outflows are exhausted" below is a praise of their virtues. "Arhat" may also be translated as "one who is worthy."

"Truth" (*satya*) may be translated as "True Person" (*pudgala-satya*), or as "The Unattached One," "The Unborn," or "The Worthy One. Alternatively, it is said that there is no direct equivalent, yet it encompasses three meanings:

first, the meaning of non-arising, because one does not undergo further existence; second, the meaning of slaying the thief, because one has severed and exhausted the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*);

and third, the meaning of being worthy of offerings, because one is fit to be a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*). These are the intended meanings of the *Vaipulya* (Shared) and *Āgama* (Distinct) teachings. If [one speaks of] the Distinct [Teaching],...

The "Perfect" (Yuan) not only slays the thief, but also slays that which is not a thief. That which is "not a thief" is *nirvāṇa*; since this too must be destroyed, it carries the meaning of "slaying the thief.

(To say it is "not a thief" is merely a designation derived from the perspective of the Two Vehicles; if, even within the Perfect and Distinct [teachings], it is still called a "thief," then it must indeed be slain.

"Not arising in arising" and "not arising in non-arising" refers to the untainted (*anāsrava*). This is "non-arising. (Taking the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as a realization, one is born outside the realms; because this "arising" is not true arising, it is [called] non-arising.)

"Causing [them] to arise" means not only being worthy of offerings, but also providing for them (to provide for what they require is called "providing"; for example, as when the Buddha transformed himself into a practitioner to deliver offerings to forest-dwelling bhikṣus).

This is a praise of the virtues from the first stage (*bhūmi*) and the first dwelling (*vihāra*) of the Perfect [Teaching] onwards. Regarding the "Original and Traces": the Original [attainment] is the obtaining of the Samādhi of Non-acceptance;
because one is unattached to the two extremes, it is called "non-arising," and because one has severed the delusions of the five dwellings (*vihāra*), it is so named.
He is named "Slayer of Thieves" (Arhat) because he can bring merit to the nine realms and benefit all sentient beings; thus he is called "Worthy of Offerings" (Arhat).

To deliver sentient beings through skillful means, he passes through the five flavors and transmits [the teaching] as non-arising. Being a Slayer of Thieves and Worthy of Offerings are both manifestations (*traces*).

Furthermore, his original nature is the Dharma-body, yet he manifests the traces of self-benefit; his original nature is Prajñā, yet he manifests the traces of non-arising; his original nature is Liberation, yet he manifests the traces [of these qualities].

"Manifesting the Slaying of the Thieves": (This is essentially the Great Wisdom of Equality, wherein there is neither breaking nor non-breaking, only then able to manifest traces; in all teachings, there is no birth, and fundamental realization is liberation—there is neither thief nor non-thief, only then able to manifest traces;

slaying the thieves is fundamentally the attainment of the Dharma-body, which is neither responsive nor non-responsive, only then able to manifest traces as the "Worthy of Offerings. Furthermore, for one who contemplates the mind, the contemplation of emptiness is Prajñā, the contemplation of the provisional is Liberation, and the contemplation of the middle is the Dharma-body.
Moreover, the contemplation of entering emptiness from the provisional also possesses three meanings, namely:
When one reaches the Middle Way and contemplates the slaying of the thief of ignorance, one should not give rise to thoughts of the two extremes;

one should honor such a person as one would honor the World-Honored One. As the Vaipulya Sūtras state: "To make offerings to the Buddha and Mañjuśrī is not as meritorious as practicing according to the Vaipulya teachings. Furthermore, this sūtra states:

"The transgression of slandering the Buddha and the merit of praising him are both light compared to the transgression of slandering or the merit of praising one who upholds this sūtra. Even a single meal that fills the body is sufficient for the practice of these teachings. This sūtra also says: "The sin of slandering the Buddha and the blessing of praising him are still slight compared to the sin of slandering or the blessing of praising one who maintains this sūtra."

The gravity of the offenses and blessings is extreme. Why is this? Because the Buddha has no thought of food; he has long been free from the eight winds (aṣṭau lokadharmāḥ) and is neither benefited nor harmed by them.
To give to one who upholds this sutra is beneficial, for it preserves the physical body, continues the retribution of life, gives rise to the Dharma-body, and increases the life of wisdom.
Conversely, to disparage such a person causes distress, regret, and decline; if one loses this favorable opportunity, it cannot be recovered, and thus the loss is great. All [should know this].
The two phrases "outflows are exhausted" and "there are no further afflictions" praise the virtue of being a slayer of thieves; "outflows" refers to the three outflows (*āsrava*).

The phrase "having attained one's own benefit" praises the virtue of being a Worthy One (*arhat*); all causes and effects within the three realms are termed "others," while the merit of wisdom and abandonment is termed "one's own benefit.
Because one is fully endowed with this own benefit, one becomes a Worthy One who has exhausted all fetters of existence and attained peace of mind.
The two phrases concerning mastery praise the virtue of non-arising. "All existences" refers to the twenty-five states of birth; "fetters" refers to the twenty-five causes of birth.
When the mind is sovereign, wisdom is necessarily sovereign; one who is fully endowed with both concentration and wisdom is a person of dual liberation.
Regarding "original and trace": non-arising and further non-arising is named Great Nirvana, which is free from the outflows of affliction.
The source of their flow having long since been exhausted, they no longer fall back into the stages of the two vehicles or those of ordinary beings;
this is the Dharma-body of original non-arising, the merit of wisdom and cessation, and the true mark of reality—this is called "original self-benefit.

Having attained the King Samādhi, one destroys the twenty-five states of existence and manifests the self-nature endowed with the eight sovereign powers; this is called "originally slaying the thief," while its traces are shown as the merits of the two vehicles.

Regarding the contemplation of the mind through the faculty of wisdom (*prajñā-śrotra*), this is the Middle Way of correct contemplation; it does not fall into the two extremes of emptiness or the provisional.

When the afflictions of these two extremes are extinguished, one is able to contemplate the nature of the mind—this is called the "robe and jewel secret treasury" of the supreme meditative concentration (*samādhi*). This is one's own possession, which constitutes one's own benefit.
Through the correct contemplation of the Middle Way, the bandits of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) are severed. Because there are no longer any fetters, both existence and non-existence are also severed.
Because the extremes cannot bind the mind, the mind is sovereign; thus, although afflictions exist, they are as if non-existent.
To enter nirvana without severing the afflictions is precisely this meaning. △ Third, the enumeration of names and the summary conclusion.
Their names were Ājñātakauṇḍinya, Mahākāśyapa, Uruvilvākāśyapa, Gayākāśyapa, Nadīkāśyapa, Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākātyāyana,
Aniruddha, Kapphiṇa, Gavāmpati, Revata, Pilindavatsa, and Bakula.
Mahākauṣṭhila, Nanda, Sunanda, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra,
Subhūti, Ānanda, Rāhula, and other such great arhats renowned among the masses.
"Ājñāta" (阿若) is the first name in this list; "thus" (如是) at the end is the summary. The listing of names briefly cites twenty-one venerable ones.

Although all the Buddha’s disciples were complete in their various practices, they concealed their perfect capabilities and each received a name based on a single virtue, solely for the purpose of guiding those with particular inclinations. ○ *Kauṇḍinya* is his clan name; this translates as "Fire-Vessel."
The Brahmin caste traces its origins to those who served the fire; from this, their clan was named after fire. Fire has two meanings: illumination and burning.
Illumination means that darkness does not arise; burning means that material things do not arise. Thus, they take "non-arising" as their surname. *Ajñāta* is the name [of his father];
this translates as "already known," or alternatively, "without knowledge. It is not that there is nothing to be known, but rather that he knows non-existence.
If "ear" (*śrotra*) is based on the two truths (*satyadvaya*), it refers to knowing the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), being designated by the wisdom of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).

Furthermore, various sūtras and śāstras refer to this as "realizing the original limit" (*mūlakoṭi*) or "knowing the original limit. If it is based on the four truths (*catur-āryasatya*), it refers to knowing cessation (*nirodha*), or alternatively, it is translated as "attaining the Path" (*mārga-lābha*).
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "In my Buddha-dharma, one is broad-minded, compassionate, and widely learned at the very first reception..."
Regarding the flavor of the Dharma, Kauṇḍinya is foremost (this is according to the *loka-siddhānta*). In the past, during a time of famine, the Buddha manifested as a great fish;
holding his breath without gasping, five carpenters were the first to cut into the fish’s flesh.

The Buddha vowed that in a future age he would be the first to deliver these men, because he had previously made a vow to grant them the state of non-arising (*anutpāda*). Why is this so? Furthermore, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, there were nine... [text fragment ends].
Among five people who studied the Way, none had yet attained the fruit; they vowed that within the Dharma of Śākyamuni, they would be the first to awaken.

Drawn by their original vows, Kauṇḍinya was the first to attain the wisdom of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna), and is thus named Ājñāta-kauṇḍinya (The One Who Has Known). This is the *puruṣa-pudgala-siddhānta* (the standpoint for individuals).

Indeed, when one sleeps through the long night of ignorance, no one can awaken them; before the sun has risen, the morning star appears first—just so did Kauṇḍinya first attain the wisdom of non-arising.
It is like the morning star at the beginning of all luminous bodies; among the wisdom and clarity of all people, none precedes it.

Just as nothing surpasses the morning star for first dispelling darkness, so too, among the darkness extinguished by all people, none precedes it; therefore, he is named Ajñāta (Thus-Known). (This is according to the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta*.
When the Prince entered the mountains to study the Way, his father the King sent five men to follow and serve him; two of these were his maternal uncles.
The three companions were of the father’s faction, while the two others regarded desire as purity; the three others regarded asceticism as purity.

When the Prince practiced asceticism, the two [of the father’s faction] abandoned him; when the Prince abandoned asceticism to accept food, ghee, and warm water, the three [others] again abandoned him.
After the Prince attained the Way, he first preached the Four Noble Truths to the five men, beginning with Ājñāta-kauṇḍinya.

Because he was the first to be called "understood," he is named Ajñāta (First Understanding). Regarding the classification of the teaching according to the doctrine (*śāsana*), since the principles of the teaching are easily distinguished by way of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), they are analyzed in detail through contemplation.

Furthermore, as the twelve thousand Kauṇḍinya were at the head [of the assembly], and non-arising (*anutpāda*) is the essence of all contemplations, this is intended so that by hearing his name one may recognize the practice, and by taking him as an example, others may understand the mind.
The Tripitaka Teaching is illustrated by the analogy of a blind man for the wisdom of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), and by the analogy of a mirror for the realm of non-arising.

The aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense bases (*āyatana*)—the six parts such as the head—are likened to the present cause; the reflected image is likened to the future fruit. If one opens one's eyes and takes up the mirror, the form confronts the image;
because of this delusion, [the cycle] is not severed. If one closes one's eyes like a blind man, then there is nothing seen; one does not perceive the six parts.
Because this cause does not arise, the reflection in the mirror does not arise as its fruit. Thus, the Āgama Sūtra says:

"If one claims there is form (*rūpa*), and that form is pure, then purity arises; it does not not-arise. If one claims there are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna*), and that consciousness is pure, then purity arises;
it does not not-arise. If one claims there is feeling, and that feeling is bliss (*sukha*), then bliss arises; it does not [not-arise]..."

If one claims that there is no arising of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, yet these—feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—are pleasant, then pleasure is indeed arising, not non-arising.

If one claims that there is no arising of feeling, perception, or mental formations, yet these—feeling, perception, and mental formations—are the self, then the self is indeed arising, not non-arising.

If one claims that there is no arising of consciousness or form, yet feeling is the self, then the self is indeed arising, not non-arising. If one claims that there is no arising of consciousness, yet consciousness is permanent, then it is indeed...

Arising is not non-arising. If one says that form exists, and that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are permanent, then that permanence is precisely arising and not non-arising.
It is like holding up a mirror and seeing one's face; the face is arising and not non-arising. If one says there are five aggregates, they are all arising and not non-arising.
If one can know that form is not pure, and so on up to knowing that consciousness is not permanent, then one can further know [the truth].
That form is impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure, and so on up to consciousness being impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure—this is non-arising, not arising.
It is like a blind person holding a mirror who does not see the reflection; this is non-arising, not arising.
Since one knows it is non-arising, why would one further reckon within it: "I am form," or "I am distinct from form"?
To reckon that "I am within form" or that "form is within me," and so on up to consciousness—viewing it in this manner, both present causes and future fruits do not arise.
It is like a blind person facing a mirror and not seeing their reflection; this is called the wisdom of contemplation regarding the non-arising of the aggregates (*skandha*).
As for contemplating the sense bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*): though the ocean is deep and vast, it still has this shore and that shore.

It is merely a small amount of water; yet, when one has seen a form with the eye and becomes attached to it, craving for its pleasure, and gives rise to bodily, verbal, and mental karma—this is the great ocean that submerges all the world, including devas, humans, and asuras.
You should know that the eye is the great ocean and forms are the waves; because of this attachment to forms, there is a whirlpool within which unwholesome thoughts arise.
Evil fish and dragons give rise to jealousy and malice; male rākṣasas give rise to lustful attachment; female rākṣasas give rise to [attachment] through body, speech, and mind.
This is like drinking salt water and sinking of one's own accord. This is what is meant by: due to ignorance regarding forms and the eye, ignorance and craving arise;

because craving arises, it is called "volitional formations" (*saṃskāra*); because volitional formations arise, it is called "karma"; karma binds consciousness to become the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). This is what is meant by...

Consciousness enters the womb it has received; this is the arising of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). Once the five swellings—the hands, feet, and head—have formed, this is called the arising of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).

When the six sense bases encounter the six objects, contact (*sparśa*) arises. From the distinction between pleasant and painful objects, feeling (*vedanā*) arises. From the arising of defilement toward objects, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) arises.
From rushing about in the four directions in search [of gratification], grasping (*upādāna*) arises. From this, one produces bodily, verbal, and mental karma.
The arising of what is called "existence" is named "the arising of birth"; the transformation of future aggregates is named "the arising of aging";

the disintegration of future aggregates is named "the arising of death"; the internal fever within the mind is named "the arising of sorrow"; the loud wailing that issues from the voice is named "the arising of lamentation";
and the withering and trembling of body and mind is named "the arising of suffering and affliction. These are the three [feelings] that arise immediately when the eye sees a form.
The twelve links of dependent origination in this world give rise to a great mass of suffering; it is not that they do not arise.

The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, as well as to forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects—from the eye-element up to the mind-object-element. This is called the arising of the elements;
it is not that they do not arise. How is it that they do not arise? When one contemplates the eye and forms, one does not plant the seeds of suffering, nor does one produce the sprouts of suffering.
Foul-smelling fluids do not attract maggots and flies; if the seed does not grow, the sprout will not grow;

if the foul fluids do not arise, maggots and flies will not arise. Therefore, it is called "non-arising. When the eye sees a form and gives rise to perceptions of greed or anger, this is the seed of suffering.
To dwell upon the phenomena of the five desires is the sprout of suffering. The six sense organs grasping the six sensory objects is called "foulness."
When the "juice" flows out into the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), good and evil arise in competition; this is called maggots and flies.

If one knows that the eye and forms are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, then greed and anger will not arise, thoughts of desire will not arise, grasping for objects will not arise, and the performance of good or evil deeds will not arise.
This is called "non-arising. It is the same for the ear and sounds, and so on, up to the eye-faculty and its objects.
The Dharma-realm is also like this. Because Kaundinya was the first to attain this wisdom of the three baskets (*tripiṭaka*), he was named Ajñāta.
For one who contemplates according to the general teaching, it is like a phantom person holding a phantom mirror and facing a phantom mirror with the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).

When beholding the phantom image, the image does not arise from the mirror, nor does it arise from the six sense-bases, nor does it arise from the combination of the mirror and the six sense-bases, nor does it arise apart from them.
Since the mirror and the six elements do not arise from the four propositions, they are neither internal, external, nor intermediate;
they do not exist eternally of themselves, nor is there a place where they cease. They do not go to the directions of east, west, south, or north.
Their nature is fundamentally non-arising, yet it is not non-arising; their nature is fundamentally non-ceasing, yet it is not non-ceasing. Thus, there is neither arising nor ceasing.
Therefore it is said that there is no arising of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; the twelve bases (*āyatana*) and eighteen elements (*dhātu*) are likewise so.

For one who contemplates according to the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavasthāna*), the analogy is as follows: the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is like a mirror, and contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanājñāna*) is like the eye.

Blue, yellow, red, white, small, large, long, and short represent the ten Dharma-realms: blue represents the causes and effects of hell; yellow represents the causes and effects of hungry ghosts; red represents the causes and effects of animals; white represents the causes and effects of humans and devas; and "small" refers to form.

The image-like [causes and fruits] of the Two Vehicles, the great form-like [causes and fruits] of the universal Bodhisattvas, the short form-like [causes and fruits] of the particular Bodhisattvas, and the long form-like [causes and fruits] of the Buddhas—all these are distinguished within the mirror without error.
If one wishes to rectify oneself, one must ensure that the nine causes and fruits do not arise and that the one cause and fruit arises;
if one wishes to rectify others, one must cause them to ensure that their nine causes and fruits do not arise and that their one cause and fruit arises, by relying upon the *dharmadhātu*.

In the sequence of practicing the bodhisattva path, one first employs the wisdom of analytical contemplation of the essence (*tattva*) to sever the four abidings (*catur-vāsa*), ensuring that birth does not arise.
Next, one employs the Buddha-dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges to sever the afflictions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, ensuring that ignorance (*ajñāna*) does not arise.

Finally, one employs the wisdom of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) to sever ignorance (*avidyā*), ensuring that the root itself does not arise. If the four abidings are absent, then birth in the realm of segmented existence (*prādeśika-bhava*) will not arise.

If there were no ignorance (*avidyā*), then skillful means would not arise; if there were no ignorance, then true retribution would not arise—arising does not arise, and non-arising also does not arise; therefore it is called "non-arising.

For one who contemplates according to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), it is like contemplating a round mirror (the roundness symbolizes the realm of principle, while the contemplation symbolizes wisdom). One does not contemplate the back or the front (the back symbolizes ignorance, the front symbolizes the clarity of wisdom, and the mirror symbolizes the causes of the ten realms).

One does not contemplate forms and images (where "forms" are likened to the causes of the ten realms and "images" are likened to the effects of the ten realms); it is neither turned away nor dark, neither facing forward nor bright.

One does not grasp at various appearances or various reflected images, but contemplates only that which is perfectly round, without boundaries, without beginning or end, without light or darkness, and without distinctions of unity or difference.
This perfect contemplation is likewise such that one does not grasp at the characteristics of the ten dharma-realms.
Regarding appearances, there is neither good nor evil, neither heterodox nor orthodox, neither large nor small; all such distinctions are extinguished.

One contemplates only the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), and the Buddha-dharma—whether form or fragrance, none are not the true mark. One observes that afflictions, karma, and birth are all *anutpāda* (non-arising), for they are fundamentally neither arising nor non-arising;
thus it is called "non-arising. The aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), as well as suffering, are likewise [non-arising].
This Dharma-body is not something manifested; therefore, it is called the "obstruction of the Dharma-body. Attachment, aversion, and delusion are themselves the Prajñā;
because they are not capable of illuminating, it is called the "non-illumination of Prajñā. Its nature is inherently lucid—this is the activity of Prajñā.
All that is bound by karmic conduct is termed "liberation"; there is no liberation attained through the severing of bonds, nor does it have any substantial essence.
Because that which is bound and that which binds are both non-existent, it is called liberation. Liberation is the non-arising of karma; Prajñā is the non-arising of afflictions;
the Dharma-body is the non-arising of suffering. These three non-arisings are a single non-arising, and this single non-arising is the three non-arisings.
Because they are neither three nor one, they are called "non-arising. How much more so for the transformation and the afflictions?

The karma of affliction is suffering, yet it is not non-arising (this should include the ten vehicles and ten objects, as well as the skillful means; this refers entirely to the text of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* treatise). As for "original and trace": Kauṇḍinya was originally non-arising, yet he is not non-arising from the beginning. To lead those who desire milk toward curd, the trace is the non-arising of the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-yāna*). To lead those who have curd toward clarified butter (*navanīta*), the trace is the non-arising of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*). To lead those who have clarified butter toward [ghee], the trace is the Distinct Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*). To lead those who have milk toward [curd], the trace is the Teaching of the Non-Arising of the Unimpeded (*anāvaraṇa-anutpāda-yāna*). To lead those who have curd toward [clarified butter], the trace is the Teaching of the Arising of the Unobstructed (*anāvaraṇa-utpāda-yāna*). To lead those who have milk toward [curd], the trace is the Teaching of the Non-Arising of the Unequaled (*asama-anutpāda-yāna*). In order to bring [beings] to maturity, the manifested traces (*nirmāṇakāya*) appear as distinct; yet because they do not give rise to [new] maturation but rather provide the recompense for what has already matured, the manifested traces are non-arising and perfect.
Their fundamental ground, however, abides in the gateway of the letter *A*, meaning that all phenomena are primordially unarisen.

If one hears this gateway of the letter *A*, one understands that all meanings are neither arising nor non-arising; thus, the manifested traces can perform the work of guiding and transforming beings.
If sentient beings who are both born and unborn can realize that non-arising is perfect, they will be identical to the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness);
being neither fundamental nor derivative, neither born nor unborn, the great causal conditions for the work of the Buddha will here be complete. Therefore, the text below says:
"If I were to fully describe all the various transformations of Pūrṇa, and if sentient beings were to hear this, their minds would become distressed."
"Doubt" (*vicikitsā*) is precisely its meaning. The *Āgama* states: "Ānanda followed behind the Buddha holding a parasol and a lamp;
Mahābrahmā followed behind Cunda holding a parasol and a lamp. These are all manifestations of traces intended to reveal the fundamental reality.

One should understand that the non-arising of the observation of the mind is to be known through the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*). Those who explain it in this manner [should] follow whatever they hear.
Whether regarding phrases, persons, or dharmas, all constitute the ritual of transformation and may entirely serve as objects of contemplation.

They enable those of future generations to initiate practice upon hearing the names, to receive the teachings and recognize the essence, to contemplate the traces and perceive the source, and to extensively illuminate the beginning and end by investigating their causes and conditions.
If one grasps this intent, then even with respect to a single person or a single phrase of a sutra, it can be taken as the supreme object of seeking; it can be taken as...

One can understand the capacities of those to be transformed by observing the manifestations of the Sage; one can comprehend the benefits received by ordinary beings by discerning the similarities and differences in names and meanings;
one can know the distinct principles of practice and realization; one can understand how meditative contemplation is formed according to what is heard;
one can interpret the provisional traces as pointing toward the fundamental reality; one can believe in the long-term nature of the transformative deeds; and one can look up in reverence to the Sage.
One can know that kindness is difficult to repay; one can know that sentient beings are difficult to transform; one can know that realizing the principle is most difficult.
He did not see this, which is why it is called "Proliferation. This concludes the explanation for Kauṇḍinya. Mahākāśyapa is translated here as "Great Kūṭi" (Kui-shi).
It is also translated as "Light-Wave" (Guang-bo) and "Drinker of Light" (Yin-guang). The account concerning his name, Pipphala, is the most extensive; here it is given briefly.

Those who require the literal text should seek it out for themselves. Regarding the first patriarch of the Western Land, who was personally entrusted by the Buddha and was foremost in *dhūta* practice:
the Sanskrit term *dhūta* means "to shake off. By means of twelve practices, one shakes off twelve kinds of faults:
first, by dwelling in an *araṇya* (wilderness), one shakes off the fault of worldly clamor; second, by constantly practicing alms-gathering, one shakes off [the fault of] the *saṃgha*...
1. Eating at the midday meal and not accepting invitations more than three times; 2. begging for alms in sequential order to avoid the fault of being selective; 3.
observing the practice of eating only one meal a day to avoid the fault of excessive seeking; 4. restricting the quantity of food to avoid the fault of craving flavors; 5.
not drinking fruit juices, honey, or other syrups after midday to avoid the fault of seeking sensual desires; 6. wearing rag-robes to avoid the fault of desiring fine garments.
Eighth, by possessing only the three robes, one avoids the fault of increase or decrease; ninth, by dwelling among tombs, one avoids the fault of the perverted calculation of constant pleasure;
tenth, by staying under trees, one avoids the fault of fear; eleventh, by sitting in the open air, one avoids the fault of craving for trees;
twelfth, by sitting and not lying down, one avoids the thieves of affliction—these are fully described as the twelve *dhūta* practices.
The Sūtra extensively clarifies that five things are the requisites for dwelling, five are the requisites for sustenance, and two are the requisites for clothing.

Now, taking alms-gathering as an illustration to clarify "shaking off" [the dust]: if it is easily obtained, joy arises; if it is difficult to obtain, anger arises. If one obtains what is good, attachment arises; if one obtains what is bad, anxiety arises.
This anxiety and joy arise dependent upon form (*rūpa*); thus, this is the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). To experience this anxiety and joy is precisely feeling (*vedanā*).
