To inwardly grasp the signs of sorrow and joy is the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*); sorrow and joy themselves are the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*); the discrimination of sorrow and joy is the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
Sorrow and joy are also the two bases of mind and mental objects (*manāyatana* and *dharmāyatana*), as well as the three realms of mind, mental objects, and mental consciousness.

These realms, bases, and aggregates constitute the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). To think "I am able to beg for food" is the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*); to calculate that there is a self or that there is no self is the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*).
To take begging as the path is the clinging to precepts; to take begging as reality is the clinging to views. To regard these as true is wrong view;
to praise and rejoice in them is greed; to revile and resent them is hatred; to think "I am capable" is pride; to be struck by reproach is doubt;

and not understanding is ignorance. These constitute the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*). When these are applied across the three realms and the four truths, they are termed the eighty-eight underlying tendencies; this is called the "Origin" (*samudaya*).
If one truly understands that within the practice of alms-gathering, the four inversions (viparyāsa) are concealed by a continuous stream of similar [delusions]:

namely, conceiving of the impermanent as permanent and of what is unsatisfactory as pleasant; conceiving of the non-self as self because of the concealment of the movements and activities [of the mind];

and conceiving of the impure as pure because of the concealment by thin skin—then this consciousness, being free from these four inversions, diligently prevents the arising of the two evils and cultivates the two virtues through the four dhyānas, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path. This is the Path.
If one is attentive while begging for alms and does not conceive of a self, then delusion ceases; because delusion ceases, craving ceases; because craving ceases, aversion ceases;
because aversion ceases, one does not exalt oneself, and thus pride ceases; because pride ceases, there is no doubt when being rebuked, and because there is no self, the view of self ceases;
because the view of self ceases, the view of extremes ceases; and by not clinging to this as the path, the [attachment to] precepts ceases.
When one perceives cessation and does not reckon it as real, then the grasping for cessation ceases; when there is no false attachment, then false views cease.

Because these ten types of cessation occur, the eighty-eight latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) that bind as seeds are extinguished. Because the seed-bonds are extinguished, the fruit-bonds—the twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*)—are extinguished.

This is the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). If, within the practice of begging for alms, one does not perceive the Four Noble Truths, for this reason one will long remain in the cycle of wandering.
To turn back the great ocean of the suffering of birth and death: if one can perceive the Four Noble Truths, then one attains the severance of birth and death;

once birth and death are exhausted, one will no longer undergo further existence (*bhava*). This is the method of the "shaking off" (*dhūta*) contemplative wisdom within the practice of begging for food;
the methods regarding the dwelling place are also like this. This constitutes the *dhūta* of the Tripiṭaka Teaching. As for the "shaking off" of the Shared Teaching (*pāṭha-sādhāraṇa-śāsana*):
Taking true reality as the condition for realizing tranquility is the dwelling place; emptiness-wisdom is the food; the mind of emptiness is the heart; practicing all activities is the robe;
and the constant nature of emptiness—wherein there is no time that is not empty—is the wisdom that shakes off all things as being like illusions and transformations.

Because delusory thoughts and all evils are stilled and do not arise, and because mental states and their concomitants do not function due to their unattainability, all marks [of phenomena] are likewise absent.
Among all ascetic practices (*dhūta*), that which corresponds to emptiness is the foremost; among all ascetic practices, the practice of emptiness is the foremost;

among all ascetic practices, the shaking-off of wisdom is the foremost. As for the distinct teaching on the shaking-off (*dhūta*), it takes the Dharma-body as its dwelling place (because one directs the mind toward the Dharma-body to cultivate the two virtues). Prajñā is its food, and all various practices serve as its adornments and protections.
The wisdom that covers and shakes off the evil of black karma, the dharma-body that shakes off the evil of afflictions, and the body that shakes off the evil of the suffering of birth and death—

first shaking off the suffering of karmic afflictions pertaining to the stage of segmented existence (*paricchinna-bhava*), and subsequently shaking off the suffering of karmic afflictions pertaining to the stage of transformation (*pariṇāma-bhava*)—
this is the Middle Way of Right Contemplation, the ascetic practice (*dhūta*) that transcends the conduct of the Two Vehicles.

For one who practices the asceticism of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao), their dwelling is both clothing and food (originally possessing the three virtues, which are likewise attained through cultivation).
Yet, this is but a single dharma; it is explained as three: first, shaking off everything (the practice of clothing); second, shaking off everything (the wisdom of food);
and third, neither one nor many (the abiding of the body). Within all that is shaken off, there is nothing that is not the true mark (dharmatā). All dharmas...
The conduct of the Buddha is the conduct of the Tathāgata, surpassing the conduct of all Bodhisattvas. Regarding the purity of his original and manifested traces:

fundamentally, he sat together with the Tathāgata in the principle of ultimate emptiness; he equally attained the vast Dharma-body, equally attained unimpeded wisdom, and equally attained immeasurable merit.
Internally, he relinquished attachment to phenomena; externally, he was free from defilement; thus, both internally and externally, he was utterly purified.

Having shaken off the fundamental [delusions], one is already pure. To extract the flavor of milk, one shakes within the realm of phenomena; next, to extract the flavor of curd, one shakes within emptiness;
next, to extract fresh butter, one shakes within the distinct; next, to extract clarified butter, one shakes within the round.

For the contemplation of the mind, one shakes within emptiness; for grasping at marks, one shakes within the provisional; for the dust-like [delusions], one shakes within the middle. There is nothing [left].
"Clarifying the shaking off [of defilements] within the single mind across the five stages of abiding (etc.). ○ *Uruvilvā* is translated as "Pumpkin Grove";
*Nadī* is translated as "River" or also as "Stream"; *Gayā* is translated as "City. These three brothers were all non-Buddhist practitioners who worshipped fire.
The causal conditions regarding them appear in the *Śrī-mālā-sūtra* (*Ruìyìng jīng*) and various sections of the Vinaya. As for the provisional teaching (*jiàojiào*), it is as follows:
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa is foremost in being able to protect the fourfold assembly and provide them with the four requisites so that they lack for nothing;
Nadi-Kāśyapa is foremost in mental tranquility, having subdued all fetters through diligence;
Gayā-Kāśyapa is foremost in skillfully teaching and transforming others by observing that all phenomena are entirely without attachment."

Regarding the pedagogical intent within the milk: if one enters the stage of curdled milk (*maṇḍa*), one should feel shame for the small and aspire to the great; this principle may be understood accordingly.

If one enters the stage of fresh butter (*navanīta*), one should diligently attend to one's practice and receive the teaching. If one enters the stage of clarified butter (*ghṛta*), it is as described in this sutra:
receiving the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of attaining Buddhahood. As for the "Original and Traces" (*honjaku*): abiding in the forest of the three virtues is precisely the city of Prajñā.
The Dharma-body is water, and liberation is water; this constitutes the secret fundamental treasury. As for its traces, it relies upon the waters of the city to deliver sentient beings.
One who contemplates the mind correctly observes that the nature of the mind is the Middle Way, immovable like a city wall that remains still while defending against enemies.
Like water, it purifies all extremes and inverted views; like a forest, it simultaneously illumines both decay and flourishing in lush abundance.
The three dharmas supporting one another are like brothers joined at the hip. ○ Śāriputra is translated here as "Body-Son" (Shenzi) or "Jewel-Son" (Zhuzi);
his name is Upatiṣya, which is translated as "Treatise on Meaning" (Lunyi). He is foremost in wisdom; the full details of the causes and conditions are as found in the *Wenju*.
Regarding the classification by teaching: if this is the wisdom of the Tripiṭaka, it consists of the ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*) of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), which sever the afflictions.
He is the one who attests to the realization and assists the Buddha in spreading the transformation; the *Śāstra* calls him the "Great General on the Right.

Regarding those of penetrating wisdom, as explained within the *Prajñāpāramitā* itself, the reason he is called a *mahāsattva* (Great Being) is that he has abandoned such views as the view of a self (*ātman*), the view of sentient beings (*sattva*), the view of a Buddha, the view of bodhi, and the view of turning the wheel of the Dharma; because he has destroyed these views, he is named "Mahā."
This wisdom of the Bodhisattva differs from the initial teaching. Regarding the wisdom of the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), one should distinguish it according to the five flavors.

If, from the very beginning, one hears only of milk and curd but not the other flavors, and one awakens the mind and practices by performing only those acts of milk and curd, this is the wisdom of the Initial Teaching.
If one hears only of curd—whereby the curd does not arise from milk—and [understands] the nature of good and evil as being inherent in their own nature...
If one holds that emptiness is inherent from the beginning and does not arise through the cultivation of good to destroy evil, nor through the extinction of form to attain emptiness,
but rather that one simply cultivates what is already empty— this is the wisdom of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao). If, from the very beginning, one hears of the *amṛta* (the supreme nectar),

then for the sake of that *amṛta*, one must churn the cow for milk, boil the milk to make curd, transform the curd into fresh butter (*navanīta*), and further refine the fresh butter into clarified butter (*ghṛta*) before finally attaining the *amṛta*.
To practice in this manner is the wisdom of the Separate Teaching (Pratītyasamutpāda).

If, from the very beginning, one hears only that the cow eats the *kṣānti-grass* and thus produces *ghṛta*, and if one is able to consume it, all ailments are eliminated and all medicinal herbs are contained within it;
to cultivate this practice is the wisdom of the Perfect Teaching (Ekayāna). As for "Original and Traces" (*honjaku*):...
The Prajñāpāramitā of the wisdom of the primordial abiding true reality serves as the mother; from the objective realm arises wisdom, and that objective realm is the body, while wisdom is the child.
Out of compassion for sentient beings, he manifests the traces of the five flavors.
Śāriputra wishes to transform the evil blood of afflictions into wholesome milk, and thus manifests as an outsider who acts as a great master of treatises, intending to boil milk into curd.

The wisdom of the Tripitaka serves as the second [stage]. The World-Honored One, wishing to extract the cream from curdled milk to produce fresh butter, manifested the great while appearing small, accepting the humiliation of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* in order to benefit his fellow practitioners of the Brahma-faring life. Wishing to extract fresh butter from that cream to produce clarified butter, he received the teachings of the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Finally, wishing to extract the essence of clarified butter (*ghṛta*) to produce the finest cream (*amṛta*), he first attained awakening through the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
All these are long-hidden realities: the traces manifest externally while the fundamental ground remains secret within.
One who contemplates the mind employs the threefold contemplation within a single mind, thereby encompassing all wisdoms. Contemplating the mind as empty encompasses the wisdom of *dadhi* (curd);

contemplating the mind as provisional encompasses the wisdom of the two *mantha*s (fresh butter) as well as worldly wisdom; contemplating the mind as the Middle encompasses the wisdom of *ghṛta* (clarified butter).
The *amṛta* (ghee) of wisdom is called the single wisdom within the mind, which is all-wisdom; all-wisdom is single-wisdom; it is neither single-wisdom nor all-wisdom (and so forth).
○ Mahāmaudgalyāyana is his clan name; it is translated as "Praise and Recitation," also translated as "Radish Root," and also translated as "Horsebean.
His personal name is Kauṣṭhila, and he is foremost in supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*). The *Śāstra* states: [text continues].
The disciples on the left, who follow the provisional teachings, rely upon the four dhyānas to give rise to the fourteen transformations;

by relying on the contemplation of the ten all-encompassing *sarvadharmas* through the refinement and cultivation of the untainted (*anāsrava*) *dharma-dhyāna*, they are able to perform the eighteen transformations—this refers to the supernormal powers within the Initial Teaching (Tripitaka Teaching).

They give rise to wisdom based on emptiness, cultivating various supernormal powers with a mind of empty wisdom—this refers to the supernormal powers within the Shared Teaching (Pratyekabuddha and Bodhisattva Teachings). Next...
Next, by practicing according to the three truths, one attains supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) that penetrate ever deeper, surpassing those of the Two Vehicles;

this is the supernatural power of the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavasthāna-śāsana*), which relies on the ultimate reality (*bhūtatathatā*) to obtain supernatural powers. One does not perceive the Buddha-lands through dualistic marks;

arising from the truth as a response (*nirmāṇa*) without moving from the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), it pervades the ten dharma-realms. This is the supernatural power of the Perfect Teaching (*paryanta-śāsana*). (And so forth.)

Regarding the phrase "not by means of dualistic characteristics" (*advaya-lakṣaṇa*): non-duality is the true reality (*dharmatā*). To perceive the land is itself supernatural power (*abhijñā*), for it is perceived in reliance upon the principle; thus it is called "perceiving through non-dual characteristics. As for the repeated "and so forth" (*ādi-ādi*):

it causes one to distinguish that the former two are attained through cultivation, while the latter two are manifested through realization. The former rely on phenomenal meditation (*dhyāna*) and supernatural powers, while the latter rely on the true principle. The former are distinct [powers] prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), whereas the latter arise spontaneously as an aid to the perfect [path]. The former two are named "penetrating" (*sāmānya*) and "transformative" (*nirmāṇa*); the latter two are named "secret" (*guhya*) and "responsive" (*anurūpa*).

The former two subdue sentient beings; the latter two perceive the capacities of sentient beings. The former two are subject to destruction; the latter two are indestructible. The former two pertain to the path of teaching (*śāsana-mārga*); the latter two pertain to the path of realization (*adhigama-mārga*). Regarding the former two, the supernormal power of the body (*kāyābhijñā*) exists only in the present; the latter two pervade the three periods of time. Furthermore, the former two are cultivated only at the level of the sages (*ārya*).

Regarding the two [categories] that follow, ordinary beings cultivate both; regarding the two that precede them, they may cultivate either according to their basis. As for the latter two, one must necessarily have a superior basis. Regarding "Original and Traces":

the Original dwells in the *bhūtakoṭi* and the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, able to universally respond to the ten directions in a single thought-moment through various manifestations, performing Buddha-works out of compassion.
The Traces consist of the supernatural powers of the five flavors, which guide beings to enter the ultimate contemplation of the mind. As for "contemplation," it refers to...

When one mind suddenly becomes all minds, and upon observing all minds, they suddenly vanish; since these minds are neither existent nor non-existent, one penetrates to the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*).
Mahākātyāyana—this is translated as "Ornamentation," also as "Fanning-Rope," and also as "Fine Shoulders.

He was foremost in expounding the meaning of the teachings. Regarding the classification by teaching: he relies on impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self to refute the view of annihilationism.

The view of permanence and so forth is the doctrinal meaning of the Initial Teaching (Śrāvaka-yāna), which relies on emptiness (*śūnyatā*), non-existence, and non-apprehensibility to refute and sever the views of permanence and annihilation.

The view of permanence and so forth is the doctrinal meaning of the Shared Teaching (Pratyekabuddha-yāna), which relies on the dhāraṇīs and the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) to observe capacities and illuminate the provisional, applying medicine to suit the illness to refute and sever the views of permanence and annihilation.
The view of permanence and so forth is the doctrinal meaning of the Distinct Teaching (Bodhisattva-yāna), which relies on the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) that is neither existent nor non-existent.

The absence of the breaking of [extremes] such as the views of permanence and annihilation constitutes the fundamental meaning of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). Regarding the "Original" (*ben*) and the "Traced" (*ji*):

the Original resides in the two kinds of adornments—merit and wisdom—and is capable of both questioning and answering; for the sake of pitying sentient beings, the Traced serves as the teacher of the meaning of the Five Flavors (*wumi*).

As for "contemplating the mind" (*guanchin*), it is the contemplative wisdom (*guan-zhi*) that examines the object (*jing*), and the object gives rise to wisdom; this mutual interplay between wisdom and the object is itself contemplation.
The *Cittaviveka* (Heart Treatise) is its doctrinal meaning. ○ *Aniruddha* is translated here as "Free from Poverty" (*Apauṇya*) and also as "As One Wishes" (*Yathābhiprāya*).

He was the Buddha’s younger cousin and was foremost in the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). Regarding the classification of teachings: those who develop the divine eye based on worldly meditation (*laukika-dhyāna*) are ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

Those who develop the divine eye based on the meditative concentration of untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-vastu-dhyāna*) are the perspective of the Tripiṭaka [teaching]. [Those who develop it] based on the untainted wisdom of the essence of dharmas (*dharmatā-anāsrava-prajñā*) belong to the [Mahāyāna] intent.

The provisional teaching (*bye-rgya-pa'i chos*) holds that the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) arises from conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); the intentional teaching (*dgongs-pa-can*) holds that it arises from scattered virtues; the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*) arises from meditative concentration (*dhyāna*);

the divine eye arises from the ultimate (*paramārtha*); the wisdom eye (*prajñācakṣus*) arises from the conventional (*saṃvṛti*); the dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣus*) arises from the middle way (*madhyamā*); and the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*) arises from the distinct teaching (*khyad-par-ba'i chos*).

The intentional teaching holds that the divine eye arises from the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*), and that the divine eye is itself the Buddha-eye. The perfect teaching (*rdzogs-pa chen-po'i chos*) further holds that [the divine eye] also arises from scattered virtues.

The cultivation of the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*) is based on *dhyāna*; the cultivation of the heavenly eye (*divya-cakṣus*) is based on the Tripiṭaka; and the cultivation of the fleshly and heavenly eyes through the supernormal power (*abhijñā*) is based on emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
This is the sequential meaning according to the teachings. To cultivate the five eyes non-sequentially is the perfect (*pariniṣpanna*) meaning. Regarding the fundamental and the trace:
the fundamental resides in the true reality (*bhūtata-lakṣaṇa*), which is the true heavenly eye that perceives the Buddha-lands without the duality of marks.

The provisional traces show that regarding the contemplation of the mind through the "half-head" divine eye: when one contemplates the good mind produced by causes and conditions, this is the contemplation of the physical eye;

when one contemplates the concentrated mind produced by causes and conditions, this is the contemplation of the divine eye; when one contemplates the emptiness of the mind produced by causes and conditions, this is the contemplation of the wisdom eye;

when one contemplates the mind produced by causes and conditions as being conventional (provisional), this is the contemplation of the dharma eye; and when one contemplates the mind produced by causes and conditions as being the Middle Way, this is the contemplation of the Buddha eye. (Thus it is said.)
(Kyun). ○ Kapphiṇa (劫賓那) is translated here as "Lunar Mansion" (房宿). His parents prayed to the lunar mansion (房星) for his birth, and he became foremost in his knowledge of the stars;
furthermore, because he attained the fruit of realization while sharing a single lunar mansion with the Buddha, he was named accordingly. Regarding the interpretation according to the teachings:
to dismantle the house of sense-faculties and objects is to dwell together with the Buddha in the chamber of the True Truth (眞諦). This is the essential meaning of the Tripiṭaka.
When one realizes that the faculties and objects are identical to the True Dharma-realm, one dwells together with the Tathāgata in the chamber of ultimate truth.

According to the intent of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*), by discerning the faculties, objects, and chambers of the ten dharma-realms, one attains the vision of the Buddha. According to the intent of the Distinct Teaching (*pratyeka-yāna*), within the chamber of a single faculty or object, one sees all chambers and sees all Buddhas.
Regarding the original and the trace according to the Perfect Teaching (*ekayāna*): the original is identical to the Tathāgata.
Coming together to dwell in the trace of the true reality (*dharmatā*), one merely shows [the practitioner] the various rooms and lodgings. For the practitioner who contemplates the mind:

by analyzing the house of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as empty, they dwell with the *nirmāṇa*-buddha; by contemplating the house of the five aggregates as provisional (*upāya*), they dwell with the *saṃbhoga*-buddha;
by contemplating the house of the five aggregates as the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*), they dwell with the *dharma*-buddha (and so forth). ○ Kapphiṇa (憍梵波提): this...
Regarding the first point, the provisional teaching (*yijiao*): dwelling in the celestial garden indicates a "good existence," while chewing like an ox indicates "evil";

this is the meaning of the *Tripitaka* (Śrāvaka) teaching. Furthermore, that one attains the Way while having a body that chews like an ox shows that "evil is not evil," and that while dwelling in the celestial garden one still chews like an ox shows that "good is not good";
this is the meaning of the *Common* (Shared) teaching. These demonstrate both the internal and external realms.

The distinction between good and evil represents the intent of the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*); the revelation of the true reality (*shixiang*) of good and evil represents the intent of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). Regarding origin and trace (*benji*):
the origin is abiding in the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*), dwelling securely as a Holy Lord like a bull-king, the sovereign of the ultimate truth;

the trace is manifesting as a cow-chewing being who delights in dwelling in the heavens. Regarding the contemplation of the mind (*guanchin*): it is to contemplate the principle of the Middle Way within the nature of the mind, walking with steady steps.

"His gait is level and upright; his speed is like the wind. (This refers to employing the Bull-King among men to generally take the white ox as the draft animal. ○ *Revata* is translated here as "Constellation" and also as "Provisional Conjunction.
Because he attained the Way after two spirits contended over a corpse, he sits in meditation and enters samādhi with a mind that does not fall into confusion.
First, regarding the teaching through analysis: he analyzes and shatters the five aggregates (*skandhas*) as not being his own possession. Three.

The intention of the *Zang* (Treasury) school is that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are fundamentally not mine; the intention of the *Tongjiao* (Shared Teaching) is to distinguish that the five aggregates within the ten dharma realms are all not mine;
the intention of the *Biejiao* (Distinct Teaching) is to realize that the five aggregates are neither mine nor belong to another, seeing the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of the aggregates;

and the intention of the *Yuanjiao* (Perfect Teaching) regarding "original" and "traced" is that the original state dwells in the *Sūrya-tāraka-samādhi*, while the traced manifestation displays this name.

Regarding the contemplation of the mind: when one contemplates the mind while reciting the Buddha’s name, one sees the Buddhas of the ten directions as numerous as the stars seen at night (and so forth).

[The preceding section on the provisional teaching relied upon the conjunction of the provisional; now, in this section on the fundamental and trace aspects, the contemplation of the stars likewise relies on the constellations, both being adapted to the occasion. Seeing the Buddhas like stars is the intention of the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra*. Regarding "contemplating the mind" and what follows, one should extensively cite the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra*.
○ Piliṅgavatsa (translated as "Habitual Remnants") sat beneath trees in the bitter cold, avoiding neither wind nor rain. First, regarding the provisional teaching (*yijiao*): he extinguished pride;
thus, according to the Tripiṭaka [teaching], there is no pride. According to the general meaning, pride and non-pride are both present.

According to the specific meaning, one distinguishes the high and low of the ten dharma-realms. According to the self-mastery of the eight [realms], he was fully endowed with the Buddha-dharma. According to the Perfect [Teaching], it is the fundamental [nature].
The "traces" (likenesses) are the manifestations of the fundamental abiding in permanence, bliss, self, and purity—the eightfold sovereign mastery—and the subtle Brahma-voice;

these traces are shown to counteract pride and harsh speech. As for the contemplation of the mind: one contemplates that coarse words and gentle speech alike ultimately converge in the primary meaning (paramārtha).

[In this context, both the general and specific aspects of the three contemplations are the primary meaning, and the delusions to be eliminated are equally considered "coarse"]. ○ Bakula is translated here as "Good Appearance"; he was one hundred and sixty years old.
Free from illness and untimely death, one always delights in dwelling in seclusion. First, regarding the provisional teaching: entering the truth by extinguishing clamor;
the *Tripitaka* [teaching] is tranquility, wherein clamor itself is the truth. The *Shared* [teaching] is tranquility, wherein one enters the Middle Way by departing from the two extremes.

The *Distinct* [teaching] is tranquility, wherein the extremes themselves are the Middle. Regarding the fundamental and the trace: the fundamental abides in the samādhi of great tranquility, possessing longevity that is eternal.
Freedom from illness is bliss; not meeting an untimely death is my tranquility; this is purity—these are the fundamental traces of the four virtues.
To observe the mind through the stillness of the six sense faculties means that within the nature of the mind, the Middle Way is simultaneously emptiness, provisionality, and the middle;
it is the contemplation of permanence, bliss, self, and purity. ○ Mahākauṣṭhila is translated as "Great Thigh"; Śāriputra’s mother—

My maternal uncle was foremost in eloquence (*pratibhāna*). Regarding the provisional teachings (*yijiao*): externally he mastered the four Vedas and internally he mastered the three baskets (*tripiṭaka*).

His eloquence in the initial teaching (*shichiao*) was such that he claimed, "I have nothing to obtain. His eloquence in the shared teaching (*tongjiao*) involved names and meanings pervading the ten dharma-realms.

His eloquence in the distinct teaching (*biejiao*) relied upon the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) to pervade all forms of eloquence. His eloquence in the perfect teaching (*yuanjiao*) was likewise pervasive.

Regarding "Original and Trace" (*honjaku*): the Original is the inconceivable transformation of the mouth-secret and the mouth-wheel, consisting of great meditative concentration and great wisdom; the Trace is the manifestation of Mahākāśyapa.
As for "Contemplating the Mind" (*kanjin*): contemplating the mind as being simultaneously emptiness, concentration, the provisional, and wisdom serves to adorn the mind (and so forth).
○ Nanda also said: "Nanda the Cowherd"; this is translated as "Good Joy. Some say that...
Regarding the *Vinaya*, the "joy" (*pramuditā*) mentioned in the context of the teachings of Upananda refers to joy in phenomena (*dharma*), whereas in principle there is no such joy.
According to the meaning of the Tripiṭaka, this is joy in phenomena; according to the meaning of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*), it is the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*);

according to the Distinct Teaching (*pratyeka-yāna*), it is the Abode of Joy (*pramuditā-vihāra*); and according to the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*), it is [the same]. (Although the Abode of Joy lacks the specific name "joy," because the realization of the path is identical to that of the distinct stages, the name of the stage is borrowed to designate the abode. Regarding the "original and the trace": the original resides in reality.

The limit that is neither joy nor non-joy is called the "contemplation of joy. As for the contemplator of the mind, when the contemplation of the mind accords with and corresponds to the principle, it is called the "contemplation of joy.
○ *Sundara* is translated here as "lovely" or "handsome"; he was named after his wife, Nanda, who was explained previously.
He was the Buddha’s own younger brother. Regarding the teaching, from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), there is [joy].
The meaning of the *Tripiṭaka* [teaching] is that true reality (*satya*) is without joy, yet conventional joy is itself true joy.

The meaning of the *Shared Teaching* (*pāryāyika-yāna*) is that from the joy of the shared Dharma, there arises both conventional joy and the joy within the middle way. The meaning of the *Distinct Teaching* (*pratiniyata-yāna*) is that the joy of the shared [teaching] possesses all dharmas of joy.
The meaning of the *Perfect Teaching* (*vaipulya-yāna*) is that the fundamental and the manifested are the contemplation of the mind, as explained regarding Nanda. ○ Pūrṇa is translated as...
Pūrṇa is his father’s name; Maitrāyaṇī, translated as "Compassionate Woman," is his mother’s name. Because he received his name from his parents, he is called Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra.
Regarding his being foremost in preaching the Dharma: in terms of the teaching, he diligently analyzes the dharmas and has accomplished what was to be done.
In the Tripiṭaka, his vows are fulfilled and he realizes the essence as emptiness; having attained realization within emptiness, he possesses supernormal powers.
The fulfillment of the vow through the Teaching refers to the complete perfection of the Dharma-eye; the fulfillment of the vow through the Separate Teaching refers to abiding in the secret treasury;

the fulfillment of the vow through the Perfect Teaching refers to the original and the manifested, wherein the original vow has long been fulfilled and the manifested aspect serves as the foremost teacher of the Dharma, manifesting to sentient beings what constitutes a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).

Regarding the contemplation of the mind, as explained in the *Mohe Zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation), it involves contemplating the person, the principle, and so forth as the spiritual friend; "person" refers to Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Arhats, while "practice" refers to...

The principle of these six perfections and the factors of the path is the *dharmatā* and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Subhūti is here called "Born of Emptiness" (*Śūnyatā-ja*) and also "Good Auspiciousness" (*Kalyāṇa-bhadra*), "Good Deeds" (*Kalyāṇa-karman*), or "Good Manifestation" (*Sudarśana*).
He is foremost in understanding emptiness. Regarding the interpretation according to the teachings: In the *Zangjiao* (Tripitaka/Āgama) sense, the wisdom of the emptiness of form arises.

In the *Tongjiao* (Shared) sense, the essence of the body is the wisdom of the emptiness of form. From the wisdom of existence arises the wisdom of emptiness; from the wisdom of emptiness arises conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).

From the conventional wisdom (*sāṃvṛtijñāna*) arises the middle wisdom (*madhyamajñāna*); this is the meaning of the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddhayāna*), where emptiness gives rise to existence, and that which is existence is also conventional wisdom.

Middle wisdom is the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulyayāna*). Regarding the fundamental and the manifested (*honji-suijaku*): the fundamental resides in the Dharma-body of the true reality (*dharmakāya-bhūtatathatā*);

the manifested shows the arising of contemplation of the mind from seeing emptiness. This contemplation of the mind does not abide within, without, or in between; it is not self-existent. This is the Dharma-body of the contemplation of the mind.
○ Ānanda is here called "Joyful" (Huanxi) or "Untainted" (Wuran). He was the Buddha’s cousin and foremost among those of great learning (*bahuśruta*).
Regarding the classification by teaching (*jiao*), Joyful Ānanda represents the Tripitaka; Worthy Ānanda represents the Shared; Treasury Ānanda represents the Distinct;
and Ocean Ānanda represents the Perfect. Regarding the fundamental and the manifested (*benji*), his fundamental state dwells neither in joy nor in non-joy.
The Dharma-body is like empty space, and wisdom is like clouds and rain; it can sustain and receive, manifesting as joy.

One who contemplates the mind corresponds to the immediate emptiness, provisionality, and the Middle Way, and thus experiences joy from the stage of names through to correspondence with true contemplation.
*Rāhula* means "obscuration"; he is the son of the Buddha. The causes and conditions are as stated in the text.

Regarding the first [category], the "Secret Practice of the Sentences" (*gumi gyō*), the provisional teaching (*kyōkyō*) is as follows: the analytical dharma (*shakuhō*) of the Path Truth (*dōtai*) obstructs the four abodes; this is the intent of the Tripiṭaka Teaching.

The dharma of the Path Truth obstructs the four abodes; this is the intent of the Shared Teaching. The three successive wisdoms (*sanji*) obstruct the five abodes; this is the intent of the Distinct Teaching.

The single mind and three wisdoms (*isshin sanchi*) obstruct the five abodes; this is the intent of the Perfect Teaching. Regarding the fundamental and the trace (*honjaku*): the fundamental resides in the Middle Way and is obstructed and blocked.
The second [aspect] is the trace that demonstrates the obscuring of the contemplation of the mind:
namely, that "provisionality" obstructs *nirvāṇa*, "emptiness" obstructs *saṃsāra*, and "the Middle" obstructs "that which is neither *saṃsāra* nor *nirvāṇa*. The conclusion states:
"Known by all" means that some say "knowing" is simply "cognition," while others say that hearing the name is "knowledge" and seeing the form is "cognition"; seeing the form is "knowledge."

Regarding the knowledge and vision of the mind as the fundamental and phenomenal aspects of consciousness: the fundamental aspect constitutes the knowledge of the "full characters" for sentient beings, while the phenomenal aspect constitutes the knowledge of the "half characters.
As for the contemplation of the mind, it is as explained in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*. Thus far, the section on the various types of knowledge is concluded.
△ Second, the assembly of those with limited knowledge.
Furthermore, there were two thousand persons, both learners (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*).
Next, the assembly of those with limited knowledge is listed; however, their number is indicated by their status alone, and their virtues are not extolled, hence they are termed "limited."
Ordinary people with mere knowledge cannot fathom the sages; yet the sages do not distinguish between superiority and inferiority based on whether one has much or little learning.

Those who aspire to the lofty and admire the distant are led by means of extensive knowledge, while those who conceal their names, hide their virtues, and practice humility are led by means of limited knowledge.

Because they accord with the capacities of sentient beings, there appear various manifestations; one must not lose sight of the ultimate truth because of these outward traces of much or little learning.

Regarding the provisional teachings (*yàojiào*) based on the original [classification]: in the *zàng* (Āgama) teaching, those in the first, second, and third fruits are called "learners" (*xuérén*), while those in the fourth fruit are called "those beyond learning" (*wúxuérén*).

In the *tōng* (Shared) teaching, those prior to the stage of detachment from desire are called learners, while those in the stage of having completed their task (*yǐbiàndì*) are called those beyond learning. Furthermore, all nine stages are called learners, while the tenth stage, the Buddha-stage, is called that beyond learning.
In the *bié* (Distinct) and *yuán* (Perfect) teachings, this distinction may be made either in terms of effortful practice (*yònggōng*) or the state beyond effort (*wúgōng*).
This clarifies the distinction between those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), whether in terms of their full or incomplete attainment of such states.
Furthermore, within the *Āgamas*, when an outsider asked the Buddha whether an Arhat still trains further, the Buddha replied: "An Arhat does not perform unwholesome dharmas;

he abides in wholesome dharmas. Training therein is what is called 'training' (*śikṣā*). If this is so, then one who is still in training (*śaikṣa*) might also be designated as "beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*).
Why is it that one who has completed what was to be severed and has nothing further to sever is called "beyond training" (aśaikṣa)? This constitutes four propositions.

When applied to the five skillful means, these combine with those who are neither in training nor beyond training to form five propositions. By analogy with the four teachings, this should likewise apply;
thus there are twenty propositions. Regarding the fundamental and the trace: the fundamental refers to the Mahāsattvas of the Dharma-body, who abide in the study of the *mañjuṣā* (full letters).
Sentient beings at the stage of training (*śaikṣa*) should use the "half-syllables" to adorn those who are both trained and beyond training (*śaikṣa-aśaikṣa*) within the twin trees;

through successive transmission, they lead the contemplator of the mind to correctly contemplate the Middle Way. Not taking the two extremes as objects, that which is in the middle is the state of being beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
To be able to contemplate in this way is called "training. Furthermore, not taking [the extremes] as objects while yet taking them as objects is called "beyond training. Training is always thus.

Regarding the contemplation of "names" (*nāman*), when contrasted with those who have not yet cultivated the paths of learning (*śaikṣa*) and no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), it constitutes the fifth proposition. Furthermore, from the perspective of principle (*li*), it may also be established as the fifth proposition.

Thus, each of the three contemplations can individually constitute five propositions. If one clarifies the enumeration according to the gate of contemplation, then for both matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*), there are the ten realms (*dhātu*) and the ten suchnesses (*tathatā*);
when these realms and suchnesses are discussed in mutual relation, they total two thousand. This concludes the first section on the assembly of bhikṣus. △
There were two assemblies of bhikṣuṇīs:
the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī together with her retinue of six thousand,
and the bhikṣuṇī Yaśodharā, the mother of Rāhula, also together with her retinue.
Mahāprajāpatī—translated here as "Great Path of Great Affection"—was the Buddha’s maternal aunt. Originally, she dwelt in the dharma-gate of the *Prajñāpāramitā* (Perfection of Wisdom);
in her manifested traces, she became the mother of the thousand Buddhas, giving birth to the Teacher. For those who contemplate and understand her: her vast and extensive insight is called "Great";

her unconditional compassion is called "Affection" (*prajā*); and her principle of emptiness and pervasive penetration is called "Path" (*pati*). "Great" refers to her own practice, while "Affection" refers to...
Transforming others is like taking birth out of love and traversing the path of existence out of compassion; this thus encompasses both self-cultivation and the transformation of others.
"Six thousand" refers to the number. Regarding the contemplative understanding, one contemplates that the purity of the six sense faculties possesses a thousand merits.
Yaśodharā is translated as "Flower-like Color" (Huase) and also as "Renowned Name" (Mingwen). When the Buddha was still a householder, he had three consorts.

First, Gopī; second, Yaśodharā; third, Mṛgajā. Regarding their original and manifested forms (*honjaku*): they were his wives in the same lifetime. How could those who are ordinary beings become the wives of a Bodhisattva?
Thus we know that in his original state he dwelt in the subtle joy of the Dharma within tranquil meditative concentration, while in his manifested form he became the wife of the Prince.

For one who contemplates the mind, the joy of the Dharma is the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) joy of emptiness; thus, one uses Mṛgajā to symbolize the wife (because she did not give birth to a son). This is the contemplation.
The joy of the Dharma through the provisional *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) is represented by Yaśodharā as his wife (because she gave birth to Rāhula);

the joy of the Dharma within contemplation is represented by Gopī as his wife (because her status is the most supreme). Above, each section has clarified the original and the trace (*honji-suijaku*) regarding the contemplation of the mind;

now, we shall further discuss them collectively to reveal the subtle skill of expedient means (*upāya-kauśalya*) and clarify the subtlety of contemplative practice. Regarding the collective clarification of the original and the trace: first...

Within the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, various manifestations are displayed to suit the capacities of sentient beings, such that there is nothing he does not perform. To discuss this briefly from a proximate perspective:

when the World-Honored One entrusted his traces to a royal palace and descended as a spirit into a noble queen, the great Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-body all assisted the Buddha in his work of transformation, dispersing their reflections into other households.
Likewise, when the thirty-two golden-jeweled forms were born in response to the world, each of the great Bodhisattvas also [manifested accordingly].
Each manifested either an empty room (Subhūti), a rain of jewels (Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra), or the interpretation of dreams (Śāriputra).

Just as when a crown prince abandons his kingdom and royal status to leave the city and study the Way, all great beings follow their teacher to request instruction, becoming masters of that school through their mastery of both talent and art;
so too was it when the Tathāgata first turned the Wheel of Dharma and opened the gate of ambrosia.

The Great Beings, knowing that the conditions for their transformation were not yet ripe, manifested as if they did not accept [the offerings], maintaining a formal distance and opposing [the worldly] with their own true Way.

Thus, the transformer and the transformed were entirely like milk; yet when the conditions for transformation ripened, the plain silk was easily dyed, the lotus in the pond bloomed early, the ordinary was transformed into the holy, and the milk was turned into curd. The Master became the foremost leader among the Buddhas, and his disciples followed him.
These sons, each supreme in wisdom, supernatural powers, eloquence, and samādhi, together assist the Dharma King;

they further deliver those not yet delivered and bring to full maturity those already matured. At the assembly of the Vaipulya sūtras, upon hearing of the inconceivable merit of the Bodhisattvas, they feel shame for the Lesser Vehicle and aspire to the Great;
this is like the transformation of curd into fresh butter. Next, they hear the Prajñāpāramitā Mahāyāna.

The gate begins with the sequential traversal of form and mind, culminating in the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñā). It encompasses and holds both the Small and Great Vehicles, involving taking out and bringing in, receiving and giving, whether in common or distinct, partial or perfect.
Having received the mandate and mastered this understanding, the mind gradually becomes open and expansive, like transforming raw butter into refined butter.

Subsequently, hearing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, one realizes that the nature of heaven and earth is fixed, the father and son are granted their respective prophecies (*vyākaraṇa*), and the Mahāyāna is entrusted as the ultimate teaching.

The three refuges are one, just as the other four flavors are the same single *amṛta* (clarified butter). Not allowing even a single person to attain *nirvāṇa* alone, all are brought to extinction through the *nirvāṇa* of the Tathāgata.
This is the great task of the Dharma King and his Dharma ministers appearing in the world, skillfully employing expedient means:
first using the "half-syllable" teachings to cut down the thick undergrowth of the twenty-five states of existence, thereby achieving the "four kinds of withered trees."

First, the twin trees benefit sentient beings by employing the methods of the "half" and "full" to break the solitary goodness of the Two Vehicles and establish the vast perfection of the Bodhisattvas;

this constitutes the fourth stage of flourishing. Subsequently, the twin trees benefit the sages by employing the eternally abiding "full" character to break the preceding and succeeding extremes of the Two Sides, thereby establishing the Buddha’s secret treasury—which is neither withered nor flourishing—as the ultimate benefit.
The merit of the General-in-Chief has been fully realized and the vows of the Great Oath have been fulfilled;
therefore, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana have ceased their transformative activity within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. That the Holy Lord redeems their lives is likewise not for long.
As the text says: "My original vow is now fulfilled; before long, the Tathāgata shall enter nirvāṇa. The proclamation of his passing originated from this very point.
The twenty thousand Buddhas, such as Dīpaṃkara and Kāśyapa, all reached ultimate realization through the Lotus Sūtra;

likewise, the present Buddha and his disciples have all revealed their origins through this sūtra. Internally they secretly practiced the conduct of Bodhisattvas, while externally they manifested as Śrāvakas.
In truth, since my attainment of Buddhahood, immeasurable billions of kalpas have passed. By this inference, one may see that the great Arhats look down from the stage of the Dharmakāya.

The shadow follows its conditions and traces appear upon ten thousand waters; for those in training and those beyond training, manifesting as male or female, and appearing in both the monastic and secular worlds—the power of the *Śūraṅgama* enables it to perform all things.

Such is the nature of these skillful means and expedient devices. If one attempts to explain the "original" and "traced" aspects through these two layers of general and specific interpretations, I fear one may still miss the essential meaning. How much more so when merely translating a single phrase—what difference does that truly make?

Regarding the general clarification of contemplating the mind within the various teachings for the assembly of *śrāvakas*: the aforementioned purpose of the Dharma-body manifested through the instruction of master and disciple is that if one does not employ the skillful means of contemplation, it will be of no benefit to the practitioner—like a poor man counting his treasures or a blind person holding a torch.
Although mental factors (*caitta*) are exceedingly numerous, we shall provisionally rely on the wholesome ones; and even among those, though disciples are many, we shall cite only ten.
The ten wholesome mental factors assist the sovereign mind-king; they enable one to reform evil and pursue good, transform the mundane into the sacred, and accomplish all dharma-gates.

Taking these ten mental factors as the foundation is like having ten disciples assist the Buddha in his transformative work, together maturing sentient beings and establishing them in the Buddha-dharma.
Each of these ten persons is endowed with manifold virtues, serving as guides for their respective specialties and proclaiming the teachings.

The Buddhas manifest their paths according to the inclinations of sentient beings: for those who desire wisdom, they appoint Śāriputra as teacher; for those who desire extensive learning, they appoint Ānanda as teacher.
Together they assist the Dharma King, each presiding over a specific office. Now, observing the mind is also like this:

within each and every thought, all the "kings" (the mental factors) are fully present. For the sake of accomplishing contemplation, these kings support one another so that awakening may be attained. Or...

Whether entering the path through the category of perception (*saṃjñā*) or entering the path through the category of desire (*kāma*), one should, as appropriate, employ the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and its mental factors (*caitta*) to collectively attack them.

One transforms and takes up the various minds of affliction (*kleśa*) to perform the work of a Buddha. When contemplating in this manner, if one has not yet awakened to the practice of contemplation, it is like milk;
if the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) practice of contemplation arises, it is like curd; and if the dust-like [delusions] are shattered, it is like the state between raw and cooked.
If ghee breaks through ignorance, it is viewed as clarified butter (*ghṛta*); if the mental afflictions (*kleśa*) are not fully exhausted, the contemplation will not be completed.
Thus, the Sūtra states: "I shall not attain perfect enlightenment until all sentient beings have been delivered"—this is precisely that meaning.
Master Xu maintains that the twenty-one great Arhats should be categorized according to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, collectively representing the twenty-one types of wholesome minds.

The factors of enumeration (saṃskāra-dharma) are: contact, attention, feeling, perception, volition, desire, resolve, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, faith, shame, dread, diligence, non-attachment, non-hatred, non-delusion, pliancy, heedfulness, equanimity, and non-harming.
Each of these is mutually associated and each possesses manifold virtues; together they assist the King of the Mind, benefiting oneself and others until the end of the future.
There are cases where [the categories] are divided, yet it is not necessary to labor over assigning each one to a specific group; the essential point lies in grasping the underlying meaning.

This concludes the section on the assembly of Śrāvakas. Second, regarding the assembly of Bodhisattvas: The *Śāstra* asks, "Since Bodhisattvas are subsumed within the fourfold assembly of monastics and laypeople, why are they listed separately?
The answer is: there are Bodhisattvas who fall within the fourfold assembly, yet there are also those among the fourfold assembly who do not fall within the category of Bodhisattvas.
Because those among the assembly who have not resolved to attain Buddhahood are excluded, those who have likewise resolved to seek Buddhahood are now listed separately as the "Bodhisattva Assembly.
The text is divided into three parts: first, the general category and its magnitude; second, clarifying their stages and praising their virtues;
third, listing their names and providing a concluding summary. This is the first part.
"Eighty thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
To preserve the full form, it should be called *bodhisattva-mahāsattva*. Master Śikṣānanda abbreviated it. *Bodhi* is translated as "the Way";
*sattva* is translated as "sentient being" (*sattva*); *mahā* is translated as "great. This refers to sentient beings who possess the mind of the Way and the great mind of the Way.

This refers to the "affinities" (*qìlèi*). There are many types of bodhisattvas, namely the partial (*piān*), the universal (*tōng*), the distinct (*bié*), and the perfect (*yuán*), as explained in the *Śāstra* which cites Kātyāyanīputra regarding the limits of the six perfections. Those who fulfill them desire to transform blood-like sentient beings into milk;
if the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* speaks of bodhisattvas whose resolve corresponds to *sarvajñatā*, they desire to transform that milk into cream.
If, as in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, it is explained that there are bodhisattvas who resolve their minds to sport with supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) and purify buddha-fields,

this is like desiring to refine curd into fresh butter (*navanīta*) or clarified butter (*ghṛta*). If, as in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, it is explained that there are bodhisattvas who, upon resolving their minds,

immediately sit at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), attain perfect awakening (*abhisambodhi*), turn the wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*), and deliver sentient beings, this is like refining clarified butter into the finest essence, *amṛta* (ghee).
Therefore, the subsequent text states: "When the Bodhisattva hears this Dharma, the net of doubts is entirely removed. It further states:
"If a Bodhisattva does not hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, they are not practicing the Bodhisattva path well; if they hear this sutra, they are practicing the Bodhisattva path well.

Thus, there are briefly four kinds. Regarding the "Original and Traces" (*honji-matsuji*): the Original Ground is difficult to fathom, for [the Buddha] may dwell at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Alternatively, the Dharma King is equal to Mañjuśrī, who was originally the Buddha Uṣṇīṣa-rāja;
as a trace-emanation assisting Śākyamuni, he acts as a guide for bodhisattvas and others, leading them through the four flavors so they may all return to the *amṛta* (the finest essence).

Yet, as for his original ground and ultimate accomplishment, how could it be that he only entered the Mahāyāna today? Nor is it that he first shone upon the high mountain at the site of enlightenment (Bodhimaṇḍa) all at once.
If [the assembly] were gradual, it would merely be a matter of outward traces. For one who contemplates the mind, the Middle Way’s correct contemplation simultaneously illuminates the two truths;

this is called the Great Penetration to the Ultimate Fruit. "The Way" refers to the breaking of the five abodes of defilement, and "accomplishing sentient beings" refers to the number eighty thousand.
In other sutras, the gathered assemblies are very large; why is this sutra so small? It may be that these numbers refer to the general total.
Or, for example, it is like a king discussing secret matters that cannot be deliberated upon by the entire realm;
now, opening this secret treasury, those who testify to its authenticity do not involve those of provisional capacity, but are necessarily perfect beings (*paripūrṇa-pudgala*) with a distant root.

As for the contemplation of the mind, one contemplates that a single wholesome mind possesses the hundred realms and the thousand suchnesses; the ten wholesome acts are thus the myriad dharmas, according to the eight [categories].

The Right Path consists of the eighty thousand dharma-gates (the ten wholesome actions as the objects of observation and the eightfold right path as the observing subject). △ Second, clarifying the stages and extolling their virtues:
they have all attained non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; they have all acquired *dhāraṇī* and the eloquence of joyful speech;
they turn the irreversible wheel of Dharma; and they have made offerings to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Buddhas. Regarding these Buddhas...

Having planted the roots of all virtues, they are constantly praised by all Buddhas; cultivating their bodies with loving-kindness, they skillfully enter the Buddha’s wisdom, penetrate great insight, and reach the other shore;
their fame is heard throughout immeasurable worlds, and they are able to deliver countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings.

The first phrase clarifies both the stage and extols the virtues; the subsequent twelve phrases extol only the virtues. Together, these thirteen phrases extol the virtues both horizontally and vertically.
*Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is translated here as "Unsurpassed Perfectly Equal and Right Enlightenment," a meaning that applies across the four teachings.
Regarding "non-retrogression" (*avaivartika*), it refers to non-retrogression in terms of stage, practice, and mindfulness.
There are four distinctions: if one says that one will not be born in the three evil realms, this is called "non-retrogression in status";

if one is not born in borderlands, possesses complete faculties, and does not receive a female body, this is called "non-retrogression in practice"; if one constantly knows past lives, this is called "non-retrogression in mindfulness.
To possess these is the meaning of the stage of *avaivartika* according to the Tripiṭaka school. Alternatively, from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the sixth stage...

Non-retrogression for ordinary beings is called "retrogression of name and position"; although their afflictions (*āsrava*) may already be exhausted, they have not yet been able to cultivate the myriad practices universally, and thus their practice still regresses.
At the seventh stage, it is called "retrogression of practice," because one still gives rise to thoughts of the two vehicles.
At the eighth stage, where path and contemplation proceed together and one enters the flow of the Dharma, it is called "retrogression of thought."
The name "Avivartika-bhūmi" (the stage of non-retrogression) refers merely to the meaning of the ten stages common to the three vehicles within the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*).

Master Di stated: "The Ten Abidings are non-retrogression through realization; the Ten Practices are non-retrogression of position; the Ten Dedications are non-retrogression of practice; and the Ten Stages are non-retrogression of mindfulness.
This is the meaning of the Distinct Teaching (*pratyeka-yāna*). The *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* (or *Yingluo jing*) states: "In the first stage, the three contemplations manifest before one."
"The mind-mind is quiescent and naturally flows [into the Way]" is the meaning of the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao).

If the *Avataṃsaka* clarifies that one attains the Tathāgata’s single body and infinite bodies and possesses the three non-regressions at the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*), this is the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (Yuan-jiao); it is a single reality.

Now, this is used to judge the wondrous stages. Regarding "Original Ground" (*ben*) and "Trace" (*ji*), if even the Original Ground of quiescence does not yet equal the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*), how much less so [the lower stages]?

If even the first stage (*bhūmi*) of this [Perfect Teaching] is not yet the true first stage, how much less so the stages of the Separate and Common [Teachings]? These positions of the Separate and Common can be explained as referring to other sutras’ enumerations of assemblies;
the position of the Perfect Teaching resides precisely in this present sutra. Since one does not yet recognize the traces (*traces of the teaching*), how could one know the source?

As for the contemplation of the mind: the three contemplations are themselves the three non-regressions, and the three contemplations within a single mind are themselves the three non-regressions within a single mind.

"Regressing must be discussed in terms of the six stages of realization. This phrase vertically praises [the Bodhisattva] on the first stage, the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), for being non-regressive and not falling into the two extremes, thereby entering the Middle Way;

it horizontally praises [the practitioner] in the first dwelling, the Dwelling of Initial Resolve (*prathama-cittotpāda-vihāra*), for transcending the two extremes, transforming the ordinary and surpassing the sages.
"All have attained *dhāraṇī*": *dhāraṇī* is translated here as "obstructing and maintaining"—obstructing evil and maintaining good. This is a vertical praise.

The phrase "the precept-paramita is purified on the Stainless Ground" is a horizontal praise of the first dwelling (prathama-bhūmi), which obstructs the three hindrances and maintains the three virtues.

The phrase "eloquence of joyful speech" is a vertical praise of the Radiant Ground (arciṣmatī-bhūmi), wherein one attains great dhāraṇī and possesses the four types of unimpeded eloquence (*pratisaṃvid*).

The phrase "turning the irreversible wheel of Dharma" is a vertical praise of the Blazing Wisdom Ground (*arcismatī-bhūmi*). The phrase "the mouth-secret virtue of the first dwelling" is a horizontal praise. The phrase "turning the irreversible wheel of Dharma" is a vertical praise of the Blazing Wisdom Ground.

The phrase "The ground itself shatters its own delusions and destroys the darkness of others' confusion" is a horizontal praise of the initial stage (*ādikṣaṇa*) manifesting as a Buddha to preach the Dharma and deliver sentient beings.

The phrase "Making offerings to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Buddhas" is a vertical praise of the Difficult to Conquer Stage (*sudurjayā-bhūmi*), wherein one universally raises offerings through the power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and supernormal faculties (*abhijñā*).
The phrase "Horizontally praising the initial stage, being able to universally serve all [Buddhas] of the ten directions" [is a horizontal praise of the initial stage].

The phrase "the Buddha also planted the roots of all virtues under various Buddhas" praises vertically the *prajñā* of the Present Stage (*Abhimukhī-bhūmi*), wherein present wisdom is the root of virtue, like planting seeds in the earth.

The phrase "planting [them] in the earth" praises horizontally that those dwelling in the first stage attain the original nature of true reality (*dharmatā*), which is capable of planting all virtues.
The phrase "constantly praised by all Buddhas" praises vertically the second stage, the Far-Reaching Stage (*Dūraṃgamā-bhūmi*).
The phrase "Wisdom and skillful means transcend all" praises [the Bodhisattva] for extensively cultivating benefits that accord with the Buddha’s mind;

the phrase "transversely praising the first stage" refers to opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, which is identical to that of all Buddhas, and is thus praised by the Buddhas. The phrase "cultivating the body through compassion" praises [the Bodhisattva] vertically from the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*):
compassion permeates the three karmas, permeates the body as it enters the five destinies, and permeates the mouth as it preaches the Dharma.

The phrase "the Dharma perfumes the mind" establishes the skillful means by horizontally praising the power of the unconditioned compassion (*anālambana-karuṇā*) of the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*), which can universally manifest form-bodies (*rūpakāya*) pervading the entire Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

The phrase "skillfully entering the Buddha-wisdom" vertically praises the profound penetration into the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) at the stage of Excellent Wisdom (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*), while horizontally praising the entry into the secret treasury (*guhyagarbha*) at the first stage. The phrase "thoroughly penetrating great wisdom" [is as follows].
The vertical praise extols the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) on the Dharma-Cloud Stage (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*) as being preeminent;

the horizontal praise extols that the single mind and threefold wisdom of the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) are without obstruction and have reached the further shore. The phrase "reaching the further shore" vertically praises the internal virtues of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), which has reached the further shore of the Three Truths;
horizontally, it praises the ultimate realization of both phenomena and principle at the first stage. Thus, its fame is heard everywhere.
The phrase "immeasurable worlds" is a vertical praise of the external virtues of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambuddha*), wherein the dharma-realm hears the conferral of the empowerment of office;
the phrase "pervading all" is a horizontal praise of the perfect virtues of the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*), wherein reality accords with its name and designation.

The phrase "able to deliver countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings" is a vertical praise of the grace of Equal Enlightenment in transforming others, which, when compared to the lower stages, is most supreme and most vast.
This horizontal praise asserts that the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) can serve as the locus of support for all ten realms (*dharmadhātu*).

Now, although all stages (*bhūmi*) are fully endowed with manifold virtues, the explanation here is given in terms of vertical emergence and submergence because people’s dispositions favor novelty, because it follows the convenience of the ten-stage schema, and because the vertical principle is easier to understand;
thus, this particular approach is adopted merely to interpret the text. Furthermore, regarding the first stage...
Although there are immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable merits, they are here expressed briefly in only thirteen phrases;

if even the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) is thus, one may know that this holds true for the second stage up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"The initial letter A-gate possesses the merits of all forty-one letters, and the final letter Ḍha likewise possesses the merits of all letters."

The middle [stage] is likewise; the merits of the letters and the words are also equal. Regarding the contemplation of the mind: the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is the *svādhiṣṭhāna-dhāraṇī*;
the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti*) is the *śatasahasra-svādhiṣṭhāna-dhāraṇī*; and the contemplation of the middle way is the *dharmasvara-upāya-dhāraṇī*.
Furthermore, in the contemplation of emptiness, observing the mind as having only names is the *śruta-dhara-dhāraṇī*. The provisional...
Contemplating the contemplating mind—wherein immeasurable minds and mental factors are all dharma-gates—is the practice of the *dhāraṇī* of contemplation;

this contemplation of the contemplating mind is the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), which is the *dhāraṇī* of upholding the meaning. Contemplating the contemplating mind through conventional contemplation (*saṃvṛti-darśana*) as possessing the dharmas of the ten realms is the *dhāraṇī* of unimpeded eloquence regarding phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*);
contemplating the contemplating mind such that the ten realms all enter into true reality is the *dhāraṇī* of unimpeded eloquence regarding principles (*artha-pratisaṃvid*).

The meaning of the mutual identity [of phenomena] is the unimpeded eloquence of emptiness; contemplating the mind through the ten realms, one sees that they are merely names and words, which is the unimpeded eloquence of dharma.

Contemplating the single mind as the three minds, the three minds as the single mind, and the rotation without obstruction between one realm and all realms, is the unimpeded eloquence of joyful speech. This contemplation of emptiness is the stage of non-retrogression.

The provisional contemplation of the wheel is the turning of the Dharma-wheel of non-retrogression in practice; the contemplation within the wheel is the turning of the Dharma-wheel of non-retrogression in thought.

To make offerings to the Buddha is simply to accord with the Buddha’s words; now, to cultivate the three contemplations of the mind in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching is itself making offerings to the Buddha.
Because this serves to shatter the five abodes and attain liberation, it is making offerings to the Dharma—the principle of the Three Truths.

Harmony is the mind that makes offerings to the Sangha; furthermore, the mind of various practices is the basis for the mind of contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*), and this mind of contemplative wisdom is the offering to the Buddha.
When the mind of contemplative wisdom unfolds its objective realm, it is the offering to the Dharma. The harmony between the objective realm and the wisdom of the mind is the offering to the Sangha.

The mind of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is the basis of the mind of contemplative wisdom, and the mind of contemplative wisdom is the basis of the mind of various practices. Thus, when one attains and plants these roots, [the three jewels are fulfilled].
Because it is established, it is said to "plant the roots of all virtues. Contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā*) merges with its object, and the object seals contemplative wisdom;

when wisdom has a constant object, it is always united with that object. This is precisely what the Buddha praised as the empty contemplation (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), which is perfumed by the compassion for phenomena (*dharmālambana-maitrī*);

the provisional contemplation (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*), which is perfumed by the compassion for sentient beings (*sattvālambana-maitrī*); and the middle-way contemplation (*madhyamā-vipaśyanā*), which is the unconditioned compassion (*anālambana-maitrī*).

The contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) enters the wisdom of the Buddha of the Shared Teaching; the contemplation of the provisional (*upāya-vipaśyanā*) enters the wisdom of the Buddha of the Distinct Teaching;

and the contemplation of the middle (*madhyama-vipaśyanā*) enters the wisdom of the Buddha of the Perfect Teaching. Through the contemplation of emptiness, one reaches the other shore of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*); through the contemplation of the provisional, one reaches the other shore of the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*); and through the contemplation of the middle, one reaches the other shore of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
By means of the contemplation of emptiness, one hears the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); by means of the contemplation of the provisional, one hears the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
The Middle Way of the Universal Renown is also universally known as the First Noble Truth of the Ultimate Meaning (*paramārtha-satya*).

Through the contemplation of the emptiness of the Three Truths, one delivers hundreds of thousands of sentient beings from the four abodes (*catvāraḥ sthitayaḥ*); through the contemplation of the provisional (*upāya*), one delivers hundreds of thousands of sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;

and through the contemplation of the Middle, one delivers hundreds of thousands of sentient beings from ignorance (*avidyā*). This single mind of the three contemplations possesses immeasurable virtues that cannot be fully extolled; this is merely a brief explanation.
[End of section] △ Third, the enumeration of names and the concluding summary.

Their names were: Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva, Nityodyukta Bodhisattva, Anikṣiptadhura Bodhisattva, Ratnapāṇi Bodhisattva, Bhaiṣajyarāja Bodhisattva, and Śūradatta Bodhisattva.
There were eighty thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas present together with him,
such as the bodhisattva Ratnacandra, Candraprabha, Pūrṇacandra, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, Anantavikrama, Trailokyavikrama, Bhadrapāla, Maitreya, Ratnākara, and Nāyaka.
The Great Being (Mahāsattva) and the Great Name (Mahānāman) may be derived from a dharma-gate, from conduct and virtue, or from original vows;
though they are but single names, they encompass immeasurable meanings. Now, relying on the sūtras and based on contemplation, I shall explain the names of the eighteen bodhisattvas.
Regarding Mañjuśrī, this is translated as "Wondrous Virtue" (Miaode). As the *Great Sūtra* says: "To see the Buddha-nature clearly is to be like Mañjuśrī. Contemplate thus.
The *Fangguang bore jing* (Larger Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra) states: "Although one speaks of all dharmas, one does not give rise to the mark of dharmas, nor does one give rise to the mark of non-dharmas;
therefore, one is named 'Wondrous Virtue' (*Miaode*). The *Beihua jing* (Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra) states:

"I vow that when I practice the bodhisattva path, all the sentient beings I transform shall first attain perfect enlightenment in the ten directions, so that my divine eye may see them all, and my land shall be entirely uniform."
He caused all those born as bodhisattvas to follow his exhortation to resolve upon the path of enlightenment. He said, "I shall practice the bodhisattva path without limit.
The Buddha Baozang (Treasure Store) said, "The merit you have cultivated is most profound, most profound. You shall take a wondrous land;
for this reason, I now name you Mañjuśrī. In the northern world-system of Abhirati, you shall become a buddha named Abhirati."
The Tathāgata Maṇiratnasaṃcaya is still present today; merely hearing his name extinguishes the four grave offenses. Furthermore, the *Śūraṅgama Samādhi Sūtra* states:
"In the past, immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Nāga-uttara-rāja (Dragon-Species Supreme Honored King), who is also the contemplation of the mind of Mañjuśrī.
Because the secret treasury of the three virtues is neither vertical nor horizontal, it is called 'wondrous' (miao)."
The virtue of Avalokiteśvara—whose Sanskrit name is *Bhagavat-avalokiteśvara*—is explained in detail as in the "Universal Gate" (*Pumen pin*) chapter.

Regarding the contemplation of the mind: the three types of wisdom are called "contemplation" (*guan*), and the three truths are called "the world" (*shi*). Because these are the basis of the verbal expression, it is called "sound" (*yin*).

(In the following section, it is explained according to phenomena, taking that which is addressed as "sound"; here, however, it is explained according to the contemplating subject, taking that which is proclaimed as "sound"). Mahāsthāmaprāpta is also named Mahāsthāmaprāpti; this is according to the *Siddhi-vivardhana-sūtra*.
It is said that wherever he places his feet, the three thousandfold world-system and the palaces of Māra tremble; therefore, he is named Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
The *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra* states: "If one sees even the light from a single pore of this Bodhisattva, one immediately beholds the pure and wondrous radiance of all Buddhas of the ten directions;
for this reason, this Bodhisattva is named Amitābha (Boundless Light) by virtue of his wisdom."
The light of wisdom universally illumines all, causing them to leave the three miserable realms and attain supreme power; therefore, this Bodhisattva is named Mahāsthāmaprāpta.

For one who contemplates the mind, the three types of cessation (śamatha) serve as the feet, and by stepping upon the ground of the three truths, all abodes of views and attachments within the ten dharma-realms are shaken and overturned. He who is ever-diligent is a great jewel.
The *Jiyun* (Accumulated Clouds) Sūtra states that for the sake of a single sentient being, a bodhisattva follows them for immeasurable kalpas without abandoning them;
even if they do not undergo transformation, the bodhisattva does not relinquish them for a single thought-moment. Because both body and mind advance together, there is no rest.
The *Sìyì* (Thought-Benefit) Sūtra says: "A kalpa as numerous as the sands of the Ganges constitutes one day and night; thirty such days constitute a month, and twelve months [constitute a year]."
After passing through hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, one may encounter a single Buddha;

encountering Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in this way, one practices the various pure conducts (*brahmacarya*) and cultivates meritorious virtues, whereupon one receives the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). One whose mind does not cease thus contemplates the mind:

contemplating emptiness (*śūnyatā*) without dwelling in emptiness, entering the provisional (*upāya*) without dwelling in the provisional, and entering the middle (*madhyama*) without dwelling in the middle, illuminating both truths (*satyadvaya*) simultaneously.
The term "unremitting" (*aśithila*) has a meaning roughly equivalent to "constant diligence" (*nityavīrya*). To distinguish between them:
entering [the practice] without interruption is called "diligence," while continuing for a long duration without cessation is called "unremitting.
Therefore, since contemplative understanding is termed "non-abiding," the explanation of "unremitting" is also based on a long duration; it merely records the distinction regarding its benefits.
