These are the realms perceived within the sixth auspicious omen of this land—the emission of light—intended to facilitate understanding and to draw parallels; thus they are divided into six parts. First, the vision:

Sixth, the auspicious sign of the six realms; second, the auspicious sign of seeing all Buddhas—this is the pair of the superior sages and the inferior commoners. Third, the auspicious sign of hearing the preaching of the Dharma;
fourth, the auspicious sign of seeing the fourfold assembly attain the Way—this is the pair of persons and the Dharma. Fifth, the auspicious sign of seeing the bodhisattvas perform their practices;
sixth, the auspicious sign of seeing the parinirvāṇa of all Buddhas—this is the pair of the beginning and the end. Since there are sentient beings who can be transformed, [the Buddha appears].
There is a Buddha who can manifest transformation; where there is a Buddha, there is the preaching of the Dharma; where there is the preaching of the Dharma, there are disciples;
and disciples are the beginning of practice, for the beginning of practice must lead to its completion.

Furthermore, the six auspicious omens in this land collectively signify that sentient beings shall attain self-awakening, while the six auspicious omens in that land collectively signify that sentient beings shall awaken others. Moreover—
Those six auspicious omens signify that the paths of those Buddhas and this one are identical;

among them, the first five omens manifest that his land is already the same as this one, while the sixth omen manifests that this land shall likewise become the same as that one. First, there was the omen of seeing the six realms of existence.
From the Avīci Hell below up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven above, they see all the beings of the six destinies within this world and that land.
"Avīci" is translated here as "Uninterrupted," being located at the very bottom of the world; "Akaniṣṭha" is translated as "Formless."
The Ultimate Peak (Akaniṣṭha) is situated at the very top of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*). This follows from the preceding text:
as the light illuminated eighteen thousand lands in the eastern direction, reaching from that Avīci Hell up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, there was nothing that did not appear within the light.
At that time, the great assembly in this realm saw all the sentient beings of the six destinies (*ṣaḍgati*) in those lands, namely:
The hells, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans, and devas—these [beings] in that land manifest the five turbidities just as they do in this land.
△ Second, seeing the auspicious signs of the various Buddhas:
one also sees the various Buddhas currently residing in that land.
The Buddhas appearing in those lands manifest in the world for the sake of the five turbidities; their intent is the same as that of Śākyamuni Buddha’s appearance in this land.
△ Third, the auspicious omen of hearing the preaching of the Dharma.
Furthermore, he hears the sutras and teachings expounded by all the Buddhas.

This manifestation is identical in intent to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* taught here on this earth by Śākyamuni Buddha—how that original Buddha first, from the single dharma of formlessness, suddenly and instantaneously expounded the Great *Avataṃsaka*. △ Fourth, the auspicious signs of the fourfold assembly attaining the Way.
Furthermore, one sees those bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās who have attained the Way through various practices.
Although this present Buddha is not gradual, he teaches the Dharma of the Three Piṭakas in a gradual manner for the sake of those with dull faculties; the fourfold assembly relies upon this.
The attainment of the four supramundane fruits and the path of the *pratyekabuddha* is identical in intent to the teaching of the Tripiṭaka by Śākyamuni Buddha in this land.
△ Fifth, seeing the auspicious signs of the Bodhisattva’s practice.
Furthermore, he saw various bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practicing the bodhisattva path through diverse causes and conditions, diverse faiths and understandings, and diverse manifestations.
These [bodhisattvas] appeared before that Buddha, who— though not gradual himself— gradually taught the Vaipulya Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of those of the Mahāyāna.
The intent of the *Mahāyāna-vaipulya-tathāgatagarbha-sūtra* and the two "milk" teachings (*kṣīra-dharma*) spoken by Śākyamuni Buddha in this land is the same:
the good roots planted in the past through the four teachings serve as the cause, while the present reception of the dharma-gates of the four teachings serves as the condition.

Each of the four teachings possesses its own faith and understanding (*śraddhā-vimukti*) as that which evokes [the response], and since there are four gates for the practice of each teaching, it is said that there are "various appearances. △ Six: Seeing.
There were auspicious signs of the parinirvāṇa of various Buddhas;
furthermore, he saw various Buddhas entering parinirvāṇa, and after the parinirvāṇa of those Buddhas, he saw stūpas made of the seven precious jewels being erected for their relics.
This manifestation of that Buddha, having completed the work of transformation, withdraws immeasurable dharmas and returns them to the single dharma;

he demonstrates extinction to cease his transformative activity, even to the point of erecting stupas to perform Buddha-work. Thus, from his initial appearance in the world until the end of the Semblance Dharma period, all the provisional and ultimate benefits he enacted shine forth, illuminating that land so vividly they appear before one's eyes. By using that as an analogy...
Since these five preceding [teachings] are identical to the one subsequent [teaching], how could they be different?

It should be known that from the moment of his initial attainment of enlightenment, Śākyamuni brought forth immeasurable dharmas from a single dharma of non-characteristic (*animitta*); this was neither sudden nor gradual, yet it appeared both sudden and gradual. That matter is now concluded;
today he must surely gather the immeasurable dharmas back into the single dharma, revealing the provisional to manifest the real, and proclaiming his entry [into parinirvāṇa].
The cessation [of the teaching] is the same as that land. Question: Why is that land not manifested within the light while preaching the Lotus Sūtra? Answer:

If it were to be clearly and fully manifested, then the introduction would not be established; furthermore, it would not allow for the assembly’s doubts, nor for Maitreya to pose the question and Mañjuśrī to provide the response through reflection.
Thus, there would be no way for the two discourses on the Trace and the Origin to be initiated. Why is this so?

Because it will ultimately bring about boundless benefit both in the present and after the extinction [of the Buddha], some claim that the true purport of the *Lotus Sūtra* lies solely in the single ray of light shining toward the East.
This is a one-sided view, failing to realize that both preaching and silence possess the four *siddhāntas*.
When entering meditative absorption, the four *siddhāntas* reach only those of the highest capacity; when preaching the Dharma, the four *siddhāntas* universally reach those of all three capacities.
The four *siddhāntas* within meditative concentration pertain exclusively to the present; the four *siddhāntas* for the circulation of the Dharma extend universally to the future.

Because those who realize through darkness (*andhakāra*) lack knowledge, they hold many divergent views. [Objection: When that which is illuminated is perceived all at once in the light, how can you say there is first the sudden and later the gradual, even until their ultimate convergence?
[Response: Since both the distant and the near can be made to see and hear simultaneously, this applies equally to the past and the future.

Since all difficulties have been resolved so that everyone may see and hear, making the beginning and end of the ten directions as clear as if before one's eyes, how can you use such ordinary sentiments to measure the realm of the Sage?
You ask whether what is seen within the light is not purely sudden, but perhaps gradual.
Answer: The assembly at that time merely obtained sight because of the light; the great skillful means, however, resides with the World-Honored One. It was he who caused them to see.

The original purpose was to manifest the same realization; the light emitted was for the sake of achieving the single reality. Thus, while the phenomena differ, the principle is absolute—those who do not partake of this light are not moistened by it.

Question: This term *parinirvāṇa* is here translated as "entering nirvana" and also as "extinction and deliverance. Since the *śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha* (the *āgama* and *vaipulya* teachings) involve the severance of the ashes [of the aggregates], they achieve *parinirvāṇa*.

Now that the perfect, eternal nature has been revealed, how can one say they have "entered extinction"? Answer: When a Buddha appears in the realm of shared existence (*sahā-loka*), his activities must necessarily...
If one knows that what is shown as extinction is not birth, then showing birth is immediately known to be non-birth;

if one knows that what is shown as extinction is not extinction, then showing extinction is immediately known to be non-extinction. By reading the "Chapter on the Lifespan," these doubts will be resolved of themselves.
*Śarīra* is sometimes called *śilā*, which translates as "sacred bone. A *stūpa* is fully called *tāpa*, or *stūpa*, which translates as [relic-mound].
"Square mound" (fāng fén) is alternatively translated as "round tomb" (yuán zǒng), and also as "lofty and manifest. This concludes the Preface on the Manifestation of Auspicious Omens.
△ Third, the Preface on Doubtful Reflections, in two parts: 1. Maitreya’s Doubtful Reflection; 2. The Great Assembly’s Doubtful Reflection. Now, the first: Maitreya’s Doubtful Reflection.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva had this thought: "Now the World-Honored One manifests signs of spiritual transformation;
by what causes and conditions does this auspicious omen arise? The Buddha, the World-Honored One, has now entered samādhi and manifested this inconceivable and rare event—whom should I ask about it?
Who is able to answer? He further thought: "This is Mañjuśrī Dharma..."
The Prince has already personally approached and made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas of the past;
he must surely perceive this rare and wondrous sign, so I shall now question him.
Maitreya has three reflections: first, from "Now" downward is the reflection on the six auspicious omens; second, from "Now the Buddha" downward is... [the reflection on the Buddha].

Reflecting on the question of who [is present], he repeated this thought three times, resulting in the following: "Mañjuśrī, Mañjuśrī. As the second thought arose, it removed [the previous one], leaving only the first thought remaining;
thus, there was but a single doubt. Regarding "spiritual transformations" (*ṛddhi-vikurvaṇā*): "Spirit" (*shen*) refers to the Heavenly Mind, which is innate internal wisdom;
"transformation" (*bian*) refers to shifting and changing, which is the manifestation of the six auspicious omens externally. This is from the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra*.
It is said that the Buddha, abiding in the dharma of non-duality, is able to manifest supernormal powers; as a Dharma King, his power surpasses all.
Because Maitreya could not fathom these external transformations nor understand his internal wisdom, he gave rise to doubts. Indeed, the common person does not know the arts;
the scattered person does not know meditative concentration; the ordinary being does not know the sage; and the lesser sage does not know the [Buddha’s] body.
The Śrāvakas do not know the Bodhisattvas; the Bodhisattvas do not know those in their final birth (ekajātipratibaddha); and those in their final birth do not know the Ultimate Honored One.
This is the realm of the Ultimate Honored One, and for this reason Maitreya does not know it. Yet, since Maitreya has planted so much merit, how could he fail to have even a vague perception of it?
He must have concealed what is manifest and revealed what is obscure, speaking thus "of not knowing" as a skillful means. Question 1.
Question: Since all bodhisattvas are sons of the Dharma-king, why is Mañjuśrī alone singled out for praise? Answer: There are two reasons.
First, among the sons of the Dharma-king, Mañjuśrī is preeminent in virtue. Second, in various sutras, Mañjuśrī is consistently designated as the foremost leader of the bodhisattvas.
△ Second, the doubts of the great assembly.
At that time, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, as well as the devas, nāgas, and spirits, all had this thought:
"This is the sign of the Buddha’s light and supernormal power; whom should we now ask about it?"

The great assembly has two thoughts: first, the thought of the six auspicious omens and right mindfulness; second, the thought of asking who [will succeed]. If one anticipates the following verse, it may also be understood as having three thoughts.
The verse says: "The fourfold assembly looks up with joy toward you and me. There is no third thought here of "what is the reason for looking up to you?
This absence is intended to indicate that [the Buddha] wishes to promote the Holder of the Succession (Anantarya-bhūmi) to the foremost position. This is the textual inquiry.
Maitreya’s virtue is extraordinary; his rank is nearly equal [to that of the Buddha]. Why, then, is there one who asks and one who answers? Answer: Sentient capacities (*nengquan*) vary.

Although their status may be equal, the roles of host and guest differ according to what is appropriate. The Sage responds to these capacities; it is not possible for the questioner to provide the answer.

(Based on causes and conditions) Furthermore, within the Dharma-gates there are provisional and real aspects. One who occupies the position of the "Successor" (*upapadya*) requires questioning, while one who possesses the Real requires answering. (Based on the teaching) Furthermore, regarding the traces...

There is the sequence of questions and answers regarding the near and the distant (the *honji* and *suijaku* aspects), where the near asks and the distant answers; alternatively, there is the sequence of ease and convenience: Maitreya is named "Kindness" (*Maitreya*), and as kindness is for the sake of sentient beings, he must ask;
Mañjuśrī is named "Wondrous Virtue" (*Mañjughoṣa*), and as virtue is that which should respond, he must answer. This concludes the introductory section on the three doubts and reflections.

△ Fourth, the section on the introduction of the inquiry, in two parts: first, the long prose; second, the verse recitation. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, the narrative by the scribe (*sūtrakāra*).
The second part concerns the formal posing of the question. First:

At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva, desiring to resolve his own doubts and also observing the minds of the fourfold assembly—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—as well as the multitude of devas, nāgas, ghosts, spirits, and others, [addressed the Buddha].
The two [sections] describing his own doubts and the doubts of others are as stated in the text. △ Second, the formal posing of the question:

He addressed Mañjuśrī, saying, "By what causes and conditions has this auspicious sign of supernatural power appeared—this emission of great radiance that illuminates eighteen thousand lands in the eastern direction, such that all the adornments of those Buddha-lands are clearly seen?"
The two questions regarding this land and other lands are as in the text. △ Second, the verse summary has two parts: first, summarizing the preceding questions;
second, summarizing the request for an answer. Why are there verses? The *Vyākhyāyukti* (Lung-shu pi-p'o-sha) states: "First, regarding the obstruction of the land:

in India, there is the tradition of 'scattered flowers' and 'garlanded flowers,' which is like the postscripts following the prefaces here [in China]. Second, it follows their inclinations and desires."
1. Differentiation according to whether there is delight in discursive exposition or delight in verses (the second is the worldly); 2.
Differentiation according to the difference in the arising of understanding—some attain understanding through discursive exposition while others attain it through verses (for the person); 3.

Differentiation according to sharpness or dullness—the sharp-witted realize upon hearing once, while the dull-witted realize only after a second explanation (the ultimate truth); 4. Furthermore, this expresses the Buddha’s earnestness in repeating the teaching (the fifth).

Furthermore, because it is for the sake of people and for the assembly gathered before and after, there are verses. (As for the "remedial" [treatment]: because it can remove subsequent doubts, the ten meanings in the treatise now list only six;

the first five are as cited above. Sixth, causing later people to generate faith in the sutra is also for the sake of people. Seventh, easily changing the phrasing and shifting the momentum when preaching the Dharma is also remedial. Eighth, demonstrating that the meaning is inexhaustible.

Ninth, clarifying that the person of realization has boundless teachings—these two are the same as the first "ultimate meaning. Tenth is the sixth passage cited here. First, the verse summarizes the preceding question. Second, the initial inquiry into this land has six parts.
Section Two: Questions on the Six Auspicious Omens in Other Lands. This is the first.
Thereupon, Maitreya Bodhisattva, wishing to restate this meaning, asked in verse:
"O Mañjuśrī, Guide, for what reason does the great light from the white tuft between your eyebrows universally shine and rain down *māndārava* flowers?"
The fragrance of *mañjūṣaka* flowers and sandalwood wafted on the wind, gladdening the hearts of the multitude.

By these causes and conditions, the earth was everywhere adorned and purified, and as this world shook in six ways, the fourfold assembly was filled with joy; their bodies and minds were refreshed and delighted, attaining what they had never experienced before.

This long passage poses a general inquiry regarding the six auspicious omens of this land. Within the verses, there is a lengthy description of fragrant winds and the purification of the earth, yet it lacks mention of preaching the Dharma or entering meditative absorption.

Examining the text, one might argue that these elements are expanded or contracted; however, upon investigating the underlying meaning, this is not the case. Preaching the Dharma is the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*), while entering meditative absorption is the mind of the celestial realm (*deva*).

Because of the nature of wisdom and the mind of the celestial realm, one is able to emit light and cause the earth to tremble. By observing the "branch" (the external manifestations), one immediately knows the "root" (the internal reality).
Therefore, "contraction" is not merely contraction; furthermore, the two characters for "Guiding Master" (Dǎoshī) themselves constitute the inquiry.
This is because preaching the Dharma and entering meditative absorption can guide others. Since heavenly flowers are supremely wondrous, how could they have color without fragrance?

Thus, where there are flowers, there is fragrance. As the flowers gather upon the ground, the ground becomes adorned and pure, symbolizing that if one proceeds toward the cause, [the result will follow].
As for the fruits of these fruits, they are solemn and pure like the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, for the Dharma-body is adorned by the accumulation of merit and virtue;

thus, through the fragrant wind and the purity of the ground, the four flowers are manifested as full, yet not full. △ Second, the inquiry regarding the six auspicious omens in other lands, which consists of six parts:
first, the inquiry regarding sentient beings in the six realms; second, the inquiry regarding seeing those Buddhas and hearing their preaching of the Dharma; third...

The first section consists of six questions: (1) asking about the fourfold assembly in other lands; (2) asking about the four fetters, with the first three being opened and the fifth remaining; (3) asking about the practice of the bodhisattva path in other lands; (4) asking about the making of offerings to the *śarīra* relics in other lands, which is equivalent to asking about the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa. Now, the first [question]: Question: Why does the World-Honored One not manifest the appearance of the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa in this Sahā world? Furthermore, why does he not manifest the appearance of the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa in the lands of the ten directions? Answer: It is because the sentient beings here have heavy afflictions and dull faculties. Because their afflictions are heavy, they do not believe that the Tathāgata is eternal. Because their faculties are dull, even though they hear that the Tathāgata is eternal, they cannot produce faith. For this reason, the Tathāgata does not manifest the appearance of his parinirvāṇa here. In the lands of the ten directions, there are two types of sentient beings: those with heavy afflictions and dull faculties, and those with light afflictions and sharp faculties. Among them, those with heavy afflictions and dull faculties do not believe that the Tathāgata is eternal. Those with light afflictions and sharp faculties, although they hear that the Tathāgata is eternal, are unable to produce faith. Therefore, the Tathāgata does not manifest the appearance of his parinirvāṇa in those lands either. Furthermore, it is because the lifespan of the sentient beings here is short. Because their lifespan is short, they do not believe that the Tathāgata is eternal. Even if they were to hear that the Tathāgata is eternal, they would not believe it. For this reason, the Tathāgata does not manifest the appearance of his parinirvāṇa here. In the lands of the ten directions, there are two types of sentient beings: those with short lifespans and those with long lifespans. Among them, those with short lifespans do not believe that the Tathāgata is eternal. Even if they heard that the Tathāgata is eternal, they would not believe it. Those with long lifespans, although they hear that the Tathāgata is eternal, are unable to produce faith. Therefore, the Tathāgata does not manifest the appearance of his parinirvāṇa in those lands either. Furthermore, it is because the sentient beings here have little merit and virtue. Because they have little merit and virtue, they do not believe that the Tathāgata is eternal. Even if they heard that the Tathāgata is eternal, they would not believe it. For this reason, the Tathāgata does not manifest the appearance of his parinirvāṇa here. In the lands of the ten directions, there are two types of sentient beings: those with little merit and virtue, and those with great merit and virtue. Among them, those with little merit and virtue do not believe that the Tathāgata is eternal. Even if they heard that the Tathāgata is eternal, they would not believe it. Those with great merit and virtue, although they hear that the Tathāgata is eternal, are unable to produce faith. Therefore, the Tathāgata does not manifest the appearance of his parinirvāṇa in those lands either. Furthermore, it is because the sentient beings here are attached to the five desires. Because they are attached to the five desires, they do not believe that the Tathāgata is eternal. Even if they heard that the Tathāgata is eternal, they would not believe it. For this reason, the Tathāgata does not manifest the appearance of his parinirvāṇa here. In the lands of the ten directions, there are two types of sentient beings: those who are attached to the five desires, and those who are not attached to the five desires. Among them, those attached to the five desires do not believe that the Tathāgata is eternal. Even if they heard that the Tathāgata is eternal, they would not believe it. Those not attached to the five desires, although they hear that the Tathāgata is eternal, are unable to produce faith. Therefore, the Tathāgata does not manifest the appearance of his parinirvāṇa in those lands either. Furthermore, it is because the sentient beings here are attached to the three poisons. Because they are attached to the three poisons, they do not believe that the Tathāgata is eternal. Even if they heard that the Tathāgata is eternal, they would not believe it. For this reason, the Tathāgata does not manifest the appearance of his parinirvāṇa here. In the lands of the ten directions, there are two types of sentient beings: those attached to the three poisons, and those not attached to the three poisons. Among them, those attached to the three poisons do not believe that the Tathāgata is eternal. Even if they heard that the Tathāgata is eternal, they would not believe it. Those not attached to the three poisons, although they hear that the Tathāgata is eternal, are unable to produce faith. Therefore, the Tathāgata does not manifest the appearance of his parinirvāṇa in those lands either. Furthermore, it is because the sentient beings here are attached to the five aggregates. Because they are attached to the five aggregates, they do not believe that the Tathāgata is eternal. Even if they heard that the Tathāgata is eternal, they would not believe it. For this reason, the Tathāgata does not manifest the appearance of his parinirvāṇa here. In the lands of the ten directions, there are two types of sentient beings: those attached to the five aggregates, and those not attached to the five aggregates. Among them, those attached to the five aggregates do not believe that the Tathāgata is eternal. Even if they heard that the Tathāgata is eternal, they would not believe it. Those not attached to the five aggregates, although they hear that the Tathāgata is eternal, are unable to produce faith. Therefore, the Tathāgata does not manifest the appearance of his parinirvāṇa in those lands either. Furthermore, it is because the sentient beings here are attached to the twelve links of dependent origination. Because they are attached to the twelve links of dependent origination, they do not believe that the Tathāgata is eternal. Even if they heard that the Tathāgata is eternal, they would not believe it. For this reason, the Tathāgata does not manifest the appearance of his parinirvāṇa here. In the lands of the ten directions, there are two types of sentient beings: those attached to the twelve links of dependent origination, and those not attached to the twelve links of dependent origination. Among them, those attached to the twelve links of dependent origination do not believe that the Tathāgata is eternal. Even if they heard that the Tathāgata is eternal, they would not believe it. Those not attached to the twelve links of dependent origination, although they hear that the Tathāgata is eternal, are unable to produce faith. Therefore, the Tathāgata does not manifest the appearance of his parinirvāṇa in those lands either. Furthermore, it is because the sentient beings here are attached to the eighteen realms. Because they are attached to the eighteen realms, they do not believe that the Tathāgata is eternal. Even if they heard that the Tathāgata is eternal, they would not believe it. For this reason, the Tathāgata does not manifest the appearance of his parinirvāṇa here. In the lands of the ten directions, there are two types of sentient beings: those attached to the eighteen realms, and those not attached to the eighteen realms. Among them, those attached to the eighteen realms do not believe that the Tathāgata is eternal. Even if they heard that the Tathāgata is eternal, they would not believe it. Those not attached to the eighteen realms, although they hear that the Tathāgata is eternal, are unable to produce faith. Therefore, the Tathāgata does not manifest the appearance of his parinirvāṇa in those lands either. Furthermore, it is because the sentient beings here are attached to the twelve sense bases. Because they are attached to the twelve sense bases, they do not believe that the Tathāgata is eternal. Even if they heard that the Tathāgata is eternal, they would not believe it. For this reason, the Tathāgata does not manifest the appearance of his parinirvāṇa here. In the lands of the ten directions, there are
The radiance from between his eyebrows illuminated eighteen thousand lands in the eastern direction, making them all appear golden.
From the Avīci Hell up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), within all the worlds, he clearly beheld the destinies of birth and death for sentient beings of the six realms,
as well as their good and evil karmic conditions and the resulting retributions of beauty and ugliness.
The sentient beings of the six realms are the provisional designation for those who go; birth and death are the five aggregates that are gone toward;

wholesome and unwholesome karmic conditions are the causes of going; and beauty and ugliness are the fruits of going. "The Peak of Existence" (bhavāgra) refers to the summit of the three realms of existence, specifically indicating the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana). As the *Dīrgha Āgama* states, "Akaniṣṭha" refers only to the Ultimate Form Realm (akaniṣṭhabhavana).
"World-Honored One, if it is as you say— that seeing from afar by receiving light means that because the Formless Realm lacks form and color,
it cannot be seen— then since the various retributions received through the karmic conditions of birth and death are all clearly seen,
it would logically follow that [the Buddha's light] should universally illuminate the Formless Realm as well. △ Second, the question regarding seeing those Buddhas and hearing them preach the Dharma.
Furthermore, he beheld the Buddhas, the holy lords and lions, expounding the sutras that are subtle and supreme;
their voices were pure, emitting gentle sounds as they instructed countless billions of bodhisattvas with profound and wondrous Brahma-voices that all delight in hearing.
In each world, they preached the True Dharma through various causes and conditions, illuminating the Buddha-dharma with immeasurable parables.
It awakens sentient beings.
Those who dwell in the distinct stages and the perfect stage are called "Sages" (ārya); because the Buddha is further most honored, he is called the "Holy Lord.
Because he teaches the Mahāyāna Dharma with certainty and fearlessness, he is called the "Lion. Because the sudden teaching is purely great, it is termed the "First among Explanations."
Because it accords with principle, its sound is pure; because it conforms to the Dharma of the true mark (*dharmatā*), its resonance is supple;

because there is no assembly of the Two Vehicles, it is said that it "teaches all Bodhisattvas. As for the sequence of what is expounded: the three truths (*trīṇi satyāni*) are profound, while the three truths as perfectly interfused (*pariniṣpanna*) are wondrous.

Because it accords with principle and is appropriate to the capacities of the audience, it is said that it "causes people to delight in hearing it. Because it is present throughout the seven locations and nine assemblies, it is said that they are "respective[ly]."
Because there are two teachings and eight gates within the world, it is said to be "various"; because it does not involve the Three Vehicles, it is called the Buddha-dharma;
and because those who hear it immediately enter the Buddha-wisdom, it is called "opening and awakening. This is precisely the same as the *Avataṃsaka* teaching in this land.
△ Third, [the question concerning] the fourfold assembly in other lands.
If there are people who encounter suffering and weary of old age, illness, and death, he preaches for them *nirvāṇa*, the end of all suffering.

If there are people with merit who have previously made offerings to the Buddha and aspire to the supreme Dharma, he preaches for them the path of the *pratyekabuddha*. If there are sons of the Buddha who cultivate various practices in pursuit of unsurpassed wisdom, he preaches for them the pure path.

If a person encounters suffering, this refers to those who open themselves to the Śrāvaka-yāna. If, while encountering suffering, they further create evil karma, then their suffering will not come to an end;
such are the base beings. If, while encountering suffering, they create wholesome karma, loathing the lower realms and aspiring for the higher, then their suffering likewise will not come to an end;
such are those who observe the precepts and cultivate meditative concentration in order to be born among humans or devas. Encountering suffering...
Furthermore, those who seek liberation within the teachings of non-Buddhists do not exhaust their suffering;

this is because they do not know the Three Jewels, the Four Noble Truths, or the four foundations of mindfulness, and can only increase their views and prolong the accumulation of the roots of suffering.

Only when one encounters suffering and is able to develop universal revulsion for the birth, aging, sickness, and death of the triple world, as well as revulsion for the accumulation [of karma], can one move the Buddha to appear.

To say that one attains Nirvana by practicing the supramundane path from this point onward to forever exhaust the limits of suffering means that one knows suffering and thereby abandons its origin, and yearns for cessation and thereby cultivates the path.
If a person possesses merit, they are opened to the Pratyekabuddha vehicle; because Pratyekabuddhas plant the seeds of merit over a hundred kalpas, it is said that they "possess merit.
To briefly contemplate the general characteristics of the Four Noble Truths is considered inferior, as [the Pratyekabuddha path] involves twelve [aspects].

Detailed observation of the specific characteristics of causes and conditions is superior; furthermore, because the Four Noble Truths take suffering as their primary gateway, they are inferior, whereas the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination take the Truth of Origination as their primary gateway, and thus are superior.
One who attains awakening by contemplating the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination is therefore called a *Pratyekabuddha*.
If there is a "Son of the Buddha," this refers to one who opens the way for the Bodhisattva Vehicle through the practice of the six perfections. There is the Great... [text ends]

Because they possess compassion and are capable of continuing the lineage of the Buddhas, they are called "sons of the Buddha" (*buddhaputra*). Because the practices of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) are vast, they are called "various practices.

Because they aspire to attain Buddhahood, it is called "unsurpassed wisdom" (*anuttara-jñāna*). Because there are no six obscurations within the six perfections, it is called the "pure path" (*viśuddha-mārga*).
This takes the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*) as its primary gateway. It is identical in meaning to the three vehicles (*triyāna*) within the Tripiṭaka teachings of this land. △
Fourth, this concludes the preceding section and introduces the subsequent one:
"Mañjuśrī, I dwell here and have seen and heard such things as these, as well as thousands of millions of other events; though they are thus numerous, I shall now speak of them briefly."
"Seeing and hearing [the Dharma] as such" concludes what preceded; "now I shall briefly explain this" opens what follows.

△ Fifth, the inquiry regarding the cultivation of the bodhisattva path in other lands is identical in its essential meaning to that of the various Mahāyāna teachings of this land, such as the *Fangdeng* and *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras.
The text is divided into three parts: first, a general inquiry; second, sequential inquiries; and third, miscellaneous inquiries. The sequence is modeled after that of this land.
The gradual teachings and miscellaneous questions are modeled after the indeterminate teachings of this land. First:
I see bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in that land seeking the Buddha-way through various causes and conditions.
"Constant Sands" (Héngshā) is also called "Ganges Sands" (Hénghéshā) or "Gaṅgā Sands" (Jīngjiāshā). From the Silver Ox Mouth on the east of Lake Anavatapta, the Gaṅgā River flows out to the south;
from the Golden Elephant Mouth on the west, the Sindhu River flows out to the north; from the Lapis Lazuli Horse Mouth on the north, the Vakṣu River flows out to the east;
and from the Crystal Lion Mouth on the south, the Sītā River flows out to the west. The sands of the Gaṅgā are fine and...
Because many Buddhas preached the Dharma near this river, it is used as a metaphor. △ Second, there are six sequential questions:

first, the question on giving; second, the question on precepts; third, the question on patience; fourth, the question on diligence; fifth, the question on meditation; and sixth, the question on wisdom.
First: There are those who practice giving gold, silver, coral, pearls, mani-jewels, tridacna shells, agate, diamonds, and various other treasures;
they give away slaves, vehicles, precious ornaments, and palanquins with joy, dedicating their merit toward the Buddha-way and vowing to obtain this vehicle.

There are Bodhisattvas who give away precious chariots drawn by four horses, adorned with railings, flowered canopies, and elegant decorations—praised by the Buddhas as supreme within the three realms.
Furthermore, one sees Bodhisattvas giving their own flesh, hands, feet, wives, and children in pursuit of the unsurpassed path;
and one also sees Bodhisattvas joyfully giving away their heads, eyes, bodies, and limbs in pursuit of the Buddha’s wisdom.

The first four verses inquire about the relinquishing of wealth; the fifth verse inquires about the relinquishing of the body—wherein flesh, hands, and feet constitute the internal body, while wife and children constitute the external body;
the sixth verse inquires about the relinquishing of life, as the relinquishing of head and eyes is equivalent to relinquishing life.
The reason *dharma-dāna* (the gift of Dharma) is not mentioned here is to defer it to the subsequent *prajñā-pāramitā*. △ Second, the inquiry regarding precepts (*śīla*).
Mañjuśrī, I have seen various kings go to the presence of the Buddha to inquire about the unsurpassed path, whereupon they abandon their pleasant lands,
palaces, ministers, and consorts, shave off their hair and beards, and don the dharma robes.
Regarding the observance of the precepts from the perspective of renunciation, the Bodhisattva vows apply universally to all seven classes of practitioners;

however, the *bhikṣu-śīla* (the monastic code) is restricted specifically to the Great Sangha. Among all the precepts, these *bhikṣu-śīla* are the most honored and most noble, for they constitute the foremost of the seven classes.
Nevertheless, if one maintains them with a mind focused solely on one's own liberation, they then become the precepts of a Śrāvaka.
To maintain the mind that seeks the unsurpassed path constitutes the Bodhisattva’s *śīla-pāramitā*.

Furthermore, there are four distinctions regarding the attainment of the unsurpassed path, namely the four great vows (*mahāpraṇidhāna*) arising from the four kinds of Four Noble Truths: those of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*), non-arising (*anutpāda*), the immeasurable (*apramāṇa*), and the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*).
The four great vows of arising and ceasing belong to the preceding category of the mundane perfections (*laukika-pāramitā*); here, one should refer specifically to [the latter three].

Later, Hongsan-si and others also left the household life; they took the various kings as examples to show that the noble may serve as a model for the humble, and the superior may encompass the inferior.
This does not mean that the precepts and degrees of attainment are restricted solely to human kings.
It is because, for instance, when the Bhikṣu Dharmākara relinquished his royal throne to attain the Pure Land, it was called the Bodhisattva Precept Pāramitā. △ Third, the question on patience.
Alternatively, one may see a bodhisattva who has become a bhikṣu dwelling alone in a secluded and quiet place, delighting in the recitation of the sūtras.

In the remote forests and deep valleys, enduring wicked people and fierce beasts without anger, he gives rise to the patience of forbearance; by self-restraint and guarding his resolve, he practices the patience of asceticism;
and by reciting the sūtras in pursuit of Buddhahood, he practices the patience of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). These three types of patience are universally attained through the four teachings.
This is patience. △ Fourth, the inquiry regarding progress:
Furthermore, one sees Bodhisattvas who, with courageous and diligent effort, enter deep mountains to contemplate the Buddha-way.
This is like the example of the Prince’s ascetic practices in the Snowy Mountains; the Buddha-way thus contemplated also penetrates the four [noble truths].
[The section on] Teaching. △ Fifth, the inquiry regarding dhyāna:
Furthermore, one sees those who, having detached from desire, constantly dwell in seclusion and deeply cultivate meditative concentration, thereby attaining the five supernatural powers;
and one also sees Bodhisattvas, settled in dhyāna with palms joined, praising the Kings of Dharma with ten million verses.
The first verse asks about the cultivation of mundane pure dhyāna and dhyānas such as those refined through contemplation, practice, and perfuming;

the second verse asks about the cultivation of supramundane, supreme dhyāna—namely, the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, which manifests all majestic deportments without arising from or entering the meditative state of cessation.
Regarding the first [verse], "detachment from desire" means being free from the afflictions of the lower realms and attaining the fundamental [dhyāna].

The first dhyāna is shallow; progressing further to depart from the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) in order to attain the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) is what is called "deep.
This is merely the intent of the Hīnayāna (Tripitaka) teachings. It does not only involve departing from the desires of the three realms, but also from the craving for the dharma of nirvāṇa;

it does not only involve departing from the desires of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), but also from the craving for the dharma of emerging into the provisional (*upāya-niḥsaraṇa*); and it does not only involve departing from the desires of the two extremes, but also...
To be detached from the Middle Way while still possessing attachment to the Dharma that accords with the Path—this is what is called "profound" in its distinct sense.
However, if one is detached from all things and practices the complete subduing and complete cultivation, this is then called "profound" in the sense of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

The separate stages (*bie di*) obtain the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) and the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*), yet because they defer to the Buddha, they are merely termed "five. The *Śūraṅgama Samādhi* belongs precisely to the Perfect School.
One should also attain the same realization as those in other stages. △ Sixth, the inquiry concerning wisdom:
Furthermore, one sees Bodhisattvas whose wisdom is profound and whose resolve is firm; they are able to question the Buddhas and hear all that is taught, receiving and upholding it.

One also sees these sons of the Buddha, endowed with both meditative concentration and wisdom, who expound the Dharma for the sake of the multitude using immeasurable analogies, delighting in the teaching of the Dharma to transform and guide all Bodhisattvas.
Having shattered the hosts of Māra’s armies, he strikes the Dharma drum.

The first verse asks about his own practice; the following two verses ask about his transformation of others. That wisdom which exhausts the root of principles is called "profound knowledge" (*jñāna*);
that vow which is vast and firm is called "steadfast resolve" (*adhyāśaya*). This constitutes the possession of the two adornments.

"Capable of questioning and capable of upholding" refers to those who possess both concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). If one says that when they have not yet reached [the higher stages], wisdom is predominant; in the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), concentration is predominant;

and in the four *dhyānas*, both are equal. Furthermore, regarding the liberations (*vimokṣa*), wisdom is predominant; in the nine attainments (*navānupūrva-vihāra-samāpatti*), concentration is predominant; and in the ten totalities (*daśakṛtsnāyatana*), both are equal. This is the explanation by way of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).

Moreover, in the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), concentration is predominant; in Bodhisattvas, wisdom is predominant; only in the Buddha are they equal. This is the explanation according to the teachings (*yathā-śāsana*).

The commentary further explains that the *śūnyatā-vipaśyanā* (contemplation of emptiness) emphasizes *samādhi*, while the *prajñapti-vipaśyanā* (contemplation of the provisional) emphasizes *prajñā*. The *madhyama-vipaśyanā* (contemplation of the Middle) involves equalizing these mental states.
Regarding the "immeasurable metaphors," this refers to the various analogies within the various teachings used to assist in revealing the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

As for "destroying the armies of Māra," in the *Tripiṭaka* and *Pratyekabuddha* vehicles, one destroys the four māras within the realm; in the *Distinct Teaching* (*bipōjiào*), one sequentially destroys the eight māras of both the internal and external realms.

The Dharma Drum that strikes all demons—having already shattered the eight demons and all demonic forces through the Perfect Teaching’s perfect refutation—is now turned as the fourfold wheel of the Dharma across the four teachings.
Having completed the two successive inquiries [regarding the four teachings], △ third, the miscellaneous inquiries are divided into seven parts:

first, an inquiry on meditation; second, an inquiry on diligence; third, an inquiry on precepts; fourth, an inquiry on patience; fifth, a further inquiry on meditation; sixth, an inquiry on giving; and seventh...
Questioning Prajñā: First, I see that when the Bodhisattva remains in tranquil silence and is honored by devas and nāgas, he does not consider this a cause for joy;
yet I also see him dwelling in the forest, emitting light to relieve the sufferings of those in the hells and lead them into the Buddha-way.

The first verse asks about entering the dhyāna of equanimity (*upekṣā*), which refers to one's own practice; the next verse asks about entering the dhyāna of compassion (*karuṇā*), which refers to transforming others.

Regarding the dhyāna of equanimity, it is the fourth dhyāna. It may also refer to the equanimity of forgetting the mind in the Separate and Perfect [Teachings], so called because one forgets that very dhyāna.
Regarding the dhyāna of compassion, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "It is easy to cultivate compassion in the first dhyāna, but difficult in the second."
It is easy to cultivate joy through the first dhyāna, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) through the second, equanimity (*upekṣā*) through the third, and compassion (*karuṇā*) through the fourth.

Since it is stated here that the meditation on compassion involves transforming others, how could it pertain solely to the first dhyāna? In the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, there are both general and specific discussions;
how much more so in the Great Teaching (Mahāyāna)? Therefore, for each dhyāna, one should state that from loving-kindness up to joy and equanimity, light is emitted to rescue beings from suffering.
As stated in the *Suyāma-sūtra*, the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha emits light that universally illuminates incalculable lands in the ten directions;

all afflictions and all diseases encounter this light and attain peace and happiness. Furthermore, when the Buddha himself emits the lights of the six perfections, those touched by them receive benefit.
Regarding the mention of "all" afflictions and "all" diseases, these should be understood according to the four teachings (*catur-yāna*), just as in the case of the Buddha.
He told Brahmā Viśeṣacintin: "To be able to teach sentient beings the mind of omniscience is called generosity (*dāna*); not abandoning the bodhicitta is called ethical discipline (*śīla*);

not perceiving the arising and ceasing of mental characteristics is called patience (*kṣānti*); seeking the unattainable mind is called diligence (*vīrya*); eliminating the coarseness of body and mind is called meditation (*dhyāna*);
and being free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) is called wisdom (*prajñā*). Is this not the Tripiṭaka and the six [perfections]?"

Regarding the characteristics of deliverance, it is further said: "I declare that giving is called nirvāṇa, because the foolish person who possesses great wealth enters into the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena;
precept-keeping is nirvāṇa, because it is non-doing and non-arising; patience is nirvāṇa, because it perishes moment by moment;
vigor is nirvāṇa, because there is nothing to be grasped; and meditation is nirvāṇa, because there is no greedy attachment."

Wisdom is the non-apprehension of the characteristics of *nirvāṇa*. Furthermore, it is said that the equality of giving is itself *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), and so on up to wisdom (*prajñā*), which is itself *sarvajñā*.
It is also said that giving is neither giving nor stinginess, and so on up to wisdom, which is neither wisdom nor folly.
Are these not all the characteristics of the six perfections of the Shared Teaching (*p’ung-chiao*)? Moreover, it is said that one is able to penetrate the One.
The fact that all dharmas have nothing to discard is called *dāna-pāramitā*; that all dharmas have nothing to lose is called *śīla-pāramitā*;
that all dharmas have nothing to injure or damage is called *kṣānti-pāramitā*; that all dharmas are equal is called *dhyāna-pāramitā*;

and that all dharmas have no characteristic of arising is called *prajñā-pāramitā*. Are these not the characteristics of the distinct and the perfect six perfections? Furthermore, it is like the *Bhūmisaṃgraha* (Earth-Holding).

The six perfections each have nine [stages], all of which are signs of receiving benefit through the light; for the names of the Buddha-ways apply to the four teachings, and compassion and dhyāna are not restricted to the first dhyāna.

Thus, they separately pertain to the first stage (bhūmi) and the first abiding (vihāra) of the Perfect Teaching, as well as generally to the seventh stage, all of which allow entry into the four marks.
Since these marks are distinct, the five periods can be discerned. △ Second, the inquiry regarding progress.
Furthermore, one sees sons of the Buddha who never sleep, but practice walking meditation (*caṃkrama*) in the groves, diligently seeking the Buddha-way.
This is like the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi* (Banzhou) and other such Dharma-gates. "Pratyutpanna" here means "the Buddha standing.

For ninety days, they constantly walk without sitting or lying down, making the elimination of sleep their primary focus. This section belongs to the Vaipulya (fangdeng) class and also encompasses the four teachings.
Now, it is said that "diligently seeking the Buddha-way" distinguishes [the bodhisattva] from the two vehicles. △ Third, the question on precepts:
Furthermore, one sees those who possess the precepts and whose dignified demeanor (*īryāpatha*) is without deficiency, pure as a precious jewel, as they seek the Buddha-way.
Having no deficiency in dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*) is the first, the "unimpaired precept"; being pure like a precious jewel is the tenth, the "complete precept.
These ten precepts are named after the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. The first, the "unimpaired precept," means not committing grave offenses (*ānantarya*);

if one commits a grave offense, it is like a leak in a life-preserving bag (*uragaṇḍa*). The second, the "unbroken precept," means not committing intermediate offenses; if one commits an intermediate offense...
The three aspects of "unpierced" precepts refer to not committing even minor offenses; this is because if one commits a minor offense, it is like a leak in an air-filled float.
These three belong to the category of restraint (*saṃvara*). The four aspects of "unmixed" precepts refer to not giving rise to unwholesome thoughts;
for if unwholesome thoughts arise, then although body and speech may be pure, the mind is defiled by afflictions. This one aspect is [the category of non-affliction].

1. The precept concomitant with meditative concentration (*samādhi-sahagata-śīla*) consists of the five precepts that follow the Path, such as the separation of four inches from insects when tilling the soil at the stage of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*).
2. The precept of non-attachment (*anāsakta-śīla*) refers to the Arhat’s permanent freedom from craving for the six objects of the sensory realms within the three worlds;

these two are the precepts concomitant with the Path (*mārga-sahagata-śīla*) and are also the precepts of the True Truth (*satya-śīla*). 3. The precept praised by the wise (*jñāna-praśasta-śīla*) refers to being skillfully able to emerge from the conventional and engage [with the ultimate].
The eighth is the precept of mastery, which is praised by the wise for benefiting sentient beings in the mundane world;

it refers to manifesting supernatural powers through play and demonstrating both the forward and reverse orders of phenomena without violating either natural or proscribed prohibitions, thereby always remaining in this state—these two constitute the precepts of conventional truth.

The ninth is the precept of accordance with meditative concentration, which means manifesting various dignified demeanors while remaining within the meditative absorption of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. The tenth is the precept of fulfillment.

"Precepts" refers to the ultimate perfection of the precept-pāramitā, wherein there is neither dharma nor preparation; these two constitute the precepts of the Middle Way, the primary truth (paramārtha-satya).
Taking the former four precepts as the objects of contemplation and the latter six as the matters of contemplation, one contemplates the mutual identity of phenomena and principle.
While those of the Two Vehicles in the two teachings possess only the former six, bodhisattvas who have emerged from the provisional may possess seven or eight.
In the Separate Teaching (biejiao), the ten stages are cultivated sequentially; in the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao), the ten are cultivated with a single mind.
The present statement, "seeking the Buddha-way," also serves to exclude the two types of *śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*. △ Fourth: Questioning on Patience (*kṣānti*).

Furthermore, one sees sons of the Buddha abiding in the power of patience (*kṣānti-bala*), who are able to endure all insults and beatings from those of overweening pride (*adhimāna*) in their quest for the path of the Buddha.

Regarding the two types of patience—the patience regarding the arising of phenomena (*dharmasamutpāda-kṣānti*) and the patience regarding the turning of the wheel (*cakrapravartana-kṣānti*)—the four teachings differ. If one is able to endure amidst respectful offerings and veneration...

If one is unattached, one does not give rise to arrogance or negligence. If one can endure being reviled, struck, or harmed, as well as mosquitoes, gadflies, and the like, then anger and affliction do not arise;

this is called the patience toward living beings (*sattvakṣānti*). If one can endure external conditions such as cold, heat, wind, rain, hunger, thirst, old age, and illness, remaining unmoved, and if one can endure internal conditions such as greed, anger, sorrow, pride, and wrong views— [...this is called the patience toward phenomena (*dharmanidhyānakṣānti*)...]

The meaning of the Tripiṭaka is that forbearance toward the non-arising [of phenomena] constitutes *dharmakṣānti*. Combining this with the preceding two types of forbearance constitutes *sattvakṣānti*, while taking the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) as *dharmakṣānti* is the general meaning.
Furthermore, observing that both the realms of sentient beings (*sattva*) and phenomena (*dharma*) are empty constitutes the general sense of *paramārtha*;

observing these two realms through the sequence of emptiness, then the provisional (*upāya*), and finally the Middle Way constitutes the specific sense. Observing that both realms are empty is [the first].

Within the provisional [teaching], this is the perfection [of patience]. Now, by singling out harsh abuse and physical assault as the objects of endurance, the author uses what is difficult to illustrate what is easy.
△ Fifth, further inquiry regarding meditation:
Furthermore, one sees the Bodhisattva who has distanced himself from all frivolous laughter and foolish companions, and who draws near to the wise, single-mindedly eliminating distraction.
Gathering one's mindfulness in the mountain forests for hundreds of millions of years to seek the Buddha-way;

abandoning frivolous laughter to dispel the hindrance of restlessness and regret; distancing oneself from foolish associates to eliminate the hindrance of ill-will; drawing near to the wise to remove the hindrance of doubt;
maintaining single-mindedness to eliminate distraction and dispel the hindrance of sensual desire; and gathering mindfulness in the mountain forests to remove drowsiness.
The first six phrases clarify what is to be abandoned, while the final two phrases clarify the intent of abandoning them.

Since both mundane and the four teachings of the Buddha involve the cultivation of dhyāna to abandon the five hindrances (*pañcanīvaraṇa*), the present intent concerns the path of the Buddha, which differs from that of ordinary people, non-Buddhists, and those of the two vehicles.
For a detailed explanation of the five hindrances according to contemplation, one should consult the fourth fascicle of the *Mohe Zhiguan* (*Mahā-śamatha-vipaśyanā*). △ Question Six.
He practices giving.
Or he sees a bodhisattva bestowing a hundred kinds of fine foods, delicacies, and medicinal decoctions upon the Buddha and the Sangha;

or bestowing famous robes and superior garments worth ten million, or even priceless robes, upon the Buddha and the Sangha; or bestowing ten million billion kinds of sandalwood jewel mansions upon the Buddha and the Sangha.

They give various exquisite bedding to the Buddha and the Sangha; they give pure gardens and groves with flourishing flowers and fruits, flowing springs, and bathing pools to the Buddha and the Sangha.
Giving such various and subtle offerings, they rejoice without weariness, seeking the unsurpassed path.
The first four verses clarify the offering of the four requisites for sustenance; the final verse clarifies the intent behind making such offerings.
The first verse concerns the two matters of food and drink and medicine; the second verse concerns clothing; the third and fourth verses both pertain to bedding and seating.
The "Unsurpassed Way" (anuttara-mārga) further encompasses all four teachings. △ Seventh, the inquiry into wisdom.
There are some bodhisattvas who preach the Dharma of quiescence, instructing and transforming countless sentient beings through various teachings;

or one sees bodhisattvas contemplating the nature of all phenomena as being without dual characteristics, like empty space; and one also sees these sons of the Buddha whose minds are free from attachment, seeking the unsurpassed path through this wondrous wisdom.
The first verse explains the *prajñā* that is ineffable yet spoken; the next verse explains the *prajñā* that is unobservable yet observed;
and the final verse—that the path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity ceases—discusses the *prajñā* that is spoken through the ineffable and observed through the unobservable.
One should contemplate how this *prajñā* also permeates all teachings. (Fifth question from another.)
The practice of the bodhisattva path on this earth is concluded. △ Sixth, questioning the offering of relics in other lands is equivalent to questioning the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
Mañjuśrī, furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who, after the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, offer worship to his relics and also behold the sons of the Buddha.
He constructed countless *stūpas* and temples as numerous as the sands of the Ganges to adorn the realm;

these jeweled *stūpas* were five thousand *yojanas* in height and two thousand *yojanas* in both length and breadth. Each temple featured a thousand banners and pennants, with canopies of interlaced pearls and hanging curtains, while jeweled bells chimed in harmony.
Gods, dragons, spirits, humans, and non-humans constantly made offerings of incense, flowers, and music.
Mañjuśrī and the sons of the Buddhas adorned the stūpas and temples to make offerings to the śarīra;
the realms naturally became exceptionally marvelous and beautiful, like the celestial king of trees with its flowers in full bloom.
The first verse provides a general summary of the offerings to the *śarīra* after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa; the second verse clarifies the number of stūpas;
the third verse clarifies the dimensions of the stūpas; the fourth verse clarifies the adornments of the stūpas; the fifth verse clarifies the offerings;
and the sixth and seventh verses conclude by praising the magnificent decorations. The "King of Heavenly Trees" (*devatarāja*) refers to the *pārijātaka* tree. First.

The preceding verses have concluded the inquiry. △ Second, the verses on the request for an answer, in two parts: first, raising doubts to state the request; second, resolving four underlying difficulties. Now, the first part:
"The Buddha emitted a single ray of light, and I, along with the great assembly, beheld this land with its various and wondrously sublime manifestations of the supernatural powers of all Buddhas."
The wisdom [of the Buddha] is rare and marvelous; emitting a single pure light, it illuminates immeasurable lands. We have seen this and attained what we have never experienced before.
O Son of the Buddha, Mañjuśrī, we pray that you resolve the doubts of the assembly.
The first verse cites the events witnessed in this land; the white tuft of hair symbolizes the Middle Way as the foundation of all dharmas; therefore, it is mentioned first.
The first verse enumerates the various and wondrous signs, which are the six auspicious omens (*ṣaḍ-prātihārya*). The second verse enumerates the events of seeing other lands;
the six auspicious omens in those lands are all seen by means of light, and that light, in turn, arises from spiritual power (*ṛddhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).

The third verse is the formal request for an answer. To explain this: the phrase "attaining what was never before" (*abhūtapūrva*) regarding the six auspicious omens in both lands refers to the *Avataṃsaka*.
Even up to Prajñāpāramitā, all possess distinctions. △ Second, the explanation of four latent difficulties: The four assemblies look up to you with joy;
O World-Honored One, for what reason do you emit this radiance? O Son of the Buddha, answer now to resolve their doubts and bring them joy.
What benefit does this radiance provide? It is the wondrous Dharma attained by the Buddha while seated at the site of enlightenment.

Desiring to speak of this, and intending to bestow a prophecy while revealing the various Buddha-fields adorned with myriad jewels and causing one to behold the Buddhas—know, Mañjuśrī, that this is no small cause;
the fourfold assembly, along with the nāgas and spirits, gaze upon you, venerable sir, wondering what you will proclaim."
The first four verses correctly explain the underlying difficulties (*vighna*), while the final verse concludes with a request.

Regarding "underlying difficulties," Mañjuśrī internally formulated objections and was unwilling to answer immediately; his intention had three aspects: first, these auspicious signs were rare and marvelous, and thus could not be lightly judged in haste;
second, he humbled himself before this ocean-like assembly of the wise; third, he was hesitant and reluctant to respond.
Because the assembly yearns with thirst, they suppress their objections and remain hidden to resist [the teaching]. Maitreya’s explicit explanation of these objections also has three intentions:
first, because the auspicious signs are great, the doubt is great; if he does not explain them, anxiety will linger in the hearts of the assembly, hindering their hearing of the true teaching.

Second, although the ocean-like assembly is vast, the capacity for understanding lies with the Benevolent One (Maitreya). Third, the entire assembly gazes upon the Benevolent One; therefore, it is known that they focus their sincere devotion upon him.
The term "reverent" (*yīnzhòng*) serves to clarify the request for the resolution of difficulties, entitling one to an immediate response.

First, regarding the anticipation of an objection: this arises from the formal request. The request states: "O Son of the Buddha, Mañjuśrī, may you resolve the doubts of the assembly. From this point, Mañjuśrī first anticipates an objection:
"You say there are 'doubts of the assembly,' yet the assembly has never doubted. If they were in doubt, they should have asked; since the assembly does not doubt, why do I [ask]?"
Maitreya, having resolved this, then explained it with the first verse: "The fourfold assembly looks up to you with joy; I too look upon you.
They wish for me to ask you, and they desire that you provide the answer. Because of this, Mañjuśrī raised a second preliminary objection:
"The assembly shares this same doubt; it would not be easy to answer. Once the Buddha has emerged from his meditative absorption, he will naturally resolve the doubts."

Maitreya then explained with the second verse, saying: "If there is doubt lingering in one's breast, one is distressed and uneasy, not knowing when the Tathāgata will arise from his meditative absorption;
therefore, he must answer at the proper time to bring joy. The phrase "answering at the proper time" means urging him to answer immediately.
Based on this, Mañjuśrī raised a third preliminary objection: "I and you, O Virtuous One, are alike..."
Dwelling on the stage of learning, we wish to fathom the Buddha’s intention; may we together deliberate upon this rather than leaving me alone to answer, for that would be contrary to reason.
Maitreya then explained with the third verse: "I too hesitate and reflect:
is it the wondrous Dharma attained at the site of enlightenment that he speaks of, or is it the bestowal of a prophecy? Thereupon, Mañjuśrī raised the fourth preliminary objection: "If..."
What you have said already resolves the doubt; why trouble me to decide it? Maitreya then explains with the fourth verse, saying: "This is no small matter;
how can one judge such a great affair with a mind of hesitation? Mañjuśrī, having reached this point, has exhausted his objections;
his humble brilliance has also ceased. Therefore, the final verse concludes the request for an answer. (4)
The introduction concerning the posing of the questions is concluded. △ Fifth, the section on answering the questions has two parts: first, the long prose; second, the verse summary.

Within the first part, there are four sections: first, answering by means of reflection; second, answering by briefly citing what was previously seen; third, answering by extensively citing what was previously seen;
fourth, answering with a clear and definitive judgment. Now, the first section.
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya and the other great beings, sons of good family, saying: "As I contemplate it, the Buddha, the World-Honored One,
now intends to proclaim the Great Dharma, to rain down the rain of the Great Dharma,
to blow the conch shell of the Great Dharma, to beat the drum of the Great Dharma, and to expound the meaning of the Great Dharma."

The "good man" (kulaputra) opens the seven stages of expedient means; he is fit to hear the uniquely wondrous [Dharma] and is thus called a "man" (*puruṣa*), which may also be translated as a "virtuous person.
The designation "person" (*puruṣa*) applies across all four teachings, but here it must refer specifically to the Perfect Teaching. As for "contemplation" (*cintā*) and "reflection" (*manasikāra*):

"contemplation" means to contemplate the present as being like the past, and to reflect on the past as being like the present. Yet, how could Mañjuśrī—who is an ancient Buddha—be anything other than such?
Not knowing that this was merely a trace left to prompt reflection, those who wished to hear the Great Dharma answered by citing the auspicious sign of preaching the Dharma:
"In the past, after all Buddhas had preached the *Ananta-artha* (Infinite Meanings), they revealed the provisional to manifest the real, gathering the infinite back into the one.
Considering this, since the present Buddha has already preached the *Ananta-artha*, he too should now reveal and manifest it, bringing the infinite back into the one. "The one" refers to—
This is the Great Dharma itself. "Raining down the rain of the Great Dharma" answers the omen of the raining of flowers.

Consider that in the past, after the various Buddhas rained the four kinds of flowers from heaven, [beings] universally entered the perfect cause, proceeding through the stages of abiding, practice, and direction (*caryā-bhūmi*).

By inference, after the present Buddha has rained the flowers, they must likewise all become Buddhas by passing through the stages of abiding, practice, and direction. "Blowing the great Dharma conch" means blowing the conch to transform [sentient beings].
The title "Answering the Great Assembly: A Portent of Joyful Mind" means that in the past, when the fourfold assembly saw this portent, they were filled with unprecedented joy;
their obstructions were removed and their spiritual capacities were stirred, whereby human teachings, practices, and principles were all transformed into a single reality.

Considering that the present assembly’s joy likewise signifies the removal of obstructions and the stirring of their capacities, the transformation of human teachings, practices, and principles from the former state must be even more profound. This is the striking of the great Dharma drum.
Regarding the auspicious sign of the earthquake: In the past, following an earthquake, there were six successive occasions on which the thieves of ignorance were destroyed;
I surmise that following this present earthquake of the Buddha’s ground, there shall likewise be six successive occasions on which the delusions of ignorance are destroyed.

This oral teaching is most sublime. [The Buddha] expounded the great Dharma principles. Regarding the auspicious sign of emitting light: In the past, after all Buddhas emitted light from the white tuft between their brows, they preached the Dharma.

The Lotus Sūtra states that the paths of these Buddhas are identical; by inferring from this, one should understand that after the Buddha emitted light, he likewise preached the Lotus Sūtra to extensively clarify that the paths of the five Buddhas are the same.
Thus, these five phrases all consist of using the past to judge the present and using the present to infer the past, attaching the meaning to the text.
There is only a slight omission regarding the single auspicious sign of entering samādhi—namely, the raining of flowers, the shaking of the earth, and the emission of light.
All such [phenomena] arise from entering meditative concentration; thus, the intention is to encompass both [aspects], so there is no need for laborious doubt.

Because this one item was omitted, it is called a "brief answer. This is merely a response based on inference, answering the six auspicious omens of this land. △ Second, briefly citing what has been seen to provide the answer.
"O sons of good family, in the past, when I saw this auspicious sign from the Buddhas of former times—after they had emitted such light—they immediately preached the Great Dharma.
Therefore, you should know that the present Buddha’s manifestation of light is likewise so;
he manifests this auspicious sign because he desires to cause all sentient beings to hear and know the Dharma that is difficult for all the world to believe."

This is a brief citation of what was previously seen; it clarifies only the single matter of emitting light, which serves as the answer regarding the six auspicious omens in other lands, because all six omens in those lands are illuminated by this emission of light.
"Hearing" refers to faith and understanding, while "knowing" refers to practice according to the Dharma.
That which is called "the Dharma difficult to believe in throughout all worlds" means gathering the immeasurable into the one and causing it to unfold.
The sixfold demonstration, awakening, entry, transformation of persons, teaching, practice, and principle refute the lack of clarity;
it is evident that the equality of the Buddhas' Way is not something that can be believed by those with the capacities of the nine dharma-realms.

△ Third, the extensive citation of what was previously seen serves as a dual response to the questions regarding this land and other lands. Maitreya, due to the light, perceived horizontally toward the east and took this as the basis for his inquiry.
This specifically cites the past story of the boy who saw many Buddhas as a response, correctly revealing that the Way of all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time is identical.
The text is divided into three parts: first, citing the identity with one Buddha; second, citing the identity with twenty thousand Buddhas;

and third, citing the identity with the final Buddha. Within the first part, there are three sections: first, the time period; second, the designation of names; and third, the preaching of the Dharma. Now, the first section.
Good sons, in the past, immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago.
△ Second, the designation of the name:
At that time, there was a Buddha named Candrasūryapradīpa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata...
The World-Knower, the Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
"At that time" refers to a period prior to inconceivable eons in the past. Now, time possesses no substantial dharma;

it is a provisional designation established based on the states of form and mind, following worldly convention and not destroying conventional names—this is the perspective of the world (*loka-samvṛti*).

Hearing that there are immeasurable kalpas, one knows that the affairs of birth and death are long-lasting, thereby giving rise to a mind of weary detachment; this is the *sarvajñatā* (knowledge for the sake of others).

Furthermore, knowing that before a kalpa there was no kalpa, one does not give rise to the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*); and knowing that after a kalpa there is again a kalpa, one does not give rise to the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*);

this is the *pratipakṣa-sarvajñatā* (knowledge as an antidote). To contemplate that which is distant as if it were today—such that ten ages of past and present do not depart from the present moment—is the *paramārtha* (ultimate truth).
When that Buddha appeared in the world, he also taught the Three Vehicles; this is the same as the present Buddha appearing in the five turbidities.
If one says that Buddhahood is achieved by accumulating practice over three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, this is the characteristic of the Tripiṭaka [Hīnayāna] approach.

"Buddha" is translated here as "the Knower" or "the Awakened One.
