To explain these ten titles, one must rely upon the four teachings and the revelation [of the ultimate truth];
this will not be described in detail here. The same applies to the examples of the fundamental and manifested traces (*honjaku*) and the contemplation of the mind (*kanjin*).
This can be understood. △ Third, the preaching of the Dharma:
He expounds the True Dharma, which is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end;

its meaning is profound and far-reaching, its phrasing is skillful and subtle, it is pure and unadulterated, and it possesses the characteristics of the complete, stainless Brahma-conduct. For those seeking the state of a Śrāvaka, he preaches the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths.

To deliver beings from birth, old age, sickness, and death and lead them to ultimate nirvana, he teaches the Dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination for those seeking the state of a Pratyekabuddha;
and for all Bodhisattvas, he teaches the six pāramitās so that they may attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and achieve the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).

This clarifies that the past Buddhas, for the sake of bestowing the ultimate truth, employed provisional means by teaching both the sudden and the gradual, revealing the provisional to manifest the ultimate;

thus, they all converge in that which is neither sudden nor gradual. This is identical to what is seen within the light [of the present Buddha], and it is also the same as the Dharma taught by Śākyamuni Buddha.
The initial statement, "expounding the True Dharma," refers to the Sudden Teaching. The three excellences of beginning, middle, and end pertain to the sequence of the Sudden Teaching.

The three sections of the True Propagation (Zhengliutong) possess a profound and far-reaching meaning; that is, as the definitive teaching of the Sudden Vehicle (Dun jiao), its depths cannot be fathomed by those of the Two Vehicles (Er sheng).
Its phrasing is skillful and subtle; that is, the texts of the Sudden Vehicle accord with principle through direct exposition, delighting the minds of Bodhisattvas.
It is "pure and without admixture," meaning that the Sudden Vehicle is not shared with the Two Vehicles. As for "complete" (ju zu):
The Sudden Teaching clarifies the Dharma-gate of the full letters; its purity refers to the Sudden Teaching being free from the defilements of the two extremes;

its pure conduct refers to the Sudden Teaching’s unconditioned compassion. The above clarifies that the Sudden Teaching taught by the Buddhas of the past and the *Avataṃsaka* taught by the Buddha of the present are identical in responding to the question of the Supreme Holy Lord, the Lion, regarding the subtle and supreme nature of the preaching of the Dharma.

Next, the phrase "for the sake of those seeking śrāvakas and so forth" clarifies that the intent of the former Buddhas bestowing the three [vehicles] and the present Buddha’s teaching of the Tripitaka, as well as the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā sūtras, is identical;

this answers the question posed above regarding how people encounter suffering and how the sons of the Buddha cultivate various practices. The fourfold nature of the Four Truths is fully explained as set forth in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning).

Now, for the sake of the śrāvakas, I shall briefly explain the dharmas associated with arising and ceasing: the retributive fruits of the three realms are truly suffering and cannot be made into happiness;
afflictions (*kleśa*) and karma are truly the causes of suffering, and there is no other cause. When the cause ceases, the fruit ceases;
this is the path to the ultimate peace and happiness that extinguishes suffering. It consists solely of morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*), and nothing else.

The other paths also have four types of dependent origination, as explained in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning). Here, for the sake of the pratyekabuddha, we shall briefly explain the characteristics of the conceivable arising and ceasing that correspond [to this process].

Namely, ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*) are the "projecting factors" (*ākṣepaka-aṅga*); consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and feeling (*vedanā*) are the "projected factors" (*ākṣipta-aṅga*);
craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*) are the "generating factors" (*janaka-aṅga*); and birth (*jāti*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) are... [the generated factors].
That which is produced by the factors of arising is itself the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*); that which draws forth and produces it is the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*).

The cessation of ignorance up to the cessation of old age and death is the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*); the wisdom that contemplates dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).

Because the faculties of the śrāvakas are dull, the Dharma of the Four Truths is taught to them in terms of general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*); because pratyekabuddhas are somewhat sharper, the causes are taught to them in terms of specific characteristics (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*).
Regarding the Dharma of conditions, the characteristics of the Six Pāramitās and the Four Teachings have been briefly explained as before.

If one explains the Three Piṭakas and the Six Pāramitās directly, they belong to the Āgama. If one discusses phenomena and principle in contrast, and frequently subordinates phenomena to principle, it belongs to the Vaipulya.
If one speaks of principle while retaining phenomena, and frequently integrates phenomena with principle through that principle, it belongs to the Prajñāpāramitā. Hereafter...

The phrase "causing them to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi," and so forth, clarifies that the ancient Buddhas' opening of provisional means (*upāya*) and manifestation of the ultimate reality (*bhūtārtha*) is identical in intent to the present *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* Dharma.
If one observes the textual flow superficially, it appears as though "causing them to attain" and so forth refers solely to the preceding section concerning the bodhisattvas;
however, if one carefully examines the underlying logic of the discourse, these phrases serve as a comprehensive conclusion for the entire exposition of the True Dharma (*saddharma*).
The underlying intent here is that, from the very beginning, the teaching of the Sudden [Vehicle] was intended to enable sentient beings to attain all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*).

For those who have not yet attained it, one gradually and skillfully guides them through various expedient means—such as the Three Baskets (*tripiṭaka*), the Shared, Distinctive, and Perfect [Teachings], and the combined or alternating methods—whether they be fixed or unfixed, manifest or esoteric; for these matters are not uniform.

In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, whether they be śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, those who practice through ritual acts, or even those mentioned incidentally in the *Avataṃsaka*, there are none who are not led to attain unexcelled bodhi and achieve all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*).
This is the response to the previous question regarding seeing the Buddhas of other lands entering nirvana and having stupas erected for them within the light. Regarding that light:

Among the Buddhas of the past and the Buddhas of the future, there are none who do not bestow both the sudden and the gradual teachings, converging upon that which is neither sudden nor gradual;

yet Mañjuśrī skillfully expounds it without resorting to elaborate rhetoric. Therefore, although the previous Buddha explained the sudden and the gradual in detail, they are essentially no different from what is here presented, which is merely concise.

Opening [the text] now reveals that among the twenty thousand Buddhas, it is clarified that their names are identical, their surnames are identical, and their ten titles are identical, as well as the identity of their skillful teaching of the Dharma;

Before that final Buddha went forth from home, there were eight princes: the first was named Meaningful, the second Good Meaning, the third Immeasurable Meaning, the fourth Jewel Meaning, the fifth Increasing Meaning, the sixth Doubt-Dispelling Meaning, the seventh Resonance Meaning, and the eighth Dharma Meaning.
These eight princes possessed majestic power and sovereignty, each ruling over four continents.
When the princes heard that their father had left the household life and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
they all renounced their royal positions and followed him into the homeless life. They resolved upon the Mahāyāna, constantly cultivated pure conduct (*brahmacarya*),
and all became Dharma-preachers who had already planted roots of goodness under tens of millions of Buddhas.
In the past, the Buddha had eight sons; now, the Buddha has one son. Although their numbers are unequal, they both emerge from and dwell within the same land.

This land contains both *darśana-heya* (afflictions to be abandoned by insight) and *bhāvanā-heya* (afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation), and thus manifests both having sons and the reality of having sons. These matters are identical:

the eight sons each respond to conditions to manifest what they represent, while the one son represents the single path of purity. Furthermore, the eight sons represent the Eightfold Noble Path. Moreover, the sons of the former Buddha... [have] set forth.
Regarding the intention of the Mahāyāna: if the present Buddha’s disciples now abide in the fruits of the Hīnayāna, how can they be the same as those of former times?

Since the path of transformation has already been completed, this reveals their original state; thus it is said that they have "aroused the intention for the Mahāyāna. Although their true identity has not yet been revealed, they are still called Arhats.
When the text below reveals their origin, they are seen to be Bodhisattvas; in this sense, their intention is the same. Each presides over a four-continent world-system; this is the golden [nature].

At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Wonderful Light who had eight hundred disciples. Then, the Buddha Sun Moon Lamp Brightness arose from samādhi and,
for the sake of the bodhisattva Wonderful Light, preached a Mahāyāna sūtra titled *The Lotus of the Wonderful Dharma*,
which teaches the Dharma for bodhisattvas and is protected by the Buddhas.

In the past, the Buddha arose from meditative absorption because of the Bodhisattva Wonderful Light’s exposition of the sutra; now, the Buddha arises from meditative absorption because of Śāriputra’s exposition of the sutra.
Śāriputra was the teacher of Rāhula, just as in the past Wonderful Light was the teacher of the eight princes; therefore, it is said that they are the same.
Furthermore, since Śāriputra has already received his prediction of enlightenment, he is truly a bodhisattva; in the past, Wonderful Light heard the Dharma [from him].
When he manifested as a flower, why must he not also manifest as a śrāvaka? △ Second, the identity of time:

for sixty minor kalpas he did not rise from his seat, and those in the assembly who were listening likewise sat in one place for sixty minor kalpas with body and mind unmoving, listening to what the Buddha taught as if it were the duration of a meal; at that time, there was not a single person among the multitude [who perceived the passage of time].
Whether in body or mind, weariness arises;
this is the same as the passage below which states that fifty intermediate kalpas are perceived as being like half a day.

It is due to the empowerment of the Buddha’s power that one forgets the length [of time] and perceives it as short; this shall be explained in detail below. △ Third, the similarity in proclaiming extinction.
After the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa had preached this sutra for sixty intermediate kalpas,
he spoke these words amidst the assembly of Brahmās, Māras, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, devas, humans, and asuras: "Today, at midnight,
the Tathāgata shall enter parinirvāṇa without remainder."

In the past, when preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, he immediately proclaimed his entry into extinction; now, in the "Jeweled Stūpa" chapter, the Buddha likewise says that the Tathāgata shall soon enter *nirvāṇa*.
His work of transformation and guidance is complete, and the matter of proclaiming extinction is identical. Brahmā is the lord of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*);

Māra is the lord of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). "Śramaṇa" is translated here as "diligent rest"; it is the general name for those who have left the household life. "Brāhmaṇa" [is the term for those of the priestly caste].
The term *muni* is here translated as "Pure Lineage" (*jingyi*) and also as "Brahmin" (*fanzhi*). These are the noble clans among householders;

the gods, humans, and asuras are briefly cited as three types of those in the wholesome paths, all of whom are selected for their excellence because they are easily able to enter the Buddha-dharma. △ Fourth, the bestowal of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) is the same.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Guṇakośa. The Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa immediately bestowed upon him a prophecy, addressing the bhikṣus:
"This bodhisattva Guṇakośa shall next become a buddha, named Viśuddhakāya Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."
The bestowal of the prediction for the śrāvakas constitutes the main body of this sutra and should not have been disclosed prematurely;

however, the statement that the prediction for the "Successor" (Bodhisattva) is now bestowed is identical to Śākyamuni’s bestowal of the prediction upon Maitreya. Question: In the *Lotus Sūtra*, no prediction was ever bestowed upon Maitreya;
how can you cite them as being the same? Answer: It is sufficient for the purpose of the meaning that the overall scope of their respective single-era teachings be equal; what further need is there?

One must certainly be cautious regarding these minute details and not force an analogy. Since the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* in its Sanskrit original extends to eight *li*, those who have arrived here are few indeed.

How can one know that the Sanskrit manuscript lacks the passage concerning the entrustment to the Future Buddha (Maitreya)? Within the section on the predictions (*vyākaraṇa*), three titles are briefly cited;
whether three or ten, they are all equally equal. △ Fifth: After the Extinction, the Propagation of the Sutra is Identical to the Three [Periods]. First, the explicit explanation.
First, the entry into parinirvāṇa; second, the benefits of the universal teaching of the sutras after his passing; third, the reconciliation of ancient and modern accounts. Regarding the first:
After the Buddha had bestowed his prophecy, he entered the nirvana without remainder during the middle watch of the night.

Regarding those who receive a prediction of enlightenment and immediately enter *nirvāṇa*: although they may appear in a shared realm (*sahā-loka-dhātu*), because the five corruptions (*pañca-kaṣāya*) there are not yet severe, it is not necessary for them to further preach the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.
This is similar to how in this land, Kāśyapa Buddha also entered *nirvāṇa* immediately after finishing his preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
However, the meaning of *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa without remainder) applies to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna; this point must briefly be clarified, as some people hold differing views.

It is said that in the Hīnayāna, because the fetters of the fruit still remain, it is called "with remainder" (*sopadhiśeṣa*); when both body and wisdom are reduced to ashes, it is called "without remainder" (*nirupadhiśeṣa*).
In the Mahāyāna, only when the five stages (*pañcavihāra*) are fully exhausted is it called "without remainder. This is merely an explanation from one perspective;

if we discuss *nirvāṇa* comprehensively, there are three kinds: first, *prakṛti-viśuddha-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa of intrinsic purity), which is equal for both ordinary beings and sages, and is the *dharmakāya*.
The second is the perfection of merit: Nirvana as the manifestation of clarity beyond obstructions, which is the virtue of *prajñā*. The third is the perfection of skillful means:
Nirvana for the sake of sentient beings, wherein non-arising is manifested as arising and non-extinction is manifested as extinction;

this is the virtue of *vimukti*. Furthermore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* clarifies that there are four types of nirvana: first, the nirvana of intrinsic purity, which is equal for both Buddhas and sentient beings.

There are two types of *nirvāṇa with remainder* (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*) that are not attained through cultivation: first, the *tathatā* (suchness) which has emerged from the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) while the remaining basis (*upadhi*) has not yet been extinguished;
this is what is attained when those of the three vehicles first realize the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*).

Second, *nirvāṇa without remainder* (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*), which occurs when the afflictions have been exhausted and the basis of suffering has also been extinguished; this is when the body and wisdom of those of the three vehicles in the state of no-more-learning are fully spent.

That which is realized is the nirvana of non-abiding (apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa). This refers to True Suchness (tathatā) accompanied by the transcendence of the cognitive obstructions (jñeyāvaraṇa), and constantly assisted by great compassion (mahākaruṇā) and prajñā;

it neither abides in saṃsāra nor abides in nirvāṇa, extending to the end of the future, being quiescent yet ever-illuminating as it benefits sentient beings. Now, by correlating these four with the three [bodies], the meaning may be understood.
The purity of nature (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*) is precisely the purity of nature with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa*) and without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa*);

emerging from the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and non-abiding, it emerges from the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), which is the perfection of purity (*pariśuddhi*). From its essence, it gives rise to its function;

though it repeatedly proclaims arising and ceasing, in reality it neither arises nor ceases—this is the purity of skillful means (*upāya-viśuddhi*). Furthermore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states that all sentient beings possess only the first [of these purities].
The two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) who have attained the stage of no-more-learning may possess the first three [qualities], but only our World-Honored One can be said to possess all four.
This is because the nature-pure dharma-body is shared by all living beings; thus, all possess the first.

When those of the two vehicles realize the state of no-more-learning, they are said to have a "remainder" (sopadhiśeṣa) and are not called "without remainder" (nirupadhiśeṣa). However, when they enter parinirvāṇa, they are called "without remainder" and are not called "with remainder. This is because...
Since the preceding and succeeding states do not coexist, it is said that there may be the former three [nirvāṇas].

When a Tathāgata sits at the Bodhi tree and attains equal and perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), his body and mind are no longer subject to outflows (*āsrava*); because all suffering-conditions are eternally exhausted, it is called "nirvāṇa without remainder" (*anupadhiśeṣa*).

Because the basis of suffering no longer exists, yet the true and eternal five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) remain, it is called "nirvāṇa with remainder" (*sopadhiśeṣa*). Not abiding in either extreme is called "non-abiding" (*apratiṣṭhita*).
Abiding herein, the four meanings of *nirvāṇa* are simultaneously and fully present; thus it is said that one may be said to possess all four.
By this it is understood that from the very moment he first attained perfect enlightenment, he had already fully entered the four kinds of *nirvāṇa*.

His current entry into quiescence at midnight is merely a manifestation for those of dull faculties in the *sahā* world, appearing to share the extinction (*parinirvāṇa*) of the two vehicles; it is, in fact, the *upāya-śuddha* (Pure Land of Expedient Means).

The wondrous function is not extinction; how could that which proclaims extinction ever truly be extinguished? △ Second, clarifying the benefits of the scripture’s transmission after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa:
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Bodhisattva Wonderful Light upheld the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for a full eighty minor kalpas.
The person preached that the eight sons of the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa were all disciples of Prabhāsa;
Prabhāsa taught and transformed them, causing them to become firm in their resolve for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

After these princes had made offerings to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas, they all attained the Way of the Buddha. The last among them to attain Buddhahood was named Dīpaṃkara. Eighth.
Among his hundred disciples, there was one named Seeking Fame (Yaśaskāma), who was greedily attached to gain and offerings.
Although he recited many sutras, he did not penetrate their meaning and forgot much of what he had learned; for this reason, he was called Seeking Fame.

Nevertheless, because of the causes and conditions of having planted various roots of goodness, he encountered immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas, whom he served, honored, revered, and respected.

Praise. Regarding the period after [the Buddha’s] parinirvāṇa when the profound sutras were elucidated, the person who elucidated these profound sutras was endowed with wondrous radiance. For eighty intermediate kalpas, the elucidation of the profound sutras continued for a long duration.
As for the eight sons, including those seeking fame and others, those who firmly established the benefits of elucidating the profound sutras endured for a long time.

Having already established that those who seek fame are next to fill the place of a Buddha, this dual manifestation of the causes and conditions for the Buddha-way shows that it relies entirely upon teachers and friends, and is likewise entirely dependent upon cultivation and realization;
thus, both points are beyond dispute. △ Third, the conclusion correlating the ancient and the modern.
Maitreya, you should know that the Bodhisattva Wonderful Light of that time was none other than my own self; the Bodhisattva Seeking Fame was none other than you.
As for the one who clearly mastered the sutras, benefited others, led the eight sons and eight hundred disciples, and finally brought together the ancient and the modern—this was, in fact, myself.

This clarifies the secret opening of the *āyus-pramāṇa* (lifespan). Some may doubt that Maitreya, being a *kṣetrapratyaya* (one destined for succession), should not ask [questions], and that Mañjuśrī, not being a *kṣetrapratyaya*, should not answer.
Here it is clarified that Maitreya is included among the eight hundred [bodhisattvas] and thus ought to have asked;

furthermore, Mañjuśrī was previously his teacher who propagated and disseminated the wondrous Dharma. Thus, the resolution of these doubts is not erroneous. Furthermore, the youngest of the eight sons attained [realization].
Dīpaṃkara Buddha lit the lamp and bestowed the prediction upon Śākyamuni Buddha; yet now Mañjuśrī, who was originally his teacher and patriarch, has become a disciple of Śākyamuni.
This shows that the relationship between teacher and disciple is not fixed, revealing through mystery that birth is not truly born and extinction is not truly extinguished.

Question: Maitreya has previously seen various Buddhas and heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*; why does he pose these questions? Answer: It is because of the spiritual capacities of the assembly at that time.

"It is fitting that one should strike and awaken the ear. Having thus extensively cited what he had previously seen to provide his answer, [the section] concludes. △ Fourth, the clear and definitive response:
"Now, seeing this auspicious omen, which is no different from before, I therefore reflect that today the Tathāgata shall preach the Mahāyāna."
The title of this sutra is *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, which teaches the Dharma for bodhisattvas and is protected by the Buddhas.
Since the six auspicious omens of both the past and the present are identical, I reflect that they are certainly not in error; they must signify that the Mahāyāna will surely be expounded.

These are the auspicious signs preceding the preaching of the Dharma; they are called the "Auspicious Signs of the Rain of Flowers" preceding the preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. They teach the bodhisattvas.
The "Dharma-determination" (*dharmavyākaraṇa*) was a portent of joy for the assembly; the "earth-trembling" was a portent of the Buddha’s protective mindfulness. Regarding the method of answering:
because it begins subtly and later becomes manifest, this present clear judgment reveals that what preceded was not a matter of doubt.
How could the great sage Mañjuśrī have first deliberated and only then responded? This concludes the initial long prose section of the "Introduction to Questions and Answers. II. Verse Recitation.
Regarding the two parts: first, the two verses that extensively cite what was previously seen to provide the answer; second, the two verses that clearly judge and provide the answer.

Within the first part, there are two sections: first, one verse on the similarity to a single Buddha; second, two verses on the similarity to the final Buddha. The [verses] do not include the section on "contemplation" (*vitarka*) or the brief citation; they only include the extensive citation.
Within the extensive citation, only the beginning and the end are cited while the middle is omitted, yet this is sufficient to clarify the meaning.
This serves to avoid excessive prolixity. Now begins the first [chapter].
At that time, Mañjuśrī, wishing to reiterate this meaning within the great assembly, spoke these verses:
"I recall that in the past, through immeasurable and incalculable kalpas, there was a Buddha, a Honored One among men, named Candrasūryapradīpa."
The World-Honored One expounds the Dharma, delivering immeasurable sentient beings and countless billions of bodhisattvas, causing them to enter the Buddha’s wisdom.

This verse summarizes the aforementioned time period, names, and the preaching of the Dharma. △ Second, the verses on the final Buddhas being identical [to the present one] are divided into three parts:
first, a verse on how past events are already the same as the present; second, a verse on how past events are currently the same as the present.
The three verses concern events seen in the past that are identical to those of the present. First:
When the Buddha had not yet left the household life, his eight princes, seeing the Great Sage renounce the world, also followed him in practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
△ Second, the verses on how past events are identical to the present; this also has two parts. First, the verse on the identity of the manifested omens;

second, the verse on the identity of the doubts and reflections. The first part also has two sections: first, the verse on the identity of the six omens in this land; second, the verse on the identity of the six omens in other lands. Now, the first section.
At that time, the Buddha preached a Mahāyāna sūtra titled *The Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings*. Within the great assembly, he extensively analyzed and expounded it.
Having finished preaching this sūtra, the Buddha sat cross-legged upon the Dharma-seat in a samādhi called "The Abode of Immeasurable Meanings.
Heavenly *māndārava* flowers rained down, and celestial drums resounded spontaneously. Gods, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits made offerings to the Honored One among Men.
All Buddha-lands immediately shook with a great trembling, and the Buddha emitted light from between his eyebrows, manifesting various rare and wondrous events.
In the verse, the addition of "the celestial drum sounds of its own accord" represents the fact that at the beginning of the *Upāya-paryāya*, the Buddha spoke spontaneously without being asked.
The phrase "manifesting various rare and wondrous events" is a general summary of all the auspicious omens. △ Second, the verses on the six auspicious omens in other lands, likewise expanded.
The prose merely states briefly that "what is seen here and now is the land of all Buddhas," whereas the verse expands upon this;
yet although the prose and verse differ in their arrangement and transformations, they do not go beyond the meaning of the six auspicious omens.

This light shines upon eighteen thousand Buddha-lands in the eastern direction, revealing to all sentient beings the places where they undergo the retribution of birth and death according to their karma;
there they see those Buddha-lands adorned with various jewels, possessing the colors of lapis lazuli and crystal—all of which arises from the illumination of the Buddha’s light.
This verse observes the auspicious omens of the six realms of existence in that land while simultaneously revealing the differences between the purity and defilement of various lands;
it further observes the various devas, humans, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and kiṃnaras, each making offerings to their respective Buddhas.
The meaning of this verse reveals that within the six realms of existence there exists the capacity for Buddhahood.

Furthermore, one sees the Tathāgatas spontaneously attaining the path of Buddhahood, their physical bodies as golden mountains, majestic and exceedingly subtle, like a statue of pure gold appearing within clear lapis lazuli;
the World-Honored Ones, amidst the great assembly, expound the profound meanings of the Dharma.
This verse describes the auspicious signs of seeing that Buddha and hearing him preach the Dharma. Regarding those who naturally attain the Way of the Buddha:
the path of skillful means involves applying the mind through cultivation; the arising of the true path, however, occurs spontaneously and naturally, in accord with principle.

A Tathāgata of the *garbha* (womb-treasury) attains it spontaneously in a single sitting through thirty-four moments of mind; a *sambhogakāya* Buddha corresponds to it in a single thought-moment without the addition of effort.
The separate, perfect, and wondrous enlightenment is fundamentally attained through spontaneity; thus, attaining the Buddha-way spontaneously is the *sambhogakāya*.

The lapis lazuli is the *dharmakāya*, and the originally pure golden image is the manifestation of form in accordance with conditions. This profound meaning of the Dharma is precisely the sudden teaching of the Mahāyāna.
In each and every Buddha-field, the assemblies of śrāvakas were incalculable; through the illumination of the Buddha’s light, all those great congregations were seen.
Among them were bhikṣus dwelling in mountain forests who diligently maintained the pure precepts as if guarding a bright mani-jewel.
This verse shows the auspicious signs of the fourfold assembly in that land attaining the Way. By mentioning the śrāvakas, the three vehicles of the Tripitaka are encompassed;
by mentioning the bhikṣus, the fourfold assembly is encompassed. Alternatively, the second verse may also be attributed to the six perfections that follow.
Furthermore, I see various bodhisattvas practicing giving, patience, and so forth, their number as vast as the sands of the Ganges; this is due to the illumination of the Buddha’s light.
I also see various bodhisattvas deeply entering various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), their bodies and minds tranquil and unmoving, seeking the unsurpassed path.
I also see various bodhisattvas who, knowing the mark of the cessation of all phenomena (*dharmas*), each preach the Dharma within their own lands, seeking the path to Buddhahood.

This verse reveals the auspicious signs of the bodhisattvas’ practices in that land. Since the six perfections are common to all four teachings, they are here compared to those of the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā sutras;
in every respect, they are identical to those in the Eastern Quarter and in this land. This concludes the section on the verses describing the manifestation of auspicious signs.
△ Second, the verses on the identity of their doubts and reflections.
At that time, the fourfold assembly, seeing the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa manifest such great supernormal powers, their hearts were filled with joy,
and they each asked one another about the causes and conditions for this event.
The two verses on the similarity between past events seen and present reality are concluded. △ Third, the three verses on the similarity between past events seen and what will occur in the future:

first, one verse on the person who preaches the Dharma; second, two verses on the time and season; third, three verses on the proclamation of extinction; fourth, four verses on the bestowing of predictions;
fifth, five verses on the propagation of the sutra after extinction. Now, the first [section].
The Honored One, revered by devas and humans, having just arisen from samādhi, praised the Bodhisattva Wonderful Light:
"You are the eye of the world, the refuge and object of faith for all; you are able to uphold the treasury of the Dharma. As I have taught the Dharma, only you can realize and know it.
Having thus praised him, the World-Honored One caused Wonderful Light to rejoice and spoke this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
△ Second, the verse on the duration:
For sixty full intermediate kalpas, he did not rise from this seat; the sublime and wondrous Dharma he preached was entirely received and upheld by the Dharma Master Sublime Light.
When the preceding section of parables concludes, [the Buddha] tells Śāriputra: "Do not preach this sutra among those who lack wisdom," and so forth.
One should know that the fact that Wenguang (Prabhāketu) received and upheld it entirely is identical to the present time when Śāriputra receives the Buddha’s entrustment.
△ Third, the verses on the proclamation of extinction.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and had brought joy to the assembly, he immediately on that very day addressed the multitude of devas and humans:
"I have already explained for you the meaning of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena. Tonight, at midnight, I shall enter parinirvāṇa.
You must practice with single-minded diligence and remain free from negligence; Buddhas are extremely difficult to encounter, appearing but once in an interval of billions of kalpas."

This second chapter, "Expedient Means," is the primary teaching of this sutra and the confluence of all dharmas; it serves as the evidence of faith and the catalyst for this [teaching].

The analogies illustrate this, extending even to its circulation; explaining this constitutes two parts: first, the brief, and second, the detailed. Within the brief section, there are two further divisions:

The Dharma has its squareness and roundness, while function has its variations and convergences. The three provisional [means] are the compass and the square. One.
It is truly so: when wisdom reaches the compass, one skillfully employs the method of partiality to accommodate sentient beings;
when wisdom reaches the square, one skillfully employs the method of totality to accommodate sentient beings.

As the Sūtra says, "To cause them to leave behind all attachments and emerge from the suffering of the triple world"—therefore, the Tathāgata earnestly extols expedient means, for they accord with the capacities of sentient beings.
The claim that desire is not the Buddha’s fundamental intention may explain other sutras, but it is not the intent of this chapter. Second, regarding "expedient means" (*upāya*):
it is a gate. A gate is that which enables passage; it leads to what is to be reached. Expedient means and skillful strategies all serve as gates for the manifestation of the ultimate truth.

Since the manifestation of the truth is achieved through expedient means, and because it is named after that which makes it manifest, the term "gate" (*mukha*) is used here to explain "expedient" (*fang*).

"Thus, it is as the Sūtra says: 'Opening the gate of expedient means (upāya-mukha) to reveal the mark of reality (bhūta-lakṣaṇa). This meaning may be explained in reference to other sūtras, but it is not the intent of this present chapter.
Third, 'fang' (方) means secret; 'bian' (便) means marvelous. That which was kept secret in the past is now opened and becomes marvelous.
To reach this marvel through the secret is precisely the true secret. It is like the priceless jewel within one's own clothes that is pointed out to the King."
At the summit there is but a single jewel, neither two nor distinct; likewise, the hired laborer and the son of the elder are neither two nor distinct.
The skillful means and the gate are precisely the secret and wondrous. As the sutra says: "Only I know this mark, and so it is with the Buddhas of the ten directions.
"Cease, cease! There is no need to speak, for my Dharma is subtle and inconceivable. This is explained by way of secrecy.
The interpretation that [the expedient means] are "wondrous" precisely accords with the intent of this present chapter. Regarding the subsequent analysis:

the first interpretation holds that these are expedient means external to the essence, the provisional methods for transforming sentient beings through speech that conforms to the intentions of others; the second interpretation also holds that these are expedient means external to the essence, the provisional methods for both self-cultivation and the transformation of others through speech that conforms to the intentions of both self and others; the third interpretation holds that they are identical [to the essence].
The essence of skillful means (*upāya*) is the provisional method of one's own practice; this constitutes speech according to one's own intention. Furthermore, regarding the first interpretation:

skillful means is neither that which enters nor that which is entered. Regarding the second interpretation: skillful means is that which enters, but not that which is entered. Regarding the third interpretation:
skillful means is both that which enters and that which is entered. Moreover, according to the first interpretation, skillful means is secret.

The first [explanation] is that it is not the marvelous; the second explanation is that the secret expedient means (*upāya-guhya*) are capable of entering the marvelous; the third explanation is that the secret expedient means are themselves the marvelous.

According to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, this chapter is titled "On Skillful Means" (*Upāyakauśalya-parivarta*). Since "skillful means" (*upāya*) and "expedient means" (*upāya*) are non-dual and without distinction, even lowering the head or raising a hand leads to the attainment of the Buddha-way;

Regarding the extensive commentary: it refutes the ancients and does not record their views. This chapter demonstrates that the Tathāgata’s skillful means encompass all phenomena, just as space contains form or the ocean receives flowing streams.
How could one possibly explain the great expanse of the Dharma-realm using but a single branch or a single stream?

Regarding all phenomena as provisional: as the text says, "The characteristics, nature, substance, function, causes, conditions, fruits, retributions, origins, and ends of all dharmas—even a mere utterance of words—all these are provisional. Regarding the reality of all phenomena, as the text states: "The Tathāgata skillfully teaches all dharmas to gladden the minds of the multitude;

It is not the true reality as it is. If all dharmas are merely provisional, what could not be subverted?

Since all things possess both the provisional and the real, how can one alone be a single path while others are divergent interpretations?
Within each and every dharma there are both the provisional and the real; they cannot be categorized as exclusively provisional or exclusively real.
If all dharmas were neither provisional nor real, what would there be to refute, and why such fuss over forcefully establishing [a position]? It is simply a matter of listing them directly.

Whether fundamental or derivative, their essence and principle are no different; though spoken, they are not spoken.

Principle refers to True Suchness (*tathatā*); True Suchness is fundamentally pure, and whether a Buddha appears or not, it remains eternally unchanging. Therefore, principle is called "real.

Phenomena refer to the mind, consciousness, and mentation, which give rise to pure and impure karma and are subject to constant fluctuation and instability; therefore, phenomena are called "provisional."
If expediency (*upāya*) were not based on principle, there would be no means to establish practice; if practice were not based on phenomena, it could not manifest principle.

Regarding the "Expedient Means" (upāya): from the dharma-nature of ignorance up to all dharmas outside the realms, these are all that is expressed (*vācya*). This mind, consciousness, and mentation—both in name and in essence—are fully endowed with all dharmas outside the realms.

Having already cited an entire fascicle as proof, I shall further cite another chapter. Although not presented in sequential order, the text is complete in its entirety:
"The wisdom of all Buddhas is profound and immeasurable; its gate of wisdom is difficult to understand and difficult to enter.

These are the four *siddhāntas* (doctrinal positions) that explain the provisional and the ultimate—the first rare and difficult-to-understand dharmas accomplished by the Buddha.

Teaching through two modes—provisional and ultimate—as gateways for the sake of transforming others: those who are sharp-witted may enter, but those who are dull-witted do not.
(Prajñāpāramitā) This too is unsuitable for certain beings and thus cannot be taught. Abandoning the three modes of teaching for the sake of transforming others, one speaks only of the ultimate.
Those who practice this, whether they be of sharp or dull faculties, all gain entry; from beginning to end, it takes skillful means as its gateway.

It does not simply state that all things are immediately beneficial, nor that both the sharp and dull faculties can immediately perceive reality through skillful means (*upāya*) (as in the *Lotus Sūtra*).

Since you have earnestly requested this three times, how could I not speak? Up to the "Chapter on Bestowing Predictions upon Those in Training and Those Beyond Training," there is a broad exposition of the Three Vehicles to reveal the One Vehicle, which serves to sever doubts and engender faith.
This section consists of two parts: first, the brief opening and revelation; second, the raising of doubts and the request for further teaching.
The first part, again, has two sections: first, the prose and verse praises of the Buddha’s twofold wisdom; second, the verses that formally provide the brief opening and revelation.

The first section, "Manifesting the Arising of Doubt through Adherence to Movement," also has two parts. The first part, the long prose, has two sub-sections: first, praising the two wisdoms through words; second, praising the two wisdoms beyond words.
The first of these [praising through words] also has two parts: first, clarifying the provisional and real aspects of all Buddhas;

second, clarifying the provisional and real aspects of Śākyamuni. The first of these [clarifying the provisional and real of all Buddhas] further has three parts: first, a dual praise; second, a dual explanation; third, a dual conclusion.
First: At that time, the World-Honored One arose calmly from samādhi and addressed Śāriputra: "The wisdom of all Buddhas is profoundly deep and immeasurable;
its gateway to wisdom is difficult to understand and difficult to enter, and is not within the reach of any śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha."
"It can be known.
At that time refers to the moment when Mañjuśrī had finished answering the question. Since the Buddha is always in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), why does he say "arising"?
This is intended to show that in the past, whenever the various Buddhas spoke this sutra, they would invariably first enter the *Anantārtha* (Infinite Meaning) samādhi.
"Entering the Lotus [Sūtra], the present Buddha is likewise. This indicates the world-siddhānta (worldly standpoint). Out of compassion, he arises from samādhi;

having observed both the principle and the capacity of beings with thorough discernment, his teaching is necessarily free from error, thereby increasing the faith of sentient beings. This indicates the person-siddhānta (standpoint for individuals).

Out of compassion, he arises from samādhi. If even a Buddha, who is eternally luminous in his tranquility, must still enter samādhi before preaching the Dharma, how much more so [is this required for others]?
Furthermore, when the distracted mind falsely utters speech, this demonstrates the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the therapeutic standpoint).

Out of compassion, one arises from meditative concentration to enter it, and by taking the principle as an object, one settles the mind in the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*). Upon emerging from concentration, one causes others to settle their minds in true reality;

this demonstrates the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the ultimate standpoint). Out of compassion, one arises from concentration to establish these four dharmas; therefore, it is said that "one arises with composure. (All four teachings possess these.)

Regarding the four *siddhāntas*, they must now be understood in terms of the revelation of the Perfect [Teaching]. As for the address to Śāriputra: among those of the Small Vehicle, he was foremost in wisdom;
the Buddha intends to use him as a means to shatter small wisdom and reveal great wisdom. This is a passage initiated by the compiler of the sutra. Question:

What is the difference between this address to Śāriputra and that in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*? Answer: How could it be limited to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* alone? It begins with the *Catuṣ-āgama*.
In the end, this sutra is taught in various places with different purposes: in the *Āgamas*, it is taught to initiate the wheel of the Dharma of arising and ceasing;
in the Vaipulya, it is taught for the purpose of censure; in the *Prajñāpāramitā*, it is taught for the purpose of empowerment;

and in the present sutra, it is taught for the purpose of revelation. As Vasubandhu’s commentary states: "The teaching is addressed to Śāriputra and not to other śrāvakas because his wisdom is profound."

There are five reasons why [the Buddha] did not inform the bodhisattvas: first, because of matters to be performed for the śrāvakas; second, because of the dedication toward great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*);
third, so as to prevent cowardice; fourth, so as to inspire wholesome mindfulness in other people;
and fifth, so as to prevent the arising of the thought that "what was to be done has already been accomplished. One should know that these five intentions differ from those found in other sūtras.
The explicit teaching does not state that Śrāvakas can enter the Buddha-wisdom.

The phrase "the wisdom of all Buddhas is extremely profound and immeasurable" praises their true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*). It is not because there are three kinds of provisional or real [wisdom] for transforming others;

rather, it says "all Buddhas" to manifest their own practice, and it says "wisdom" to indicate that this essence of wisdom is the threefold wisdom within the one mind, vertically penetrating the Dharma-realm as vast as space.
Because it is the ultimate ground of principle, it is called "profound"; because it extends horizontally to the very limits of the Dharma-realm, it is called "immeasurable.
These are words of true praise. Just as the roots being deep ensures that the branches are luxuriant, and the source being distant ensures that the stream is long, so too is it with true wisdom;
expedient wisdom follows this same analogy. Thus, the gateway of wisdom is difficult to understand.

"Difficult to enter," and so forth, praises the provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*). Because one possesses the power of progress through the preliminary expedients prior to the path of self-cultivation, it is called a "gate" (the forty stages of the true cause).

Entering through the gate, one arrives at the midst of the path (the stage of wondrous enlightenment, the fruition). That which is within the path is called the real, while that which precedes the path is called the provisional.

(This refers to the discussion of the provisional and the real regarding cause and effect within the aforementioned ten pairs. Because the Ten Abidings mark the beginning of understanding, they are difficult to comprehend; the Ten Grounds are likewise profound.

"Because it is difficult to enter for the sake of entry"—this is a praise of the provisional [means] (upāya), stating that it cannot be fathomed by those who have not yet attained the seven stages of expedient means (the two vehicles of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha, the Bodhisattvas of the Shared and Distinct teachings, and the three stages of the Ten Faiths of the Perfect teaching).

The separate mention of the inability of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas to know it is because their attachments are heavy; thus, they are specifically refuted. The fundamental intent of the Dharma-body is originally based on the provisional means of one's own practice.

In truth, because they are like those who flee from a mechanism, it is said they do not know (those who have not yet established a karmic connection are said to be in the *dharmakāya*; after the connection has been established, they are said to be "without capacity," etc.).

Because the *Avataṃsaka* illuminates all at once, they are like the deaf and the mute, hence it is said they do not know. Because the *Vaipulya* (Prajñāpāramitā) rebukes and challenges while maintaining the thatched hut, it is said they do not know.
Because the *Prajñā* turns the teaching and has no mind to seek or grasp, it is said they do not know. Now, in the Great [Sūtra]...
When the opportunity is opened and the light is emitted, the earth shakes; thus, the paths of all Buddhas of the past and present are identical.

Because they harbor doubts, they claim not to know; yet even those of sharp faculties who understand bit by bit, or those of dull faculties who are equal to the Two Vehicles, likewise do not know. △ Second, the dual explanation.

Why is this? Because the Buddha has personally attended upon hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of countless Buddhas, fully practicing the immeasurable Dharma of the paths of all those Buddhas with courageous diligence, so that his fame is heard everywhere.
“The Buddha once drew near [to them]” and so forth explain actual wisdom (*bhūtajñāna*). This is because, externally, one encounters the Buddha and receives many essential teachings;
thus, actual wisdom is profoundly deep because, internally, one’s practice is pure and thick, having fully cultivated the path of the Dharma. Actual wisdom is immeasurable;
“immeasurable” explains its horizontal breadth, while “profoundly deep” explains its vertical height. “Valiant and energetic” and so forth provide the further explanation.

Skillful means and wisdom arise precisely from courageous and diligent exertion; because one is able to enter the gate that is difficult to enter, and having entered the gate, one’s benefits extend boundlessly such that all beings revere these supreme virtues, one’s name and fame become universally renowned.

Thus, being able to enter the Dharma-gate through courageous and diligent exertion explains the profundity of skillful means and wisdom, while the universal renown of one's name explains the vastness of skillful means and wisdom.
Although there are no words of profound breadth to serve as examples, this meaning is established through actual wisdom. △ Third, the double conclusion:
He has accomplished the most profound and unprecedented dharmas; the underlying intentions of his teachings, given according to what is appropriate, are difficult to understand.

Because it accords with principle and is ultimate, it is said to be "accomplished"; because it has reached the bottom of the other shore, it is said to be "profound"—this concludes the establishment of true wisdom (*jñāna*).

Because it accords with capacities and meets [the needs of] the occasion, it is said to be "expedient"; because it is not something known through the seven stages of expedient means (*upāya*), it is said to be "difficult to understand"—this concludes the establishment of provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).
Alternatively, "accomplished" and "profound" refer to the unprecedented dharmas that establish one's own [nature].
The provisional and the real are taught according to what is appropriate; their underlying intent is difficult to comprehend.

The provisional and the real regarding the transformation of others are both termed "real," while the provisional and the real regarding one's own practice are both termed "provisional. This concludes the initial clarification of the provisional and the real of all Buddhas.
△ Second, the clarification of the provisional and the real of Śākyamuni, which has three parts: first, a double eulogy; second, a double explanation; third, a double conclusion.
Now, first: Śāriputra,
since my attainment of Buddhahood, I have extensively expounded the verbal teachings through various causes and conditions and various parables,
using countless skillful means to guide sentient beings and cause them to leave all attachments behind.
If true wisdom were not perfected, the Buddha-way would not be accomplished; since it is said that "once one attains Buddhahood, all is attained," this is a praise of true wisdom.
The section beginning with "various causes and conditions" below praises expedient wisdom.

For more than forty years, he has used three types of teachings to transform others, employing both the expedient and the real to accommodate sentient beings; thus, it says "various causes and conditions. As for the "parables":
In the Hīnayāna, there are similes such as the plantain tree and water bubbles; in the Mahāyāna, there are similes such as the city of the *gandharvas* and magical illusions.
"Extensively expounding" means being able to produce immeasurable meanings from a single dharma. "Innumerable skillful means" refers to the seven kinds of skillful means.

Regarding "guiding" and so forth: it refers to teaching the ten ordinary wholesome deeds (*daśa-kuśala*) to lead away from the three miserable realms, and teaching the ten pure [wholesome deeds] to lead away from attachment.

Skillfully departing from attachment to the desire realm, he speaks of the Tripitaka; departing from attachment to views and afflictions, he speaks of the Bodhisattva Dharma; departing from attachment to the nirvana, he speaks of the Buddha Dharma;
and departing from attachment to the craving for dharmas that accord with the Path. △ Second, the dual explanation.
Why is this so? Because the Tathāgata has fully perfected the *pāramitās* of expedient means (*upāya*) and knowledge-and-vision (*jñāna-darśana*).
The two characters "Tathāgata" explain his true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*), which arises from and attains Buddhahood through the true nature of reality (*tathatā-satyalakṣaṇa*);
thus he is called the Tathāgata. The two characters "expedient means" explain his skillful wisdom (*upāya-kauśalya*), by virtue of which he employs skillful means.
Therefore, one is able to extensively expound the verbal teachings through various causes, conditions, and parables.

"Knowledge and vision of the *pāramitā*" refers to the simultaneous presentation of the provisional and the real: the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) is called real knowledge; the Buddha-eye is called real vision; the path-knowledge (*mārgajñatā*) is called provisional knowledge;
and the dharma-eye is called provisional vision. Because they all reach the ultimate limit of both phenomena and principle, they are all so named.
"Having fully perfected all the *pāramitās* means that both the provisional and the ultimate have been completely realized. △ Third, the double conclusion:
"Śāriputra, the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision is vast and profound, immeasurable and unobstructed;
through his powers and fearlessnesses, his meditative concentrations, liberations, and samādhis, he has entered deeply into the boundless and accomplished all unprecedented dharmas."
The "vast and great" refers to the horizontal clarity; the "profound and far-reaching" refers to the vertical reality-wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*).

This wisdom is neither horizontal nor vertical, yet by means of provisional words, its horizontal and vertical illumination is praised as being limitless and infinite, like a large box requiring a large lid. "Immeasurable" refers to the great loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity of the Buddha-ground.
"Unimpeded" refers to the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) of the Buddha-ground. "Power" refers to the ten powers (*bala*) of the Buddha-ground.
That which is "feared" refers to the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) of the Buddha-ground. "Dhyāna" is the dhyāna of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*).
"Samādhi" is the Śūraṅgama Samādhi. "Samāpatti" is the King Samāpatti. To penetrate deeply into the boundless and thereby perfect the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*);

to achieve vertically the profound and accomplish all unprecedented dharmas, thereby perfecting the wisdom of skillful means; and to extend horizontally in vast breadth—this is the initial reliance upon words.

The praise of the two wisdoms is concluded. △ Second, the praise of the two wisdoms through words of ineffability, which is divided into two parts: first, citing the reason for the words of ineffability;
second, the actual words of ineffability. Regarding the first part, there are two sub-sections: first, the actual citation of the reason for the words of ineffability;
second, pointing to the realm of ineffability. Now, the first [sub-section].
Śāriputra, the Tathāgata is able to skillfully analyze and expound all dharmas in various ways, using supple and gentle speech that delights the hearts of the multitude.
By skillfully analyzing and expounding all dharmas in various ways, he repeatedly demonstrates his skillful means (*upāya*), using supple and gentle speech that delights the multitude.
"Mind" (*citta*) emphasizes the reality [of the teaching]. In the preceding passage, when describing the other lands, it is said that they "emit gentle sounds";

in the subsequent passage, Śāriputra’s realization states, "I have heard the Buddha’s gentle sound. Thus, it is said to emphasize reality, for the minds of the assembly find joy precisely in attaining the real.
The preceding section praises the prior reality and the subsequent expedient means; this clarifies that the expedient is extended from the real.
Now, by severing words to praise the prior provisional and the subsequent real, he intends to roll back the provisional to return to the real. △ Second, pointing to the realm beyond words:
Śāriputra, to speak of it in brief, the Buddha has fully accomplished immeasurable, boundless, and unprecedented dharmas.
To take the essential point: "briefly indicating" (*lue er yan zhi*) means to speak in summary.
"Immeasurable and boundless" refers to the provisional (*quan*), while "unprecedented phenomena" (*weizengyou fa*) refers to the ultimate (*shi*). These two matters the Buddha has fully accomplished;

having attained them through the cultivation of the path, how could they be described? If one were to clarify only a single matter, one should not say "fully" (*xi*). "Fully" (*xi*) indicates both simultaneously.
This is the provisional and the real. Furthermore, that which is immeasurable and boundless is entirely unprecedented;

thus, it is the inconceivable, unprecedented dharma wherein the provisional is itself the real. That which is immeasurable and boundless is itself the inconceivable, wherein the real is itself the provisional.
This concludes the initial section on the grounds for this ultimate praise. II. The actual expression of ultimate praise beyond words, in two parts: first, the silence regarding words.
This concludes the praise of the two Śākyas and the intent behind the cessation of that praise.
First, [the Buddha] stops Śāriputra, saying there is no need to speak further.
Because this Dharma is profound and tranquil, transcending the path of language and its essence being ineffable, he ceases his speech to praise it through the exercise of compassion.

Out of compassion, he spoke for them, yet they could not understand upon hearing it; grieved that their roots of goodness were thus stunted, he therefore ceased. △ Second, explaining the intent behind ceasing and praising. Why is this?
It is because the Dharma accomplished by the Buddha is the foremost, most rare, and difficult to understand; it is known only by Buddhas and Buddhas.
He is thus able to exhaustively investigate the true reality of all phenomena— that is to say, that all phenomena have such characteristics,
such natures, such essences, such powers, such activities, such causes, such conditions, such fruits, and such retributions, being equal in their fundamental essence and their ultimate consummation.
This commentary on the cessation of praise contains two intended meanings: first, because the Buddha is the supreme person who has accomplished and attained the supreme Dharma, he is "inexpressible";
this refers to the wisdom capable of exhaustive investigation. Second, because his profound realm is inconceivable, he is "inexpressible";
this refers to the various [dharmas] that constitute the object of exhaustive investigation.

The term "Dharma-reality" (dharmatā) refers to the following pairs of opposites: accomplishment versus non-accomplishment, the foremost versus the non-foremost, the marvelous versus the non-marvelous, and the difficult to understand versus the not difficult to understand.
When considering the fruit in relation to the cause, these are paired as self and other. One must rely on the flavor of the teaching to discern them thoroughly;

by distinguishing the other [the disciple], one reveals that the Buddha’s supreme authority—whether provisional or ultimate—is horizontally pervasive, and for this reason, [this teaching] is not [limited].

It can be said that only a Buddha and a Buddha are able to exhaustively fathom [the truth]; those who have attained it in its initial and middle stages have not yet reached its source, like the moonlight on the fourteenth night, which is not yet full.
Only a Buddha and a Buddha reach the ultimate depths, like the moon on the night of the full moon, whose substance is nowhere not round and whose light is nowhere not pervasive.
This reveals the provisional and the real, and the vertical profundity of the path of cultivation.
Because it has been attained, it cannot be spoken of. The true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is a brief indication of the profound realm of the provisional and the real.
"All phenomena" refers to the thousand suchnesses within the hundred realms; this is the provisional aspect of the real. "True reality" refers to the essence of the Middle Way principle;
this is the real aspect of the provisional. What is called "the suchness of all phenomena" and so forth extensively explains the profound provisional [nature].
The actual reality must be explained in four ways: first, in terms of the ten dharma-realms; second, in terms of the Buddha-dharma realm;
third, in terms of separation and conjunction; and fourth, in terms of stages. The scripture says "all dharmas," therefore it is explained by means of the ten dharma-realms.
The scripture says "the rare dharmas accomplished by the Buddha," therefore it is explained by means of the Buddha-dharma realm. The scripture says "Stop, stop, do not... [and so forth].
It must be explained that my Dharma is subtle and inconceivable; therefore, the *parikarma* (analytical) method of *yuan-li-he-shi* (separation and combination) is employed.
Since the Sūtra states, "Only Buddhas and Buddhas can exhaustively fathom it," the method of *wei-shi* (classification by stage) is employed. First, regarding the ten dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*):

although the dharmas of the six classes of ordinary beings and the four classes of sages are immeasurable in number, they do not exceed eleven realms. Furthermore, though each realm may branch into many divisions, they do not exceed ten.

Just as the hell realm inherently possesses its own specific characteristics from beginning to end, so too does it possess the characteristics of the animal realm from beginning to end, and even the characteristics of the Buddha-dharma realm from beginning to end, without any deficiency.
Thus, the *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā* states: "The path of the hells accomplishes the dharmas of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven."
This is an illustration; one should know that the same applies to the other nine dharma-realms. Each individual realm mutually contains the other nine realms.
If one contemplates the ten suchnesses of the nine realms within its own position, they are all termed "provisional" (*upāya*);
if one contemplates the ten suchnesses of the Buddha-realm within its own position, it is termed "real. Within the one, there are the infinite; within the infinite, there is the one.

Therefore, it is called "inconceivable. Although ordinary beings possess [the capacity for realization], their emotions are deluded as they are cut off from principle (it is said they are "cut off from principle" because they despise themselves as having no share [in it];

it is said they are "deluded in emotion" because they hold divergent views according to their perceptions). Although those of the Two Vehicles possess [the capacity for realization], they abandon and seek liberation (the three paths are abandoned and not contemplated; avoiding emptiness while seeking emptiness instead serves only to support their minor liberation).

Although Bodhisattvas possess [the capacity for realization], their illumination is not all-pervasive, and thus it is called "not yet clear" (because the *Zang* and *Tong* [teachings] illuminate the six [realms], while the *Bie* [teaching] illuminates them in succession, it is so called).

The Tathāgata’s non-limiting [wisdom] penetrates and surveys both the horizontal and the vertical; being fully endowed with this, the infinite is contained within the one (horizontal), and the one is identical to the infinite (vertical). Because many and one are mutually identical, it is said to be "fully endowed."
It is understood only by oneself and not seen by others; because it cannot be proclaimed or shown, one simply ceases and halts all speech.
This has already been explained in the "Profound Meaning" (*Xuan yi*) above, so it is not recorded here in full. Second, regarding the explanation according to the Buddha-dharma realm:
the Buddha-realm is neither a mark nor a non-mark, yet it is designated as "such a mark," referring to the causal conditions of the myriad virtues. As stated in the passage below:
"Adorned with various jewels" refers to the Buddha-realm being neither a nature nor a non-nature, yet being designated as "such a nature";

this indicates the wisdom of the discerning cause (*vijñapti-hetu*), as the subsequent text says, "there is a great white ox. The Buddha-realm is neither an essence (*ātman*) nor a non-essence, yet it is designated as "such an essence";
this indicates the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) of the causal source (*nidāna-hetu*), as the subsequent text says, "the chariot is high and wide."

Furthermore, the Buddha-realm is neither possessing power nor lacking power, yet it is designated as "possessing such power," referring to the power of the bodhicitta, the roots of goodness of compassion, and so forth;
thus the subsequent text says: "Moreover, upon it, canopies and awnings are spread.

Furthermore, the Buddha-realm is neither acting nor not acting, yet it is designated as "acting in such a way," referring to the spontaneous path of effortless exertion (*anābhoga-mārga*); thus the subsequent [text] says...
The text says, "Its speed is like the wind. The Buddha-realm is neither cause nor non-cause, yet it is designated as such a cause;
this refers to the forty-one stages. As the subsequent passage states, "Riding upon this precious vehicle, one travels through the four quarters.
The Buddha-realm is neither condition nor non-condition, yet it is designated as such a condition; this refers to all factors that assist the path to enlightenment.

The subsequent text states: "Furthermore, he is attended and guarded by many servants. The Buddha-realm is neither fruition nor non-fruition, yet it is designated as such a fruition because it refers to the realization of the wondrous enlightenment (*miao-jue*) attained through the radiant and perfect cause; hence the subsequent text says, "He proceeds directly to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
The Buddha-realm is neither retribution nor non-retribution, yet it is designated as such a retribution because it refers to the Great Parinirvāṇa.
Because it is *nirvāṇa*, the subsequent passage states that one attains the immeasurable, untainted, and pure fruit of retribution.

The Buddha-realm is neither beginning nor end, yet it is neither not-beginning nor not-end; to speak of beginning and end, "beginning" refers to the Buddha’s manifestation (*dharmakāya*) and "end" refers to the Buddha’s retribution (*vipākaphala*), which constitutes the provisional means of self-cultivation. The Buddha-realm is neither equal nor unequal, yet it is spoken of as ultimate.
Because "equality" (等) refers to the true reality (*dharmatā*), the heading states that "true reality" is the reality of one's own practice (*sva-caryā*).

Since it is real while being provisional, it is called "root and branch"; since it is provisional while being real, it is called "equality. [Question: What is the distinction between the Buddha-realm (*buddha-dhātu*) mentioned here and the Buddha-realm within the ten realms mentioned previously?

[Answer: The former pertains to both delusion and the cause, as well as both awakening and the fruit; the latter pertains solely to the fruit and does not extend to the cause or delusion. Therefore, every single phenomenon employs the "double negation": it is neither identity nor difference, neither non-identity nor non-difference.

Although it is not emptiness, it emerges from the intention of the "double negation" (neither-nor); one should know that the nine levels below the three truths follow accordingly, up until the ultimate equality of the beginning and the end. Only in this way can it be called the ultimate Buddha-vehicle. Therefore, the text concludes with the passage on the "great carts.

Thus, within the text of this present chapter, these are the true marks of all phenomena (*dharmas*) belonging to the stage of Buddhahood; in the preceding parable, they are the great carts that adorn the site of enlightenment; in the previous lives, they are the precious sites where the Buddha of the ultimate fruit opened the provisional means;

and in the Chapter on the Original [Nidāna], they are the wondrous Dharma realized by the One who attained Buddhahood long ago. If the main body of the teaching can be understood, how could one be confused regarding the circulation [of the sutra]? Even a single sentence or a single verse is utterly trustworthy. The discourse on the Three Virtues and the Three Tracks is as clear as the light of day.

If one now grasps this intent, then the extensive exposition over eight years does not transcend a single thought-moment (*citta-kṣaṇa*), and fifty minor kalpas do not stir for even an instant. By this analogy, one should know that the teachings of a single lifetime to suit various capacities reside within the nature of the mind;

the Buddha-activities of the ten directions are vividly present before one’s eyes, and the faculties and natures of the Dharma-realm are easily understood upon inspection. Whatever is taught according to suitability all points toward the principle of the *garbha* (the womb-treasury).

This is the Tathāgata’s own practice of the provisional and the real, the most supreme among the supreme aspects, even unto the supreme fruit and retribution—vast horizontally and profound vertically, yet without end.

Therefore, the heading of this chapter states "the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena"; by analogy, one should also speak of the "true nature," the "true substance," the "true power," and even the "true ultimate" of all phenomena.

However, it merely cites one instance to encompass them all. The Tathāgata’s universal illumination pervades both the horizontal and vertical dimensions, as complete as observing fruit in the palm of one's hand;
yet for ordinary beings, he is like two people born blind, and for those of the Two Vehicles, he is like a person with cataracts.
The Bodhisattva Miǎomù (One-Eyed) sees indistinctly at night; because it cannot be described, he remains silent—“Stop, stop! Cease speaking!

Third, the explanation by way of separation and integration: if one observes within the Buddha’s mind the ten realms and the ten suchnesses, they are all supreme marks, even up to the supreme fruit and retribution;
these are solely the Buddha’s Dharma-realm, like the ocean that encompasses the myriad streams.

Just as a thousand chariots share the same ruts, this refers to the provisional and real aspects of one's own practice (*svayam-pratipatti*). If one follows the intentions of others, there are the nine realms of existence, the ten suchnesses, and the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*);
these constitute the provisional and real aspects of transforming others (*parārtha*). Although the transformation of others possesses reality, all are subsumed under the provisional;
although one's own practice possesses the provisional, all are subsumed under the real. This is precisely the distinction between one's own practice and the transformation of others.
Regarding provisional and ultimate truth: following others, they are opened; following oneself, they are closed. Transversally and vertically, they illuminate all; opening and closing are sovereign.
Though opened as the infinite, the infinite is one; though closed as the one, the one is infinite.
Though infinite and one, it is neither one nor infinite; though neither one nor infinite, it is both one and infinite. Only the Buddha [knows this].

Only with a Buddha can this be thoroughly investigated; ordinary beings slander it and do not believe in it, those of the Two Vehicles are confused and do not accept it, and Bodhisattvas have not yet clarified the dust and stumps [of their delusions]. For these reasons, [the Buddha] says "Stop, stop," and cuts off further speech.
Fourth, explaining according to the stages: such characteristics mean that all sentient beings possess the true mark (dharmatā), which is inherently present from the beginning.
This is the appearance of the Tathāgatagarbha. Such a nature is the wisdom of the original virtues (*prakṛti-guṇa*), which is the ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
Such an essence is the principle of the Middle Way, the *dharmatā*. These three virtues pervade the ten dharma-realms;
they are present in every stage. If one investigates these three virtues and enters the stage of the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), it is then called...
When such power and such activity enter the forty-one stages, they are called "such cause" and "such condition.
When one reaches the stage of Buddhahood, they are called "such fruit" and "such retribution. The first three are called the "root," and the latter three are called the "branch.
Since the beginning and the end are identical in these three virtues, they are termed "ultimate equality. The three virtues of the initial stage pervade both the unwholesome and the wholesome.
It penetrates the worthy and the sage, the small and the great, the beginning and the ultimate. Though it is in evil, it does not sink; though it is in good, it does not rise.
Though it is in the worthy, it does not descend; though it is in the sage, it does not ascend. Though it is in the small, it is not narrow;
though it is in the great, it is not expansive. Though it is at the beginning, it is not new; though it is at the ultimate, it remains as it is.
Furthermore, it is because this is inconceivable and cannot be expressed that one ceases, ceases, and cuts off speech.

Moreover, regarding the ultimate equality of the three virtues: although the ten realms possess various distinctions in their characteristics and natures, provisional and real aspects, and their opening and closing, when one contemplates them as they truly are with the great wisdom of equality, they are ultimately all equal. If one is deluded regarding this realm...

There are the characteristics and nature of the six elements, which are called the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). If one understands this realm, there are the characteristics and nature of the two vehicles, which are called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

When one realizes that this is neither delusion nor understanding, there are the characteristics and nature of the Bodhisattva and Buddha realms, which constitute the Middle Way, the supreme truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
If one uses this wisdom to view the conventional truth as equal [to the ultimate], then the conventional truth is not delusion.

Regarding the True Truth (*satyārtha*), the True Truth is neither understanding nor non-understanding, neither delusion nor non-delusion; being free from both delusion and understanding, it is merely termed "equality" (*samatā*).

If one illuminates both simultaneously, the provisional (*upāya*) is precisely the real (*bhūta-artha*), and the real is precisely the provisional; though they are two, they are not two, and this is also called ultimate equality.

(This refers to [the relationship between] affliction and understanding, etc. Furthermore, regarding the realm where the provisional and the real are non-dual, the seven kinds of skillful means (*upāya*)—[text fragment ends].

Only the Buddhas are able to equalize the non-dual realm through non-dual wisdom; because they equalize the non-dual realm with non-dual wisdom, it is called "ultimate equality" (this refers to equality in terms of persons).
Furthermore, the capacities of those in the present Mahāyāna are such that they do not clearly perceive the characteristics and natures of the nine realms;
rather, it is directly taught that all characteristics and natures enter entirely into the characteristics and nature of the Buddha-realm—a teaching that was not present in the past.
"Explanation" means that because the past was not equal to the present, the present teaching explains it so that one knows the past is equal to the present;
