therefore, it is called "ultimate equality" (this refers to equality in terms of the teaching). Furthermore, the reason for the fourfold interpretation is as follows: the interpretation in terms of the ten realms clarifies the universal inclusion of principle;

the interpretation in terms of the Buddha-realm clarifies the ultimate nature of self-realization; and the interpretation in terms of separation and combination clarifies the Buddha’s transformative activity.
Because the three virtues are all-pervasive, they are explained according to the various stages. First, the praise of the Buddha’s two wisdoms; within this, the initial long prose section concludes.

△ Second, the verse recapitulation, which has two parts: first, the verse recapitulating the praise of the two wisdoms through words; second, the verse recapitulating the praise of the two wisdoms beyond words.

These verses vary in detail from the preceding prose so that the meaning may be more clearly revealed. Within the first part, there are two sections, the first of which is the combined verse recapitulation.
The praise of the two Buddhas, the two wisdoms, and their combination consists of two verses; the explanation of this praise by the two Buddhas and its conclusion consist of a long prose passage.

The two Buddhas each offer praise to indicate that their conditions for transformation differ, while the combined praise of the two Buddhas within the verses demonstrates that their two wisdoms are identical. First, [the verses]: [Verse 1] The Tathāgata’s wisdom is most profound and subtle; It is difficult to fathom even for the Śrāvakas. Only the Buddha can fully know it; No one else can comprehend it. [Verse 2] The Tathāgata’s wisdom is most profound and subtle; It is difficult to fathom even for the Pratyekabuddhas. Only the Buddha can fully know it; No one else can comprehend it. Now, the first [section].
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“The Hero of the World is immeasurable; among all classes of beings—gods, humans, and all other sentient creatures—none can know the Buddha.
The Buddha’s powers, his fearlessnesses, his liberations, his various samādhis, and all his other dharmas cannot be measured by anyone.”
The first verse summarizes the two Buddhas’ wisdom of reality (*bhūta-jñāna*), while the second verse summarizes the two Buddhas’ wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*).
As for "all other dharmas," this refers to the skillful means and reality for the sake of transforming others; that is, one takes one’s own practice as the means of transforming others.

From within a single dharma, immeasurable skillful means are manifested, all of which are such that they are simultaneously both skillful means and reality; therefore, there is nothing that is not so.
[He] is able to measure it. △ Second, the two Buddhas join their verses to praise and conclude the praise.
"Originally, following countless Buddhas, you have fully practiced all paths and the profound, subtle, and wondrous Dharma that is difficult to see and difficult to comprehend.
Having practiced these various paths for immeasurable billions of kalpas, you attained the fruit at the site of enlightenment; I have fully known and seen this."
This verse serves as a concluding summary for the preceding two chapters; however, the phrasing is varied and need not be assigned to each line individually.
It means that the two dharmas of provisional and ultimate truth—profound and subtle—are most difficult to perceive and comprehend.
This is because both I and all Buddhas have, from time immemorial, attended upon countless Buddhas and fully practiced the immeasurable dharmas of the Path.
Having practiced this path for immeasurable kalpas, one then sits at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and attains the fruit of Buddhahood;

therefore, one is able to fully know and fully see these subtle and wondrous teachings of the provisional and the real. Because one has fully accomplished the practice of the path for immeasurable kalpas, the wisdom of skillful means (upāya-jñāna) is perfected at the site of enlightenment, and the fruit is realized;
thus, the wisdom of reality (tattva-jñāna) is perfected. This, too, is a discussion of the provisional and the real in terms of cause and effect.
The first verse concludes the praise of the two wisdoms by means of words. △ Second, the praise of the two wisdoms through the transcendence of words is divided into three parts:
first, the verse explaining the intent behind the praise of cessation; second, the actual verse on the transcendence of words; third, the concluding verse on the realm beyond words.
Now, the first part.
"Such matters as the various natures and characteristics of these great fruits of retribution can be known by me and the Buddhas of the ten directions.
This verse means that only a Buddha and a Buddha can exhaustively fathom the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmas*).

Having first raised the topic of the fruits of retribution, the following section raises the topic of their natures and characteristics; from this, one may infer by analogy that 'great fruits of retribution' refers to the Sublime [Dharma]."
The various natures and characteristics of the retributive fruits refer to the meaning of the distinctions among the hundred realms and thousand dharmas;
this very meaning is ultimate equality. △ Second, the verse on the ineffable praise.

This Dharma cannot be demonstrated; its verbal signs are quiescent, and among all other classes of sentient beings, there is none capable of comprehending it, except for those bodhisattvas whose power of faith is firm and stable.

This verse precisely captures the purport of not needing to speak further regarding cessation (*śamatha*). This Dharma is the wondrous realm of provisional and ultimate truth illuminated by the two wisdoms of all Buddhas;
it is the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, consisting of the hundred realms and thousand suchnesses, which is inconceivable.
Because this true reality has no spatial location, it cannot be pointed out; because it transcends the path of language, its verbal expressions are quiescent.
Although the Buddha is able to speak this ineffable Dharma, because sentient beings are incapable of understanding it, he desists and deems it unnecessary to speak.
Yet, if there is no one capable of understanding, does this mean that the Dharma will ultimately never be transmitted?
Therefore, it is said: "Except for the assembly of Bodhisattvas whose power of faith is firm and solid, perhaps they may be able to understand. This refers to the power of faith.

"Solidly established" refers to the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) of the Perfect Teaching (*ekayāna*). From this point downward, the text correctly and extensively clarifies that all other sentient beings are unable to understand [this].
The assembly of the Buddha’s disciples, having made offerings to various Buddhas, have exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*) and abide in their final bodies (*antima-deha*).

The strength of such people as these is insufficient; even if the entire world were filled with those like Śāriputra, and they were to exhaust their thoughts to measure it together, they could not fathom the Buddha’s wisdom.

Even if the ten directions were filled with those like Śāriputra and all other disciples, and they were to fill the lands of the ten directions and exhaust their thoughts to measure it together, they still could not know it.
Pratyekabuddhas of sharp wisdom, free from outflows, in their final bodies, also fill the ten directions, their number like that of bamboo groves;
though these together with one mind for immeasurable billions of kalpas should wish to contemplate the Buddha’s true wisdom, they cannot know even a small fraction of it.
A newly resolved Bodhisattva who has made offerings to countless Buddhas understands all meanings and principles and is also able to skillfully expound the Dharma.
Suppose fields throughout the ten directions were filled with rice, hemp, bamboo, and reeds;

even if those who possess sublime wisdom were to contemplate them together with single-minded focus for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges, they could not know the Buddha’s wisdom. Nor can the number of non-retrogressive bodhisattvas, which is like the sands of the Ganges, be known even if they were to seek it together with single-minded focus.
The first six phrases exclude those disciples who have exhausted their outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) yet lack such knowledge; the next four phrases exclude Śāriputra’s lack of knowledge;

the third section with six phrases excludes the other great disciples’ lack of knowledge; and the fourth section with eight phrases excludes the Pratyekabuddhas’ lack of knowledge—because Pratyekabuddhas contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) both in direct and reverse order, they are termed "those of sharp wisdom" (*tīkṣṇajñāna*), whereas the Buddha possesses true [knowledge].

The wise practitioner’s own practice of both the provisional and the real is called "real. The fifth section contains ten phrases that distinguish those bodhisattvas who have awakened the mind from others—namely, those who do not understand, or who refer to practitioners of the six perfections over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* who have not yet severed their afflictions, or those who have awakened the mind according to the two teachings (the Shared and the Distinct).
Each of these individuals is able to thoroughly comprehend the meaning and intent of the Four Noble Truths within their respective teaching, and they rely upon them accordingly.
Arising from the Four Great Vows, each is able to expound the teachings and the Way of the Dharma; as these unfold one after another toward the ultimate goal, they are all termed "wondrous wisdom.
Thus, the Tripitaka Teaching is called "wondrous" for its transcendence of the mundane world; the Shared Teaching is called "wondrous" for its thorough realization of emptiness;
and the Distinct Teaching is called "wondrous" for its reverent faith in the Middle Way. The sixth section contains four phrases for discernment.
The non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas do not know that, through the Shared Teaching (tongjiao), one severs the delusions within the realm;

though they have attained non-retrogression, they do not know the distinct principle and distinct teaching of the Middle Way. The three stages of the Sages (sanxian) of the Distinct Teaching, though they have attained non-retrogression in rank and practice, do not know that the Middle Way possesses all dharmas such that it is identical to all dharmas. △ Third, a retrospective verse on the ineffable realm.
Again he addressed Śāriputra: "The untainted, inconceivable, profound, subtle, and wondrous Dharma that I have now fully attained—only I know its characteristics;
the Buddhas of the ten directions are likewise."
This verse correctly praises how the Buddha has fully accomplished immeasurable, boundless, and unprecedented dharmas.
The final two lines are also a restatement: "Only a Buddha and a Buddha can exhaustively fathom the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
Regarding "untainted" (*anāsrava*): it refers to the pure, singular true nature; outside of this true nature, there are no other dharmas. Regarding "inconceivable": it refers to the mind.
The sphere of practice is the severance of the path of speech; "profound and subtle" refers exclusively to that which is realized and accorded with by all Buddhas.

Furthermore, based on the meaning of the untainted (*anāsrava*), the preceding explanation of the ten suchnesses (*daśa-tathatā*) in terms of the ten dharma-realms shows that the ten realms and ten suchnesses encompass the untainted nature-reality (*dharmatā*) of all ordinary beings and sages, and encompass the untainted nature of the three truths, thereby subsuming both the provisional and the ultimate.

Wisdom is without loss because it relies on the meaning of the inconceivable; as previously explained regarding the ten suchnesses in terms of their opening and closing, they are provisional yet real, and real yet provisional, and are therefore inconceivable. It relies on the meaning of the profound and subtle;
as previously explained regarding the ten suchnesses in terms of the Buddha-dharma realm, it relies solely on the fact that "this meaning is known only by me. As previously [stated],...
Regarding the ten suchnesses, the explanation according to their stages and the clarification of both [the provisional and the real] can be understood.

First, within the brief opening and manifestation, the long prose and the verse praise of the Buddha’s two wisdoms are concluded. △ Second, the verses that correctly and briefly open and manifest, which move [deep-seated] attachments and give rise to doubt, consist of two parts:
first, clarifying how all Buddhas reveal the reality; second, clarifying how Śākyamuni opens [the teaching]. These are explained alternately from one perspective. Now...
First: "Śāriputra, you should know that the words of all Buddhas do not differ; regarding the Dharma taught by the Buddha, you should give rise to great power of faith.
After a long time, the World-Honored One’s Dharma will surely proclaim the ultimate truth."
The statement that "the words of all Buddhas do not differ" reveals that the transformative teachings of all Buddhas are identical.
The following two lines exhort one to have faith, while the final two lines explicitly reveal the truth. One should see that everything previously explained was not ultimately real;

this is why past attachments were shattered and present doubts were born. The subsequent passage, which questions whether it might be a Māra manifesting as a Buddha, arises precisely from hearing these words.

Since the Buddha has already spoken these true words to encourage faith, for what reason would he instead provoke doubt? It is precisely to prevent slander arising from doubt that he must encourage faith.
△ Second, explaining how Śākyamuni opened the three [vehicles].
I address the assembly of śrāvakas and those seeking the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas—those whom I have caused to be liberated from the bonds of suffering and attain nirvāṇa.
By the power of skillful means, the Buddha has displayed the teaching of the three vehicles; for sentient beings are attached everywhere, and he leads them out by drawing them forth.
The first verse correctly identifies the three types of śrāvakas previously mentioned as recipients of gifts:

those of the Hīnayāna, those of the Pratyekabuddhayāna as the middle vehicle, and those who, through the six perfections over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, are liberated from the bonds of suffering and attain nirvāṇa as the Mahāyāna.
The next two lines directly refute these by stating that they are all merely provisional designations and collectively not real. The final two lines provide an explanation.
The intention to emerge from the three [realms] and lead others out of attachment is merely what cannot be avoided; this concludes the brief initial exposition.

△ Second, raising doubts and requesting instruction, which has two parts: first, describing the doubts; second, requesting a resolution. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, the narration by the sutra compiler;
second, the actual arising of the doubts. Now, the first section.
At that time, among the great assembly, there were twelve hundred śrāvakas, Arhats whose outflows were exhausted, such as Ājñātakauṇḍinya and others,
as well as bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās who had resolved their minds upon the paths of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha;
each of them thought to themselves:

Above, it was refuted that the three vehicles are all merely expedient means; now, the presentation of doubts focuses specifically on the two vehicles because their attachments are heavy and their doubts are deep, and thus they are singled out for mention.

However, in the subsequent section where the doubts are set forth, it says, "Those who seek Buddhahood, including the various bodhisattvas, number eighty thousand," from which we know that those of all three vehicles harbor these doubts. △ Second, the actual arising of the doubt.
Now, for what reason does the World-Honored One so earnestly praise skillful means and speak these words:
"The Dharma attained by the Buddha is extremely profound and difficult to understand; its intended meaning is hard to discern, and it is beyond the reach of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas"?
Yet the Buddha speaks of the single principle of liberation, saying that we too have attained this Dharma and reached nirvāṇa.
Now, I do not know where this meaning leads.
Why is it said that "the Dharma attained by the Buddha is extremely profound and difficult to understand"? This is a doubt regarding the Buddha’s ultimate wisdom (*bhūtajñāna*).

Why is it said that "his spoken words and underlying intentions are difficult to discern"? This is a doubt regarding the Buddha’s expedient wisdom (*upāyajñāna*). This is because the Buddha previously spoke of the three [vehicles]...
Riding upon wisdom, we realize the same truth without deviation; it is merely a matter of whether residual habits have been exhausted or not.
Now, you have suddenly praised the Tathāgata’s two types of wisdom as being beyond my reach, and for this reason, doubt has arisen.

When the Buddha speaks of the single meaning of liberation, [I previously] doubted whether the noble paths of the Three Vehicles that I have attained were truly the means of escape. I cultivated these principles...
Having reached Nirvana, he now suddenly says that all are merely expedient means (*upāya*) and we do not yet know which is the reality;
therefore, he says he does not know where this meaning leads. This concludes the initial narration of the doubt. II. Requesting a Decision.

This section contains three requests and two refusals; together with the preceding text, there are three refusals. The first refusal is because the principle is profound and difficult to understand. The first request is for his own sake.

Regarding his successive requests for a definitive resolution: the first instance of hesitation was due to alarm, doubt, and lack of faith; the subsequent request was because [the seeds of understanding] had been planted long ago and he would certainly comprehend;

the later instance of hesitation was due to slander and the certainty of falling into evil realms; the final request was because he possessed sharp faculties and would thereby obtain benefit—or because the Buddha knew in advance that benefits would accrue over three cycles and not all at once—and thus He suppressed him three times to await his third petition. Regarding this first petition, there are two parts. First:

The long prose section consists of two verses; the first long prose section has two parts: first, the expression of doubt, and second, the request for instruction. Now, regarding the first, the expression of doubt, there is doubt concerning the two types of wisdom.
At that time, Śāriputra, knowing that the fourfold assembly harbored doubts and that he himself had not yet fully understood, addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One..."
For what cause and for what reason do you so earnestly praise the Buddhas' foremost skillful means—the profound, subtle, and difficult-to-understand Dharma?
△ Second, the formal request; having finished [the initial inquiry], he requests the assembly to join him in the request.
Since time immemorial, I have never heard such a teaching from the Buddha as this. Now, the fourfold assembly all harbor doubts;
I only pray that the World-Honored One will expound upon this matter. For what reason does the World-Honored One so earnestly praise this most profound, subtle, and difficult-to-understand Dharma?

△ Second, the verses in praise [of the request] consist of five parts: first, a verse praising the doubt regarding the two wisdoms; second, a verse praising the doubts of the four assemblies regarding the three vehicles;
third, a verse praising one’s own doubt; fourth, a verse praising the doubts of the Buddha’s sons; and fifth, a general clarification of the shared doubts and requests. Now, the first part:
At that time, Śāriputra, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:

"The Great Holy Honored One, the Sun of Wisdom, has long since preached this Dharma. He himself declares that he has attained such inconceivable dharmas as the powers, the fearlessnesses, the samādhis, the dhyānas, and the liberations.
Regarding the Dharma obtained at the site of enlightenment, there is no one capable of posing a question about it."

My intention is difficult to fathom and there is none able to question me; yet, without being asked, I shall speak of my own accord, praising the path I have practiced—the wisdom that is most subtle and sublime, attained by all Buddhas.

"This Dharma" refers to the power of wisdom regarding reality (*tattva-jñāna-bala*) and the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), which point to the provisional wisdom; "attained at the site of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa-labdha*) points to the provisional and real of one's own practice (*sva-caryā*).

"My intention is difficult to fathom" points to the provisional and real of transforming others (*para-parivartana*)—it is difficult to fathom because these are skillful means (*upāya*) of the same essence.

"The path practiced" concludes the provisional of one's own practice, while "that which the Buddha has attained" concludes the real of one's own practice. "Spontaneous declaration without being asked" (*apṛṣṭa-svayaṃ-vyākaraṇa*) immediately establishes the transformation of others.
If his intention were not to transform others through his own practice, why would he praise himself spontaneously without being asked?
△ Second, the verse on the doubts of the three vehicles and the fourfold assembly:
"The various arhats free from outflows and those seeking nirvana now all fall into the net of doubt; for what reason does the Buddha preach this?"

Those bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs seeking pratyekabuddhahood, as well as the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and others, looked at one another with hesitation and gazed up at the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings, wondering: "What is this matter? We pray that the Buddha will explain it for us."

The first line clarifies the Hīnayāna; the second line clarifies the Mahāyāna of the Six Perfections; the subsequent verse clarifies the Madhyamāyāna as well as the fourfold assembly and so forth. △ Third, the verses express his own doubts:
"Among all the śrāvaka assembly, the Buddha declared me foremost; yet now, regarding my own wisdom, I am in doubt and cannot comprehend it."
Is this the ultimate dharma, or is it the path to be traversed?
The ultimate dharma is the fruit, while the path to be traversed is the cause. In the preceding passage, the Buddha rejected the three vehicles he had shown as being merely expedient means;
yet now one may wonder whether each of these three vehicles possesses its own cause and fruit, and that practicing and realizing them according to the teachings has never been erroneous.
If it is said that the skillful means are not ultimate reality, does this mean that the fruit which is realized is not real, or that the cause which is practiced is not true?
△ Fourth, the verse on the doubts of the Buddha’s sons.
"The sons born from the Buddha’s own mouth join their palms and gaze upward in expectation, wishing for the emergence of subtle and wondrous sounds; pray, speak at this time according to reality.
This refers to whether the Bodhisattvas of both the general and specific teachings have doubts or not; if they have no doubts, why do they join their palms and gaze upward in expectation?
△ Fifth, a general clarification of the shared request made out of doubt.
The devas, nāgas, spirits, and others, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; the bodhisattvas seeking buddhahood, numbering eighty thousand;
and the wheel-turning sage-kings from ten trillion lands, all joining their palms with reverent hearts, desiring to hear the complete path.
The first request was concluded. △ Second, to stop [the discourse] because of the fear that doubt might arise:
At that time, the Buddha told Śāriputra, "Stop, stop! There is no need to speak further.
If this matter were explained, all the devas and humans in the entire world would be struck with alarm and doubt."
△ Second, because their faculties were sharpened by past roots of merit, they harbored no doubt.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha once more, saying: "World-Honored One, we pray that you will speak; we pray that you will speak. Why is this?
Because the countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* beings in this assembly have all seen various Buddhas in the past, and their faculties [are matured]."
Those with sharp and penetrating wisdom who clearly understand what the Buddha has taught will be able to revere and believe it.
At that time, Śāriputra, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"O Dharma King, Supreme Honored One, please speak; have no concern. Among the immeasurable multitude in this assembly, there are those capable of revering and believing."
△ Third, because of the need to restrain and protect against overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
The Buddha again addressed Śāriputra: "If this matter were spoken, all the world—including devas, humans, and asuras—would be struck with alarm and doubt;
those monks possessed of overweening pride would fall into a great abyss. At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
He said: "Stop, stop! There is no need to speak; my Dharma is subtle and difficult to conceive. Those who possess overweening pride will certainly not show respect or faith upon hearing it.
△ Third, the request for an exposition on those who receive great benefit: throughout successive lifetimes they have been transformed by the teaching and do not give rise to overweening pride.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha again, saying: "World-Honored One, we pray that you will speak of this; we pray that you will speak of this.

Those in this assembly who are like us—hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of beings who have already been transformed by the Buddha throughout successive lifetimes—will surely be able to believe with reverence;
they will find peace and security for a long night and receive great benefit. At that time, Śāriputra...
Wishing to restate this meaning, he spoke these verses:
"O Unsurpassed Honored One among Two-legged Beings, I pray you will preach the supreme Dharma. I am the eldest son of the Buddha; please deign to analyze and explain it for me.
The immeasurable multitude in this assembly is able to reverently believe in this Dharma, for the Buddha has already taught and transformed such as these throughout successive lifetimes."
With single-minded devotion and palms joined together, we—these twelve hundred and others who seek Buddhahood—desire to hear and receive the Buddha’s words.
For the sake of this assembly, we pray that you will deign to analyze and expound them; upon hearing this Dharma, they shall give rise to great joy.
The first section, "Briefly Opening the Three to Reveal the One, Ending the Movement of Attachment and the Arising of Doubt," is complete.

△ Second, "Extensively Opening the Three to Reveal the One, Severing Doubt and Generating Faith," consists of three cycles. First, from this point until the end of the second fascicle, "Dedicating toward the Buddha-way," constitutes the first cycle of the Dharma-exposition (*dharmadeśanā*), through which those of superior faculties attain awakening. Next, from the passage where Śāriputra addresses the Buddha at that time...
The passage from "I now have no further doubt or regret" up to the "Chapter on Bestowing Prophecy" constitutes one cycle of teaching through parables for those of medium capacity to attain awakening.
The three chapters beginning with the "Parable of the Three Transformation Cities" constitute one cycle of teaching through causes and conditions for those of inferior capacity to attain awakening;

this is also termed the three cycles of principle, phenomena, and practice. Now, these shall be analyzed according to ten points: first, there are both general and specific aspects. Second... [and so forth].

1. There are those who are śrāvakas and those who are not śrāvakas; 2. there are differences in the thickness or thinness of the three delusions; 3. the four faculties may either transform or not transform;
4. the five faculties may either awaken or not awaken; 5. there is comprehension or lack of comprehension; 6. there is receiving a prediction or not receiving a prediction;
7. awakening has degrees of depth; 8. benefit is either provisional or ultimate; 9. there is waiting for the time or not waiting for the time. First, to clarify the general and the specific:

In its specific sense, the first week is called the "Teaching of the Dharma" (*dharmadeśanā*); in its general sense, it possesses all three [modes of teaching]. The phrase "like the *udumbara* flower, appearing only once in an age" is the "Exemplification" (*upamādeśanā*).
The statement "If I encounter sentient beings, I teach them all the Buddha-way" is the "Causal Narration" (*nidānadeśanā*).

In the second week, the specific name is the "Exemplification"; in its general sense, it likewise possesses all three. Previously, I did not say that all were for the sake of the Single Buddha-vehicle.

Therefore, the further differentiation of the single Buddha-vehicle into three is the teaching by way of Dharma (*dharmadeśanā*). Upon hearing this, the elder was startled and entered the burning house;

that he should then provide rescue and relief is the teaching by way of causes and conditions (*nidānadeśanā*). In the third week, the specific title "Causes and Conditions of Past Lives" (*pūrvayatanidāna*) also generally possesses these three [teachings]:
when the time for *nirvāṇa* arrived and the assembly was again purified, he caused them to enter the Buddha-wisdom (*buddhajñāna*). This is the teaching by way of meaning (*arthadeśanā*).
The "Dharma-explanation" (dharmadeśanā) refers to the direct teaching, while the "analogy-explanation" (aupamyadeśanā) refers to the metaphorical teaching.

Here, because we wish to follow the majority, the primary meaning, the concise, and the peripheral, and so that the terminology does not become confused, we employ a general term to capture a specific sense. Second, regarding the existence or non-existence of śrāvakas:
Guangzhai asserts that there must certainly be śrāvakas of actual practice; if one says there are no real ones, then what would the provisional ones be based upon?
The Kai-she (Kāśyapīya) school should be refuted as follows: They claim that there are certainly no śrāvakas who practice according to reality.

Citing the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*, they argue that those who have first engaged in the practices of the three vehicles are not deluded regarding the Dharma; since ordinary worldlings already know of the One Vehicle, how could there be two vehicles?

As for the fact that the sūtras speak of them, this is merely a provisional teaching (*upāya*). These two schools are biased in their attachments, deviating from the sūtras and losing the true meaning. If [the two vehicles] truly existed, why would the sūtras [speak otherwise]?
It is said that [the Buddha] merely transforms bodhisattvas and has no śrāvaka disciples; if these were definitively non-existent, who would enter the "transformed city" (nirvāṇa)?
Furthermore, if there were no three [vehicles], what provisional means (upāya) could there be to lead them? An objection is raised:

If it is said that there are actually śrāvakas who are led by provisional means, then there must also actually be a Tripiṭaka-Buddha who is led by a provisional Tripiṭaka-Buddha. If this is the case, [then...]
Question: If there are no Buddhas of the Tripitaka and only provisional Buddhas, for what reason do you not allow that there are only provisional Śrāvakas and no real Śrāvakas?
Answer: This point is not analogous. Those who truly sever the afflictions within the realm [of desire] are called real Śrāvakas, and the provisional ones correspond to them.
Where could there be a Buddha who merely severs the afflictions within the realm [of desire]?
Yet there is the Buddha of Expedient Means who responds to this Buddha. Now it is clarified that existence and non-existence must not be clung to one-sidedly:

if one observes from the perspective of the elder’s true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*), there is no hired laborer; yet if one approaches according to the faculties and nature of the impoverished son, he then considers himself a hired laborer.

The *Fahua lun* (Treatise on the Lotus Sutra) clarifies four kinds of śrāvakas: first, those of fixed destiny; second, those with overweening pride; third, those who regress; [and fourth, those who transform].
Regarding the four types of those who should be transformed, the first two are not granted predictions because they are not yet mature; the latter two are granted predictions.
According to this present sutra, there should be five types: first, those who have long practiced the Hīnayāna and whose path has now matured;

upon hearing the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle, they realize the fruit—these are identical to the "definitive śrāvakas" mentioned in the treatises. Second, those who were originally bodhisattvas who have cultivated the path for many kalpas.
In the interim, becoming weary of saṃsāra, they regress from the Great Vehicle and take up the Lesser; these are termed "distinct roots of goodness" in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
The Buddha, for their sake, establishes them in the Lesser Path and teaches them the *Saṃyukta-prajñāpāramitā*, enabling them to sever their fetters and attain the fruit.

Having regressed from the Great Vehicle not long ago and having practiced the Lesser for some time, it stands to reason that they should easily awaken; these correspond to the śrāvakas who have regressed from the Great Vehicle mentioned in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*.

Third, because of these two reasons, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas internally conceal [their true nature] while externally manifesting [as disciples], thereby accomplishing the guidance and reception that leads others to enter the Great Path;
this is the same as the "transformed śrāvakas" mentioned in the treatises.

Fourth, by seeing both the provisional and the ultimate types of śrāvakas as causes for escaping birth and death, they joyfully delight in nirvāṇa and cultivate the precepts, concentration, and wisdom to a slight degree.

When their contemplative wisdom has not yet entered the stage resembling the fruit (*sādṛśāvasthā*) and they perceive some slight attainment, claiming it to be the realization of the fruit—this is called "claiming what has not been attained as attained" and "claiming what has not been realized as realized. This is identical to the "arrogant śrāvakas" mentioned in the treatises.

Fifth, regarding Mahāyāna śrāvakas, this refers to those who cause all beings to hear the sound of the Buddha-way. If we categorize them according to the two types of those who definitely regress from the Mahāyāna:

Thus, regarding śrāvakas: from the perspective of Mahāyāna principle, they lack the "ash-like severance" (nirvāṇa) and do not dwell in the "transformed city," but ultimately return to the "jeweled destination.
Since this is the reality, there can be no provisional [status]. Therefore, there are no śrāvakas [in the ultimate sense].
Furthermore, those with overweening pride have not yet entered the stages and thus are not called "real"; nor are they emanations and thus are not called "provisional. If one grasps this meaning...
Existence and non-existence are perfectly clear; why must one struggle so bitterly in debate? Furthermore, regarding the existence or non-existence of śrāvakas within the Buddha-way:
if they are skillful means manifested as transformations, appearing externally with minor traces while internally concealing great virtues, then it is said that there are no Mahāyāna śrāvakas.
If, however, one follows their own practice to reveal their origins and manifest their fundamental nature, then it is said that there are Mahāyāna śrāvakas. Now, this is opened up.
The provisional revelation of reality is precisely for the purpose of leading the two types of śrāvakas who are certain to regress from the Great Vehicle so that they may become Mahāyāna śrāvakas;
once their own practice is established, they are able to serve as transformation śrāvakas. If one grasps this intent, one will penetrate both existence and non-existence.
Third, regarding the thickness or thinness of delusions, this refers to the distinctions among ignorance and secondary afflictions, as well as to the faculties of the Mahāyāna.

Regarding their dispositions (*gotra*), there are four permutations: first, those with light afflictions and sharp faculties; second, those with heavy afflictions and sharp faculties; third, those with light afflictions and dull faculties;
and fourth, those with heavy afflictions and dull faculties. If one has light secondary afflictions and sharp faculties, one attains awakening upon the first hearing.
If one has heavy afflictions and sharp faculties, one attains awakening upon the second hearing. If one has light afflictions and dull faculties, one attains awakening upon the third hearing. If...
Those whose delusions are heavy and whose faculties are dull cannot attain awakening even after hearing the teaching three times; they merely serve as an assembly for establishing karmic connections.

Alternatively, the first two lines may represent those with sharp faculties who constitute the superior root, the third line represents the middling root, and the fourth line represents the inferior root.
Or again, the first line may represent the superior root, while the second and third lines together represent the middling root.

The fourth phrase regarding the faculties refers to those of inferior capacity. Furthermore, with respect to the first category of ignorance, there are three layers that can obscure the Middle Way of the initial stage.
For those of superior capacity, it is taught that upon hearing this initial method of practice, these three layers of ignorance are exhausted simultaneously;
they open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, enter the rank of Bodhisattvas, and receive the prediction of enlightenment (*bodhi*). Those of middling capacity sever only two of these layers.

Those of inferior capacity sever only the first stage; subsequently, an analogy is provided for those of middling capacity, who sever the third stage completely, opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and receiving the prediction of Bodhi.

Later, when those of inferior capacity advance to sever the second stage, a causal explanation is given, at which time those of inferior capacity sever all three stages completely and receive the prediction of Bodhi. Fourth, regarding whether the faculties transform or not: according to the old [commentary]...

It is said that those of superior faculties (agradhika) attain awakening immediately upon hearing the Dharma-discourse (dharmadeśanā); those of middling faculties (madhyendriya) subsequently become equal to those of superior faculties;

and those of inferior faculties (mṛdvindriya) subsequently become equal to those of middling faculties. When the discourse of parables (avadāna) is given, those of middling faculties—who had previously become superior—can now attain awakening;

those of inferior faculties—who had previously become middling—now subsequently become equal to those of superior faculties. When the discourse on causes and conditions (nidāna) is given, those of inferior faculties—who had previously become superior—[attain awakening].
Therefore, regarding the attainment of awakening, if it were as you say, then all who awaken would possess superior faculties; how then could they be designated as having three grades of faculties?

If all were called those of superior faculties, what purpose would there be in distinguishing between the sharp and the dull? Indeed, the minds of sentient beings are unstable: when they encounter adverse conditions, their sharp faculties turn dull;
when they encounter favorable conditions, their dull faculties turn sharp. This is because in previous lives they encountered Buddhas and heard the Dharma.
Among those who have transformed their faculties, there are some who transform from the lower or middle grades to the superior grade and attain awakening through the direct teaching of the Dharma;

there are some who transform from the lower to the middle grade and attain awakening through the parable-based teaching; and there are some who did not transform in previous lives and must wait for all three cycles before attaining awakening.
Such differences in the transformation of faculties are explained by the old commentators as being like using three types of axes to chop wood: the sharp axe [requires only one strike].

When cutting, that which is sharp severs in two strokes, while that which is dull severs in three strokes; yet the designation "sharp" or "dull" does not change, for the place where the wood is severed remains the same.
The blade is a metaphor for the faculties (indriya) and the teaching; the wielder of the blade is a metaphor for the practitioner and the instruction;

the act of cutting is a metaphor for the Buddha; the recipient of the teaching is a metaphor for one who hears the Dharma; the brandishing of the blade is a metaphor for the application of contemplation (vipaśyanā); and the severing of the wood is a metaphor for realization and entry (praveśa).

The analogy of the whetstone refers to the transformation of faculties (*indriya*) from previous lives; because the conditions for whetting differ, there are those who are sharp and those who are dull.

In this context, attaining awakening upon hearing the Dharma seems to pertain primarily to the practitioner by faith (*śraddhādhimukta*), yet it is not without inclusion of the practitioner by dharma (*dharmānusārin*).

This is because, due to the differing ways in which faith and the Dharma mutually supported one another during past lives, they manifest differently. However, within a single sitting, there should not be sixty-four rounds of questioning.

Question: At the stage of the first dwelling (*ādikṣānti*), are there still distinctions between those of sharp and dull faculties? Answer: When the essence of true cultivation (*bhūtayoga*) is manifested, there are no longer such gradations. Question:
If that is so, from the first dwelling upward, when one again engages in cultivation through conditions (*pratyaya-yoga*), are there still differences of excellence or inferiority?

Answer: For those within this same stage, there is no further distinction of victory or defeat; since the essence of true cultivation is fused, how could there be any difference? This clarifies that there is awakening according to one's faculties.
Regarding those who do not awaken, the sutras frequently clarify that Bodhisattvas constitute the superior faculty, Pratyekabuddhas the middling faculty, and Śrāvakas the inferior faculty.
If this were the case, would it necessarily follow that all Bodhisattvas attain awakening during the first three weeks? This is not necessarily so;
from the three weeks onward, through the dissemination of the teaching and the *Nirdeśa-parivarta*, there are various Bodhisattvas who attain the realization of non-arising at each successive stage.

Question: Why must the Śrāvakas be restricted to the scope of the "Teaching of the Dharma" (dharmadeśanā-parivarta), while the Pratyekabuddhas are not restricted to the scope of the "Simile and Parable" (aupamya-parivarta)?

This can also be understood. Answer: One might ask whether the awakening of Bodhisattvas extends through both the beginning and the end [of the three assemblies], and whether the awakening of the Two Vehicles should likewise extend to the latter [assembly].

The answer is that once the nature of the father-son relationship has been definitively established across the three assemblies, they are all designated as Bodhisattvas, even if their realization occurs later.
Regarding the sixth point, "The Bodhisattvas of the Same Name Attain Enlightenment," it clarifies those who have attained understanding and those who have not.

If the three vehicles attain enlightenment equally, for what reason do we see only the Śrāvakas attaining understanding while the other two do not? Herein it is clarified that those who appear in the world when no Buddha is present and attain enlightenment upon hearing the Buddha’s teaching on the law of causes and conditions are called Pratyekabuddhas (Solitary Realizers), such as Mahākāśyapa of the householder’s life.

Śāriputra and the others all possess the faculties and nature of the Middle Vehicle; having entered among the ranks of the śrāvakas, they attained awakening and understanding no differently than the bodhisattvas.

As for those who have not yet attained such understanding, the Śrāvaka teachings do not clarify the attainment of Buddhahood. This present sutra opens the path for them to return to the Great Vehicle.
Fearing that their own understanding might be erroneous, they recount their realization before the Buddha; the bodhisattvas do not do so.
Furthermore, there are three reasons why there is no need for formal acknowledgment (*anujñāna*): first, the original intention of the Bodhisattvas was to seek Buddhahood;
even if they held divergent attachments, those attachments were slight, and since they would ultimately attain Buddhahood, they had no anxiety that they might fail to do so.

Now, hearing the teachings of the three turnings of the wheel merely serves to rectify their contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*), and thus formal acknowledgment is unnecessary. Second, there are many instances where the Bodhisattvas have already realized the Great [Truth].

The text concerning the two vehicles attaining Buddhahood begins with the present teaching; as it was transmitted according to its essential points, the Bodhisattva’s realization of the Sanskrit original is abbreviated, or perhaps certain Chinese omissions were not recorded.
Third, the stage and practice of the Bodhisattvas are profound and transcendent, such that all junior Bodhisattvas do not dare to explain their realization.
The explanation of the *āyus-pramāṇa* (lifespan) is concluded. Maitreya now provides a comprehensive summary of the realization, beginning from "From the beginning... [until] "no... [etc.].

When the patience regarding the arising of dharmas (*utpatti-dharma-kṣānti*) is perfected and only one final birth remains, one has fully realized and understood [the truth]; what further thing could one seek? 7.

Regarding those who have received a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) and those who have not: if both equally possess full realization, why do the Śrāvakas receive a prediction while the Pratyekabuddhas and Bodhisattvas do not?
This also has three meanings. First, it clarifies that the two vehicles [Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha] entered [the path] in the past...
Those established in the correct position (*samyaktva-niyāma*) are unable to resolve their minds toward enlightenment; how, then, could they receive a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*)?

Now, having awakened to the Great [Vehicle] and rejoicing in this distinct certainty, he is therefore granted a prediction regarding his eon and realm. Because a Bodhisattva resolves their mind to seek Buddhahood and achieves it through the fulfillment of their practice, they do not rejoice in seeking Buddhahood with haste, nor is the prediction conferred prematurely.
Furthermore, in the previous teachings, predictions were conferred upon Bodhisattvas at various points; this is the constant rule.

It is said that here we are merely following the essential points of the transmission and translation; yet, since there are also predictions for the two bodhisattvas, as well as for Devadatta and the dragon girl, are these not also predictions?

Furthermore, the "Chapter on the Dharma Master" states: "Those who seek the vehicle of the śrāvaka, those who seek the vehicle of the pratyekabuddha, and those who seek the path of the Buddha—all such types as these, having heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* in the presence of the Buddha, I bestow upon them all the [prediction of]..."

When it is said that Bodhi bestows this prediction, does this not mean that all have been predicted? This is because the followers of the Two Vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas) have never previously received a prediction regarding the eight signs [of a Buddha's life];
thus, he predicts their eon and land. As for the Bodhisattvas, they have already received predictions previously, so they are not explained again here.

Predictions concerning the near-term are obtained at the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), which is what Bodhisattvas rejoice in; however, this is a prediction of the ultimate, wondrous enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) in the distant future, and therefore [the text speaks of] his lifespan.
In the *Pramāṇa-pariccheda*, from the initial generation of the bodhicitta until the attainment of the wondrous cause in one lifetime, the ultimate fruit is suddenly perfected;

this is the bestowal of the prediction of the Dharmakāya. Why, then, is it called "unpredictable" (*avyākṛta*)? Question: If those of the Hīnayāna have already awakened to the Great Way, they should likewise receive the prediction of the Dharmakāya.
How is it that they instead receive the prediction of the eight phases [of a Buddha]? Answer: The eight phases are the prediction for the Nirmāṇakāya (the responsive body). Since...

The reason for granting a definitive prediction (vyākaraṇa) is that [the Buddha] knows there must be a fundamental cause, and wishing to lead sentient beings to hear this and together form karmic conditions, he grants the prediction accordingly.

Furthermore, if these followers of the Two Vehicles hear of the lifespan, they will likewise increase their progress on the path, diminish their remaining births, and obtain the prediction of attaining the Dharma-body.
Eighth, regarding the clarity that there are varying depths of awakening: at first glance, it is the same as destroying ignorance and entering the first stage of the Perfect Teaching (Vimalā-bhūmi).

If one investigates minutely, one must surely clarify what was initially obscure. Having first heard the teaching of the Dharma and already entered the Buddha’s wisdom, upon hearing the teaching through parables, how could it not be further clarified?
Furthermore, hearing the principle of causes and conditions will surely lead to progress; hearing the teaching on the lifespan even more so, becoming increasingly profound and deep.

This is like a person who hears the Dharma again and thus excels their former understanding, just as one who receives clothing in the cold finds that single or double layers differ in their thickness and warmth.

9. Clarifying that there are both provisional and real benefits for those in existence: some say that those of real practice obtain benefit, while those of provisional practice are merely intended as a means to guide and attract followers, regardless of whether they actually receive benefit.
Now it is clarified that this is not so. If one reaches the stage of the Lifespan (Āyuṣpramāṇa), both the provisional and the real obtain benefit;

the path is further enhanced and birth is further exhausted until one approaches the ultimate limit of the Perfect (Samantabhadra) and remains with only one more birth—how could this not be the provisional?
Is this not beneficial? For this reason, at the beginning, [the Buddha] acts as an influence and a shadow to bring about the maturation of the practice of reality (*satyābhisamaya*).

Later, when the ultimate fruit is explained, it is stated that the path is self-evident: "The profit from the inhalation and exhalation of breath, as well as the profit from throughout other lands, being within oneself is one's own benefit.

The benefit gained through the practice of reality arises due to the power of provisional guidance and transformation; since this merit returns to oneself, the provisional [teachings] also gain benefit. Therefore, the Buddha...
When preaching the Dharma with a single voice, sentient beings each attain understanding according to their own kind;

why then must one necessarily wait for the full span of a lifespan before allowing them to benefit through provisional means? The Bodhisattvas emerging from the earth say, "We ourselves also wish to obtain this truly pure Great Dharma," which is itself self-benefit.
Regarding the distinction between waiting for the time and not waiting for the time, it refers to the period prior to that.

Those who have not yet awakened and must wait for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* to awaken are said to "wait for the time"; those who have already awakened through the previous teachings are said to be "not waiting for the time.

Why is this? Because the Buddha has two modes of teaching, the exoteric and the esoteric. If we rely on the exoteric teaching, before the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the followers of the Two Vehicles had not yet awakened to the Great Way;
they required the ripening of the five flavors [of the Dharma] before finally converging in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Therefore, it is so called.

The reason why [the Buddha] had not yet spoken was that the time had not yet arrived; now, precisely, is the time. He has definitively expounded the Mahāyāna—this is what it means for [the teaching] to "await the time.
If one speaks according to the esoteric [teachings], it is not necessarily required to await the five flavors; it is only in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* that this is fully realized.
As for those who entered [the path] through the esoteric teachings prior to that, it is called "not awaiting the time. This is a general distinction between the timely and the untimely.
If we consider the three turnings of the wheel, these are also categorized as "dependent on time" and "independent of time.

Regarding the two gates of the trace and the source, these likewise involve being dependent or independent of time, which accounts for the sequential nature of awakening and entry. Within the three turnings, specifically concerning the esoteric [teaching], at the time of the Dharma-exposition, one hears the secret revelation of the Great Vehicle and the event of the Great Universal Penetration to attain awakening and entry; this is precisely what is meant by being "independent of time."

In the middle [section], it is known that this can be understood by analogy with what was heard in the *Zhōuzhì* (Threefold Profound). Question: If the three cycles and the original existence (*benyǒu*) are spoken of as "profound" (*mì*), why does the *Xuánwén* (Profound Text) state that only the *Fahua* reveals [the truth]?
Answer: Regarding "revealed" (*xiǎn*) and "profound" (*mì*): prior to this, the partial (*piān*) and the complete (*yuán*) were mutually unknown;

now, upon reaching this sutra, they enter together into the single completeness. Although it is profound, it is revealed because it is of a pure, single flavor. It is only within... *(Note: The provided source text ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion of the text.)*
In one assembly, [the Buddha] knew both those who waited and those who did not wait, and his proclamation was manifest;

he bestowed predictions upon the followers of the Two Vehicles with clear and explicit clarity, and regarding their long lifespans, there was no one present in that assembly who did not hear and know it—therefore, this is called "manifest" (khyāta). Question:

There is a certain class of root-nature who received no secret benefit during the previous four periods, nor did they attain the manifest [benefit] until the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*; how is it that they are said to have attained both?
Question: Does "missing the time" mean that one will never attain awakening because the opportunity has been lost? Answer: In other sutras, this may indeed be called missing the time;

however, this is not the case here. Although such a person does not awaken during either the esoteric or the exoteric periods and conceives the thought of having attained parinirvāṇa, they shall hear this sutra in that land; therefore, there is no such thing as missing the time.
Question: Is this merely waiting for the time of that land? Question: Should the five thousand [disciples] who rose and departed not be considered having missed their opportunity? Answer:

These individuals will likewise receive benefit from those who propagate the sutra after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa; this too is a matter of waiting for the proper time. The threefold exposition, analyzed according to ten meanings, is concluded.
Regarding the first, the Exposition of the Dharma, it is divided into five parts: first, the formal exposition of the Dharma; second, Śāriputra...

The section on the understanding [of the teaching] consists of four parts: (1) the three Tathāgatas’ exposition and confirmation, (2) the bestowing of the prophecy, (3) the joy of the fourfold assembly, and (4) the initial and intermediate sections.

Within the first [section], there are two parts: (A) the prose text and (B) the verse recitation. Within the first of these, there are three parts: (i) the granting of permission, (ii) the receiving of the mandate, and (iii) the actual discourse.
Within the first of these [three], there are again three sub-sections: (a) the permissive grant, (b) the admonitory grant, and (c) the selective grant. This is the first.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra: "Since you have already made your request with such earnestness three times, how could I not speak?
Since you have been so persistent and compliant, how could I not speak? This is the granting of permission. △ Second, the admonition and permission.
Listen attentively now and reflect upon it well; I shall explain it to you in detail for you.

The first two phrases are an exhortation, and the last phrase is a promise. "Listen attentively" refers to the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*); "reflect well" refers to the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*);
and "keep it in mind" refers to the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). A great sutra states: "First, associate with virtuous friends; second, listen [to the Dharma]."
First, hearing the True Dharma; second, contemplating its meaning; third, practicing according to the teaching—these four factors alone are the causes for Nirvana.
To say that ascetic practices are the cause of Nirvana is impossible. A single "Good Friend" refers to the Tathāgata.
Since the latter three phrases correspond to the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*), the Buddha cautioned [the practitioners] regarding this Nirvana.
"Pan" (槃) refers to the proximate causes and conditions. △ Third, the exclusion and acceptance:

At the time these words were spoken, there were five thousand people in the assembly—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—who immediately rose from their seats, prostrated to the Buddha, and withdrew. Why was this? Because the roots of transgression for these individuals were deep and heavy.
Furthermore, there are those with overweening pride who claim to have attained what they have not attained and claim to have realized what they have not realized;
because such faults exist, the World-Honored One remained silent and did not restrain them. At that time, the Buddha said to Śāriputra:

"In this assembly of mine now, there are no longer any branches or leaves, but only the pure and the substantial. Śāriputra, it would be well indeed if such people of overweening pride were to withdraw."
"Listen well now; I shall speak for you.
From the beginning up to the point of their withdrawal is also excellent. "Listen well now" is the selection [of the audience], and it is also the permission [to speak].

Because five thousand people were seated in the assembly, the Tathāgata had previously halted him three times; now, as he is about to grant permission to speak, he uses his majestic spiritual power to have them depart, which is why this is called "selecting the assembly. (5)
To perceive many obstacles as turbid while regarding minor ones as significant; to hold that great obscurations are deep-rooted while failing to realize one has attained the three fruits;

to claim one has attained the three fruits when one has not; or to claim one has realized the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) when one has not—such as mistakenly identifying the four dhyānas as the four fruits—these are termed "overweening pride" (*adhimāna*).
To possess such faults refers to the three defects of obscuration, attachment, and pride. [The text concludes with: "Remaining silent..."
Regarding the prohibition [of the teaching]: when the three were briefly revealed and the one was manifested above, the words were concise yet the meaning was profound;

as such, slander had not yet arisen, and it served as a sufficient cause and condition for fastening the jewel. Departing [from this land] would have been beneficial. However, if the three were extensively revealed and the one manifested, it would have contradicted their sentiments and incited slander;
remaining [in this land] would have caused harm. For this reason, I did not prohibit it. As for "no more branches or leaves": the branches and leaves are minute.

"At the end, they are not fit for the vessels of utility"—this refers to those who cling to the expedient means of expedient means (wherein the four fruits of the Lesser Vehicle are already expedients, yet they falsely reckon the stages of *ūṣmagata* and *mūrdhan* as ultimate).
Because they are not vessels for the Great [Vehicle], the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "To grasp at branches and cling to leaves while abandoning the root—such a person is not wise.
This is precisely that meaning. "It would even be better to retreat" means that since one has already obscured oneself with the small.

Furthermore, it would have obstructed the great radiance of others; now that he has withdrawn, there is no fault of slandering the Dharma, nor is there the transgression of hindering others—thus it is said to be "excellent.
Since the branches and leaves have not yet been removed, the Tathāgata’s three refusals were sincere, and his true wish was for [Śāriputra] to hear [the teaching].

Therefore, when Śāriputra made his four requests, the Master and Disciple discerned the capacity [of the assembly]; it was not merely a matter of being parsimonious or withholding. Question: The Buddha possesses great compassion; why does he not employ supernatural powers?
He forcibly causes them to remain [in their state] so that they do not hear, like the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) who are deaf and mute within the *Avataṃsaka*. Why?

Because there is a specific reason for each case. At the conclusion of the *Avataṃsaka*, the gradual teaching (*ānupūrvika-dharma*) had already been opened, yet the attachments of the Lesser Vehicle had not yet been destroyed;
thus, while they were seated, they were separated from the truth. Now, at this very moment, one intends to extinguish their delusions and destroy those attachments.
The hermitage must be cleared of those who would slander; if they depart together, they will slander. One should speak firmly, as in the case of Nandika:
"If you go now, there will be benefit; why then do you insist on staying? If you stay, there will be harm; why then do you refuse to leave?

By speaking firmly out of compassion so that Nandika might gain benefit from being sent far away, the Tathāgata protects him from slandering out of his protective care (*maitrī*), and dispatches him out of his compassion (*karuṇā*).
Mañjuśrī asked, "If those who were destined for suffering have been removed and only five thousand remain in the assembly, they will not receive benefit; what then is the use of their departure?

The Buddha replied, "These are not those for whom the teaching is intended (the *dharmapātra*), but merely people with whom I have formed a karmic connection (*pratyaya*). In the past, during the time of the Buddha Mahāvairocana, there were also immeasurable sentient beings whose minds gave rise to doubt.
They have been born together with their teacher life after life, and now they have all attained deliverance—even until the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata."
Even later, these five thousand people have still not exhausted [their faults]; it should be known that the same applies to them.

Furthermore, when this Great Sūtra was being preached, there were eighty-five thousand *koṭis* of people who did not give rise to faith in this sūtra; such persons shall also attain faith in the future.
By analogy with this case, their benefit will likewise be realized before long. The first section, "The Initial Granting," concludes. II. Receiving the Mandate.
Śāriputra said, "So be it, World-Honored One; I wish most earnestly to hear it.
This was the fourth request, following the three previous ones.

First, the formal exposition of the long passage on the preaching of the True Dharma: first, the granting of permission; second, the receiving of the mandate, concluded. △ Third, the actual exposition, which is divided into two parts.

The first four chapters on the Buddhas extensively explain the provisional and real aspects of the various Buddhas; the chapter on Śākyamuni extensively explains the provisional and real aspects of Śākyamuni.

The fewer phrases in the former sections are due to textual brevity, while the general statement "all Buddhas" is a brevity of person; however, the principle of "opening the three to reveal the one" is a brevity of meaning.
In this [chapter], the majority of the sections and phrases are extensive in text, clarifying the five Buddhas as the extensiveness of person, and extensively clarifying [the teaching].
The sixth section consists of six parts for the broad exposition of this meaning: first, praising the rarity of the Dharma; second, declaring that there is no falsehood;

third, revealing the provisional means (*upāya*); fourth, demonstrating the ultimate reality; fifth, citing the five turbidities to explain the provisional; and sixth, distinguishing the false to encourage faith. Praising the Dharma is intended to engender respect;
declaring that there is no falsehood is to stop slander; and revealing the provisional means is so that one does not remain attached to them.
The "Small Exposition of Reality" is intended to cause awakening; the "Great Exposition" uses the five turbidities to demonstrate that the three [vehicles] must be bestowed.
To exclude the false and ensure reality, each of the five Buddha-chapters should fully contain the six meanings, though these appear interchangeably throughout.
Where they are not complete, it is because the Tathāgata’s skillful teaching employs brevity without deficiency and directness without prolixity.

Furthermore, regarding the six meanings, their sequence is likewise indeterminate. (Their manifestation is vivid; the general principle is that these six meanings together accomplish the revelation of the great purport.

For instance, the Buddhas of the three periods each have only two chapters—is this not extremely concise yet complete in its revelation? By omitting four chapters, the text avoids prolixity. "Reaching" means "attaining. Regarding the indeterminacy of sequence:

among the essentials of the six chapters, none surpasses the revelation of the truth. As for the mutual indeterminacy of sequence, the remaining four chapters merely exist as meanings within the six; they collectively form a single intent and need not follow a fixed order. The first four Buddha-chapters constitute two [sections].

First, a general clarification regarding all Buddhas; second, a listing of the Buddhas of the three periods. Regarding the first [section], there are only four parts: first, praising the rarity of the Dharma;

second, stating that there is no falsehood; third, opening up the provisional means; and fourth, revealing the ultimate reality. As for the "lacking two meanings," this refers to the subsequent text. Now, for the first part:
The Buddha told Śāriputra: "Such a wondrous Dharma as this is preached by the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, only at rare intervals;
it appears but once in a long while, like the udumbara flower.
Herein, both the teaching and the simile together praise the Buddhas: whenever they appear in the five turbidities, they must first open the Three Vehicles, as is the case in the present world."
For over forty years, the Honored One has manifested the truth; because it was rare and long withheld, it is said that he speaks only at the proper time.
That he did not speak for so long was because people were not yet capable, the time had not yet arrived, and the five thousand [unworthy] had not been dismissed.
Now that people are capable, the time has arrived, and the five thousand have departed; since he will definitely preach the Mahāyāna, it is said that he speaks only at the proper time.

Regarding the udumbara flower—here called the "Auspicious Omen" (ling-shui)—it appears once every three thousand years; furthermore, its appearance coincides with the emergence of a Golden Wheel-turning King.
This signifies that only after the beings of the Three Vehicles have been matured through training does one preach the Sublime Dharma and bestow the prediction of Buddhahood upon the Dharma King.

Moreover, it is only after passing through the three flavors of curd, cream, and ghee that one finally speaks of the clarified butter (sarpirmanda). As for the interpretation through the contemplation of the mind, this refers to the "Middle" and the "Sublime."
Contemplating that all phenomena penetrate to the true reality (dharmatā) is called "spiritual" (*ling*);

because one possesses this contemplation, one necessarily receives the Buddha’s prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), which is termed "omen" (*shuai*). Because one attains the fruit of Buddhahood through this contemplation, it is termed "flower" (*hua*).
△ Second, the teaching is not false.
Śāriputra, you all should believe what the Buddha has spoken; his words are not false.
This principle is most profound and differs from the provisional principles of the past; this teaching is most subtle and contrasts with the provisional teachings of the past;
this practice is most universal and diverges from the provisional practices of the past; this person is most supreme, surpassing those who were inferior in the past—this refers back to the guest.
Having previously practiced the four kinds of coarse [teachings], they now all perceive them as sublime;

fearing that sentient beings might harbor doubts or slander, he first exhorts them to have faith, so that they may believe that the person who speaks the non-false dharma is himself without falsehood. △ Third, the opening of the skillful means (upāya): first, the opening;
second, the explanation; third, the conclusion. Now, the first.
Śāriputra, the Buddhas teach the Dharma according to what is appropriate; their underlying intentions are difficult to comprehend.
They skillfully employ expedient means to teach in accordance with the three types of capacities, yet people are unable to understand that the Buddha’s intent lies in the ultimate reality.
△ Second, the explanation.
Why is this so? Because I have expounded all dharmas through innumerable skillful means, various causes and conditions, parables, and verbal expressions.
By citing the sovereign power of the present Buddha, one explains that the skillful means, ingenuity, and wisdom of all Buddhas are identical;
thus, by using this to explain that, one should know that the Buddhas' revelation of their provisional teachings is also like my own. △ Third, the conclusion.
This Dharma cannot be understood through deliberation or discrimination; only the Buddhas can know it.
This passage establishes the intent of "opening the provisional" (kaiquan), for its meaning is difficult to comprehend.

Generally, those who receive the teachings all say that there are three [vehicles] and that only the Buddhas know the one. This text has two directions: if it is taken as revealing the reality (shizhenshi), then...
This pertains to the initial section of the subsequent text, which designates the person of superior capacity and the Dharma. The non-conceptual Dharma can only be known by a Buddha;

because the Buddha understands and realizes the non-conceptual Dharma through non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), this reveals the reality. △ Four: Demonstrating the True Reality. 1. First, designating the person of superior capacity and the Dharma.
2. Second, designating the intention for appearing in the world. 3. Third, reiterating the demonstration. 4. Fourth, the formal explanation. 5. Fifth, the summary.
The opening text of the first section is as before. Second, the intention for appearing in the world is indicated:
Why is this? It is because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world solely for the sake of the one great causal matter.
This is explained in two parts: first, the general overview; second, the detailed analysis. Regarding the first, the general overview:
following the preceding text, it asks why this Dharma cannot be understood through conceptual thought or discrimination, and why only the Buddhas are able to know it.

This is because the Buddhas have awakened to the aspect of reality as it truly is (*yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa*), and by riding upon this true path, they appear in the world solely to enable sentient beings to attain [enlightenment].
This true reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa) has no other reality; because its true reality is signless (animitta), subtle, and supreme, it cannot be understood through conceptualization or discrimination.
Next, regarding the analysis by means of characters: "One" refers to the one true reality. It is not three, not five, not seven, and not nine;

therefore, it is called "one. (The "three" refers to the Three Vehicles; the "five" adds humans and devas; the "seven" adds the two vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; the "nine" adds the common and distinct Bodhisattvas.)
Its nature is vast and expansive because it encompasses three, five, seven, nine, and so forth; thus it is called "Great.

It is called "Affair" (事) because it is the ritual procedure for the appearance of all Buddhas in the world. It is called "Cause" (因) because sentient beings possess this capacity for resonance and response.

It is called "Condition" (緣) because the Tathāgata responds by seizing upon that capacity. This constitutes the fundamental intent of appearing in the world, and thus he first opened the Three [Vehicles].

This is merely a preliminary lead-in; just as when a person wishes to take something, they must first give it to him, so too, although various paths are taught, in reality, they constitute a single vehicle (*ekayāna*). △ Third, the demonstration.
Śāriputra, what is meant by saying that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world solely for the sake of one great cause and condition?
Being about to provide an explanation, [the Buddha] again raises this question as a starting point for his discourse; furthermore, this "Great Matter" is that which the Buddhas hold most sacred.
This is as clarified in the *Śāstra*: the King, our father, desired to hear the names and enumerations of the Crown Prince so many times that he never grew weary of speaking them.
△ Fourth, the correct explanation refuting past [interpretations] and not recording [them]: Since reality is now revealed, all immeasurable dharmas are one.
As in the *Xuanyi*, the Ten Subtleties (*daśa-prakaraṇa*) are ten kinds of oneness. If one briefly harmonizes [this with]...

The ancient commentary provisionally establishes four "onenesses. First, regarding the "oneness of the immeasurable": it means that every single form and every single fragrance is none other than the Middle Way;
this meaning is readily understandable. Regarding the "oneness of the ten [meanings]": although the textual arrangement is not sequential, the ten meanings remain complete without deficiency.
The statement, "This Dharma cannot be understood through deliberation or discrimination," reveals the oneness of principle (*li-yi*); there is only the various...
That the Buddha alone is able to know this reveals that wisdom is singular; "only for the sake of the one great matter" means that "one" is principle (*li*) and "great" is wisdom (*zhi*).

(Wisdom can illuminate objects, and only then does one realize the greatness of the object; therefore, "great" refers to wisdom. "Matter" (*shi*) refers to practice (*xing*) (both self-cultivation and transforming others are called "matter").
Principle gives rise to wisdom, and wisdom guides practice; following this meaning, it reveals that practice is singular. As for "knowing and seeing," wisdom knows [the object].

The principle-eye perceives the Truths; when the principle of the Truths is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), there is no discrimination. Based on these unconditioned dharmas, distinctions are established.
Through this, the exposition of knowledge, vision, realization, and entry—from the concise to the extensive—is presented, comprising forty stages.

This is the manifestation of the stages. Furthermore, taking the concluding phrases, it clarifies that each [stage] is the Dharmakāya and the Great is Prajñā. This is the aspect of phenomena (*dharma*).
That liberation is the secret treasury; this reveals the oneness of the three dharmas. Its appearance in the world reveals the oneness of response and resonance (*saṃgati*).
Its teaching solely for bodhisattvas reveals the oneness of the retinue. All that it performs reveals the oneness of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).
It reveals the oneness of benefit by using only the Buddha’s knowledge and vision to instruct and awaken sentient beings; it does so solely because of the One Buddha Vehicle.

Expounding the Dharma for sentient beings, this sutra text clarifies the meaning of the "Seal of the Single Dharma" (dharmaparyāya-mudrā); its truth is like a tally and its seal. Now, I shall briefly harmonize the ancient commentaries into four points:
first, the identity of number but difference in meaning. The ancients spoke of "one fruit," whereas now we speak of "one principle.
This relies on both the meaning and the text. Regarding reliance on the meaning: if there were no single principle, all matters would be inverted, and everything would be the teaching of Māra.
Since this is no longer a Buddhist scripture, it is necessary that the principle be one and the text be followed. The text speaks of the Buddha’s "knowledge and vision" (*jñāna-darśana*);

taking what is known and what is seen, that which is known is the truth (*satya*), and that which is seen is the object (*viṣaya*). Since the object and the truth are the reality-mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), they are called the "one principle.
