The old translation says "causes are one," where the term is singular but its meaning is distinct; the current translation says "practice is one," which universally encompasses both cause and effect for the person.

The first teaching and its title are identical in wording to the previous [text], which consists of four parts: first, clarifying the principle; second, clarifying the person; third, clarifying the practice; and fourth, clarifying the teaching. Now, for the first [part]: [The text continues: "The first teaching and its name are the same as the old version; this constitutes the four [sections]: first, elucidating the principle; second, elucidating the person; third, elucidating the practice; and fourth, elucidating the teaching. Now, for the first [section].
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world because they desire to cause sentient beings to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision so that it may become pure;

they appear in the world because they desire to show sentient beings the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; they appear in the world because they desire to cause sentient beings to awaken to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
and they appear in the world because they desire to cause sentient beings to enter the path of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
World-Honored One, Śāriputra, it is for this one great causal matter that all Buddhas appear in the world.
To explain this principle, there are further four meanings: first, regarding the four stages; second, regarding the four wisdoms; third, regarding the four gates;
and fourth, regarding the contemplation of the mind. Regarding the four stages: the realm of the Truth (satya) is unknowable and invisible, and thus depends upon wisdom.
The [ordinary] eye can only know and see; the two types of wisdom and the four eyes cannot know and see, whereas only the *sarvākārajñatā* (all-aspect wisdom) and the Buddha-eye can know and see.
As the Sūtra says: "In order to cause sentient beings to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. If one speaks exclusively of the Buddha-fruit, one loses sight of sentient beings;
if one speaks exclusively of sentient beings, it is not the Buddha's knowledge and vision. Therefore, one must not be partial.

Regarding the practitioners of the three previous teachings, although they are sentient beings, because they have not yet attained the Buddha-eye and Buddha-wisdom, they are unable to know or see the true reality (*dharmatā*).
In the four stages of the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*), these individuals are likewise sentient beings;

yet, because they have partially attained the Buddha-eye and Buddha-wisdom, the sense of being "sentient beings" is fulfilled and the sense of "Buddha-knowledge and vision" is also fulfilled. Therefore, these four stages are employed as a metaphor to explain the principle.
First, regarding the auspicious signs: the rain of four kinds of flowers from the heavens symbolizes that all myriad virtues converge to enable entry into the four stages (*bhūmi*).
By employing the flowers of these four stages to advance toward the fruit of Buddhahood, the principle is revealed through the stages.

"Opening" refers to the initial stage of the Perfect Ten Abidings, where ignorance is shattered and the *tathāgatagarbha* is opened, revealing the principle of the true reality (*dharmatā*). Why is this? Because the wondrous principle of the inherent virtues is...
The defilement and attachment caused by both the general and specific delusions are difficult to discern.

Although those at the initial stage can achieve perfect faith (the stage of names), perfect reception (the five ranks of practice), and perfect subduing (the ten stages of faith), they have not yet severed them; thus, this is not called "opening.

Internally, through meditative cultivation, and externally, aided by the rain of Dharma, one assists in breaking through the general and specific delusions, thereby revealing the true cultivated nature and the knowledge and vision of the treasury.

It is brilliantly developed like the sun rising to extinguish darkness, for the eyes have become functional; thus it is called "opening. By practicing the conditions that destroy delusions, it is made pure.
The *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* states: "The prajñā that enters into principle is called 'abiding';

it abides in the stage of the ten abidings, the position of the white flower. As for "manifesting," once the obstacles of delusion are removed, the essence of knowledge and vision is revealed. This is the essence.

Because the myriad virtues and all the qualities of the dharma-realm are displayed with perfect clarity, it is called "Manifestation" (*śū*), which corresponds to the stage of the Great White Flower in the Ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*).

For the awakened one, hindrances are removed and the essence is revealed; the practices of the dharma-realm become clear, and phenomena and principle are harmoniously integrated so that there is no longer any dualistic course.

Because the wisdom that accords with reality (*yathābhūta-jñāna*) and the wisdom that accords with phenomena (*yathāvasthita-jñāna*) are non-dual in their principle and measure, it is called "Awakening" (*bodhi*). Thus...

The ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) correspond to the stage of the Red Flower (*rakta-puṣpa*). As for "entering," since phenomena and principle have already been harmonized, one enters spontaneously and without obstruction, flowing freely into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (omniscience).

Through mastery in penetrating according to reality (*yathārtha*) and according to measure (*yathāmātra*), one possesses the knowledge and vision according to measure (*yathāmātra-jñāna-darśana*) that can sustain all virtues, and the knowledge and vision according to reality (*yathārtha-jñāna-darśana*) that can obstruct all delusions; this is the Great Red of the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*).

This refers to the stage of the Flower (the Bodhisattva stages). However, within a single stage of the wondrous path of the Perfect Teaching (*yuan dao*), the merits of all forty-one stages are fully contained.
Merely by opening [this stage], the phases of Opening, Showing, Entering, and Realizing are fully manifested; it is not a matter of different minds.

It is simply that, through knowledge and vision in accordance with reality (*yili*), there are no marks of distinction between shallow and deep; yet, in order to manifest knowledge and vision in accordance with phenomena (*ru liang*), the four stages are distinguished.
"The initial resolve and the ultimate resolve are not two; yet between these two states of mind, the former is more difficult.
Since it speaks of "difficult" and "easy," one knows that there must be a distinction of clarity and obscurity, as well as depth and shallowness, between the initial resolve and the ultimate resolve.

It is like the body of the moon, which is full both at the beginning and at the end, yet differs according to the phases of the new moon and the full moon. The insights of these four stages all clearly illuminate the true reality (*dharmatā*).

Furthermore, the distinctions between "opening," "showing," "awakening," and "entering" are explained as follows: Second, regarding the four types of wisdom (*catur-jñāna*): (The names originate from the *Prajñāpāramitā*; while they generally apply to all three teachings, here they refer exclusively to the Perfect Teaching.
First, the wisdom of the path (*mārga-jñāna*) perceives the true nature (*dharmatā*) through the Path of Vision; within this true nature, one attains the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

Second, the wisdom of the varieties of the path (*mārgajñatā-jñāna*) knows the distinct characteristics of the various paths and seeds within the ten dharma-realms, as well as the aspects of delusion and awakening; it reveals each and every one of these as the Buddha’s [knowledge].
1. Knowledge and Vision (*jñāna-darśana*): This refers to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajña-jñāna*), which knows that all phenomena are of one mark—quiescence;
this quiescence is precisely the awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. 2. Knowledge of All Aspects (*sarvākāra-jñatā*):

This refers to the knowledge of all phenomena as being of the mark of quiescence, while simultaneously cognizing their various types, categories, and characteristics; this is entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. (Note: The two terms "wisdom" [prajñā] and "knowledge" [jñāna] both encompass cause and effect, as well as the general and the specific.)

Now, it is simply said that "the wisdom of the path" (mārgajñatā) refers to the cause and the general, adding one character; "the wisdom of the aspects of the path" (mārgākārajñatā) refers to the cause and the specific, as there are the two characters "all" (sarva) upon the wisdom; and "omniscience" (sarvākārajñatā) refers to the fruit and the general, again adding one character, while referring to the fruit and the specific.

Furthermore, the wisdom of the path, being according to principle (yathārtha), is called "opening"; the wisdom of the aspects of the path, being according to measure (yathāmātra), is called "indicating.
The non-duality of principle and measure is termed "awakening," and the simultaneous illumination of both principle and measure is termed "entry. This, too, is based on reality.

In principle, there is no shallow or deep; it is within the middle that the distinctions of shallow and deep arise. (Just as with conventional objects and their numerical quantities, when they accord with ultimate reality, principle and quantity are mutually identical.

They are neither cause nor effect, nor general nor particular; yet, for the sake of convenience, one speaks of cause, effect, generality, and particularity. Thus, the principle is the same from beginning to end. Third, an horizontal explanation of the four phrases according to the four gates of the Perfect Teaching:
through the gate of emptiness, all is empty; this is the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Through the gate of existence, all exists... [and so forth].
"All existence is both emptiness and existence" is the gate of revealing and instructing the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;

"all is both emptiness and existence" is the gate of awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision as neither empty nor existent; "all is neither empty nor existent" is the gate of entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
That which enables penetration consists of four, while that which is penetrated is one. Revealing, instructing, awakening, and entering are the gates of that which enables penetration.
To know that which is seen is to understand the principle through which one penetrates. Fourth, regarding the explanation by way of contemplating the mind (*guanxin*):
one contemplates the principle of the three truths within the nature of the mind, which is inconceivable. This contemplation is clear and pure, and is thus termed "opening" (*kai*).

Although it is inconceivable, one is nevertheless able to distinguish emptiness, the provisional, and the middle; these are perfectly distinct without confusion, and are thus termed "indicating" (*shi*) emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.
The mind is three yet one; the one is three. This is called "awakening to emptiness, the provisional, and the middle" (*kong-jia-zhong*).

The mind is not itself empty, provisional, or middle, yet it simultaneously illuminates emptiness, the provisional, and the middle. This is called "entering. Thus, there is the single mind and the three contemplations (*san guan*), which are distinguished and presented as the differences between the stages of separation, opening, awakening, and entering.
Therefore, the fourfold interpretation [of the Lotus Sūtra] is established because the principle is seen through the stages, and the stages are established by the principle.
Wisdom arises from wisdom; the gates are opened through the gates; penetration is achieved through contemplation. Because the gates are penetrated, wisdom is perfected;
because wisdom is perfected, the stages are established; because the stages are established, one perceives the principle. Because one perceives the principle, it is called the "Unity of Principle.

(Although it is said that the principle is one, the gates are the unity of teaching, contemplation is the unity of practice, and the stages are the unity of persons. This is the method of distinguishing the three—teaching, practice, and person—by means of the principle. Since the principle is thus, the other three are likewise so. There is nothing more subtle than this for explaining the meaning.)

Furthermore, regarding the previous discussion on the stages (*bhūmi*) and wisdom (*jñāna*), it seems that only upon reaching the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) can one be said to have attained "opening" (*kai*). This appears to be a realm beyond the reach of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). However, regarding the gates (*mukha*) and contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), even those at the initial stage of the "name-and-word" (*nāma-pada*) level have ground for cultivation;

how much more so for sentient beings whose knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*) are fundamentally the very essence of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Just as ice is essentially water, yet through the obstruction of delusion and the freezing of cold, water is raised up to become ice—if one truly believes that the gate of the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*) holds that contemplating the mind is itself [the Way], then there is the sequence of name, word, opening, showing, awakening, and entering, up to the ultimate opening, showing, awakening, and entering.

How could one then loftily defer to the state of the Sage while disparaging oneself as having no share in it? Nor could one recklessly calculate that the initial mind is itself the Buddha, thereby conflating the ordinary with the ultimate. Herein, the discussion of stages is not intended as a vertical progression; rather, it is a vertical analysis based on...

Regarding the "gates," they are not horizontal; yet when discussed in terms of horizontal [expansiveness], they are horizontal. Regarding wisdom, it is neither horizontal nor vertical; yet when discussed in terms of both horizontal and vertical, it is both horizontal and vertical. Regarding contemplation, it is neither non-horizontal nor non-vertical; yet when discussed in terms of being neither horizontal nor vertical, it is neither horizontal nor vertical.
Furthermore, it simultaneously illuminates both the horizontal and the vertical. From "Śāriputra" onwards, the text concludes by establishing the single principle.

Although in the past the teachings of the provisional methods were each presented as opening, showing, awakening, and entering, these were not the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; therefore, they were provisional. Now, because this clarifies the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, it is the reality—the ultimate truth.
This is the identity of principle. △ Second, the identity of persons.
The Buddha told Śāriputra: "The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, teach and transform only bodhisattvas.

This refers to the expedient means of the past, wherein they are said to teach and transform the three vehicles; in reality, however, they teach and transform only bodhisattvas, just as in the case of that impoverished son.
He considered himself a lowly hired laborer, yet when the Elder looked upon him, he was truly his own son; this is the first point regarding the person.
△ Third, the clarification of the practice:
In all that he does, he always performs but one task—solely to reveal and awaken sentient beings to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
The various practices of the Three Vehicles are termed "all" because they are complete; thus, "all" is precisely "one.
As for what these practices reach, they lead solely toward the Buddha’s knowledge and vision—this is the single intent of practice. △ Fourth, clarifying the One Teaching.
Śāriputra, the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma for sentient beings solely by means of the Single Buddha Vehicle (Ekayāna);
there is no other vehicle, whether a second or a third.
The Perfect and Sudden Teaching is called the Single Buddha Vehicle, while all teachings from the Distinct Teaching (Bhinnayāna) onwards are termed "provisional" (śeṣa) teachings. Thus it is said:
The statement that "the provisional meaning is not the One Buddha Vehicle and there is no other vehicle" means:
first, there is no "distinct [vehicle]" as included within the *Avataṃsaka*; second, there is no "pair" as carried along within the *Prajñāpāramitā*;

and third, there is no "trio" as confronted within the Vaipulya (*Vaipulya*). However, each of these four passages has two meanings; regarding the first passage, if one takes it from the perspective of the "knower":

Regarding the first passage, if one takes "seeing" as the person, it is more convenient to take "one" (the person) as the principle; if one takes "what is known and seen," it is more convenient to take "principle" as the one.

Regarding the second passage, if one takes "teaching and transforming," it is more convenient to take "teaching" as the one; if one takes "the Bodhisattva," it is more convenient to take "person" as the one.

Regarding the third passage, concerning "whatever is done," if one speaks from the perspective of the teacher of the doctrine, it is more convenient to take "teaching" as the one; if one speaks from the perspective of practice, [it is more convenient to take "person" as the one].

If one takes the meaning of "acting for oneself," then practicing the One Vehicle is most expedient; this is the fourth textual point. If one takes the meaning of "riding and transporting [others]," then practicing the One Vehicle is most expedient.
Now, taking the sense of preaching the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, teaching the One Vehicle is most expedient. This is merely an explanation according to what is most expedient.
The fourfold correct explanation is concluded. △ Fifth, the summary.
Śāriputra, the Dharma of all Buddhas of the ten directions is likewise thus.
This sentence summarizes the four sections; although the text is concise, its meaning is vast. Why is this so?

In the introduction, by means of the light, eighteen thousand lands were seen horizontally, and Mañjuśrī cited the past to clarify vertically the twenty thousand Buddhas—all of whom are none other than the Real.
The employment of provisional means (*upāya*) to open up the provisional and reveal the real is fundamentally identical in intent to the present Buddha’s appearance in this world of five turbidities;

this, of course, requires no further elaboration. Furthermore, regarding the infinite worlds within the ocean of lands throughout the ten directions—distinguished by their purity or defilement—and the appearances of the infinite Buddhas therein:
there are those who teach exclusively the Great [Vehicle], and there are also those who teach exclusively the Small [Vehicle]. Pure...
If one speaks in terms of the Great [Vehicle], it is not necessarily the case that three are bestowed; this is indeed the "four-in-one.

If one speaks purely in terms of the Small [Vehicle], one cannot manifest the reality (dharmatā), yet after a long, long time, in the ultimate sense, there is likewise no failure to become "four-in-one.

This, however, cannot be calculated by the duration of kalpas, nor can it be measured by the supernatural powers or the divine eye of those from the stage of Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi) downward.
This is all. The subsequent text reveals the provisional traces to manifest the fundamental reality; the Tathāgata’s transformative merit across the three periods of time is such as this.
If one does not believe in this, how can they be said to rejoice with accord? The first section, which generally clarifies all Buddhas, is concluded.
II. Listing the Buddhas of the Three Periods, divided into three parts: 1. Buddhas of the Past; 2. Buddhas of the Future; 3. Buddhas of the Present. Within this, there should be six [subsections].

The meaning consists of only two aspects: first, revealing the provisional means; second, manifesting the ultimate reality. "Both" refers to the two preceding sections; "both" also refers to the two following sections.

(The praise of the rarity of the Dharma and the statement that it is not false point back to the previous general chapter. The citation of the five turbidities to explain the provisional and the selection of the false to encourage faith point forward to the subsequent Śākyamuni chapter. First, regarding the Buddhas of the past:

Śāriputra, the Buddhas of the past, by means of immeasurable and innumerable skillful means, various causes and conditions, parables, and modes of expression, have expounded the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings; all these teachings were for the purpose of the Single Buddha Vehicle.
Consequently, those sentient beings, having heard the Dharma from the Buddhas, ultimately all attain the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
The "immeasurable and innumerable skillful means" and so forth constitute the disclosure of the provisional; "these dharmas are all equal" constitutes the manifestation of the real.

This refers to the One Buddha Vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*), which is the oneness of teaching, the oneness of person—the sentient being who can attain the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*)—and the oneness of principle, which is that which is known by this single knowledge. △ Second, the Buddhas of the future.
Śāriputra, in the future, all Buddhas who shall appear in the world will likewise, by means of immeasurable and innumerable skillful means,
various causes and conditions, parables, and modes of expression, expound the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings; all these teachings are for the purpose of the Single Buddha Vehicle,
so that all these sentient beings, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, shall ultimately attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā).
△ Third, the Buddhas of the Present.

Śāriputra, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, currently residing in immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddha-lands throughout the ten directions, bring great benefit and peace and happiness to sentient beings; these Buddhas likewise employ immeasurable and innumerable skillful means.
By employing various causes, conditions, parables, and expressions,
he expounds all dharmas for the sake of sentient beings because all these dharmas are for the purpose of the Single Buddha Vehicle. Śāriputra,
these Buddhas teach and transform only bodhisattvas, desiring to reveal to sentient beings the knowledge and vision of a Buddha.
It is because he wishes to awaken sentient beings with the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and because he wishes to cause sentient beings to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

Since the present Buddha is precisely the principal teacher of transformation, he first indicates the intent of his appearance in the world; next, he clarifies the opening of the provisional to reveal the real;

and finally, he concludes by establishing the sequence of opening, showing, awakening, and entering. The few abbreviated phrases are merely due to the brevity of the text; the first four [phrases] are as follows.
The Chapter on the Buddha concludes. △ Second, the Chapter on Śākyamuni extensively explains the provisional and the real aspects of Śākyamuni through six meanings;
herein, there is no expression of the rarity of the Dharma, but rather five sections: first, the opening of the provisional; second, the manifestation of the real;

third, citing the five turbidities to explain the skillful means; fourth, distinguishing the false to encourage faith in the one reality; and fifth, clarifying that there is no falsehood. Now, the first section.
Śāriputra, I am now likewise thus: knowing that sentient beings have various desires and deep-seated attachments,
I preach the Dharma for them through the power of skillful means— using various causes, conditions, parables, and modes of expression— in accordance with their fundamental natures.
"First three, then one," as with the four Buddhas, because they are not different; thus it is said, "likewise, various desires and so forth.
These refer to the faculties, dispositions, and inclinations of the five vehicles. That which is called "faculties" (*indriya*) in the past has the meaning of being able to produce [results];

that which is called "desires" (*chanda*) in the present has the meaning of grasping objects; that which is called "disposition" (*gotra*) in the future has the meaning of being unchanging. It is that which is deeply attached to in the mind.

That which is difficult to transform due to past habitual tendencies is precisely the "faculty" (indriya). The "expedient means" (upāya) refers to the provisional teachings of the three vehicles opened according to what is appropriate.
Herein, "resonance" (ganying) refers to the various faculties, dispositions, and desires of sentient beings that evoke [a response];
"response" (ying) refers to our Buddha’s knowing this and preaching the Dharma through the power of expedient means. △ Second, revealing the reality.
Śāriputra, all of this is for the sake of enabling [beings] to attain the One Buddha Vehicle and the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
△ Third, citing the five turbidities to explain the skillful means, which has three parts: first, stating the intent; second, citing the five turbidities; third, concluding the explanation.
First: Śāriputra, in the worlds of the ten directions there are not even two vehicles, let alone three.

This is intended to first state the underlying meaning before raising the topic of the five turbidities. Previously, it was explained that the Buddhas open up the provisional and reveal the real, yet this point had not yet been clarified.

The provisional teachings were hidden while the ultimate was established; now, by observing according to the reality of the ultimate, one sees that throughout the worlds of the ten directions there is nothing that is not the wondrous principle of the Dharma-realm and True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Since even the duality of the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddha*) does not exist, how much less could there be the three—the *śrāvaka*, *pratyekabuddha*, and Separate Teachings?
As for the name "Two Vehicles" in the context of the Separate Teaching, the Middle Way transcends the two extremes and is not identical to those two extremes; this is the Middle.

Because the extremes constitute two, it is called the Second Vehicle. Since even these two of the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao) cannot be found, how much less could there be the three provisional [teachings] consisting of the Shared (Tong), the Treasury (Zang), and the Separate?

It is only because we have emerged from a world of the five turbidities that we cannot help but conceal the One Truth and manifest the three provisional [teachings]. △ Second, citing the five turbidities.

Śāriputra, all Buddhas appear in the five turbidities of an evil world, namely: the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*), the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*), the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*), the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*), and the turbidity of lifespan (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*).
An "eon" refers to time; since time has no substantial reality, it is a conventional designation established based on the states of form and mind. Now, these are called "turbidities."
This refers to the fact that the four turbidities (*caturkaṣāya*) have intensified and gathered in this period; as the subsequent text states, it is "the time of the chaos of the *kalpa*-turbidity.
Regarding the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*): speaking generally, the three delusions of the five stages of dwelling are all termed afflictions.

For now, however, the five dull underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) within the realm of desire are designated as the turbidity of afflictions—namely, greed, hatred, ignorance, pride, and doubt. As for sentient beings...
Furthermore, it has no separate substance; this provisional name is established based upon the five aggregates of form and mind.
What is here called "the turbidity of sentient beings" (*sattva-kaṣāya*) refers to the coarse, inferior, and base retribution of form and mind produced by the afflictions of views;

thus it is named the turbidity of sentient beings. As for the "turbidity of views" (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*), speaking in general terms, all delusions of discrimination within and beyond the realms are termed "views."

For now, let us consider the five afflictive views within the realm [of desire] as the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*), namely: the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), the view of attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and false views (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*).

Furthermore, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is not a substantial dharma; it is a provisional designation based upon a portion of the seeds of consciousness that functions to maintain the continuity of matter and mind without interruption.
As for what is called "turbidity" here, it refers to the seeds of consciousness produced by unwholesome karmic maturation (*vipāka*), which cause...
Because the physical form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*) that sustain existence are short-lived, it is called the turbidity of life (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*).

If one considers the mutual dependence of cause and effect, views and afflictions (*kleśa*) serve as the cause, while the physical form and mind of the three realms (*tridhātu*) are the result produced by them. Based on these results, the designation "sentient being" (*sattva*) is established;

based on the single period of birth and death of a sentient being, the term "life-faculty" (*jīvitendriya*) is established. It is based on these four factors, all of which are turbid, that [the turbidity of life] is established.

Regarding the name "Kalpa-turbidity" (*kalpa-kaṣāya*): if one follows the sequence of various sutras, the Kalpa-turbidity stands at the beginning, while the turbidities of views, afflictions, and life are listed subsequently.
In this present text, the order is not sequential, yet there is no specific doctrinal significance in this deviation. Question:
Is this identical to or different from the five turbidities explained in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*? Answer: The five turbidities in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* encompass all nine [categories].

Question: Since only a Buddha can purify the realms (*dhātu*), why are the five corruptions (*pañca kaṣāyāḥ*) mentioned in this sutra restricted to the defiled lands (*sāśrava-bhūmi*) and the aeons of decline (*apacaya-kalpa*), rather than being applied to the pure lands (*viśuddha-bhūmi*) or the aeons of increase (*upacaya-kalpa*)?

Answer: This is because it clarifies that the Buddhas conceal their ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) and manifest the three vehicles (*triyāna*) due to the unavoidable necessity of acting within the world of the five corruptions.
This clearly demonstrates that skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) are inconceivable; how then can the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* be categorized as belonging to the same class as those [other] sutras?

[Objection: If the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) can act as obstacles, why is it that in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, one hears and awakens to the truth even before the turbidities have been eliminated? [Response: This should be analyzed according to four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).

There are three further categories: first, those with sharp faculties but heavy obstacles who, because their faculties are sharp, cannot be hindered by heavy obstacles—these are those in this land who hear the Mahāyāna for the first time upon hearing the *Avataṃsaka*;
second, those with sharp faculties and light obstacles who suddenly hear the Mahāyāna in the pure lands of other directions;
and third, those with dull faculties and light obstacles who first hear the Three Vehicles in the pure lands of other directions.

Those who later realize the One Vehicle are such people. Those with dull faculties and heavy obstructions who hear the gradual teachings in this land and only then remove their turbidity before hearing the Mahāyāna are also such people.

Question: Do the five turbidities also obstruct those of the Hīnayāna? Answer: Even regarding the Hīnayāna, one should apply a fourfold analysis: 1. Those with sharp Hīnayāna faculties and light obstructions whom the turbidities cannot hinder, such as Śāriputra.

2. [Those with sharp faculties but heavy obstructions. 3. [Those with dull faculties and light obstructions. 4. Those with dull faculties and heavy obstructions whom the turbidities hinder. (Note: The second and third categories are implied by the context of the fourfold analysis.)
1. Although Kāśyapa and others possessed sharp faculties of the Two Vehicles (Hīnayāna), their heavy and turbid obstructions could not act as a hindrance, as seen in the *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra*. 2.
Although Aṅgulimāla possessed dull faculties of the Three Vehicles and his obstructions were light and turbid, they likewise could not act as a hindrance, as seen in the case of the bhikṣu Paṇḍaka.
3. Those with dull faculties of the Four Vehicles and heavy obstructions do indeed constitute a hindrance; such individuals did not hear [the Dharma] during the Buddha’s lifetime.

Question: Regarding those who cannot attain liberation through the Hīnayāna, why is it that some hear both the Mahāyāna and the Hīnayāna even though they do not rely on the *Avataṃsaka* nor the Tripiṭaka?
Answer: This should be explained by applying four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) based on the four teachings (*catur-yāna*).

Furthermore, one may apply four permutations for each of the four teachings individually. As for the total four permutations: those with sharp faculties and light hindrances follow [the teaching] accordingly.
At what time should those with sharp faculties and heavy hindrances hear the Perfect Teaching? At what time should those with dull faculties and light hindrances hear the Distinct Teaching?
At what time should those with dull faculties and heavy hindrances hear the Common Teaching? And at what time should those [with dull faculties and heavy hindrances] hear the Treasury Teaching?
The Buddha, through his secret power of speech, responds accordingly to each, causing them all to obtain benefit as they individually act.
Regarding the four propositions: each of the four teachings has its own four gates. Those with sharp faculties and light hindrances enter through the gate of "neither empty nor existent.
Those with sharp faculties and heavy hindrances enter through the gate of "both empty and existent.
Those with dull faculties and light hindrances enter through the gate of emptiness. Those with dull faculties and heavy hindrances enter through the gate of existence. To summarize:

In discussing this, it does not matter whether one has obstacles or lacks them; what is valued is simply having the roots and the seeds of the vehicle. Obstacles arise from breaking the precepts, while the seeds arise from cultivation.
Roots depend on past habits and may be sharp or dull. This results in encountering a Buddha now and awakening—some requiring the right time and others not.
If one lacked the seeds of the vehicle in the past and had not planted the roots of supramundane goodness, then even if...
How can one help those who are hindered by light attachment to pleasure and fail to awaken—neither included within the four propositions nor subsumed by the four gates? Question:

Regarding the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*), why, in the first instance, do they obstruct the Great [Vehicle] but not the Small? (This question concerns the fourth of the first four propositions. Answer: The turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*) is heavy;

they falsely reckon the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as the four virtues. (This constitutes the heaviness of the obstruction. If they hear of the permanence, bliss, [self, and purity] of the Mahāyāna...
To hold that "I am pure" is itself an attachment (this is due to dull faculties). The former physician was stubborn and foolish;

he did not know whether the milk was good or bad (he did not recognize the medicine), he did not know the root source from which the illness arose (he did not recognize the disease), and he did not know the prescriptions for administering or withholding the medicine (he did not know the method of dispensing the medicine).
Because he lacked understanding, his turbid obstructions were great. As the text says: "If one merely praises the Buddha Vehicle, sentient beings will sink [into despair]."

"To abide in suffering" is precisely this meaning. If one hears of impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity, one will then grow weary of birth-and-death and rejoice in Nirvana, thereby destroying false attachments and conceptions;
thus, the five turbidities do not obstruct [the path]. As the Minor Text says:
"When one reflects in this way, the Buddhas of the ten directions all appear and console me with Brahma-sounds"—this is precisely that meaning. △ Third, the conclusion and explanation.
Thus, Śāriputra, because sentient beings during the period of the defilement of the kalpa have heavy impurities, are stingy, greedy, and jealous, and have accomplished various unwholesome roots,
the Buddhas, through the power of skillful means, distinguish and teach three vehicles within the single Buddha-vehicle.
The first phrase refers to the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*); the second phrase refers to the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*).

Stinginess, greed, jealousy, and envy constitute the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*) and the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*); the cultivation of various unwholesome roots constitutes the turbidity of life (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*).

Had he not graciously bestowed expedient means (*upāya*), how could he have drawn them out from the wheel of suffering? This concludes the third section, which explains the expedient means by citing the five turbidities. △ Fourth, distinguishing the false and exhorting [the true].
"Faith in the One Reality": If a disciple of the Buddha can personally believe and understand this, yet does not believe or understand it, they are neither a true disciple nor an Arhat.
[The text] urges the assembly to accept and believe it. The commentary has two parts: first, distinguishing the true from the false;
second, providing exemptions and resolving doubts. The first part also has two sections: first, if one has not heard or does not know [this], one is not a true disciple; second, if...
To hear this and not believe or accept it is the arrogance of overweening pride. First:

Śāriputra, if among my disciples there are those who consider themselves Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas, yet do not hear or know that the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, teach and transform only Bodhisattvas—these are not disciples of the Buddha, nor are they Arhats.
Pratyekabuddhas.
Just as the disciples of the world follow the Teacher’s Dharma to continue the Way and transmit the lamp, if one now neither hears nor knows it, there would be no Dharma to follow.
What then would be called a "disciple"? In the past, the Tathāgata, for the sake of governing the five turbidities, expediently bestowed the three [vehicles].
That you have been able to hear and know [the Dharma] and practice it in accordance with it is what defines you as a disciple.
Now that the five turbidities have been removed, for the sake of you, I shall manifest the One. Why do you not hear and not know? Not hearing means you do not hear the teaching;
not knowing means you do not know the practice. One who is neither a disciple nor a human being is one who is entirely deluded regarding the Principle. △ 2.
If one hears this and does not believe or accept it,
that is overweening pride (*adhimāna*). Furthermore, Śāriputra, these bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs claim for themselves that they have already attained arhatship,
that this is their final body, and that they have reached ultimate nirvāṇa, and thus they no longer aspire to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
You should know that these people are all those of overweening pride. Why is this?
If there were a bhikṣu who had truly attained arhatship and yet did not believe in this Dharma, such a thing would be impossible.
The Buddha established the Two Vehicles originally for the sake of those whose afflictions are heavy due to the five turbidities, so as to temporarily allow them to cease from suffering;

thus he provisionally taught that the complete severance of the views and thoughts is called Arhatship, and that one who no longer receives a subsequent existence within the three realms is said to have attained "finality," emerging from the cycle of segmented suffering in the land of shared habitation and calling this Nirvana.
However, even if one were to truly attain the path of an Arhat, it would still be subject to the realization of existence.
Those who have attained other forms of liberation should now, upon hearing this sutra, immediately accept it with faith and strive to seek supreme bodhi.
Why is this? Since the turbid obstructions have already been removed and they have further heard this Great Dharma, they ought to carefully examine themselves:

if ignorance and secondary delusions still remain, how can one be called an Arhat? How can the cycle of death and rebirth through transformation be called "vast"? And how can the city of transformation be called the "final body"?
Since this is not yet the place of treasure, how can it be called ultimate *nirvāṇa*?
Therefore, among those who have truly attained the state of an Arhat, there is none who would fail to believe in the Buddha’s teaching of this Dharma.

If one considers oneself sufficient and no longer aspires to seek Bodhi, you should know that such a person has not yet realized Arhatship, but is merely possessed of overweening pride (*adhimāna*). This concludes the initial examination of the true and the false.
△ Second, the opening of exceptions and the resolution of doubts, which is further divided into two parts: first, the opening of exceptions; second, the resolution of doubts. Now, the first part.
[The exception] concerns the period after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa when no Buddha is present before one. Why is this?
Because after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, those who receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain the meaning of such sūtras as these are difficult to find.
Fearing that someone might ask: "If that is so, then do all Arhats necessarily aspire to seek unexcelled Bodhi?
he now provides an exception, saying: "Excepting the period after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa when no Buddha is present;

in such cases, those who have received the provisional teaching and attained the state of an Arhat are not necessarily able to immediately aspire to seek Bodhi. Furthermore, another asks: "Even though the Buddha..."
"Even though this sutra remains in the world after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, why would they not believe it? To this, the commentary now explains: Why is this so?
Although the sutra remains in the world after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, those who can receive, uphold, read, recite, and understand its meaning are difficult to find.
If one does not encounter such a person, how could a practitioner of the Lesser Vehicle (hīnayāna) possibly resolve these matters for themselves? △ Second, resolving doubts.
If one encounters other Buddhas, one will then attain definitive understanding within this Dharma.
Fearing that there might be doubt— namely, that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, those Arhats who do not encounter this sutra,
nor meet anyone who upholds, recites, or explains its meaning, would then enter into a permanent, limited nirvana— I shall now provide an explanation:
Although such a person conceives the thought of extinction and enters into *nirvāṇa*, they are born into the Land of Skillful Means with Remainder (*upāya-śeṣa-kṣetra*).

There, they still encounter a Buddha who preaches this Dharma for them; they then attain definitive understanding that the "transformed city" was not real, and they must once again resolve to seek unexcelled *bodhi*.
Thus, there is no principle by which they could enter *nirvāṇa* forever. Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
The *Vyākhyā* on the "Chapter on Certainty" states: "If one asks where the body of an Arhat must cease and where he dwells to fully realize the Buddha-way, the answer is:
outside the three realms, there is a pure Buddha-land free from afflictions.
In that land, having heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* from the Buddha, one fully realizes the Buddha-way. It then cites this sūtra as proof, saying: "There are Arhats who..."
Those who have not heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and yet claim to have attained extinction (nirvāṇa) will hear me say in other lands,
"You shall become Buddhas," and they shall likewise attain definitive resolution upon encountering those in this land who receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain its meaning. Thus,
Master Nanyue said that "other Buddhas" refers to the four reliances (*catur-śaraṇa*), and that Arhats encounter them and hear [the teaching].

The *Jue-liao jing* (Sūtra of Definitive Resolution) further states: "Arhats who practice the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha see the Buddhas of the ten directions, who then preach this sūtra for them, whereby they immediately attain definitive resolution.

(If one says they are mindful of the Buddhas of the ten directions, it means they have already awakened the Great Mind; if, on the other hand, they only mindfully contemplate Śākyamuni Buddha, it is because a small cause has elicited a great response—this is simply due to the arousal of their spiritual capacity.
This concludes the fourth section: Distinguishing the False to Encourage Faith in the One Reality. △ Fifth: Clarifying that there is No Deception.
Śāriputra, you all should with single-minded faith, understanding, and resolve accept and uphold the words of the Buddha;
for the Tathāgatas speak no falsehoods, and there is no other vehicle—there is only the One Buddha Vehicle.
First, he exhorts faith in the true words of Śākyamuni; next, he exhorts faith in the sincere words of all Buddhas;

finally, he concludes by establishing the Single Buddha Vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*) in order to cease doubt and slander. Within the first section, the "Proper Exposition of the Dharma" (*saddharmadeśanā*), the long prose passage is now complete.
II. The Verse Recitation is divided into two parts: first, the verses on the promise to answer; second, the verses on the actual exposition. Now, the first part.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“Bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs harboring overweening pride; upāsakas with arrogance and upāsikās lacking faith—these fourfold assemblies numbered five thousand.
They did not perceive their own faults, for they were deficient in the precepts.”
Those who cherish their own flaws possess but small wisdom; they are the chaff removed from among the masses.

It is by the Buddha’s majestic power that such persons have departed, for they lack sufficient merit to be able to receive this Dharma. This assembly is now free of branches and leaves, consisting only of those who are steadfast and true.
Śāriputra, listen well.
The four assemblies all commonly possess overweening pride (*adhimāna*), pride of self (*māna*), and lack of faith.

However, among the two groups of the ordained, many who practice the path attain meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and mistakenly claim it to be the fruit of sainthood, giving rise to overweening pride (*abhimāna*). Those in secular life, being conceited, frequently give rise to pride of self (*māna*).

Women, having shallow wisdom, often produce lack of faith; those who do not perceive their own faults suffer from these three losses, which cover the mind, conceal flaws, and promote [their own faults].
One who cannot reflect inwardly upon their virtues is a person devoid of shame (*anapatrāpya*). If one perceives one's own faults, one possesses a sense of modesty (*hrī*).

Those with deficiencies in the precepts have a failure in their restraint (*saṃvara*); this is termed a "deficiency. Those with failures in that which is concomitant with meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the Path are termed "leaks" (*āsrava*), because they lack concentration and the Path.
Thus, when evil thoughts arise within like a jade containing a flaw, the restraint is impaired, and consequently, there is outward movement.
When one’s body and speech are like jade or dew, yet one conceals transgressions and remains complacent without confessing them, this is called "protecting and cherishing small wisdom.

Such individuals possess neither the wisdom of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) nor that of those still in training (*śaikṣa*), but instead harbor worldly, minor wisdom. They falsely reckon tainted (*sāsrava*) states to be untainted (*anāsrava*);
because it is the smallest among the small, it is termed "small wisdom. They have not yet attained the nourishment of untainted meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*).
The "moisture" refers only to mundane-flavored dhyāna, which is like dregs; it lacks supramundane wisdom of principle.

The "words" refer only to a thin understanding of the text that merely uncovers the phrasing while losing the essential meaning, and is thus like husks. Furthermore, the dregs and husks are metaphors for those lacking great capacity, while the branches and leaves are metaphors for those who are not excellent vessels;
since none are fit for employment, they must be discarded. These four verses all praise the selection and acceptance of the latter [the true dharma].
One verse summarizes the exhortation and permission; it is a concise summary that follows and accords with the prose. △ Second, the verse on the actual exposition has two parts:
first, the verse on the four Buddhas; second, the verse on Śākyamuni. Within the first part, there are four sections: first, the verse on all Buddhas; second, the verse on past Buddhas;
third, the verse on future Buddhas; fourth, the verse on present Buddhas. The first verse on all Buddhas corresponds to the long prose.

There are three differences: first, in this [text], the long passage praises the Dharma while lacking mention of the five turbidities (*pañca kaṣāyāḥ*), whereas here there are the five turbidities but no praise of the Dharma;

second, in the previous [text] the long passage appears intermittently, first praising the Dharma and subsequently clarifying that it is not in vain by revealing the provisional to manifest the real, whereas here the provisional is first revealed to manifest the real, and only later is it clarified that it is not in vain; third, regarding the opening and closing [of the sections], they do not correspond.

In the preceding long passage, the exhortation to believe was combined with the statement that [the teaching] is not in vain; here, the exhortation to believe is separated from the statement that it is not in vain.

Furthermore, in the long passage, Śākyamuni’s skillful means were used to explain the provisional nature (*upāya*) of all Buddhas; here, Śākyamuni’s manifestation of the One is used to establish the reality (*bhūta*) of all Buddhas.
These are the four differences. The text is divided into five parts: first, a verse on the bestowal of skillful means; second, a verse on... [text fragment].

The three verses on revealing the reality, the four verses on exhorting faith, and the five verses on the non-futility [of the teaching] regarding the five turbidities constitute the first part. First:
"The Dharma attained by all Buddhas is taught to sentient beings through immeasurable powers of skillful means.
The Buddha fully knows the thoughts in the minds of sentient beings, the various paths they travel, their manifold desires and dispositions, and the good and evil karma of their past lives."
By means of the power of skillful methods—employing various conditions, parables, and verbal expressions—they cause all beings to rejoice;
they preach the *sūtras*, *geyas*, *itivṛttakas*, *jātakas*, and *adbhutadharmas*, as well as the *nidānas*, *avadānas*, *geyās*, and *upadeśas*.
To those of dull faculties who delight in inferior teachings and are attached to birth and death, [they teach] regarding the infinite Buddhas.
For those who do not practice the profound and wondrous path and are afflicted by manifold sufferings, [the Buddha] speaks of *nirvāṇa*.
"The Dharma attained by the Buddhas" refers to attaining the various provisional dharmas through the cultivation of the path.

This is truly because, when the causes of one's own practice are fulfilled, the subsequently attained non-conceptual wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*)—also called differentiated wisdom—is realized; this precisely constitutes one's own practice.
The internal power—that is, this Dharma-body—likewise cannot be described; yet, for the sake of sentient beings, it is explained through skillful means as the "power of transforming others.

It is taught according to the capacities of those in the nine realms, wherein the seven stages of expedient means are expounded. These nine realms are the objects of the teaching, which does not exceed the seven stages;
thus, the seven are taught to reach the nine, gradually leading them to enter the reality. Within these seven and nine, whichever capacity hears [the teaching]...

Regarding what dharmas are taught: because they encounter various capacities and opportunities and do not remain fixed from the outset, it is said that he teaches sentient beings through the power of immeasurable skillful means (*upāya*).

The manifestation of hope is termed "what is contemplated" (*nitya*); this contemplation is itself the habituation of desire (*chanda-vāsanā*), which, as an established nature, serves as a subsequent seed.
Furthermore, there are differences in prior karma—whether good or evil—which manifest in manifold ways.
It cannot be delivered by means of a single condition, a single parable, or a single expedient method; only the Buddha can fully know this.
Therefore, he is able to preach the ninefold canon (navāṅga-dharma-pravacana) according to what is appropriate, so that all may rejoice.

When they rejoice, they will inevitably give rise to the wholesome, extinguish the unwholesome, and enter into the principle. This mentions the beginning to encompass what follows. Regarding the ninefold canon, in general discussion:

The Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna each consist of twelve distinct divisions; if discussed separately, the Hīnayāna may consist of eleven or even only nine divisions, as explained in detail in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning).
The six phrases beginning with "those of dull faculties who delight in the Lesser Dharma" conclude the intention behind the provisional application of skillful means (*upāya*).

Because their faculties were dull in previous lives and they lack the spiritual capacity (*indriya*) in the present life to hear the Great [Vehicle], it is said that they do not practice the profound and wondrous Way. This is because they were greedy in previous lives... [text truncated].

Those whose attachments and hindrances are heavy and who are afflicted by the sufferings of this present life can only hear the Small [Vehicle]; therefore, it is said that for them, this is taught as *nirvāṇa*.
II. The Verse Exposition Revealing the Reality (4 sections): A. One verse on Principle; B. Two verses on Persons; C. Three verses on the Teaching;
D. One verse on Practice. Now, the first [section]: A. One verse on Principle.
I have established these skillful means to enable you to enter the Buddha’s wisdom, yet I have never said that you shall attain the path of Buddhahood;
this was because the time for such a teaching had not yet arrived. Now is precisely the right time, and I shall definitively proclaim the Mahāyāna.

These nine divisions of my Dharma were taught in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings, but they are fundamentally intended to lead them into the Mahāyāna; for this reason, I preach this sutra.
The Buddha’s wisdom is precisely this one great matter of causal conditions (*ekamahākaruṇā-pratyaya*). If considered from the perspective of the knower, it is the unity of practice;

if considered from the perspective of that which is known, it is the unity of principle (*liyi*). Furthermore, if considered from the perspective of the preaching of the sūtra, it should be the unity of teaching;

if considered from the perspective of what is expounded, it is the unity of principle. This is because taking what is convenient, it is designated as the "unity of principle. △ Second, the verse on the person.

There are sons of the Buddha whose minds are pure, gentle, and pliant, and who possess sharp faculties; having practiced the profound and wondrous path under immeasurable Buddhas, for these sons of the Buddha I preach this Mahāyāna sūtra.

I grant this prediction to such people that they shall attain the path of Buddhahood in a future age, because they mindfully recollect the Buddha with a deep heart and maintain the pure precepts. Upon hearing this, these individuals will experience great joy that pervades their entire bodies.

Because the Buddha knows their mental activities, he preaches the Mahāyāna for them; whether they be śrāvakas or bodhisattvas, if they hear even a single verse of the Dharma I preach, they will all undoubtedly attain Buddhahood.
This verse correctly summarizes that all Buddhas and Tathāgatas teach and transform only bodhisattvas. To elaborate on the various skillful means:
when all people become true persons, they possess the mind of a Buddha-son; those whose minds are pure are the distinct teaching (biejiao) persons for whom the Buddhas preach Mahāyāna sūtras.
Upon receiving their prediction (vyākaraṇa), their hearts rejoice, and they thus become true persons of the perfect teaching (yuánjiào). As for the śrāvakas, if they [become] bodhisattvas...

"Sā" refers to the śrāvakas who also attain the state of pratyekabuddhas—this constitutes the two vehicles of the two teachings—and the bodhisattvas who also attain the Mahāsattvas of the *zàng* and *tōng* [teachings].
Since all shall undoubtedly attain Buddhahood, it is clear that these seven kinds of skillful means are none other than the sons of the Buddha.
This is the sincere teaching of the Ultimate Sage; how can one fail to believe it? △ Third, the verse on the teaching (1).
Within the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the One Vehicle Dharma; there is no second and no third, except for the Buddha’s skillful means of speaking.
He uses only provisional names to guide sentient beings, doing so in order to speak of the Buddha’s wisdom.

This verse correctly summarizes the above point: the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma to sentient beings solely by means of the Single Buddha Vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*), and there is no other vehicle, whether dual or triple.
It is merely by using provisional names for the three teachings that he guides them to enter the Buddha-wisdom.

Thus, while from the perspective of skillful means (*upāya*) it may temporarily appear as if there were more than one, when discussed from the standpoint of the ultimate, there is definitively no duality.
3. △ Fourth, one verse on practice:
The Buddhas appear in the world; this alone is the one true reality, while the other two are not real. They never deliver sentient beings by means of the Lesser Vehicle;
the Buddha himself abides in the Great Vehicle, adorned with the power of the Dharma he has attained through wisdom and meditation.
By means of this, I deliver sentient beings and personally realize the unsurpassed path—the Dharma of equality of the Mahāyāna.
If I were to transform even a single person by means of the Hīnayāna, I would fall into stinginess and greed; such a thing is not permissible.
The verse beginning with "This alone is the one true reality" praises the aforementioned fact that all activities are constantly for the sake of the One Great Matter.

The verse beginning with "The Buddha himself abides in the Mahāyāna" praises the aforementioned teaching, awakening, and enlightenment of sentient beings solely through the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
The final six lines explain the intention not to deliver [beings] by means of the Lesser Vehicle. The two verses clarifying the reality are concluded. △ Third, the verses of exhortation.
Regarding the two parts of the first section—first, exhorting faith by citing the fruit; second, exhorting faith by citing the cause—the first is as follows:
"If a person has faith and takes refuge in the Buddha, the Tathāgata does not deceive, nor does he harbor greed or envy.
Because he has severed all evils within all dharmas, the Buddha alone among those in the ten directions is free from fear. I adorn my body with marks, and my radiance illuminates the world."
Venerated by immeasurable multitudes, he proclaims the Seal of the True Nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇamudrā*).
With a pure mind and all evils utterly severed, he fearlessly expounds the Dharma; these internal virtues are trustworthy.
Adorned with wondrous marks and resplendent with brilliant light, he is venerated by the multitudes as he proclaims the Seal of the Mahāyāna; these external virtues may be relied upon.
This is faith. △ Second, citing the cause to exhort faith:
"Śāriputra, you should know that I originally established a vow, desiring to make all sentient beings no different from myself.
As I vowed in the past, my wish is now fulfilled; I transform all sentient beings, causing them all to enter the Buddha-way."
In the past there was a sincere vow; now, in order to repay that vow, he speaks of this ancient aspiration, which is therefore credible.
Since the vow for enlightenment is fulfilled and others are transformed to enter together into the cause of attaining the fruit, that cause is not in vain and is thus even more credible. Question:

If the original vow was universal, yet sentient beings still abound today, how can the vow be said to be fulfilled? Answer: The Buddha benefits all beings throughout the three periods of time; there is no [time when he does not do so].

Now, for the time being, we shall discuss the present state where the conditions have ripened; this is termed the fulfillment of the vow. The three verses exhorting faith are concluded. IV. Section on the Five Corruptions (*pañca-kaṣāya*). 1.
First, a general explanation of how the five corruptions obstruct the greatness [of the Buddha's teaching]. 2. Second, a detailed explanation of the five obstacles. 3.

Third, explaining that it is because of the five corruptions that the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) is taught. 4. Fourth, explaining that by means of the Great [Vehicle], the small [vehicle] refines the five corruptions, and the great vow is attained.
Section One. Now, first:
if I were to encounter sentient beings and teach them all the Buddha-way, those without wisdom would become confused, deluded, and unable to accept the teaching.
Sentient beings torment themselves with suffering, while the Buddhas rescue beings through great compassion; thus, compassion and suffering stand in opposition.
Therefore, it is said that they "meet. Furthermore, the Buddha’s suchness and the suchness of sentient beings are one suchness, without duality;
because their natures are interrelated, it is said that they meet. Now, to exhaustively teach through the Buddha-way is the fundamental intention of the Buddha.

That there are those who, due to ignorance and delusion, do not accept the teaching, is because the five turbidities constitute a great obstruction. Since they possess such obstructions, how could expedient means not be established?
To gradually entice them, the Sūtra states: "In the past, there was a Buddha named Dwelling in Non-dwelling (*Anālaya-sthita*).

He made a vow that the sentient beings of his own land would attain Buddhahood on the same day and at the same time as himself, and he entered parinirvāṇa on that very day. Furthermore, prior to the Bhadrakalpa, there was a Buddha named Equality (*Samatā*).
He also vowed that the sentient beings of his own land and those of the ten directions would attain Buddhahood on the same day as himself, and he entered parinirvāṇa on that very day."
Dù asked, "If that is so, how is it today that there are both Buddhas and sentient beings? The Buddha said, "Stop, stop!
What I spoke of previously referred only to those who have attained a human body. Is there anyone who has made a vow to attain Buddhahood on the same day as the five destinies?
The Buddha said, "It is impossible to achieve the Unsurpassed Way with a body that is not a fit vessel; one must first transform the three woeful realms."
Only after causing people to attain the human state can one then fulfill their aspirations; otherwise, how could one achieve Buddhahood by following the three non-virtuous paths?
△ Second, a detailed explanation of the five obstacles:
"I know that these sentient beings have never cultivated the roots of goodness; because they are stubbornly attached to the five desires and deluded by craving, they give rise to affliction."
Due to the causes and conditions of various desires, one falls into the three evil realms and transmigrates within the six destinies, undergoing all manner of bitter poisons and suffering.
These two verses specifically clarify the defilement of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*). True Suchness (*tathatā*) and the ultimate reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) are called the root of goodness;
because one does not rely on these roots of goodness, one cannot be moved by the Great Dharma. The five desires are the root of all evils, arising from ignorance.
When there is craving, manifold afflictions arise in competition.
The subtle form within the womb constantly grows and develops from lifetime to lifetime; those of meager virtue and little merit are oppressed by manifold sufferings.
This single verse specifically clarifies the turbidity of lifespan (*āyuṣkaṣāya*). According to the *Garbhāvakrānti-sūtra*, this process continues from the first seven days up until the thirtieth.
The eighth week fully explains the signs of gradual growth; this is what is called "constant growth from lifetime to lifetime.
Regarding the contemplation of the mind as something truly to be renounced: the moment a single thought arises, it constitutes karma for the future.
This karma is the embryo (*garbha*), and the karma of the embryo is inexhaustible. That it continues without interruption from lifetime to lifetime is precisely what is meant by "growth."
"Entering the dense forest of wrong views—whether through [theories of] existence or non-existence—one relies upon these various views, which fully comprise the sixty-two [types].
This single verse specifically clarifies the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*). The five views intermingle like a lush, dense forest:

'existence' refers to the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*), and 'non-existence' refers to the view of annihilationism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*). Based on these two views, the sixty-two views are established, as detailed [in the scriptures]."
Regarding the categories of dharmas:

being deeply attached to false and illusory phenomena, stubbornly grasping them so that they cannot be relinquished, possessing the pride of self-exaltation, and having a mind that is crooked and insincere—this single verse specifically clarifies the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*).
This is a brief enumeration from among the fundamental [afflictions], such as greed and pride, and the minor derivative afflictions (*upakleśa*).
"Using flattery to win over the rest;
for thousands of millions of billions of kalpas they shall not hear the name of the Buddha nor hear the True Dharma—such people are difficult to save.

This single verse specifically clarifies the *kalpa-kaṣāya* (the defilement of the age). Not hearing the Buddha-dharma for a long period is precisely what constitutes the *kalpa-kaṣāya*. Furthermore...
The four preceding turbidities are gathered within the period of time, and are therefore called the *kalpa-kāṣāya* (the turbidity of the eon).

Because these five turbidities act as obstacles, one does not believe in the One Vehicle and is thus difficult to save. Regarding the interpretation through the contemplation of the mind: in every thought-moment there is only evil discernment and no right contemplation;
because one’s own awakening is [obscured], one does not hear the name of the Buddha, and never accords with the Eightfold Noble Path, which is to say one does not hear the True Dharma.
This mind is indeed difficult to transform. (2) The detailed explanation of the five obstacles is concluded. △ Third, explaining that the Lesser Vehicle was taught because of the five turbidities:
"Therefore, Śāriputra, I established skillful means to teach the various paths for exhausting suffering and pointed them toward Nirvāṇa."
△ Fourth, it is explained that for the sake of great giving, the minor remedies for the five turbidities and the great vows may flourish.
Although I speak of *nirvāṇa*, this is not yet the true extinction; all dharmas have been eternally in a state of quiescence from the very beginning.
When the sons of the Buddha have practiced the Way, they shall become Buddhas in future ages.
If one analytically exhausts the delusions of the three realms and extinguishes form to attain emptiness, this is not true extinction;

for as long as the specific delusions of ignorance remain, the *pariṇāmi-cyuti* (transformative birth and death) beyond the realms continues to flourish naturally. If one realizes that ignorance is fundamentally empty, how could all phenomena exist?
It is like seeing flowers in the sky due to an eye disease—the appearance of the flowers is inherently void. Although phenomena are fundamentally quiescent, [they appear otherwise through ignorance].
If one does not cultivate the Path, there is no way to achieve union [with the Dharma]; therefore it is said: "The Buddha-son, having practiced the Path, shall become a Buddha in a future age.
This is like a flower in the sky: though it is inherently quiescent, if the cataract is not removed, one cannot perceive the pure void.
(4) The exposition of the five turbidities is concluded. △ 5. Verse on the Non-Vainness [of the Teaching].
I possess the power of skillful means to reveal the Dharma of the three vehicles; yet all the World-Honored Ones preach the path of the single vehicle.
Now, this entire great assembly should eliminate all doubt and confusion: the words of the Buddhas do not differ; there is only one, and no second, vehicle.
First the provisional, then the real; skillfully, for the sake of those in the five turbidities, this expedient means is bestowed. These sincere words are not false; do not harbor doubts.
The first verse, concerning all Buddhas, is now concluded. △ Second, the verses on past Buddhas, in two parts: first, a brief summary of the revelation and manifestation;
second, an extensive summary of the revelation and manifestation. Now, the first part.
In the past, throughout incalculable kalpas, there were immeasurable Buddhas who have entered parinirvāṇa—hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis, their number beyond measure.
These World-Honored Ones, through various causes, conditions, and parables, and by means of countless powers of skillful expedience, expounded the characteristics of all dharmas.
All these World-Honored Ones taught only the Single Vehicle Dharma (Ekayāna), transforming immeasurable sentient beings and causing them to enter the Buddha-way.
The first two verses clarify the three types of giving, while the final verse clarifies the revelation [of the One Vehicle].

Explaining the Dharma of the One Vehicle constitutes the "One" of teaching; transforming immeasurable multitudes constitutes the "One" of persons; causing them to enter the Buddha-way constitutes the "One" of practice; and the principle itself constitutes the "One" of principle.

△ Second, the extensive verses on the revelation, which have two parts: first, a general clarification of how expedient means assist in the revelation; second, a specific demonstration of the characteristics of the revelation.
First: Furthermore,
the Great Holy Lords, knowing the deep-seated desires of all classes of beings among the devas and humans of the world,
employ further diverse skillful means to assist in manifesting the primary meaning.
"Gods, humans, and all living beings" refers to the various vehicles (*yāna*) to clarify the skillful means (*upāya*) regarding the identity and difference of persons.

"The one practice" refers to the various teachings and practices to manifest the single teaching. This "one ultimate truth" (*paramārtha*) is the oneness of principle; the Buddha-nature as the true cause is precisely this ultimate truth.
If one employs the perfect and wondrous right contemplation, it is the skillful means of the true nature (*dharmatā*), and is not merely termed [a conventional means].
It differs from the present [teaching] in that it employs the five vehicles (*pañca-yāna*) and the seven skillful means (*sapta-upāya*) and so forth to assist in its manifestation;
thus, what is called "different skillful means" refers to the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) and even such acts as making offerings and chanting the name, which will be discussed below.

This is truly because the inclinations and desires of sentient beings differ, causing the skillful means of the Buddhas to vary. Although the skillful means differ, their assistance in manifesting [the truth] is the same. Since—

Having revealed the reality, this excellence of being neither different nor non-different is earnestly praised precisely because of this. II. Specifically showing the characteristics of the revelation has two parts: A.

First, revealing the merit of the conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*) by means of various virtues; B. Second, revealing the merit of the causal factor of understanding (*pariniṣpatti-hetu*) by means of hearing the sutra.
In the first part [A], there are seven sections: 1. Clarifying the revelation by means of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*); 2. By means of the mind of longing and devotion...
The clarification and revelation [of the meaning] is fivefold: first, regarding the offering of relics; second, regarding the construction of Buddha images;
third, regarding the painting of Buddha images; fourth, regarding the offering to stupas and images;
fifth, regarding the recitation of the Buddha’s name. Now, for the first:
If there are any classes of sentient beings who encountered the various Buddhas of the past, and whether they heard the Dharma, practiced giving, observed the precepts,
practiced patience, diligence, meditation, or wisdom— performing such various cultivations of merit and wisdom— all such people have already attained the path to Buddhahood.
Because the Buddha-nature as the true cause is identical in essence to that of the Buddhas, if delusive obstructions are profound, one will never encounter a Buddha.
However, those who do encounter a past Buddha do so because the power of their internal causes is strong, thereby evoking supramundane conditions.
Nevertheless, because the desires of their deep minds differ, the teachings of the various Buddhas also differ; at a particular time, some may hear the sudden [teaching].

Regarding the Dharma, there are those who hear the gradual teachings, or practice generosity, or practice ethical discipline, or practice patience, or practice diligence, or practice meditative concentration, or practice wisdom;
some cultivate a single dharma or a single practice alone, while others cultivate various dharmas and practices concurrently;
these differ in being either transformative or supportive; furthermore, some may practice with a mind focused on signs.
Regarding the six perfections, some may practice them through the signless (*animitta*), some through that which is neither sign nor signless,
and others may practice the six perfections sequentially; though these various approaches differ, when viewed from the present perspective,
since they have all attained Buddhahood and all realized the single principle (*ekārtha*), these individuals are thus one in person, and the merit and wisdom they cultivated are one in practice.

Hearing all dharmas is the teaching of the One; herein, hearing the Dharma and wisdom seem appropriate to belong to the *vidyā-hetu* (revealing cause), yet because they follow the hearing of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, they belong only to the *pratyaya-hetu* (conditioning cause). △ Second, clarifying the opening and revealing through the mind of compassionate longing.
After the parinirvāṇa of the Buddhas, if there are people with virtuous and gentle minds—such sentient beings have all already attained the path of Buddhahood.
Following the preceding text, it is not only those who encountered the Buddha, heard the Dharma, and practiced the six pāramitās who have become Buddhas;

even those who, upon the manifestation of the Buddhas' passing into extinction, were able to give rise to a heart of sorrowful longing for the Tathāgata and, in a single thought-moment, abandoned evil [have also attained it].

Transforming the good into the firm and making the firm soft—though at that time this may seem to pertain to humans, devas, and those of the Two Vehicles, when viewed from the present perspective, they have all already attained the Buddha-way.

Since the realization of the Buddha-way is one in principle, it follows that all sentient beings are identical to the person [of the Buddha], one virtuous and soft mind is identical to the practice, and the manifestation of extinction is identical to the teaching. △ Third, regarding the provision of dwellings.
To clarify and reveal this benefit: those who,
after the parinirvāṇa of the Buddhas, make offerings to their relics by erecting billions of kinds of stupas—
adorned, purified, and extensively embellished with gold, silver, crystal, *śukti*, *musāragalva*, *muktikā*, and *vaiḍūrya* beads— upon all these stupas.
There were some who erected stone shrines, or made them of sandalwood, aloeswood, *mukūla* wood, or other materials such as brick,
tile, clay, and earth; or those who, in the midst of wildernesses, piled up earth to create Buddha temples, even children playing games who gathered sand to make Buddha stupas—
all such people have already attained the path of Buddhahood.
Continuing from the preceding passage: not only those who, out of sorrowful longing for the Tathāgata, have given rise to a virtuous and supple mind and have already attained Buddhahood,
but also those who, after the parinirvāṇa of the Buddhas, have shattered their own bodies into various *śarīra* relics,
and those among them who have erected jeweled stūpas to offer to these relics— ranging down to those who have built stone shrines or even earthen shrines— and so forth.
Those who built sand stupas in childhood play may have contained relics the size of mustard seeds, or they may have been without relics;
whether made with a sincere heart or a playful mind, at that time they were said to possess either great or small merit, or to have them or not.
