Yet, viewed from the present perspective, they have all already attained the Buddha-way. Since the principle of the Buddha-way has been realized, [the distinction between sincerity and playfulness no longer applies].
First, it is like this: when such people together erect stupas and temples, piling up earth and gathering sand, they are practicing one [aspect] of the teaching;

when they break their own bodies into relics (*śarīra*), they are practicing another aspect of the teaching. According to the account, after Śākyamuni manifested his parinirvāṇa and the cremation was completed, Mahākāśyapa said:
"The relics of the Tathāgata are not our concern; there are kings, princes, and others [who shall take them]."

"Ministers, officials, elders, lay devotees, Brahmins, and others who delight in the field of merit and who perform extensive offerings and services for us should now convene a council to compile the Three Pitakas, lest the True Dharma perish too soon.

From this perspective, since Kāśyapa has transmitted the Buddha’s seal of mind, he regards this as his primary duty; likewise, those among gods and humans who delight in planting seeds in the field of merit [should do the same]."

Thus, making offerings takes precedence; when performing these offerings, although the vows and aspirations generated for the Three Vehicles or Five Vehicles differ, by virtue of the skillful means (*upāya*) of the Buddhas of the past, after a long period of time there is none who does not ultimately return to the Buddha-way.
Furthermore, according to the methods for constructing stūpas found in the sūtras, the Tathāgata’s [stūpa] consists of thirteen tiers.
The Pratyekabuddha has five tiers; the Arhat, four; the Anāgāmin, three; the Sakṛdāgāmin, two;
and the Srotāpanna, one. The Wheel-Turning King has no tiers, for "tier" refers to the marks of the wheel.

In the present age, ordinary people frequently erect stupas, conflating the common with the noble—a transgression against which the Venerable Nāgārjuna spoke when he said, "The gentleman loves others..."
Even granting that disciples revere their masters, how could one allow them to fall into the sin of falsely claiming sainthood?

Furthermore, even granting that the deceased remain in the dark and obscure, would this not nonetheless reveal the meager worth of the living? △ Fourth, clarifying the manifestation [of the teaching] by means of creating Buddha images.
If people, for the sake of the Buddha, establish various images, carving them to form all the marks and signs, they have all already attained the path to Buddhahood.
Whether made of the seven treasures, brass, bronze, red or white copper, white wax, lead, tin, iron, wood, or clay;
or whether adorned with lacquer and cloth to create an image of the Buddha—all such persons have likewise already attained the path to Buddhahood.
Continuing from the preceding text: it is not only those who erect stupas or temples for the sake of making offerings to the *śarīra* who have already attained Buddhahood.

Regardless of what material is used to establish an image, at that time the objects may be coarse or exquisite, their price high or low, the mind sincere or insincere, and the vow far-reaching or limited; thus, it appears that the merit may likewise be great or small accordingly.
Observing them now, we see that they have all already attained the Buddha-way. The Buddha-way is the oneness of principle; these people are the oneness of person;
the creation of images is the oneness of practice; and the Tathāgata’s differentiation of the merit of creating images is the oneness of teaching.
However, while the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* prohibits the use of glue for creating images—stating that doing so incurs the offense of losing right mindfulness—this sūtra permits its use.
The ancient masters said that in foreign lands, resin from trees is used [for sealing]. Some say that soybean juice may serve as a substitute for resinous glue.
Furthermore, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* does not permit the use of yellow arsenic or foul-smelling substances; the *Śīla-sūtra* does not permit the creation of half-body images.
Moreover, one should not sit before a Buddha image, nor should one lie down before a Buddha image. Also, there is the *Sūtra on the Merit of Creating Images*.
A brief explanation of the eleven merits: first, one’s eyes shall be clear and pure in every lifetime;
second, one shall never be born in an evil place; third, one shall always be born into a noble family; fourth, one’s body shall be like the color of purple-polished gold;

fifth, one shall abound in rare treasures; sixth, one shall be born into a virtuous and good family; seventh, one shall be born to become a king; eighth, one shall become a Golden Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakravartin).
Ninth, one will be born in the Brahma Heaven with a lifespan of one kalpa. Tenth, one will not fall into the evil realms.

Eleventh, in future births, one will again be able to revere and honor the Triple Gem. It is further said that if, at the time of death, a person speaks the words to have an image made—even if it is as small as a grain of wheat—it can eliminate the sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas throughout the three periods of time. One should know this.

Such merits as these are all the provisional rewards (*puṣpa-vipāka*), with their ultimate fruit residing in the stage of Buddhahood. △ Fifth, clarifying the manifestation [of the Buddha-nature] by means of painting images of the Buddha:
Whether one paints an image of the Buddha oneself or has another do so, adorning it with the marks of the hundred blessings, all such persons have already attained the Way of the Buddha.
Even those who, as children at play, drew images of the Buddha with grass, wood, brushes, or even their fingernails—
all such people gradually accumulated merit, perfected the mind of great compassion, and have all attained the Way of the Buddha;
they merely transform bodhisattvas and deliver immeasurable multitudes.
Continuing from the preceding passage: it is not only those who have constructed images of the Buddha who have already attained Buddhahood.

Whether one paints an image of the Buddha oneself, commissions another to do so, or even if a child draws one in play—at that very moment, it is said that their merit may be great or small, or perhaps existent or non-existent;
yet when viewed from the present perspective, they have all likewise already attained the path of Buddhahood.
The Way is the oneness of principle, and all people are the oneness of persons. By gradually accumulating merit and fulfilling the mind of great compassion, one practices the "one";
this is precisely to transform all bodhisattvas, which is the teaching of the "one. Furthermore, the two phrases "merely transforming" clarify the matters after that person has attained Buddhahood;

it is the self-realization of the fourfold oneness, whereby one again uses the fourfold oneness to deliver sentient beings. △ Six: Regarding... (Note: The final character "約" [yue] indicates a section heading or transition marker, likely referring to the sixth point concerning the application of the fourfold oneness.)
Making offerings to stupas and images clearly reveals [the truth].
If a person, with a reverent mind, makes offerings of flowers, incense, banners, and canopies to stupas, temples, precious images, or painted images;
or if they cause others to perform music by beating drums, blowing horns, conchs, and ocarinas, or playing flutes, lutes, harps, and lutes (*vīṇā*), or cymbals and gongs—

Those who offered all such various wonderful sounds as an act of worship, or those who with a joyful heart sang hymns in praise of the Buddha’s virtues—even a single small sound—all have already attained the path to Buddhahood.

If a person, even with a distracted mind, offers so much as a single flower to a painted image, they will gradually see countless Buddhas. Or there may be someone who prostrates, or perhaps merely joins their palms in reverence.
Even if one merely raises a single hand or slightly bows the head to make such an offering to the image, one will gradually see immeasurable Buddhas,
personally attain the unsurpassed path, and extensively deliver countless multitudes before entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, like a fire extinguished when the fuel is exhausted.
Continuing from the preceding text: it is not only those who erect stupas, build temples, or fashion statues and paintings who have already attained Buddhahood;

rather, whoever performs various offerings before any stupa, temple, precious statue, or painting shall all attain Buddhahood. A full discussion of these offerings does not go beyond the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*):
flowers, banners, canopies, and so forth, which pertain to the sense-object of form (*rūpa-dhātu*); and musical sounds, which pertain to the sense-object of sound (*śabda-dhātu*).
The sound of chanting is the object-field of sound; incense is the object-field of fragrance; prostration is the object-field of touch.

Furthermore, clothing is the object-field of touch, and food and drink are the object-field of taste—these are not mentioned here in brief, yet they must logically exist. Moreover, making offerings requires discussion of the three karmas:
the mind of reverence is the karma of the mind; praising virtues is the karma of speech; and prostrating, joining the palms, raising the hands, and bowing low [are the karma of the body].
The head refers to bodily karma; regarding these five objects of the senses, the three karmas may be more or less predominant, and the activities may be either focused or dispersed.
At that time, it was said that there must be distinctions in merit; yet viewed from the present perspective, they all equally constitute the "four ones.
Furthermore, by means of these four ones, one extensively delivers sentient beings until the fuel of the three delusions is exhausted and the fire of the two deaths is extinguished.

This refers to entering the Great Parinirvāṇa of non-abiding. Regarding the scriptural passage that speaks of "causing others to make music," whether they be ordained bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs, śrāmaṇeras or śrāmaṇerikās, or laypeople such as kings, elders, officials, or householders, there is no principle by which any of them would personally perform musical performances;
therefore, it must necessarily say "causing others" to do so. As for singing...
Regarding the chanting of praises for virtues, both monastics and laypeople are permitted to perform it; however, one must also understand its fundamental principles.

If the *brahmanic* sounds (*brahma-svara*) are harmonious and elegant, they are suitable for both clergy and laity alike. If, however, these are confused with secular lyrics and tunes, such practice is not permitted by the Vinaya.

I have frequently observed that in recent times, those who chant praises often employ the melodic modes of professional musicians, and furthermore, when performing liturgical repentance (*li-chan*), they do not adhere to the *brahmanic* style.
The ancient custom was to compete in drawing out long tones, fearing only that it would increase greed and arrogance and augment negligence;
blessings are few while transgressions are many—reflect upon this and choose wisely. △ Seventh, clarifying the manifestation by means of invoking the Buddha’s name.
If a person with a distracted mind enters a stupa or temple and recites "Namo Buddha" even once, they have all already attained the path of Buddhahood.
Following the preceding text, it is stated that not only those who make offerings to stupas and images through the five sense objects and three karmas have become Buddhas;
even those who, with a distracted mind, recite the name of the Buddha even once, shall all attain Buddhahood. "Namo" is translated here as "taking refuge" (or "dedicating one's life").
I, too, translated it as "Namo. When Devadatta was at the point of death, he recited "Namo," but before he could say "Buddha," his physical body sank into the earth and he fell into hell.
The Buddha prophesied that upon emerging from hell, he would become a Pratyekabuddha named Namo.
In the Western Regions, there were those who worshipped celestial images; they fashioned the heads of these images out of gold. When bandits came to steal them, [the heads] vanished.
The thief was unable to seize it; however, as soon as he uttered "Namo Buddha," the golden head was obtained.
The next day, the multitude gathered and deliberated, saying, "The celestial image has lost its head; this must mean that the gods have departed.
One who had been possessed by a deity spoke, saying, "When the thief came to take the head, he recited 'Namo Buddha,' and all the devas [were present]."
Because he was so startled and agitated, he obtained his head; because he was thus [fearful], he lost it. The crowd asked, "Is Heaven not as good as the Buddha?
Since it is not as good, why do you not serve the Buddha? Even a bandit who merely utters "Namo Buddha" can still obtain his head;
how much more so for a worthy person who recites the name of the Buddha? How could the honored deities of the ten directions ever dare to withstand him? Simply be diligent and do not be indolent!

A previous sutra states: "It is like a person holding a single stone and placing it in water; it will surely sink without doubt. Yet if one holds a hundred stones and places them upon a boat, they will certainly not sink.
Likewise, a person who has committed evil karma will inevitably fall into hell upon death, just as a stone sinks when placed in water.
However, if at the moment of death one recites 'Namo Buddha,' by the power of the Buddha, that person shall not enter hell, just as [the stones do not sink] by the power of the boat."
Therefore, it was caused that the stone did not sink. Furthermore, a sutra states:
"At the third great assembly in Huālín Garden, ninety-two billion people—each of whom had once uttered 'Namo Buddha' during the period of Śākyamuni Buddha’s bequeathed Dharma—shall behold Maitreya.
Additionally, during the Buddha’s lifetime, there was an old man who sought out five hundred senior elders (sthaviras) for ordination; the elders examined him...

Those who lacked roots of goodness in their past lives were all denied permission; however, this person finally encountered a Buddha at the very end and was immediately ordained by him, attaining the state of an Arhat.
When the Elder questioned the Buddha about this, the Buddha said: "In immeasurable kalpas ago, this person entered the mountains to gather firewood and encountered a tiger.
In his terror, he once called out, 'Namo Buddhāya. Because the roots of goodness from that single utterance have now ripened, he has attained this."
That one attains deliverance is due solely to this [practice] and no other virtue;
that one wanders through birth and death for such a long time is because the duration of kalpas is so vast that it is neither seen nor known by the eye of the śrāvaka path.
Since one who has attained the realization of arhatship must necessarily also realize unsurpassed bodhi, it is clear. Even the scattering of the mind while chanting the name must necessarily...

If one can attain Buddhahood through various good deeds, how much more so for one whose mind is undistracted! A single thought in accord with reality is a Buddha; a single day in accord with reality is a Buddha.
This mind makes the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha. If you do not believe this, I have no further means to help you.
The first section, which clarifies the merit of the *nidāna-condition* (緣因) by means of various good deeds, is concluded. △ Second, clarifying [the merit] by means of hearing the sutra.
This clarifies the merit of the causes [of enlightenment]:
"If there were those who heard this Dharma during the lifetimes of the Buddhas of the past or after their parinirvāṇa, they have all already attained the path to Buddhahood.
This Dharma specifically points to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the teaching that reveals the ultimate reality by opening up the provisional means. The above constitutes the six perfections.
Even making offerings during the Semblance Teaching, or merely reciting the names of the Buddhas, are all skillful means employed by the Buddhas to assist in revealing the ultimate truth;
if these can open the way for one to become a wondrous *nidāna-hetu* (causal condition), how much more so this sutra, which directly reveals the ultimate truth?

If there are those who hear it, they will immediately possess the seeds of the *vijñapti-hetu* (revealing cause); how could they fail to attain Buddhahood? However, depending on the time of hearing the sutra, or...
Whether one understands or not, whether there are signs or no signs, whether the mind is focused or distracted—these matters are not uniform;

yet they can all be discussed in terms of the distinctions between the five vehicles. Even if it passes through the ear only once, it will forever serve as a seed for the Path. Whether far or near, one will ultimately be liberated by means of this;
there is not a single person who will not attain Buddhahood. This is the true word and the real word of all Buddhas.
This should indeed be deeply believed. Question: What is the meaning of explaining in detail that the five vehicles of the past Buddhas all equally enter the reality?

Answer: All Buddhas of the three periods of time possess the opening of the provisional; however, because the future [Buddhas] have not yet arisen and the present [Buddhas] have only recently begun their practice, their realization of this principle is weak.
The Buddhas of the past opened the provisional long ago, and those who were transformed by them have all achieved the fourfold oneness (*catur-eka*). Therefore...
Regarding the meaning of "manifesting the real through the provisional" throughout the ten directions, such forced and empty words are not as good as verifying it through actual facts;
therefore, in relation to the Buddhas of the past, the reality is extensively revealed by means of the five vehicles. This concludes the two verses concerning the Buddhas of the past.
△ Three verses on the Buddhas of the future; the first verse concerns the employment of skillful means, and the second verse reveals the ultimate truth. Now, the first:
"The World-Honored Ones of the future shall be immeasurable in number; these Tathāgatas likewise employ skillful means to preach the Dharma."
△ Second, the verses that reveal the reality [of the Buddha-body] consist of four parts: 1. One verse on the person; 2. Two verses on practice; 3. Three verses on the teaching;
4. One verse on the principle. Now, for the first:
All Tathāgatas, by means of immeasurable skillful means, deliver all sentient beings and cause them to enter the untainted wisdom of the Buddha.
If there are those who hear the Dharma, not one among them will fail to become a Buddha.
Because it is certain that no one who hears the Dharma fails to attain Buddhahood, this refers to the "one" in terms of the capacity to deliver others, which is the unity of teaching.
That which is realized through the Buddha’s wisdom is the unity of principle. To enter into the Buddha’s wisdom is the unity of practice. △ Second.
The first verse concerns the single practice:
"The fundamental vows of all Buddhas are that the Buddha-way which I have practiced, I desire all sentient beings to likewise attain;
for my own practice and the transformation of others are nothing other than the Buddha-way, this is the single practice. △ The third [section] concerns the single teaching in one verse.
Although the Buddhas of future ages shall preach hundreds of thousands of billions of countless Dharma-gates, in reality they are but the One Vehicle.

The Buddhas, the Honored Ones among two-legged beings, know that all phenomena are eternally without self-nature and that the Buddha-seed arises from conditions; for this reason, they preach the One Vehicle.
Regarding the "hundreds of thousands of billions of countless dharma-gates," this refers to all provisional teachings such as the five vehicles and the seven stages of skillful means.

To state that their ultimate reality is the Buddha-vehicle is precisely to clarify the intent behind teaching through skillful means. Although the teaching resides in the provisional, the intent is fundamentally rooted in the real;
since the provisional is the provisional of the real, it can be opened up so that both together accomplish the cause of enlightenment. This is knowing the Dharma.

"Perpetual absence of nature" means that the true mark (*dharmatā*) is eternally abiding, lacking self-nature (*svabhāva*), lacking other-nature (*parabhāva*), lacking common nature (*sāmānyabhāva*), and lacking causeless nature (the emptiness of nature).
That there is no nature even in the absence of nature (the emptiness of marks) means that the single term "absence of nature" encompasses two absences of nature;

this is the nature of the absence of nature, which is the nature of signlessness (*animitta*). Because it has existed from the very beginning, it is called "perpetual. "Knowing" refers to illumination.

As fully explained in the fifth fascicle of the *Mohe Zhiguan*, regarding the inconceivable realm (*acintya-viṣaya*), the "three thousand worlds in a single thought-moment" (*ekakṣaṇa-trisāhasra*) is neither self nor other;

since it lacks the four modes of being (*catuṣkoṭi*), the single thought-moment is likewise non-existent. This is precisely the emptiness of nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*). Since there is no single thought-moment, even "no-thought" (*amanasikāra*) is non-existent;
this is the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*). These are the two kinds of emptiness within the inconceivable. If these two are originally empty by nature, then...

If these inherent virtues are investigated and analyzed until they enter into emptiness, this constitutes "attainment through cultivation. If one investigates them and finds they cannot be established, then one must cultivate the myriad practices, combining the primary and auxiliary.
When all practices are fully present within these acts, it is only then called the "conditioning cause" (*pratyaya-hetu*).

Having heard this meaning, one then understands what is called "opening. One may inquire about worldly causes and conditions through the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) to comprehend birth and non-birth.
Question: Since the nature (*prakṛti*) is fundamentally pure and does not depend on dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), why is it necessary to analyze it by means of these four propositions?

Answer: Worldly phenomena (*loka-dharma*) are also fundamentally non-arising; they are merely designated as "arising" due to conceptual attachment (*saṃjñā*). The nature of reality (*dharmatā*) is likewise so.

Because one speaks of "self" and "other" and so forth, it is necessary to analyze it through the two types of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). If these two emptinesses are not yet manifest, one must further analyze them in terms of continuity (*anubandha*) and dependence (*apekṣā*).

Question: Is this established through causal conditions? Question: For what reason is this contemplation not set forth in the present text? Answer: The Sūtra opens [this teaching] for those of sharp faculties.
As for "the Buddha-seed arises from conditions," the Middle Way of non-substantiality (*niḥsvabhāva*) is itself the Buddha-seed.
Those who are deluded regarding this principle give rise to sentient beings due to ignorance acting as a condition; those who understand this principle do so through the practice of the teachings.
When conditions arise, there is the emergence of perfect enlightenment; because one desires to give rise to the Buddha-seed, the teaching of the One Vehicle is required.
Thus, this verse teaches the One [Vehicle]. Furthermore, "those without nature" refers to the true cause of Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*).

That "the Buddha-seed arises from conditions" refers to the conditional and developmental causes (*pratyaya* and *pariniṣpatti-hetu*), whereby the conditional aids the developmental so that the true seed may arise. When one arises, all arise; such are the three.

The nature (*prakṛti*) is called the One Vehicle. (Because the three causes do not change, they are collectively termed "nature"; because the entire substance is restored, it is further designated as "conditions" and "understanding"). Thus, within the stage of the principle (*tattva*), suffering is the *dharmatā-nature* as the direct cause (*hetu-pratyaya*) of Buddha-nature;

afflictions are the *dharmatā-nature* as the understanding-cause (*prajñā-pratyaya*); and karma is the *dharmatā-nature* as the condition-cause (*pratyaya-pratyaya*). These three Buddha-natures are neither vertical nor horizontal, neither simultaneous nor separate; they are inconceivable. They lack self-nature, even lacking the nature of being causeless;

yet this very absence of nature is designated as the *dharmatā-nature* as the direct cause of Buddha-nature. Within the stage of names (*nāman*), there is a slight degree of subtle understanding and a slight degree of subtle practice; this is precisely the nature of the absence of nature, which constitutes the entirety of that subtle understanding and subtle practice.

Upon reaching the stage of "semblance" within the practice of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), the conduct of understanding gradually becomes more manifest; this too is the nature of that which lacks a fixed nature, accomplished by the totality of its essence. Within this stage of names and semblance, the three inconceivable causes are designated as the *pratyaya-hetu* (conditional cause) of Buddha-nature.

In the stage of partial realization (*bhūmi*), at the first dwelling (*prathama-bhūmi*), there occurs the "simultaneous arising of all through one arising. The principle-mind of the direct cause (*samyag-hetu*) arising is named the virtue of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya-guṇa*); the wisdom-mind of the discerning cause (*vijñapti-hetu*) arising is named the virtue of Prajñā; and the virtuous mind of the conditional cause arising is named the virtue of Liberation (*vimukti-guṇa*).

These are inconceivable in that they are neither vertical nor horizontal, neither simultaneous nor distinct. Within this stage of partial realization, these three inconceivable causes are designated as the *vijñapti-hetu* (discerning cause) of Buddha-nature. In the ultimate stage, the qualities of nature are fully manifested, and cultivation is brought to completion.

Because virtue culminates in the fulfillment of its function, it is called the "correct seed" (*samyag-bīja*). That which arises once causes all things to arise; this reveals that the fruit-vehicle (*phala-yāna*) depends upon the correct [seed], with the primary and its attendants, even down to the repayment of causes, where a single atom, a single practice, and a single moment arise simultaneously.

"Arising" (*utpāda*) means "accomplishment. When the cultivated nature (*bhāvanā-dharmatā*) and the innate nature (*prakṛti-dharmatā*) are unified, there is no further division; this is because the three causes of the rational nature (*dharmatā-svabhāva*) are ultimately and perfectly manifested. Therefore, it is said that these three natures are called the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). △ Fourth, the verse on the unity of principle (*tattva-ekatva*):

"This Dharma abides in its fixed position; the characteristics of the world are eternally constant. Having realized this at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), the Teacher explains it through skillful means (*upāya*).
"This" refers to the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) of the non-duality of nature and cultivation. This One Vehicle is precisely the abiding of the Dharma, also called the fixed position of the Dharma.
From the root of non-abiding, all dharmas are established; this root of non-abiding cannot [be grasped].

Because it is subject to movement, it is called the "abiding of phenomena" (*dharmasthiti*). All various phenomena do not transcend this scope; thus, it is called the "fixed position of phenomena" (*dharmaniyāmatā*).
Taking this abiding of phenomena and fixed position as the characteristics of the world’s perfect awakening, the abiding of phenomena and the fixed position are eternally constant.
Therefore, the characteristics of the world’s perfect awakening are also eternally constant. Taking up these phenomena...
Abiding in the station of the Dharma, one acts for the sake of the world of sentient beings and the world of the vessel;
because the phenomena abiding in the station of the Dharma are eternally abiding, the characteristics of both the world of sentient beings and the world of the vessel are likewise eternally abiding.
Thus, each and every characteristic of the three worlds is without exception eternally abiding, and each and every one is without exception a phenomenon abiding in the station of the Dharma.
Each and every thing is none other than the One Vehicle; yet sentient beings, deluded and obscured, are unable to awaken to this knowledge.
Within the eternally abiding, they falsely perceive arising and ceasing; within the One Vehicle, they falsely perceive distinctions.
Only the Greatly Awakened Teacher, seated at the site of enlightenment, having known it as it truly is, [realizes] the ineffable, quiescent nature of reality, free from all conceptual proliferation.
One can explain this principle of unity through skillful means (*upāya*), and furthermore, one can use diverse skillful means to assist in manifesting this principle of unity.

Question: To awaken to this rational nature is called "Perfect Enlightenment" (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Since the mundane world accords with this nature, it follows that the nature is eternal and its manifestations (*lakṣaṇa*) are likewise eternal; this would be acceptable.

However, sentient beings are deluded regarding this rational nature, and since the mundane world thus deviates from the nature— *Note: This passage sets up a dialectical inquiry regarding the relationship between the ultimate nature (*dharmatā*) and its phenomenal manifestations within the context of the Tathāgatagarbha and Huayan thought.*

Therefore, although the nature (*svabhāva*) is fundamentally eternal, its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) must necessarily be impermanent. How then could the characteristics of the world of sentient beings and the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*) also be eternally abiding?
Answer: It is like ice and water, which both share moisture as their nature; moisture is the characteristic of both ice and water.
Since the ice and water are impermanent, the nature of moisture is likewise impermanent. Thus, this nature of moisture is designated as "naturelessness" (*niḥsvabhāvatā*).

Since the characteristic of moisture is permanent, the characteristics of both ice and water are likewise permanent; therefore, these characteristics of ice and water are designated as "permanently abiding.
Furthermore, the principle of the non-substantiality of the One Vehicle is like a house that fundamentally does not move:
the Tathāgata awakens to it as one who has sobered up sees its immobility, while the nine realms of existence are deluded by it as those who are intoxicated falsely perceive it.
Although that [world] appears to undergo transformation, the fundamental house does not transform;

therefore, while the characteristics of the sentient world and the characteristics of the vessel-world appear to undergo birth and extinction through false perception, they are in fact eternally abiding.

This is because both the sentient beings and the vessel-world are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), are the abiding of phenomena (*dharmasthiti*), and are the fixed position of phenomena (*dharmapratisthā*). Furthermore, it is like the false vision of one with cataracts.
The arising and ceasing of flowers in the sky are such that these flowers have no actual arising or ceasing, because they lack intrinsic nature and are identical with emptiness.
The eternal abiding of the world follows this same principle. All sentient beings possess this constant reality; to hear of it and be able to understand it is called "constant through name.
To examine and investigate it moment by moment, mind after mind, without interruption, is called "constant through contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*)," which removes coarse defilements.
First, the purification of the six sense organs is "semblance permanence," as it is a sudden and vast awakening that realizes the true cause of the forty-one stages.
Second, the "partial realization permanence" is the complete manifestation without remainder or deficiency; this is "ultimate permanence.

Because these states are equal from beginning to end, they are called "immediate. Yet, because there are vast differences between ascending and sinking, one must distinguish the six based on their equality.
The essence of equality itself possesses the distinction between rising and sinking, just as one must rely upon empty space to discuss distance and proximity;

therefore, it is said that "the entirety of nature gives rise to cultivation" (referring generally to both the two types of cultivation: the adverse and the compliant). Regardless of how greatly rising and sinking may differ, they never depart from the single body of equality, just as distance and proximity do not exist apart from empty space;
therefore, it is said that "the entirety of cultivation resides within nature. It is for the purpose of explaining this that the teachings have come forth.
Because the teaching is for the sake of one practice that accords with this; because the practice is for the sake of one person who must realize this;
because the person is for the sake of one—these three verses conclude the section on future Buddhas. △ Fourth, the verses on present Buddhas.

The Buddhas currently residing in the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who are honored by devas and humans, have appeared in the world for the sake of bringing peace and security to sentient beings;

they likewise preach this Dharma. Knowing the supreme tranquility, yet through the power of skillful means, they manifest various paths, though in reality there is but the Buddha-vehicle. They know the various conducts of sentient beings and what their deep minds intend.

He teaches by means of various causes, conditions, parables, and verbal expressions, employing appropriate skillful means according to the karma practiced in the past, the nature of one's desires, the power of diligence, and the sharpness or dullness of the faculties.
The first verse clarifies the intent of the transformation; the second verse reveals the reality; and the third verse demonstrates the provisional means.
Such a teaching refers doubly to both the provisional and the real teachings. "First, quiescence" refers to the oneness of principle;

"conveniently demonstrating various paths" refers to the oneness of teaching from the perspective of what is demonstrated, and the oneness of practice from the perspective of what is shown; it is for the purpose of knowing the various [capacities] of sentient beings.

The practice [of the three vehicles] and so forth represent the provisional application of skillful means; this concludes the first verse, the section on the four Buddhas. II. The second part, the section on Śākyamuni, has two sub-sections: A.

First, a brief versification of the preceding provisional and ultimate teachings to serve as the basis for the general analogy that follows. B. Second, an extensive versification of the preceding six meanings to serve as the basis for the specific analogies that follow.
Within section A, there are two further parts: 1. First, a versification of the revelation of the ultimate reality. 2. Second, a versification of the application of skillful means.
Now, first:
"Now I, likewise, for the sake of bringing peace and security to sentient beings, proclaim the Buddha-way through various gateways of Dharma.
This passage fully explains the four points [of the preceding verse]. Regarding "Now I, likewise": it means that I am identical to all Buddhas in this regard.

To teach and transform sentient beings through the One Reality is a general verse that reveals the reality. "Peaceful and secure" refers to the secret treasury of *nirvāṇa*, which is the place of peace and security;
the Buddha himself dwells therein and also establishes sentient beings so that they likewise enter this place of peace and security.
This "place" is the oneness of principle, and "sentient beings" is the oneness of persons. Entering the Buddha-way through various Dharma gates is—
The single practice that is proclaimed is the single teaching. △ Second, the verse on the provisional application of means:
"By the power of my wisdom, knowing the dispositions and desires of sentient beings, I employ skillful means to preach all dharmas so that they may all attain joy."

The power of wisdom (*prajñā-bala*) is precisely skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*): knowing their dispositions and desires constitutes the discernment of limited capacities; preaching the various dharmas constitutes the correct application of skillful means;

and all being filled with joy constitutes responding to what is appropriate for their capacities. Although the two preceding verses briefly encompass the beginning and end of the Buddha’s single transformation, exhausting it without exception, they are thus called "abridged verses" (*saṃkṣipta-gāthā*). The above discussion of the provisional and the real serves as a general summary for what follows.
The six analogies constitute the foundation. First, "I am now likewise" refers to myself, Śākyamuni, who am the principal figure of this single transformation;

for those below, there is the analogy of the great elder, which serves as the basis. Second, "peace and security" refers to the Great Nirvāṇa—eternal, blissful, self, and pure—and is contrasted with the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) of the triple world, which are termed "lack of peace and security."
1. The burning house is the basis for the third [point], namely that sentient beings—the multitudes who receive transformation across the five destinies—are the "five hundred people" below.
2. The teaching of the secure and peaceful Dharma corresponds to the insecure dharmas of the five turbidities;
this is the basis for the metaphor of the fire breaking out below. 3. The various gateways of the Dharma correspond to that which is not diverse; this is the basis for the "below."

There is only one gate, which serves as the basis for the six [sections] below: knowing the dispositions and natures of sentient beings refers to the distinctions in the capacities of the three vehicles within the five destinies;
this serves as the basis for the thirty similes below. The first brief verse above concludes the provisional and the real.
△ Second, the detailed verses on the six meanings above serve as the basis for the individual similes in the subsequent text. First, the verse:

1. The five turbidities serve as the basis for the lower [view] of the analogy of fire; two verses are composed as the basis for this. 2. Bestowing skillful means and transformations serves as the basis for the lower [view] of the analogy of discarding a stool and using a carriage;
three verses are composed as the basis for this. 3. Revealing the reality serves as the basis for the lower [view] of the analogy of equally bestowing the great carriages;

four verses are composed as the basis for this. 4. Five verses praise the rarity of the Dharma. 5. Six verses show that it is not in vain. 6. Six verses distinguish the assembly and exhort them toward faith; these collectively constitute the lower [view] of non-existence.
First, regarding the analogy for falsity:
Śāriputra, you should know that with my Buddha-eye I behold the sentient beings of the six realms who are impoverished and lacking in merit and wisdom;
they enter the perilous paths of birth and death where suffering continues without interruption, and they are deeply attached to the five desires, just as a yak loves its tail.
Blinded by their own craving and ignorance, they see nothing; they do not seek the Buddha of Great Power nor the Dharma that cuts off suffering.
Deeply immersed in various false views, they seek to abandon suffering through further suffering. For the sake of these sentient beings, he gives rise to great compassion.
The first eleven characters clarify that the Buddha possesses the eye capable of seeing; the subsequent text states, "The master of the house stands outside the gate.
This implies that the Buddha, abiding in the realm of the *dharmakāya*, uses his eternally quiescent Buddha-eye to universally illumine all sentient beings.
If their faculties are sharp and their afflictions light, he teaches the One Vehicle Dharma through the form of Vairocana; if their faculties are dull and their afflictions heavy, then...
By manifesting as an aged bhikṣu, he enters the burning house as a skillful means to bestow the three vehicles;

this was done at that time because he discerned their capacities, and thus he said, "I observe with the Buddha-eye. Now, when observing material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), one should employ the *divya-cakṣus* (heavenly eye), and when distinguishing the faculties and capacities of beings, one should employ the *dharma-cakṣus* (Dharma-eye). Here, however, it says "observing with the Buddha-eye" to indicate that the superior includes the inferior. Furthermore, there are four [meanings].
The eye-faculty and the Buddha-eye are both called the Buddha-eye. Regarding the sentient beings of the six realms, the following clarifies what they perceive:
the five turbidities. As the text below states: "You sons, because you previously came into this house while playing, you were immature and ignorant, delighting in worldly pleasures.
Being poor and lacking merit, wisdom, and blessings—this verse refers to the turbidity of sentient beings. The two lines concerning entering birth and death refer to the turbidity of views.

The verse on the *kaṣāya* of lifespan (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*) consists of four lines beginning with "deeply attached" (*gāḍhābhiniveśa*). The verse on the *kaṣāya* of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*) consists of two lines beginning with "not seeking" (*anarthin*).

The verse on the *kaṣāya* of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*) states that because there is no Buddha within the eon, it is called a "defiled eon" (*kaṣāya-kalpa*); yet, if there were a Buddha, even though it is defiled, one would be able to break through it.

This is expressed by the two lines beginning with "penetrating deeply" (*gambhīra-praveśa*). The verse on the *kaṣāya* of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*) consists of four lines beginning with "or not seeking," which collectively describe the *kaṣāya* of views because of [the presence of] false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).

Not seeking the Buddha of Great Power, nor seeking the Dharma that severs suffering, yet falsely hoping to abandon the fruit of suffering by means of the very causes that summon it—how could this ever be possible?
Since the four turbidities are concentrated in this period, it is termed the *kalpa-turbidity*; therefore, there is no need for a separate verse.
The two lines beginning with "For the sake of these sentient beings" clarify the arising of great compassion and the responsive manifestation described in the following text.

It is said that when the elder heard this, he was startled and entered the burning house. △ Second, the verse on the application of skillful means as a transformation, which serves as the basis for the subsequent parable of discarding the small table and using the carts;

this section has two parts: first, the thought of employing the Mahāyāna as a provisional fit which cannot be attained; second, the thought of employing the Three Vehicles like all Buddhas, which is suitable and can be attained.

The first of these again has three parts: first, clarifying the employment of the Great Vehicle as a provisional fit. (Note: The provided text fragment ends mid-sentence regarding the first sub-point. The translation reflects the structure and content as presented.)
[The Buddha] clearly perceives that sentient beings lack the capacity [to understand], and thus his three types of supernormal knowledge reflect upon the desire to cease his transformative ministry.
First: "When I first sat at the site of enlightenment, observing the tree and walking back and forth for twenty-one days, I contemplated this matter:
'The wisdom I have attained is subtle and supreme.'"

Regarding "initially sitting at the site of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*): from the perspective of ultimate truth, there is no time; yet, because he uses time to transform sentient beings, it is called the "beginning" as the start of his transformative activity.
Regarding the literal explanation: because he first cultivated and attained the Way at this place, it is called the "site of enlightenment.
Because he attained *samyak-saṃbodhi* while sitting beneath this tree, it is called the "Tree of the Way. Out of gratitude for the tree's kindness, he contemplates and reflects upon its virtues.
Therefore, as he walked upon the ground beneath the trees, there was no discrimination; how could he have required gratitude?
The *Adbhutadharmaparyāya-sūtra* states that it is solely through universal transformation and the transmission of the Dharma that one is said to repay kindness.

The *Past Causes and Effects Sūtra* states that during the first seven days after attaining enlightenment, the Buddha contemplated that his Dharma was so subtle and wondrous that no one would be able to receive it; during the second seven days, he contemplated the superior [capacities] of sentient beings.
Those of middling and inferior faculties contemplate for twenty-one days who should first hear the Dharma;
thus [the Buddha] went to Vārāṇasī to preach the Four Truths to the five bhikṣus, and Kauṇḍinya attained the purity of the Dharma-eye (this refers to what is perceived by those of limited capacity).

Now it is clarified that when the Buddha abides in the stage of the Dharmakāya, he is quiescent yet ever-illuminating, constantly surveying all things with the Buddha-eye without omission—how could he have only arrived at the site of enlightenment [at that time]?
"Staying for twenty-one days, he then contemplated this matter. To say "twenty-one days" is to indicate that he intended to preach the Dharma in three cycles.

During the first week, he contemplated the *dharmadeśanā*; during the second week, the *aupamyadeśanā*; and during the third week, the *nidānadeśanā*. Finding no receptive capacity [among the listeners], he was unable to do so;

therefore, he ceased the Great [Vehicle] and bestowed the Small [Vehicle]. This explanation applies specifically to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) of the Mahāyāna; if taken in a general sense, however—

Regarding the explanation according to the Mahāyāna: the first seven contemplations explain the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao); the next seven contemplations explain the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao); and the final seven contemplations explain the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao).
Since there are no sentient beings with the capacity [for these teachings], they cease their Mahāyāna discourse and instead teach the three vehicles as expedient means of the Tripitaka.
Regarding the explanation through the contemplation of the mind: the "tree" refers to the great tree of the twelve links of dependent origination; one must deeply contemplate this conditionality.
Having given rise to the aspiration for self-awakening to Bodhi, and wishing to benefit sentient beings with the shade of the forest of untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*), he says:
"The *Vṛkṣapracchāyā-sūtra* practitioner [practices] the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharmāḥ*) of the Mahāyāna; these are the dharmas for practicing the Path.

By personally traversing the ground of the true nature (*bhūtala*) through these factors of enlightenment, one attains the Buddha-way. Wishing to transform and deliver sentient beings by means of these dharmas, one therefore gives rise to this practice. (3)
Seventh: The first seven [days] clarify that the contemplation of the Middle Way is subtle and difficult to contemplate, such that one cannot attain it through the subsequent seven;
the next seven clarify that the contemplation of the Provisional is difficult for discerning wisdom to arise, such that one cannot attain it through the final seven;

and the last seven clarify that the contemplation of Emptiness is difficult to skillfully traverse through Emptiness alone, thereby elucidating the expedient analytical methods of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) contemplations. △
Second, it clarifies that sentient beings lack the necessary capacity.
Sentient beings have dull faculties, are attached to pleasure, and are blinded by ignorance; how can such types as these be saved?
Since his wisdom is subtle, wondrous, and supreme, it cannot be grasped or understood by those with dull faculties who are blinded by ignorance. Below...
The text says: "The sons, being ignorant, although they heard their father’s instruction, still delighted in and clung to their play, never ceasing.
△ Third, the cessation of the teaching due to the remembrance of desire.
At that time, the various Brahma Kings, the various Śakras, the Four World-Protecting Heavenly Kings, and Maheśvara...
Furthermore, hundreds of thousands of millions of other celestial hosts and their retinues, with palms joined in reverence, entreated me to turn the wheel of Dharma.
I then reflected: "If I were to praise only the Buddha Vehicle, sentient beings submerged in suffering would be unable to believe this teaching.
Because they would reject the Dharma and lack faith, they would fall into the three evil realms. It would be better for me not to preach the Dharma at all, but to quickly enter parinirvāṇa."

Although Brahmā and Śakra requested [the teaching], the Buddha knew there was no spiritual capacity [for them] and therefore did not preach it; as the subsequent text says: "The sons are young and have not yet attained any realization;
they might fall and be consumed by fire. His initial thought was to employ the Mahāyāna, but finding it unsuitable, he desisted. △ Second thought:
To act in accordance with all Buddhas by employing the Three Vehicles (Triyāna) so that it may accord with their suitability. This has two parts; first, the explanation.

Regarding the first part of the "Transformation" section, which clarifies the two points that resolve doubts, there are four subsections: first, explaining the provisional suitability for the three vehicles; second, explaining the existence of those with small capacities;
third, explaining the bestowal of transformation; and fourth, explaining the reception, practice, awakening, and entry. Now, the first [subsection].
Reflecting upon the power of the skillful means practiced by the Buddhas of the past, [the Bodhisattva] thinks: "The path I have now attained should likewise be taught through the three vehicles.
He reflects that although those beings lack the great capacity for enlightenment, they must not be abandoned forever; rather, they must be guided and saved through skillful means.

It is not that he is unaware of this intention to bestow the three vehicles, but because he wishes to align himself with all the Buddhas, it is said that he "reflects. As stated in the subsequent text:
Even though he contemplated and devised various skillful means. △ Second, clarifying that there are those of small capacity; this section has two parts: first, clarifying the praise by all Buddhas;
second, clarifying Śākyamuni’s response in accordance with their desire for a great transformation. Because they lacked the capacity for that [great] transformation, the Buddhas did not praise them.
Now, wishing to preach the Small Vehicle to accord with their faculties and conditions, they shall attain deliverance from beginning to end; therefore, the Buddhas praised them.

"If one does not first employ the small, then both the small and the great will be lost; if one first employs the small, then in the end there will surely be great benefit—hence it is said that 'from beginning to end, one attains deliverance'. Now, the first [section].
While I was reflecting in this way, the Buddhas of the ten directions all appeared and comforted me with Brahma-sounds: "Excellent, Śākyamuni!
You, the foremost guide, have attained this unsurpassed Dharma; following the example of all Buddhas, you employ the power of skillful means.
We, too, have all attained the most wondrous and supreme Dharma, which we shall analyze and expound as the three vehicles for the sake of all classes of sentient beings."
Those with little wisdom who delight in inferior teachings and lack self-confidence regarding their own buddhahood are taught various fruits through skillful means;
although the three vehicles are thus explained, it is solely for the purpose of instructing bodhisattvas.

The first three lines constitute Śākyamuni’s own account of why the Buddha appears: it is because, through the power of the skillful means of mindfulness of the Buddha, he accords with the Dharma and accords with the capacities of sentient beings;
this is why the Buddha appears. The subsequent five lines consist of the various Buddhas’ praise of Śākyamuni:

because he is able to establish the provisional based on the ultimate, they say "Excellent!"; because he introduces [beings] into the Buddha-wisdom by bestowing the three [vehicles] for the sake of the one [vehicle], they call him "Supreme."
Because the Teacher has realized the subtle, supreme, and ultimate true wisdom, it is said that he has "attained the unsurpassed Dharma.
Because he follows all Buddhas in concealing the ultimate and manifesting provisional means, it is said that he "employs the power of skillful means.

The next four phrases clarify that the Buddhas themselves conceal the ultimate and manifest the provisional; the following four phrases explain the dual meaning of this concealment and manifestation for the sake of sentient beings of inferior intelligence.
Because they lacked self-confidence in attaining Buddhahood, they concealed the reality and delighted in the Lesser Dharma; thus, provisional means were employed to speak of various fruits.
The latter two phrases together conclude these two meanings: although three vehicles were initially taught, in the end, one vehicle must be revealed.
△ Second, explaining Śākyamuni’s response to their compliance.
Śāriputra, you should know that when I heard the holy lion’s voice—profound, pure, subtle, and exquisite—proclaiming "Namo to all Buddhas," I further thought to myself:
"I have emerged from this world of turbid evil; as all the Buddhas have taught, I too shall practice in accordance with them."

The first verse speaks in response, meaning "Namo," which here [in Chinese] signifies "reverence" (*namas*) and "to follow. The latter verse contemplates and accords with the capacities of sentient beings.
This concludes the second section, clarifying those with small capacities. △ Third, clarifying the bestowing of transformation.

Having reflected on this matter, he proceeded to Vārāṇasī; [realizing that] the mark of the cessation of all dharmas cannot be expressed in words, he nevertheless taught it to the five bhikṣus by means of skillful power.
Vārāṇasī is the Deer Park. The principle of the Buddha-seed within the Middle Way is beyond calculation and is inexpressible;
yet, through skillful means (*upāya*), it is taught by way of the three vehicles. Furthermore, that which is neither arising nor ceasing is, through skillful means, taught as arising and ceasing.
Even the principle of partial truth (*ekadeśa-satya*) is not expressible, yet it is spoken of for the sake of skillful means.

The exposition of the four gates begins with the teaching for the five bhikṣus, which is the gate of impermanence. First, by contrasting the provisional and the real: the Real is ineffable, whereas that which is spoken belongs to the provisional;

thus, the three provisional [aspects] are numerical while the one Real is non-numerical. Next, by contrasting arising-and-ceasing with non-arising-and-non-ceasing—this is the Mahāyāna gate: because it is non-arising-and-non-ceasing, it is ineffable; yet to speak of arising-and-ceasing is to contrast the Great and the Small.

Finally, by contrasting the partial truth of the Small Vehicle’s four gates with the Small: the principle of partial truth is likewise unspeakable. Thus, both the Great and Small principles are ineffable; yet, through skillful means for the sake of sentient beings, both may be spoken. Although both may be spoken...

The Buddha’s intention in teaching was that it was not yet appropriate for beings in their actual state to grasp [the truth] directly; therefore, he intentionally employed skillful means to speak of arising and ceasing. △ Fourth, clarifying the reception, practice, awakening, and entry: when the opportunity arises, one receives [the teaching];

as one contemplates and transforms in accordance with what has been heard, this is called the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth up to the first stage of the Worldly First Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), which is termed "awakening. If one attains the first fruit (*srotāpatti-phala*), it is termed "entry."
This is called the turning of the wheel of Dharma, whereby there arise the sounds of *nirvāṇa* and the distinct designations for the *arhat*, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha.
The transformation of the Buddha’s mind—the method for edifying others—so that it enters the minds of others is called the turning of the wheel of Dharma.

As previously stated, upon first seeing the Truth (*satyadarśana*), one abandons the delusions of conceptual discrimination (*vikalpavikalpa*) and partially realizes *nirvāṇa with remainder*; from this, the sound of *nirvāṇa* arises within oneself.
In this regard, by virtue of this, one attains the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) and thereby receives the name Arhat;
the one capable of teaching is called the Buddha; that which is taught is the Dharma of the Three Vehicles; those who have seen the Truth, such as the Arhats, constitute the Sangha.
Thus, the Three Jewels manifest in the world. The first section, clarifying the attainment through transformation, is concluded. △ Second, resolving doubts.
"Since time immemorial, I have constantly taught that the Dharma of Nirvana reveals the eternal exhaustion of the suffering of birth and death.

Fearing that others might suspect the Teacher, saying, "The Buddha was initially unable to discern the capacities of beings, and only after reflecting upon the Buddhas did he first come to know their root-natures," this commentary explains:

It was for the purpose of leading others along with him that he reflected upon the Buddhas; it was not only now that he reflected and thereby came to know [the capacities], but rather from time immemorial.
When they come to see that the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) brings happiness, [the Buddha] praises and demonstrates it to them so as to lead them to the exhaustion of all suffering;

thus, upon hearing the Lesser Vehicle, they immediately attain liberation. Furthermore, fearing that disciples might doubt—asking how it is that by merely hearing it for a brief moment in one lifetime, they can realize the state of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa)—he now explains:
because he has praised and demonstrated it to them from long ago, in accordance with their original habituation, they quickly attain the Way.

"Long ago" (*ch'iu yüan*) refers to the period after [the Buddha] established a karmic connection with Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū; thus, the subsequent passage states: "The father knew that each of his sons had previously harbored their own preferences.
These two verses describe the application of skillful means for transformation, corresponding to the later parable of discarding the small table and providing the carts.
(End of the main section). △ Third, these three verses reveal the ultimate truth, corresponding to the later parable of equally bestowing the great carts. (Main section).

Śāriputra, you should know that I see these sons of the Buddha, numbering in the immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis, who all seek the path of Buddhahood with a heart of reverence and have come to the presence of the Buddha.

Having heard from various Buddhas the Dharma taught through skillful means, I immediately thought: "The reason the Tathāgata has appeared is to proclaim the wisdom of the Buddhas; now is precisely the time for this."
Śāriputra, you should know that those of dull faculties and small wisdom, who are attached to signs and possessed by pride, cannot believe in this Dharma.
Now I rejoice and am fearless; among all the bodhisattvas, I directly abandon expedient means and teach only the unsurpassed path.
When the bodhisattvas hear this Dharma, the net of their doubts is entirely removed. The twelve hundred arhats shall all likewise become buddhas.

"Sons of the Buddha, having come to the presence of the Buddha with a mind of reverence, you have heard the various Buddhas skillfully teaching the Dharma"—this reveals that practitioners of the three vehicles are all sons of the Buddha;

this is the first verse on the "Unity of Persons. "For the sake of explaining the Buddha-wisdom"—that is, the omniscience which is the Buddha’s knowledge and vision—this is the second verse on the "Unity of Principle. "He speaks only of the Unsurpassed Way"—this is the third verse on the "Unity of Teaching."
The first [section] concerns the teaching; the second concerns the removal of the Bodhisattvas' doubts regarding Arhats attaining Buddhahood, as illustrated by the verses on practice.

Furthermore, the first two stanzas clarify the arousal of the Mahāyāna faculty (*indriya*), which is also called "seeking the fruit" and serves as the analogy for the children seeking their respective carts.

The next two stanzas—one line each—clarify the Buddha’s joy because sentient beings are capable of receiving the benefits of the Mahāyāna, and thus serve as the basis for the subsequent "seeing the children."
The analogy of rejoicing upon being freed from danger corresponds to the first three lines of the main text, which clearly manifest the reality for those of inferior capacity.
The analogy of bestowing great chariots upon the sons corresponds to the final verse of the main text, which clarifies the reception, practice, awakening, and entry.

The analogy of the sons’ joy at receiving the chariots corresponds to the beginning of the main text, which explains that because the capacity is activated, there is a request for the fruit; this should consist of four points, the first of which is the removal of obstacles.

When the potential has not yet been activated, it is like the various arhats during the period of the Tripiṭaka: because they delighted in the Lesser Vehicle, although their turbid obstructions were removed, their great faculties were dull, and thus their wondrous potential had not been activated;
consequently, certain obstructions remained unremoved. When the great potential is activated, it is like the ordinary people in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*:
although they have not yet severed the fetters, because their great faculties are sharp, their potential is activated and their inherent obstructions are spontaneously removed.

That is to say, when the capacity [of the listener] is present, it is immediately triggered; as when the *Anantārthika* (Infinite Meanings) was preached, those with the capacity for the Lesser Vehicle realized its fruits right there in that very seat.
Conversely, when one's own obstacles have not yet been removed and the capacity has not yet been triggered—as in the case of the five thousand who withdrew from their seats—it does not manifest.

To "seek the Buddha-way" means to seek the Great Fruit. There are three meanings to this seeking: first, the sense that the Great Capacity possesses the principle of responding to and producing fruit.

The "two searches" within the capacity [of the audience] and the "secret search" within their disposition are as stated in the following passage: "Whether it is obtained or not obtained. The "three verbal searches" refer to the three earnest entreaties.
Although the two searches already existed within the teachings of the past, they did not yet involve verbal expression;
however, on this day, these three searches are fully present. If one asks whether the "search for leaving the house" of the past was merely a matter of capacity and disposition: it was.
Regarding the objection that the text says "as previously promised," this refers to seeking the three [vehicles]; how does it relate to seeking the one? The answer is:
having gone outside and not seeing [the others], there must be a different path; taking what was previously promised to seek a different intention is also equivalent to seeking the one.
"All come to my presence with a heart of reverence" is as Śāriputra requested, saying: "All..."
The devas, nāgas, spirits, and others joined their palms with reverent hearts, desiring to hear the complete path.

Those who had previously heard from various Buddhas the teachings on skillful means fully received [the teaching] during the first four periods of ripening. Second, regarding the removal of obstacles and the Buddha’s joy:
for the sake of the Buddha-wisdom, the Buddha appeared; because his past obstacles were heavy and the capacity [of beings] was lacking, he could not speak immediately.

Although the obstacles had been removed during the intermediate period of wisdom, because the capacity [of the disciples] was not yet mature, he had not yet attained the opportunity to preach. Now that their capacity has been awakened, it is precisely the time for preaching.

Formerly, the faculties of the masses were dull and their wisdom small; fearing they would slander the Dharma and fall into evil states, [the Buddha] did not preach. Now, their faculties are sharp and their resolve is great; hearing [the teaching], they will certainly believe and understand.
Therefore, he rejoices and is without fear, having no dread that they will cling to the small vehicle, slander the Great, and give rise to the karma of falling into evil states.
Third, the explicit revelation of the reality: the five vehicles are crooked rather than straight, and partial or peripheral rather than central;
now, all such deviations are abandoned, and only the single, upright path is taught. Fourth, regarding reception, practice, awakening, and entry:
upon first hearing this brief exposition, one realizes that after a long time, the reality must indeed be taught, and that the three vehicles are nothing other than skillful means. Furthermore...
This means that because non-retrogressive bodhisattvas did not understand the Buddha’s wisdom, both bodhisattvas and arhats alike fell into the net of doubt.
Now, by opening up the provisional to reveal the real, not only do the arhats have their doubts removed, but there are no bodhisattvas of the three teachings whose doubts are not likewise removed;
not only do the bodhisattvas become Buddhas, but the arhats all likewise become Buddhas as well. △ Fourth, the verse praising the Dharma.
How rare! Just as the Buddhas of the three periods of time have employed this ritual for preaching the Dharma, so do I now preach this non-conceptual Dharma.

It is extremely difficult for a Buddha to appear in the world; it is difficult to encounter one when he has appeared; and it is even more difficult for him to arise in the world and preach this Dharma.
To hear this Dharma throughout immeasurable and incalculable kalpas is difficult; likewise, those who are able to listen to this Dharma are also rare.
It is like the udumbara flower, which all cherish and love, yet is rarely seen by gods and humans, appearing only once in a great while.
To hear the Dharma with joy and praise, even uttering but a single word, is to have already made offerings to all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Such a person is exceedingly rare, surpassing even the udumbara flower.
This verse correctly praises this wondrous Dharma, which the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, preach only at certain times—just as the udumbara flower appears but once in a long while.
Regarding the fact that the wondrous Dharma does not manifest apart from provisional and ultimate rituals: these are the provisional means by which the Buddhas guide sentient beings.

The non-discriminative Dharma is the reality revealed by all Buddhas; furthermore, since from the outset there is no distinction between the provisional and the real, it is only those of dull faculties and small wisdom who discriminate between the provisional and the real, calling this "ritualistic form. Now, to again awaken to and enter into the non-duality of the one and the three is called "non-discrimination.
The two lines beginning with "The Buddhas appear in the world" clarify that such people are rare; the following two lines [clarify] the next point.
The first two lines clarify the difficulty of the Dharma being taught, as it has remained in silence for over forty years.
The next two lines clarify the difficulty of hearing the Dharma, as five thousand people withdrew from their seats and did not hear it during the Buddha’s lifetime.

The subsequent two lines clarify the difficulty of listening with faith, as among the entire assembly, Śāriputra alone was able to comprehend it first. Finally, a simile is presented which corresponds only to the aspect of listening with faith.
The difficulty of this point can be resolved by other examples. △ Fifth, the verse on "not being in vain" serves as the basis for the subsequent parable of "absence of falsehood":
"Do not harbor doubts; I am the King of all Dharmas. I universally address the great assembly:
I teach and transform all bodhisattvas solely through the path of the One Vehicle; I have no śrāvaka disciples. You, Śāriputra, whether you are a śrāvaka or a bodhisattva..."
One should know that this sublime Dharma is the secret essence of all Buddhas.
The first six lines admonish one not to harbor doubts regarding trustworthy persons; the subsequent four lines admonish one not to harbor doubts regarding trustworthy teachings.
Now, in the world, even a human king’s word is non-dual; how much more so for the Buddha, the King of Dharma—how could there be [any discrepancy]?
If even false teachings and expedient, provisional explanations can eliminate turbidity, how much more so the secret and essential wondrous Dharma—how could it not be the ultimate truth?
△ Sixth, the verse distinguishing the assembly and exhorting faith; this section has two parts: first, the verse distinguishing the assembly, and second, the verse exhorting faith.
First: In this world of the five turbidities, sentient beings such as these—who take pleasure only in attachment to various desires—will ultimately not seek the Buddha-way.
When wicked people of future ages hear the Buddha preach the One Vehicle, they will become confused and fail to believe or accept it; they will destroy the Dharma and fall into the evil realms.
For those who possess a sense of shame and dread of blame, whose pure resolve seeks the Buddha-way, one should extensively praise the path of the One Vehicle for such as these.
The first four lines of verse respond to the preceding [text]: "These are not disciples of the Buddha. Why? Because if one delights in various desires, this constitutes the work of Māra;

thus, they must be excluded. In the previous text, it was stated that even those attached to *nirvāṇa* are not disciples of the Buddha; here, it is stated that those attached to birth [are likewise not].
That "death" refers merely to the mutual exclusion [of the Buddha's disciples] from the ordinary and the small; only when one has abandoned both can they be worthy of receiving a prediction.

Furthermore, the phrase "never seeking the Buddha-way" also serves as a verse for those aforementioned people of overweening pride (*adhimāna*), who, because they have not attained the supreme Dharma, claim to have attained it, and therefore no longer seek the Buddha-way. In future ages, there will be four kinds of evil people.
Regarding the preceding verse and its commentary: those who, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain the meaning [of this teaching] are difficult to find.
Regarding the subsequent four verses and their commentary: if one encounters other Buddhas, one shall then attain definitive understanding. Next, the verses exhort faith.
Śāriputra, you should know that the Dharma of all Buddhas is thus: by means of billions of skillful expedients, they preach the Dharma according to what is appropriate.

Those who have not practiced it cannot understand this. Now that you have already understood these matters regarding the skillful expedients of the Buddhas, the Teachers of the World, you should no longer harbor any doubts;
let your hearts give rise to great joy, knowing for yourselves that you shall become Buddhas.
This verse [demonstrates] that for one who has truly attained arhatship, it is impossible not to believe this Dharma.

The first six lines exhort faith in the provisional (upāya), while the latter six lines exhort faith in the ultimate (paramārtha). This concludes the initial section on the formal exposition of the Dharma within the "Complete Exposition of the Dharma" (Dharmaparyāya).

△ The explanation of the "Expedient Means" chapter is concluded; next, the "Parable" chapter is explained.

Regarding the third chapter, the "Parable," this explanation also has two parts: first the general, then the specific. As for the general explanation: "parable" (譬) refers to comparison, while "analogy" (喻) refers to instruction and elucidation.
Relying on this to illustrate that, and using the shallow to convey the profound, the preceding long prose and verses extensively elucidated the provisional and the real aspects of the five Buddhas.

Those of superior faculties and sharp wisdom attained awakening through hearing the teaching in its entirety; however, those of middling and inferior capacities still harbored delusions that had not yet been dispelled.

Out of inexhaustible great compassion and boundless skillful wisdom, [the Buddha] further employed analogies and parables to enlighten them and lead them to realization; therefore, these are called "parables" (dṛṣṭānta).
Regarding the separate explanation: the causal conditions (*nidāna*) are categorized according to teaching, origin and trace (*honjaku*), and contemplation of the mind.

As for the causal conditions, they use the analogy of worldly father and son to illustrate the transcendental relationship between teacher and disciple. Based on having heard what was never heard before, there is leaping joy and delight;

this is the benefit to the world. Furthermore, they use the analogy of worldly requisites to illustrate transcendental requisites, ensuring that those who receive the Buddha’s voice and teachings do not lose them.
"Mahāyāna: that which you all practice is the path of the bodhisattva, which benefits others;

furthermore, by comparing worldly extinction with supramundane extinction, one uproots their suffering and hardship to enable them to escape being burned and boiled—this is the benefit of the remedy through hearing that I have attained the exhaustion of outflows;
furthermore, by comparing worldly non-arising and non-extinction with supramundane non-arising and non-extinction—"
The vehicle of cessation is the precious vehicle; by reaching the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and abiding within true wisdom, I shall certainly become a Buddha.

This is the benefit of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Because the Buddha, with a single voice, skillfully employs parables to enable those of superior, middling, and inferior capacities to obtain the four benefits (*caturvidha-artha*), it is called the "Parable Chapter.
Regarding the teaching according to the doctrine: the Buddha’s original intention was to praise the Buddha-vehicle for the sake of sentient beings.

One who is capable of recollecting the great compassionate skillful means of the former Buddhas, proceeding to the Deer Park and praising the three vehicles for those of the two vehicles and below—who save themselves through their own merit but whose kindness does not extend to others—the Bodhisattva yokes oxen to transport others out of the fire; therefore, he is called a Mahāsattva.
This is an allegory within the Tripiṭaka Teaching. Furthermore, these three types of persons equally fear being burned and boiled by the sound.
Hearing [the Dharma] is like a roe deer that goes straight ahead without looking back; the Pratyekabuddha is like a doe that gallops alongside while glancing back;
and the Bodhisattva is like a great elephant that wards off swords and arrows with its body so that the entire herd may escape. These are metaphors from the Shared Teaching (Pāṭha-sādhāraṇa).

Furthermore, those of the Two Vehicles who resolve their minds have a proximity to conditions that is near and a realization of principle that is shallow; their wisdom is weak, such that they can only sever the delusions common to all [vehicles] but cannot exhaustively reach the ultimate limit.

The "Ultimate" (Di) is not a *pāramitā*; it refers to Bodhisattvas who have long since resolved their minds, whose principles are profound and whose wisdom is powerful, enabling them to sever distinct delusions and exhaust the source and nature of reality.
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "The two vehicles are like fireflies, while Bodhisattvas are like the light of the sun.
This is an analogy used within the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*). Furthermore, as soon as they first see my body and hear what I preach, they all immediately believe and accept it.
For such a person who has entered the wisdom of the Tathāgata, it is easy to transform and deliver them, so as not to cause the Tathāgata to give rise to weariness or distress.

In the *Avataṃsaka*, truth is realized through phenomena themselves (*yathābhūta*), requiring no further metaphors (though the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is not without metaphors; however, those [teachings] lead one into the Path in an incorrect manner).
For those who have not yet entered, for more than forty years, he has again employed various skillful means (*upāya*) to assist in manifesting the Supreme [Truth].
Today, on this Vulture Peak, the Dharma is definitively proclaimed as the Mahāyāna, universally causing all to open, show, awaken to, and enter the Buddha’s wisdom;
not allowing even a single person to attain extinction alone. As it was at the beginning, so it is now; as it is now, so it was at the beginning—without duality or distinction.
Those of superior faculties and sharp wisdom can understand it upon hearing it, so that the Tathāgata does not give rise to weariness.

Regarding suffering, there is no need for further analogies; however, because those of middle and lower capacities may hesitate at the crossroads, it is necessary today to employ the analogy of the Great Vehicle to enable them to attain benefit.
