This is called the analogy within the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). As for the "Original and the Traced" (*benji*):

since the four teachings and their analogies already exist within the Traced, by using the Traced as a model for the Original, one should likewise apply these [analogies] to the Buddha’s initial attainment of the Way in the Original state.

The parables for maturing sentient beings—such as the lotus, the flower, and so forth—are based on metaphors. The traces of the giving [of the Dharma] and other details are fully explained in the *Xuánwén* (Profound Text).
For the practitioner of contemplation of the mind (*guānxīn*), emptiness is like the white ox; the provisional [truth] is like the carriage body within the "Means" chapter.

(The title of this section should have appeared after the verses spoken by the devas and before the Parable of the Burning House; it has been placed here by the editor of the scripture for the purpose of adjusting the fascicle. At the beginning of the "Exposition of the Dharma" (*fǎshuō*), there is a middle section.
In the preceding five sections, the first part—the formal exposition of the True Dharma—is completed. Second, Śāriputra’s reception and understanding of the teaching has two parts:
first, the narrative by the Sūtra compiler; second, Śāriputra’s own statement. This is the first.
At that time, Śāriputra leaped for joy and, rising immediately, joined his palms and gazed up at the Honored One’s countenance.
His leaping for joy expressed his internal understanding, while joining his palms and gazing up expressed his external demeanor.
To have faith and understanding in one's heart is called "joy"; for joy to move the physical form is called "leaping. Having heard the wondrous Dharma from the Wondrous Person, he attained it.
To have a profound understanding of the harmony between the internal and external, thereby attaining this joy, is the worldly interpretation (*loka-vyākhyā*).

Furthermore, to abandon small learning for great learning, to cast aside the affairs of poverty to inherit the estate of a wealthy family, and to realize today that one is truly a son of the Buddha—therefore, one rejoices;
this is the human interpretation (*pudgala-vyākhyā*). Moreover, when both sorrow and regret are dispelled and doubts and difficulties are simultaneously removed within...

Because external hindrances have been cleared away and there is vast, expansive clarity, it is said: "I have attained the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*)," and "Hearing [the Dharma], my afflictions and distress are also removed.
This is the explanation of joy as an antidote. Furthermore, that which a son of the Buddha ought to attain has all been attained;
abiding within true wisdom (*bhūtajñāna*), one thinks, "I shall certainly become a Buddha," and thus feels joy. This is the explanation according to the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*).
Regarding the provisional teaching (*yōkyō*), "joy" refers to rejoicing at entering the stages;

however, for an Arhat, who has escaped the cage of the triple world and shattered the seeds and fruits of the four abidings, there is no sorrow when encountering harm nor joy when meeting profit. What is here called "joy" is certainly not worldly joy.

Whether it be the manifestation of the patience regarding suffering (*kūnin*) or the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising (*jinmushōchi*), these have already been attained previously; they are not [attained] now.

One should rejoice deeply if three people together attain the essence of the path through the Way of Non-words (*avacanātmaka-mārga*); although their analytical understandings differ, they are like space, which is of one consistency.
One does not rejoice deeply if one has already long ago attained that joy of single consistency.

If two attain the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) as the path of means (*upāya-mārga*), the provisional contemplation clears away the narrowness and vulgarity of the Two Vehicles, while the contemplation of emptiness clears away the clamor and congestion of ordinary beings. This is the transcendence.

The two extremes having been eliminated, they attain great joy; upon realizing the Way and attaining perfect fulfillment, this is the Stage of Initial Resolve (Prathamacittotpāda-vihāra), which may also be called the Stage of Joy (Pramuditā-vihāra).
Furthermore, the initial practice is called the Practice of Joy, and the first stage is also named the Ground of Joy (Pramuditā-bhūmi).
Since Śāriputra possesses superior faculties and sharp wisdom, he may have entered [the path] by leaping over stages; even if he did not leap over them, he would certainly [attain this].
This is the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*). Regarding its fundamental and manifested aspects (*honjaku*): Śāriputra attained Buddhahood long ago, titled Kinnara;

his manifested aspect is that of an assistant to Śākyamuni as a disciple of wisdom. Beginning from his time as a non-Buddhist, he led others from heterodoxy to the correct path, demonstrating the "milk-flavor" joy to benefit ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), followed by demonstrating the "curd-flavor" joy to benefit those who are noble (*ārya*). Next, he demonstrated the third... [text ends]

The Bodhisattva Ghee-Delight-and-Benefit now demonstrates that for those who study the Buddha-way, this "Ghee-Delight-and-Benefit" is such that all these forms of delight are merely manifestations of traces.

For one who contemplates the mind, contemplating the mind as empty, provisional, and middle constitutes everything from "delight by name" up to "ultimate delight. As for immediately rising to join the palms, this signifies...
In the past, the provisional and the real were two, like the palms of the hands not joined; now, understanding that the provisional is itself the real is like the joining of the two palms.
"Gazing up at the Honored Face" signifies that his realization of the Real is without any other thoughts, as he contemplates only the realm of the Buddha.
"Rejoicing and leaping for joy" generally clarifies the realization through the three karmas: "rejoicing" is the mind, and "rising and joining the palms" is the body.
Kāśyapa gazed upon the Honored One’s countenance; this constitutes the mental karma (*manas-karma*). What follows, where he addressed the Buddha, constitutes the verbal karma (*vāk-karma*).
Together, these clearly illustrate his understanding through the three types of karma. II. Śāriputra’s Personal Declaration A. The Extended Prose 1.
The Initial Statement of the Three Joys 2. The Explanation 3. The Conclusion Now, the first [of the three joys]:
He addressed the Buddha, saying: "Now, having heard this Dharma-sound from the World-Honored One, my heart leaps with joy at what I have never before experienced.
Because I have now been designated by the World-Honored One as one who is personally near to the Buddha’s body, it is called 'joy of the body.
Because I have heard this Dharma-sound from the Buddha’s own mouth and rejoice, it is called 'joy of the mouth. This unprecedented attainment is my intention."
Because one is able to understand the Buddha’s intention, it is called "joy of mind. △ Second, the commentator explains that this reveals the attainment of the present by relinquishing past errors;
furthermore, through the sorrow felt for the past, one achieves the joy of the present.

Why is this? In the past, I heard such a teaching from the Buddha, seeing that various bodhisattvas received the prediction of attaining buddhahood, while we ourselves were not included in this matter;
I was deeply moved by the thought that we had lost the Tathāgata’s immeasurable knowledge and vision.
Although they have likewise heard such a Dharma from the Buddha, because their own persons do not participate in this matter, their bodies remain distant from the Buddha;
thus, they lack physical joy—what is called being "distant despite being near. Furthermore, because they hear it as if they had not heard it, they lack verbal joy.
Being deeply moved by their own condition, they lack mental joy when they see the various bodhisattvas receiving the prediction of attaining Buddhahood.
This specifically refers to the Vaipulya sūtras, praising the Perfect [teaching] and extolling the Great; furthermore, it is because of the censure and rebuke that one feels such sorrow.
"World-Honored One, whenever I dwell alone in the mountains, forests, or beneath trees, whether sitting or walking, I constantly think:
'We have all entered the same Dharma-nature; why does the Tathāgata deliver us by means of the Hīnayāna teachings?'"
In mountain forests and beneath trees, these are the places for contemplation; whether sitting or walking, these are the postures for contemplation.

Regarding those who say they have entered the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) together [with the Buddha]: both the *Zang* (Tripitaka/Agama) and *Tong* (Shared) vehicles take the partial truth (*pradeśa-satya*) as the name for *dharmatā*.

However, when one is correctly hearing the Tripitaka, one falsely conceives that the Great Being (the Bodhisattva) truly requires only three *kalpas* to subdue the afflictions, and thus rejoices in having first realized the "Dharma-lineage" (*dharmagotra*).
One should reflect that it is precisely because of hearing the Vaipulya teachings that one secretly attains comprehensive benefit.

Since all three types of people attain [realization] upon hearing the exposition of the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, and as they have equally entered the *dharmatā* of ultimate truth, why is it that the Bodhisattva alone receives the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), while we remain forever fixed in the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle? Such is our doubt and indecision; we simply do not realize that [the path] relies upon the Great [Vehicle].

It is only by riding upon the Middle Way of the Dharma-nature that there is the meaning of receiving the prediction of attaining Buddhahood. As for those who are delivered by means of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) dharma:

because they have not heard the Great Dharma, they lack joy in speech; because they falsely calculate that they have entered the Dharma-nature equally [as the Bodhisattvas] without understanding the principle of skillful means, they lack joy in mind;
and because they dwell alone in secluded practice, their physical conduct remains distant from the Buddha, and thus they lack joy in body.

"This is our own fault, not that of the World-Honored One. Why is this so? Had we waited for the Buddha to explain the underlying causes for the realization of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, we would certainly have attained liberation through the Mahāyāna.
However, we did not understand his skillful means and provisional teachings; upon first hearing the Buddha’s discourse, we immediately accepted it with faith and contemplated it accordingly."
They attained realization.
When they first formed this thought, they believed that the Tathāgata was partial; thus, they sought deliverance through the perspective of the Hīnayāna.
After reflecting for a long time, they took the blame upon themselves and said, "This is our own fault, not the World-Honored One's. Why is this so?

The following passage explains and clarifies one's own faults: it is because the *prajñā* was transmitted through a transformative teaching and the "wealth" was entrusted [to others] that a distinct benefit was secretly obtained.
It is already known that the Middle Way *dharmatā* beyond the realms (*dhātu*) is the true cause for accomplishing unsurpassed *bodhi*.
Yet, as our faculties are dull, we were unable to receive it; we waited for the time when the high mountain would first be illuminated, and furthermore, we acted out of desire.
They quickly sought to see the small and inferior [attainments] and realize them, yet they did not know to pause and wait for the teachings of the Vaipulya Prajñāpāramitā.

Thus, they took the blame upon themselves; nevertheless, they still did not know that what they had realized was not true extinction (*nirvāṇa*), nor that what they were practicing was the path of the Bodhisattva.
Without waiting for the causes to be explained, they did not understand the reality, nor did they understand the skillful means (*upāya*). Following [their own views],...

Because they do not understand that what is being taught is precisely the subtle realization of the provisional and the non-provisional, as well as the real; because they lack the joy of the mind in accepting the initial teaching with faith;
because they lack the joy of the mouth in contemplating and attaining the realization of the partial truth of *nirvāṇa*, thereby remaining far removed from the Tathāgata’s body of eternal bliss;
and because they lack the joy of the body—all these are explained by showing how what was previously lost is now attained. The two explanations are complete. △
The three fetters are bound today; this constitutes the third joy. [The text] has two parts: first, the binding, and second, the completion. Now, for the first:
"World-Honored One, from the past until now, throughout the day and through the night, I have constantly reproached myself.

But now, having heard from the Buddha this unprecedented Dharma never heard before, all my doubts and regrets are severed; my body and mind are at ease, and I have attained a refreshing sense of peace and security."
Recapitulating the previous points, acknowledging one's faults and returning to the source is called "self-reproach," which manifests present joy pervading the three karmas.

"Following the Buddha" refers to the physical body; being near the Buddha’s body binds the joy of the body. "Hearing the Dharma" refers to the golden mouth and perfect voice; this binds the joy of the mouth.
"Swiftly attaining peace and stability" refers to the mind being identical to the Buddha’s mind; this binds the joy of the mind. As for the phrase "hearing what has never been heard before":

The High Mountains were first illuminated, yet they did not participate in the Dharma assembly; therefore, they did not hear the provisional teachings of the Tripiṭaka, which do not expound the Middle Principle.
Therefore, they did not hear the Vaipulya [teachings], which rebuke and scorch those who are ruined and devoid of merit.

Therefore, they did not hear the Prajñāpāramitā, which transmits the teaching solely for the sake of Bodhisattvas. Furthermore, regarding the Tripiṭaka, they heard only the partial truth; as for the Shared Teaching...

To hear [the teaching] and immediately realize it as the True Distinct Teaching (*bhūta-bhinna-śikṣā*)—to hear that emerging from the two extremes is itself called the Middle Way—and yet not to have heard that these very skillful means (*upāya*) are themselves the ultimate reality; this is why it is called an "unprecedented dharma" (*adbhuta-dharma*).
As for the question, "How can you judge us with such a small view?"—this was our fault in doubting the Buddha. We now repent of ourselves; we no longer doubt, nor do we regret.
Therefore, they are profoundly at ease and secure. △ Second, the fulfillment:
"Today I finally know that I am truly a son of the Buddha, born from the Buddha’s mouth, transformed by the Dharma, and having obtained a portion of the Buddha-Dharma."
Truly, as a son of the Buddha (*buddhaputra*), one’s body is close to the Buddha-body; the joy of the meaning is accomplished through being born from the Buddha’s mouth.

The joy of the meaning is accomplished through being transformed by the Dharma from the Buddha’s mouth; the joy of the mind is accomplished through attaining a portion of the Buddha-Dharma—meaning the partial realization of the secret treasury of the three virtues (*triguṇa-guhya-kośa*).
Indeed, when Śāriputra first realized arhatship, it was also said that he was the eldest son of the Buddha, born from the Buddha...
The mouth-born are born from the transformation of the Dharma; looking back from the present to the past, the former existed only as a provisional means and thus was not called "true.

Today, it is truly so—this is according to the meaning of relative contrast. Furthermore, during the period of the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā teachings, it was said that only Bodhisattvas were called "sons of the Buddha," while Śrāvakas had no share in the Buddha-dharma; today, one knows that they have originally been true Buddhas.
This concludes the initial section on the long prose, which summarizes the meaning of the opening and manifestation. △ Second, the verses in three parts: first, the verses on the heading;
second, the verses on the explanation; third, the verses on the conclusion. Now, the first part.
At that time, Śāriputra, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Having heard this sound of the Dharma, I have attained what I never had before; my heart is filled with great joy, and the net of doubt has been entirely removed."

"I who have heard" refers to hearing directly from the Buddha; this establishes both body and speech as never having been attained before, while establishing the mind [as such]—the rest may be understood.
△ Second, the verse explanation has two parts: first, supplementing the verse on what was not lost; second, correctly versifying what was previously lost. Now, the first:
Since long ago I have been graced by the Buddha’s teaching and have not lost the Mahāyāna; the Buddha’s voice is most rare and marvelous, for it can eliminate the afflictions of sentient beings.
Having already attained the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), hearing it has likewise removed my grief and distress.

"Not losing the Mahāyāna" explains the joy of the body; "the Buddha’s voice is rare and marvelous" explains the joy of the mouth; "the outflows are exhausted and afflictions removed" explains the joy of the mind.
Originally, there was never any loss; it was only because of one's own delusion that one falsely claimed to have lost it.
△ Second, the actual verse on the former loss.
Whether dwelling in mountain valleys or beneath forest trees, whether sitting or walking in meditation, I constantly contemplate this matter, sighing with deep self-reproach:
"How can we deceive ourselves? We too are sons of the Buddha, having entered together into the outflow-free Dharma;
yet we are unable to proclaim the unsurpassed path in the future—the golden body, the thirty-two marks, the ten powers, and the various liberations."
While sharing in the same Dharma, I have failed to attain these qualities—the eighty minor marks, the eighteen unique dharmas, and other such merits—and thus I have lost them all.
As I was walking alone, I saw the Buddha amidst the great assembly, his fame filling the ten directions and bringing vast benefit to sentient beings;
reflecting on this, I thought to myself that I had lost this benefit and was merely deceiving myself.
Having heard this verse, which critiques the Vaipulya [sūtras], one secretly attains the benefit of universal penetration.

The "outflow-free dharma" (anāsrava-dharma) is what is referred to in the long prose as "dharma-nature" (dharmatā); it refers to the partial truth of nirvāṇa because it does not leak or fall back into saṃsāra.
Day and night, I have constantly contemplated this matter, wishing to ask the World-Honored One whether I have erred or not.
I have often seen the World-Honored One praise the bodhisattvas; therefore, throughout the day and night, I have deliberated upon these matters.

Now, hearing the Buddha’s voice preaching the Dharma according to what is appropriate—this outflow-free teaching that is difficult to conceive—I see that it causes all beings to reach the site of enlightenment.

This verse concerns the matter of secretly attaining a distinct benefit through the teaching of the *Prajñāpāramitā* after it has been heard. If one interprets this as a symbolic representation of phenomena (*dharmaparyāya*) by day and night:

"day" refers to *nirvāṇa*, while "night" refers to birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*). Furthermore, the birth-and-death of ordinary beings and the *nirvāṇa* of the two vehicles are both termed "night," whereas the Middle Way and the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) are termed "day. That which is untainted (*anāsrava*) is inconceivable.
This is because the dharma-nature of the Middle Way does not fall into either of the two extremes.
Originally, I was attached to false views and served as a teacher to various brahmins; the World-Honored One, knowing my mind, uprooted my errors and preached nirvana to me.
I completely eliminated all false views and attained realization within the dharma of emptiness. At that time, I thought to myself that I had reached extinction.
This verse describes how, upon first hearing the Buddha’s teaching, one immediately encounters it with faith, contemplates it, and realizes its truth. The second verse concludes the explanation.
△ Third, the concluding verses; this has two parts: first, the verse that concludes; second, the verse that establishes [the realization]. Regarding the first, there are three further sections:
first, the actual concluding verse; second, a retrospective account of the net of doubt; third, an account of the present understanding and realization. Now, the first section:

Now I have realized for myself that this was not true extinction; only when I attain Buddhahood, endowed with the thirty-two marks and revered by the assembly of devas, humans, yakṣas, nāgas, and spirits, shall it be called the eternal exhaustion of all things without remainder.
When the Buddha spoke among the great assembly, "I shall become a Buddha," hearing such a sound of the Dharma, my doubts and regrets were entirely removed.
To manifest the marks of a Buddha is to bind the body with joy; to proclaim "I shall become a Buddha" is to bind the mouth with joy; to eliminate doubt and regret is to bind the mind with joy.

To realize for oneself that one has not truly attained *nirvāṇa* means that although one has severed *dṛṣṭi-āsrava* (afflictions of views) and *bhavāsrava* (afflictions of existence), thereby emerging from the *paricchinna-bhava* (segmented existence), one still possesses *avidyā* (ignorance) and remains subject to *pariṇāmi-kāya* (the transformative body).
If one attains Buddhahood, one transforms the impermanent five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of the nine realms and realizes the eternal.
When one delights in the five aggregates, yet at that time the five abodes are utterly exhausted and the two deaths are forever extinguished, this can be called true extinction (*nirvāṇa*).
Regarding the thirty-two marks, let us speak here of the wondrous form of the *dharmakāya*:

every mark is non-mark, and every sea of marks is none other than the perfect manifestation of essential virtue; therefore, it is said to be "endowed" with them. △ Second, a retrospective account of doubt and regret.
Upon first hearing what the Buddha had spoken, his heart was greatly struck with alarm and doubt: "Could it be that a Māra has become a Buddha to disturb and confuse my mind?
This clarifies that it was not only during the period of the Vaipulya (fangděng) teachings that he gave rise to doubt, nor only during the Prajñāpāramitā teachings that he felt regret;
even upon first hearing this sutra—which briefly reveals the One by opening up the Three—he was already startled and remorseful, which is why he made his request three times without ceasing. △
Third, the present summary of understanding:
The Buddha, through various causes, analogies, and skillful speech, has taught that his mind is as peaceful as the ocean; having heard this, my net of doubts is severed.
The Buddha has further explained that the immeasurable Buddhas who attained parinirvāṇa in past ages likewise all dwelt within skillful means and preached this very Dharma.

The Buddhas of the present and future are infinite in number, and they too expound this Dharma through various skillful means, just as the World-Honored One now has—from his birth, his renunciation, his attainment of the Way, and his turning of the wheel of Dharma—also taught through skillful means.
The World-Honored One speaks of the true Path; Pāpīyas could not have done so. Therefore, I know with certainty that this is not Māra acting as a Buddha.

Because I had fallen into the net of doubt, I thought this was the work of Māra; yet, upon hearing the Buddha’s gentle voice—profound, far-reaching, and most subtle, as he eloquently expounded the pure Dharma—my heart was filled with great joy, my doubts and regrets were forever exhausted, and I came to dwell securely within true wisdom.
This verse concludes the three joys by correctly embodying the purport of the five Buddhas’ revelation; the first verse of the conclusion is finished.
II. The Verse on Accomplishment:
"I shall certainly become a Buddha, revered by devas and humans, turning the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma to teach and transform all bodhisattvas."

However, if one can recite even a single phrase of a portion of the Buddha-dharma, the three joys will be simultaneously accomplished. If one wishes to distinguish them: being honored by devas and humans is the accomplishment of the body;
turning the unsurpassed wheel [of Dharma] is the accomplishment of the mouth; and teaching and transforming bodhisattvas is the accomplishment of the mind.
This concludes the second section: the two sons of Śāriputra’s realization and understanding. △ Third, the Tathāgata’s confirmation and completion. Part One: Former Teachings.
When [Śāriputra] forgot the second [level of] Great and took up the third [level of] Small, the Buddha again explained the Great for him.
At first, by recounting his past teachings on the Great, [the Buddha] demonstrated that Śāriputra’s understanding gained from the Buddha’s instruction since the past was not erroneous.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra: "I am now, amidst this great assembly of devas, humans, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas..."
In the middle [section] it is said: "I have previously, for the sake of the unsurpassed path, constantly taught and transformed you at the abodes of twenty trillion Buddhas;
you also followed and studied under me throughout the long night. Because I guided you through skillful means, you were born within my Dharma."
Regarding the "Unsurpassed Path," the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā* states: "Unsurpassedness of body" refers to the primary and secondary marks (the first phrase is the fruit).

"Unsurpassedness of upholding" refers to self-benefit and benefiting others (through the perfection of body, speech, and mind). "Unsurpassedness of fulfillment" refers to livelihood, views, and precepts (these two phrases constitute the six points of harmony in the Mahāyāna).
"Unsurpassedness of wisdom" refers to the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*). "Unsurpassedness of the inconceivable" refers to the six perfections (*pāramitā*).
Pāramitās (these two phrases refer to merit and wisdom); Unsurpassed Liberation refers to the ability to destroy the two obstacles;

Unsurpassed Practice refers to the noble conduct, the Brahma-conduct, and the celestial conduct (only these two are mentioned because they represent the fruit and its function that are realized; the subsequent six phrases all pertain to the cause).
Furthermore, Unsurpassed Body is named the Great Man; Unsurpassed Reception is named Great Compassion; and Unsurpassed Fulfillment is named Reaching the Other Shore.
Supreme wisdom is called "all-knowledge" (sarvajñā); supreme inconceivability is called "Arhat"; supreme liberation is called "Great Nirvana";
and supreme practice is called "Samyak-saṃbuddha. (These seven are all established from the perspective of the fruit; thus, six causes are designated by the names of their fruits.
This present sutra clarifies the unsurpassed path of perfect penetration. As for "the long night," although there was formerly a great transformation, it had not yet...

Having shattered the darkness of ignorance and delusion within the mind, one follows and trains under the Buddha. Regarding those who are skillfully guided to be born into my Dharma, there are two types:
first, those who were previously transformed by the Great [Vehicle] and now attain great understanding; second, those who were temporarily led by the Small [Vehicle] and caused to realize its fruits.
Regarding the second point, it describes the causes of their sorrow, doubt, and regret for having forgotten and grasped the Small [Vehicle].
“Śāriputra, in the past I taught you to aspire to the Buddha-way, yet now you have forgotten it all and instead claim that you have already attained parinirvāṇa.
△ Third, he again explains the Great [Vehicle] for him, describing how his present attainment of understanding is not in vain.
Now, because I wish to cause you to recollect your original vow and the path you have practiced, I shall preach for all the śrāvakas this Mahāyāna sūtra entitled *The Lotus of the Wondrous Dharma*,
which teaches the Dharma for bodhisattvas and is protected by the Buddhas.
The third section, the Tathāgata’s confirmation, is concluded. △ Fourth, the bestowing of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), which has two parts: first, the long prose; second, the verse summary.

Now that they have attained great understanding and know for themselves that they shall become Buddhas, why wait for a prediction? There are four reasons for the prediction: first, because the Two Vehicles had not previously received a prediction, they must now receive one;
second, because those of dull faculties have not yet awakened, the prediction serves to encourage and spur them on; third, to cause... [text continues]

For those who hear this, it establishes the conditions for their karmic connection and fulfills their four original vows. This long introductory section consists of ten parts, beginning with the time period and ending with the duration of the Dharma’s abiding. Now, for the first:
"Śāriputra, in a future age, after immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable kalpas have passed..."

Question: Since Śāriputra attained awakening during the first cycle of the teaching, having already opened the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and entered the first stage of the Perfect Teaching (*vimalā-bhūmi*), he should be able to attain Buddhahood on the spot, just like that dragon girl.
Why, then, has he been granted a prediction [of future Buddhahood] that requires him to pass through so many kalpas?
Answer: For a Buddha to achieve [his own] realization, there must be the appropriate conditions and opportunities (*pratyaya*). These śrāvakas have, from the past until now, never...
Having taken up the purification of Buddha-lands, they now receive their prediction; subsequently, they establish karmic conditions with sentient beings.
Because the capacities of these beings differ, the duration of the kalpas varies. Although the Dragon Girl is of the female form, because her vehicle is swift, she first practices skillful means.

Furthermore, this should be discussed separately according to the provisional traces [of the teaching], for it is merely to accommodate the suitability of beings and follow the length or brevity of their individual capacities. △ Second, the causal practice.
They made offerings to several tens of billions of buddhas, upheld the True Dharma, and fulfilled the path practiced by bodhisattvas. First, making offerings to the buddhas;
second, upholding the Dharma—only through these can one fulfill the bodhisattva path, which is the complete perfection of the two kinds of adornments:
merit and wisdom. △ Third, attaining the fruit.
He shall attain Buddhahood, known by the name Flower Radiance Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct,
Well-Gone, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One.
Regarding the possession of both the general and specific names: the general name has already been explained as before.

As for the specific name "Flower-Light" (*Puṣpārāma*), it is because he was the very first to receive the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) upon witnessing the Buddha emit light and preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; thus he obtained this name.

Furthermore, "flower" refers to the Buddha-nature as the conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*), while "light" refers to the Buddha-nature as the revealing cause (*vijñapti-hetu*). These four—[the flower, its fragrance, the light, and its radiance]—are [the attributes].
The teachings all discuss merit and wisdom, and all discuss the conditions and the fulfillment; now, however, we are concerned solely with the Perfect [Teaching].

Furthermore, having long ago realized the *Miaohua Guangming Samādhi* (Flower-Light Radiance Samādhi), he manifests traces for the sake of future Buddhahood. Moreover, regarding the contemplation of the mind: that which is both empty and the Middle is provisionally named "Flower";
that which is both provisional and the Middle is named "Light"; and that which is both empty and provisional is the Middle, named "As It Is" (*tathatā*).
Come. △ Fourth, the lands:
The name of the land is Vimalā (Stainless). Its terrain is level and upright, pure, adorned, peaceful, and prosperous; gods and humans are numerous and flourishing.
The ground is made of lapis lazuli, with eight intersecting roads marked on its sides by cords of gold. Beside each [road], there are...
The rows of trees made of the seven treasures are always in bloom and bear fruit.

First, the ground emerges from the earth; next, the characteristics of the land are clarified: being without high or low is called "level," and being without partiality or crookedness is called "straight. It is peaceful and secure.
Below this, the enjoyment of the land by its inhabitants is clarified; below that again, the superior characteristics are further elucidated—all of which are the result of pure conduct.
He acts as a dominant condition for all sentient beings. △ Fifth, the teaching of the Dharma:

The Tathāgata Padmaprabha also teaches and transforms sentient beings by means of the three vehicles. Śāriputra, although the time when that Buddha appears is not an age of evil, he nonetheless preaches the Dharma of the three vehicles due to his original vow.
This is explained in accordance with the case of Śākyamuni; thus it says, "Also by means of Śāriputra," which serves to resolve a doubt. The doubt is as follows:
"As clarified above, the Buddha appeared in the five turbidities and, having no choice but to employ skillful means, taught the three vehicles.

Now, since the land of the Buddha Flower-Light is so pure, why does he also transform beings through the three vehicles? The explanation is: "Because of his original vow. It is because of his original vow.
According to the *Mahākaruṇā-gaṇḍavyūha-śūnyatā-kośa-sūtra*, Śāriputra once practiced the bodhisattva path for sixty kalpas;
however, when a brāhmaṇa begged for his eyes and he was about to retreat, he made a vow that upon his attainment of Buddhahood, he would open the Dharma of the Three Vehicles.

Furthermore, in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, Amitābha likewise employs the Three Vehicles to transform beings; this is truly because his compassionate vows are profound and heavy, gathering them in through their power.
Regarding those who attain rebirth by virtue of having taken up [the path], they cannot enter gradually without relying on the Three Vehicles;

this is generally the case within the Land of Common Abode for Ordinary Beings and Sages, whether pure or impure. Among those who practice all three vehicles, there are many who are "pure" (exclusive) and few who are "mixed" (inclusive).

Furthermore, there are two types of Bodhisattvas: first, those who begin their training in the Mahāyāna; second, those who practiced the Hīnayāna and subsequently entered the Mahāyāna. These distinctions are discussed in terms of their sharpness or dullness of faculties.
Thus, it appears that those who have studied directly from the beginning possess the power and efficacy of sharp discussion, while those who enter gradually through refinement possess strength;
this is why the Bodhisattvas of the Fragrant Accumulation further study the "double flow.

One should know that direct study involves a brief acquaintance with various practices—just as one who begins from the small furrows must test all offices, pass through successive stages from shallow to deep, and only then understand the suitability of things.
Only upon ascending the throne can one drape the ceremonial robes and bring peace to the world.
△ Sixth, the name of the kalpa. Why is this kalpa named "Great Jewel Adornment"? Because within that land, bodhisattvas are regarded as the great jewels.
△ Section on the Sevenfold Assembly.

Those bodhisattvas are immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, beyond the reach of calculation or analogy, and cannot be known except by the power of a Buddha’s wisdom. When they wish to walk, precious lotuses receive their feet. These bodhisattvas...

They are not those who have merely first resolved [to attain enlightenment], but are all those who have long planted the roots of virtue, having purified their Brahma-conduct under immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas;
they are constantly praised by all Buddhas, always cultivate the Buddha-wisdom, possess great supernormal powers, and are well-versed in the gateways of all dharmas;
being upright and without guile, their resolve and mindfulness are firm—such Bodhisattvas fill [the world].
As for that land:
△ Eighth, the lifespan.
Śāriputra, the lifespan of the Buddha Flower-Light was twelve small kalpas, excluding the time when he was a prince and had not yet become a Buddha.
The lifespan of the people in that land is eight *kṣudrakalpas*.
The mention of twelve *kṣudrakalpas* refers merely to the duration of time. In the Pure Land, there are no minor calamities;
it is not that weapons, epidemics, or famine cause damage to the people and things that constitutes what is called a *kalpa*. Nevertheless, when discussing the duration of a *kṣudrakalpa*:

Regarding the duration, it can be properly understood by taking one *utsarpiṇī* and one *avasarpiṇī* of this world-system as the measure for its number; the following sections should be understood accordingly.
△ Nine: The Stage of the Future Buddha.
After twelve minor kalpas have passed, Tathāgata Padmaprabha bestows the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* upon the Bodhisattva Dṛḍhavati.
He gave the prediction of supreme enlightenment to the bhikṣus, saying:
"This Bodhisattva Sthiramati shall next become a Buddha named Padmapratiṣṭhita, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; his buddha-field shall likewise be such as this."
Because his resolve and mindfulness are firm and he skillfully knows all dharma-gates, he is named "Firmly Full" (Kṣemadatta);
because when he wishes to walk, precious flowers receive his feet, he is named "Flower-Footed Peaceful Gait" (Padmavyūha).

Thus, the Tathāgata Padmaprabha transforms beings through the three vehicles, yet the adornments of that Bodhisattva’s supreme land are such as these; how can worldly people hold the three vehicles in contempt?
By traversing the one reality, how can one know that the essence of the provisional and the real is non-dual? How can one know the principle of opening up the provisional to reveal the real?
△ Tenth, the duration of the Dharma’s abiding:
Śāriputra, after the parinirvāṇa of the Buddha Padmaprabha, the True Dharma shall abide in the world for thirty-two intermediate kalpas.
The Semblance Dharma will also remain in the world for thirty-two intermediate kalpas.
This concludes the initial prose section. II. Verses in Praise (Gāthā): A. Verses corresponding to the prose; B. Concluding praise. In the first part [A], there are eight sections:
1. Verses on attaining the fruit (skipping ahead); ... [up to] 8. Verses on the duration of the Dharma’s abiding (briefly omitting the section on the Bodhisattva in the position of succession).
Now, first:
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"In a future age, Śāriputra shall become a Buddha, a Honored One of Universal Wisdom, whose name shall be Padmaprabha; he shall deliver immeasurable multitudes."
△ Second, the verse on the causes of his practice:
Having made offerings to countless Buddhas, he fulfilled the bodhisattva practices and attained the unsurpassed path through merits such as the ten powers.
△ Third, the verse on the time period and the name of the kalpa.
After immeasurable kalpas had passed, there was a kalpa named Mahāratnavyūha.
△ Fourth, the verses on the land:
The world was named Vimalaviśuddhānupakleśa; its ground was made of lapis lazuli, and its paths were demarcated by golden cords.
The trees of seven precious substances, variegated in color, are always laden with flowers, fruits, and seeds.
△ Fifth, the verse on the number of the assembly:
The bodhisattvas in that land are always firm in their resolve and mindfulness, and they have all fully perfected the *pāramitā* of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).
Under countless Buddhas, they have skillfully trained in the bodhisattva path.
(6) The verse describes their preaching of the Dharma:
"Such great beings as these were transformed by the Buddha Flower Radiance."
△ Seventh, the verse on the lifespan:
When the Buddha was a prince, he abandoned his kingdom and worldly glory; in his very last body, he left the household life and attained the Way of Buddhahood.
The World-Honored One Flower-Light Buddha (Puṣyarasmi) dwelt in the world for a lifespan of twelve minor kalpas, and the people of that land had a lifespan of eight minor kalpas.
△ Regarding the duration of the Dharma’s abiding in eight verses:
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma shall remain in the world for thirty-two minor kalpas, extensively delivering all sentient beings.
Once the True Dharma has been extinguished, the Semblance Dharma shall remain for thirty-two [minor kalpas], and the relics shall be widely disseminated, universally worshipped by devas and humans.

During the period when the True Dharma (Saddharma) abides, there is teaching, practice, and realization of the fruit; because this is no different from when the Buddha was in the world, it is said that he "widely delivers sentient beings.
During the period when the Semblance Dharma (Pratirūpaka-dharma) prevails, there is teaching and practice, but the realization of the fruit is rare;

yet, because the relics (śarīra) are universally used for the sake of the Buddha’s work, it is called the Semblance Dharma. The initial verse of the long prose section concludes here. △ Second, the concluding praise.

All the deeds performed by the Buddha Padmaprabha were exactly like this; that most supreme and peerless Honored One among two-legged beings was none other than your own self—you should truly rejoice in this.
The fourth [section], the conclusion of the bestowal of the prophecy, is finished. △ Fifth: The Joy of the Fourfold Assembly. Part One: The Long Text; Part Two: The Verses.

Within the first part, there are three sections: First, the sūtra-master describes the joy of the assembly; Second, the presentation of offerings; Third, the formal realization and understanding. Now, the first section.
At that time, the great assembly— the fourfold community of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, as well as devas,
nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and others—
saw Śāriputra receive the prediction of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi before the Buddha, and their hearts were filled with great joy.
They were filled with immeasurable joy and exultation.
△ Second, the presentation of offerings:
each person removed the upper garment they were wearing to offer it as an offering to the Buddha, Śakra-devānām-indra, Brahmā-deva-rāja, and the others.
Together with countless sons of the gods, they also made offerings to the Buddha with celestial fine garments, celestial *mandārava* flowers, and *mahāmandārava* flowers.
They scattered these celestial robes while remaining suspended in mid-air, revolving of their own accord.
Hundreds of thousands of kinds of celestial music simultaneously resounded in the sky, as a rain of various celestial flowers fell.
"Upper garment" (*shangyi*) refers here to noble attire; this is a general term for the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings.

If speaking specifically of *bhikṣus* and *bhikṣuṇīs*, it refers to the *saṃghāṭī*, the great robe. In the Western Regions, most *bhikṣus* follow the practice of receiving only the three robes (*tricīvara*).
Since these three robes cannot be discarded, how could one remove them to offer to the Buddha? This is illustrated, for example, in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
In the Sūtra, three hundred bhikṣus, having heard the Prajñā[pāramitā], all used their saṃghāṭī robes as an offering.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains this by stating that it may mean they offered them because they had realized the signless (*animitta*) Dharma, or that they obtained them anew on that very day.
If one interprets this according to the symbolism of the Dharma, the dyed color of the kāṣāya is fundamentally the path for śrāvakas to realize the Truth; now, they have removed them to offer them.

The Buddha symbolizes his relinquishing of attachment to the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle and his pursuit of unsurpassed Bodhi. Furthermore, the celestial robes symbolize the patience regarding the dharma of quiescent extinction (*śānta-nirvāṇa-dharma-kṣānti*);
the celestial flowers symbolize the wondrous wisdom of the Mahāyāna; and the celestial music symbolizes the liberation of eternal bliss.

As for their abiding in the void and revolving of their own accord, this symbolizes that cause and effect, the environment and its inhabitants, and self and others, all rely upon the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) itself.
Nevertheless, he turned [the wheel]. △ Third, the formal understanding and realization.
He spoke these words: "In the past, the Buddha first turned the wheel of Dharma at Vārāṇasī; now he has again turned the unsurpassed, greatest wheel of Dharma."
First, one receives the provisional teachings bestowed in the past; next, one receives the revelation of the ultimate truth bestowed in the present.

Because it exclusively clarifies the perfect principle, it is called "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*), differing from those [teachings] that possess a "superior" (*uttara*) in relation to the "combined," "partial," or "corresponding" [vehicles]. Because it is absolute, without peer, and all-encompassing, it is named the "greatest.

It is able to open up the various [teachings] within the combined, partial, and corresponding categories—whether great or small—so that they all together constitute one Great Vehicle. This is the first section, the long prose passage.

[End of section. △ Second, the verse summary, which has two parts: first, the summary of the opening of the provisional to reveal the one true reality; second, the personal account of attaining understanding, rejoicing, and dedication. Now, the first:
At that time, the various devaputras, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
In the past, at Vārāṇasī, you turned the wheel of the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths and analytically taught the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates of phenomena;
now, once again, you turn this most wondrous, unsurpassed, great wheel of Dharma—a teaching so profound and subtle that few are able to believe it.

The five aggregates (pañca-skandha) are the five *skandhas*; these *skandhas* constitute the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). Because of their origination, they arise; once arisen, they inevitably perish.

Since arising and perishing have ceased, this is called the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). That which can extinguish suffering and its origination is called the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).
The remainder may be understood accordingly. △ Second, a personal account of attaining understanding, rejoicing, and dedication.
"Since ancient times, we have frequently heard the World-Honored One preach various teachings, yet never before have we heard such a profound, wondrous, and supreme Dharma as this.

We all rejoice in the World-Honored One’s preaching of this Dharma. Now that the Greatly Wise Śāriputra has received the prediction of his future enlightenment from the Honored One, we too shall likewise surely attain Buddhahood, becoming the most honored and unsurpassed among all worlds."

The Buddha-way is inconceivable; he teaches expedient means according to what is appropriate. All the meritorious deeds I have performed, whether in this life or past lives, as well as the merit from seeing the Buddhas—I dedicate them all toward the Buddha-way.
The first four lines describe the understanding [of the Dharma], the next ten lines express sympathetic joy (*anumodana*), and the final four lines dedicate the merit (*pariṇāmana*).
"We, too, are likewise" means that we are like Śāriputra in our realization, like Śāriputra in being established [in the teaching], and like Śāriputra in receiving the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*).
Question: Why is it that Mahākāśyapa, Subhūti, and the other great śrāvakas have not yet attained such understanding, while the fourfold assembly has?
Who was the first to attain awakening? The answer is that among the fourfold assembly and the devas, there were those who possessed all three faculties (*indriya*):
those above were equal to Śāriputra, those in the middle were equal to the four [great disciples], and those below were equal to the five hundred [bhikṣus] and others.

Furthermore, since Śāriputra, Kāśyapa, and the others were all practicing through provisional means, their middle and lower faculties had not yet been opened; thus, Kāśyapa and Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra manifested as if they did not understand, as Vimalakīrti said: "Sentient beings..."

The bodhisattvas who have not yet attained healing have likewise not yet attained healing (and so forth). First, the section on the "Exposition through Dharma" concludes. Second, the section on the "Exposition through Parable" consists of four parts:

first, the text of this chapter provides the formal parable that opens the teaching by revealing the One Vehicle; second, the "Parable of the Faith and Understanding" clarifies how those of medium capacity attain realization;
third, the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" is the Tathāgata’s confirmation of their attainment; fourth, the "Bestowal of Prophecy" is the granting of predictions.
The first part of the first section of the decision consists of two parts: the request and the response. Now, for the first [part]:
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I now have no further doubt or regret;
having personally received the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* before the Buddha, these twelve hundred [disciples] who have mastery over their minds..."

Those who formerly dwelt on the stage of training were constantly taught by the Buddha, who said: "My Dharma can bring about liberation from birth, old age, sickness, and death, culminating in ultimate Nirvana.

These persons, both those in training and those beyond training, each thought for themselves that they had attained Nirvana by being free from the view of self and views such as existence and non-existence.
Yet now, in the presence of the World-Honored One, hearing what they have never heard before, they all fall into doubt and confusion. How excellent! World-Honored One!
"World-Honored One, we pray that you will explain the causes and conditions for the sake of the fourfold assembly, so that they may be freed from doubt and regret.
Herein, the first part is the Master’s own statement that he has no doubts; the section beginning with "These various... describes how his peers have such delusions;

and the section beginning with "Excellent... is a request on behalf of the entire fourfold assembly for him to speak, as these peers are fellow practitioners who cherish their old ties and thus require this instruction.
The request to the fourfold assembly is made because this newly manifested realm of transformation universally invokes great compassion;

"hearing what was never heard before" refers to the preceding Dharma-exposition, up to the confirmation and bestowal of the prophecy, which differs from the teachings previously mounted and the realizations therein attained.
As for the "causes and conditions," why is it that three were previously taught and now one is taught? This must be clarified.

As for the reason why this is so, one asks: "If even ordinary beings can attain awakening upon hearing [the Dharma] once, and now these twelve hundred people have heard both the brief and the extensive explanations and the detailed exposition, and having heard Śāriputra receive his prediction, even dragons and spirits were able to cite examples and rejoice—why do they still remain deluded?
The answer is that there are two reasons: first, long-standing attachment; second, having entered a fixed stage.

The explanation that immediately shatters attachments—once attachments are shattered—one enters and abides [in the truth]; ordinary beings lack this, or perhaps it will be easy for them to comprehend.
△ Second, the response is divided into three parts: first, the introduction; second, the formal analogy; third, the exhortation to believe and circulate [the teaching]. Now, the first part.

At that time, the Buddha said to Śāriputra: "Did I not previously state that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, teach the Dharma through various causes and conditions, parables, and skillful means for the sake of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
All that has been taught is for the purpose of transforming bodhisattvas. Nevertheless, Śāriputra, I shall now further employ a parable."
To further clarify this meaning, those who possess wisdom shall attain understanding through parables.

In the text, there is first a suppression followed by an induction. When it says, "I did not say before," it refers back to the clarification that all provisional [teachings] are for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
When it says, "all manifesting the real," it refers back to the revelation that these are all for the purpose of transforming bodhisattvas. Whether provisional or real, they all enter the Buddha-way.
In the section on *apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa*, it was already clearly stated: "How can you cling to the teachings, being deluded and ignorant, failing to understand?

This reprimand is intended to suppress [the opponent] until they are moved to indignation and resolve. However, from the passage beginning with "Śāriputra," there is an invitation and consolation to cause him to advance quickly.

Since the previous censure was so severe, there was a fear that he might feel contemptuous resentment and sink into despair; thus, it is now permitted through the use of parables that if he can understand them...

This refers to what is still called "wisdom" (*jñāna*). △ Second, the actual parable and explanation, in two parts: first, the long prose; second, the verse summary. Within the first part, there are two sections:
first, establishing the parable; second, the application to the Dharma. Now, regarding the parable and its application, each may be either concise or detailed.

If the parable is concise and the application is detailed, one must first condense the text of the application to correspond with the parable; once that is complete, when reaching the application itself, it must be explained in full detail. If [the parable is...]

The extensive [explanation] synthesizes the concise. World-Honored One, how could you merely utter idle words? You must provide a detailed analysis of the analogies and their synthesis; however, the concise version corresponds only to the beginning.

Furthermore, there are two parts: first, the general analogy; second, the specific analogies. Within the first, there are six sections: first, the analogy of the elder; second, the analogy of the house;
third, the analogy of the single gate; fourth, the analogy of the five hundred people; fifth, the analogy of the fire breaking out; sixth, the analogy of the thirty sons.
First, the analogy of the elder refers to me, Śākyamuni. Śāriputra,
suppose there were a great elder in a kingdom, city, or village who was advanced in years, possessed immeasurable wealth,
and owned many fields, houses, and servants.
The phrase "kingdoms, cities, and villages" clarifies their names; the phrase "there was a great elder" correctly designates his rank and title.
The description that "his years were advanced" and so forth elucidates his virtuous achievements. His name is like a guest, while his conduct is like that of a host;

his conduct has degrees of intimacy (substantive conduct is intimate, while expedient conduct is distant), and his name has degrees of proximity. Therefore, he is cited by his location to manifest his name and conduct; a defined territory constitutes a kingdom.
The most distant administrative seat is the central town; the neighboring villages are the closest settlements.
An elder whose name and conduct are renowned throughout these three places is one who does not see their own minor flaws when near, but only admires their lofty character from afar.

His speech is free of censure, his conduct is free of censure, and his mind is free of censure regarding the Dharma; his name and conduct are in perfect accord. He is a true great man, as illustrated by this analogy.

The three karmas of the Tathāgata proceed in accordance with wisdom; he bestows transformation according to the capacities of beings, so that his fame is universally heard and his virtue pervades the Dharma-realm.

The "country" represents the Land of True Reward (*niṣyanda-bhūmi*), the "city" represents the Land of Expedient Means (*upāya-bhūmi*), and the "village" represents the Land of Shared Residence (*sahā-bhūmi*).

From the fundamental state of the Land of Quiescent Light, these three lands descend as traces; by gathering these three lands as traces back into the fundamental state of the Land of Quiescent Light, one is called "the manifestation of conduct and its characteristics being in accord."

"Yi" (overflowing) means pervasive. A worldling householder must be endowed with ten virtues: first, noble lineage—either descended from emperors or belonging to a family where the official rank is indicated by the "ermine-tipped cap";
second, high position—serving as a minister or counselor such as Ai-heng; third, great wealth—abundant in gold, grain, and treasures;
fourth, majestic authority—dignified and imposing, achieving results without the need for sternness; fifth, profound wisdom—their inner mind is like an armory.

1. Extraordinary and transcendent, for six years he was venerable, with hair as white as frost and a majestic bearing that caused all things to submit; 2. His seven modes of conduct were pure and white, like a flawless jade; 3.
His eight observances were complete and perfect, moving with rhythmic harmony; 4. Above, he was praised by the One Man (the Buddha) as one whom all revere; 5.
Below, he was honored by the four seas as one whom all take as their master. Possessing these ten virtues, he is called a Great Elder; he is likened to the Tathāgata appearing in the world.

The Elder is born from the true suchness (*tathatā*) and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) of the three periods of time; thus, his noble lineage is supreme. His merit is perfected and his Way is manifest, with the ten titles being infinite;
thus, his two stations are exalted. He is fully endowed with the ten thousand virtues of the Dharma-wealth; thus, he possesses the three great riches.
His ten powers are fierce and valiant as he subdues Māra and restrains externalists; thus, his fourfold majesty is formidable. His single mind and triple wisdom are without exception...
Thoroughly penetrating the five wisdoms is profound; attaining perfect enlightenment so early is as remote as this. Six years have passed—this is old age.

The three karmas move in accordance with wisdom without error—this is the purity of the sevenfold conduct. Possessing the majestic deportment of a Buddha, the mind is like the great ocean—this is the perfection of the eight modes of respect.
Praised and compared by the Great Awakened Ones of the ten directions—this is the supreme eulogy. These are the seven aspects of direction.

Thus one comes to rely upon the ten virtues of the lower [stages] of the four teachings. (In the fruit-stage Buddhas of the four teachings, each is discussed according to its respective teaching; even in the first stage of the Perfect Teaching, one may partially realize the ten virtues of the Perfect family.

As for the contemplation of the mind: the wisdom of contemplating the mind arises from the true reality (*dharmatā*), and being born into the Buddha-family, one’s lineage is truly authentic—this is "noble birth.
Although the three delusions have not yet ceased and the true [path] has not yet been realized, one already dwells as a Tathāgata.
The robe symbolizes the patience of quiescent extinction (*śānti-kṣānti*), which signifies high status; the three truths (*trīṇi satyāni*) containing all merits signify great wealth;
the wisdom of correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana-prajñā*) subduing craving and views signifies majesty and ferocity;

the Middle Way illuminating both the provisional and the real simultaneously signifies profound wisdom. One who has long accumulated roots of goodness is able to cultivate this contemplation; this contemplation arises from...

The "seven expedients" (saptavidha-upāya) above refer to the stage of advanced age (*vṛddha*). This contemplation observes the nature of the mind and is called the "supreme concentration" (*uttama-samādhi*);

it can cause the three karmas to be free from transgression, which is the purity of conduct (*caryā-śuddhi*). Throughout all conditions and encounters with objects, one's dignified demeanor (*īryāpatha*) remains without fail, which is the perfection of ritual propriety (*vidhi-sampad*).
To be able to contemplate in this way constitutes the mark of profound faith and understanding; all Buddhas will rejoice and praise such a person.
The "upholding of the Dharma" refers to the praise mentioned above; the "heavenly dragons and the fourfold assembly reverently making offerings" refers to the homage mentioned below.
As the subsequent text states: "The Son of the Buddha abiding in this stage is the very enjoyment of the Buddha.

This is called the Elder who Contemplates the Mind. (These ten virtues do not transcend the three categories of object, wisdom, and practice. Although one has not yet entered the [bodhisattva] stages, because one is like a prince in the womb, it is termed "contemplative practice. If these ten virtues of the Tathāgata are contrasted with the supramundane, they correspond respectively to their teachings, contemplations, distinct fruits, and standards according to the scriptures.)

Regarding the contemplation of cause and effect for oneself, one immediately applies the three contemplations (*trividha-darśana*) to the four teachings (*catuṣ-prakāra-deśanā*), surveying the marks of virtue (*guṇa-lakṣaṇa*) to praise these contemplations. This is so that future students may cultivate the causal stage with full equipment, using the contemplation of the ten virtues to realize the resultant stage of the ten virtues.

Because one can, with a single mind, fully illuminate the three dharmas, this is the "contemplation of the mind" (*citta-darśana*). Since these ten virtues are fully present, the passage beginning with "O Son of the Buddha" (*buddhaputra*) is cited as proof for the contemplation of the mind. Furthermore, these ten virtues correspond to the sequence of the "Ten Dharmas Accomplishing the Vehicle" (*daśa-dharma-yāna-sampanna*); when combined, they possess profound significance. Why is this? The true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is precisely the inconceivable realm (*acintya-viṣaya*).

Because one arouses vows based on the principle (*tattva*), it is called "abiding in patience" (*kṣānti-sthiti*). Because the mind rests in the principle and accords with the principle, it is called "containing [the seeds]. By eliminating the delusions of the three truths and attaining the pervasive penetration, it is called the "Middle Way" (*madhyamā-pratipad*), which is the simultaneous [negation and affirmation].

Illuminating that which is unobstructed and penetrating that which was previously impassable, these articles of the path of non-action transcend the seven stages of expedient means (*upāya*). They assist the three karmas so that they accord with principle without fault and encounter objects of perception without error.

Because one relies on the true stage and one’s faith and understanding are already profound, one is able to practice patient endurance (*kṣānti*) and does not give rise to attachment to dharmas (*dharmatṛṣṇā*); only then can one receive the offerings of the lower [levels]. The ten dharmas of the three teachings are explained progressively to form the ten dharmas of contemplating the mind in this present sutra. These ten contemplations do not merely exist horizontally within the stage of contemplative practice; from the initial stage to the final stage, all ten contemplations are fully present.

Furthermore, the meaning of these ten virtues is vertically profound, merging seamlessly with the horizontal and vertical ten vehicles (*daśayāna*). Regarding the virtues within the "Brilliant Virtuous Deeds" (*ming de ye*), there are internal and external aspects; internally, it is as follows:
Wisdom and strategy correspond externally to wealth; being advanced in years corresponds to a broad mastery of antiquity and the present. The Buddha’s wisdom and virtue are like this;

his decline in vigor corresponds to the ripening of the faculties and will, which is like the Buddha’s virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa*). Wealth represents external virtues that are immeasurable, collectively representing all virtues.
A field can nourish one’s life, specifically representing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) which relies upon *prajñā*. A house is where one may take refuge, specifically [representing the body].
For example, the true realm serves as the basis for wisdom (such as the eighteen gates of emptiness). If one discusses merit, there is no practice that is not cultivated;
if one discusses wisdom, there is no realm that is not illumined. Therefore, it is said that he possesses many fields and houses.

"Servants" refers to attendants and laborers, which are metaphors for the complete perfection of skillful means and insight (*upāya-jñāna*). He blends his light with the six paths, complying with them in all their twists and turns.

The various vehicles are the servants of true wisdom. △ Second, the analogy of the house: this illustrates the aforementioned "peaceful security" in contrast to the "unfixed," where "unpeaceful insecurity" refers precisely to the three realms.
That house is vast and expansive.

Sentient beings are busily occupied, all dwelling within the triple world; because the Tathāgata, through his responsive transformations, presides over and governs this household, it is said to be vast and expansive.
△3. The Parable of the Single Door illustrates how, as mentioned above, the Buddha-way is proclaimed and revealed through various Dharma-gates.
There is only one gate. The text states:
"By means of the Buddha’s gate of teaching, one exits the suffering of the triple world and attains the realization of nirvāṇa.

One should know that the principle (*tattva*) is what is elucidated by the teaching; thus, we take the teaching that elucidates this principle as the gate. Since the principle is singular, the teaching cannot admit of two.
Furthermore, it is said that these are one and the same. Moreover, there are the "house gate" and the "chariot gate. The "house" refers to birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*);
the "gate" refers to the path for emerging from birth-and-death; this is the interpretation according to the provisional teachings (*upāya-deśanā*). The "chariot" refers to the Mahāyāna Dharma;

the "gate" refers to the interpretation according to the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya*). If the house gate is identical to the chariot gate, then at the moment of exiting the burning house, one should immediately attain [enlightenment].

Why should the great vehicle require waiting for a rope? If the gate of the house were not the gate of the vehicle, then at the very moment one seeks the vehicle, one would simply be exiting from the burning house;
how could there be another path? Furthermore, once the gate of the house has been reached, yet the gate of the vehicle has not been reached—where would one be staying?
One should know that if they are excluded, the vehicle and the house are eternally distinct; if they are opened, the two gates are no different, for the house and the vehicle are one.
How do the first and second gates differ? Therefore, the three vehicles all possess these two meanings. Having emerged from the house by means of the teaching, one does not see the small carts;
yet, having already been matured through the two intermediate flavors, one then requests from the father the very vehicle previously promised.

Since it has been requested, it must be granted; thus, the small gate is opened for that purpose. There is nothing that is not the Great Teaching, for beneath the gate, the minor principles ultimately have no separate path.
The principle is severed and non-dual; the essence of the coarse and the subtle is one. Dharmas abide in their own positions, and the characteristics of the world are eternal.

How could there be any distinction within the three realms? If there were no prior difference, what would there be to discuss as being the same? Those who have sunk into suffering are all gathered here now.
△ Fourth, the parable of the five hundred people illustrates the aforementioned sentient beings, which are precisely the five destinies.
Many crowds of people—whether one hundred, two hundred, or even five hundred—dwell therein.
"One hundred" refers to devas, "two hundred" to humans, and so on up to "five hundred," which refers to the three evil destinies (*durgati*).

Asuras are not mentioned because asuras are either included within the destiny of hungry ghosts (*preta-gati*) or are subsumed under the four destinies, as stated in the *Mahābuddhapiṭaka-śikhara-sūtra*.
△ The fifth analogy, the Arising of Fire, illustrates the aforementioned dharma of peace and security in contrast to the dharma of insecurity;

"insecurity" refers here to the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*). The text is further divided into two parts: first, it sets forth the characteristics of the burning house as an analogy for the retributions of the six realms;
second, it clarifies the fire that burns as an analogy for the eight sufferings and the five turbidities. This is the first part.
The hall and pavilion are decayed and ancient; the walls and partitions have collapsed; the bases of the pillars are rotten;

and the beams and rafters are tilting and perilous. The hall is a metaphor for the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); the pavilion is a metaphor for the form and formless realms (*rūpa- and ārūpyadhātu*). "Decayed" is a metaphor for the three realms being worn out, evil, and impermanent; it is thus a metaphor for the three realms not being newly created.

The "walls and partitions" are a metaphor for the four great elements (*mahābhūta*); "collapsed" is a metaphor for their diminution; the "bases of the pillars" [are a metaphor for the roots of existence].

It is like a life that has rotted; it is like a precarious state that will not last long. The beams and rafters represent the consciousness; their tilting and collapsing represent the ceaseless flux of change.
Although the formless realm lacks the coarse colors of the four great elements, in terms of conventional resultant form, it is nonetheless like walls and partitions.

All three realms are maintained by consciousness; however, if one explains this solely in terms of the causes and effects of the primary retribution (*vipāka*) within the three realms, then [the formless realm] is already included.

The dependent retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*) need not be combined with the primary retribution (*adhiṣṭhāna-vipāka*) for the sake of the analogy; the dependent retribution is merely a small portion of the *pariṇāma-bhāga* (evolving aspect) of the eighth consciousness.

Furthermore, since there are already no sentient beings during the twenty eons of dissolution and formation, how could one explain the meaning of the "turbidities" (*kaṣāya*) and "burning" (*jvalana*)?

Because they are somewhat removed [from that state], they are not employed here. Moreover, regarding the contemplative interpretation: the hall (*kūṭāgāra*) is a metaphor for the lower part of the body, and the pavilion (*kūṭa*)...
The upper parts, such as the head, are likened to the walls; the falling away of skin and flesh is likened to decrepitude;
the rotting of the base of the pillars is likened to the failing of the two feet; and the tilting and perilous state of the beams and rafters is likened to the great end [of life].
△ Next, the fire that burns is explained.
Simultaneously and suddenly, fire breaks out on all sides, burning down the house and its dwellings.

Because the eight sufferings pervade the four elements and the four modes of birth, it is said they "surround" [the house]; because all are equally impermanent, it is said they arise "simultaneously and suddenly.
This is an analogy for that which was originally non-existent now coming into being; originally there was no such suffering, yet through ignorance, the five fires arise.

The analogy concludes. △ Sixth, the analogy of the thirty sons illustrates the aforementioned "knowing the dispositions and desires of sentient beings," which refers specifically to the practitioners of the Three Vehicles.
It is as if the elder’s sons—whether ten, twenty, or even thirty—are within this house.
Having previously studied the Buddha-dharma, our natures are naturally attuned; those who have already formed a karmic connection with me upon seeing me are my sons.
If there are ten such people, they are the sons of Bodhisattvas; if twenty or thirty, they are the sons of the Two Vehicles. Such individuals are all capable of escaping from the house.

If one lacks this capacity, then they are merely among the five hundred [disciples]. Alternatively, it may be that their modes of emergence and disappearance differ—whether as Pratyekabuddhas or followers of the Lesser Vehicle.

Whether categorized as belonging to the Śrāvaka-vehicle or the Pratyekabuddha-vehicle, all are said to possess "ten" because they all inherently possess the nature of the ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*). [The ten knowledges are:

(1) knowledge of the conventional (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), (2) knowledge of the minds of others (*paracittajñāna*), (3) knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*), (4) knowledge of the origin (*samudayajñāna*), (5) knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), (6) knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*), (7) knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), (8) subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), (9) knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), and (10) knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*). The first section, the general analogy, is concluded.
△ Second, the four specific analogies: 1. The analogy of the elder seeing the fire; 2. The analogy of discarding the stools and employing the vehicles; 3. The analogy of the equal bestowal...

The great carriage is a metaphor for the four [means of conversion]; the absence of falsehood is a metaphor for the initial scene where the elder sees the fire, which illustrates how the Buddha, seeing the five turbidities, gives rise to a heart of great compassion.
When the elder saw this great fire arising from all four sides, he was immediately seized with great alarm and fear, and thought to himself: "Although I..."

While he was able to emerge safely from this gate that was being consumed by fire, the children within the burning house were so attached to their play that they were neither aware nor cognizant of it;
they were neither startled nor terrified, and as the fire approached and tormented their bodies with piercing pain, their hearts felt no aversion or distress,
nor did they have any intention to seek escape.

In this passage, there are four textual sections, but their meaning is but threefold: first, the elder sees the manifestation of the seer, which illustrates my [the Buddha’s] statement, "I observe with the Buddha-eye";
second, the great fire arises from the four directions, illustrating that which is seen, namely the sentient beings of the six realms mentioned above;
third, he is immediately seized by great terror, illustrating the phrase "for this reason" mentioned above.
For the sake of sentient beings, one gives rise to the mind of great compassion (4).

Now, the passage beginning with "the sons" and so forth extensively explains the second point previously mentioned—the fire seen there—and further elucidates the meaning of being terrified. Body, sensation, mind, and phenomena constitute the four sides of the house;
from these four sides arise the four inversions of purity, pleasure, permanence, and self, whereby the eight sufferings all accumulate. If...

When one knows that the body is impure, suffering, impermanent, and non-self—and that feeling and the other aggregates are likewise—then the fire of the afflictions is extinguished and the suffering of karma is simultaneously quenched.
At this point, "great alarm" refers to the mindfulness of falling away from the Great Good;
"alarm" refers to the anxiety over the imminent arising of grave evils; "fear" is great compassion for those who lack happiness; and "terror" is the sorrow for those who possess [suffering].
"Although I am capable [of escaping], I have safely emerged from this gate of burning" explains the meaning of "terror.

Although these are words that do not exhaust the full sense, they clarify that because the Buddha, by the power of his wisdom, is able to seek the true teaching and perceive the truths it elucidates, he is not endangered by the five turbidities or the eight sufferings; thus, he is not shaken by the violent winds of the four inversions.
Because it is capable of movement, it is hidden; because it is remote and beyond all burdens, it is said that it has emerged. Yet sentient beings are not so; they are burned by fire.
Because the Tathāgata’s compassion is likewise inflamed by the fire of anxiety, it is said that he too is "burned. As for the "gate of what is burned," a gate must necessarily have components.
There is emptiness, yet it is not a component; without something to mark the gate, there would be no gate. Without emptiness, there would be no way to pass through.

The aforementioned items can be reduced to ashes and emptiness cannot be burned; this serves as a metaphor for the teaching consisting of the expressive medium (*vācaka*) and the expressed content (*vācya*).
If there were no expressive medium to explain it, it could not constitute a teaching; if there were no expressed content, how could one emerge from the expressive medium?
