the one kind is the knowledge of all modes, which is the virtue of wisdom (*prajñā*); and that which can produce pure, wondrous, and supreme bliss—bliss being the absence of suffering—is the virtue of liberation (*vimukti*).
These three virtues are inconceivable and are called the "high, vast, and great vehicle," for these three are equal.
The analogy of bestowing the great chariots is concluded. △ Fourth, the analogy of the absence of falsehood has two parts: first, restating the analogy; second, the formal application.
Now, the first:
"Śāriputra, just as that elder first used the three vehicles to entice his children and subsequently gave them only the great [chariots],"
The chariot is adorned with precious treasures, supremely secure and stable; yet that elder is free from the fault of falsehood.
△ Second, the formal application:
The Tathāgata is also like this, being without falsehood; he first teaches the three vehicles to guide sentient beings, and thereafter...
They deliver them solely by means of the Mahāyāna. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata possesses immeasurable power of wisdom, the fearlessnesses, and the treasury of all dharmas;
he is able to bestow the Dharma of the Mahāyāna upon all sentient beings, yet they are not all capable of receiving it.
Śāriputra, for these reasons, you should know that through the power of the skillful means of the Buddhas, [they teach] within the single Buddha-vehicle.
I distinguish and explain three vehicles.

This is because I can provide the Dharma of the Mahāyāna to all sentient beings—just as it is said that even if one were to distribute these goods of mine throughout an entire kingdom, they would not be exhausted—yet they are unable to receive it all. Therefore, having no other choice, I bestow one [vehicle] while establishing three.
Third, because it was not the Buddha’s original intention for sentient beings [to hear this], yet teaching the Mahāyāna now does not contradict his original mind, it is not false.
Previously, Śāriputra asked, "I pray that you will explain the causes and conditions for the fourfold assembly";
thus, he now answers, "For these reasons, I distinguish and teach the three [vehicles]. This concludes the initial long prose section within the second part, the section on correct analogies.
*The Collected Meanings of the Tiantai School on the Lotus Sutra*, Fascicle Two, Part One;
*The Collected Meanings of the Tiantai School on the Lotus Sutra*, Fascicle Two, Part Two.
Composed by the later scholar of Ancient Wu, Ouyi Zhixu.

△ Within the section on the formal parable, there are two sets of double verses. Of these, the first set establishes the parable, and the second set applies it to the Dharma. Within the former, there are two parts:

the first verse provides a general parable, and the second set of verses provides specific parables. The former further consists of four parts: the first verse concerns the elder; the second verse concerns the house;
the third verse concerns the five hundred people; and the fourth verse concerns the outbreak of fire—briefly omitting the mention of the single gate and the thirty [pillars].
This is the first instance.
The Buddha, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse: "Suppose there were an elder...

This verse refers to his rank and title, which simultaneously implies his conduct and praises his virtues; it is like how by uttering the name of a Buddha, one immediately knows of his myriad virtues. △
The second verse describes the house:

There was a great house, which was ancient and had long been in decay; its halls and chambers were perilously high and unstable, the bases of its pillars were crushed and rotten, the beams and rafters were slanting and leaning, the foundations and steps were collapsed and ruined, the walls were crumbling and split apart, the plaster was peeling away, and the thatched roof was falling down in disarray.
The rafters and eaves are broken and detached, the surrounding walls are crooked and warped, and filth and impurities fill every corner.
To explain this by way of analogy: there is a great house, which refers to the cohabitation within the trichiliocosm of the three realms (*tridhātu*).

Since these three realms have no beginning, they are ancient and were not created recently; thus, they are termed "old," "impermanent," "lowly," and "debased. Furthermore, the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is designated as "suddenly dilapidated."
The desire realm is its hall; failing to escape falling is its high peril; the life-faculty is its supporting pillar;
being transmuted by the four marks is its crumbling decay; consciousness is its beams and rafters; being destroyed by various sufferings is its tilting collapse;
past karma is its foundation and steps; the shifting and extinction of karmic destiny is its ruin; and the four great elements are its walls.
The mutual injury of the walls results in their crumbling and splitting; the skin serves as the plaster and mud coating; the lack of enduring vigor leads to decay and falling away;

the lack of rectitude in the four modes of deportment is like a thatched roof collapsing in disorder; the five consciousnesses being unwholesome and failing to govern their respective objects is like rafters and eaves becoming misaligned and detached;
and the mental consciousness racing about everywhere, seizing upon objects through all six sense faculties, is like a pervasive enclosure that wanders throughout.
The objects of the senses are crooked and pervade the six sense-fields; the arising of greed, anger, and delusion constitutes the impurities that fill them.
This, in general, refers to the three realms, where form and mind constitute the substance of the house. Regarding the interpretation through the contemplation of the mind:

the present single thought-moment of the five aggregates, body, and mind, is by its very nature fundamentally vertical and pervasive, and is thus called "one great house" that has been dark since beginningless time.

The succession of consciousnesses is said to have no creator and is called "ancient"; yet moment by moment it is impermanent, and its deluded nature is so base and evil that it is called "suddenly decayed.
The belly is the hall and the back is the house; the two feet are the pillars and the backbone is the ridgepole;
the buttocks and thighs are the foundation steps; the skin and flesh are the walls, and the complexion is the plaster; the beard and hair are...
The teeth and bones and joints form the rafters and eaves; the interior of the entire body forms the surrounding walls;
the small and large intestines and so forth form the winding passages; and the various great and small impurities fill it with filth.
Such is this single body, and outside of it there is nothing else that can be called a "great house. This is the actual dwelling belonging to the elder. If one is able to...
Moment by moment, through contemplation, one realizes that the nature of suffering inherent in these five aggregates of body and mind is the virtue of the *dharmakāya*;
that all defilements and afflictions are the virtue of *prajñā*; and that all karmic activities are the virtue of *vimukti*.
Thus, one transforms from being a nominal elder to becoming an ultimate elder, awakening oneself and awakening others in inexhaustible benefit.

If they do not observe this, they will dwell forever within the burning house until the end of the future, being burned again and again without ever realizing that the very substance of this great mansion is the vehicle of the great white ox. Alas, alas! △ Third, the verse on the five hundred people.
Five hundred people dwell within it; this is like the five destinies (*pañcagati*).
Since there are five destinies, there are the root-natures of the three vehicles (*triyāna*), which together comprise the thirty sons.

△ Fourth, the verse on the fire breaking out has four parts: first, the verse on the events upon the ground, which is a metaphor for the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); second, the verse on the interior of the pit.

The internal analogy refers to the three verses on the form realm (*rūpadhātu*); the external analogy refers to the four [verses] on the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). To summarize, the various difficulties are not one. Question:
Since the scriptural text already contains both analogies and their applications (*upanaya*), why is there further explanation through analogy within the analogies themselves?

Answer: The analogy is extensive while the application is concise; logically, one should explain the analogy by way of its illustrative instances. For example, the comparison of the owl, the screech-owl, the eagle, the vulture, and even the *yakṣa* and *preta*.
If [the faculties] such as the equal, the sharp, and the dull were not [discussed], for what purpose would these redundant and miscellaneous names and categories be listed?
Could it be that the Buddha spoke words devoid of meaning? Regarding the first four [sections]: first, clarifying the things to be burned; second, clarifying the cause by which the fire arises;
third, correctly clarifying the momentum of the fire’s arising; fourth, clarifying the characteristics of being burned. First, clarifying the things to be burned:
They resemble the ten classes of sentient beings driven by the afflictions.

Owls, crows, eagles, vultures, ravens, magpies, doves, pigeons, vipers, snakes, adders, scorpions, centipedes, millipedes, lizards, geckos, many-legged insects, weasels, badgers, mice, and various other malevolent creatures run about crosswise; in places reeking with excrement and urine, impurities flow and overflow.
Dung beetles and various other insects swarm upon it; foxes, wolves, and jackals gnaw, trample, and bite the corpse, tearing its flesh and bones to pieces.

Because of this, packs of dogs come rushing to seize and snatch at them, emaciated with hunger and terror, seeking food everywhere while fighting, clawing, snarling, and barking; the house is thus filled with such terrifying transformations.
This first analogy refers to the five dull afflictions (*pañca-mṛdu-kleśa*). The eight birds, such as the owl and the screech-owl, serve as metaphors for the affliction of pride (*māna*).

Sentient beings exalt themselves and look down upon others, just as these birds soar high and gaze downward; looking down upon others is called "pride" (*māna*), while relying on oneself is called "haughtiness" (*mada*). Therefore, haughtiness is used to explain pride.
The *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-sūtra* clarifies the eight types of haughtiness, which are now applied here to correspond with the eight birds. For instance, the haughtiness of physical vigor is like...
Pride in lineage is like the *chī* (owl); pride in wealth is like the hawk; pride in power is like the vulture; pride in longevity is like the crow; pride in intelligence is like the magpie;

and pride in performing good deeds is like the pigeon. Pride in physical beauty is like the dove. Next, the two phrases concerning the lizard and the snake serve as metaphors for the latent tendency of hatred (*dveṣānuśaya*).
The "lizard" refers to the black snake; because the lizard-snake inhales [its prey] without even touching it, it serves as a metaphor for irrationality (*ayoniśomanasikāra*).

The "wrathful viper" (*zhenfou*) is a kind of snake; it is three inches long, as thick as a finger, and has needles upon its snout. When touched by such a viper or a scorpion, one is stung; this is a metaphor for wrath regarding the grasping of principles.

The "wrathful red-headed creature" is named the centipede (*wugong*); those that are not red are called millipedes (*youyan*). This is a metaphor for wrath regarding frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*).

Next, the eight phrases beginning with the *shougong* (gecko) collectively serve as metaphors for the latent tendencies of delusion (*moha-anuśaya*). The *shougong* is the same as the *yan-yan* (lizard).
The lizard and the centipede are motionless and devoid of cognition, which is analogous to the "isolated" (*mūla*) ignorance.
The weasel resembles a rat yet also devours rats; the *lī* is a species of cat; and the *khīra* is the "sweet-mouthed" rat.

These four analogies correspond to the various classes of evil insects that represent the two types of ignorance—both the isolated and the associated—which run rampant and cross paths, universally conditioning the three [realms].

Because of the realms, they arise crosswise and in confusion; because of their swiftness, they "run about. This means that from the root of delusion (*moha*), all fetters (*saṃyojana*) arise together.
The two lines concerning excrement and urine clarify that the objects to which the deluded mind clings are all impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure.
The two lines concerning dung beetles clarify that through the ignorance of deluded phenomena, one falsely discriminates them as being permanent, blissful, and self.
From purity, defiled attachment arises. The eight phrases beginning with "foxes and wolves" collectively illustrate the latent tendencies of greed (*rāga-anuśaya*).
"Foxes and wolves" illustrate powerful greed that seizes by means of its majesty; "jackals" illustrate weak greed that begs from others.
"Chewing" illustrates seizing what is useful, while "trampling" illustrates seizing what is useless. Furthermore, when [the objects] are few, one chews them; when they are many, one tramples them.
"Treading" and "gnawing" are metaphors for insatiable greed and voracious devouring; the "corpse" is a metaphor for the coarse and debased five desires (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*);
the "scattered bones and flesh" are metaphors for the accumulated five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*).

Because they do not know contentment, a pack of dogs comes vying with one another to seize and snatch them—this refers to kings, thieves, and others who possess great power, who are able to take away all the accumulated goods of both the powerful and the powerless.
"Taking by force" refers to being constantly insatiable during times of hunger; "emaciation" refers to seeking that which does not accord with one's desires;
and "panic-stricken confusion" refers to various kinds of frantic searching—this is what is meant by the saying that a person of excessive desire is poor despite being wealthy.

Furthermore, the "loving heart" covets the "flesh" of the five sensory objects (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*); when the seeing-mind covets the "bones" of the principles of the Way, it pursues knowledge and views until they become numerous.
That which they understand is like many dogs with gnawed bones and missing bones vying with one another to seize them;

their minds, upon seeing this, have not yet obtained the food of the True Dharma, which is called "hunger. Being unable to subdue or sever the delusions of views is called "emaciation. Seeking understanding everywhere is called "trepidation.
Mutual contention over right and wrong is called "strife. Their intention is to regard what is not as being so, just as before.

"Seizing again" means that, as previously mentioned, one drags [the opponent] back and forth, engaging in verbal debate to determine the principle of right and wrong, like the snarling and barking of dogs.
This combines with the preceding section; thus, the four lines concerning the "pack of dogs" and so forth comprise six lines in total, all serving as metaphors for doubt.

They illustrate how one causes the abandonment of fear and the transformation of its manifestations. This concludes the summary of the aforementioned five dull afflictions (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*). (See *Shǔ*)

Regarding the phrase "the sharp faculty of discernment is sovereign" (li-shi zizai) in the subsequent text: here, it refers to the "sharp among the dull," and thus one gives rise to doubt by inferring from the underlying principle. (To purse the lips and bare the teeth is called *jiaishi*; to let out a loud roar is called *haofei*.)

Everywhere there were *chī-mèi wǎng-liǎng* (goblins and imps), *yakṣas*, and malevolent ghosts who devour human flesh, along with various species of venomous insects and evil birds and beasts that breed and give birth, each guarding its own young. The *yakṣas* vied with one another to seize and eat them;
once satiated, their malevolence flared up even more, and the sounds of their quarreling were most terrifying, as were those of the *kumbhāṇḍa* ghosts.
Crouching on mounds of earth, sometimes at a height of one or two feet, they wander back and forth, indulging in wanton play;
they seize dogs by their two hind legs, pin them down until they cry out, and place their own feet upon the dogs' necks, taking pleasure in terrifying them.
Furthermore, there are various ghosts whose bodies are tall and large, naked, black, and emaciated, who constantly dwell therein, emitting great evil sounds, shrieking and crying out for food.
Furthermore, there are various ghosts whose throats are like needles; others have heads like those of oxen. Some eat human flesh, while others devour dogs.
Their hair is disheveled and matted; they are cruel and predatory, driven by hunger and thirst, crying out as they run about.

This current analogy refers to the five *drṣṭi-āsravas* (five deluded views). The two lines, "present everywhere," collectively clarify that these five types of deluded views pervade the three realms, the five aggregates (*skandha*), and the four noble truths, existing at all times and in every circumstance.

The mountain monsters are called *chī*, the house monsters are called *mèi*, and the transformations of wood and stone are called *wǎnglǎng*. The three verses concerning the *yakṣas* and so forth separately illustrate those who hold false views.
Flesh is a metaphor for the excellent retributions of the supramundane; devouring human flesh is a metaphor for repudiating the existence of supramundane cause and effect.

Poisonous insects, birds, and beasts breeding and giving birth, each protecting and concealing their offspring, is a metaphor for mundane cause and effect: because a cause can produce an effect, it is called "concealment" (*gupti*);
because one will certainly obtain [the result] without loss, it is called "protection" (*rakṣā*). To scramble for and eat them is a metaphor for repudiating mundane causes.
The fruit, having been eaten until one is full, is a metaphor for the fulfillment of wrong views; the further intensification of the evil mind is a metaphor for the expansion of those wrong views;

the sound of quarreling and strife is a metaphor for the denial of cause and effect; and the fact that such heterodox doctrines are utterly terrifying is a metaphor for how hearing these doctrines can cause one to fall into the three miserable realms.
The two and a half verses beginning with "Ghūṇa" (the woodworm) separately illustrate the precepts.
The *kumbhāṇḍa* refers to a fearsome ghost; "sitting empty" (*xūzuò*) means squatting (*dūn*), while "sitting solidly" (*shízà*) means crouching (*jù*).

A "mound of earth" (*tǔduǒ*) refers to a high place on the terrain, which serves as a metaphor for non-Buddhists who, relying on the grasping of precepts (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), practice the ten wholesome actions and are thus able to be born in the high places of the six heavens of the desire realm.
When they occasionally rise one or two feet off the ground, this serves as a metaphor for practicing based on the grasping of precepts.
Attaining the four dhyānas and being born in the realm of form is called "leaving the ground by one chi";
alternatively, attaining the four formless absorptions through the power of precepts and being born in the formless realm is called "leaving the ground by two chi.

"Wandering back and forth" refers to ascending to birth in the two higher realms and returning to birth in the desire realm; "indulging in idle play" is a metaphor for failing to enter the right path.
In the end, there is no actual attainment. Grasping the two hind legs of a dog is a metaphor for falsely calculating asceticism as being pure;

making it cry out by striking it is a metaphor for falsely calculating that asceticism cannot yield the fruit of suffering. Placing one's foot upon its neck is a metaphor for seeking the fruit of happiness through asceticism.
Terrifying the dog while enjoying oneself is a metaphor for temporarily subduing the afflictions (*kleśa*) through asceticism, occasionally gaining slight results.

This is the meditation on flavors (*rasa-dhyāna*). Furthermore, there are six phrases beginning with "various ghosts whose bodies are tall and large," which serve as distinct metaphors for the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*):
calculating a self by entering vertically through the three periods of time is called "tall"; calculating a self by extending horizontally throughout the five aggregates is called "large";
calculating a self as autonomous while failing to cultivate wholesome dharmas is called "naked" because of a lack of shame and dread of blame; and being adorned with evil is called "black."
Because they lack the provisions of merit, they are called "emaciated. Because they falsely conceive of a self that can never transcend the triple world, it is said they "permanently dwell therein.
Because they utter words proclaiming various marks of a self, it is said they "emit great evil cries.
Because they falsely conceive of a self that can attain *nirvāṇa*, it is called "crying out for food. Next, there are further various *pretas*.

Their throats are like needles; this is a specific metaphor for the view of grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*). Their throats are so narrow that life is perilous, yet they preserve their lives—this is like the realm of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), which is impermanent, yet they falsely reckon it to be *nirvāṇa*. Next, there are various ghosts with heads like oxen and so forth;

these two verses specifically illustrate the extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). Based upon the view of self-existence (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the two views of annihilationism and eternalism arise, just as an ox’s head has two horns.
The two views of annihilationism and eternalism sever the supramundane roots of goodness, just as eating human flesh severs mundane roots of goodness.
Sometimes they calculate [existence] as annihilated and sometimes as eternal, revolving back and forth like disheveled hair.
The view of eternalism destroys the correct principle of impermanence, while the view of annihilationism destroys the correctness of dependent origination.
Because their rational calculations constantly cause them to fall into the pit of eternalism and the pit of nihilism, they are said to be "cruel and fierce.

Because they consume no wisdom and drink no meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they are said to be "tormented by hunger and thirst. Because they proclaim the heterodox doctrines of eternalism and nihilism, they are said to be "shouting and crying out.
Because they cycle through birth and death without ceasing, they are said to be "running about."
Yakṣas, pretas, and various evil birds and beasts, driven by the urgency of hunger, peer out from all four directions through the windows and lattices;
such calamities and fears are immeasurable.
This is a summary of the characteristics of sentient beings with sharp or dull faculties who possess afflictions within the desire realm; these are all of the nature of outflows (*āsrava*).

Because the mind is constantly lacking the flavor of the Way, it is said to be "hungering in haste. Because one falsely contemplates the principle of emptiness while yearning for the flavor of the Way, it is said to "peep through four directions.
With a mind full of attachment, one fails to accord with the true principle, like looking at the sky through a window or a lattice; one cannot attain unobstructed freedom.
This concludes the first section clarifying the things burned. △ Second, clarifying the cause by which the fire arises, illustrated by the arising of the five [fires].
This is the source of its turbidity.
It was like an old, dilapidated house belonging to a certain person who had recently left it not long ago;
subsequently, a fire suddenly broke out within that dwelling.

The three realms are the places where the Buddha manifests through transformation; because he has vowed from the moment of his initial resolve to deliver all beings, they are said to belong to this one person alone.

Just as the elder in the house was able to ensure his children were careful regarding the fire while he was inside, yet allowed the fire to break out once they had gone outside because they were ignorant—this is a metaphor for when the Buddha was near the time of Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū Buddha, constantly teaching these people to subdue the five [desires].
Sentient beings in an age of turbidity perceive that the Tathāgata has exhausted his lifespan and abandoned this realm; subsequently, these [beings] give rise to the five turbidities.

Because he goes to other lands to respond to conditions rather than departing forever, it is said that he "recently emerged. Furthermore, because he has already realized non-arising and does not take birth within the triple world, he is called "emerged";
yet because he will soon return to respond [to beings], he is called "near. As the *Ayuṣpramāṇa-parivarta* states: "He appears repeatedly."
Nirvana is the intention of exiting the house; the three realms constitute the house and the five aggregates constitute the dwelling.
△ Third, the correct elucidation of the force of the fire’s arising is a metaphor for the actual emergence of the five turbidities.
Simultaneously from all four sides, its flames blaze together; the rafters, beams, purlins, and pillars crack with explosive sounds and collapse, while the walls crumble and fall.
The four sides are likened to the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena (*dharmas*); because the four inversions, the five turbidities, and the eight sufferings suddenly arise, it is said to be "one."
At that time, as the flames blaze together, his life is severed like a blast of wind; his body is dismembered like being cut by a blade; his joints are severed like a crackling gas;
his bones are separated like being broken and crushed; and the four great elements dissolve like walls collapsing.
Because of these turbid inversions, his physical life is impermanent. △ Fourth, the appearance of being burned illustrates the sharp and dull afflictions of the eight sufferings and five turbidities.

The sentient beings as well as the various spirits and ghosts raised their voices in loud cries; the vultures, eagles, and other birds, along with the kumbhāṇḍas, were so overwhelmed by panic and terror that they could not escape.
The various ghosts and spirits collectively seize all the dull and sharp latent tendencies (*anuśaya*); they raise their voices in loud cries, so terrified that they know not what to do.
The eagles and vultures represent the most prominent among the dull latent tendencies, while the *kumbhāṇḍas* represent the most prominent among the sharp latent tendencies.
Yet all are utterly distraught and fearful, unable to escape on their own; thus we know this.

If one lacks the Three Jewels, the Four Noble Truths, and the Dharma of the Four Foundations of Mindfulness, then even if one were a celestial being, a dragon, or a deity, one would certainly not escape the cycle of saṃsāra.
The first verse concludes the analogy for matters on the ground, representing the Desire Realm. II. The second part [of the section] verses the events within the cave, representing the Form Realm.
This has three sub-sections: 1. An analogy for the types of beings to be burned; 2. Clarifying the cause by which the fire arises, and the manner in which the fire arises.
First, regarding the signs of the three knowledges (*vidyā*) being consumed by fire:

even though the holes and burrows where wild beasts, venomous insects, and *piśāca* demons dwell are not as open and spacious as those outside the door, they are still able to escape the fierce flames; this serves as a metaphor for the four [meditative absorptions].
Although dhyāna does not reach the bliss beyond the realms, it still allows one to escape the coarseness and evil of the desire realm.
"Evil beasts and venomous insects" refers generally to sentient beings with dull afflictions (*mṛdu-kleśa*); *piśāca* demons refer briefly to sentient beings with sharp afflictions (*tīkṣṇa-kleśa*).
Both are able to attain dhyāna and be born in the form realm. *Piśāca* is translated here as "those who devour vital energy. △ Second.
[He understands] the causes from which the fire arises and the manner in which the fire spreads.
Because their merit is meager, they are oppressed by fire and mutually slaughter one another, drinking blood and devouring flesh.
The phrase "because their merit is meager" refers to the cause from which the fire arises; "oppressed by fire," and so forth, refers to the manner in which the fire arises.
This is the nature of the situation. Although there is no fierce flame within the hollows, there is still the affliction of heat;
this is like how, within the fourth dhyāna, although the evil dharmas of the desire realm are absent, there is nevertheless the subtle suffering of attachment to its flavor.

One gradually grows weary of the lower levels and rejoices in the higher ones, using the higher to subdue the lower—this is called mutual harm. Yet one remains silent and attached, like drinking blood, clinging merely to the branches and twigs.
The merit is like devouring meat. △ Third, the signs of being burned:
the jackals and their ilk have all already died beforehand, and various great evil beasts compete to come and devour them; foul-smelling smoke and flames fill the four directions.

The jackal is a metaphor for the craving of the desire realm; the various great predatory beasts that died previously represent the craving of the form realm, which is able to swallow the craving of the desire realm.
The four inversions and eight sufferings of the desire realm are like fierce flames, while the four inversions of the form realm are likened to foul-smelling smoke.
This is because they pervade the body, sensations, mind, phenomena, and the four great elements; therefore, it is said that they fill the four directions.

When centipedes, millipedes, and other venomous insects are scorched by fire, they scramble to flee their burrows;
the kumbhāṇḍa spirits seize and devour them.

Because one loathes the coarse obstruction of the form-aggregate (*rūpa-skandha*) as suffering and yearns for the immaterial realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*) as purity, excellence, and liberation, it is said [that this is the cause].
When burned by fire, they scramble to exit their holes; once they have reached the upper level, the lower objects of perception (*ālambana*) necessarily cease.

Therefore, it is said that the *kumbhāṇḍa* spirits seize and devour them as soon as they arrive. However, speaking generally, both the sharp and dull latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are capable of attaining the formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samādhi*).

Now, specifically regarding the dull dispositions, because they feel aversion toward the lower realms, they grasp for the upper ones; whereas the sharp dispositions, having realized the upper realms, cause [the lower] to cease.
This is the lowest [realm]. △ Second, explaining the signs of being burned:
Furthermore, the heads of various hungry ghosts (preta) are ablaze with fire; tormented by hunger, thirst, and heat, they wander about in agitation and distress.

Because the gods of the four formless heavens (ārūpyadhātu) likewise lack untainted food and drink (anāsrava-āhāra), although they dwell within the triple world (tridhātu), they are like hungry ghosts.
At the summit, one cannot escape being burned by impermanence, just as when fire burns upon the head; because there is no food of the True Path, one suffers from hunger;
because there is no drink of the aids to the Path, one suffers from thirst; still being oppressed by the eight subtle sufferings, one suffers from heat;
and because subtle afflictions still manifest, one suffers from distress, remaining within the cycle of birth and death without knowing the way of escape.
Therefore, it is said that they "wander about in panic and distress. These three verses conclude the analogy for the external affairs of the [formless] realm.
△ Fourth, a summary of the manifold difficulties:
"The house is thus; it is most terrifying, with poisonous harms, fires, and manifold disasters."
The general analogy in the first verse is concluded. △ Second, the verses on the specific analogies, which consist of three parts: first, the verse on the elder seeing the fire;

second, the verse on abandoning the stools and employing the carts; third, the verse on equally bestowing the great carts. The analogy of there being no falsehood is omitted from the summary. Now, the first part:
At that time, the owner of the house was standing outside the gate when he heard someone say:

"Your sons, having previously come into this house while playing, are young and ignorant, and they take delight in their amusements. Upon hearing this, the elder was startled and entered the burning house.
The first three lines of the verse describe that which sees; the next five lines describe that which is seen; and the final two lines describe the state of alarm and fear.

"Outside the gate" refers to the stage of the Dharmakāya. "Standing" means constantly harboring great compassion, desiring to save sentient beings, rather than remaining seated upon the throne of ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
The preceding text speaks of "seeing," whereas the current verse speaks of "hearing"; by substituting "hearing" for "seeing," the meaning is made manifest.
Seeing and hearing are non-dual. There are those who say that the Dharma is the Teacher of the Buddha; this refers to the dharma of samādhi.
If one enters samādhi, one is able to perceive the capacities [of beings]; because samādhi enables the Buddha to see, it is said that there is "hearing.
Regarding the statement that he previously entered this house by way of sport, there are two meanings: first, at the very moment of first generating the aspiration for enlightenment...

The phrase "named 'emerging'" refers to those who have not yet attained the stage of non-retrogression; because they still give rise to views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), it is said that they "enter this house while sporting.
Second, the nature of reality is fundamentally pure and is not a phenomenon of the triple world;

however, due to ignorance (*avidyā*), they give rise to conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and falsely perceive birth and death, hence it is said that they "enter this house while sporting. "The young children" refers to those in whom the great goodness has not yet taken root.
"Those who lack knowledge" refers to being entangled by delusion; "startled and entering" refers to the arising of great compassion in response.

△ Second, the verse on the analogy of discarding the bench and using the carriage, in two parts: first, the verse on discarding the bench; second, the verse on using the carriage. Regarding the first, the verse on discarding the bench:

in the previous section on the correspondence of the Dharma, only the gate of exhortation was correlated; here, only the gate of admonition is versified, which serves to mutually illustrate them both.
It is now appropriate to provide relief so that no one suffers from the conflagration; I shall admonish my sons by describing the many calamities:

how evil spirits and venomous insects spread a disastrous fire, and how various sufferings follow one another in an unceasing succession—snakes, vipers, and pythons, as well as yakṣas, kumbhāṇḍas, jackals, foxes, dogs, vultures, eagles, owls, hawks, and centipedes—all tormented by hunger and thirst.

This place of suffering and hardship is truly terrifying; how much more so when great fires are present! Although the sons are ignorant and have heard their father’s instructions, they still delight in play and do not cease.
The first four and a half verses praise the gate of admonition as being appropriate; the final verse praises what is not appropriate, which is precisely what is suitable.
This is intended to accommodate them through the Great Teaching. "Exhorting and instructing" refers to the gate of admonition, which explains the various calamities and hardships.

The phrase "evil spirits and venomous insects" establishes the general locus of what is burned; that is, the fires of disaster spreading among sentient beings of both sharp and dull faculties due to the ten afflictions (*kleśa*).
The three subsequent phrases collectively clarify the intensity and characteristics of the burning. The two verses beginning with "venomous snakes" provide a detailed explanation.

The various afflictions (*anuśaya*), both dull and sharp, that are being burned away no longer follow a fixed sequence; this phrase regarding "this place of suffering and difficulty" serves as an illustration (*upamā*) and conclusion.
Having already been unable to endure the causes and effects of the three realms, how much more so when the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) arise?
These sons, being ignorant, lack the capacity for the Mahāyāna and are unwilling to believe or accept it; since they are deeply attached to views and thoughts, they sport [in them].
The phrase "the play did not cease" implies that the father’s instructions failed to transform [the sons], thereby containing the sense of their transformation through the cessation of breath.
△ Second, the verse on the use of the carts, in three parts: first, the verse on the provisional application of the three carts; second, the verse praising the rarity of the three carts;
third, the verse on satisfying the sons' wishes (briefly omitting the verse on knowing the sons' prior disposition). Now, the first part.
At that time, the elder thought to himself: "My sons are like this; they only increase my grief and distress.
Now, in this house, there is not a single thing to be enjoyed, yet these sons are so immersed in their play that they do not accept my instructions and will surely be harmed by the fire.
He then reflected and devised various skillful means.

The first verse clarifies the intention of the preparatory application; the next verse clarifies the reason for employing the Lesser Vehicle—namely, that because they are attached to views and afflictions (*kleśa*), one must employ only the Lesser Vehicle.
The following two lines clarify the purpose of employing the Lesser Vehicle: if the Lesser Vehicle were not employed, both the Great and the Small would perish;
hence it says, "lest they be harmed by fire. The final two lines explicitly contemplate the employment of the Lesser Vehicle. △ Second, the verse of praise.
"These three vehicles are rare and marvelous.

I tell you, my children: I have various kinds of precious playthings and wonderful, excellent vehicles—ox-carts, deer-carts, and great bull-carts—which are now outside the gate. Come out, and I shall provide these vehicles for you."
"You may sport as you please according to your desires.

The first four lines of the verse praise the encouragement to turn [the wheel]; the next three lines praise the demonstration of turning; the phrase "Come forth, all of you" reiterates the praise for the encouragement to turn;
and the final verse praises the realization of turning. "I am able to create the chariot" refers to citing what one has personally realized.
And thus it was clearly shown to be without error. △ Third, the verse on the sons' fulfillment of their wishes:
Upon hearing these words regarding the various chariots, the sons immediately vied with one another to run out and reach the open space, thereby escaping all suffering and distress.

The first verse describes hearing the teaching; the wisdom of hearing rushes toward the verses. The second verse describes reflection and cultivation; they gallop forth from the verses. The third verse describes the realization of the Truth;
they arrive at the open space, which represents the stage of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa*). These two verses conclude the analogy of discarding the small stools for the use of chariots.
△ Third, the analogy of the equal bestowal of great chariots has four parts: First, the verse on the father seeing his sons escape the calamity and rejoicing; Second, the verse on the sons...

The analogy of seeking the carts consists of three verses; the analogy of bestowing great carts upon the sons consists of four verses; and the analogy of the sons’ joy at obtaining the carts follows. Now, for the first:
seeing that his sons have emerged from the burning house and are sitting upon lion thrones at the crossroads, the elder rejoices, saying:

I am now joyful; these sons of mine were so difficult to raise and bring forth, yet they were foolish, ignorant, and entered a perilous house filled with many venomous insects and terrifying goblins and spirits, while a great fire with fierce flames broke out on all four sides.
These sons, greedy for pleasure and play, have now been rescued by me and enabled to escape. Therefore, O people, I am now joyful.

"Staying at the crossroads" means clearly perceiving the Four Noble Truths. Regarding "sitting upon the lion throne," previously, when the householder was outside the gate, he still possessed anxiety and fear;
thus it is said he was "standing. Now, seeing that his son has escaped calamity, he finally attains fearlessness;
thus it is said he is "sitting. This is the same meaning as what is stated in the "Expedient Means" chapter: "Now I rejoice and am fearless. Furthermore, the former [state] was...
Because the great-capacity [beings] have not yet assembled, it is said "standing"; because the minor transformation has already been completed, it is said "seated.

"Standing" refers to secret benefit; "seated" refers to manifest benefit. As for the words of self-congratulation, it is because one has obtained the capacity of those to be transformed, and thus there is joy and fulfillment.
Since the teaching of two trillion Buddhas was by means of the Mahāyāna, it is said that they were "born" therein; since they were subsequently matured through the minor [vehicle], it is therefore...

It is said that he has been raised here for a long time and nurtured repeatedly; hence it is said, "it is extremely difficult. Because his roots of goodness are still slight, he is called "foolish and small.
Because he is shrouded by delusive confusion, he is called "ignorant. Being ignorant, he gives rise to turbidity; giving rise to turbidity, he invites karmic fruition;
hence it is said, "entering the house where there are many venomous insects. These two lines summarize the sharp and dull faculties within the three realms.
The two lines beginning with “Behold the great fire’s fierce flames” summarize the force of the eight sufferings within the three realms;
the two lines beginning with “And these sons” clarify how they give rise to views and attachments and are unable to extricate themselves;
the two lines beginning with “I have already rescued them” clarify the reason for his joy; and the two lines beginning with “Therefore, all these people” conclude the sentiment of his joy. △ Second.
The verse illustrates the parable of the sons seeking carts.
At that time, the sons, knowing their father was sitting at ease, all went to where he was and addressed him, saying:
"We pray you grant us the three kinds of precious carts as previously promised; when we come forth, you shall provide the three carts according to our desires."
Now is precisely the right time; please grant us what we seek.
To know that the father is sitting at ease is the very moment he is about to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Their requesting the chariots is the ritual of requesting the Dharma, identical to this present assembly. All have come together with hearts of reverence.
"O Buddha, we pray that you grant us three kinds of precious chariots" is a formal request for what was previously promised;

"as previously granted" refers to holding onto the past while doubting the present. Previously it was said that there truly are three vehicles according to our desires, but now that they have been dismissed as being merely expedient means, you must surely bestow something else upon us. △ Third, the verse on equally bestowing [chariots] upon all the sons.
The parable of the great chariots:
The elder was immensely wealthy, possessing many treasuries filled with gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, and agate.
He had constructed great chariots out of various precious materials, adorned and decorated with ornamental railings on all sides, with bells suspended from them and crisscrossed with golden cords.
A net of pearls was spread over it, with golden flower tassels hanging down everywhere; it was surrounded on all sides by various colorful ornaments.
Soft silk and cotton served as carpets and cushions, while exquisite, fine woolens worth hundreds of billions—fresh white and pure—were spread upon them.
There were also great white oxen, fat, strong, and of beautiful form.
He yokes precious chariots and provides them with numerous attendants and guards, bestowing such exquisite vehicles upon his sons.

The first two lines are an anticipatory verse (*kṣepaka*) explaining the reason for the chariots; the subsequent six and a half verses all constitute the main body of the verse, clearly elucidating the nature of the chariots;
and the final two lines are a retrospective verse summarizing the headings, omitting the mention of the "mind" (*citta*) and so forth. However, the "chariots" and the "sons" are indeed the "mind."
It must be clearly understood that a house containing objects is called a "storehouse" (*kū*), which can be used as a metaphor for the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) containing all dharmas;
the earth containing objects is called a "treasury" (*kośa*), which can be used as a metaphor for all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) containing all dharmas.

Furthermore, the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*) containing all dharmas can be metaphorically represented by a treasury, because in terms of principle (*tattva*), they are like the earth. Thus, the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) and the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) also contain all dharmas.
This may be illustrated by the analogy of a treasury, for cultivation is like building a house; in reality, within each and every dharma, all practices and all dharmas are complete.
Because every single practice contains all dharmas and all practices, it is called a "treasury," being manifold and greatly wealthy.
The various dharmas inherently present are collectively termed "many jewels," which arise from nature through cultivation.
To name it "the maker," "many practices," or "many vehicles" is to follow after manifold names;

to name it "each and every one" is because the substance of the vehicle is not without height and breadth, and thus it is named "Great. Furthermore, one must demonstrate the direction so that the practitioner may know:

cultivation is named "making" (creation), yet when cultivation is extinguished by its own nature, that which returns to the original existence is the very substance of the vehicle. The adornments below are all fully equipped for crossing over. First.
The four lines are explained as before. The two lines concerning the "pearl net" (*muktājāla*) are a verse on the "canopy of the gateways of compassion.
They are not merely one; just as there is a single pearl within each mesh of a net, so too do all the various gateways of compassion correspond to reality.
The two lines concerning the "various golden flower tassels" are a verse on the hanging of various flower tassels, thereby clarifying that [the teaching] pervades all capacities.
"Delightful" refers to the various colorful decorations; "brightly suspended in the place of transformation" indicates that the arrangements differ according to the occasion.

"Surrounded on all sides" signifies the suitability of gathering sentient beings, leaving nothing deficient. "Soft silks and cotton" corresponds to the character *wan* (婉) in the verse as the rugs and cushions;

"exquisite fine woolen cloth" corresponds to the character *xian* (筵) in the verse for the mats; and the four lines [of the following verse] correspond to the two characters *chongfu* (重敷), meaning "layered spreadings."
This indicates that the various meditations on phenomena are, in their essence, identical to the true mark (*dharmatā*);

because they differ from those of ordinary people and *śrāvakas* who are entangled in various afflictions, they are "fresh, white, pure, and supremely sublime. The "great white ox" is explained as before. "Retinue" refers to servants and attendants;
the rest can be understood accordingly. △ Fourth: A verse on the analogy of the sons obtaining the carts and rejoicing.

At that time, the sons were filled with joy and leaped for gladness as they rode these precious chariots, traveling through the four directions, sporting and delighting with sovereign ease and without obstruction.
Riding upon the wondrous wisdom of the Middle Way, they traveled horizontally through the fourfold gates and the fourfold Four Noble Truths, and traveled vertically through the forty [aspects].

This is the realization of the four ultimate virtues of permanence, bliss, self, and purity. The first verse, establishing the analogy, is concluded. △ Second, the second verse, the application to the Dharma, has two parts:
first, the verse applying the general analogy; second, the verse applying the specific analogies. Within the first part, there are four sections: first, the verse applying [the analogy of] the elder;
second, the verse applying [the analogy of] the five hundred people; third, the verse applying [the analogy of] the house; fourth, the verse applying [the analogy of] the fire.
[The Sūtra] begins. First:
"I, Śāriputra, am likewise the most honored among the assembly of sages and the father of the world.
Likewise, the first line of the verse combines with the position [of the title], while the second line of the verse combines with the name; this simultaneously extols his virtues.
[End of section]. △ Second, the verse summarizes the meaning of the five hundred people and their simultaneous attainment of the state of being the thirty sons:
"All sentient beings are my children; they are deeply attached to worldly pleasures and lack the heart of wisdom."
"All" refers to the three realms and five destinies; "thirty" are the factors of causal conditions, and "all" are the factors of direct causes.
△ Third, the verse encompasses the meaning of the entire household and one gate.
The three realms are without peace, like a burning house.
△ Fourth, the verse on the simultaneous outbreak of fire:
They are filled with manifold sufferings and are most terrifying; there are always such fires as birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, and affliction.
Blazing without ceasing.

The first two lines present the heading, the next two lines provide the explanation, and the final two lines offer the conclusion. This concludes the first verse, which synthesizes the general analogy.

II. The second section: The verses synthesizing the specific analogies, in four parts. First, the verse synthesizing the sight of the fire; second, the two verses synthesizing the abandonment of the bench and the use of the carriage.
The three verses together correspond to the granting of the great chariots; the four verses together correspond to the absence of falsehood. Now, for the first [section]:
"The Tathāgata has already departed from the burning house of the triple world and dwells in tranquil seclusion, securely settled in the forest wilds.
This triple world is now all mine, and the sentient beings therein are all my children. Yet, this place is now full of many afflictions and perils."
"I alone am able to provide protection.

The first verse corresponds to that which is able to see; it is precisely because [the Buddha] abides in the King Samādhi (*rāja-samādhi*), being tranquil yet constantly illuminating, that he is able to see.
The next six lines correspond to that which is seen. The final two lines correspond to the entry into alarm and fear.
The Dwelling. △ Second, the verse on the combined abandonment of the stool and the use of the carriage. First, the verse on the combined abandonment of the stool:
Although he was instructed and exhorted, he did not believe or accept it, because his deep attachment to and craving for various sensual desires were profound.

The first line of the verse is intended as a proposal; the second line states that it is not permitted, while the final two lines explain the reasons for this lack of faith and simultaneously contain the intention to cease the teaching. △ Second, the verse on the application of the vehicles.
By these skillful means, he preaches the three vehicles for them, causing all sentient beings to know the suffering of the triple world and revealing and expounding the supramundane path.
Among these sons, some whose minds are resolute attain the three types of supernormal knowledge (*traividyā*) and the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*),
becoming either pratyekabuddhas or non-retrogressive bodhisattvas.
The first two lines of the verse correspond to the section on what is appropriate; the following four lines correspond to the praise of the rarity of the three vehicles;
and the final six lines correspond to the fulfillment of the sons' wishes. If the mind is determined, these collectively correspond to the stage of rushing forth via the three vehicles.
The four lines beginning with "fully equipped" specifically correspond to the stage of competing to emerge via the three vehicles; the meaning of "non-retrogression" applies universally to both.
The first three teachings and two verses conclude the section on "Abandoning Various Vehicles. △ Third, the two verses conclude the section on "Equally Bestowing the Great Vehicle.
First, one verse concludes the "Equal Bestowal"; two verses conclude the "Joyful Response. The sections on "Avoiding Calamity" and "Seeking the Vehicle" are omitted from the verses.
Now, first:
"Śāriputra, for the sake of sentient beings, I have used this parable to teach the Single Buddha Vehicle.
If you all can believe and accept these words, you shall all attain the path of Buddhahood."
These preceding verses all concern my sons and others who [enter] the Mahāyāna, up to the point where they are brought to extinction by means of the Tathāgata’s own extinction;
this refers to those whose minds are in accord [with the Dharma].
This vehicle is subtle, wondrous, pure, and supreme; it is unsurpassed among all worlds and is what the Buddhas delight in.
All sentient beings should praise, make offerings to, and prostrate before this.
This verse describes that which is of a single characteristic and a single kind, praised by the noble ones, capable of producing pure,
wondrous, and supreme bliss, and is the essential body of the vehicle.

Having attained such a vehicle—consisting of immeasurable billions of powers (*bala*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and the other dharmas of a Buddha—this verse summarizes how I possess an immeasurable and boundless treasury of the Buddha-dharmas, such as wisdom, powers, and fearlessnesses, which serves as the reason for the assembly of the carts.
The first verse concludes the summary of the bestowal of these equal gifts. △ Second, the verse summarizes the joy.
He causes his sons to constantly sport day and night for kalpas, together with the assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas,

riding upon this precious vehicle straight to the site of enlightenment; by this cause and condition, if one seeks truthfully throughout the ten directions, no other vehicle exists, except for the skillful means of the Buddha.
The first seven lines correctly clarify that each attains the joy of the Mahāyāna Dharma; the subsequent four lines conclude by exhorting faith. Regarding "day and night":
initially attaining the Buddha’s knowledge and vision—the light of wisdom of the Middle Way—is like day; while residual ignorance remains, it is like night.
Attaining the wisdom of the Middle Way for oneself is like day, while entering birth-and-death through compassion is like night; one constantly practices these two dharmas.

Therefore, it is said that he "plays freely"; because he extensively transforms those of the three vehicles so they equally attain the One Vehicle, it is said that he "together with the bodhisattvas and the assembly of śrāvakas, mounts this precious vehicle.
Because this vehicle is perfect and sudden (*yuan-dun*) and lacks any circuitous characteristics, it is said that he "goes straight to the site of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
Next, the conclusion establishes that there is only the One and not three; the causes and conditions for this may be understood. These three verses together constitute the equal bestowal.
The section on the Great Vehicle concludes. △ Fourth, the verse on the absence of falsehood:
"Śāriputra, you and all these people are my children, and I am your father. For kalpas upon kalpas, you have been scorched by manifold sufferings;
I have rescued and delivered you all, causing you to emerge from the triple world. Although I previously said that you had attained *nirvāṇa*..."
They have merely exhausted birth and death, yet in reality they do not cease; what they ought to practice now is solely the wisdom of the Buddhas.

If there are bodhisattvas among this assembly who can listen with a single-minded focus to the true Dharma of all Buddhas, then all those beings whom the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, transform through skillful means are indeed bodhisattvas.
The first four lines first establish that the natural affection between father and son is the ultimate expression of human feeling;

this corresponds to the verse stating that the Tathāgata is likewise thus, being without falsehood. The next four lines correspond to the initial teaching of the three vehicles used to guide sentient beings.
The subsequent fourteen lines correspond to the statement that he subsequently delivers them by means of the Mahāyāna alone.
If there are people of limited wisdom who are deeply attached to craving and desire, for their sake he speaks of the Truth of Suffering;
these sentient beings rejoice and attain what they have never had before when the Buddha says that the Truth of Suffering is real and without deviation.

If there are sentient beings who do not know the root of suffering and are so deeply attached to the causes of suffering that they cannot abandon them even for a moment, for their sake he employs skillful means to speak of the path, [explaining] the cause of all sufferings.
With craving as its root, if craving is extinguished, there is no further basis for existence; the total cessation of all suffering is called the Third Truth, the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-satya).
Therefore, by practicing the Path (mārga), one becomes detached from the bonds of suffering and is said to have attained liberation.

Because these beings surpassed the verses and were unable to fully receive the Mahāyāna Dharma, the Buddha, through the power of skillful means (*upāya*), taught the Four Truths of arising and ceasing.

That which is the root of suffering is the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*); "skillfully speaking the Way" refers to the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) as spoken by skillful means; the remainder can be understood accordingly.
"By what means does this person attain liberation? Merely being free from falsehood is called 'liberation,' yet in reality they have not attained complete liberation.
The Buddha says that this person has not truly entered parinirvāṇa, because they have not yet attained the Unsurpassed Way.
It is not my intention that they should reach final extinction; for I am the Dharma King, sovereign over all dharmas, and I bring peace and security to sentient beings."
Therefore, he appears in the world.

This verse in praise extols that the Tathāgata possesses immeasurable power of wisdom and fearlessness, is a treasury of all dharmas, and is able to bestow the Mahāyāna Dharma upon all sentient beings.
"Only those who are free from delusion" means being free from the afflictions of views and thought.

"All who are liberated" refers to the Great Parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata; "those who have not yet truly entered extinction" refers to those for whom the death-and-rebirth of transformation still persists.
"The Unsurpassed Way" is the Knowledge of All Modes (sarvākārajñatā). The Dharma King appears in the world to bring peace to sentient beings;
having promised the Three and granted the One, how could there be any falsehood? This concludes the verse summary. The analogies explaining the four major sections are now complete.
In the first part of the middle section, the primary analogy opens up the three to reveal the one; this consists of a request and a response. Within the response, there are three parts:

first, the initiation; second, the actual analogy; and third, the conclusion of the analogy. Third, the exhortation to believe and the transmission of that belief. "Belief" refers to whether the Buddha’s teaching is to be understood or not.

"Exhortation" means to urge [the acceptance of] both these meanings—that it can be understood and that it cannot be understood. Therefore, it is called "exhortation to believe. The text is divided into two parts.
First, there is the brief presentation of two chapters, followed by their explanation. Now, for the first:
"O Śāriputra, I have proclaimed this Dharma-seal for the sake of benefiting the world;
wherever you travel, do not propagate it recklessly."
The first four lines indicate what is taught and what is not taught: "I have taught this Dharma-seal of the true mark (*dharmamudrā*) for the sake of benefiting the world;
if forty-odd years have not yet passed, it is not the time to teach it; if the five thousand [monks] have not yet regressed, then I do not teach it.
The next two lines indicate what may be communicated and what may not: "Do not propagate it recklessly," lest evil [occur].
To force those who are wicked to fall into suffering by preaching to them, while not misleading the virtuous so that they may attain happiness—this is what great compassion entails.
Thus, it is inappropriate to apply [the teaching] to the wicked, yet it is appropriate to apply it to the virtuous.
According to this passage, the Buddha’s entrustment to Śāriputra is identical to the entrustment of Candrasūryapradīpa to Prabhāsa; it reaches Śāriputra even before the Buddha.
His entry into parinirvāṇa was merely what those of limited capacity could perceive; that we are now able to hear the *Lotus Sūtra* has never ceased to be due to the power of Śāriputra’s propagation.
△ Second, the explanation is divided into two parts: first, explaining what can be spoken and what cannot be spoken;
second, explaining what can be understood and what cannot be understood. Now, the first part.
If there are those who hear this and rejoice in it, receiving it upon their heads, you should know that such persons are *avaivartika*.
If there are those who believe in and accept the Dharma of this sutra, these persons have already seen past Buddhas, have paid them respectful offerings, and have also heard this Dharma.
If anyone is able to believe what you have spoken, they shall see me, as well as you and the assembly of bhikṣus.
Together with all the bodhisattvas, this Lotus Sutra is taught for those of profound wisdom; those of shallow understanding, upon hearing it, will be bewildered and fail to comprehend it.
All śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are beyond the reach of its power. You, Śāriputra, have already gained entry into this sutra through faith;
how much more so the other śrāvakas, who enter by virtue of their faith in the Buddha’s words?
That this sūtra accords with one's own capacity for wisdom is not the case;
this correctly clarifies the manner in which the Tathāgata benefits the world. Generally speaking, this concerns the benefit across the three periods of time;
specifically, it concerns leading the two vehicles into faith. The first verse contemplates the present benefit and is spoken using the Sanskrit term *arhat*.

Now, regarding the passage "Only those who reach this state" and so forth: the next six lines explain the contemplation of past goodness; the subsequent six lines explain the contemplation of future goodness.
As the text below states, "If one has deep faith and understanding, one sees that the Buddha is always present on Vulture Peak"—this is precisely the meaning here.
The final four lines conclude the preceding section and introduce the following: the Tathāgata contemplates their depth.
The wisdom [of the Buddha] benefits those of the three periods of time; therefore, he teaches for their sake. If those of shallow understanding do not comprehend it, he does not teach them.
The final three verses clarify that the followers of the Two Vehicles enter by means of faith, as this is not within the scope of their own wisdom.

Since they truly attain the state of an Arhat only by believing the Buddha’s words, even though their power of wisdom is weak, they may still be taught. This applies even to the five thousand who possessed overweening pride.
If they are human Buddhas, one does not preach for them. △ Second, explaining what is accessible and what is inaccessible; this has two parts:

first, regarding the gate of great compassion, one must not preach to those who do evil; second, regarding the gate of great kindness, one should preach for those who are good people. Now, the first part.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, do not preach this sutra to those who are arrogant, indolent, or possessed of the view of self.

Do not preach it to worldlings of shallow understanding who are deeply attached to the five desires, for they will not understand it upon hearing it. If a person does not believe and instead slanders this sutra, they sever the seed of the Buddha in all the worlds.
The teaching expounded in this sutra discusses exclusively the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*), for the Seal of True Reality universally seals all phenomena;

thus, even the slightest goodness or subtle understanding becomes integrated with the conditions and causes [of enlightenment]. However, those whose afflictions of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *vicikitsā*) are heavy will incur two faults upon hearing it:
first, lack of faith; second, erroneous interpretation. Regarding "lack of faith," because of their shallow intelligence, they cling to the provisional and doubt the ultimate.

Regarding those who provide erroneous interpretations, because they rely solely on the literal text, they directly equate the eternal, blissful, self, and pure (*nitya-sukha-ātma-śubha*) as conceived by non-Buddhists with this perfect principle, claiming there is no difference between them. This is like an old physician who exclusively uses poisonous milk.
These two errors are both termed "slander" of this sutra; they sever the Buddha-seed in the world. Why is this? Because this sutra [teaches] through conditions...

To realize this is to possess the seed of Buddhahood; yet, if one clings to expedient means while doubting the ultimate reality, one will not believe that even minor good deeds can lead to Buddhahood—this severs the worldly *pratyaya-hetu* (causal condition) seed and likewise severs the *jñāna-hetu* (wisdom cause) seed.

If one erroneously interprets "permanence and bliss," one fails to distinguish between the quality of milk—this severs the worldly *jñāna-hetu* seed and furthermore, to claim that delusion itself is [enlightenment]...
The activity of *prajñā* is itself liberation; one no longer cultivates various wholesome dharmas, and furthermore, one severs the causes and seeds of conditions.

Now, the first verse concerns the gravity of the afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava*), the second verse concerns the gravity of the afflictions of thought (*bhāvanā-āsrava*), and the final verse summarizes their faults.
Or again, there may be those who frown and harbor doubts; you should now listen as I describe the retribution for the sins of such people.

Whether the Buddha is in the world or has entered parinirvāṇa, if there are those who slander such a sūtra as this, or who, upon seeing one who reads, recites, copies, or upholds it, treat them with contempt, hatred, and jealousy, harboring resentment within their hearts—you must now listen further to the retribution for the sins of these individuals when their lives come to an end.
They enter the Avīci Hell and remain there for a full kalpa; when that kalpa ends, they are reborn again, continuing in this manner through countless kalpas.
Upon emerging from hell, they fall among the animals as dogs or jackals, their forms emaciated, dark-skinned, and afflicted with scabies and leprosy;
they are tormented by those who touch them and are further despised and loathed by humans, constantly suffering from hunger and thirst until their flesh and bones are withered away.
In life they suffer bitter agony, and at death they are struck by tiles and stones; because they have severed the seed of the Buddha, they receive such retributive punishment.
Some are born as camels or among donkeys, their bodies constantly burdened with heavy loads and further afflicted by whips and lashes; they think only of water and grass, knowing nothing else.
Because they slandered this sutra, they incur such offenses. Others become jackals that enter villages, their bodies covered in scabs and sores.
Furthermore, having lost one eye, he was beaten and pelted by various children, undergoing all manner of agonizing pain that sometimes even led to death.
Having died there, he further received the body of a python; his form was vast, measuring five hundred yojanas in length.
He was deaf and witless, lacking feet, crawling about on his belly, and being bitten and eaten by small insects. Day and night he suffered without any respite.
Because they slander this sutra, they incur such offenses as these: even if they obtain human birth, their faculties will be dull and dark;
they will be short, ugly, hunchbacked, lame, blind, or deaf; whatever they say, people will not believe or accept; their breath will always stink; they will be possessed by malevolent spirits;

they will be poor, lowly, and base, serving at the beck and call of others; they will suffer from many ailments and emaciation, having no one to rely upon; and though they may seek the company of others, they will remain alienated.
People do not take heed; even if they seem to have attained something, they soon forget and lose it.

If they practice the way of medicine, treating illness according to prescriptions, they may instead increase another's ailment or even cause death. If they themselves fall ill, there is no one to provide relief;
even if they take excellent medicine, their condition worsens. If others commit acts of rebellion, plunder, robbery, or theft, such people will suffer the calamities resulting from these crimes.
Such a person of sin shall never see the Buddha, the King of Sages, preaching the Dharma to transform and teach beings.
Such a person of sin will always be born in difficult circumstances—mad, deaf, and mentally deranged—and shall never hear the Dharma for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
From birth to birth, they will be deaf and mute with impaired faculties, constantly dwelling in hell as if it were a pleasure garden, while other evil realms become their abode.
Just as one’s own home has camels, donkeys, pigs, and dogs as its inhabitants, so too does one who slanders this sutra incur such offenses.
If they should obtain a human birth, they will be adorned with deafness, blindness, muteness, poverty, and various misfortunes;
with dropsy, consumption, scabies, leprosy, carbuncles, and abscesses as their clothing, their bodies shall always be foul-smelling, filthy, and impure.
Deeply attached to the view of self, their anger and lust increase and blaze forth; they do not distinguish between humans and beasts, and because they slander this sutra, they incur such offenses.
I tell you, Śāriputra, that if one were to speak of the offenses of those who slander this sutra, they would not be exhausted even at the end of an eon.
For these reasons, I say to you: do not preach this sutra among people who lack wisdom.
This section fully elucidates the evil retribution summoned by slandering the sūtras, serving as a warning not to propagate them recklessly. Question:
If slandering the sūtras gives rise to sin, does it mean that the sūtra itself is the cause of that sin? Answer: The Buddha’s preaching of the sūtras was solely for the purpose of generating merit;

those who are deluded and do not believe incur the calamity of sin themselves. It is like the Four Great Elements, which are fundamentally intended to nourish all sentient beings, yet the foolish commit offenses against them.

One merely brings harm upon oneself. Now, the Buddha has repeatedly and earnestly admonished us, commanding that we propagate the Dharma while observing the capacities of others, and further ensuring that they know how to avoid suffering;
this may truly be called ultimate great compassion. The first section, concerning the gate of great compassion, concludes with the instruction not to speak of evil.
△ Second, concerning the gate of great kindness, one should speak for the sake of good people. This is further divided into two parts: first, explaining the five pairs.
The characteristics of virtuous persons may be proclaimed; two summaries may be stated. First:
if there are those with sharp faculties, clear wisdom, extensive learning, and strong memory who seek the Buddha-way—such persons may be taught this.
Furthermore, if a person has previously seen hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas, planted various roots of goodness, and possesses a firm and resolute deep resolve.
It is for such persons that one may preach this.
Those with sharp faculties and strong memory who see the Buddha in the present are those who have planted roots of goodness in the past; this constitutes the pair of the present and the past.
If there is a person who is diligent and constantly cultivates a mind of loving-kindness, not begrudging even their own body or life, then for such a person one may preach it.

If there is a person who is reverent and free from dualistic thoughts, who has distanced themselves from all the vulgar and foolish, and dwells alone in the mountains or marshes—for such a person one may preach it.

Cultivating loving-kindness is to have compassion for those below; showing reverence is to honor those above. Furthermore, through diligent cultivation of loving-kindness, one does not stagnate in nirvana—thereby remaining apart from all ordinary fools—and does not stagnate in saṃsāra. This is the pair of merit and wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, if you see someone who has abandoned evil associates and draws near to virtuous friends,
such a person may be taught this. If you see a son of the Buddha who maintains pure precepts like a polished,
clear pearl and seeks the Mahāyāna sūtras, such a person may be taught this.

Abandoning evil and befriending the good is called "shame" (*hrī*) when seeking renown externally; guarding the precepts like a precious pearl is called "modesty" (*apatrāpya*) when protecting oneself internally.
This pair constitutes shame and modesty.
If a person is free from anger, upright, gentle, and flexible, always compassionate toward all beings, and respectful toward all Buddhas—such a person [is endowed with these qualities].

One may then explain it to those sons of the Buddha who, amidst the great assembly, preach the Dharma with an unobstructed eloquence using various causes, conditions, parables, and expressions, with a pure mind; to such persons as these, one may indeed explain it.
Being upright and sincere while revering the Buddha is the practice for oneself; teaching the Dharma through parables is the transformation of others—this constitutes the pair of self and other.
If there is a bhikṣu who seeks the Dharma in all four directions for the sake of omniscience, receiving it with palms joined at his crown and solely delighting in its upholding and retention...
To those who would not accept even a single verse from any other sutra, but only from the Mahāyāna scriptures—such persons may be taught.
Just as a person with a sincere heart seeks the relics of the Buddha, so too they seek these sutras; having obtained them, they receive them upon the crown of their head.
Such a person no longer aspires to seek other sutras, nor do they ever think of the texts of the non-Buddhists. To such a person, one may indeed teach.

Seeking the Dharma in all four directions is the beginning of requesting instruction; receiving it upon the crown of one’s head and practicing it with single-minded devotion is the end of relying upon it.
This constitutes a pair of beginning and end. Question: The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that to accept one [teaching] while rejecting others is called a demonic activity.
Why, then, can it now be said that one may even refuse to accept a single verse from other sutras? Answer: If one remains stuck in explanations that follow mere personal sentiment, then...
To receive [the teaching] as one alone and not as anything else is called the work of Māra;

however, if one upholds the discourse that reveals and clarifies [the truth], then because there is nothing other than the one, one can thereby unify the one with the rest, and thus becomes a vessel for the Dharma.
This concludes the initial clarification of the characteristics of the five pairs of virtuous persons. △ Second, the summary of what may be taught.
"Śāriputra, I tell you that those who seek the Buddha-way through these signs would not reach the end of them even after the exhaustion of kalpas;
such persons as these are able to believe and understand. You should preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for them."
The faithful who believe are exceedingly numerous; I have briefly cited ten aspects merely to demonstrate the method for its circulation.
This concludes the second section, the Parable, specifically the primary analogy that opens the three to reveal the one.

△ The preceding explanation of the "Parable Chapter" is concluded; next, the "Chapter on Faith and Understanding" (Adhimukty-adhikāra) is explained. Regarding the fourth chapter, the "Chapter on Faith and Understanding":

faculties have their sharpness or dullness, delusions have their thickness or thinness, teachings have their direct or analogical exposition, and awakenings have their priority or posteriority. As the text says:
World-Honored One, in the past when you had been teaching the Dharma for a long time, I was seated among the assembly;
my body was weary and exhausted, and I thought only of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. I did not give rise to a single thought of joy or interest in the Bodhisattva teachings.
