His father, filled with anxiety and longing, searched for him in four directions. The following verses describe how he eventually encountered his father at the city.
First: "For example, a young boy, immature and ignorant, abandoned his father and fled, wandering far away to another land and traveling through various countries for more than fifty years."
Wandering through various countries is like transmigrating through the three realms; being thus for over fifty years is like having fully experienced the six destinies.
△ Second, the verse on seeking the son and desisting midway:
His father, filled with anxious concern, searched in all four directions; having grown weary from his quest, he settled in a certain city and built a house and dwelling.

He delighted himself with the five desires; his family was immensely wealthy, possessing abundant gold, silver, tridacna shells, agate, pearls, lapis lazuli, elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, palanquins, carriages, fields, and estates, as well as numerous servants and subjects.

His income and profits extended throughout other countries, and there was no place where his merchants and traders did not exist. Surrounded by a multitude of thousands of millions of billions, they paid him reverence.
He is constantly cherished by the king, and the ministers and noble clans all revere him together;
because of these various circumstances, those who come and go are numerous, and he possesses such great wealth and power.
Seeking in the four directions is like contemplating the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*) to find sentient beings who are ready to be saved.

Coming to rest in a single city is like the "Nirvana with remainder" (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*), which is the land of skillful means (*upāya*). Building a house of compassion and kindness within a dwelling of intrinsic emptiness (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*) and enjoying the sublime sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) that accord with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) is due to the Buddha’s abiding in skillful means; this is precisely the Land of Real Reward (*vipāka-bhūmi*).
This is because it is the very realm of tranquil light (*śāntaprabhāsa*). The "King" is a metaphor for the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) and the Body of Self-Enjoyment (*svasaṃbhogakāya*);
since this [Bodhisattva] is a supreme emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), he is cherished by the King. The "ministers and noble clans" are metaphors for the Mahāsattvas of the Dharma-body;

the "great crowds coming and going" are metaphors for the Bodhisattvas of the various lands who come and go to hear the Dharma. △ Third, the verse transcends [the previous section] to describe the father’s anxious concern.

Now that I am advanced in years, my anxiety for my son increases; day and night I think only of how the time of my death is approaching, and as my foolish son has abandoned me for more than fifty years, what shall become of the treasures and goods in my storehouses?
△ Fourth, the verse summarizing the encounter at the father’s city:
At that time, the impoverished son sought food and clothing, traveling from town to town and from kingdom to kingdom; sometimes he obtained something and sometimes he obtained nothing.
Starving and emaciated, with sores and scabs breaking out upon his body, he gradually made his way until he reached the city where his father resided.

Traversing the twelve bases (*āyatana*) and eighteen elements (*dhātu*) in order to seek the right path and its auxiliaries, it is said that one goes "from village to village" and "from country to country.
In terms of mundane wholesome states (*sāsrava-kuśala*), there may be something gained; in terms of supramundane wholesome states (*anāsrava-kuśala*), there may be nothing gained.
Lacking the Dharma-food of the Mahāyāna, one suffers from hunger; lacking great power and function, one is emaciated.
Lacking great merit, one becomes emaciated and deluded regarding the principles of the Truths; giving rise to views and afflictions as the substance [of this state], sores and scabs begin to form.
The first verse, concerning the father and son losing each other, is concluded. △ Second, the verse on the father and son meeting. Part One: The verse on the son seeing the father.
Part Two: The verse on the father seeing the son. Now, the first.

Through successive shifts of labor, he eventually arrived at his father’s house. At that time, the elder was within his gate, seated upon a lion throne beneath a great jeweled canopy, surrounded by his kinsmen and attended by his retinue.
Some were calculating gold, silver, and precious objects, while others were recording the accounts of income and expenditure on written ledgers.
When the impoverished son saw his father’s magnificent wealth and majestic dignity, he thought him to be a king.
If a king or others become terrified and wonder why he has come here, he reflects to himself:
"If I remain for long, I may be coerced or forced into labor. Having thought this, he flees and seeks out a poor neighborhood, intending to go there to seek employment.
The first two lines of the verse describe the cause for seeing his father; the subsequent ten lines describe the appearance of the father.
The preceding section clarified that the place where he saw his father was by the side of the gate; the present statement that "the elder was inside his gate" thus includes the location as well.

Because the Bodhisattva’s practices and vows frequently clarify specific details and numbers, the term "calculating" is used here; this is annotated to extensively illustrate what was previously stated briefly.
Bestowing the prediction [of enlightenment] serves as the record, and the Four Great Vows serve as the bond; practicing these constitutes the commentary.

Next, regarding the fourteen lines beginning with "The impoverished son sees his father," it can be understood that they express the arising of fear and avoidance. II. Verses on the Father Seeing the Son:
These verses only describe the act of seeing the son and the immediate recognition upon seeing him; they do not describe the father’s joy or the fulfillment of his wishes.
At that time, the elder was upon his lion throne; seeing his son from afar, he recognized him silently.
The two verses on the meeting of father and son are concluded. III. The three verses on the pursuit and enticement. First, the verse on the bystander’s pursuit.
Second, the verse on the two men’s enticement. Now, the first.
He immediately commanded his messengers to pursue and seize the impoverished son, who, startled and crying out in confusion, fell prostrate on the ground, thinking, "This man has seized me;

he will surely kill me. Of what use are food and clothing that have brought me to this state? The elder, knowing his son was foolish, narrow-minded, and inferior, did not believe his words nor recognize him as his father.

△ Second, two verses on the two types of people who entice [the laborers]. First, one verse on hiring them for work and instructing them collectively; second, one verse on instructing them in their work and leading them according to their intentions. Now, the first:
He immediately employs a further expedient and dispatches another person—one who is blind in one eye, short and ugly, and lacking in majesty—and says to him: "You should speak to them thus..."

He said, "I shall hire you to remove all manner of filth and excrement, and I will pay you double the wage. When the impoverished son heard this, he was filled with joy and followed him to clear away the filth and clean the rooms.

The one-eyed man is a metaphor for partial emptiness and limited wisdom; the short and stunted man is a metaphor for failing to exhaustively reach the source of the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*). "Ugly" refers to the lack of such realization.
"Those who are narrow-minded and lacking the adornment of the ten thousand virtues, because they do not possess the four fearlessnesses, have no majesty;

because they do not possess permanence, bliss, self, and purity, they have no pure virtue. 'Purifying all the rooms' refers to purifying the rooms of the six sense organs and the houses of the five aggregates.
△ Second, the verse on the instruction to act.

The elder constantly observed his son from the window; seeing that his son was foolish and inferior, delighting in menial tasks, the elder put on tattered, filthy clothes, took up a dung-removal tool, and went to where his son was.
Adopting a tactful approach, he spoke to him, urging him to work diligently, saying:
"I shall increase your wages, provide oil for your feet, ensure you have sufficient food and drink, and give you thick, warm bedding. Thus he spoke with such earnest words.
"You should diligently apply yourself and use gentle words, as if toward my own son.

The first two lines of the verse praise the provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) that has long desired to provide what is appropriate; the next two lines praise the long-standing knowledge that the minor teachings (*hīnayāna-dharma*) were his cherished playthings;
the following four lines praise the long-standing knowledge that he must praise the three vehicles; and the final ten lines praise the long-standing knowledge [of the ultimate truth].

"Appropriately, you should receive and practice this. These words form a four-line verse on the Four Foundations of Mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). "Exert yourself diligently" forms a three-line verse on the Four Right Efforts (*samyakpradhāna*).

"Since I have increased your value" consists of six lines on the Four Bases of Psychic Power (*ṛddhipāda*). As for "anointing the feet with oil," oil can dispel wind, which is a metaphor for meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*);
furthermore, being able to walk upon water is a metaphor for supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). "Food and drink" refers to rice, flour, salt, vinegar, and condiments.
The metaphor of a thick and warm seat illustrates the practice of contemplating and cultivating the various *dhyānas*.
Such words of exhortation as "You should exert yourself diligently" and "O man, you should constantly perform this [practice]" serve to summarize what was stated previously.

Furthermore, with gentle words such as "If you are like my son," he then recites three verses beginning with "Be well-composed in mind," which treat the five faculties (*indriya*), the five powers (*bala*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*).

The pursuit and enticement are concluded. △ Fourth, the verse on receiving and entrusting the family estate has two parts: first, the verse on receiving the estate; second, the verse on entrusting the estate.
Now, the first:
The elder, possessing wisdom, gradually led him in and out for twenty years, having him manage the household affairs and showing him the gold and silver.

Whether pearls, crystal, or other such items were brought in or out, he was made to know of them all; yet, while staying outside the gate in a thatched hut, he would think of his own poverty, reflecting, "I have no such things.

The first two lines praise the mutual trust in their inner dispositions; the following six lines praise receiving the command and taking charge of the affairs; and the final four lines [praise his humble state].

The verse states that there was no expectation of gain; "twenty years" refers to the teaching for Bodhisattvas to sever the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) beyond the realms, which differs from the previous twenty years of removing filth.
II. Verse on Entrusting the Task. Part One: Verse on the Actual Entrustment of the Task. Part Two:
Verse on the Joy of Receiving the Entrustment. Now, the first part.
The father, knowing that his son’s mind had gradually become expansive, desired to bestow wealth upon him.
He immediately assembled his kinsmen, the king, ministers, kṣatriyas, and householders, and addressed this great assembly: "This is my son who abandoned me and went abroad fifty years ago.
It has now been twenty years since I saw my son return. Long ago, in a certain city, I lost this son; I have wandered about searching for him everywhere."
He then came here, and all my houses and people were entirely entrusted to him, to be used as he pleased.
Regarding the "twenty years," it may refer to twenty years of practicing the path of the Two Vehicles (*dviyāna*) oneself;

or, it may mean that only after the period of clearing away filth has passed is one called a "son," thus designating twenty years by the time spent teaching others and performing manual labor; or, it may be interpreted according to...
The names of the two vehicles [are used] for twenty years. △ Second, a verse on obtaining the entrustment with joy:

The son reflects that formerly he was poor and his aspirations were lowly; now, from his father, he has obtained great treasures as well as houses and all manner of wealth and property, feeling immense joy at having attained what he had never experienced before.

The first verse concludes the establishment of the analogy. △ Second, the verses on the application of the Dharma (the dharma-yojanā) have three parts: first, the verse on the application of losing the marks and seeing the marks;
second, the verse on the application of pursuing and inducing; third, the verse on the application of receiving and entrusting the family estate. Now, the first [part].
The Buddha is likewise aware that I delight in the small;
because I delight in the small, I have been separated from my father, yet the Buddha, knowing me, has come to meet his son.
△ Second, the verse on the reunion and enticement.

It has never been said that "you shall become Buddhas," yet it is said that we have attained the various outflows-free states (*anāsrava*) and achieved the status of disciples of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) Śrāvakas.
The first two lines of the verse correspond to the retrospective [explanation], while the subsequent four lines correspond to the inducement. △ Third, the verses correspond to the entrustment.

Regarding the two sections on inheriting the family business: first, the two verses on receiving the mandate to inherit the family business; second, the two verses on having no desire for acquisition.
Of these, the first [section] consists of: first, the verse on receiving the mandate to take charge; second, the verse on having no longing in the mind. Now, the first.
The Buddha commanded us, saying, "Explain the supreme path; those who practice this shall attain Buddhahood.
Receiving the Buddha’s instruction, we, as great bodhisattvas, have used various causes and conditions, diverse parables, and manifold expressions to explain the unsurpassed path.
When the sons of the Buddhas hear this Dharma from us, they contemplate it day and night and practice it with diligent effort; at that time, the Buddhas—
He then bestowed upon him the prediction: "In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood.
While all Buddhas expound the secret treasury of the Dharma solely for the sake of Bodhisattvas by manifesting its actual reality, they did not explain this essential truth to me."
The synthesis of the synthesis: the body of the teaching on entrusting the task is now merely summarized in verse as the synthesis of entrusting the task.
The "Supreme Path" is the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*. II. Verse on the Synthesis of the Mind Being Without Hope or Grasping. This passage is extensive and is further divided into three parts:

first, citing the analogy to generally clarify the absence of hope or grasping; second, explaining the meaning of being without hope or grasping; third, concluding the section on being without hope or grasping.
First: Just as that impoverished son, though he drew near to his father, had no desire to take possession of the various goods even though he knew of them;
so too it is with us: although we speak of the treasure-house of the Buddha-dharma, we ourselves lack any aspiration for it.
△ Second, the explanation of the intention of having no aspiration for acquisition:
We consider our own internal cessation to be sufficient; we understand only this matter and believe there is nothing further.
Thus, when we hear of purifying Buddha-lands or teaching and transforming sentient beings, we feel no joy or delight whatsoever. Why is this? Because all dharmas...
"All things are entirely empty and quiescent—without arising and without ceasing, without great and without small, without outflows and unconditioned.

Contemplating thus, they do not give rise to joy or pleasure, thinking: "For a long night we have been without craving or attachment toward the Buddha’s wisdom, and no longer possessed of any aspiration for it;
yet we considered our own [limited] dharmas to be the ultimate. For a long night we have practiced the dharma of emptiness and attained liberation from the three realms."

Regarding the affliction of suffering, those who dwell in their final body and attain *nirvāṇa with remainder*, having been taught by the Buddha and attained the Way so that it is not in vain, have thereby repaid the Buddha’s kindness.
The first verse is due to possessing small abandonment, and thus does not aspire to great abandonment; the next verse is due to possessing small wisdom.
Therefore, there is no delight in great wisdom. The next two verses explain and establish the minor abandonment; the following one and a half verses explain and establish the minor wisdom;
the subsequent one and a half verses re-explain the minor abandonment; and the final verse re-explains the minor wisdom. △ Third, the conclusion on the absence of longing for attainment.
Although we have expounded the Bodhisattva teachings for the sake of the sons of the Buddhas in order to seek the path to Buddhahood, we have never had any aspiration or delight in these teachings;
yet the Teacher, seeing that he disregarded us, observed our hearts and from the beginning did not encourage us or speak of the actual benefits therein.
Because I lacked aspiration and desire, the Teacher abandoned me; this was due to his observation of my mind, not because he was stingy regarding the Great Dharma.
The first verse concludes the section on receiving the task. II. The second part, the verse on receiving the family inheritance, has two sections:
first, the verse on receiving the task; second, the verse on rejoicing. Regarding the first: the initial six lines cite the analogy, and the subsequent six lines provide the formal explanation.
It is the same. Just as a wealthy elder, knowing his son’s inferior disposition, uses the power of skillful means to soften and subdue his mind before finally entrusting him with all his wealth,
so too does the Buddha manifest rare and marvelous events, knowing those who delight in the Lesser Vehicle, and through the power of skillful means [guides them].
Having tamed their minds, he then teaches them great wisdom.
△ Second, the verse on shared joy:
"Today we have obtained what we never had before; it was not what we previously hoped for, yet now we have attained it ourselves, just like that impoverished son."
"O World-Honored One who has attained immeasurable treasures, we have now attained the Way and realized the fruit; regarding the untainted Dharma, we have attained the eye of purity.
For a long night we have upheld the Buddha’s pure precepts, and only today do we receive their retribution.
Within the Dharma of the Dharma-King, we have long cultivated the Brahma-faring life, and now we have attained the untainted, unsurpassed, great fruit. We are now truly śrāvakas."
By means of the sound of the Buddha-way, we cause all to hear; we are now true Arhats, who among all the worlds—among devas, humans, Māras, and Brahmās—should universally receive offerings.
Those who attain the Way attain the path of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*); those who attain the fruit partially attain the unsurpassed bodhi of the Mahāyāna;
those who practice the fruit of the outflow-free dharma (*anāsravadharma*) do not leak into the two extremes via the Middle Way;

and those who obtain the pure eye partially attain the Buddha-eye—this clarifies the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Because pure precepts constitute the true conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*), one attains wondrous retribution.

Because the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) constitutes the true cause of realization, one attains the wondrous fruit; that which is known and seen is precisely the merit of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), the rational nature of the True Cause.
Those who are truly Śrāvakas and true Arhats occupy the stage of the first *bhūmi* of the Perfect Teaching;

they are "true in one part" yet "true in all parts," meaning they are partially realizing the Three Virtues (*triguṇa*) of the ten realms. This is merely an opening up from the perspective of their original station.
Because it is manifest, they are called Śrāvaka-Arhat. The initial long prose and the repeated verses have finished correctly presenting the attainment of understanding.
△ Next, thirteen verses praise the profound kindness of the Buddha.
The World-Honored One, with great kindness, has out of compassion taught and benefited us through this rare occurrence; who could ever repay such a debt over immeasurable billions of kalpas?
Even by providing for our hands and feet, prostrating with our heads at his feet, and making every possible offering, none could repay it.

Furthermore, even if one were to carry him upon the crown of one’s head or on both shoulders for as many kalpas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, serving him with the utmost reverence and the finest delicacies—
Even if one were to use immeasurable precious robes, various bedding, diverse medicinal decoctions, ox-head sandalwood,
and all manner of rare jewels to construct stūpas and temples, and spread precious robes upon the ground— performing such acts of offering for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges—
one still could not repay the Buddhas’ rare, immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable power of great supernormal faculties.
The King of all dharmas—taintless and unconditioned—is able to endure such matters for those of inferior capacity.
For ordinary people who grasp at signs, he teaches according to what is appropriate. The Buddhas have attained supreme mastery over the Dharma;

knowing the various inclinations and aspirations of all sentient beings, as well as their mental capacities and what they are able to bear, they teach the Dharma through immeasurable parables, in accordance with each sentient being.
Furthermore, having discerned through various deliberations and distinctions whether the roots of goodness from past lives have matured or not,
he teaches the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) as three vehicles according to what is appropriate.

The Great Benevolence of the World-Honored One is such that the Buddha, from the beginning, established compassion to extract beings from the suffering of the six realms and grant them the bliss of the four noble ones.

The ten dharmas universally pervade the four great vows; this is the Tathāgata’s chamber. Second is the Tathāgata’s practice: practicing the bodhisattva path to instruct, transform, benefit, and gladden others.
[He said: "In the past, you taught me the Mahāyāna; though I may have forgotten it in the interim, my wisdom and vows have not been lost.
This is the Tathāgata’s chamber—cooling and warm—wherein great compassion bestows happiness; this is the third kindness. When sentient beings encounter suffering, he regards them as his own children.
The Buddha observes the appropriate timing, like a calf following its mother, fully practicing the six pāramitās to benefit sentient beings.
This is the chamber of the Tathāgata, which wards off cold and obstructs heat; with great compassion, he uproots suffering.

Although the four Buddhas, having attained enlightenment, ought to enjoy the bliss of quiescent non-action, they conceal their spiritual virtues to employ the Dharma that accords with the preferences of the impoverished. [The five precepts and the ten...]
First, to sprinkle cool water on his face to cause him to regain consciousness is the grace of the Buddha’s robe that wards off the heat of greed.
Fifth, appearing as an old bhikṣu to approach him through skillful means and provide him with a day’s wage is the grace of the Buddha’s robe that removes the cold of views and the heat of craving.
Sixth, after this has passed, causing him to realize the nature of his own mind through trust, and then rebuking and censuring him to induce shame, is [the grace of the Buddha’s robe].
The small aspiration for the great canopy is the Buddha’s robe that conceals all ugliness; this is my seventh debt of gratitude.
To entrust me with the family estate, the gold, silver, and treasuries, making me fully aware of them all, is the Buddha’s robe that provides me with adornment; this is my eighth debt of gratitude.

To assemble my kinsmen, establish my status as his son, and hand over the family estate so that the unsurpassed treasury of jewels is obtained without seeking, is the Tathāgata’s seat; this is my [ninth] debt of gratitude.
Having sat upon the seat, his body and mind became serene and he attained a state of profound peace and stability.
By means of the sound of the Buddha-way, he caused all to hear, becoming universally worthy of offerings among devas and humans.

This is what is meant by the Tathāgata’s seat, which enables him to fulfill his own practice and transform others; the grace borne upon his two shoulders is such that it cannot be repaid even by equals. This is called the "Ox."
Regarding "head-sandalwood," the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that it comes from Mount Vimala; if used to anoint the body, fire cannot burn it.
Herein, one should understand the three aspects of the room, the three robes, and the four seats. Because the room provides the robes, there is the grace of protection and nourishment.
Because the room contains the seats, it fulfills the function of bestowing refuge. The seats rely upon the robes and the room to benefit both oneself and others.

By establishing the practice of wearing robes and using provisional seats and rooms, the principle of the beginning and the end is made manifest; therefore, these three meanings together constitute the Great Benevolence.
Since the *Zhenglun* (Treatise on the Correct) states that the benevolence received is difficult to repay, one must not simply explain it as being repaid through death.
This concludes the second section of the "Two Parables" within the "Exposition of the Middle Capacity."

Volume Three, Part One.
△ The explanation of the "Parable of the Faith and Understanding" is concluded; next is the explanation of the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs."
The Parable of the Herbs, Chapter Five.

Herein, although mountains, rivers, clouds, and rain are all present, the title is designated solely by "herbs" because the earth is that which gives birth, the clouds and rain are that which moisten, and the herbs are that which are born and moistened;
thus, both that which is born and that which is moistened are universally applicable.

If one follows the meaning as described by the Tathāgata, then the entire earth is nothing but medicine; yet, from the perspective of Kāśyapa and others who are able to grasp the meaning, they are precisely the "medium-grade herbs.
This is like how all mundane wholesome dharmas can eliminate evil, yet the untainted (anāsrava) is supreme.

Now, among this assembly of the untainted, the four great disciples serve as analogies for those who grasp the Buddha’s analogy; they have profoundly harmonized with the Sage’s mind, and thus the Buddha praised them, saying, "Excellent!"
This is most rare; because it describes their attainment of understanding through metaphors applicable to those individuals, it is called the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" (the *loka-siddhānta*).
Now, medicinal herbs have grown together for a long time, yet upon receiving the rain from the clouds, they flourish and bloom, their sprouts and stems becoming lush and abundant;

externally, they are nourished by external forces, and internally, they are moistened by internal power. This is likened to those who dwell in the final body of an *anāsrava* (one free from outflows), possessing the *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana with remainder).

Having attained *nirvāṇa*, they no longer aspire for the Buddha-way; now, having heard this sutra, they themselves mount the Buddha-vehicle and simultaneously transport others by means of the sound of the Buddha-way, so that all may hear it.
Because both self and others, internal and external, possess superior power and function, it is called the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" (the *puruṣapudgala-siddhānta*).
Now, as for medicinal herbs, they are able to treat the four great elements and nourish the five viscera. Furthermore—

In former times, we were like those who dwell in the world, using the three grades of medicinal herbs to treat the four great elements and benefit the five viscera; though they may restore youth and preserve the complexion, these are neither true medicines nor kings of medicine. They merely remove the diseases of the four abidings and nourish the five aggregates, returning one to the provisional truth while preserving the complexion against the changes of transmigration.

Now, having encountered the clouds and rain [of the Buddha’s teaching], we have suddenly become kings of medicine. By ingesting it, we universally treat all ailments, transforming our very bodies into immortals.
This is like us, the anāsravas, hearing this sutra to shatter the delusions of ignorance and open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Today is truly a day when the sons of the Buddha obtain a supreme treasury of jewels without seeking;

hence it is called the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" (the breaking of delusions and the comprehensive treatment of all ailments corresponds to the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta*, while the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and the formation of the analogy of the immortals corresponds to the *paramārtha-siddhānta*). Regarding the classification by teaching (*yàojiào*):

the three types of grasses represent the *āgama* (Tripitaka) teaching, the small trees represent the *pratyekabuddha* (Shared) teaching, the large trees represent the *vaipulya* (Distinct) teaching, and the earth and rain represent the *vaipulya* (Perfect) teaching. Thus it was in the past.

When not yet revealed, the provisional and the real were vastly different; now that they have been revealed, the three types of grass and two types of trees are all produced from the same ground and moistened by the same rain—how could their roots, stems, branches, leaves, and four subtle elements differ?

One should fully traverse the five flavors to reveal the unique wondrousness of the original and the trace. As for the "original," it abides in the ground of wisdom where clouds and rain were once bestowed; as for the "trace," it serves as...
The passage on "Grasses and Trees" leads to the contemplation of their growth, as explained in the profound text regarding the benefits of the wondrous [teachings] in the latter section.
△ Within the third major section of the analogies, "The Tathāgata’s Confirmation," there are two parts: first, the brief confirmation; second, the extensive confirmation.
Within the first part, there are two sub-sections: first, the dual exclamation of "Excellent!"; second, acknowledging what has not yet been reached. Now, the first:
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mahākāśyapa and the other great disciples: “Excellent, excellent, Kāśyapa!
You have well spoken of the Tathāgata’s true merits; it is exactly as you have said.”

Because Kāśyapa occupies the foremost position among the monks, he is addressed separately. Although the four types of those with faith and understanding are listed in full, and although Subhūti occupies the foremost position in his own declaration, the lead in this proclamation belongs to Kāśyapa; therefore, he is addressed separately now.

Furthermore, by mentioning the various great disciples, it is made known that those who have attained awakening are not limited to these four alone. "Excellent" is said to describe the analogy for the Dharma.

In both places [the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* and the *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra*], the realization of the ultimate truth (*dharmatā*) is praised as "excellent," describing its dharma through metaphors; in both places, the provisional means (*upāya*) are likewise acknowledged.
Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* is intended to lead toward the realization of the ultimate, while the Tripiṭaka teachings are designed to guide and lead by means of the provisional.

The profound essence of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* and the transformative teaching of the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtras* together encompass both the provisional and the ultimate. Finally, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* entrusts the Dharma-treasure and reveals that the provisional is itself the ultimate.
Because the phrasing is exquisitely refined and the expressions are skillful, it is said that all these eloquent expositions are the Buddha-dharma;
because they are sealed by the seal of true merit and established as unerring, it is said, "It is truly as you have stated. △ Second, acknowledging what one has not yet attained.

First: At that time,
the Tathāgata observes the sharpness or dullness of these sentient beings' faculties, their diligence or indolence, and according to what they are capable of,
he preaches the Dharma for them.

This precisely corresponds to the analogy of the simultaneous pouring down of rain; however, the great clouds and rain serve as but a partial metaphor for the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma. Why is this?
Clouds and rain are produced by the collective karma of sentient beings; they are manifestations transformed by the consciousnesses of sentient beings and are categorized among non-sentient things.
Consequently, they belong only to the category of the unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), and for that reason, [they cannot [serve as a perfect analogy]].
While those who observe the faculties of beings to suit their capacities may cause benefit or harm to various things, the Tathāgata is not like this;

he possesses great vows, great compassion, and great wisdom. Although his appearance in the world is induced by the dominant and collective karma of sentient beings, and although each being perceives the Buddha's form as a transformation within their own consciousness, [the Buddha] is nonetheless the primary essence.
Since the objective realm is the functional application arising from the entire substance of the retribution-body of untainted wholesome dharmas,
one is able to observe the sharpness or dullness of the faculties and the diligence or indolence of these sentient beings by means of the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation; subsequently,

by means of the Wisdom of Accomplishing What is Done, one preaches the Dharma according to what they can bear, while simultaneously maintaining universal equanimity through the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom.
It is that which is sealed and illuminated by the wisdom of equality (*samatā-jñāna*). "At that time" refers to the time when sentient beings come to the Buddha's presence to listen to the Dharma.
Regarding the sharpness or dullness of the faculties: those who cannot receive the Way are dull, while those who can receive the Way are sharp.
Furthermore, those who cannot uphold the precepts are dull, while those who can uphold the precepts are sharp. Those who cannot cultivate meditative concentration (*samādhi*) are likewise dull.

Those who are dull-witted are able to cultivate meditative concentration; those who are sharp-witted cannot sever delusions. Those who are dull-witted are able to sever delusions and exit the triple world; those who are sharp-witted analyze through contemplation to sever delusions.

Those who are dull-witted sever delusions through essential contemplation (*tǐguān*); those who are sharp-witted are able to realize the true emptiness. Those who are dull-witted provide guarantees for the realization of true emptiness;

those who are sharp-witted emerge from the provisional to transform sentient beings. Those who are dull-witted take the two contemplations as skillful means; those who are sharp-witted directly contemplate the Middle Way.
The transmission of benefits varies, and furthermore, regarding the five vehicles and the seven stages of expedient means (*saptopāya*), each is discussed in terms of sharp or dull faculties.
The same applies to diligence and indolence; according to what each can endure, it accords with their individual capacities without the error of addition or subtraction.
Thus, from the *Avataṃsaka* at the beginning to the *Prajñāpāramitā* at the end, within each respective period, there is the secret and the indefinite.
The Buddha’s power of preaching the Dharma through sound—wherein each being understands according to their own kind—is an unshared, inconceivable sovereign power.
Because it causes beings only to gain benefit and never to fall into suffering, he rains down equally upon all at once;

thus, within that single moment, each possesses the five flavors, universally and completely adapting to the faculties and natures of sentient beings, even unto the assembly of the Lotus Sūtra where the five thousand who withdrew from their seats were moved elsewhere.

Although from another perspective, a single seat may be called "manifest and definitive" (*kyōryoku kettei*), when viewed in relation to the ten directions, it does not hinder its being termed "esoteric" (*himitsu*).
The Buddha’s transformation through the three mysteries is like the universal drenching of rain and clouds; yet, it differs from the insentient nature of ordinary rain and clouds.
This is how it is. If one relies on the five periods of teaching as understood by Kāśyapa, what name would it bear?
At one time, [the rain] falls equally upon all. Second, as for the convergence of what is moistened:
all the various and immeasurable [beings] are made to rejoice and swiftly obtain wholesome benefits.

Having heard this Dharma, these sentient beings attain peace and security in the present life and are reborn in good realms in future lives; they experience happiness through the Path and likewise obtain the hearing of the Dharma. Having heard the Dharma...
Being free from all obstacles, one enters the Path gradually according to one's capacity among all phenomena.
This possesses the benefits of hearing the Dharma—namely, the ripening of seeds across the three periods of time and liberation—which are manifold and immeasurable;
even in this present life, there is peace and security, and its moisture universally permeates all, serving as a metaphor for being reborn in favorable realms and even hearing the Dharma once again.
To speak collectively of their spiritual lineage (gotra) and their growth therein is an analogy for having already heard the Dharma and gradually being led into the Path;
this corresponds to the analogy of flowers blooming and fruits ripening. Causing all to rejoice is the benefit for the world (*loka-anugraha*);

bringing about peace and the arising of wholesome states is the benefit for persons (*pudgala-anugraha*); and becoming free from hindrances and obstacles is the benefit of remediation (*pratipakṣa-anugraha*). Thus, one gradually attains entry into the Path.

Regarding the benefit of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), for those who first hear the Dharma and plant roots of goodness, there is maturation in the next life and liberation in a subsequent life;

or, if they have already planted them in the past, there is maturation now and liberation in the next; or, if they have already matured in the past, they are liberated immediately upon hearing it now.
These matters are not uniform. Furthermore, the benefits of the four *siddhāntas* encompass both the provisional and the real, each consisting of four aspects.
The various approaches of sudden and gradual teachings differ; were one to explain them in full detail, they would be as vast and boundless as the great void.
Here, I shall merely present the general outline so that you may understand how the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma benefits all future beings.

Furthermore, all these methods cause beings to rejoice, allowing them to grow according to their respective dispositions (gotra) and swiftly attain wholesome benefits. These encompass the four teachings, wherein both the provisional and the ultimate are fully present.

"Benefit" refers to the blossoming flowers and ripening fruits of this present life; it signifies the peace and security of the current existence and the attainment of supreme joy and virtuous advantages—these being the four benefits in the present life.
"Rebirth in a good realm" means that through the path, one receives the fruit of retribution induced by the cause of enjoyment;

furthermore, one obtains the hearing of the Dharma, which is the fruit of cultivation induced by the cause of cultivation. The enjoyment of the Path one receives must necessarily consist of both the provisional and the ultimate.
Regarding the provisional and ultimate paths, one further discusses their relative shallowness and depth; the Dharma thus heard is likewise so.

This immediately follows with the discernment of the four benefits within this world. Having heard the Dharma, one becomes free from all obstacles, and these obstacles abandoned also differ in degree of shallowness and depth.
All of these constitute the retributive causes that evoke retributive fruits; according to one's capacity and ability, one gradually attains entry into the Path.
The entry [into the teaching] also possesses both provisional and ultimate aspects; these are all causes of habituation that evoke fruits of habituation.

This constitutes the third section, which distinguishes the four benefits within future lives. The capacities of those to be benefited span horizontally across the ten realms, and the benefits they receive penetrate vertically through the four teachings.
Thus, in texts such as the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Prajñāpāramitā*, even those in the hells are enabled to obtain benefit; the rest may be inferred accordingly.
The initial formal correspondence is concluded. △ Second, the citation of the analogy and its application:

Just as that great cloud rains upon all the grasses, trees, thickets, forests, and medicinal herbs, each receiving its full measure of moisture according to its own nature and attaining growth accordingly.
The great clouds and rain represent the ability to moisten and harmonize the Tathāgata’s three secrets (*triguhyaka*) and his vocal teachings (*śabdopadeśa*).

The two characters "all" (*sarva*) represent the conventional designation (*prajñapti*) of sentient beings. The various plants, trees, thickets, and medicinal herbs represent the five vehicles (*pañcayāna*) and the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidhopāya*).

The "seed-natures" (*gotra*) represent the sharpness or dullness of the faculties (*indriya*) as well as indolence and diligence. "Fully receiving the moisture" represents that all [sentient beings] are equally benefited.

This causes them to rejoice and swiftly obtain excellent benefits; each attains growth, and they achieve peace and security in the present life, as well as rebirth in a good realm in future lives, and so forth.
Thus, that which was initially non-differentiated becomes differentiated at the end. △ Second, the section on the convergence of differentiation and non-differentiation.

This has two parts: first, the formal convergence; second, the concluding explanation. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, the convergence of what is produced by a single earth and moistened by a single rain.
Second, there are differences among grasses and trees. First:

the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata has a single characteristic and a single flavor—namely, the characteristic of liberation, the characteristic of detachment, and the characteristic of cessation—which ultimately culminates in all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
"Single characteristic" means that the mind-nature of sentient beings is identical to True Suchness as its characteristic, uniting them into a single stage.
"Single flavor" means that the Dharma of the One Vehicle equally explicates a single principle, uniting it into a single rain. This explains the "single characteristic and single flavor" in pairs.
"The characteristic of liberation" means that karma is itself liberation; fundamentally, there are no two sides to the characteristics of karmic bondage.
Furthermore, "separation from characteristics" means that delusion is fundamentally the separation from the characteristics of both the general and specific afflictions;

"extinction of characteristics" means that suffering is fundamentally the quiescent extinction of the two kinds of birth-and-death within the Dharmakāya. The nature of the mind of sentient beings is precisely the characteristic of liberation as an inherent virtue;
these characteristics of separation and extinction are such that they are three while being one, and one while being three. Thus it is said:
When the One Sound comes to preach this, it is the principle that the one is three and the three are one;
it is the teaching that the single flavor is three flavors and the three flavors are the single flavor.

When sentient beings uphold this teaching and practice, they take the three aspects and the one aspect of their own inherent virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*) as the object of contemplation, relying upon the Buddha’s teaching of the three flavors and the single flavor.

As the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), the practice of the three aspects and one aspect within the Middle Way is brought to ultimate fulfillment, thereby achieving the fruit of the omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) of the three aspects and one aspect.
Indeed, the Buddha skillfully unfolds the single reality-mark (*ekalakṣaṇa-dharma*) into three, five, seven, nine, and so forth;
he differentiates the teaching of a single flavor (*ekarasa*) by expounding it as the "combined," the "exclusive," and the "corresponding."
Sentient beings who possess various tastes [of faculties] uphold the teachings and practice them, each attaining their respective fruits and realizations;

who is able to know this? Only a Buddha can know that these ultimately all return to a single mark and a single flavor. △ Second, combining the analogy of grasses and trees to show that each has its own distinctions.

This section has three parts: first, the formal application of the analogy, showing that sentient beings are like grasses and trees because they do not know for themselves; second, clarifying that there is only suchness...

Because it can be known through its arrival, it is similar to a great cloud yet not identical to one; this is the third analogy, which addresses the fact that sentient beings do not understand. First:
if there are sentient beings who hear the Dharma of the Tathāgata, and if they uphold, read, recite, and practice it as taught, the merit they thereby obtain—
They do not realize or know this themselves.
"Those who have sentient beings" refers collectively to those ignorant people, encompassing the three types of grass and two types of wood.
"Dharma" refers to the Dharma of a single sound and a single flavor. If one upholds, recites, and practices according to the teaching, it clearly clarifies that they do not know.

For this reason, the upholding and preaching [of the Dharma] differ, and the practices are distinct; humans and devas form conceptions of precepts and wholesome deeds, while those of the Three Vehicles form conceptions of the Truths, Conditions, and the Paramitas. Since these conceptions are not the same, they constitute differentiation.

Those who do not realize the merit they have attained are unaware that the Buddha’s teaching is of a single flavor and without differentiation, but instead remain within the seven kinds of provisional [teachings].
Within these merits, each obtains one kind and forms its own interpretation;

yet they do not know their ultimate convergence upon the reality, nor do they know that what they have attained is provisional—that it is both provisional and real. They are merely deluded by names and thus lack self-awareness.
△ Second, explaining that only the Tathāgata can know this, he is thus the same as a great cloud yet different from it.

Why is this? Only the Tathāgata knows the species, characteristics, and essential nature of these sentient beings; he knows what they have contemplated, what they have reflected upon, and what they have cultivated;

how they have contemplated, how they have reflected, and how they have cultivated; by means of what dharmas they have contemplated, by means of what dharmas they have reflected, and by means of what dharmas they have cultivated;
and by means of what dharmas they have attained what dharmas—sentient beings who abide in various stages.
Only the Tathāgata perceives it as it truly is, with clarity and without obstruction.
That which the Tathāgata can know is the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*); that which he perceives as it truly is is the vision of the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*);
and that which is clear and unobstructed is that which penetrates from beginning to end and from within to without.
Externally, all are thoroughly understood. If one restricts this to that which can know and see, there is only Buddha-wisdom and the Buddha-eye;

however, if one restricts it to that which is known and seen, then reducing the number and briefly citing ten objects, they are combined into four meanings, each of which is without error—that is, non-differentiation is itself differentiation. As for the four meanings: first, regarding the four dharmas; second, regarding the three... [text ends].

Regarding the three dharmas as pertaining to two dharmas, the four dharmas as pertaining to one dharma, and the one dharma as pertaining to four dharmas—these refer to the categories (*gotra*), characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), essence (*svabhāva*), and nature (*dharmatā*).
There are two meanings to "category" (*gotra*): if categorized in terms of their mutual relationship, the three paths are the categories of the three virtues.

Thus, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states: "The entire host of afflictions constitutes the category of the Tathāgata. (This is because the path of affliction itself possesses the category of *prajñā*. Furthermore, it says: [...]* *Note: The ellipsis indicates the omission of the intervening text from the source.*
The five *ānantarya* [sins] all possess the characteristic of liberation (for even through unwholesome karma, there exists the seed of liberation that is wholesome Dharma).

It is further said that all sentient beings possess the characteristic of *nirvāṇa* and cannot be extinguished again (the path of the suffering of birth and death is itself the seed of the *dharmakāya*).

If one discusses seeds according to their categories, then every lowering of the head and raising of the hand is the seed of liberation; so too are all worldly wisdom and the understanding of the three vehicles.
The mind is the seed of *prajñā*; all who possess a mind shall become Buddhas—this is the seed of the *dharmakāya*.
These various distinctions among seeds can only be known by a Buddha. That all seeds are but a single seed, which is non-distinctive, can also only be known by a Buddha.
That distinction is non-distinction, and non-distinction is distinction—this too can only be known by a Buddha. As for "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*)...

That which relies on external forms and takes substantiality as its primary nature is based on internal endowment, as explained in the section on the ten realms and the ten suchnesses (*daśadhātu-daśatathatā*).
If one discusses their distinctions, they are the characteristics of the ten dharma-realms (*daśadharma-dhātu*), which only a Buddha can know.

If one discusses their non-distinction, they are the characteristics of the single Buddha-realm, which likewise only a Buddha can know. That distinction is itself non-distinction, and non-distinction is itself distinction; this too only a Buddha [can know].

The principle for knowing their essential natures (*svabhāva*) is likewise twofold. Regarding the three dharmas, these are the three types of wisdom: that arising from hearing, reflection, and cultivation. Furthermore, there are three layers:
first, as for what is remembered, what is reflected upon, and what is cultivated—these are the objects apprehended by the three wisdoms.

According to the teachings, the categories, characteristics, and essential natures (*lakṣaṇa-svabhāva*) explained therein differ; thus, the modes of reflection and cultivation vary in accordance with those teachings, corresponding to the respective realms (*dhātu*).

One should understand that the differences or non-differences between the objects of observation, their extent, the increase or decrease [of practice], and the skill or clumsiness of the meditative essence correspond to their respective meanings.
Regarding the two—expedient means and reality—and so forth: what is mindfulness, what is reflection, and what is cultivation?

These are the essential natures of the three types of wisdom. This essence is precisely that which is capable of hearing, reflecting, and cultivating; it likewise possesses instances of difference and non-difference.

The preceding [section] can be understood. As for the three questions—by what dharma does one recollect, by what dharma does one contemplate, and by what dharma does one cultivate—they refer to the causal conditions (*pratyaya*) of the three types of wisdom (*trividya*).
Because one apprehends objects only through hearing the Dharma, hearing the Dharma serves as the causal condition.

Thus, regarding these three vehicles and the three types of wisdom, it was previously said that there are differences because the objects, essences, and causal conditions are distinct; this constitutes their differentiation.

If one enters the perfect and wondrous threefold wisdom, there is no distinction; yet this existence of distinction can only be known by a Buddha, and this absence of distinction can also only be known by a Buddha.
Furthermore, that distinction is itself non-distinction, and non-distinction is itself distinction—this too can only be known by a Buddha.
Thirdly, regarding the two dharmas, they are cause and effect. By means of what dharma as a cause does one attain what?
The fruits of the Dharma and the causes of the five vehicles each obtain their respective results; this is differentiation, which only a Buddha can know.
Sentient beings are like Buddhas, identical as one suchness, without duality; being thus a single cause and a single fruit, there is no differentiation, which likewise only a Buddha can know.
Furthermore, that differentiation is non-differentiation, and non-differentiation is differentiation—this too only a Buddha can know.
To know that the four [stages] are subsumed within a single dharma means that sentient beings dwell in various stages;
that is, the seven types of persons in the preparatory practices (saptavidha-upāya) dwell in seven positions. This differentiation can only be known by a Buddha, who perceives it as it truly is:

that it is in fact a single stage, which is non-differentiation. Furthermore, this very differentiation is non-differentiation, and non-differentiation is differentiation. Only a Buddha can know this.
Since even their differentiation can only be known by the Buddha, it is said that he is "clearly aware and unimpeded.

Herein, these four aspects encompass all phenomena—namely, their categories (*jāti*), characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), essence (*svabhāva*), and nature (*dharmatā*)—as the objects apprehended by the three types of wisdom. These four factors do not transcend cause and effect;
the substance of cause and effect is simply the true nature (*bhūtatathatā*). △ Third, the analogy is raised and applied: sentient beings... [text breaks off]
It is known that, just as those grasses, trees, forests, and medicinal herbs do not themselves know their superior, middling, or inferior natures, so too,
when they have not yet blossomed, those of the seven stages of expedient means are all like the grasses and trees; they are merely able to receive moisture and grow.

Once one has realized this for oneself after it has been revealed, one then understands that whether it be the roots, stems, branches, leaves, flowers, or fruits of the three types of grasses and two types of trees, each and every part is nothing other than the four subtle elements (*catur-aṇu*) of the earth.

Thus, one can fully awaken to the ground of principle (*li-di*) within the nature-virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*) of sentient beings, which constitutes the ultimate ground of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) of all Buddhas; from this ground of wisdom, [one proceeds].

Raising the clouds of great compassion, he pours down the rain of provisional and ultimate teachings to transform beings without end; this is why the Tathāgata preaches the Lotus Sūtra, desiring only that people awaken to this nature and cultivate its secret essentials.
