The Tathāgata knows that this is a dharma of a single characteristic and a single flavor— namely, the characteristic of liberation, the characteristic of detachment,
the characteristic of cessation, and ultimate nirvāṇa, which is the characteristic of eternal quiescence and ultimately returns to emptiness.
The "one mark" and "one flavor" have already been explained as before.

For the sake of sentient beings, these are distinguished and taught as the dharma of liberation, detachment, and cessation—that is, the one within the immeasurable, the ultimate *nirvāṇa*, the eternally quiescent mark that ultimately returns to emptiness; this is the one within the immeasurable, which thus establishes the ultimate.
There is no distinction. When it says "ultimate nirvāṇa," it is not like the two types of nirvāṇa with remainder and without remainder belonging to the two vehicles.
When it says "the mark of eternal quiescence," it does not mean that liberation is named by severing bonds;

since the Dharma is fundamentally without bondage, there is now likewise no liberation. It does not mean that detachment is named by abandoning attachments; since the Dharma is fundamentally without attachment, now...

Furthermore, there is no departure from this, for it is not by the exhaustion of birth that it is called the mark of cessation. Dharmas are fundamentally without birth, and now they are likewise without cessation;
what is called "all dharmas" has, from the very beginning, always been the mark of inherent quiescence.

This is not like the three marks of the Two Vehicles, which ultimately resolve into emptiness—meaning they return to the emptiness of the ultimate truth of the Middle Way, rather than the "ash-emptiness" of the Two Vehicles.

The emptiness that severs [delusion] is explained with such diligent repetition because the simple reality differs from the provisional; the Great Compassion of the Buddha is truly most earnest and profound.
△ Second, explaining the intention for not teaching immediately.

Having known this, the Buddha observes the inclinations of the minds of sentient beings and protects them; for this reason, he does not immediately preach the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Since the Tathāgata knows that the beginning and the end are fundamentally one, why does he not at all times speak only of the single reality?

The present commentary states: observing the desires of the minds of sentient beings, [the Buddha] nurtures and protects them, fearing that they might slander [the teaching] and thus does not speak immediately.
This concludes the first section, which correctly elucidates the inconceivability of the provisional and the real. △ Second, the conclusion, praise, and summary.
"O Kāśyapas, it is truly rare that you are able to understand the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma according to what is appropriate, and are able to believe and accept it. Why is this?
Because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, teach the Dharma according to what is appropriate; it is difficult to comprehend and difficult to know."
The immeasurable merits of the Tathāgata explained previously could not be fully exhausted even if you were to speak for immeasurable billions of kalpas;

they are like the inconceivable rain from a great cloud. Fearing that people might doubt whether these four disciples truly attained realization through the uniform teaching, the Buddha recounted this:
although it does not yet reach the ultimate stage of Buddhahood, it is nonetheless complete.

To lead [beings] through the provisional and the real across the five periods, to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and to realize the fruit of Buddhahood—both partialy and fully—is truly not in vain;
furthermore, it is intended to inspire those of inferior faculties so that they may likewise attain awakening. First, regarding the praise of its rarity:

ordinary beings may repeatedly hear [the teaching] and gain benefit, while Bodhisattvas already understand it as their own affair, so this is not considered extraordinary. Now, however, it concerns the station of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).

Yet, because they are able to relinquish [conceptualization] and enter into reality, this is most rare. To know how to preach the Dharma according to what is appropriate describes their capacity for comprehension;
to open up the three [vehicles] and describe their capacity for comprehension reveals the one [vehicle]. Why is this?
The following section explains and establishes this rarity, which can be understood. Furthermore, whereas it was previously said, "You cannot fully express it," it is now said, "You..."
This is truly rare and extraordinary: previously, it was established that the Buddha’s grace universally covers all, like clouds and rain that moisten everything without exception;
the Buddha’s grace universally sustains all, like the great earth that brings all things to life and growth. How could it be intended for only one region or one individual?
Therefore, it is said that words cannot fully express it. Now, although the Buddha’s grace is universal, sentient beings...

It is because you are unable to realize this for yourselves—just as the three types of grass and two types of trees, though rooted in the earth and nourished by the rain, remain unaware of it—that your ability to know the beginning and end of these ten kinds of grace is truly rare.

To enable those who have not yet crossed over to cross over, and so forth, you have described how knowing the grace of the Buddha’s Four Great Vows is exceedingly rare; through this, there shall be peace and security in the present life and a favorable rebirth in the future.

He establishes beings in wholesome states so that they may experience happiness through the Path; describing his knowledge of the grace of bestowing happiness through Great Loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is most rare.
He causes them to leave behind all obstacles and gradually enter the Path; describing his knowledge of the grace of extracting suffering through Great Compassion (*karuṇā*) is most rare.
Universal Monarchs, Śakra, and Brahmā are but minor medicinal herbs; describing his knowledge of the grace of exhorting toward goodness and eliminating afflictions is most rare.
It is rare to know the untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) that can attain *nirvāṇa* and the realization of a *pratyekabuddha*;
herein, the medicinal herbs describe the rarity of their knowledge in removing the suffering of cold and heat, as well as the craving and attachment [of sentient beings].
The superior herbs and small trees describe the rarity of their knowledge in concealing ugliness and their aspiration for the Great [Vehicle]. The great trees describe their...
The knowledge of the grace of adornment is most rare and is the ultimate reality;
it describes the grace of knowing how to bestow wealth and provide seats, wherein body, mind, material goods, and the Dharma are sovereign and at peace—a grace that is most rare.
The Buddha describes its distinctions in the passage praising the ten graces; when the text concludes and describes its non-distinction, that is precisely "One."
The extensive exposition of the Great Kindness within the first section of the "Establishment" concludes. △ Second, the Verses in Repetition (Ge-yo), which has three parts:
first, verses on the Dharma-exposition; second, verses on establishing similes; third, verses on the application of the Dharma. Now, the first part.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
The Dharma-King who destroys existence appears in the world to preach various teachings according to the desires of sentient beings.

The Tathāgata’s wisdom is profound and far-reaching; having long remained silent on this matter, he does not strive to speak it hastily. If those with wisdom hear it, they will be able to believe and understand.

If one lacks wisdom, harbors doubt, or feels regret, then one will suffer eternal loss. For this reason, Kāśyapa, I teach according to people's capacities, using various causes and conditions to enable them to attain right view.
That which destroys the King of Dharmas yet whose cause and effect do not perish is called "existence. Ordinary beings take [the afflictions of] view and thought as...

Taking segmented birth-and-death as the cause and the two vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas as the fruit; taking dust-like sands as the cause and the expedient transformation-death (*parināmika-vaiparītya-maraṇa*) as the fruit for Bodhisattvas;

and taking ignorance as the cause and the self-nature transformation-death (*svabhāva-pariṇāmika-maraṇa*) as the fruit—only when the Buddhas have extinguished the causes of the five abodes and lost the fruits of the two deaths do they attain great mastery over all dharmas and appear in the world.
The interval [between teachings] is for the sake of benefiting sentient beings; thus, all provisional and ultimate teachings ensure that those who receive them derive benefit without fail.
The two lines beginning with "According to the desires of sentient beings" (*yathā-jana-kāma*) praise the teaching of provisional doctrines through provisional wisdom.

The four lines beginning with "The Tathāgata is honored" (*tathāgato gurukṛta*) praise the teaching of ultimate doctrines through ultimate wisdom. The four lines beginning with "If one possessing wisdom hears [this]" (*dhīmatā śrutvā*) explain why [the Buddha] does not speak immediately.

This is the basis for [the distinction between] the provisional and the real. Therefore, Kāśyapa, the four lines [of verse] reveal the skillful means of first employing the provisional and subsequently revealing the real.
By means of various conditions, one first bestows the provisional so that right view may be attained;
this subsequent revelation of the real is because this single reality alone is called "right view. Thus, in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the youth Kāśyapa’s realization states: "Prior to this..."
"We are all people of false views. △ Second, the verses establishing the analogy, in two parts: first, verses on the non-differentiated yet differentiated;
second, verses on the differentiated yet non-differentiated. In the first part, there are two sections: first, an anticipatory verse on the non-differentiation of that which moistens;
second, a retrospective verse on the differentiation of the produced and the produced-recipient of moisture. Now, the first:
Kāśyapa, you should know that it is like a great cloud arising in the world, completely covering everything. This cloud of wisdom contains moisture;
its lightning flashes brilliantly and its thunder resounds afar, bringing joy to all beings. It eclipses the sunlight, making the earth cool and refreshing.
Lofty and dense, it hangs low as if one could reach out and grasp it. Its rain falls equally upon the four quarters, pouring down in immeasurable torrents.
The entire realm is thoroughly saturated.

The cloud is likened to the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body), for the response body follows the movement of wisdom; thus it is said that the "wisdom-cloud" is able to possess the twelve divisions of the Dharma.

Therefore, it is said to contain moisture. The flashing brilliance of lightning is likened to the body emitting great radiance, while the distant resonance of thunder is likened to [the proclamation of the Dharma].
The proclamation of the four analytical knowledges is like the sun’s radiance eclipsing all else; the ninety-five kinds of heterodox lights do not appear.
It is like the earth becoming cool and refreshing, where the ninety-eight kinds of afflictive fevers are removed. It is like dense clouds hanging low as if they could be grasped;

the marks and signs of the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and its majestic deportment seem identical to those of the three realms of existence, yet though one may go toward it with a mind intent on grasping it, it is truly unattainable.
Furthermore, the rain falls universally and equally upon the four directions, which is like the eight tones and four forms of eloquence responding universally to the capacities of all beings;
its continuous flow is immeasurable, which is like each single period of time fully containing the five periods and the eight teachings;

it saturates the entire land, which is like all who possess a mind receiving benefit and profit, with each individual period of time allowing them to attain the *zang*, *tong*, *bie*, *yuan*, and *dun* [teachings].
This is the gradual, secret, and indeterminate benefit of the five flavors. △ Second, a summary verse on the distinctions among the moisture-receiving capacities of the produced and the producers:
"The plants, medicinal herbs, and trees—large and small—growing in mountains, rivers, steep valleys, and deep recesses; as well as the various grains and sprouts."
Sugarcane and grapes, moistened by the rain, were all abundantly fulfilled; even parched lands were universally saturated, and medicinal herbs and trees flourished together.
From that cloud issued water of a single flavor, yet the grasses, trees, and forests received its moisture according to their respective capacities.
All the various trees—superior, middling, and inferior—each attained growth according to their size, with their roots, stems, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits attaining radiant color.
Wherever the single rain falls, everything attains freshness and luster.

The mountains, rivers, precipitous valleys, and ravines—though briefly mentioned—are capable of producing growth; their profound seclusion is like the habitual causes planted by sentient beings over a long period, hidden within the fruits and the mind-and-matter (nāma-rūpa).
The hundred grains are like the ten wholesome actions (daśa-kuśala-karma-patha), which mutually adorn one another. As for the ten wholesome actions:

A single piece of sugarcane can be used as an analogy for the object of focus in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), while many bunches of grapes can be used as an analogy for the numerous delusions destroyed by wisdom (*prajñā*).
The thorough moistening of dry land serves as an analogy for causing those who have no faith to gain faith. The rest is as stated in the initial verse;
thus, the section on "the different being non-different" is concluded. △ Second, the section on "the non-different being different."
Just as their physical forms and natures differ in size, yet that which moistens them is one and each grows lushly;

the first two lines of the verse praise the produced and the moistened, the third line directly praises the non-differentiation of the moisture itself (omitting a brief mention of the producer), and the fourth line praises the fact that they do not know their own distinctions. The capacity to produce is implicitly included within the "produced."

The two verses establishing the analogies are concluded. △ Third, the two verses on the application of the Dharma [to the analogy] have two parts: first, one verse on the application of non-differentiation within differentiation;

second, two verses on the application of differentiation within non-differentiation. Within the first part, there are three sections: first, one verse on the application of that which moistens; second, two verses on the application of that which produces and that which is produced;
third, three verses again on the application of that which moistens and that which is moistened. Now, the first [section].
The Buddha is likewise manifested in the world like a great cloud that universally covers all;
having appeared in the world, he analytically expounds the reality of all dharmas for the sake of all sentient beings.
The Great Sage, the World-Honored One, proclaims these words amidst the assembly of devas and humans: "I am the Tathāgata, the most honored among two-legged beings, who has appeared in the world."

Just as a great cloud saturates all withered beings, causing them all to leave suffering behind and attain peace and happiness—the worldly joy as well as the bliss of Nirvana—let the multitudes of devas and humans listen with single-minded devotion;

you should all come here to behold the Unsurpassed Honored One. For the sake of bringing peace and security to sentient beings, I, who am the World-Honored One beyond compare, have appeared in this world.

For the great assembly, he expounds the pure Dharma of ambrosia; this Dharma is of a single flavor—liberation and nirvana—and with one wondrous voice, he eloquently elucidates this meaning, constantly acting as the causal condition for the Mahāyāna.
The three verses beginning with "Having appeared in the world" briefly praise the Ten Epithets; "To moisten and nourish all" and the following six phrases briefly praise the Four Great Vows.
The remaining four Dharma-gates are not praised here. The four verses following "The assembly of devas and humans" praise the exhortation to listen to and receive the Dharma.
"Of one flavor" means that the seven kinds of skillful means do not fail to return to the One Vehicle, though they differ [in their manifestations].

There is no difference; those who constantly act as the causes and conditions for the Mahāyāna, having already established these causes and conditions, must employ skillful means—thus, while there is no difference, there is difference. △ Second, the verse combines the producer and the produced.
I contemplate all things as universally equal, without any mind of attachment or aversion toward self or others.
I am free from greed and possess no hindrances; I constantly preach the Dharma with impartiality to all, whether to one person or many.
I always expound the Dharma without other concerns, and whether walking, coming, going, sitting, or standing, I never grow weary, fully satisfying the world.
Just as rain universally moistens all things,

the preceding prose explains the correspondence between the producer and the produced by stating that "countless thousands of myriads of kotis of sentient beings come to the Buddha's presence to hear the Dharma.
Now, this verse clarifies that the Buddha regards all beings with universal equality.

The Buddha’s teaching for those of his own capacity is for this [audience], while his teaching for other capacities is for that; the Buddha speaks with impartiality, neither favoring those of his own capacity nor hating those of other capacities.
It is like the falling rain, which makes no distinction between mountain streams and valleys. The Buddha’s work is "self" and Māra’s work is "other.

That which corresponds to the future is "going," while that which corresponds to the beginning is "coming. Entering into reality is "sitting," while emerging through skillful means is "standing. The rest is as previously explained.
The Text. △ Third, the verses on the reunion of the moisture and the moistened. First, one verse on the reunion of the moisture; second, two verses on the reunion of the moistened. Now, the first:

the noble and the lowly, the high and the low, those who uphold the precepts and those who violate them, those whose deportment is complete and those whose it is incomplete, and those with right view and those with wrong view.
He rains down the Dharma rain upon those of sharp faculties and dull faculties alike, without weariness or indolence.

This verse describes how the Tathāgata, at that time, observes the sharpness or dullness of the faculties of these sentient beings, their diligence or indolence, and according to what they are capable of bearing, he expounds the Dharma for them.
[The distinctions of] noble and base, high and low refer to their status; [the distinctions of] upholding or violating the precepts refer to their conduct.
Regarding the practice of those with sharp and dull faculties, it should be explained in relation to the five vehicles and seven stages of skillful means, as they develop one after another.

△ Second, the verse on the synthesis of that which is moistened has two parts: first, a verse on the joy, excellent benefit, and present-world peace and security, which corresponds to the analogy of universal soaking;
second, a verse on being born in good realms in future lives and gradually attaining entry into the Path, which corresponds to the growth, spreading, and ripening of fruit.
First, as for the analogy:
all sentient beings who hear my Dharma receive it according to their capacity and abide in various stages, whether among humans, devas, universal monarchs (*cakravartin*), Śakra, or Brahmā kings;
these are the small medicinal herbs, who know the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) Dharma and are able to attain *nirvāṇa*.

Those who give rise to the six supernormal powers and attain the three insights, dwelling alone in mountain forests and constantly practicing meditative concentration to realize the fruit of a pratyekabuddha—these are the medicinal herbs.
Those who seek the place of the World-Honored One and resolve, "I shall become a Buddha," practicing the concentration of diligence—these are the superior medicinal herbs.

Furthermore, those sons of the Buddha who single-mindedly focus on the path of the Buddha, constantly practicing loving-kindness and compassion, and who know for themselves that they will become Buddhas with absolute certainty—[they are the supreme medicinal herbs].
This is called the small tree that dwells securely in supernatural powers, turns the irreversible wheel, and delivers immeasurable billions of hundreds of thousands of sentient beings.
Such a bodhisattva is called a great tree. The Buddha speaks with impartiality like a rain of a single flavor;

yet according to the dispositions of sentient beings, what they receive differs, just as the various plants and trees each absorb nourishment differently. The Buddha uses this analogy as a skillful means to reveal and instruct.
To expound a single Dharma through various modes of expression is like a single drop of water in the ocean of the Buddha’s wisdom.
The first verse generally clarifies receiving the moisture; the subsequent seven verses specifically clarify receiving the moisture;

and the final three verses conclude by clarifying that the capacity to moisten is inconceivable. Since both humans and deva-kings have not yet severed their afflictions (*kleśa*), they are collectively categorized as "Small."
Because the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) both possess [the stages of] abandonment and realization, they are combined as the "middle grass.

Because bodhisattvas of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) have resolved to seek Buddhahood, their initial aspiration (*cittotpāda*) is already superior to that of the two vehicles; thus, they alone are designated as the "superior grass.

Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching (*pāryāya-yāna*) have already severed the delusions common to all levels, yet they vow to sustain their remaining habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) while transforming sentient beings; therefore, they are called "small trees. As for the bodhisattvas of the Distinct Teaching (*prthak-yāna*), themselves...
Because their practice of transforming others brings about lofty and vast merit and wisdom, they are called "great trees.

Furthermore, in terms of meaning, this may be applied to the Bodhisattvas of the three teachings, each forming small, medium, and large trees—resulting in six trees when the six *pāramitās* are correlated with the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*. In the *Tongjiao* (Common Teaching), it refers to the seventh, eighth, and ninth stages;
in the *Biejiao* (Distinct Teaching), it refers to the thirty minds. Regarding the Buddha’s wisdom as being like a drop in the ocean, it is able to provide moisture.
Just as a single drop is moistened by the ocean, the merit of that single drop cannot be fully exhausted even if explained for immeasurable billions of kalpas.
△ Second, the verse on being born in good realms and gradually attaining entry into the Path combines the analogies of growth,
expansion, and fruition.
I rain down the rain of Dharma to fill the world with the Dharma of a single flavor, which beings practice according to their capacity.

Just as the medicinal herbs and trees in a forest grow more lush and flourish according to their respective sizes, so too do the teachings of the Buddhas always employ a single flavor to cause all in the world to attain fulfillment;
through gradual cultivation, both Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas attain the fruits of the Path.
Those dwelling in mountain forests in their final existence who hear the Dharma and attain the fruit are called medicinal herbs that each attain growth.
If bodhisattvas possess firm wisdom, thoroughly understand the three realms, and seek the Supreme Vehicle, they are called small trees that attain growth.
Furthermore, there are those who dwell in dhyāna, attain supernormal powers, and upon hearing that all dharmas are empty, experience great joy in their hearts.
Emitting countless rays of light to illuminate all sentient beings is called the growth of the Great Tree.
The first two verses provide a general summary of this growth; the subsequent six and a half verses provide a detailed exposition of it.
Within this detailed exposition, the six lines beginning with "The Dharma of all Buddhas" clarify the growth of humans and devas, followed by the six lines beginning with "The śrāvakas."
This passage clarifies that for the followers of the Two Vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas) who abide in their final existence (*caramabhavika*), there are two meanings:

first, if the followers of the Two Vehicles do not encounter a Buddha, they may not necessarily be in their final existence; however, by encountering a Buddha, they become those in their final existence—this is the meaning of "increase" (*vṛddhi*).
Second, when the followers of the Two Vehicles have already abided in *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, they are designated as being in their final existence. Now...
To hear the Mahāyāna Dharma and attain the fruit of the Mahāyāna is precisely the meaning of "increase. Next, the six lines beginning with "If all bodhisattvas...

clarify the body of the Dharma-wisdom of the Shared Teaching (p’ung-chiao); because it is sharp, it is called "firm," and because it severs the delusions of the three realms, it is called "thoroughly penetrating.
Next, the two verses beginning with "Furthermore, there are those who dwell in dhyāna... clarify the Distinct Teaching (pieh-chiao).

Increasing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) constitutes entering the power of the provisional. Hearing that all phenomena are empty of self-nature, one experiences great joy;

this means hearing the Middle Way, the emptiness of the primary truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), and being able to accord with and contemplate it accordingly. [The text] briefly omits verses on the increase of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*).

As for "increase," the six perfections are the most provisional among the provisional; they involve the teaching but not the person, and since afflictions have not yet been severed, they may be subsumed [within the category of the provisional].

Entering the realms of humans and devas: the initial verse combines non-differentiation with differentiation, which is now concluded. Second, the prose section extensively combined differentiation with non-differentiation;
this verse now provides a concise summary.
Thus, the Dharma taught by Kāśyapa Buddha is like a great cloud, moistening the flowers of humanity with rain of a single flavor.
"Kāśyapa, you should know that the attainment of the true fruit was achieved by me through various causes, conditions, and diverse parables to reveal the Buddha-way;
this is my skillful means, and all Buddhas act likewise. Now, for your sake, I shall speak of the most ultimate reality:
none of you śrāvakas have attained final nirvāṇa. The path you have practiced is the bodhisattva-way; by gradually cultivating and training in it, you shall all become Buddhas."

The first six lines present the analogy and its application; where there is no difference, yet there is difference—this very difference is non-difference. The "single-flavored rain" is without difference.
Its "moistening of people and flowers" refers to the seven causes of goodness as flowers, which do indeed differ.

Each attains the formation of fruit, ultimately returning to the same ground; thus, the four subtle differences are themselves non-difference. The subsequent three and a half verses conclude by establishing the provisional [teachings].
In truth, there is no duality; through various causes, conditions, and parables, the provisional is precisely the real, and the revealing of the Buddha-way is the real within the provisional.

What I now declare to you as the most ultimate reality is the "revealed" reality, which differs from the "reality contrasted with the provisional" found in the *Avataṃsaka*, *Vaipulya*, and *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras—this refers to the unity of the teaching. As for the sound...
To hear that all are not yet in *parinirvāṇa* is the "one person"; that what you practice is the bodhisattva path is the "one practice";
and that through gradual cultivation and study one shall all attain Buddhahood—that which the Buddha knows and sees is the "one principle.
This concludes the third section of the parables, wherein the Tathāgata provides his confirmation.
△ The explanation of the "Parable of the Herbs" chapter is concluded; next is the explanation of the "Bestowal of Predictions" chapter (*Vyākaraṇa-parivarta*).

The sixth chapter, "Bestowal of Predictions," in the Sanskrit language is *vyākaraṇa*, which here is translated as "bestowal of prediction" (*shouji*), also called "receiving prediction" (*shouji*), "receiving the decision" (*shoujue*), or "receiving the prophecy" (*shoubie*). "Shou" (to receive) means...
"Receiving" (*pratigraha*) means to obtain; "prediction" (*vyākaraṇa*) means to record events; "deciding" (*niścaya*) means to determine; and "proclamation" (*vyākaroti*) means to fully declare.

In various sūtras, there are instances where predictions are refuted, such as when the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa* asks: "Is one predicted to attain enlightenment by arising from Suchness, or by ceasing from Suchness?
Since there is neither arising nor ceasing, one knows there is no prediction. Furthermore, the *Sangītisūtra* says: "I pray that I may not hear a prediction."
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Great Treatise) states that "receiving a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*)" is conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

How, then, do you respond to this? If one perceives a prediction as being for a person who exists [as a substantial entity], such a view must be refuted. However, if it is a prediction based on the vow of a Bodhisattva, then this prediction must be granted. (This is the general response.

Furthermore, predictions are made from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), whereas from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), there are none. (Since all four teachings discuss the two truths, how can the ultimate be used to challenge the conventional? Moreover, they are appropriate according to the four *siddhāntas* (the four purposes) suited to the occasion.

The records are as explained below (each of the four teachings discusses the four *siddhāntas*). In this sutra, there are five [types of prediction]: if recorded according to the general path, it is as at the beginning of the "Dharma Master" chapter;
if recorded specifically, it is as after the three weeks [of teaching] (one general and one specific); if a prediction of the direct cause (*dharmatā-hetu*), it is as in the case of Sadāparibhūta;

if a prediction of the contributing cause (*pratyaya-hetu*), it is as the ten kinds of offerings in the "Dharma Master" chapter; if a prediction of the completing cause (*vyañjana-hetu*), it is as in the "Bestowal of the Three [Baskets]."

Regarding the prediction of roots and persons: if it is based on the direct cause (*nidāna-hetu*), the prediction is broad; if it is based on the conditions (*ālambana*), the prediction is narrow (the two causes).

Or there is a prediction given slowly, or a prediction given quickly (the three aspects of slowness and speed; slowness is like that of the Śrāvakas, while speed is like that of the Dragon Girl). Or there is a prediction by a Buddha as in this text, or a prediction by a Bodhisattva as in the case of Sadāparibhūta;

although there is no fixed determination regarding the kalpa or the land, such a prediction may still be obtained (the four aspects of teacher and disciple). Furthermore, there are predictions made from afar (*vyākaraṇa*).

The Chapter on the City of Transformation concerns future disciples (the fifth [category], present and future). The *Śūraṅgama Samādhi Sūtra* clarifies four kinds of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*), which this present sūtra fully possesses:
the prediction for those who have not yet resolved their minds, as in the "Never-Disparaging" chapter; the prediction for those who have resolved their minds in the present;
and the threefold prediction regarding the non-arising of dharmas. Regarding the four *siddhāntas*: fundamentally, all Buddhas act for the sake of the Great Matter.
By means of this supramundane [teaching], all sentient beings have been enabled to open, reveal, awaken to, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;

now that this great matter has been manifested and the Buddha’s teaching is complete, and sentient beings have entered [the path], the Buddha’s original intention has been fulfilled. The aspirations of sentient beings are satisfied, and the Dharma ought to grant them a prediction of enlightenment.
Is it not as when a father meets his son and does not entrust him with his wealth? Furthermore, for immeasurable eons, practitioners have cultivated vows and aspirations.

In the present-day Buddha’s text, it says: "Because his original vow was such, he has obtained this prediction. These two conditions constitute the *loka-siddhānta* (worldly standpoint), and thus the prediction is given.

(The first concerns the correspondence between the capacity of the recipient and the response of the teacher; the second concerns the rapid capacity alone. Furthermore, when those of the two vehicles hear the sutra, they transform their Lesser Vehicle practice into the Great Vehicle;
since the perfect cause is already sufficient, the cause must inevitably bring forth its fruit. Therefore, the Tathāgata grants them the prediction, and the entire assembly knows it.

Making a vow to become an internal or external retinue for the *nirmāṇakāya* and *dharmakāya*, or vowing merely to be born in that land to benefit sentient beings—these two are recorded as being for the sake of the *puruṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint for persons), because [the first] has already produced one's own goodness and [the second] can produce the goodness of others.

Furthermore, the bestowal of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*) upon those of the two vehicles is intended to break the desire of bodhisattvas who would otherwise regress from the Great Vehicle and enter the Lesser Vehicle; for if there were truly fixed [realms] for the two vehicles from which one could regress, [such a teaching would be unnecessary].

1. To refute the evil of seeking to become a Lesser Vehicle practitioner now that [the two vehicles] no longer exist: "If there are no two vehicles, what is there to regress from? 2. To refute the evil of those who wish to give rise to the mind of the two vehicles:
"Since they have already abandoned me upon their realization, why would I take them up? 3. To directly refute the evil of the Lesser Vehicle for those who have not yet changed:
"Then one simply reforms the Lesser. 4. To refute [the clinging to] the Lesser for those about to realize it: "One then does not take that realization."

Furthermore, these four are recorded because they constitute the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint of remedial treatment). Moreover, the manifestation of non-arising must necessarily arise from the true understanding that opens up the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*) without error;

therefore, they are granted the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*). Furthermore, although all sentient beings possess only the correct [condition] and the objectless [condition], when those of the Lesser Vehicle hear this sutra and attain faith and understanding, their conditions for the correct and the objectless are fully complete, thereby opening up the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; thus, they are granted the prediction.
The prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) regarding these two is based on the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the ultimate established truth); thus, this fourfold prediction exhaustively encompasses all predictions.
When those of middling faculties hear the Dharma during the two weeks of the parable and the [Lotus] Sūtra, the three are opened up to reveal the One, and they attain full understanding.

Although the Tathāgata confirms their realization, even though they know for themselves that they will become Buddhas, the timing and circumstances remain uncertain; yet, were they to receive the Buddha’s sincere [assurance]...

To speak of "bestowing" means that when one receives a definitive prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) regarding the certainty of the future fruit, the kalpa, the land, and the nearness or distance [of its attainment], one experiences great joy;

because this name is received from the Buddha’s bestowal, it is called the "Chapter on Bestowing Predictions" (*Vyākaraṇa-parivarta*). Furthermore, speaking generally, recording the affairs of the ten realms is all termed "bestowing predictions.
Here, however, we record only those who will become Buddhas. Moreover, while Buddhas of all four teachings receive predictions, here the focus is solely upon [the Buddha of] the present.
Furthermore, regarding the two types of predictions—those for the *dharmakāya* and those for the *nirmāṇakāya*—for now we shall consider the *nirmāṇakāya*.

In terms of the fundamental and the manifested, the great disciples have long since received their predictions; however, here they are shown to receive them for the first time as a manifestation to lead those who practice through contemplation of the mind.

Those who can contemplate the nature of the mind as being emptiness, provisionality, and the Middle are granted predictions by all Buddhas, and they are likewise able to grant all such predictions, as is the constant rule.

Not Disparaging. △ The fourth section of the Parable Chapter consists of two parts: the bestowing of predictions upon those of middle capacity, and the granting of permission for those of inferior capacity to recount their past lives.
In the first [of these], there are two sub-sections: first, the bestowing of the prediction upon Mahākāśyapa; second, the bestowing of predictions upon three other individuals.
In the first of these, there are again two parts: first, the prose section; second, the verse section. The prose section is divided into six parts; first, the practice.
[This leads] through the six stages to purity. First:
At that time, after the World-Honored One had spoken these verses, he addressed the great assembly, proclaiming these words:
"This disciple of mine, Mahākāśyapa, shall in a future age behold and serve three hundred trillion Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones."
Having made offerings, paid homage, revered, and praised [the Buddhas], they widely proclaimed the immeasurable Great Dharma of all Buddhas.
When the World-Honored One entered parinirvāṇa, Kāśyapa addressed the great assembly: "The relics of the Tathāgata are not our concern;
our concern is that we should compile the treasury of the Dharma so that the True Dharma does not perish too quickly. Thus he widely proclaimed this.
This is a clear testimony of the Great Dharma. Having transmitted the Buddha’s Mind-Seal, he served as the First Patriarch in the Western Land with such bitter resolve;
yet even after beholding all the Buddhas of the ten directions, he was only then shown to have attained Buddhahood.
Alas, alas! that people of today, upon merely obtaining some slight glimmer of light and shadow, immediately wish to revile the Buddhas and scold the Patriarchs. △ Second, attaining the fruit.
In his final body, he attained Buddhahood, named the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha,
Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, known as Prabhāsa.
Because his body was perfectly complete with a mass of purple-gold light during the causal stage, he is named *Prabhāsa* (Radiance) as a Tathāgata in the fruit stage;
furthermore, because he maintains the Great Dharma and universally illumines all things, he is called Radiance. △ Third, the name of the kalpa and the land.
The name of the land is Radiant Virtue, and the name of the eon is Great Adornment.
△ Fourth, the lifespan:
the Buddha’s lifespan is twelve minor eons.
△ 5. The duration of the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma:
The True Dharma remains in the world for twenty minor kalpas, and the Semblance Dharma likewise remains for twenty minor kalpas.
△ 6. The purity of the land.
The borders of that land are magnificently adorned, free from all filth, evil, tiles, rubble, thorns, excrement, or impurities.

Its terrain is level and even, without elevations, depressions, pits, or mounds; its ground is made of lapis lazuli, with rows of jewel-trees and golden cords demarcating the sides of the roads, strewn everywhere with various precious flowers, and is entirely pure. In that land, there are immeasurable thousands of billions of bodhisattvas.
The assembly of śrāvakas was likewise incalculable; there were no demonic activities, for although Māra and his followers were present, they all protected the Buddha-dharma.

Because they had, during their causal stage, deeply protected and upheld the True Dharma with a sincere heart, they have now attained a pure land free from demonic interference. All other matters are as previously described.

The long prose section at the beginning of the text concludes. △ Second, the Verses in Repetition (Gāthā), in five parts: first, verses on practicing the causes to obtain the fruit; [and so forth] up to fifth, the general conclusion. Now, the first:
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
He addressed the bhikṣus: "With my Buddha-eye, I see that this Kāśyapa shall, after incalculable kalpas in a future age, attain Buddhahood.
In a future age, he shall make offerings to and attend upon three hundred trillion Buddha-Bhagavāns, purifying his brahma-conduct for the sake of the wisdom of a Buddha;
having made offerings to the Supreme Honored One among bipeds, he shall cultivate all [perfections]."
Having attained unsurpassed wisdom, he becomes a Buddha in his final body.
△ Second, the verse on the purity of the land:
His land is pure, with lapis lazuli for its ground; many jewel trees line the sides of the roads, and golden cords demarcate the paths.
Those who see it rejoice; it constantly emits exquisite fragrances and is adorned with various famous flowers of many wondrous kinds.
Its ground is level and even, without hills or pits. The assembly of Bodhisattvas is beyond measure;

their minds are harmonious and supple, they have attained great supernormal powers, and they uphold the Mahāyāna sūtras of all Buddhas. The assembly of Śrāvakas consists of those in their final bodies, free from outflows.
The sons of the Dharma King are likewise incalculable; even with the divine eye, one cannot count or know them.
△ Third, the verse on the Buddha’s lifespan:
That Buddha’s lifespan shall be twelve minor kalpas.
△ Fourth, the verses on the True Dharma and Semblance Dharma:
The True Dharma remains in the world for twenty minor kalpas, and the Semblance Dharma likewise remains for twenty minor kalpas.
△ Fifth, the summary: the names of the kalpas and the lands are omitted and not versified.
Such were the events concerning the World-Honored One Prabhāsa.
Having finished bestowing the prediction upon Mahākāśyapa, [the text proceeds to] Part Two: Bestowing Predictions upon Three Persons. This has two sections: First, the Request for Predictions;

Second, the Granting of Predictions. The first section has four parts: First, the Formal Request; Second, Establishing a Simile; Third, Applying the Dharma; Fourth, Concluding the Request. Now, the first part.
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Subhūti, Mahākātyāyana, and the others were all struck with awe;
with single-minded devotion, they joined their palms, gazed up at the Honored One’s countenance without averting their eyes for even a moment, and together spoke these verses in unison:
The Great Hero, the World-Honored One, the Dharma King of all Śākyas, out of compassion for us, has bestowed this Buddha-voice.

Those who were trembling have been transformed from the Small Vehicle into the Great Vehicle; it is not merely a shedding of skin and changing of bones—it is truly a state where heaven revolves and earth turns.
△ Second, the establishment of analogies.
If one knows that my deep intention is to grant them the prediction of enlightenment, it is like sprinkling nectar to remove heat and attain coolness; yet,
it is as if one who has come from a land of famine suddenly encounters the meal of a great king— the mind still harbors doubt and fear, and does not dare to eat immediately,
but only after receiving the king’s command does one then dare to eat.
△ Third, the Convergence of Dharmas.
We are likewise; though we constantly contemplate the faults of the Hīnayāna, we do not know how we shall attain the Buddha’s unsurpassed wisdom.
Although we hear the Buddha’s voice saying, "I declare that you shall become Buddhas," our hearts still harbor anxiety and fear, as if we did not yet dare to eat.
If we are granted a prediction of enlightenment by the Buddha, only then shall we find true peace and joy.
△ Fourth, the conclusion of the request:
O Great Hero, O Fierce World-Honored One, who ever desires to bring peace to the world, we pray that you grant us this prediction, just as one who suffers from hunger requires instruction on food.
The initial request for a prediction is concluded. △ Second, the granting of predictions, in three parts: first, the prediction for Subhūti; second, the prediction for Kātyāyana;
third, the prediction for Maudgalyāyana. Within the first [of these], there are two sections: first, the long prose; second, the verses. Within the long prose, there are five sections:
first, the cultivation of causes (extending to) the fifth, the True and Semblance Dharma periods. Now, the first [section].
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing what was in the minds of his great disciples, addressed the bhikṣus:
"This Subhūti, in a future age, shall behold three million billion nayutas of Buddhas, making offerings to them, honoring, respecting, and praising them;
he shall constantly practice the pure conduct and fulfill the path of a bodhisattva."
△ Second, attaining the fruit:
In his final body, he attained Buddhahood, being named the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna,
Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.

Now, as for the name "Born of Emptiness" (Śūnyatā-ja), those who speak of names and marks (nāma-lakṣaṇa) must understand that names and marks are fundamentally empty; emptiness itself is fully endowed with all names and marks.
This differs from merely manifesting traces in stone chambers to contemplate emptiness, which leads only to the realization of a partial principle. △ Third, the Adornment of Kalpas and Lands.
The eon was named Possessing Jewels (*Ratnavatī*) and the land was named Jewel-Born (*Ratnasaṃbhava*).

Its terrain was level and even, with ground made of lapis lazuli, adorned with jewel-trees and free from mounds, pits, gravel, thorns, or the filth of excrement and urine. Precious flowers covered the earth everywhere, making it utterly pure.
The people of that land all dwelt within jeweled terraces and exquisite pavilions, and its śrāvaka disciples were immeasurable and boundless.
The assembly of bodhisattvas, numbering in the countless thousands of myriads of koṭis of nayutas, is beyond what can be known through calculation or analogy.
△ Fourth, regarding the lifespan:
the Buddha’s lifespan shall be twelve minor kalpas.
△ Fifth, the True and Semblance Dharma.
The True Dharma shall remain in the world for twenty minor kalpas, and the Semblance Dharma shall likewise remain for twenty minor kalpas.
That Buddha constantly dwells in the void, preaching the Dharma for the sake of the assembly and delivering immeasurable multitudes of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.
Constantly abiding in the midst of empty space is the emptiness of the ultimate meaning of the Middle Way. [The long prose section ends. △ Second, the Verses in Repetition (Geya), in five parts:
first, the exhortation to listen; second, the verses on practicing the causes to obtain the fruit; ... up to fifth, the verses on the True and Semblance Dharma. Now, the first part.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"O assembly of bhikṣus, I now address you all: you should listen with a single mind to what I shall say."
△ Second, the verse on attaining the fruit through the cause of practice:
"My great disciple Subhūti shall become a Buddha named Lakṣaṇasampanna;
he shall make offerings to countless myriads of koṭis of Buddhas, follow the conduct of the Buddhas, gradually fulfill the Great Way, and in his final body attain the thirty-two marks."
He is upright and exquisite, like a mountain of jewels.
△ Third, a verse on the purity of the land:
That Buddha-land is most sublime and pure; among all beings who see it, there are none who do not love and rejoice in it, and the Buddha dwells therein.
He delivers immeasurable multitudes; within his Buddha-dharma there are many bodhisattvas, all of whom possess sharp faculties and turn the irreversible wheel.
That land is constantly adorned by bodhisattvas, while the assembly of śrāvakas is beyond counting;

they have all attained the three knowledges, are endowed with the six supernormal powers, abide in the eight liberations, and possess great majestic virtue. When that Buddha preaches the Dharma, he manifests it in immeasurable ways.
The inconceivable supernormal transformations and all the devas and humans, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, joined their palms together to listen to and receive the Buddha’s words.
△ Fourth, the verse on the lifespan.
That Buddha’s lifespan shall be twelve minor kalpas.
△ Fifth, the verse on the True Dharma and Semblance Dharma:
the True Dharma shall remain in the world for twenty minor kalpas, and the Semblance Dharma shall likewise remain for twenty minor kalpas.
The first record concerning Subhūti is completed. △ Second, the record concerning Kātyāyana has two parts: first, the long prose; second, the verse summary.
Within the long prose, there are five sections: first, practicing the causes; [up to] fifth, the True and Semblance Dharma eras. Now, the first section.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the assembly of bhikṣus:
"I now tell you, Mahākātyāyana, in a future age shall offer all manner of requisites to serve and honor eight thousand billion buddhas;
he shall revere and respect these buddhas, and after each has passed into extinction, he shall erect a stupa for each, one thousand yojanas in height and five hundred yojanas in length and breadth."

Having made offerings to the stupas and temples with flowers, necklaces, unguents, powdered incense, burning incense, silk canopies, banners, and streamers— all composed of the seven treasures of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, agate, pearl, and ruby—
and having thereafter likewise made offerings to twenty trillion buddhas, he shall fulfill the path of a bodhisattva after making offerings to all these buddhas.
△ Second, the attainment of the fruit:
He shall attain Buddhahood and be named Yaṃvunadīkanakaprabha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna,
Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
△ Third, the purity of the three realms.
Its land is level and even, with crystal for its ground, adorned with precious trees. Golden cords demarcate the sides of the paths, and exquisite flowers cover the earth everywhere, pure throughout;
those who see it rejoice. There are no four evil realms: no hells, no hungry ghosts, [no animals, and no asuras].
The realms of animals and asuras abound with devas, humans, śrāvakas, and bodhisattvas;
immeasurable tens of billions adorn that land.
△ Fourth, the lifespan.
The Buddha’s lifespan will be twelve minor kalpas.
△ Fifth, regarding the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma:
the True Dharma shall abide in the world for twenty minor kalpas, and the Semblance Dharma shall likewise abide for twenty minor kalpas.
The long prose section concludes. △ Second, the Verses in Repetition (Geya), in four parts: first, the exhortation to listen; fourth, the verses on the purity of the land. Now, the first:
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
All you assembly of bhikṣus, listen with one-pointed mind; that which I have spoken is true and without variation.
△ Second, the verse on the causes of practice:
"Kātyāyana, you should provide various kinds of excellent offerings to the Buddhas, and after the Buddhas have passed into extinction..."
They shall erect stupas made of the seven treasures and likewise offer flowers and incense to the śarīra.
△ Third, the verse on attaining the fruit:
In their final body, they shall attain the wisdom of a Buddha and realize equal and perfect enlightenment.
△ The four verses describe the purity of the land in brief; they do not mention the duration of the True and Semblance Dharma periods.
The land is pure, liberating immeasurable billions of sentient beings, all of whom are venerated by those of the ten directions.
The Buddha’s radiance is unsurpassed, and his name is Jambūnada-prabhāsa (Jambu-Golden Light). His bodhisattvas and śrāvakas—
His land is adorned with the infinite and innumerable severance of all existence and non-existence.
Second, the prediction for Kātyāyana is concluded. △ Third, the prediction for Maudgalyāyana, in two parts: first, the long prose section; second, the verses.
Within the first part, there are five sections: first, the cultivation of causes; [up to] fifth, the true and semi-dharma periods. Now, the first section.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the great assembly:
"I now tell you, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, you shall provide various kinds of offerings to eight thousand Buddhas, honoring and respecting them with reverence.

After those Buddhas have passed into extinction, you shall each erect stūpas and temples one thousand yojanas in height, and five hundred yojanas in length and breadth, made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and mother-of-pearl."
After making offerings with agate, pearls, roses, and necklaces of garlands composed of the seven treasures, as well as ointments, powdered incense, burning incense,
silk canopies, banners, and streamers, he shall likewise make similar offerings to two hundred trillion buddhas thereafter.
△ Second, the attainment of the fruit:
One shall attain Buddhahood, with the name Tāmālapatrā-candanagandha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna,
Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
Venerable One.
△ Third, the eon and the land:
the eon is named Joy-Fulfillment and the land is named Intention-Desire; its terrain is level and even, with lapis lazuli for its ground, adorned by jewel-trees.
Scattered true pearl flowers pervade everywhere, pure and causing all who see them to rejoice; there are immeasurable numbers of devas, humans, bodhisattvas, and śrāvakas.
△ Fourth, the lifespan.
The Buddha’s lifespan is twenty-four minor kalpas.
△ Fifth, regarding the True Dharma and Semblance Dharma:
the True Dharma shall remain in the world for forty minor kalpas, and the Semblance Dharma shall likewise remain for forty minor kalpas.
The long prose section concludes. △ Second, the verses in five parts: first, verses on the causes of practice (up to) five verses on the True and Semblance Dharma periods.
Now, the first:
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
After this disciple of mine, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, has cast off this body, he shall behold eight thousand two hundred myriads of koṭis of Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones;
for the sake of the Buddha-way, he shall make offerings to and revere these Buddhas, constantly practicing the Brahma-faring in their presence.
For immeasurable kalpas, he shall uphold the Buddha-dharma, and after the parinirvāṇa of those Buddhas, he shall erect stupas made of the seven treasures, complete with tall poles and golden finials.
One makes offerings to the stupas and temples of the Buddhas with flowers, incense, music, and performances.
As for *kṣetra*, the full term is *kṣetra-ma*; this is translated as "field" (*tǔtián*), referring to a pillar erected as a *kṣetra* to indicate the location where one resides.
△ Second, a verse concerning the attainment of the fruit together with the name of the land:
Having gradually perfected the bodhisattva path, he shall attain buddhahood in the land of *Manoratha*, where his name shall be *Tamālapatracandanagandha*.
△ Three verses on the lifespan:
that Buddha’s lifespan will be twenty-four kalpas.
△ Four verses on the purity of the land.

He constantly expounds the Buddha-way for devas and humans; his śrāvakas are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, possessing the three knowledges and six supernatural powers and great majestic virtue.
His bodhisattvas are countless, firm in resolve and diligent in effort, all of whom have attained non-retrogression regarding the wisdom of the Buddha.
△ Fifth, the verses on the True and Semblance Dharma:
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma shall remain for forty minor kalpas, and the Semblance Dharma shall likewise remain for that duration.
This concludes the initial bestowing of predictions upon those of medium faculties. △ Second, the promise to speak of past lives for the sake of those of inferior faculties.
"My disciples, numbering five hundred, who are endowed with majestic virtue, shall all receive predictions that in a future age they will all attain Buddhahood.
I shall now explain the karmic causes and conditions from our past lives between myself and you; listen well."

Those of inferior capacity, having already heard the Dharma and the parable for two cycles and having witnessed the bestowal of predictions upon those of superior and middling capacity, might still harbor doubts and fail to understand;

therefore, out of a desire to inspire deep shame [in them], the first six lines grant a general prediction, and the subsequent four lines grant the explanation of past conditions, thereby drawing them forward. This concludes the second cycle of the parable.

Composed by the later student of the Ancient Wu region, Ouyi Zhixu.
△ The explanation of the "Bestowal of Prophecies" chapter is concluded. Next, the "Parable of the Phantom City" chapter is explained.

In the seventh chapter, "The Parable of the Phantom City," "phantom" (hua) refers to that which is produced by supernatural power (*ṛddhi*). Because it is produced by supernatural power, that which was non-existent suddenly appears; this is termed a "phantom."

To prevent wrongdoing and ward off enemies is called a "city"; this is analogous to the *nirvāṇa* of the Two Vehicles, which is produced by provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) for the sake of transformation (*pariṇāmanā*).

By the power of provisional wisdom, that which is non-existent is taught as having utility for the purpose of transformation; to prevent conceptualization and ward off views, it is termed "Nirvāṇa" as a place of rest and relief.

This serves to introduce [beings]—first into the *Sūtra-piṭaka* (the "resting place of the two *sūtras*"), and then into the *Lotus Sūtra* (the "entrance to the reality"). Although it is not yet ultimate, it is spoken of as "extinction."

Because the crossing [of the city] is provisionally established through skillful means, it is called the "Parable of the Phantom City," as explained previously; this is an explanation based on causes and conditions (*nidāna*).

If one speaks from the perspective of the capacity of the audience (*yathā-vaineya*), that which was non-existent suddenly appears is the worldly benefit (*loka-artha*); having seen it and giving rise to joy is the benefit for persons (*pudgala-artha*); preventing wrongdoing and warding off enemies is the remedial benefit (*pratipakṣa-artha*);

and speaking of extinction (*nirvāṇa*) is the benefit of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-artha*). If one speaks from the perspective of the response [of the Buddha], the provisional establishment of this city is the worldly transformation (*loka-nirmāṇa*); generating small roots of goodness is the transformation for persons (*pudgala-nirmāṇa*); temporarily removing the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) is the remedial transformation (*pratipakṣa-nirmāṇa*); and ultimately leading them into the Great [Vehicle] is the transformation of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-nirmāṇa*). This is according to [the classification].

Regarding the "Teacher," the Three Piṭakas conceive of *nirvāṇa* as a state of security and conceive of it as final extinction; thus, their teaching for the two vehicles is identical to that of the Three Piṭakas.
It is not so for the Bodhisattva. As the *Śāstra* states: "It is like a father who, having crossed a perilous place, has one foot already inside the city and the other outside the gate.
Because he remembers his son, he returns from the city to the perilous place, vowing to support his remaining habits [of affliction] and enter into *saṃsāra*."
Yet one does not take emptiness as the final realization. In the Separate Teaching (biejiao), it is not said that the city is like an illusion;

rather, one uses the city to defend against dangers and passes through its gates directly, employing the city as a skillful means (*upāya*) to sever the delusions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*), without claiming this to be the ultimate.

In the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao), one knows there is no threat of bandits and thus no need for a city; therefore, it speaks of the "illusory city" (*nirmita-pura*). This is now the intent of the Perfect Teaching.

Therefore, it is titled "The Parable of the City of Transformation" (Hua-cheng-yu-pin). In the teachings of the Complete Teaching (*yuanjiao*), the term "transformation" (*hua*) refers to what was previously rejected and dismissed as being merely "unfit," for it had never been said that *nirvāṇa* itself is a transformation.

Only now, through the diligent application of this teaching that reveals the provisional (*kaiquan*), is it finally declared to be a transformation. Furthermore, when the provisional is revealed to be the real, the transformation becomes true; that is, it is the place of the treasure. Thus we know that in the *zang* and *tong* teachings, the ultimate is not a transformation; in the *bie* teaching, it is neither ultimate nor a transformation;

and in the *yuan* teaching, it is neither ultimate nor a transformation, yet it can be both ultimate and a transformation, and it can also be ultimate while not being a transformation. This differs in meaning from the terminology used in the *zang* and *tong* teachings. When speaking here according to the intent of the Complete Teaching, the term "transformation" is used provisionally because it serves to break through attachments; once the provisional has been opened and revealed, [the transformation is no longer such].

Regarding the non-false nature of the fundamental and the manifested (*honjaku*): if explained from the perspective of the capacity of the audience, one should say that the fundamental resides in the city of the three virtues while the manifested enters the city of transformation.

If explained from the perspective of the response, then the manifested demonstrates the teaching of transformation. Regarding the contemplation of the mind: contemplating that phenomena arising from causes and conditions are empty is entering the city of transformation;
that causes and conditions are provisional is exiting the city of transformation; and that causes and conditions are the Middle Way is [the ultimate realization].

This is the place of refuge for jewels; furthermore, observing emptiness as itself the Middle Way means that one understands transformation as non-transformation, which is the provisional as the real.

Moreover, the "transformed city" and the "jeweled abode" are discussed generally in terms of the six stages of realization (*liu ji*): when the nature of the mind is fundamentally empty, there is no time it is not empty—this principle is the transformed city.
When the nature of the mind is fundamentally the Middle Way, there is no time it is not the Middle Way—this principle is the jeweled abode. Upon hearing this principle of nature...

The "Transformation City of Names" (*nāma-nirmita-pura*) refers to the ability to generate faith and understanding; the "Transformation City of the Treasure Place" (*ratna-sthāna-nirmita-pura*) refers to the complete subduing of the five stages of dwelling (*pañca-vāsabhūmi*).

One should understand that the subsequent stages up to the ultimate fruit follow this same analogy. Question: Since this chapter explains matters of causes and conditions (*nidāna*) through which those of inferior capacity attain awakening, it should be titled the "Chapter on Past Lives" (*pūrva-janma-parivarta*).

Answer: At the beginning of the chapter, the causes and conditions are explained in detail, while at the end, the parable is concluded. Thus, it is appropriately titled according to its primary content.

If the "transformed city" were discussed from the beginning, it should have been called the "Sutra of Past Lives"; however, because the sūtra-author proceeds from the end, he speaks of the "transformed city.
Furthermore, those of superior faculties have thin doubts and thus require only the account of the seven days of contemplation under the Bodhi tree to clarify their karmic conditions;

those of middling faculties have thick doubts and thus require the addition of parables to explore and retrieve the unsurpassed path taught by twenty trillion Buddhas in order to clarify their karmic conditions.

Because the doubts of those with inferior faculties are even thicker, [the sūtra] clarifies the karmic conditions of past lives over vast eons. If one traces back from the beginning of these distant eons, it is called "past lives" (*pūrvajanman*);
if one refers to the intermediate stage, it is called the "transformed city" (*nirmita-pura*); and if one refers to the ultimate goal, it is called the "jeweled destination" (*ratnasthāna*).
Since the compiler of the sūtra adopts a middle position to encompass both the beginning and the end, he uses the term "transformed city" for the sake of this contextual convenience.

The Parable Chapter (in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, this is titled the "Chapter on the Past"; the reason for these questions and answers is as follows). Question: The conjured city is provisional, while the treasure site is real;
what is the meaning of abandoning the real to follow the provisional? Answer: Because one knows that the city is conjured, one thereby knows that the treasure site is real;

thus, by designating it as conjured, one does not lose the reality. △ Third, the exposition of the two [aspects] through causes and conditions: First, the formal exposition of the causes and conditions; second, the bestowal [of predictions].

Regarding the section on the prophecy for those of inferior faculties, there are two aspects: the recording of their realization and the restatement of the meaning. As for the sequence of these two, it is not fixed;

furthermore, their realization may be expressed either through silent contemplation or through speech. Since the textual variations are slight and insufficient to warrant a separate division, they are all included within the "Bestowal of Prophecy" section.
This section consists of two parts: first, the preliminary clarification that the vision of the distant past was attained long ago; second, the actual elucidation of his former lives.

Regarding the first two sections of the introductory causal narrative: first, the long prose; second, the verse summary. The long prose is divided into three parts: first, the presentation of what was seen;
second, the use of analogies to clarify the vastness of time; third, the conclusion that the past is just like the present. Now, for the first part:

The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: "In the distant past, immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. His land..."
The name of the eon was *Suprabha* (Good City), and the name of the bhikṣus was *Mahālakṣaṇa*. Since that Buddha passed into parinirvāṇa, a very long time has elapsed.
2. Illustrating the vastness of this duration through a simile:
Suppose there were a person who ground all the earth-element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*) within a trichiliocosm into ink.
Having passed through a thousand lands to the east, one places a dot as large as a minute mote of dust; having passed another thousand lands, one places another dot.
Continuing in this manner until all the ink from the "earth-element" (pṛthivī-dhātu) is exhausted—what do you think?
Would a mathematician or a mathematician’s disciple be able to reach the limit of those lands or know their number? "No, indeed."
World-Honored One, if one were to take all the lands through which these bhikṣus have passed and, whether marked or unmarked, grind them all into dust,

with each particle of dust representing one kalpa— since that Buddha entered parinirvāṇa, more than this number of immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of asaṃkhyeya kalpas have elapsed.
△ Third, regarding the past and the present seen through the three fetters:
"By means of the power of the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, I observe that which is long distant as if it were today.
This reveals that the Tathāgata’s three types of supernormal knowledge are far-reaching and luminous; having clearly and unfailingly recounted past events, he then proceeds to speak.
One should know that past conditions across the ten periods of time—ancient and modern—are in truth and reality never separate from the present thought-moment.
Apart from this present thought-mind, there is no other substantial dharma of coming or going to be found. Due to ignorance, one falsely conceives of transition and extinction;
within this transition and extinction, there is recollection and forgetfulness, and among those things remembered, there are those that are distant and those that are near.
However, whether the things remembered are distant or near, they are all the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) transformed by the single present thought-moment;
they do not exist as separate entities external to the mind. For instance, when we recall events from ten or twenty years ago, they appear vividly as if right before our eyes;
by this analogy, one can understand that the nature of the mind has, from the beginning, vertically penetrated through the three periods of time.
Throughout the three periods of time across all worlds, there is no appearance other than the single present thought-moment; it is solely because of ignorance that one cannot see afar.

Now that ignorance has been completely severed and the nature of the mind is transparently luminous, one’s clear perception extends vertically to the beginning and end of the three periods of time and horizontally to the furthest limits of the Dharma-realm.
How could such a brilliant vision and insight give rise to any doubt? [The long prose section concludes. △ Second, the Verse Summary:
First, the phenomena seen in the initial verse; second, the illustration through analogy to clarify the vast duration; third, seeing the past as it is now.
Regarding the first:
at that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
I recall that in the past, immeasurable and boundless kalpas ago, there was a Buddha, the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings, named Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū.
△ Second, a verse citing a simile to clarify the vast duration of time.
Suppose a person, by means of their strength, were to grind away the entire earth-element of a trichiliocosm until it was completely exhausted, using all that soil as ink.
Having passed through a thousand lands, they would drop a single speck of dust as a mark.

Continuing in this manner until all such specks of dust and ink were exhausted, let us assume that the number of these marked and unmarked lands were equal, and that they were all further ground into dust, with each single speck of dust representing one kalpa.
The number of kalpas since that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa exceeds even the number of these atoms; such immeasurable kalpas have passed since his passing.
△ Third, the verse on seeing the past as if it were now:
With unimpeded wisdom, the Tathāgata knows the parinirvāṇa of that Buddha, as well as his śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, as clearly as if they were passing away this very day.
"O Bhikṣus, you should know that the Buddha’s wisdom is pure, subtle, and wondrous; it is untainted and unimpeded, penetrating immeasurable kalpas.
It is pure because it is emptiness; it is subtle because it is the provisional; it is wondrous because it is the middle. Furthermore, the three wisdoms are one mind, thus it is pure;
one mind is the three wisdoms, thus it is subtle; it is neither one nor three, yet it is three and one, thus it is wondrous. Its essence is perfect and complete."
Therefore, because the function of the untainted [wisdom] is pervasive and all-encompassing, there is no obstruction; first, the long-term knowledge and vision of the distant past has been explained.

△ Second, the correct explanation of the causes and conditions of previous lives, which has two parts: first, the detailed narration; second, the restatement in verse. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, the cause for establishing the connection;
second, the actual establishment of the connection. Within the first of these, there are again two parts: first, the remote cause; second, the proximate cause. First [the remote cause].
Furthermore, there are two parts: first, clarifying the attainment of Buddhahood by Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū; second, clarifying the invitation of the Dharma by the Brahma Kings of the ten directions.
The first part has five sub-sections: first, the long duration of the Buddha’s lifespan; second, events prior to his attaining the Way; third, the actual clarification of his attainment of the Way;
fourth, the clarification of the offerings made by his retinue after his attainment of the Way; fifth, the request for him to turn the Wheel of Dharma. This is the first [sub-section].
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "The lifespan of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū was five hundred and forty million nayuta kalpas.
2. Matters Prior to Attaining Enlightenment.
That Buddha, having originally sat at the site of enlightenment and defeated the armies of Māra,
was on the verge of attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi when the dharmas of all Buddhas did not yet manifest before him. Thus he remained in the full lotus posture for one small kalpa,
and even up to ten small kalpas, with body and mind unmoving, yet the dharmas of all Buddhas still did not appear before him.
The Way of all Buddhas is the same, yet they differ according to the circumstances of their conditions. Śākyamuni practiced asceticism for six years, while Maitreya attained the Way on that very day;
another Buddha did not manifest for ten kalpas. This is not because their faculties are sharp or dull, nor because the Way is difficult or easy;

it is simply that the conditions require a long or short duration, and thus they manifest for a long or short time. In every place where the eight phases of manifestation are displayed, [it is the same].

First, regarding the subduing of Māra: according to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, this should also be gradual; yet, if one considers the subduing of Māra, it seems similar to a defiled land (*saṃkliṣṭa-kṣetra*).

However, if one considers the long lifespan [of the Buddha], it is not a defiled land. Therefore, we know that the characteristics of the shared lands (*sahā-loka*)—whether pure or defiled—are manifold, and matters such as the attainment of enlightenment do not necessarily coincide entirely with those of this land’s Tripiṭaka.

At that time (before the Buddha had yet sat at the site of enlightenment), the devas of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven first prepared for that Buddha a lion throne beneath the Bodhi tree, one yojana in height.
They all thought: "When the Buddha sits upon this, he shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
As soon as the Buddha sat upon this seat, the Brahma kings rained down various celestial flowers over an area of a hundred yojanas.
Every ten days, fragrant winds would come and blow away the withered flowers, raining down new ones in their place;
thus it continued without ceasing for ten intermediate kalpas as he made offerings to the Buddha. Even after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, he constantly rained these flowers.
The devas of the Four Great Kings constantly struck celestial drums to make offerings to the Buddha, while the other devas performed celestial music for ten intermediate kalpas until his passing.
The deliverance is likewise so.
△ Second, the actual explanation of the attainment of enlightenment:
"O Bhikṣus, after ten intermediate kalpas had passed, the Dharma of all Buddhas appeared before the Great Pervasive Wisdom-Victory Buddha."
He attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
△ Fourth, it clarifies the offerings made by his retinue after he attained the Way.
Before that Buddha left the household life, he had sixteen sons; the eldest was named Zhijí (Jñānakūṭa), and so were all his sons.

Each of them possessed various kinds of rare, extraordinary, and delightful objects; hearing that their father had attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they all abandoned what they held dear and went to the place where the Buddha was. Their mothers wept as they followed and escorted them.
Their grandfather, the Wheel-Turning Sage King (*cakravartin*), together with one hundred great ministers and hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of other people, all went along with them.
Surrounding him and following him to the site of enlightenment, they all desired to draw near to the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū in order to make offerings,
pay respect, honor, and praise him. Having arrived, they prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, circumambulated the Buddha, and then, with single-minded palms joined,
gazed up at the World-Honored One and spoke in verse:
