The World-Honored One of Great Majestic Virtue, for the sake of delivering sentient beings, attained Buddhahood only after immeasurable billions of years;
his vows were already fully perfected. How excellent! How auspicious and unsurpassed! O World-Honored One, you are truly rare:
for ten small kalpas while seated, your body, hands, and feet remained tranquil, peaceful, and unmoving; your mind was always serene and calm, never once becoming distracted.
Abiding in ultimate, eternal quiescence within the untainted Dharma, we now behold the World-Honored One having safely attained the Way of the Buddha;
we have gained great benefit and rejoice with immense joy. Sentient beings are constantly afflicted by suffering, blind and without a guide;
they do not recognize the path that exhausts suffering, nor do they know how to seek liberation. Thus, throughout the long night, the evil realms increase while the hosts of the devas diminish.
Passing from darkness into darkness, we have never heard the name of a Buddha until now.
That this Buddha has attained the supreme, peaceful, and untainted path brings the greatest benefit to us and all devas; therefore, we all prostrate and take refuge in the Unsurpassed Honored One.
Regarding the sixteen princes, if one explains them in terms of the manifest dharma, they represent the Eightfold Noble Path of both self-cultivation and the transformation of others.
△ Fifth, the Request to Turn the Wheel of Dharma:
At that time, after the sixteen princes had praised the Buddha with verses, they all exhorted the World-Honored One to turn the wheel of Dharma. They all said:
The World-Honored One has spoken this Dharma, bringing peace and security to many, out of compassion to benefit all devas and humans; he speaks these verses once more:
"The Hero of the World is peerless, adorned by a hundred merits; having attained unsurpassed wisdom, we pray that you will speak it for the sake of the world."
For the sake of delivering ourselves and all classes of sentient beings, please analyze and reveal this so that we may attain such wisdom.
If we are to become Buddhas, then so shall all sentient beings. World-Honored One, you know the thoughts within the deep hearts of sentient beings;
you know the paths they travel, as well as their power of wisdom, their inclinations, their cultivation of merit, and the karmic deeds performed in past lives.
The World-Honored One, having fully known this, shall turn the unsurpassed wheel.

Since it says "to cause them to attain this wisdom," and further says "if we ourselves were to attain Buddhahood," and concludes with "he shall turn the unsurpassed wheel," one should know that this is a request for the teaching of full syllables (*pūrṇa-akṣara*), such as the present *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*. This first clarifies [the request].

The Greatly Pervasive Wisdom-Victorious One (Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū) had completed his attainment of Buddhahood. △ Second, clarifying how the Brahma Kings of the ten directions requested the Dharma, in two parts:
first, the majestic light shines and moves; second, the Brahma Kings come to request the Dharma. Now, the first part.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "When the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, five million billion buddha-worlds in each of the ten directions shook in six ways.

In the regions between those lands that were dark and obscure, where even the majestic radiance of the sun and moon could not reach, there was now great illumination, and the sentient beings therein [were all made manifest]."
Each was able to see the others and they all spoke these words: "How is it that sentient beings have suddenly appeared here?

Furthermore, the various celestial palaces and even the Brahma palaces within that realm shook in six ways, and a great light shone everywhere, filling the entire world and surpassing the radiance of all the devas.

When the Buddha descended as a spirit, at the time of his birth, and at the time of his attainment of enlightenment, it is the natural law (*dharmatā*) that the world shakes and a great light shines everywhere.
Those who possess the karmic affinity perceive this even from afar; those who lack the affinity do not know of it even when nearby.

Regarding the *Śikṣānanda’s Commentary on the Contemplation of the Mind*: "The sudden arising of sentient beings occurs because the nature of the mind is fundamentally pure, yet it becomes obscured by the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*"), thereby falling into darkness.

If one cultivates contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā*), the principle of the fundamental nature is revealed; furthermore, the two mountains are the Two Truths, and that which lies between them is the Middle Way.
The light of the sun and moon is the Two Wisdoms, while the Buddha-light is the Middle Way, the non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).

When this light illuminates the original Three Truths, they are all clearly manifest. △ Second, the Brahma King comes to request [instruction]. Part five: First, the Eastern direction; second, the Southeastern direction.
3. The South; 4. A General Summary of the Remaining Six Directions; 5. The Upper Direction; First, the East: 6.1. Witnessing the Auspicious Omen with Astonishment;
6.2. Mutual Inquiry and Resolution; 6.3. Seeing the Buddha by Following the Light; 6.4. Making Offerings through the Three Karmas; 6.5. Requesting the Turning of the Dharma Wheel;
6.6. The Tathāgata’s Silent Consent. Now, the first [section].
At that time, within five hundred million worlds in the eastern direction, the palaces of the Brahmā heavens were illuminated with a radiance twice as bright as their usual light.
Each of the Brahmā kings thought to himself: "The radiance of these palaces now is unlike anything seen before;
by what cause and condition has this sign appeared?"
△ Second, the mutual inquiry and resolution.
At that time, the various Brahma kings each went to one another and deliberated together on this matter.
Then, among that assembly, there was a Great Brahma King named Savior of All, who spoke these verses for the sake of the Brahma hosts:
"The radiance of our various palaces is such as we have never known before; what is the cause and condition for this? We should each seek it together:
has a Great Virtuous One been born, or has a Buddha appeared in the world, that this great radiance shines everywhere throughout the ten directions?"
△ Seeing the Buddha by means of a three-fathom radiance.
At that time, the Brahma Kings of five million billion lands, together with their palaces,
each took heavenly flowers in the folds of their robes and went collectively toward the west to investigate this sign, where they beheld the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū.
At the site of enlightenment, seated upon the lion throne beneath the Bodhi tree, he was respectfully surrounded by devas,
nāga kings, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others; they also saw the sixteen princes requesting the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma.
△ Fourth, the offering of the three karmas.
At that moment, the Brahma Kings prostrated themselves before the Buddha and circumambulated him a hundred thousand times. They then scattered celestial flowers over the Buddha;
the flowers thus scattered were like Mount Sumeru, and they also used them to make offerings to the Bodhi tree of the Buddha. Its Bodhi...
Having made offerings of flowers from *tāla* trees ten *yojana*s high, each offered their own palace to that Buddha and spoke these words:
"May you look upon us with compassion and benefit us; we pray that you graciously accept and dwell in the palaces we have presented.
Then, before the Buddha, all the Brahma kings with one mind and in unison recited this verse:
The World-Honored One is most rare and difficult to encounter; he is endowed with immeasurable merit and is the Great Teacher capable of rescuing and protecting all devas and humans.
Out of compassion for the world, all sentient beings throughout the ten directions universally receive his benefit.
We have come from five hundred million *koṭis* of lands, having abandoned the joy of profound meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) in order to make offerings to the Buddha.
"We have previously accumulated merit such that our palaces are most magnificent and adorned; we now offer them to the World-Honored One, and pray that you will compassionately accept them.
[The Buddha] asked: "Brahmā, when the rain of flowers falls like Mount Sumeru, how do the trees, thrones, and seats remain as they were without being obstructed?
[Brahmā] replied: "Such inconceivable matters do not obstruct one another. △ Fifth, the request to turn the Wheel of Dharma.
At that time, after the Brahma kings had praised the Buddha with verses, they each spoke these words:

"We pray only that the World-Honored One will turn the wheel of Dharma to deliver and liberate sentient beings, opening the path to Nirvana. Then, the Brahma kings, with one mind and in unison, spoke these verses:
"O Hero of the World, Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings, we pray that you will expound the Dharma, using the power of great compassion to deliver sentient beings from suffering.
Since it says "to deliver sentient beings from suffering," this is a request for the teaching of the "half-syllables" (the elementary teachings), such as those given at the Deer Park.
△ Sixth, the Tathāgata’s silent assent.
At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū silently granted his consent.
It is the natural law regarding the ritual for receiving an invitation from the Buddhas that they all grant silent assent;

this is because they follow the rules established by previous Buddhas, because it engenders respect and yearning in people, because they differ from ordinary beings and non-Buddhists, and because it enables one to witness the Way directly.

The first section, the Eastern Quarter, concludes. △ Second, the Southeastern Quarter, in six parts: first, witnessing the auspicious signs and being struck with awe (up to) the sixth part, the Tathāgatas’ silent assent. Now, the first [part].

Furthermore, the great Brahma kings of five hundred million worlds in the southeastern direction each saw their own palaces brilliantly illuminated by a light never seen before; they leaped for joy and gave rise to a sense of wonder.
△ Second, mutual inquiry and resolution. That is,
when they each went to one another’s place to discuss this matter together, there was among that assembly a Great Brahmā King named Mahākāruṇika,
who spoke these verses for the sake of the host of Brahmās:
"For what cause and condition has such a sign appeared? The radiance of our various palaces is unlike anything we have ever seen before.
Is it because a Great Virtuous One has been born, or has a Buddha appeared in the world? We have never seen such a sign before;

let us together with one mind seek it out across thousands of millions of billions of lands, following this light to investigate it. It is most likely that a Buddha has appeared in the world to deliver sentient beings from suffering."
△ Third: Seeing the Buddha by means of light three *vyāma* long.

At that time, five million billion Brahma Kings, together with their palaces, each took celestial flowers in the folds of their robes and went collectively toward the northwest to investigate this sign. There they beheld the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū residing there.
At the site of enlightenment, seated upon the lion throne beneath the Bodhi tree, he was respectfully surrounded by devas, nāga kings, gandharvas, kiṃnaras,
mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others; they also beheld the sixteen princes entreating the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma.
△ Fourth, the offering of the three karmas.

At that time, the Brahma Kings prostrated themselves with their heads at the Buddha’s feet and circumambulated him hundreds of thousands of times. They then scattered celestial flowers over the Buddha;
the flowers thus scattered were like Mount Sumeru, and they also used these flowers to make offerings to the Buddha’s Bodhi tree.
Each having offered their own palace to that Buddha, they spoke these words: "May you look upon us with compassion and benefit us;
we pray that you graciously accept the palaces we have offered. Then, before the Buddha, all the Brahma kings, with single-minded devotion and in unison, spoke in verse:

To the Holy Lord, King of Devas, with the voice of a kalaviṅka, who has compassion for all sentient beings—we now pay homage to the World-Honored One, who is most rare and appears but once after a vast interval.
For one hundred and eighty kalpas, time passed in vain without a Buddha;
the three evil realms were filled and the hosts of devas diminished. Now the Buddha has appeared in the world to act as the eye for all sentient beings.
The refuge and protector for all that the world turns toward, the father of sentient beings who brings compassion and benefit—
through the auspicious merit of our past lives, we have now encountered the World-Honored One.
△ 5. Requesting the Turning of the Wheel of Dharma.
At that time, after the Brahma Kings had praised the Buddha with verses, each spoke these words:

"We pray only that the World-Honored One, out of compassion for all beings, will turn the wheel of Dharma to deliver and liberate sentient beings. Then, the Brahma Kings, with one mind and in unison, [spoke thus]...
He spoke in verse:
"The Great Sage turns the wheel of Dharma, revealing the characteristics of all phenomena to deliver sentient beings from suffering and affliction, causing them to attain great joy.
When sentient beings hear this Dharma, they attain the Way or are reborn in heaven; those in the evil realms diminish, while those who practice patience and goodness increase."
This is likewise the same as the previous request for the teaching of the "half-letters. △ Sixth, the Tathāgata’s silent assent:
At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū silently granted his permission.

The second [section], the Southeastern Quarter, concludes. △ Third, the Southern Quarter, in six parts: first, witnessing the auspicious omen and being struck with awe (up to) the sixth, the Tathāgata’s silent assent. Now, the first:
Furthermore, the great Brahma kings of five million billion lands in the southern direction each saw their own palaces.
The splendor of the palace shone with a brilliance never seen before; they were filled with joy and leaped for gladness, giving rise to a sense of wonder.
△ Second, mutual inquiry and resolution:
They immediately went to one another and deliberated together on this matter, asking, "By what causes and conditions does our palace possess such radiance?"
Now, within that assembly, there was a Great Brahmā King named Subhadharma, who spoke these verses for the sake of the Brahmā hosts:
"The radiance of our palaces is exceedingly majestic and brilliant; this cannot be without cause or condition—we should seek the reason for this sign."
"Never before in hundreds of thousands of kalpas have we seen such a sign; it must be that a Great Virtuous One has been born, or a Buddha has appeared in the world.
△ Third, seeking the light and seeing the Buddha:
At that time, five million billion Brahma Kings, together with their palaces, each took various [offerings] in the laps of their robes.
Together with the celestial flowers, they proceeded to the north to investigate this sign;
there they saw the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū at the site of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree, seated upon a lion throne, surrounded by respectful offerings from devas,
nāga kings, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, as well as seeing the sixteen princes requesting the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma.
The Wheel of Dharma.
△ Fourth, the offering of the three karmas:
At that time, the Brahma Kings prostrated themselves before the Buddha, circumambulated him a hundred thousand times, and immediately scattered celestial flowers over the Buddha.
The flowers scattered above were like Mount Sumeru, which they offered to the Buddha’s Bodhi tree.
Having made this offering, each presented their own palace to that Buddha and spoke these words: "May you look upon us with compassion and benefit us;
we pray that you graciously accept the palaces we have offered. At that time, the Brahma Kings stood before the Buddha.
With one mind, they praised him in verse, saying:
"The World-Honored One is exceedingly difficult to behold; he who has shattered all afflictions has been seen but once in over thirteen hundred kalpas.
Today, with the rain of Dharma, he satisfies all sentient beings who were once hungry and thirsty—beings such as we have never before beheld, possessed of immeasurable wisdom."
Just as the udumbara flower is encountered only today, so too have our various palaces been adorned by the light;
out of the World-Honored One’s great compassion and pity, we pray that you will graciously accept them.
△ 5. Requesting the Turning of the Wheel of Dharma.
At that time, after the Brahma Kings had praised the Buddha in verse, they each spoke these words:
"We pray only that the World-Honored One will turn the Wheel of Dharma, so that all the world—including its devas, Māras, Brahmas, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas—may all attain peace and security."
At the time of his liberation, the Brahma Kings, with one mind and in unison, spoke in verse:
"We pray that the Honored One among gods and humans will turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma; strike the great drum of the Dharma and blow the great conch of the Dharma;
rain down the great rain of the Dharma to deliver immeasurable sentient beings. We all join in this request: please manifest your profound and far-reaching voice."

Since it is called the "unsurpassed wheel of Dharma" and also the "great Dharma drum" and the "great Dharma conch," this refers to the teaching that clarifies the full [teachings] in contrast to the half [teachings], such as those of the Vaipulya period. △ Sixth, the Tathāgata’s silent assent.
At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū silently granted his consent.
This concludes the three southern directions. Fourth, a general summary of the remaining six directions:
from the southwest up to the nadir, it was likewise so.
In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the listing of the ten directions begins with the four cardinal points, followed by the four intermediate directions, and finally the zenith and nadir;
this sequence follows the translator’s intention, as it is unknown what the original Sanskrit order was. △ Fifth, the five [sections] concerning the zenith:

first, witnessing the auspicious signs and being struck with awe (up to) the fifth, the request to turn the wheel of the Dharma. Having concluded the requests from the ten directions, the World-Honored One immediately spoke; therefore, [this section] is not included here.
This is also tacitly acknowledged. First:

At that time, the Great Brahma Kings of five million billion lands in the upper direction all beheld the radiance and majestic brilliance of the palaces where they resided—unprecedented in former times—and they leaped for joy, giving rise to a sense of rare wonder.
△ Second, the mutual inquiry and resolution.
That is, each went to the other and they deliberated together on this matter: "By what cause and condition does our palaces possess such radiance?
At that time, within that assembly, there was a Great Brahmā King named Śikhin, who spoke for the sake of the host of Brahmās:
The verse says:
"For what cause and condition do our palaces now possess such unprecedented majesty, radiance, and adornment?
Such wondrous signs have never before been heard of or seen; has a Great Virtuous One been born, or has a Buddha appeared in the world?"
△ Three fathoms of light reveal the Buddha.

At that time, five million billion Brahma Kings, together with their palaces, each took celestial flowers in the folds of their robes and went together toward the lower direction to investigate this sign. There they saw the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū seated upon the path.
Seated upon the lion throne beneath the Bodhi tree, he was respectfully surrounded by devas, nāga kings, gandharvas, kiṃnaras,
mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others; they also beheld the sixteen princes entreating the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma.
△ Fourth, the offering of the three karmas.
At that time, the Brahma Kings prostrated themselves with their heads at the Buddha’s feet and circumambulated him a hundred thousand times.
They then scattered celestial flowers over the Buddha until the scattered flowers were as high as Mount Sumeru, and they also used these flowers to make offerings to the Buddha’s Bodhi tree.
Each having offered their own palace to that Buddha, they spoke these words: "May you look upon us with compassion and benefit us;
we pray that you graciously accept and dwell in the palaces we have presented. Then, before the Buddha, all the Brahma kings with one mind and in unison recited these verses:
Excellent! To behold the Buddhas, the Holy Honored Ones who save the world, who strive to deliver all sentient beings from the prison of the triple realm;
the Honored One of Universal Wisdom, Sovereign of Gods and Men, who out of compassion for all living beings can open the gate of ambrosia to extensively ferry across all.
In the past, throughout immeasurable kalpas, time passed in vain as there were no Buddhas; when the World-Honored Ones had not yet appeared, the ten directions were perpetually shrouded in darkness.
The three evil realms increase and the asuras also flourish, while the hosts of devas steadily diminish;

many die and fall into the evil realms, never hearing the Dharma from the Buddha and constantly performing unwholesome deeds. Their physical strength, vitality, and wisdom all decrease due to the causes and conditions of their sinful karma;
they lose both happiness and the perception of happiness, dwelling in false views and failing to recognize virtuous conduct and proper norms.
Those who have not been transformed by the Buddha constantly fall into the evil realms;
the Buddha, the Eye of the World, appears in the world only after a vast period of time out of compassion for all sentient beings, and having transcended them, he attains Perfect Enlightenment.
We are filled with great joy, as are all other assemblies, who marvel at this unprecedented event; our various palaces, touched by his light, are magnificently adorned.
I now offer this to the World-Honored One; I pray that you will graciously accept it out of compassion.
May the merit from this be extended to all beings, so that we and all sentient beings together may attain Buddhahood.

The inscription to the southeast states that one hundred and eighty kalpas passed in vain without a Buddha; the inscription to the south states that one saw a Buddha only after one hundred and thirty kalpas.
Now it is said that in the past, immeasurable kalpas passed in vain without a Buddha. Such vast differences in the conditions for seeing a Buddha—whether rare or frequent—are seen here.
That we have all gathered together under this light is surely no mere coincidence; let us take these ancient accounts as our precedent.
Now, since the principle is of one and the same essence, whether one sees or hears it, all follow through with responsive resonance;
those who hear the Dharma should therefore conceive the thought of joy and the realization that such an encounter is difficult to meet. △ Five: Requesting the Turning of the Wheel of Dharma.
At that time, after five million billion Brahma kings had praised the Buddha with verses, each addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We pray only that the World-Honored One will turn the wheel of Dharma, bringing peace and security to many and delivering many from suffering.
Then the Brahma kings spoke in verse:
World-Honored One, you turn the wheel of Dharma, beat the drum of the nectar-like Dharma, deliver sentient beings from suffering and affliction, and reveal the path to nirvāṇa;
we pray that you will accept our invitation and, out of compassion, expound with your great and subtle voice the Dharma practiced throughout immeasurable kalpas.

Since it is said that [the Buddha] "expounds with a great, subtle, and wondrous voice the Dharma practiced over immeasurable kalpas," and also that he "delivers sentient beings from suffering" and so forth, this is a request for a teaching that combines the partial and the full—such as the present *Prajñāpāramitā*. However, since the Way of the Buddha-Dharma is uniform, one should not request only a portion;
rather, as the present Buddha has done from beginning to end, one should request the complete turning of the Dharma-wheel of the five flavors.
Each and every instance is a response to the invitation of the Brahma King; that [invitation] should likewise be understood as such.

Now, by way of the text, we find that the initial request of the sixteen princes for the *Avataṃsaka*, up to the subsequent request from above for the *Prajñāpāramitā*, and the later request of the sixteen princes for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*—the structural nodes are perfectly clear, showing that past and present are in perfect accord. This concludes the explanation of the distant origins of the formation of karmic connections. △

The second [section] concerns the immediate [attainment], which refers to obtaining the opportunity for further exposition and establishing karmic connections because the Buddha accepted the invitation to preach the Dharma.

The text is divided into two parts: first, the turning of the wheel of the *ardha-akṣara* (half-syllable) Dharma; second, the turning of the wheel that discards the half and clarifies the full (*pūrṇa*) Dharma. In the first part, there are three sections:
first, accepting the invitation; second, the actual turning [of the wheel]; third, hearing the Dharma and attaining the Way. Now, the first [section].
At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū accepted the invitation of the Brahma Kings of the ten directions and the sixteen princes.

△ Second, the actual turning [of the wheel]: herein, one should explain the Three Vehicles according to the text of the "Introductory Chapter" (Nidāna-parivarta); however, they are not explained here.

This is specifically for those of inferior faculties; while the discourse on establishing karmic connections, the revelation of the truth, and so forth, briefly omits the mention of the six perfections, that Buddha’s attainment of enlightenment must have likewise expounded the Great Avataṃsaka Sūtra, as it was not the primary means for establishing their connection. Therefore, it is omitted here. Following the text, there are two parts:
first, the clarification of the Four Noble Truths; second, the clarification of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination. Now, the first part.
Thereupon, he turned the Wheel of Dharma with its three revolutions and twelve aspects—a wheel that no ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world could turn—namely:
"This is suffering; this is the origin of suffering; this is the cessation of suffering; this is the path leading to the cessation of suffering."
The three turnings are: first, the turning of demonstration; second, the turning of exhortation; and third, the turning of realization. The turning of demonstration means: "This is suffering.

The retributions within the twenty-five states of existence across the three realms are all the phenomena of birth-and-death suffering. Pleasure is the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*); pain is the suffering of pain itself (*duḥkha-duḥkha*);
and that which is neither painful nor pleasant is the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*). This is truly suffering and cannot be made into pleasure.

This is the origin of suffering: the afflictions of views and thoughts within the three realms, as well as the three types of tainted karma—wholesome, unwholesome, and imperturbable—which are the true causes that summon suffering; there is no other cause. This is the cessation of suffering:
because views and thoughts cease, tainted phenomena cease; because tainted phenomena cease, birth and death cease. Only in this state is there tranquility and peace.
There is no other path; this alone is the cause for the cessation of suffering. Through the cause of precepts, concentration arises; through concentration, wisdom is developed.

By relying upon the four foundations of mindfulness, one fulfills the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and enters the three gates of liberation; this is the path to the cessation of suffering, and there is no other path.
As for "exhorting the turning," it means: "This is suffering; you should know it. This is its origin; you should [abandon it]."
"This is what must be abandoned; this is cessation—you should realize it. This is the path—you should cultivate it. Regarding the transformation of realization:
"This is suffering—I have known it and shall not know it again. This is its origin—I have abandoned it and shall not abandon it again.
This is its cessation—I have realized it and shall not realize it again. This is the path—I have cultivated it and shall not cultivate it again."
Why is it that the Buddhas turn the Dharma-wheel three times? It is because sentient beings possess three faculties;

because it is for the sake of generating the three types of wisdom—listening, reflection, and cultivation; and because it is for the sake of generating the three paths of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning.

Regarding the twelve aspects: first, they are categorized by teaching; second, they are categorized by practice. As for categorization by teaching, these are namely: showing, exhorting, and realizing.
(3412) Regarding the practitioner, the three turnings each give rise to vision, knowledge, clarity, and awakening;

that is, the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) is vision, the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) is knowledge, the subsequent patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-kṣānti*) is clarity, and the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) is awakening. This applies likewise to the remaining three truths.
Thus, sixteen moments of mind are established. Since individuals of the three faculties each attain these sixteen moments of mind, forty-eight [moments] are established.

If one were to briefly summarize the twelve practices by way of the truths, there are twelve truths which constitute the Wheel of the Teaching (*dharmacakra*) and twelve practices which constitute the Wheel of Practice (*pratipatticakra*).
The twelve teachings are that which sets the wheel in motion, while the twelve practices are that which is set in motion.

Thus, the Wheel of the Teaching is that which sets it in motion—consisting solely of the single skillful wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*)—whereas that which is set in motion consists of the twelve teachings. As for the Wheel of Practice...

The teaching that can turn [the wheel] consists of twelve aspects, and the practice it turns also consists of twelve aspects. These may apply to three types of persons or be restricted to a single person.
Now, regarding the path of seeing the truths (*darśanamārga*), those of sharp faculties who hear the "turning of what is shown" each give rise to vision, knowledge, clarity, and awakening.
Because these three types of persons are presented together, it is said that there are twelve aspects of practice. As for "wheel," it means turning; it refers to the Buddha.
It is called a "wheel" (cakra) because the Dharma-gate realized within one's own mind enters into the minds of others. Furthermore, "wheel" means to crush and grind;
when sentient beings hear the teaching and give rise to practice, they crush and destroy all delusions, and thus it is called a wheel.
Even a śramaṇa who has not heard it cannot yet know it, let alone turn it. Although a pratyekabuddha has attained realization, he cannot speak of it with his mouth, much less a brāhmaṇa.

Although one may hear their names, one does not understand their underlying principle; this is likewise true for the celestial Māras and Brahmās, which is why it is said that they "cannot turn [the Wheel].
However, the meaning of these Four Noble Truths extends throughout both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, as well as the partial and the perfect teachings.

That is to say, there are the truths of arising-and-ceasing, non-arising, the immeasurable, and the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*); according to the understanding of each respective wisdom, they differ from one another, as briefly explained in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning).
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* contains the "Chapter on the Four Noble Truths," which was proclaimed by Mañjuśrī through the Buddha’s power;
how, then, can it be judged as being solely for the Śrāvakas? △ Second, the clarification of the twelve links of dependent origination.

And he further explained at length the Dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination: ignorance conditions volitional formations; volitional formations condition consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form;
name-and-form conditions the six sense bases; the six sense bases condition contact; contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving; craving conditions clinging;

clinging conditions becoming; becoming conditions birth; and birth conditions old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair. With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, [consciousness ceases...]
With the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases;
with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases;
with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases; and with the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair cease.
Furthermore, regarding the detailed exposition: the twelve links of dependent origination are explained in terms of their specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) by way of the Four Noble Truths.

Among them, the five members—ignorance (*avidyā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and existence (*bhava*)—constitute the truth of origin (*samudaya-satya*). The remaining seven members constitute the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).

The cessation of ignorance leads to the cessation of formations, and so on up to the cessation of old age and death; this constitutes the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*). This is the wisdom that contemplates dependent origination.
Since these are precisely the Truth of the Path, it is said "and so forth," referring to the extensive explanation. These twelve dharmas also pervade the Great and Small Vehicles,

as well as the Partial and Perfect teachings— namely, the conceivable arising-and-ceasing, the conceivable non-arising-and-non-ceasing, the inconceivable arising-and-ceasing, and the inconceivable non-arising-and-non-ceasing—
as briefly clarified in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) regarding the ten kinds of [wisdom] of Bodhisattvas in the sixth stage of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

When one contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) to realize the non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) of *prajñā*, how could this be judged as being merely the Dharma of the Pratyekabuddhas?

For now, following the system of Vijñaptimātra, I shall briefly indicate the characteristics of the arising and ceasing that are within the scope of conceptual thought. First, regarding "ignorance" (*avidyā*):

this refers to the ignorance that initiates karma (*karmābhisamskāra-avidyā*), which is the delusion regarding the ripened fruit (*vipākaphala-moha*). One must not assume that there is a fixed, determinate fruit for either good or evil [actions].
Because of ignorance regarding retribution and the meaning of reality, one fails to understand that the three realms are suffering and empty;

thus, one is able to produce the karma that correctly brings about birth and death. Although hatred, pride, and other afflictions can all produce karma, ignorance is the primary factor, and therefore it is specifically mentioned.
"The two types of conduct" refers to the three kinds of tainted karma—wholesome, unwholesome, and imperturbable—that are produced by that very ignorance.
That which can induce the truly matured fruit (*vipāka-phala*) of the future—these two together are termed the "projecting members" (*ākṣepaka-aṅga*). Regarding the two consciousnesses:

because ignorance and volitional formations act as the projectors, they induce the seeds of the general retribution (*sāmānya-vipāka*) for the future; this is the fourth [member], name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Because the seeds of the consciousness of general retribution exist, one possesses the *kalala* at the time of initial rebirth in the future.
The seeds of [the elements such as] earth and so forth, along with the four aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, constitute name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
With name-and-form as the seed, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are already present; that is, one possesses the seeds for the future six bases, namely:

eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. As for the six contacts (*ṣaṭsparśa*), since the seeds of consciousness, name-and-form, and the six bases are already present, one possesses the seeds for the future six [contacts].
At the time when the faculties, contact, and objects meet, the seeds of the mental factor of feeling (*vedanā*)—which consists of the seven types of feeling—are already present.

Since the seeds of consciousness, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), and contact are present, they already possess the seeds of the three types of feeling that will later experience favorable, unfavorable, and neutral objects.

These five are all called "projected factors" (*ākṣepaka-aṅga*). This is because if ignorance does not trigger the projecting karma, [the cycle] would cease; once it has triggered the projection, [the subsequent factors follow].
Because the nature of karma naturally draws forth these five seeds so that they are neither lost nor destroyed, it is called the "projected limb" (*ākṣepaka-aṅga*).

Regarding the eighth, craving (*tṛṣṇā*): once the five factors beginning with consciousness have been brought to completion by ignorance (*avidyā*) and formative forces (*saṃskāra*), there subsequently arises, due to the ignorance that is deluded regarding phenomena and fails to realize the falsity of objects, a craving for what is experienced.

Although craving (*tṛṣṇā*) also gives rise to aversion (*dveṣa*) and other afflictions toward adverse conditions, it is spoken of specifically because the habituation of craving is like water, most capable of moistening birth.
Ninth, "clinging" (*upādāna*) refers to the various pursuits of beloved objects due to craving, resulting in deep-seated defiled attachment.
Tenth, "existence" (*bhava*) refers to the power of karma produced by craving and clinging, which repeatedly nourishes [the process of rebirth].

Because they are the seeds for the five factors beginning with consciousness, these seeds are moistened and produce the sprout of existence (*bhava*), which will certainly bring about the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*) of the future;
these three are collectively termed the "generating factors" (*janaka-aṅga*). Eleventh, birth (*jāti*):

this refers to the fact that once the sprout of future existence has been fully accomplished, upon abandoning this life, one immediately undergoes birth in that [future] state. Twelfth, aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*): [this follows birth].
This refers to the fact that once born, the gradual decline and transformation is called "aging," and the ultimate return to impermanence is called "death";
these two are both termed the "branches of what is produced. The first ten [links] are causes, collectively referring to the present;
the latter two are results, specifically referring to the future. This is because the ten links of the previous life bring about the birth and death of this life.

The ten links of this present life further induce birth and death in future lives; because the cycle of cause and effect across the three periods of time revolves without end, it is called the "arising aspect" of the twelve links of dependent origination.
This is the detailed exposition of the two truths of Suffering and its Accumulation (the Truths of Suffering and Origination).
If one grows weary of old age and death, one knows that old age and death exist because of birth; next, one grows weary of birth, knowing that birth exists because of becoming (*bhava*).

Grasping arises from clinging; clinging arises from craving; craving arises from feeling; feeling arises from contact; contact arises from the six sense bases; the six sense bases arise from name-and-form;
name-and-form arises from consciousness; consciousness arises from volitional formations; and volitional formations arise from ignorance.
Since ignorance is merely a cessation of deluded conceptualization and inversion, there is no further basis for existence. Thus, through right mindfulness and observation, one is no longer deluded.
One has deep faith that within the fruit of maturation, evil brings calamity and goodness brings happiness;

one is not deluded regarding the meaning of reality, and has deep faith that being within the three realms is suffering while transcending the three realms is happiness. This is called the wisdom that contemplates causes and conditions.

By means of this wisdom, ignorance is extinguished; with the extinction of ignorance, volitional formations are extinguished, and so on, up to the extinction of old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.

Because all suffering, affliction, and distress are extinguished, it is called the "extinguishing characteristic" (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*) of the twelve links of dependent origination; this is precisely the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) within the two truths of the Path and Cessation, as explained in detail.
There are many other approaches for analyzing the meaning of the twelve branches, but as they are not urgent for the present purpose, they are not recorded here in full.

Since this is the case for the *paricchinna-janma* (segmented birth and death), it is likewise so for the *pariṇāmi-janma* (transformative birth and death), which also possesses conditions that give rise to conditions.
The characteristics of cessation in the twelvefold division of the *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (analytical cessation) are the arising and ceasing that are conceivable;

if one realizes they are empty, they are the arising and ceasing that are not conceivable. The twelvefold division of the *pariṇāma-śarīra* (transformation body) is the arising and ceasing that are inconceivable;
if one realizes they are the Middle Way, they are the arising and ceasing that are inconceivable. Furthermore, if one awakens to this inconceivable non-arising and non-ceasing...
Thus, the twelve divisions [of the scriptures] are themselves the inconceivable non-arising and non-ceasing. Therefore it is said:
delusion is itself *prajñā*, karma is itself liberation, and suffering is itself the *dharmakāya*. They are pure in their very place, sovereign in their very place, and ultimate in their very place.
One purity is all purities; one sovereignty is all sovereignties; one ultimacy is all ultimaties.
The first part, "The Ultimate Realization of All," and the second part, "The Two Correct Turnings," are concluded.

△ Third, attaining the Way upon hearing the Dharma: When the Buddha preached this Dharma amidst the great assembly of devas and humans, six hundred trillion nayutas of people—by virtue of not grasping at any phenomena—attained liberation of mind from all outflows (*āsrava*) and all attained profound and wondrous *dhyāna*.
Possessing the three clear knowledges (*vidyā*), the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*), when he preached the Dharma for a second, third, and fourth time,
hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and *nayutas* of them,

likewise attained liberation of the mind from all outflows (*āsrava*) by way of not grasping at any phenomena (*anupādāya*). From that time onward, the assembly of *śrāvakas* became immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable.
Regarding the enumeration:
"not receiving any dharmas" means not receiving the four fruits of the path and realizing the first fruit (srotāpanna);

"the mind attaining liberation from all outflows" means being freed from all bonds of views and afflictions and realizing the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa); this refers to profound and wondrous meditative concentration.
Question: Regarding those who contemplate, train in, and cultivate the various dhyānas, are they not all "liberated through both parts" (ubhayatobhāga-vimukta)?

Furthermore, since the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination are common to the four teachings, are there not also those who realize the Great [Vehicle] within them? Answer: Take, for example, when Śākyamuni first preached the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts;
even then, eighty thousand devas attained the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti). Since the Way of the Buddhas is the same in every case, how could that be otherwise?

The intent of the present text is to briefly describe the origins of this karmic connection; what leisure is there to extensively recount the benefits of the ancient secret and indeterminate teachings?

Having concluded the first turning of the Wheel of Dharma of the "Half-Characters" (the *Hīnayāna*): △ Second, the Turning of the Wheel of Dharma that Abolishes the Half and Clarifies the Full [the *Mahāyāna*], in seven parts:
1. All the Sons Enter the Monastic Life; 2. Requesting the Dharma; 3. Those Who Were Brought Along Also Enter the Monastic Life; 4. The Buddha Accepts [the Request].

I request the assembly gathered at the five times to consider whether they understand the six seasonal periods and the sevenfold exposition already entered into meditative concentration. Now, for the first:
At that time, the sixteen princes all left the household life as youths to become śrāmaṇeras;

their faculties were keen and their wisdom was clear, having already made offerings to hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas, purely cultivated the Brahma-faring, and sought [Buddhahood].

*Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. "The faculties being penetrating and sharp" refers to the purification of the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya-viśuddhi*). Furthermore, the mutual functioning of the six organs is called "penetration" (*tong*), and realizing the realm of the Buddha is called "sharpness" (*li*).

"Wisdom being clear and lucid" refers to the stages of opening, showing, awakening, and entering. (The first [explanation] is based on the stage of semblance; the second is based on partial realization.)
[The section on] the position of Śakra. △ Second, the request for the Dharma.
Together they addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, these immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of great virtuous śrāvakas have all already achieved [their goal];
may the World-Honored One also preach to us the Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. I...

Having heard this together, we all practice and study it. World-Honored One, our vows and aspirations are as the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision; we are mindful of them with a profound mind, which the Buddha himself knows and witnesses.
That Buddha, at the very beginning of his teaching, spoke of the perfect and sudden Great Vehicle for all sons, whose merits are fully complete, out of compassion for those in all directions.

He then again entreated the Buddha to reveal the provisional to manifest the ultimate. By stating that "the śrāvakas have all already attained accomplishment," he clarifies that their obstacles have been removed and their faculties have been activated;

for this reason, he makes his request. When he says, "Our aspiration is for the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision," it means that this *Lotus Sūtra* exclusively elucidates the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
to aspire solely to this is precisely to request the abandonment of the half-letters (*ardha-vyañjana*) and the fulfillment of the full letters (*pūrṇa-vyañjana*).
This is the section on the "Text. △ Third, those who were led forth also left the household life.

At that time, among the multitude led by the Wheel-Turning Sage King, eighty trillion people saw that the sixteen princes had left the household life and also sought to leave the household life; the King immediately granted them permission.
△ 4. The Four Buddhas Accept the Invitation.

At that time, after those Buddhas had accepted the śrāmaṇera’s invitation for more than twenty thousand kalpas, they preached this Mahāyāna sūtra titled *The Lotus of the Wonderful Law*, which teaches the Dharma for bodhisattvas and is protected by the Buddhas, amidst the fourfold assembly. They preached this sūtra.
The sixteen śrāmaṇeras, for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, all together received, maintained, recited,
and mastered [the teachings].
After twenty thousand kalpas had passed— since the time of the former offering by Upatiṣya was long ago and could not remain without activity in the interim— I now look down to the verses.
Within twenty thousand kalpas, he will certainly preach the Vaipulya Prajñāpāramitā, as the verse says:
"He speaks of the six pāramitās and the matters of various supernormal powers (abhijñā). Prajñā is the practice; supernormal powers are the matter.
Most Vaipulya sūtras clarify these inconceivable practices. Furthermore, the verse states: "To discern the true Dharma is precisely the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra."
This clarifies the meaning of the *prajñā* of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*). △ At that time, among the assembly, some understood while others did not.
When this sutra was being preached, all sixteen bodhisattva śrāmaṇeras believed and accepted it; within the assembly of śrāvakas, there were also those who believed and understood;
yet among the other sentient beings of thousands of myriads of koṭis, doubts and confusion arose.
Those who believe and accept [the teaching] can propagate it; those with faith and understanding can enter the reality.
As for the millions of beings who were in doubt and lacked understanding—these are precisely the sixteen princes who have established the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* connection. Question:

Since the Buddha first accepted their invitation, twenty thousand kalpas have already passed. For what reason have the sixteen princes not yet received full ordination and are still called "śrāmaṇeras"?
Question: Since Maitreya is a śrāmaṇera, why is he further called a bodhisattva? Answer: The sixteen sons were originally bodhisattvas;
because they were in haste to study the Mahāyāna, they had no leisure to undergo full ordination (upasampadā), and thus they have manifested as youths from beginning to end.
It is the constant rule of all Buddhas that a śrāmaṇera may receive the bodhisattva mahā-śīla; how can this be a cause for doubt? Although he has received the [mahā-śīla]...

Regarding his status in the precepts, he remained that of a śrāmaṇera and never presumed to overstep [his rank] as a bhikṣu, thereby disturbing the established model of the Saṃgha—the Jewel of the Sangha.
Just as the Great Sage Mañjuśrī yielded all his conduct and seating to Mahākāśyapa, this is clearly stated in the sūtras;
it is only that people themselves fail to observe it. Question: Since millions of billions of beings cannot understand [this], why not let him [be understood] like [the Buddha]?
Question: Why were the five thousand who withdrew from their seats not transferred to other Buddha-fields, rather than being allowed to give rise to doubt?

Answer: Even those who give rise to doubt are permitted to remain so that they may form karmic connections (kalyāṇamitra); therefore, they were not sent away. Only those who give rise to slander and fall into suffering must be expelled.
At this very moment when the Buddha preaches the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, how can we guarantee that there are none among them who will give rise to doubt? 6. The Time Period.
The Buddha preached this sutra for eight thousand kalpas without ever ceasing or resting.
[Some] ask: "It is traditionally said that Śākyamuni preached the Lotus Sutra for only eight years, which is already difficult to believe;

yet it is said that he 'opened the provisional to reveal the real' and 'opened the traces to reveal the source,' as these essential words were not prolix. [However,] that Buddha [preached it] for eight thousand kalpas.

It has never ceased or been abandoned, yet one does not know what it says. To answer: these four characters that "reveal the Real by opening the Provisional" (*kāuán xiǎnshí*) could not be fully expounded even in eons as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, let alone for merely eight thousand eons or eight years.
For instance, a few words regarding the true reality of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) possess a vast and profound meaning, encompassing and penetrating the hundred realms and the thousand suchnesses.

When the three dharmas of nature, cultivation, and cause-and-effect—whether viewed horizontally or vertically—are fully exhausted without exception, one may then expound them throughout the bounds of the future;
how much more so when revealing the traces to manifest the fundamental, clearly elucidating the inconceivable events of vast eons?
Furthermore, as for the Bodhisattvas emerging from the earth, they praised the Buddha with various kinds of bodhisattva praises, and then the sutra...
During fifty minor kalpas, when the Buddhas extend their broad and long tongues and manifest their supernormal powers, a full hundred thousand years pass;
how can one with the mind of an ordinary person seek to fathom the unsurpassed, most profound, and subtle Dharma of the Tathāgata?
△ Having finished the seventh exposition, he entered meditative absorption.
Once this sutra had been preached, he immediately retired to his quiet chamber and dwelt in *dhyāna* for eighty-four thousand *kalpas*.
This was precisely the proximate cause for establishing karmic connections; as the Buddha remained in absorption, the assembly of those with various doubts had no place to seek counsel.
Question: Regarding the sixteen princes, they preached the sutra again for those who did not understand.
In the text, it clarifies that the place where they entered meditative concentration (*samādhi*) was a quiet chamber; "entering concentration" refers to abiding in *dhyāna*;

and the duration of entering concentration was eighty-four thousand *kalpas*. However, since all Buddhas possess no mind that is not in concentration, how could there be any entering or emerging from it? It is merely...
Regarding the timing of the causal conditions for the various capacities [of sentient beings], the limit of the period for establishing karmic affinity among the sixteen sons was precisely this long.
This concludes the section on the origins of the initial establishment of affinity. II. The Actual Establishment of Affinity. A. Explanation through Dharma (theoretical exposition). B.

Explanation through Parable (illustrative exposition). In the first part (A), there are three sections: 1. Clarifying the mutual establishment of affinity in the past. 2. Clarifying how they encountered one another again during the intervening period.

The Threefold Clarification: Today the Buddha again preaches the Lotus Sūtra. This has two parts: first, the provisional teaching for the benefit of sentient beings; second, the Buddha’s arising to offer praise. Now, the first part:
At that time, the sixteen bodhisattva śrāmaṇeras, knowing that the Buddha had entered his room and was in silent meditative concentration, each ascended the Dharma seat.
Furthermore, for eighty-four thousand kalpas, he extensively expounded and analyzed the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* for the fourfold assembly; in each instance,
he delivered six million billion nayutas of sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, instructing, benefiting,
and gladdening them so that they all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

That a śrāmaṇera ascends the seat is not only the case for the sixteen bodhisattvas; there are also explicit texts in the present Vinaya-piṭaka stating that the emphasis lies on understanding rather than age.
If one gives rise to the great bodhicitta, one is immediately called "crossed over" (tāraka).
Having vowed to become a Buddha, one has already transcended the mundane world—this is crossing over the seven stages of expedient means.
"Shore" (*kūla*) means "meaning. △ Second, the Buddha rises and offers praise, in two parts: first, the actual praise; second, the exhortation to have faith.
Now, the first:
After eighty-four thousand *kalpas* had passed, the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū arose from his samādhi and proceeded to the Dharma-seat.
Sitting serenely, he addressed the great assembly: "These sixteen śrāmaṇera bodhisattvas are truly rare;

their faculties are keen and their wisdom is clear. They have already made offerings to immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas, constantly practicing the pure life in the presence of those Buddhas.
Having received and upheld the Buddha-wisdom, they reveal it to sentient beings, causing them to enter therein."
△ Second, the exhortation to those who are close and trusted:
"You all should repeatedly draw near to and make offerings to them. Why is this?
Because if śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas can believe in, receive, and uphold the sūtra teachings spoken by these sixteen bodhisattvas—"
"Those who disparage [this teaching] shall all attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
This is the passage from the ancient Buddha’s universal bestowal of predictions. The first section, clarifying that they collectively formed karmic conditions in the past, is concluded.
△ Second, clarifying that they further encountered one another during the intermediate period.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "These sixteen bodhisattvas always delight in preaching this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Each of these bodhisattvas has converted six million billion nayutas of sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River.

In every lifetime they have been born, they have been together with these bodhisattvas and have heard the Dharma from them; having all attained faith and understanding through these causes and conditions, they have encountered [the Buddhas]."
There are still forty trillion Buddha-Bhagavāns who have not yet passed away.

There are three types of those who encounter [the Dharma]: first, those who from the beginning constantly received the Mahāyāna and throughout the intervening period have already achieved realization, continuing until the present;
second, those who initially received the Mahāyāna but encountered a regression from it and were instead connected with the Hīnayāna; this then—
"During the interim, [the seeds] were still not yet exhausted; now they have obtained the opportunity to hear the Great Teaching once more.

Third, this refers only to encountering the Small [Vehicle] and not the Great, or where one initially received the Great but later lacked the capacity, such that during the interim they were not yet saved and even now [the seeds] are not yet exhausted—this refers to those who attain the Way after the extinction [of the Buddha].
(This person takes their initial hearing of the Small [Vehicle] as the first stage of forming a karmic connection, and furthermore...)

In the interim, they had practiced only the Lesser Vehicle; now, upon meeting the Prince, they have merely heard that among the Śrāvakas within one portion of Śākyamuni’s teachings throughout his entire life, there are those who have not yet resolved their minds for enlightenment, and they immediately judge them to be forever extinguished and incapable of awakening. This is because they do not understand the Tathāgata’s long-term transformation. Question: If, as stated above, it takes kalpas as numerous as atoms before one finally attains Arhatship, one should know that the stage of the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) must be extremely difficult to ascend. Answer: One explanation states that the Great Sage employs skillful means based on the four *siddhāntas*. Thus, he teaches that some attain the fruit of Arhatship in this very life, while others attain it after many kalpas. Furthermore, he establishes the teaching of the three vehicles to accommodate the capacities of sentient beings, and he speaks of the extinction of the Śrāvaka vehicle to encourage those of dull faculties to resolve their minds for the Mahāyāna. It is only when one has attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas that one truly realizes that all phenomena are originally empty and quiescent. Therefore, one should know that the patience of the non-arising of dharmas is not easily attained. However, because the Buddha’s compassion is vast and profound, he does not abandon even those of the smallest capacity; thus, he establishes the teaching of the three vehicles to guide them according to their respective inclinations. Consequently, although the patience of the non-arising of dharmas is difficult to reach, the Buddha’s expedient means are subtle and wondrous, allowing those who practice the Lesser Vehicle to eventually enter the Great Vehicle. This is why the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "The various paths and vehicles are all established by the Buddha. It is precisely because the Buddha’s wisdom is inconceivable that he can manifest such diverse teachings. Therefore, we should know that the patience of the non-arising of dharmas is indeed difficult to attain. Nevertheless, through the Buddha’s skillful means, even those who have long practiced the Lesser Vehicle can, upon hearing the Dharma of the Great Vehicle, immediately give rise to the Bodhi-mind. This is what is meant by the statement that "the patience of the non-arising of dharmas is not easily reached.
