He speaks in this manner: sometimes he says the Buddha-way is long and distant, or he says the Buddha-way is easy to attain;
sometimes he accords with the worldly desires [of beings], or he acts to arouse their past roots of goodness; sometimes, as an antidote for those who weary of the long path, he speaks of it as short;

or for those who conceive a sense of ease regarding the long path, he speaks of it as long; or so that upon hearing these explanations of length and brevity, they may immediately enter the foremost [stage].

One should understand that the statement that one only attains Arhatship after such a number of kalpas is merely a provisional practice of the four *siddhāntas* to lead those of true practice into the Way.
Furthermore, in principle there is no length or brevity; length and brevity reside in the capacity of the practitioner.
One need only be earnest and diligent oneself—why must one discuss whether another's time is long or short? △ Third, clarifying the return to this day.

Regarding the first part of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, there are two sections: first, the preliminary reconciliation of the ancient and the modern; second, the actual clarification of the returning teaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

Within the first of these, there are two sub-sections: first, the reconciliation of the teacher’s ancient and modern [manifestations]; second, the reconciliation of the disciples’ ancient and modern [manifestations]. This is the first.
"O Bhikṣus, I now tell you: those sixteen śrāmaṇeras who were disciples of that Buddha have all now attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
they currently reside in lands throughout the ten directions, preaching the Dharma, with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas as their retinues.
Of those two śrāmaṇeras, one has become a Buddha in the eastern direction."
The first is named Akṣobhya in the Land of Joy; the second is named Sumerukūṭa. In the southeast, there are two Buddhas:
the first is named Siṃhaghoṣa and the second is named Siṃhadarśana. In the south, there are two Buddhas: the first is named Gaganastha and the second is named Nityapraśānta.
In the southwest, there are two Buddhas: the first is named Indradhvaja and the second is named Brahmaketu. In the west, there are two Buddhas: the first is named A... [text truncated]
Amitābha has two names: [the first is Amitābha, and the second is] Deliverer from All Worldly Suffering and Affliction.
To the northwest are two Buddhas: the first is named Tamālapatracandanagandhābhijña, and the second is named Merudhvaja.
To the north are two Buddhas: the first is named Megheśvara, and the second is named Megheśvararāja. To the northeast is a Buddha named Destroyer of All Worldly Fear.
Sixteen years ago, I, Śākyamuni Buddha, attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in the Sahā world-system.
These sixteen śrāmaṇeras were those who became Buddhas in the eight directions of antiquity; they are the ones of the present. Akṣobhya—this is translated as "Immovable."
△ Second, the assembly of disciples; this has four parts: first, clarifying the original formation of the great connection; second, explaining the present doubts of those dwelling as śrāvakas;
third, formally concluding the connection between the past and the present; fourth, explaining the doubts of future disciples. Now, the first part.
"O bhikṣus, when we were śrāmaṇeras, we each converted immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings,
as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who heard the Dharma from us and [set their minds] upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

This clarifies that when first hearing the Dharma, all are directed toward unsurpassed bodhi; that is to say, those with the initial resolve of the three vehicles are not deluded regarding the Dharma.
However, it is only because there are subsequent instances of regression or non-regression that the distinctions between those who attain liberation sooner or later arise.
△ Second, the explanation of the current doubt regarding abiding as a śrāvaka.
Among these beings, those who currently abide on the stage of the śrāvakas, I constantly teach and transform toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
These individuals should gradually enter the Buddha-way by means of this Dharma. Why is this?
Because the wisdom of the Tathāgata is difficult to believe and difficult to understand.

First, it is explained why these sentient beings—who heard the Dharma from me during the time of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū—have not yet attained unexcelled bodhi but still remain on the stage of a śrāvaka even until now. The commentary states:
"I have constantly taught them with [the goal of] unexcelled bodhi; however, it is simply because these individuals should be guided by means of this provisional, lesser vehicle."
This is because the Dharma gradually leads one into the Buddha-way. Furthermore, there may be doubt as to why this person should enter [the path] through this Dharma gradually.
The explanation says: It is truly because the Tathāgata’s wisdom is difficult to believe and difficult to understand. △ Third, the formal conclusion correlating the ancient and the present.
Those immeasurable sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who were transformed at that time are none other than you, O bhikṣus,
and the śrāvaka disciples who will exist in future ages after my parinirvāṇa.
"You, all you bhikṣus, are now uniting those of the past who dwelt on the stage of śrāvakas with those of the present;
and after my parinirvāṇa, my śrāvaka disciples shall likewise unite those of the future with those of the inexhaustible present.
△ Fourth, resolving the doubts of future disciples.

After my parinirvāṇa, there will be disciples who have not heard this sutra; being unaware and unconscious of the conduct of bodhisattvas, they will conceive the notion of parinirvāṇa regarding the merits they have attained and think they shall enter nirvana.
I shall become a buddha in another land under a different name, and although these people conceive the notion of parinirvāṇa and enter into nirvana, they will [actually] be in that land.
Those who seek the wisdom of the Buddha and obtain hearing of this sutra attain extinction solely through the Buddha-vehicle;
there is no other vehicle, except for the various skillful means employed by the Tathāgatas in their preaching of the Dharma.
An objector might say: "It may be that present-day śrāvakas, upon hearing the Buddha preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, awaken to and enter [enlightenment] through its revelation."

Regarding those who have established karmic ties with us but will pass into parinirvāṇa without hearing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, how could they possibly abandon the Lesser Vehicle to enter the One Vehicle?

The commentary explains: although they conceive the thought that they have attained nirvāṇa, they are nonetheless born within the Land of Expedient Means with Remainder (*upāyika-śeṣabhūmi*) and receive a body of transformation (*nairmāṇika-kāya*). Even in that land, I shall certainly preach this sutra for them, ensuring that they enter the One Vehicle.
There is no vehicle other than the Vehicle of the Path; this excludes only the skillful means (*upāya*) by which the Tathāgatas preach the Dharma to definitively sever doubt.
These three are merely provisional designations of skillful means; in reality, there is absolutely no third [vehicle]. This concludes the initial section on reconciling the ancient and the modern.

△ Second, the formal explanation of returning to preach the Lotus Sūtra. Part one: explaining that it is preached because the time is appropriate. Part two: interpreting the three meanings previously introduced regarding the opening [of the sūtra]. Now, the first part:
"O Bhikṣus, if the Tathāgata knows for himself that the time for his parinirvāṇa has arrived, and the assembly is pure with firm faith and understanding..."

Having thoroughly realized the dharma of emptiness and entered deeply into meditative concentration, he then assembled the multitude of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas and preached this sutra for them, saying:
"In the world there are no two vehicles by which one attains extinction; it is only through the single Buddha-vehicle that one attains extinction."
"The time for Nirvāṇa has arrived" means that the Buddhas have appeared in the world and their work of transforming beings through the Way is about to be completed.
For instance, after Kāśyapa Buddha, Candrasūryapradīpa Buddha, and others had finished preaching this sutra, they immediately entered Nirvāṇa.

Śākyamuni likewise will soon proclaim his extinction at the conclusion of this sutra; therefore, this sutra is the final and ultimate proclamation. "The assembly is pure" means that [defilements] have been severed.

The accomplishment of virtue consists in the faith that is the fourfold indestructible faith; the accomplishment of wisdom consists in the untainted right understanding that realizes and penetrates the dharma of emptiness and attests to the true reality.

Once wisdom and abandonment are established, one further enters deeply into meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), possesses the two types of liberation, is capable of hearing the Great Teaching, and is able to believe and accept it. Furthermore, regarding "the purity of the assembly":
Those who have attained the benefit of the Tripiṭaka teachings have escaped the perils of the burning house;

those with firm faith and understanding have attained the benefit of the Vaipulya teachings through the mutual trust of mind and nature; those who have thoroughly realized the dharma of emptiness have attained the benefit of the Prajñā teachings and are able to transmit them to others.
The assembly of bodhisattvas constitutes the kinsmen of this gathering, while the multitude of śrāvakas are his sons whom he summons.
Furthermore, even if the time for parinirvāṇa had arrived, if the assembly were not yet pure, one could not preach this sutra.

Just as the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna was unable to preach the Lotus Sutra because there were no receptive conditions in the present world, he therefore left behind his entire-body stupa to serve as a witness in various places after his extinction. △ Second, explaining the previous "opening of the three."
"Monks, you should know that the Tathāgata, through his skillful means, penetrates deeply into the nature of sentient beings.

Knowing that their aspirations lie in inferior teachings and that they are deeply attached to the five desires, he speaks of nirvāṇa for the sake of such people; if these individuals hear it, they will immediately believe and accept it."
If, in reality, there were no two vehicles that attain extinction, for what reason did the Tathāgata previously preach the provisional teaching? The commentary explains:

"The Tathāgata deeply knows that sentient beings have small capacities and desires, and are attached to the five objects of sensory dust (*pañca-viṣaya*) and obscured by the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*);

therefore, he first preached the three [vehicles] to enable them to break through the turbidity and escape from calamity, and later preached the one [vehicle]. This concludes the initial section on the Dharma-exposition regarding the establishment of conditions. △

Second, the parable of establishing karmic connections, which has two parts: first, establishing the parable; second, the application to the Dharma. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, the parable of the guide;
second, the parable of leading the way. Now, for the first:
Suppose there were a perilous and difficult evil road five hundred *yojanas* long, desolate and devoid of people, a place of terror. If there were...

There was a great multitude who desired to pass beyond this path to reach a place of precious jewels. There was a guide there, wise, intelligent, and discerning, who well understood the characteristics of the treacherous paths, such as their obstructions and openings.
As for the "five hundred yojanas," if one refers to the retribution of karmic results, it corresponds to the three hundred directions within the realm of segmented existence (*bhavāgra*).
The place of transformation becomes four hundred; the place of real retribution and transformation becomes five hundred.
If categorized by afflictions, the views and thoughts of the three realms constitute three hundred, the "dust-sand" afflictions constitute four hundred, and ignorance constitutes five hundred.

Entering the contemplation of emptiness allows one to transcend three hundred; entering the contemplation of the provisional allows one to transcend four hundred; entering the contemplation of the Middle Way allows one to transcend five hundred.

The "hundredfold perils and difficulties of the evil paths" are a metaphor for the causes and effects of birth and death, as well as the *pariccheda* (segmented) and *pariṇāma* (transformative) forms of existence—which constitute the perils of the result—and the five stages of dwelling in views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-śīla-vrata-parāmarśa*, etc.)—which constitute the perils of the cause. Because of these causes and effects, they are called "evil paths.

There are two kinds of paths: first, those that, though vast and desolate, have people upon whom one can rely; second, those that, though vast and desolate, have no people upon whom one can rely. This serves as a metaphor.
If there were nirvāṇa within saṃsāra and bodhi within afflictions, then although [the world] might be vast and desolate, there would be someone upon whom one could rely.

However, if there were no nirvāṇa within saṃsāra and no bodhi within afflictions—just as there is no illness within medicine and no medicine within illness—then it would be a vast and desolate place where no one could find refuge from fear.

(In the Separate and Perfect Teachings, the realm is not desolate and there are people; in the Shared Teaching, the Two Vehicles are desolate yet there are people; in the Tripitaka Teaching, the Two Vehicles are desolate and there are no people.)
Because it was vast and uninhabited, he established a transformation for these people. If there were a great multitude, they would be like the unliberated multitudes transformed by the prince.
Those who wish to pass through this path to reach the place of precious jewels are like those who resolve their minds to seek unsurpassed bodhi.
The one who acts as a guide is like the sixteenth prince. His ears being pure is called "clarity of hearing," and his mind is [pure].
Purity of the ear is called the "eye of wisdom" (*prajñā-cakṣus*); purity of the nose is called "clarity" (*vidyā*); and purity of the remaining faculties is called "penetration" (*prativedha*).

In summary, this refers to the purity of the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya-viśuddhi*). Furthermore, "wisdom" refers to the threefold wisdom within a single mind (*ekacitta-trividya-jñāna*), while "clarity" refers to the possession of the five eyes (*pañca-cakṣus-samanvāgata*).

Moreover, the "three clarities" (*trividyā*) constitute "clarity," and the "ten powers" (*daśabala*) constitute "penetration. One who skillfully knows the characteristics of dangerous paths and the conditions of openness or obstruction—though...
This perilous path has both obstructions and passages; those who possess skillful means turn obstructions into passages, while those lacking in expedient artifice turn passages into obstructions.
One must fully possess provisions, implements, courage, and strength, and one must be thoroughly familiar with the water and grass along the way ahead.
△ Second, the analogy of the guide, in three parts: first, the analogy of the people being led. Second.
Falling weary and retreating midway is like the three types of extinction; being led to the place of treasure is like the present case.

First, regarding the former: leading a multitude across this perilous path is like those who originally formed karmic connections but have not yet attained liberation; though they have not yet escaped, their original connection remains intact, and they are thus led by the Guide.
△ Second, the analogy of wearying and retreating midway, which has two parts: first, the regression of the Mahāyāna; second, the connection to the Hīnayāna. Now, the first part:
The multitude they were leading grew weary and retreated midway, saying to the Guide: "We are utterly exhausted and filled with fear; we can no longer advance.
The road ahead is still long, and now we wish to turn back."
The "middle path" does not mean the halfway point; rather, it refers to the period from the initial arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) until reaching Buddhahood.

Because one gives rise to thoughts of retreat within these two pillars, it is called the "middle path. To "inform the guide" means that while the capacity for the Great Vehicle has already regressed, the capacity for the Small Vehicle may still arise;
this is a subtle resonance with the compassion of the *dharmakāya*, and its meaning is like "informing. "Exhausted" is a metaphor for the wholesome [roots].
The feebleness of the faculties is like being obscured by ignorance; "fearful" is a metaphor for dreading the suffering of saṃsāra;
"the path ahead is still long" is a metaphor for the difficulty of severing the three delusions. One becomes utterly exhausted because one lacks the courageous strength of the Mahāyāna;
one is fearful because one lacks the fortitude of the Mahāyāna as well as its provisions and equipment; and one does not recognize the path ahead because one is unacquainted with it.
Because there are aquatic plants, it is said that the road ahead is still long. △ Second, connecting to the second [section]. First, the skillful means of establishing transformation;
second, entering with joy. Now, the first:
The Guide possesses many skillful means and thinks thus: "These people are to be pitied; why should they abandon such great treasures?"

Having thus conceived the thought of turning back, he employs his power of skillful means to manifest a city within the perilous path three hundred *yojanas* away, and addresses the multitude, saying:
"Do not fear; do not turn back. You may halt here in this great city and do as you please.
If you enter this city, you will quickly attain peace and security; yet if you can proceed further..."
You may also proceed to the place where the treasure is located.
There are many skillful means, such as the Tathāgata’s provisional wisdom, which can be adapted to suit the capacity [of beings].

These [beings] are to be pitied, for it is known that they lack the great capacity [for the ultimate truth]. He manifests a city to know that they can be received through a small [means]. "Do not be afraid; do not..."
To attain the ability to retreat is a metaphor for exhorting one to advance; it is like "exhortation to turn.
To say that this great city can serve as a place of rest where one may act as one pleases is a metaphor for showing that the city is habitable; it is like "showing the turning.

To say that upon entering this city one swiftly attains peace and security is a metaphor for praising the merits of the city; it is like "realization of the turning. If one is able to proceed forward...
Even though one may reach the place of jewels, before the Buddha has yet revealed it, one cannot speak of this clearly and openly.
However, if one speaks of hearing it secretly, there is no impediment; and if one considers their past lives, such words must have existed.
For when the prince knew that they intended to retreat, he immediately exhorted them, saying: "If you fear birth and death..."
Furthermore, one may first obtain news of *nirvāṇa* and subsequently practice the Great Way; this is also permissible according to one's inclination.

Moreover, after the provisional is opened and the real is revealed, one may then expound it—as in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, where all those who have attained the rank of *arhat* embody this very meaning. △ Second, entering with joy.
At that time, the exhausted multitude was filled with great joy and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence, exclaiming,

"We have now escaped this evil path and have swiftly attained peace and security. Thereupon, the people entered the conjured city, conceiving the thought that they had already crossed over and the thought that they had attained peace and security.

Great joy is like the wisdom of hearing; exclaiming "unprecedented" is like the stage of Heat (*uṣmagata*); being freed from the evil realms is like the stage of Peak (*mūrdhan*); the sense of swift peace and security is like the stage of Patience (*kṣānti*);
entering the illusory city beforehand is like the stage of seeing the Truths (*darśanamārga*); the thought of having already crossed over is like attaining the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*);

the thought of peaceful security is like attaining the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*); furthermore, the thought of having already crossed over is like being endowed with the virtue of wisdom (*jñānaguṇa*).

The hidden thought illustrates the perfection of cessation (*nirodha-sampad*). The second section, concerning the exhaustion and retreat midway, concludes here. △ Third, the illustration of the extinction of the conjured city and the guidance to the place of treasure:
At that time, the guide, knowing that these people had already found rest and were no longer fatigued, immediately caused the conjured city to vanish.
He spoke to the multitude, saying, "Come, you all! The place of treasure is near. That great city we approached was merely a resting place created by me.

Having obtained rest, they were like those who have escaped danger; being free from further fatigue, they were like those whose capacity for the Mahāyāna has been awakened, with the place of treasure now close at hand.

The nearby analogy illustrates the true Great City, while the analogy of the transformation [of the city] signifies the setting aside of the provisional. Regarding the "Jewel Treasury," there are two meanings:

if taken in terms of the ultimate, the supreme fruit is the Jewel Treasury, as the preceding passage states, "Only a Buddha and a Buddha can exhaustively fathom the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
If taken in terms of partial entry, the first stage of the Bodhisattva path, the *Prathamacittotpādavihāra*, is the Jewel Treasury.
As stated in the preceding text, the "unsurpassed treasury of jewels" is attained spontaneously without seeking;

it is further stated that one attains a portion of the Buddha-dharma such that all which a son of the Buddha ought to attain has already been attained. Question: In five instances, the three vehicles were opened up to reveal the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*);

what is the difference between these? Answer: Generally speaking, there is no difference; specifically speaking, there are distinctions. Regarding the *Upāya-paryāya* (Chapter on Expedient Means), the distinction is based on the teaching (*śāsana*).
Regarding the opening of the three to reveal the one, it is said: "The Tathāgata teaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings solely by means of the Single Buddha Vehicle;
there is no other vehicle, whether two or three. Regarding the burning house, the three vehicles are established based on the gate of practice to reveal the one;

"vehicle" carries the sense of transport. Transport is the meaning of movement, as the text says: "Each riding upon a great vehicle, they travel through the four quarters, playing and sporting with joy."
The "Joy" [chapter] concerns the binding and releasing of people; it reveals the three to manifest the one and binds together those who have been made into disciples—namely, the son of the elder.

The text says: "We have from of old truly been sons of the Buddha. The "Herbs" [chapter] distinguishes between the differentiated and the non-differentiated to clarify the provisional and the real, without resorting to rejection or grasping.
It is simply that sentient beings do not know [the Buddha]; the Buddha causes them to know. If they know these seven kinds...

When there is differentiation, one knows that the provisional and the real are identical in their reliance upon a single principle; when there is no differentiation, one knows that the real is differentiated yet without difference, and that it is without difference yet differentiated.
This is intended merely to make this meaning known; it never says that there is neither one nor many.

This is spoken according to the Buddha’s own intention regarding the two wisdoms of the provisional and the real within his own practice; thus, while the Buddha is able to know this, sentient beings do not.

This also connects with what precedes and follows to clarify the knowledge and ignorance regarding provisional and real [teachings]. Here, the "transformed city" (*nirmāṇa-pura*) specifically refers to the principle of opening the three to reveal the one.

The "treasure destination" and the "transformed city" represent the two principles of the Great and Small Vehicles; by subverting the provisional principle of the Two Vehicles, it reveals the Tathāgata’s true, singular principle.
In the following section, where the five hundred disciples receive their understanding, the "jeweled garment" is cited as an analogy.

This analogy is also based on principle; it is explained here according to the literal sequence of the text, yet each and every phrase fully possesses the four aspects. Each of these is the Tathāgata’s ability to know what sentient beings do not know; this "knowing" is precisely the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. The initial establishment of the analogy is concluded. △ Second, the application to the Dharma (the analogy). The second part of the middle section consists of two analogies: first, the analogy of the Guide; second, the analogy of the Leader. Herein is the first.

"O Bhikṣus, the Tathāgata is likewise so: he now acts as your great guide, knowing that the various paths of birth and death, the afflictions, and the evil realms are perilous, difficult, and far-reaching, and that they must be abandoned and crossed."
The Tathāgata corresponds to the guide; you all correspond to the great multitude; birth and death correspond to the perilous difficulty of the fruit;
afflictions correspond to the perilous difficulty of the cause; the long distance corresponds to five hundred *yojanas*;

"should go" and "should deliver" correspond to being well-acquainted with the signs of passability and obstruction, and also correspond to the desire to reach the place of treasure. △ Second, the analogy of the leader and the guide.
If sentient beings were to hear only of the Single Buddha Vehicle, they would not wish to see the Buddha nor draw near to him;
they would instead think, "The path of the Buddhas is long and distant, and only after enduring toil and suffering for a long time can one attain Buddhahood.

Knowing that their minds are timid, weak, and inferior, [the Buddha], by the power of skillful means, speaks of two types of nirvana as a place of rest midway through the journey. If [sentient beings]...
When the Tathāgata perceives that [the bodhisattvas] have been established in the two stages, he then says to them: "What you have accomplished is not yet complete;
the stage upon which you dwell is close to the Buddha-wisdom. You should examine and deliberate that the nirvāṇa you have attained is not the ultimate reality.
It is merely through the power of the Tathāgata’s skillful means that the single Buddha-vehicle is distinguished and taught as three."

The phrase "if sentient beings" (若眾生) is a metaphor for the multitude of people being led along. "Merely hearing the One Buddha Vehicle" up to "can thereby achieve [enlightenment]" is a metaphor for becoming weary and retreating midway.
"The Buddha, knowing this mind" up to "preaching two forms of nirvana" is a metaphor for conjuring a single city.
This represents the interval between having already departed from the Shared Residence (tongju) and not yet having reached the True Reward (shibao).

That which is called the Middle Way, with remainder and without remainder, is termed the two nirvāṇas; these are also the two nirvāṇas realized by the two types of persons, the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
If sentient beings abide in the two stages [of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha], they are gathered and led to the place of treasure through the extinction of their transformation;
this is the analogy. The initial formal application is complete. △ Second, citing the analogy to apply it to the teaching.
Just as that guide, for the sake of providing rest, conjures a great city; and once he knows they have rested, he tells them:
"The place of treasure is near; this city is not real, it was merely a creation of mine."

The transformation into a great city and the application of the teaching on the proximity of the places where the Three Jewels are bestowed have been fully explained in the first section, "Detailed Exposition.

△ Second, the Verses in Repetition (Geya), which has two parts: First, verses on the causes for establishing the connection; Second, verses on the actual establishment of the connection. In the first part, there are two sections:
First, verses on the distant causes; Second, verses on the proximate causes. In the first of these, there are again two sections: First, verses on the attainment of Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū.
The Buddha’s two verses on the Brahma Kings of the Ten Directions Requesting the Dharma. Herein is the first.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū sat at the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas; yet the Buddha-dharma did not manifest before him, and he could not attain the path of Buddhahood."
The various devas, nāga kings, asuras, and other assemblies constantly rained down celestial flowers as an offering to that Buddha;
the devas beat celestial drums and performed various musical arts, while fragrant winds blew away the withered flowers and rained down fresh and beautiful ones.
After ten intermediate kalpas had passed, he attained the Way of Buddhahood, and the hearts of all the devas and people of the world were filled with exultation.
The sixteen sons of that Buddha, all surrounded by their retinues of thousands of myriads of koṭis, went together to the place where the Buddha was;
they prostrated themselves with their heads at the Buddha’s feet and requested him to turn the wheel of Dharma, so that the holy lion’s rain of Dharma might satisfy them and all beings.
The first three verses praise the second [section], the events prior to his attainment of enlightenment; the next single verse praises the third, the actual manifestation of his enlightenment;
and the final two verses praise the fifth, the request to turn the wheel of Dharma, while also briefly omitting a praise for the fourth, the offerings of his retinue.
They do not praise the first [section], the long duration of the Buddha’s lifespan. △ Second, the verses on the requests for the Dharma by the Brahma Kings of the ten directions (2).
The first verse concerns the majestic light that causes trembling; the second verse concerns the Brahma King’s arrival and request. Now, for the first:
"The World-Honored One is most difficult to encounter; appearing but once in a vast expanse of time, he manifests to awaken all sentient beings and causes everything to tremble."
△ Second, the verse on the Brahma King’s arrival and request:
In five hundred million worlds to the east, the Brahma palaces shone with a brilliance never before seen.
When the various Brahmas perceived this sign, they followed one another to the Buddha’s dwelling, scattering flowers as an offering and presenting their palaces.
They requested the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma, praising him with verses. Knowing that the time had not yet come, the Buddha accepted their request by remaining silent.
The same occurred from the three directions, the four intermediate points, and the zenith and nadir. They scattered flowers and offered palaces, requesting the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma:
"The World-Honored One is extremely difficult to encounter; we pray that, out of your original compassion, you will widely open the gate of ambrosia and turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma."
The first three verses praise the eastern direction, while the latter two verses summarize the praise of all nine directions. This concludes the section on the remote causes. II.

Verses on the proximate causes, divided into two parts: A. One verse praising the turning of the wheel of the *ardha-lipi* (half-syllable) Dharma; B. One verse praising the turning of the wheel that abolishes the half and clarifies the full. Now, the first part:
The World-Honored One of Immeasurable Wisdom accepted the invitation of those people and proclaimed for them various teachings:
the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, from ignorance through old age and death, all arising from birth as their condition. "Such are the manifold afflictions;
you should know this! As he expounded these dharmas, six hundred trillion nayutas attained the end of all suffering and all became arhats.
During the second discourse on the Dharma, a multitude as numerous as the sands of ten million *koṭis* of *gaṅgā* rivers attained arhatship by not grasping at any phenomena;
from that time onward, those who attained the Way were incalculable in number, such that even through calculations for ten trillion *kalpas*, one could not find their limit.

The first half-verse praises the acceptance of the invitation; the next one and a half verses praise the actual turning [of the wheel]; and the final three verses praise attaining the Way through hearing the Dharma.
Regarding the statement that "from ignorance to old age and death, all arise conditioned by birth," this means that because this exists, that exists;

it specifically points to ignorance as the condition for the arising of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), volitional formations as the condition for the arising of consciousness (*vijñāna*), and so on, up to birth as the condition for [old age and death].
Regarding the condition for the arising of old age and death, if one knows its faults and afflictions, one should employ the power of insight to extinguish that ignorance;
because this is extinguished, that is extinguished. △ Second, the verse on the turning and ceasing [of the wheel] partially clarifies the fulfillment of the Wheel of Dharma.
At that time, the sixteen princes left the household life to become śrāmaṇeras and together requested that Buddha to expound the Mahāyāna Dharma, saying:
"We and our retinues shall all attain the path of Buddhahood. We pray that you, like the World-Honored One, will grant us the foremost purity of the wisdom-eye.
May the Buddha know the deeds performed by these youths in their past lives through immeasurable causes and conditions and various parables."
He preached the six *pāramitās* and the matters of the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), analyzing the true Dharma and the path practiced by Bodhisattvas.

He spoke this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* in verses as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Having finished preaching the sutra, that Buddha entered meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) in a quiet chamber, sitting with a single mind in one place for eighty-four thousand *kalpas*.
The first two lines of the verse praise the first [section], the renunciation of the sons;
the next six lines praise the second [section], the request for the Dharma (omitting the third section, their departure, which is subsumed by the two characters "yingcong" [attendants]);
and the two verses following "The Buddha knew" praise the fourth [section], the acceptance of the invitation, wherein for twenty thousand kalpas he first preached the Vaipulya Prajñāpāramitā.

The two verses praise the acceptance of the invitation and the formal preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*; the fifth [verse], concerning those who understand and those who do not, and the sixth, concerning the time, are omitted.
The final verse praises the seventh [point]: entering meditative concentration after the preaching is finished. The first section, concluding the causes for establishing the connection, is complete.
△ Second, praising the actual establishment of the connection, which has two parts: first, praising the teaching by means of the Dharma; second, praising the teaching by means of parables. First:

Regarding the first of the three [sections] in the middle [of the chapter]: the first verse concerns the past karmic connection; the second verse concerns their subsequent encounters during the interim;
and the third verse concerns how they have today returned to hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Now, for the first:
these śrāmaṇeras, knowing that the Buddha had not yet emerged from his meditative concentration, preached the Buddha’s unsurpassed wisdom to immeasurable billions of beings.

Each sat upon a Dharma-seat and preached this Mahāyāna sūtra; after the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa, they proclaimed and assisted in the transformation of the Dharma, and among the sentient beings saved by each of these śrāmaṇeras were as many as six million *koṭis* of Ganges-sands.
△ Second, during the interval between the two verses, they encounter one another:
after that Buddha has passed into parinirvāṇa, these who have heard the Dharma will always be born together with their teacher in every Buddha-field wherever they may be.
△ Three verses on returning today to preach the Lotus Sūtra. Part one: One verse concluding the connection between the past and present; part two:
Two verses clearly explaining the return to preach the Lotus Sūtra. Now, for the first:
These sixteen śrāmaṇeras have fully practiced the path of the Buddha; they are currently in the ten directions, each having attained perfect enlightenment.

At that time, those who heard the Dharma were each at the abodes of various Buddhas; among them, those who dwelt as śrāvakas and were gradually taught the Buddha-way were included within my sixteen [disciples].
I have also previously preached this for you; therefore, by means of skillful expedients, I lead you toward the wisdom of the Buddha.

The first verse concludes the ancient and modern [teachings] of the Master; the following two verses merely praise the ancient and modern [teachings] of the present disciples in this assembly, omitting a brief mention of future disciples. △ Second, the verse correctly clarifies that he returns to preach the Lotus Sūtra.
For these fundamental reasons, I now preach the Lotus Sūtra to lead you into the Buddha-way; be careful not to harbor fear or alarm.

Because it is a verse summary suited to the occasion, I have spoken briefly without providing a prose commentary on the opening of the three meanings. The first verse, which concludes the section on the Dharma-exposition (dharmadeśanā), is finished.

II. Verses on the Parable-Exposition (aupamyadeśanā). A. First, verses establishing the parable. B. Second, verses on the application to the Dharma (dharmanirdeśa). In the first part [of A], there are two sections; first, the verses on the guide.
The Master uses two verses as a metaphor for guidance. Now, first:
Suppose there is a perilous and evil road, remote and desolate, abounding in venomous beasts and lacking water or grass—a place feared by all people.
An incalculable multitude of tens of millions of beings wishes to cross this dangerous path; the way is vast and far-reaching, extending for five hundred *yojanas*.
At that time, there was a guide who possessed strong memory, wisdom, and clarity of mind, and whose resolve was firm; he rescued the multitude from their hardships amidst the perils.
The long prose version says "vast and desolate, with no people," while the present verse says "remote and isolated, with many venomous beasts.

Here, "people" represent *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*, while "beasts" represent the afflictions (*kleśa*) of birth and death. That the beasts are both numerous and venomous refers precisely to the delusions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana* and *vitarka-vicāra*) within the limited capacities of the small vehicle.

Because the obstacles of the five turbidities are heavy and profound, one cannot practice the great direct path. "Water" is a metaphor for meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and "grass" is a metaphor for wisdom (*prajñā*).

The two lines on "strong discernment" eulogize being intelligent, wise, and far-sighted. The line on "being in danger" eulogizes skillfully knowing the characteristics of the obstructions and openings along the perilous path;
the remainder can be understood accordingly. △ Second, the eulogy on the analogy of leading the way, in two parts: first, the eulogy on those who are led.

Regarding the two verses on "the multitude becoming weary and retreating midway," which describe the cessation of the transformation and the leading to the treasure site: the first verse concerns the great retreat of the multitude, and the second verse concerns the guide’s reception of the small [group]. Now, the first [verse]: The multitude, having traveled for a long time, Became weary and lost their way; Their minds grew faint and they were terrified, And all turned back together. The second verse concerns the guide’s reception of the small [group]: At that time, the Great Leader, Seeing them turn back, Spoke these words to comfort them: "Do not fear, you who have come from afar. Knowing that the multitude delights in inferior dharmas and fears great wisdom, the bodhisattvas therefore manifest as śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."
By means of countless skillful expedients, he transforms all classes of sentient beings; though he calls himself a śrāvaka, he says that the path to Buddhahood is far from him.
Yet he delivers immeasurable multitudes, causing them all to achieve perfection. Although he appears to have few desires and to be indolent, he will gradually cause them to become Buddhas.
Internally he keeps secret his bodhisattva practices, while externally he manifests as a śrāvaka with few desires who is weary of birth and death; in truth, he is purifying his own buddha-field.
I manifest the three poisons and even display the signs of false views to the assembly; my disciples employ such skillful means to deliver sentient beings.
If I were to fully explain all these various manifestations, sentient beings who heard them would harbor doubt and confusion in their hearts.
"Small desire" means being inclined toward the Hīnayāna; "laziness" means not seeking the Mahāyāna.

Regarding the statement that he "manifests the three poisons to the assembly," it means that he does not merely manifest himself as a Śrāvaka, but also acts as a commoner possessed of the three poisons, as well as a heterodox practitioner with false views.
Furthermore, for example, Śāriputra manifested anger, Nanda manifested greed, and Devadatta manifested ignorance, and so forth. △ Second.
This verse reveals the legacy of Pūrṇa:
in the past, under a thousand billion Buddhas, this Pūrṇa diligently cultivated the path he was to travel, proclaiming and protecting the teachings of those Buddhas;
seeking unsurpassed wisdom, he appeared before each of those Buddhas as their chief disciple, preeminent in learning and endowed with wisdom.
He speaks with fearlessness, bringing joy to the assembly without ever experiencing weariness, thereby assisting in the Buddha’s work;
having attained great supernormal powers and being endowed with the four types of unimpeded knowledge, he discerns the sharpness or dullness of the faculties of others,
constantly preaching the pure Dharma and expounding such meanings to instruct trillions of beings, establishing them in the Mahāyāna while himself purifying his own buddha-field.
In the future, they shall also make offerings to immeasurable and innumerable Buddhas, protecting and assisting in the proclamation of the True Dharma, purifying their own Buddha-fields,
constantly expounding the Dharma through various skillful means with fearlessness, delivering incalculable multitudes, and accomplishing all-encompassing wisdom.

The first five verses praise the past, manifesting the original [state]; the final two verses praise the practices of future Buddhas, while briefly omitting praise for the present Buddha and the seven Buddhas.
The first verse concludes the section on the manifestation of the origin. II. Verses on the Bestowal of Prophecy (three parts): A.
Verse on the perfection of causes and the fulfillment of the fruit; B. An interlinear verse on the names of the lands and kalpas; C. Verse on the buddha-lands.

In this broad and pure [version], the Buddha’s lifespan, the duration of the Dharma’s abiding, and the construction of stupas after his parinirvāṇa are omitted from the verse. Now, for the first [section]:
Having made offerings to all Tathāgatas and upheld the treasury of the Dharma-jewel, he subsequently attained Buddhahood, and his name was called Dharmaprabhāsa (Dharma-Light).
△ Second, skipping over the names of the land, eon, and kalpa:
that land is named "Excellently Pure," composed of the seven precious jewels; the eon is named "Jewel Radiance.
△ Third, a verse on the vast purity of the land.
The assembly of bodhisattvas is vast and immeasurable, numbering in the billions; they have all attained great supernormal powers and are fully endowed with majestic virtue.
Their land is filled with them, and the śrāvakas are likewise innumerable, having attained the three insights, the eight liberations, and the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge.
With such as these as their saṃgha, all sentient beings in that land have already severed lustful desire and are born solely through transformation.
His body is adorned with the marks of excellence; he feeds on the joy of the Dharma and the delight of dhyāna, having no further thought of other food.

There are no women there, nor are there any evil realms. The merits of the bhikṣu Pūrṇa are fully perfected, and he shall attain this pure land where the assembly of sages and saints is exceedingly vast.
Such immeasurable matters as these I have now merely described in brief.
The prediction for Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra has been completed. △ Second, the prediction for the twelve hundred people. Part one: the request through reflection;
part two: the bestowal of the prediction; part three: the acceptance and understanding. Now, the first.
At that time, the twelve hundred arhats who had attained mastery over their own minds thought to themselves:
"It would be most wonderful if the World-Honored One were to grant us each a prediction of our future enlightenment, just as he has done for the other great disciples."
△ Second, the granting of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*). This has two parts: first, the long prose section; second, the verse section. Within the first part, there are three sections:
first, the general prediction for the twelve hundred; second, the specific prediction for Kauṇḍinya; third, the specific prediction for the five hundred. Now, the first.
The Buddha, knowing the thoughts in their minds, addressed Mahākāśyapa:
"I shall now, in this very presence, bestow upon these twelve hundred arhats the sequential prediction of their attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
△ Second, the individual prediction for Kauṇḍinya:
"Among this assembly, my great disciple, the bhikṣu Kauṇḍinya, shall make offerings to sixty-two thousand *koṭis* of Buddhas;
thereafter, he shall attain Buddhahood, and his name shall be the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vairocana."
The One Perfected in Conduct, the Well-Gone, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One—
because Ājñātakauṇḍinya was the first to attain deliverance and become the Elder of the Saṃgha, he was given a specific prediction. △ Third, the separate prediction for the five hundred [disciples].
These five hundred arhats— Uruvilvākāśyapa, Gayākāśyapa, Nadīkāśyapa,
Kālodāyin, Udāyin, Aniruddha, Revata, Kapphiṇa, Bakula, Cunda, Śāgata, and the rest—
all shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and all shall be exactly equal.
The first was named Puming (Universal Radiance).

Kālodāyin—translated here as "Black Light"—was the one whom the father king dispatched after the Buddha’s attainment of enlightenment to invite the Buddha, and who was subsequently ordained by the Buddha's command.
According to the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*, he attained the Way upon the Buddha’s "Welcome" call (*ehi-bhikṣu*), and through his supernormal powers, he converted [others].
According to the Āgamas and Vinaya, the father-king who was transformed [by the Buddha] was one of the group of six bhikṣus;
although he had left the household life, he continued to commit many transgressions until, at over seventy years of age, he was finally tamed and realized arhatship.

He was foremost in exhortation and transformation, for the husband and wife he converted both attained the vision of the Truths (satyadarśana), totaling more than a thousand households. Thus, we know that in both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna...
Since the perceptions of those with various capacities are each distinct in this way, it is not only the Buddha’s body-secret (*kāyaguhyaka*) that is inconceivable;
even the body-secrets of the great disciples (*mahāśrāvaka*) are all likewise inconceivable.

Udāyin is so called, and Upāli is also so called—these are merely differences in the weight of the Sanskrit pronunciation. Regarding the foremost upholder of the Vinaya, Cūḍapanthaka, this is translated as [Cūḍa-]panthaka.

The Elder Mahāpanthaka realized arhatship, mastered the Tripitaka, and became a great Dharma-master; he was the elder brother named Śagata (translated here as "Great Road" or "Successor of the Path").
The younger brother was named Cūḷapanthaka (translated here as "Small Road" or "Minor Successor of the Path").

Although the elder brother was given a single verse by the Buddha, he could not master its recitation even after one hundred days, whereupon the elder brother expelled him from his cell. Subsequently, the Buddha personally bestowed it upon the younger brother.
The six characters "I sweep away dust, I remove defilement" (我拂塵我除垢) further allow for the omission of what precedes or what follows;
they teach that only by regulating the breath can one realize the holy fruit and possess great supernatural power to subdue the poisonous fire-dragon.
Since these four venerable ones did not have their names listed among the preceding assembly, they are now explained here. Furthermore, among the assembly there is also Kauṇḍinya.

Pāṭaliputra, Piṅgalavatsa, Mahākauṣṭhila, Nanda, and Sundarananda—these five individuals were not separately mentioned [in the prediction], perhaps because the Sanskrit original has not yet been recovered, or because they are collectively included among the five hundred or the twelve hundred disciples.
The long prose section concludes. △ Second, the verse summary, which has two parts: first, the summary of the prediction concerning Chen (Cunda).
Thus, the five hundred and two verses collectively bestow the prediction of enlightenment upon all the śrāvakas. First:
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
The bhikṣu Kauṇḍinya shall see immeasurable buddhas; after an incalculable number of kalpas (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), he will attain equal and perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
He will constantly emit great radiance and be fully endowed with all supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). His fame will pervade the ten directions and he will be revered by all.
Because he constantly preaches the unsurpassed path, he shall be named Samantaprabha. His buddha-field will be pure, and his bodhisattvas will all be courageous and vigorous.
They all ascended to sublime pavilions and traveled through the lands of the ten directions, offering unsurpassed articles of worship to the Buddhas.

Having made these offerings, their hearts were filled with great joy; in an instant, they returned to their own land. Possessing such supernatural power, the Buddha’s lifespan was sixty thousand kalpas;
the period of the True Dharma lasted twice that length, and the period of the Semblance Dharma lasted twice as long again. When this Dharma perished, the devas and humans were filled with sorrow.
These five hundred bhikṣus shall successively become buddhas, all bearing the same name, Samantaprabhāsa. They shall receive their predictions in succession;

after my parinirvāṇa, such-and-such a person shall become a buddha. The world they shall transform shall be as majestic and pure as my own land today, and their supernormal powers, their assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, as well as their True Dharma and Semblance Dharma, shall be likewise.
The duration of his lifespan in kalpas is exactly as described above.

The long prose is summarized by the verses; whereas the previous verses explained the bestowal upon Cūḍapanthaka, here the first two lines clarify the causes for practice, the next two verses clarify the attainment of the fruit, the following two and a half verses clarify the purity of the land, and the final line clarifies the Buddha’s lifespan.

The two lines clarify the periods of the True Dharma, Semblance Dharma, and Subsequent Dharma, followed by the lines on the sorrow of devas and humans; these conclude the preceding section and introduce the next.
The following three and a half stanzas praise the bestowal of predictions upon the five hundred [disciples]. △ Second, praising the general bestowal of predictions upon all the śrāvakas.
"Kāśyapa, you already know that it is the same for the remaining assembly of śrāvakas who possess the fivefold mastery;
as for those who are not present in this assembly, you should proclaim [this teaching] to them."

The other śrāvakas refers to those among the one thousand two hundred who have already been granted predictions—specifically five hundred and more than seven hundred—and by extension, it refers to all śrāvakas.
As for those not present in this assembly, whether they are here or not, their attainment of the prediction is the same.
Within the granting of predictions to the one thousand two hundred, these two have now been completed. △ Third, the Acceptance and Understanding.

Part Two: The Initial Long Prose Section and the Two Verse Summaries. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, the narrative by the sūtra compiler describing their joy; second, their own declaration of realization. Now, for the first:
At that time, the five hundred arhats, having received their prediction in the presence of the Buddha, were filled with joy and leaped for gladness, and immediately rose from [their seats].
Rising from his seat, he went before the Buddha, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet, and repented and reproached himself.
He leaped for joy, celebrating that he had now attained understanding; he repented and reproached himself, feeling shame for his former lack of understanding.
△ Second, the self-proclamation of understanding. Part one: Explanation by Dharma; Part two: Explanation by Parable. Now, the first [part].
"World-Honored One, we have always harbored this thought, believing ourselves to have already attained ultimate *nirvāṇa*. Now we realize that we were like those lacking wisdom. Why is this?
We ought to have attained the wisdom of the Tathāgata, yet we instead [regarded it as having been attained] by ourselves..."
Those of small wisdom consider it sufficient;

they claim for themselves that they have already attained ultimate *nirvāṇa*. This is like a person of no wisdom who, having repented their former delusions and now realizing the truth, rejoices at having finally awakened, only to know that their previous small wisdom was ultimately identical to having no wisdom at all. They likewise [regard their attainment as final].
It is because their faculties are dull that they cannot awaken early. Why is this so? The following explains the meaning of "lack of wisdom":
only today do they realize that they ought to attain the Great Wisdom of the Tathāgata;

yet, from the very beginning, they were content with a small wisdom, clinging to the small and losing the great—is this not ultimately the same as having no wisdom at all? △ Second, the illustrative explanation, in two parts: first, establishing the analogy.

Regarding the two dharmas combined at the beginning of the first section, there are two parts: first, the analogy of being intoxicated by wine, which illustrates those of small wisdom who consider themselves to have attained *nirvāṇa* and are satisfied with that;
second, the analogy of being awakened by a kinsman, which illustrates that one now realizes what one ought to attain—the wisdom of the Tathāgata. Within the first of these, there are again two parts:

first, the analogy of tying the jewel, which summarizes the prince’s formation of a connection (*saṃbandha*) in the past; second, the analogy of sleeping intoxicated without awareness, which summarizes the preceding [section].

Regarding the intermediate regression from the two [great vehicles] and the subsequent arousal [of the aspiration], there is an analogy for leading [the practitioner] upward by means of the small [vehicle]. Now, for the first [case]:

"World-Honored One, it is as if there were a person who went to the house of a close friend and lay down after becoming intoxicated with wine. At that time, the friend had business to attend to at the government office;
he tied a priceless jewel inside the lining of the man's garment, gave it to him, and departed."
The "person" refers to the five hundred [bodhisattvas] themselves; the "intimate friend" refers to the sixteenth prince from days of old;
the "house" refers to the Mahāyāna teaching as one's home; and "lying drunk" refers to remaining in a state of unawakened ignorance.

There are two meanings to being "drunk": first, being so deeply intoxicated that one has no awareness at all, which refers to those who have not yet established a karmic connection through even a single phrase or verse.
Having previously ascended to the second stage, one is slightly intoxicated and, upon slight awakening, immediately forgets; this is also called "non-awakening.

It is like having a thin degree of *śrutamayī-prajñā* (wisdom derived from hearing) at the beginning of the five stages, yet not having entered the stage of semblance (*nirvedhabhāgīya*). "Official business that ought to be carried out" is a metaphor for the Prince [the Bodhisattva] arising his capacity elsewhere and responding to conditions as they arise.
Propagating the Dharma and transforming others is not a private matter; therefore, it is called "official business. There is no [private interest].
The precious jewel represents the jewel-like wisdom of the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the one vehicle (*ekayāna*).
"Tying it within his garment" means that the garment represents the shame, modesty, patience, and the mind of faith and aspiration at that time;

through the slight arising of faith and aspiration upon hearing the Dharma, one obtains the seeds of the causal wisdom and vows. △ Second, the analogy of being intoxicated and lying down without awareness.
That person lay drunk and asleep, completely unaware.

This is a metaphor for when the mind is heavy with ignorance and, upon seeking again, fails to remember or comprehend; being weary and regressive in the interim, one does not receive the Great Dharma.
△ Third, the metaphor of rising and wandering about.
Having arisen, he wanders to another country; for the sake of food and clothing, he seeks them with diligent effort, encountering great hardship.
If he obtains even a small amount, he considers it sufficient.
Having risen, he travels about; this is a metaphor for when the roots of goodness begin to sprout, one grows weary of suffering and seeks happiness.

Arriving in another country is a metaphor for being shrouded by ignorance, such that one does not know how to return to one’s own native land of the Mahāyāna. Food and clothing are metaphors for the two paths: the primary and the auxiliary.
The difficulty of seeking them out is a metaphor for the time before entering the True Dharma, when there is nothing to be realized or attained, yet one obtains only a meager amount.
The analogy of the feet and the grasping of authority illustrates that by practicing the teaching, one attains the fruits of the Hīnayāna;

this correctly represents the intermediate stage of using the Lesser Vehicle to lead [beings]. The section on the analogy of being intoxicated with wine concludes here. II. The analogy of the close friend’s awakening.

This represents the aforementioned primary cause and condition, wherein the Buddha now preaches the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and bestows upon his sons the great white ox-carts. The text is also divided into three parts.
First, the reprimand; second, the showing of the jewel; third, the exhortation to trade. Now, for the first:
later, when he encountered his former friend, the latter said to him, "Alas, man! Why have you come to such a state for the sake of food and clothing?"
"Meeting [the Buddha]" is a metaphor for the awakening of the Mahāyāna capacity. "Alas! How reproachable! is a metaphor for the movement of attachments and the arising of doubt.

Within the three cycles [of teaching], this meaning is present throughout. In the *dharmadeśanā* (Dharma-exposition), it says: "I cause you to be liberated from the bonds of suffering," which is a metaphor. In the *avadāna* (narrative), it says:
"Did I not previously state that all [teachings] are for the sake of *samyak-saṃbodhi*? In the *nidāna* (causal narrative), it refers to past lives.
I shall now explain the causes and conditions; these are all words of reproach. △ Second, showing the jewel:

"In the past, wishing to enable you to obtain peace and happiness and to indulge freely in the five desires, on such and such a year, month, day, and time, I tied a priceless precious jewel within the lining of your garment.
It remains there even now, yet you do not know it, and instead you seek [happiness] through toil, hardship, and anxiety."
To live for oneself is truly foolishness.

"Peace and happiness" is a metaphor for the unsurpassed Great Nirvana. "Indulging in the five desires at will" is a metaphor for the true enjoyment of the Mahayana in accordance with its nature, as it is said that the sublime five sensory objects of the "True Reward" (*sambhoga*) realm can cause even Kāśyapa to rise and dance.

"This refers to such-and-such year, month, and day; it is like when the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū again preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. 'Now he is still present' is like the actual revelation of the Truth (*dharmatā*).

Within the extensive explanation of the five Buddhas in the section on the preaching of the Truth, within the causal conditions for the bestowing of the great carts, and within the subsequent preaching of the Great [Vehicle], all demonstrate the meaning of showing the jewel. △ Third, the exhortation to trade."
"You may now trade this jewel for whatever you require; it shall always fulfill your wishes, leaving you never lacking or deficient.

Although the value of this pearl is immeasurable, it must still be traded before its utility can be realized. This is analogous to the internal understanding of the 'cause of completion' (*yuan-yin*):
though it is ultimately perfected, one must necessarily exchange the latent seed for the manifest state, trading that single past understanding of all things for a single present realization."

Because the essence of the jewel of all practices is inexhaustible and its transformation is likewise infinite, one must listen further and cultivate further for the jewel’s functional power to be revealed.

Just as in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, where one obtains a maṇi-jewel that can only rain down treasures after undergoing ten kinds of polishing, so too must practice and realization correspond before one is worthy of the Buddha’s prediction. From this point onward, one then possesses quiescent extinction (*śānti*).

Wearing the robe of patience (*śūraṅgama*), consuming the food of self-cultivation and transformation of immeasurable multitudes, and abiding in the stage of effortless mastery (*anābhoga*) where both self and others are inexhaustible, it is said that one can always have as one wishes and lacks for nothing. Within the discourse on the Dharma, Śāriputra received his prediction;

within the discourse by way of parable, four people received their predictions; and within the discourse on causes and conditions, twelve hundred and twenty thousand received their predictions—all of these.
This concludes the initial establishment of the analogy for the meaning of "encouraging trade. △ Second, the application to the Dharma, which has two parts:

first, the application to being intoxicated with wine; second, the application to awakening. The first of these [the application to being intoxicated] has three parts: first, the application to the binding of the jewel; second, the application to lying drunk and unaware;
third, the application to rising and wandering about, taking little as sufficient. Now, the first.
The Buddha was likewise so when he was a bodhisattva, teaching and transforming us so that we might give rise to the mind of omniscience.
△ Second, like being drunk and lying down without awareness,
one subsequently falls into oblivion, neither knowing nor perceiving.
△ Third, having arisen from meditative absorption, they wander about and consider what they have obtained to be sufficient.

Having attained the path of Arhatship, they claim for themselves that they have reached extinction (nirvāṇa), yet their livelihood is difficult to sustain; thus, they consider what they have obtained to be sufficient.

Because the means of subsistence within the three realms are difficult to obtain, one considers oneself satisfied with a meager fruit; yet, lacking the merit and wealth of the Dharma of the Mahāyāna, the means of subsistence remain difficult to secure. This concludes the analogy of being intoxicated by wine. △ Second, the analogy of being awakened by a kinsman, in three parts: first, the analogy of reprimand; second, the analogy of showing the jewel; third, [the analogy of obtaining the jewel]. First, the analogy of reprimand: [text follows]... This concludes the analogy of reprimand. Second, the analogy of showing the jewel: [text follows]... This concludes the analogy of showing the jewel. Third, the analogy of obtaining the jewel: [text follows]... This concludes the analogy of obtaining the jewel. This concludes the analogy of being awakened by a kinsman. This concludes the section on the parables. This concludes the chapter on the Parables.
