Chapter Ten: On the Dharma-Master. This chapter elucidates five kinds of dharma-masters: first, receiving and upholding; second, reading; third, reciting; fourth, explaining and expounding; and fifth, copying and transcribing.

The *Mahā-śāstra* elucidates six kinds of dharma-masters: first, receiving [the teachings] by means of the power of faith; second, upholding them by means of the power of mindfulness; third, ... [and so forth].
To read the text is the first; to recite it so as not to forget it in four ways is the second; to proclaim it to others is the third;

since the scriptures of the sages are difficult to understand, they must be explained—this constitutes the fourth; and to uphold them is the fifth. If one combines these, upholding and explaining together form one, and adding transcription makes five.
If discussed separately, four pertain to one's own practice (*sva-caryā*), while explaining is one type that pertains to transforming others (*parārtha*).

In general discussion, practicing the five dharmas oneself is called being a Dharma Master who practices for oneself; teaching others the five dharmas is called being a Dharma Master who transforms others.
Why is this so? "Dharma" (dharma) means a standard or rule; "Master" (ācārya) means a teacher or craftsman.

Although the Dharma serves as a standard, its essence does not propagate itself; it depends on people. One who masters these five types of scriptural penetration may all be called a Master who upholds the Dharma.
One accomplishes one’s own practice by taking the sublime Dharma as teacher; because one masters the sublime Dharma and brings one's own practice to fulfillment, one is called a "Dharma Teacher.
Furthermore, five types of persons are able to instruct and mold others through the sublime Dharma; thus, by using the term "Dharma" to designate the "teacher," they are called "Dharma Teachers.
Whether one follows the Dharma as one's own standard or acts as a craftsman of the Dharma for others, both may be designated as "Dharma Teachers. This is the Chapter on the Dharma Teacher.

This is the explanation according to causes and conditions (*nidāna*). (The distinction between benefiting oneself and transforming others is as follows: benefiting oneself refers to the accomplishment of the world; transforming others refers to generating good and eliminating evil, which is the counteractive (*pratipakṣa*) method;

when both self and others are perfected, one is called a Dharma Master, which is the ultimate meaning [*paramārtha*]). Regarding the teachings, each of the four teachings has its own expressive medium and expressed content, both of which are termed "Dharma";

in each case, discussing both self-benefit and the transformation of others, one may be called a "Master. Now, we focus solely on the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), specifically regarding its five aspects.
If one explains by reducing the number, the five are condensed into four, which are the four modes of peaceful conduct as explained later;

furthermore, they are condensed into three, namely the undertaking of the three types of action: reciting and explaining is vocal action, writing is physical action, and [the remaining] is mental action.

If discussed separately, vocal action is for the sake of transforming others, while physical and mental actions are for one's own practice; however, if discussed generally, [all three] pertain to both.
Thus, the self-regulation of the three karmas constitutes the Dharma Master who practices for oneself; the instruction through the three karmas constitutes the Dharma Master who transforms others.
Therefore, it is called the "Dharma Master Chapter. Furthermore, practicing these five dharmas by means of these three gates to cultivate oneself is the gate of merit and virtue;
extensively proclaiming these five dharmas to broadly benefit others is the gate of transforming others. Both self-cultivation and benefiting others [are contained herein].

To follow the Buddha’s teaching is the Gate of Repaying Kindness (*pratīkāra*). To discuss this specifically: cultivating it for oneself is called benefiting oneself through repaying kindness, while transforming others is benefiting them.
Generally speaking, however, following these norms for oneself and guiding others with them both constitutes being a Dharma Master; thus, it is called the "Dharma Master Chapter.
Furthermore, these three norms—reading, reciting, and copying—are the external practices, which correspond to the Tathāgata’s robe. Upholding [the Dharma] corresponds to...
Internal practice is the Tathāgata’s seat; explaining [the Dharma] for the benefit of others is the Tathāgata’s chamber.
In a specific sense, the chamber refers to clothing others while the seat refers to clothing oneself;

in a general sense, compassion that covers all things and the bestowing of benefit upon oneself is called the chamber, while warding off the evil obstructions of others and one's own faults is called the garment. Only by settling the mind in emptiness can one truly find peace.
To settle oneself and, having settled oneself, to designate this as one's seat constitutes the three dharmas of self-discipline;

these are also called the three dharmas of the Dharma-master for transforming others. To benefit beings, one must take compassion as the primary entry; to engage with the phenomenal world, one must take patience as the foundation;
to rescue others, one must take the absence of self as the essential capacity. One who can practice these three dharmas is a true Dharma-master.

Because this Great Teaching is proclaimed and disseminated, making it fit to serve as a refuge for the world, it is called the "Chapter on the Dharma Master. Furthermore, when condensed, it consists of two aspects:
self-cultivation and the transformation of others, which are easy to understand. When condensed into one, it refers to the practice of the Tathāgata, which encompasses all practices.
Discussing them in general terms, compassion extracts one from all suffering—namely, that of the four realms of existence, the three realms, the two vehicles, and bodhisattvas.
Impartial compassion bestows all happiness, namely the constant bliss of humans, devas, and nirvāṇa;
the garment of gentleness conceals all ugliness, namely the ugliness of the four abidings, ignorance, and nescience;
the seat of emptiness causes all marks to vanish, namely the marks of existence, non-existence, both, and neither. Discussed separately, compassion gives rise to all that is wholesome.
Gentleness wards off all evils; the empty seat sweeps away all marks. Furthermore, compassion and patience establish all merit;
the empty seat accomplishes all wisdom. Wisdom is the eye, and merit is the foot. Moreover, compassion and mercy surpass all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
gentleness surpasses all ordinary people and non-Buddhists; the empty seat surpasses all.

The Bodhisattvas who analyze the substance [of phenomena] as being equally partial [to emptiness and existence] further destroy the Māra of the heavens through compassion, the Māra of the aggregates through gentleness, and the Māras of afflictions and death through emptiness.
Furthermore, because they possess both compassion and patience, they are able to ask questions; because they possess emptiness, they are able to answer.

Moreover, because they possess both compassion and patience, they are able to plant [the seeds of merit], and because they contemplate emptiness, they are able to answer. Because they possess both compassion and patience, they are able to cultivate [wholesome roots].
Because it establishes that which can support the wisdom of emptiness, it is able to weed, to shatter, and to guide; furthermore, because it possesses compassion, what could obstruct it?
Because it is gentle and supple, what could hinder it? Because it is the seat of emptiness, what could cause contention?

Thus the Sūtra says: "All wholesome dharmas have loving-kindness as their root; patience is the foremost path; the signless is supreme" (the signless being the emptiness of all phenomena). If we discuss its perfection:
The practice and exposition are inexhaustible; as stated in detail in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning), the five practices of the one mind encompass all practices.

Question: For what reason is the Dharma Master explained by means of the three dharmas? Answer: If one discusses matters solely from the perspective of worldly affairs (*shi*), it is necessary to ascend the hall, adjust one’s robes, and take one’s seat before one can propagate the teaching;
therefore, it is discussed in terms of these three. However, if one discusses both affairs and principle (*li*) together, [one must consider] delusion...
Delusions do not exceed three types: first, regarding the arising of delusion with respect to the fruit of suffering, one must employ compassion to grant and remove;
second, regarding the arising of delusion with respect to fetters and karma, one must employ gentleness and patience to distance oneself from them;

third, regarding the arising of delusion with respect to the principle of the Truths, one must employ the realization of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*) to attain thorough understanding. (The first two belong to the category of "phenomena," while the last belongs to both "principle" and "phenomena"; both principle and phenomenon are the objects of delusion. If one considers only the principle alone, it is delusion.

Because one falls into suffering due to attachment to reality, one must employ the gate of compassion; because one sinks into emptiness and clings to pleasure due to delusion regarding the conventional, one must employ the gate of harmony and patience;

because one forms an obstruction to wisdom due to delusion within the midst [of phenomena], one must employ the gate of the emptiness of dharmas. These can be understood through the contemplation of the fundamental and the manifested, and the mind.

△ Section Three: The Propagation of the Trace Gate (Ji-mén) consists of five chapters in total. This is not only to provide shelter and benefit for the present age, but also to ferry and moisten those of future generations.
1. The Chapter on the Dharma Master; 2. The Chapter on the Jeweled Stupa—both clarify that the merit of propagating the sutra is profound and its blessings heavy, resulting in vast benefits.
3. The Chapter on the Many (Pú-sà-dá-duō)—this cites those from antiquity who propagated the sutra, [distinguishing] between "self" and "other."

Furthermore, to demonstrate the profound depth of his merit and virtue, [the Buddha speaks of] the Chapter on the Fourfold Sustenance, where eighty thousand great beings have perfected the power of patience;

those who propagate the sutra in this land and have newly attained the stage of retention, and those who propagate the sutra in other lands. In the Chapter on the Five Practices for Peaceful Living, ordinary worldlings at the initial stage rejoice in these supreme blessings;
yet, upon hearing of the fearsome nature of the śrāvakas or the insults and humiliations suffered by the bodhisattvas, they look back upon their own strength [and feel apprehensive].
For those who are weak and find no benefit for themselves or others, and who consequently fall into despondency, the Buddha taught the "Peaceful Practices" (Anrakugyō).

By relying upon these, one may propagate the Dharma without fearing danger or suffering. Furthermore, in the "Chapter on the Dharma Master," the World-Honored One himself spoke of the merit and blessings of propagating the sutra, urging its circulation.
In the "Chapter on the Jeweled Stupa," the Many Treasures Buddha and his emanations both bear witness to and assist this propagation, exhorting one to seek its dissemination. (Jeweled Stupa)

In order to realize the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the emanated Buddhas come to assist in opening the precious stupa; thus they assemble. Chapter One: The Chapter on the Dharma Master. Part One: First, praising those who can uphold the Dharma;
second, praising the Dharma that is upheld and showing the method for circulating the sutra. In the first part, there are two sections:

first, clarifying the profound merit and heavy blessings of the disciples who receive the Way; second, clarifying the profound merit and heavy blessings of the teachers who transmit the Way. In the first of these, there are again two sections.
There are two types of disciples of the Buddhas of the world: those from the time of the [Buddha’s] parinirvāṇa and those of the present.
This concerns the former. At that time, the World-Honored One, because of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja, addressed eighty thousand great beings:
"Bhaiṣajyarāja, do you see these immeasurable devas, nāga kings, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas within this great assembly?"
Whether they be nāgas, mahoragas, humans, or non-humans; whether they be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās;

or those seeking the path of the śrāvaka, those seeking the path of the pratyekabuddha, or those seeking the Buddha-way—should any such beings as these, before the Buddha, hear even a single verse or a single phrase of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and rejoice in it for even a single thought-moment, I [shall protect them].
All were granted the prediction that they would attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

"Cause" (*yin*) means entrustment; "proclamation" (*gào*) means a universal announcement. Because the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja burned his own body for the sake of the Dharma, and because the power of forbearance of the eighty thousand great beings was profound and firm, the sublime Dharma is now being circulated; this was first due to the universal proclamation by Bhaiṣajyarāja.
It was because eighty thousand [beings] desired to diligently protect, uphold, and assist in proclaiming [the Dharma].

When you see this great assembly, it is not merely that the four individuals headed by Śāriputra, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, five hundred, one thousand, two thousand, or two thousand others who have received their predictions;
rather, it includes all those from the eight classes and the fourfold assembly, as well as those seeking the three vehicles, who have heard even a single verse or a single [stanza].

Because it is certain and beyond doubt that one will attain Buddhahood through rejoicing in even a single phrase or a single thought-moment, I now bestow the prediction of enlightenment upon all universally.
"A single verse or a single phrase" is mentioned as a small example to illustrate the many; "rejoicing in a single thought-moment" is mentioned as a shallow example to illustrate the profound.
As for what is heard, it does not matter which verse or which phrase it may be, provided only that its meaning accords with both the provisional and the ultimate.

The ten wonders of the original and the trace, the four and the one, and the resulting merit and blessings are all likewise. Even if one does not discuss rejoicing in them, nor reading, reciting, or practicing them,
if one can deeply understand within a single thought-moment that the provisional is revealed as the real— this is the fundamental principle which is neither provisional nor real—
it is therefore able to be both provisional and real, with the provisional and the real being non-dual, such that phenomena and principle are perfectly interfused and complete.

The nature of afflictions can know the secret treasury of the Tathāgata; furthermore, within a single thought-moment, one extensively understands that all minds and all phenomena are the Buddha-dharma without obstruction.
If one wishes to analyze and expound these inexhaustible dharmas, since the dharma is thus, so too is the person—as described below regarding the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging.

Bestowing predictions upon the fourfold assembly is precisely what constitutes attaining this intent; thus, the Mahāyāna Sūtra says: "It would be better to hear little but understand much of the flavor and meaning of the Dharma.
This point will be explained further later when the *Anumodanā-parivarta* (Chapter on Rejoicing) is expounded. △ Second, the disciples after the extinction [of the Buddha].
The Buddha told Bhaiṣajyarāja: "Furthermore, after the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa,

if there are those who hear even a single verse or a single phrase of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and rejoice in it for even a single moment of thought, I shall likewise bestow upon them the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Because the merit and blessings of hearing and rejoicing in the sutra after [the Buddha’s] parinirvāṇa are identical to those when the Buddha is present, they likewise receive the same prediction.

This concludes the section clarifying that the disciples who receive the Way possess profound merit and heavy blessings. △ Second, clarifying that the teacher who bestows the Way possesses profound merit and heavy blessings, in two parts:

first, the long prose; second, the verse summary. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, the specific explanation; second, the general explanation. Within the first [section], there are two parts: first, the individual clarification; second, the collective [clarification].

Regarding the clarification of the distinctions: there are inferior and superior persons, and present and future times. As for the general [explanation], it does not distinguish between inferior and superior, nor between present and future;

it universally clarifies that one incurs transgression by acting contrary [to the teacher] and gains merit by acting in accordance with them. In the first section on the distinctions, there are two parts:
first, clarifying the present life; second, clarifying future lives. The first of these also has two parts: first, clarifying the inferior teacher; second, clarifying the superior teacher.
All of this is judged according to the stage of ordinary beings. First:

If there should be another person who receives, maintains, reads, recites, explains, or transcribes even a single verse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, and who regards this scripture with reverence as if it were the Buddha, making various offerings of flowers, incense, necklaces, powdered incense, and ointments;
Burning incense, offering silk canopies, banners, pennants, robes, music, and even joining the palms in reverent salutation—this first clarifies the characteristics of the inferior type of teacher.
These consist of five kinds of Dharma-preachers: first, those who uphold; second, those who read; third, those who recite; fourth, those who explain;
and fifth, those who transcribe. [The offerings include] first, flowers; second, incense; third, necklaces; fourth, powdered incense; and fifth, [unguents].
Anointing with incense (1), burning incense (2), silk canopies, banners, and streamers (3), robes (4), music and performance (5), and joining the palms (6)—
these constitute the ten kinds of offerings. Bhaiṣajyarāja,
you should know that these people have already made offerings to ten trillion buddhas in the presence of those buddhas.
Having fulfilled his great vows out of compassion for sentient beings, Bhaiṣajyarāja was born into this human world.
If someone should ask, "What kind of sentient beings will attain Buddhahood in future ages? you should point to these people and say that they will certainly attain Buddhahood in future ages.
Why is this? If good sons or good daughters, regarding even a single verse from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*...

If one upholds, recites, explains, or transcribes even a single phrase, and makes various offerings to this scripture—such as flowers, incense, necklaces, powdered incense, ointments, burning incense, silk canopies, banners, pennants, robes, and music—and joins their palms in reverence, such a person should be looked upon and honored by all the world;
they should be venerated with the same offerings one would offer to a Tathāgata. You should know this.
This person is a great bodhisattva who has attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
out of compassion for sentient beings, he has made a vow to be born in this world to extensively expound and analyze the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
This extensively clarifies the retribution for the merit of an inferior teacher. The phrase "having already made offerings, etc. clarifies the profundity of past causes;
the phrase "out of deep compassion for sentient beings, etc. clarifies the greatness of present merit; and the phrase "if someone asks, etc. clarifies the gravity of future retribution.
△ Second, the clarification of the superior teacher.
How much more so for those who are able to fully receive and uphold it and provide various offerings!

Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know that such persons, having relinquished their own pure karmic retribution, will—out of compassion for sentient beings—be born in an evil world after my parinirvāṇa to widely expound this sutra.

First, having already presented the characteristics of the superior teacher, next, regarding the King of Medicine (Bhaiṣajyarāja), one should know that this briefly clarifies the merit and retribution of the superior teacher.
Because they are drawn by compassionate vows, these are still karmic-born retinues and not yet those born through supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

One should form aspirations based on both karma and vows, as detailed in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) in the "Exquisite Explanation of Retinues. This concludes the first section: Clarifying the Worldly Aspects of the Sūtra. △ Second, Clarifying [the Supramundane].
In the future life, there are also two types: first, the explanation of the teacher of inferior grade; second, the explanation of the teacher of superior grade.

Now, for the first: if a son of good family or a daughter of good family, after my parinirvāṇa, is able to secretly preach even a single verse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* for the sake of a single person, you should know that this person is an emissary of the Tathāgata, one sent by the Tathāgata to carry out the Tathāgata’s work.
Regarding this matter, I venture to say that for a single person, the transformation achieved through even a single phrase is extremely limited;
indeed, one who possesses wisdom but lacks learning is not yet fit to stand before a vast assembly to expound this teaching at length. This clarifies the characteristics of an inferior teacher.
Furthermore, this sutra was spoken by the Tathāgata-jñāna (Tathāgata-wisdom) as that which accords with reality (*yathābhūta*);
now, the practitioner upholds these teachings according to reality and proclaims them in accordance with reality, and is therefore a messenger of the Tathāgata, dispatched by the Tathāgata.

Moreover, just as Tathāgata-jñāna illuminates reality as its object, the practitioner now practices in accordance with reality based on these teachings; thus, they are one who practices in accordance with reality (*yathābhūta-caryā*).
The "coming task" refers to the activity of transforming sentient beings through the principle of suchness and such-like wisdom.

Now, when a practitioner possesses great compassion and explains the principle of True Suchness found within this sutra for the sake of others, enabling them to attain benefit, they are said to be performing the task of a Tathāgata.
This clarifies the merit and retribution of the lower grade of teacher. Regarding the interpretation through the contemplation of the mind: it is the mind of wisdom.
Contemplating the object, the object itself is the realm of True Suchness (tathatā). When this realm arises to produce wisdom, that wisdom is employed by the Suchness.

That which is dispatched by the Tathāgata is the contemplative wisdom arising from within Suchness. One who carries out the work of the Tathāgata traverses all phenomena, none of which are not True Suchness;
True Suchness is itself the Buddha-work. △ Second, clarifying the superior-grade teacher.
How much more so when one extensively explains it for others amidst a great assembly?

Since it is already a grave offense to teach it in secret to a single person, how much more so to proclaim it publicly for a great assembly? And since it is a grave offense even to speak a single sentence, how much more so to provide a full exposition?
This is the superior mark of a teacher and the greatness of its karmic reward; it need not be stated explicitly, for it is self-evident. The initial detailed explanation is concluded.
△ Second, a general explanation of the transgressions incurred by opposing and the blessings gained by following the Dharma Master,

both present and future, regarding the superior and inferior [practitioners]. Medicine King, if there were evil persons who, with an unwholesome mind, stood before a Buddha for an entire eon constantly slandering and reviling him,
their sin would still be light compared to a person who, with a single evil word, disparages those— whether lay or ordained— who recite and uphold [the scriptures].
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is such that its transgressions are extremely grave.

This first clarifies the sin incurred by those who oppose it. Now, regarding the gravity or lightness of sins and blessings, one sometimes discusses them in terms of the "field" (the object), sometimes in terms of the "mind" (the intention), and sometimes in terms of the harm or benefit caused;
thus there are cases where they are grave and cases where they are light. Here, the discussion is specifically based on the gravity or lightness of the harm or benefit.

Furthermore, consider an evil person who, with an unwholesome mind—already grave—and toward the Buddha as a field of merit—already venerable—continues to revile him for an entire kalpa, thus making the karma long-lasting; yet it is said that this is still "light.

This does not mean that the retribution for the offense is light, but rather that it is still not as heavy as the sin of disparaging the reading and recitation of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Why is this so?
Therefore, the Buddha realizes impartial great compassion and constantly maintains a heart of pity for evil people;

furthermore, because he cannot be provoked or harmed by such evil people, those who revile him are, at the beginning, like those who send someone off with courtesy but are refused by them—the misfortune returns to themselves as they fall into the three miserable realms for hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas. In the end, it is like striking and reviling [an invulnerable being].

Even as sandalwood, though it possesses a fragrant scent, is further transformed by the Buddha’s influence until it ultimately becomes a cause for transcending the world, so too might a beginner practitioner who recites the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* yet has not yet perfected the power of patience easily fall back or sink away.

If such a person were to utter even a single word of disparagement, thereby obstructing this supreme matter, they would sever the seed of the Buddha; because the harm is so profound, their transgression is exceedingly grave.
Furthermore,
Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know that anyone who reads and recites the Lotus Sūtra adorns themselves with the adornments of the Buddha;
they are carried upon the shoulders of the Tathāgata, and toward whichever direction they go, one should turn and pay homage with single-minded devotion.

With palms joined in reverence, one should honor, respect, and praise them with offerings of flowers, incense, garlands, powdered incense, unguents, burning incense, silk canopies, banners, streamers, robes, and delicacies, performing various musical arts as the supreme offerings among humans.
One should hold celestial jewels and scatter them, and present heaps of heavenly treasures as offerings. Why is this so?
Because this person joyfully preaches the Dharma and those who hear it for even a moment immediately attain ultimate *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
this next section clarifies the merit obtained by following [the teaching]. The Buddha, adorned with concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), enables this person to cultivate concentration.
Because of wisdom, it is said that one adorns oneself with the adornments of the Buddha. To bear it on the back is "carrying" (he), and to carry it on the shoulders is "bearing" (dan).
Cultivating the Dharma-body, which is neither provisional nor ultimate, is precisely what constitutes the Tathāgata’s "carrying.
Possessing the functions of both the provisional and ultimate two wisdoms is precisely what constitutes the Tathāgata’s "bearing. Whichever direction one goes, one should proceed accordingly.
Ritual (*li*) refers to that which this person directs toward; all such things are in accord with the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). All are worthy of veneration and compliance;

"compliance" is precisely "direction," and "veneration" is precisely "ritual instruction. To comply with and thereby offer worship—using celestial jewels and the like as examples—is to hold what is heavy as a model for what is light.
If even celestial jewels should be offered in worship, how much more so the supreme offerings among humans?
Why is this so? The following passage explains and establishes the meaning of why [the teacher] should be honored and offered to:

because by means of him, one can immediately attain the ultimate, as he is able to perfectly manifest the ultimate, wondrous principle. Furthermore, it is necessary to distinguish between the stages from the "ultimate of names" up to the "ultimate of the ultimate.
This section clarifies the profound merit and heavy blessings of the teacher who bestows the Way; within this, the first part is extensive.

The prose section concludes. △ Second, the verses in praise have three parts: first, exhorting the practice of self-benefit and benefiting others; second, reiterating the two meanings of the specific and the general;
third, concluding with a eulogy on the sutra as being supreme. Now, the first part.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"If one wishes to abide in the Buddha-way and achieve spontaneous wisdom, one should always diligently make offerings to and uphold those who receive and maintain the Lotus Sutra.
Those who wish to quickly attain the wisdom of all modes should receive and uphold this sutra, as well as make offerings to its upholders."
△ Second, the two verses on the distinct and general meanings. Part one: the two verses that distinctly clarify [the meaning]. Part two: the two verses that generally clarify [the meaning].
Within the first part, there are two: first, the verse on the present life; second, the verse on future lives. This is the first.
If there are those who can receive and uphold the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, you should know they are sent by the Buddha to have compassion for all sentient beings.
Those who can receive and uphold the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* abandon the pure lands and, out of compassion for the masses, are born here.
You should know that such persons are sovereign over where they wish to be born and are able to extensively expound the unsurpassed Dharma in this evil world.
One should offer celestial flowers, incense, divine precious garments, and heaps of exquisite celestial jewels to those who preach the Dharma.
The first two lines of the verse praise the inferior teacher; the next two lines praise the inferior merit and reward;
the following two lines praise the superior teacher; and the final ten lines praise the superior merit and reward. △ Second, the verse on future lives.

"After my parinirvāṇa, those who are able to uphold this sutra in the evil age should join their palms in reverent salutation, as if making offerings to the World-Honored One with the finest delicacies, various sweets, and diverse garments. I hope that these sons of the Buddha may be granted even a moment’s hearing of it;
if they can receive and uphold this sutra in future ages, I shall dispatch them to act on behalf of the Tathāgata among the people."

The first two lines are a transposed verse praising the superior teacher; the next six lines clarify the karmic rewards for the superior practice (these are not mentioned in the long prose but appear here in the verse).
The following two lines are a retrospective verse on the inferior teacher, and the final two lines praise the karmic rewards for the inferior practice.
This concludes the section on the specific explanations. △ Second, the general explanation.
If one were to constantly harbor an unwholesome mind for an entire kalpa, assuming a wrathful countenance to revile the Buddha, they would incur immeasurable heavy offenses;
yet if someone were to utter even a single harsh word against one who reads, recites, and upholds this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, their offense would exceed that of the former.
Furthermore, if there were someone seeking the Buddha-way who, for an entire kalpa, stood before me with palms joined and praised me with countless verses, [the merit would be even greater].
By thus praising the Buddha, one obtains immeasurable merit; yet the merit of extolling those who uphold this sutra exceeds even that.

If for eighty billion kalpas one were to provide offerings of the most exquisite forms, sounds, scents, tastes, and textures to such upholders of the sutra, and after having made such offerings, were to hear it for even a single moment, one should rejoice within oneself, thinking: "I have now attained a great benefit."
The first two verses praise [the Buddha] by way of inversion to show that one incurs transgression; the latter four verses praise him by way of conformity to show that one attains merit.

While it is true that the Buddha’s merits are indeed immeasurable and that he does not increase because of praise, if one praises the place where this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is upheld, that place is as if the Buddha himself were present.
Since his merits are already identical [to those of the Buddha], this further causes the upholder of the sūtra to follow [the Buddha].
This is why his merit increases and becomes doubly superior. This concludes the second section, consisting of two verses that distinguish and summarize the two meanings.
△ Third, the concluding praise that this sutra is the most supreme:
"O Bhaiṣajyarāja, I now tell you: among all the various sutras I have preached, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the most supreme."

In this sutra, the phrase "throughout these various sutras" refers collectively to all that was taught during the Buddha's entire lifetime, beginning from the *Avataṃsaka* and ending with the *Nirvāṇa*.
While each of the Mahāyāna sutras individually claims to be the foremost teaching, such "firstness" is merely relative;
it does not equal the absolute firstness of this sutra, which is therefore called the "most foremost."
The first section, concluding the praise for those capable of upholding the Dharma, is finished. △ Second, praising the Dharma upheld and showing the method for circulating the sutra, in two parts:
first, the long prose; second, the two verses. Within the first part, there are five sub-sections: first, praising the Dharma in terms of its content;
second, praising it in terms of the persons; third, praising it in terms of the location; fourth, praising it in terms of... [text continues].
This is the first of the five praises based on the fruit.
At that time, the Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja:
"Of the immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of sūtras that I have spoken, am speaking, or shall speak, among them all, this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the most difficult to believe."
Bhaiṣajyarāja, this sutra is difficult to understand; it is the secret and essential treasury of all Buddhas, not to be distributed or recklessly bestowed upon others.
It is guarded by the World-Honored Buddhas and has never been openly proclaimed since the past.
If even while the Tathāgata is present in the world there are still so many who harbor resentment and jealousy toward this sutra, how much more so after his parinirvāṇa?

Having already explained the various gradual and sudden teachings preceding the *Prajñāpāramitā*, I shall now explain the *Anantaryārtha-sūtra* (the Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings) as being taught from the same seat.

Next, I shall explain the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. While the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other gradual and sudden sūtras all employ skillful means (*upāya*) so that they may be easily accepted with faith, the *Anantaryārtha-sūtra* clarifies how a single lifetime possesses immeasurable meanings.

It is clear that returning the infinite to the one makes it easy to gain faith; however, the *Dharmaparyāya of the Lotus Sūtra* is difficult to believe and understand because its doctrine integrates all distinctions into a single unity, its teachers and disciples both possess ancient origins in their fundamental and manifested forms, and both aspects stand in direct opposition to what came before.
Such matters are difficult to confront head-on, yet the *Lotus Sūtra* has already been preached, while the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* remains yet to come.

Thus, the *Yì* (the Book of Changes) may be trusted as a treasury of secret essentials. That which is hidden and not explained is called "secret" (*mì*). That which encompasses all phenomena is called "essential" (*yào*).
That which subsumes the true nature of reality (*tathatā*) and the mark of reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) without exception is called a "treasury" (*zàng*).
Because it cannot be distributed—its Dharma being so wondrous as to be difficult to believe—it can only be bestowed upon those with profound wisdom; it is not for those lacking such wisdom.
Because it would increase their transgressions, one must not bestow [this teaching] recklessly.

That which has never been explicitly taught since antiquity is that within the Tripiṭaka, it is not stated that those of the Two Vehicles attain Buddhahood, nor is the fundamental and manifested reality (honji-suijaku) of teachers and disciples clarified.

Although the Prajñāpāramitā and Vaipulya sutras speak of the principle of the true mark and the Tathāgatagarbha, they do not yet state that those of the Five Vehicles attain Buddhahood, nor do they reveal their origins.
It is called "secret" because it reveals that the various sūtras of the original, sudden, and gradual teachings have not yet been harmonized;
this sūtra fully expounds the dharmas previously kept secret, which is precisely the opening of the secret treasury (*guhyakośa*), and is itself the secret treasury.
Although this secret treasury was previously spoken in a hidden manner for a certain class of beings whose faculties had matured, for more than forty years it had never been [fully revealed].
To manifest and explain clearly yet still encounter much resentment and jealousy—as when five thousand people withdrew from their seats—shows that even in the Buddha’s own time it was so;
how much more so in the future? For the principle is that those who are difficult to transform are hard to reach. △ Second, praising by way of the person.

Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know that after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, whoever is able to write down, uphold, read, recite, make offerings to, and explain it to others will be covered by the Tathāgata with his own robe and will be protected and remembered by the Buddhas currently residing in other directions.
You should know that such a person possesses great power of faith, power of aspiration, and power of all roots of goodness. You should know that this person is...
If one stays overnight with the Tathāgata, the Tathāgata will personally stroke one’s head with his hand.
When this Dharma resides in a person, that person becomes noble and honored. That which is covered by the Tathāgata’s robe is the cultivation and study of great patience as one’s garment.
As for being protected and remembered by all Buddhas: true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is the Buddha, and true wisdom (*bhūtajñāna*) is the son; one honors true reality.

The arising of true wisdom through these marks constitutes being protected and remembered by all Buddhas. In the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), the four indestructible faiths constitute the power of great faith; the four universal vows constitute the power of aspiration; and wondrous, great wisdom constitutes the power of roots of goodness. Faith is the belief in principle, and principle is the Dharma-body; aspiration is the establishment of practice, and practice is liberation. Goodness is the perfection of the path. Thus, these three powers encompass all the Buddha-dharmas. Furthermore, the four indestructible faiths are the foundation for the four universal vows; the four universal vows are the foundation for the six perfections; and the six perfections are the foundation for the three bodies. Therefore, it is said that the three bodies are the ultimate fruit of the three powers. This is called the "Three Powers of the Perfect Teaching. It is also called the "Three Powers of the Great Vehicle," because they are the most supreme among the various vehicles. It is also called the "Three Powers of the Mahāyāna," because they are the most profound among the various vehicles. It is also called the "Three Powers of the Buddha-vehicle," because they are the most ultimate among the various vehicles. It is also called the "Three Powers of the One Vehicle," because they are the most complete among the various vehicles. It is also called the "Three Powers of the Universal Vehicle," because they universally encompass all vehicles. It is also called the "Three Powers of the Unsurpassed Vehicle," because there is no vehicle superior to them. It is also called the "Three Powers of the Supreme Vehicle," because they are the most exalted among all vehicles. It is also called the "Three Powers of the Peerless Vehicle," because there is nothing that can equal them. It is also called the "Three Powers of the Unconquerable Vehicle," because no one can overcome them. It is also called the "Three Powers of the Incomparable Vehicle," because there is nothing that can compare with them. When the initial resolve (*ādikṣānti*) dwells herein, it is no different from a Buddha; therefore, it is called "dwelling together with the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, through the power of faith, one cultivates ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), which is the wisdom of the Tathāgata. Just as the Tathāgata dwells in the abode of ultimate emptiness, this person also studies ultimate emptiness.

Therefore, he dwells together with the Tathāgata; through the power of his vows and the power of his roots of goodness, by means of his own practice of the provisional and the real, he becomes a responsive stimulus.
This "stimulus" refers to the head of this person, which the Tathāgata—by means of the hands of his two wisdoms, the provisional and the real for the sake of transforming others—unveils.
Because the resonance between the stimulus and the response is thus established, it is said that he "touches the head. "Touching the head" (mōtō) is precisely...
This is the bestowal of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*). △ Third, praising by way of location:

Wherever the Medicine King resides—whether he is preaching, reading, reciting, copying, or where the scrolls of the sutra are kept—one should erect a stupa made of the seven precious substances there, making it exceedingly high, vast, and magnificently adorned; it is not necessary to enshrine relics therein.
Why is this? Because within this [stūpa] already resides the entire body of the Tathāgata;
this stūpa should be honored, revered, respected, and praised with all kinds of flowers, incense, necklaces, silk canopies, banners, pennants, music, songs, and hymns.
If there are those who see this stūpa, pay homage to it, and make offerings, you should know that they have all drawn near to Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Bodhi. Wherever this Dharma resides, that place is noble. Indeed, the places where the Buddha was born, where he attained the Way, where he turned the wheel of Dharma, and where he entered nirvana—all these should have stupas erected.
This sutra is the birthplace of the Dharma-body and the field for attaining the Way.

Because the Dharma-wheel is the very essence of the Great Nirvāṇa Cave, one should erect a stūpa to make offerings to it; there is no need to further enshrine physical relics (*śarīra*). As the *Śāstra* states:
"The pulverized bones are the relics of the birth-body (*janma-kāya*); the sūtra scrolls are the relics of the Dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*).
Regarding those who already possess the Tathāgata’s entire body, these are the relics of the birth-body; they may be either pulverized or whole. As for the pulverized...
Śākyamuni is entirely whole, whereas the Dharma-body relics of Prabhūtaratna consist of both fragments and wholes;

likewise, the various provisional teachings are "fragmented," while the *Lotus Sūtra*—the single reality—is "whole. (In the detailed analysis of the four teachings and five periods, some are purely fragmented with no wholes, some are half-whole and half-fragmented, but only the *Lotus Sūtra* is purely whole.)
△ Fourth, praise by way of the cause:
"Bhaiṣajyarāja, there are many people, whether householders or renunciants, who practice the bodhisattva path;

yet if they are unable to see, hear, read, recite, copy, uphold, or make offerings to this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, you should know that these persons have not yet skillfully practiced the bodhisattva path."
If there are those who hear this sutra, they will be able to properly practice the path of the bodhisattva.
Other sutras, which involve expedient means as their cause, are termed "clumsy deliverance" (*duḥkha-yāna*); this sutra correctly reveals the perfect cause.

Only upon hearing and understanding this perfect cause is it termed "skillful deliverance" (*kuśala-yāna*), and skillful deliverance constitutes the proper practice. (In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the Mahāyāna gate is generally taken to be skillful; here, however, the single reality is specifically identified as skillful.)

△ Fifth, praising [the teaching] by way of its fruit; this also has five parts: first, clarifying the proximate fruit; second, establishing a simile; third, applying the analogy to the Dharma; fourth, explaining the proximity;
fifth, excluding what is not [the fruit]. Now, for the first:
"If there are sentient beings who seek the Buddha-way, and they see or hear this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, and having heard it, believe and understand it..."
Those who uphold [this teaching] should know that such persons draw near to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
There are two meanings of *anuttara-bodhi*: first, the *bodhi* of the initial mind, which corresponds to the first stage of the Perfect Teaching (*yuan-chu-zhu*);

second, the *bodhi* of the final mind, which is the ultimate fruit of Wondrous Enlightenment (*miao-jue*). What is here called "drawing near" refers specifically to drawing near to the *bodhi* of the initial stage.

Previously, it was stated that praising the cultivation of the distinct causes constitutes not yet being skilled in departing from the fruit of perfection; thus, one is far from the fruit of perfection.
Now, taking the perfect, suchness-as-it-is wisdom as the cause, it is likewise taken as the fruit.
Although there are three types of causes within the True Suchness prior to the Path—namely, the "True Cause" (the stage of Principle)—it is the True Suchness within the Path that [is meant here].

Likewise, there are three causes that share the name "conditioning cause" (*pratyaya-hetu*)—namely, the stage of designation (*nāma-tathatā*), the stage of contemplative practice (*pratipatti-tathatā*), and the stage of resemblance (*sādṛśya-tathatā*)—and they are also called "revealing causes" (*vyañjana-hetu*), which is the stage of partial realization (*praveśa-tathatā*).
Furthermore, the True Suchness (*tathatā*) subsequent to the Path is merely these same three dharmas renamed as the "Perfect Fruit" (*niṣṭhā-tathatā*).

Therefore, the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-dhyāna-sūtra* states: "The cause of the Mahāyāna is the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena; the fruit of the Mahāyāna is likewise the true reality of all phenomena."
The *Śāstra* explains: "Observing the true reality (*tattva*) at the beginning is called the cause; when the observation is completed, it is called the fruit.
Discussing this from the perspective of principle (*li*), True Suchness (*tathatā*) and true reality are neither cause nor fruit, nor do they possess sequence.
However, in terms of spiritual cultivation (*pratipatti*), there is both sequence and the relationship of cause and fruit. △ Second, establishing analogies.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, it is like a person who, parched with thirst and needing water, digs for it on a high plateau;
seeing only dry earth, he knows the water is still far off. Yet, not ceasing his efforts, he sees moist soil and gradually reaches mud;
his mind becomes certain that the water must be near.
This is explained in two parts: first, in terms of the gate of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-mukha*); second, in terms of the gate of teaching (*deśanā-mukha*). Regarding the gate of contemplation:

the minds of sentient beings are possessed of all afflictions (*kleśa*), which is likened to a high plateau. Cultivating the wisdom of contemplation is likened to digging and excavating, through which one realizes the flavor of principle (*tattva-rasa*), just as one obtains clear water.

If we consider this in terms of the general contemplations, the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi*) is like dry soil, while the Ground of Nature (*prakṛti-bhūmi*) is like moist soil and mud.
Seeing the Truth (darśana-mārga) serves as the means to obtain pure water; yet, when distinguished by specific contemplation, it involves entering emptiness from the conventional.

One sees only emptiness and does not see that which is not empty, thereby severing the delusions of the four abodes (*catur-vāsabhūmi*). This is like digging dry earth: one is still far from reaching the water.

Entering the conventional from emptiness, one first realizes what is not conventional and now realizes what is not empty. By means of these two contemplations, one attains entry into the Middle Way and is able to subdue ignorance.
When one clearly perceives that the soil is moist and that water is near, it is like the contemplation of the Middle Way as neither empty nor false, yet illuminating both emptiness and the false;

because the four abidings have been exhausted, ignorance has been suppressed, and one has attained a semblance of the perfect understanding of the Middle Way, it is said to be "like gradually reaching the mud.
If one enters the first dwelling (bhūmi) and gives rise to the true understanding of the Middle Way, one then shatters ignorance, which is like [actually reaching the water].

When the mud is cleared and purified, the Middle Way becomes visible, just as when one obtains clear water. Thus, the *Fahua lun* (Treatise on the Lotus Sūtra) states: "The Buddha-nature is like water;
one should know its sequence. Regarding the gates of teaching: "earth" is a metaphor for the sūtras and teachings, while "water" is a metaphor for the Middle Way.

The teachings explain the Middle Way just as earth contains water. The Three Baskets (*Tripiṭaka*) have not yet explained the Middle Way, which is like dry earth; the *Vaipulya* and *Prajñāpāramitā* [sūtras] are likewise.
The teaching of the Middle Way through expedient means is like moist soil; the teaching of the Middle Way in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* through direct revelation is like mud.
Because of the instruction of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, through hearing, reflection, and cultivation, one immediately awakens to the Middle Way and truly perceives the Buddha-nature.

The true wisdom thus aroused no longer relies on the literal text, just as once pure water is obtained, there is no longer any appearance of soil. Therefore, [the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* says: "The *Avataṃsaka*..."
It is said that at the very moment of first generating the mind of enlightenment, one attains perfect awakening and achieves the body of wisdom, not through realization by means of another.
△ Third, the analogy of the Dharma:
A bodhisattva is also like this; if they have not yet heard, nor understood, nor been able to practice this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, then...
One should know that such a person is still far from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
yet if they hear, understand, contemplate, and practice it, one must know that they will certainly draw near to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
To obtain hearing and contemplation within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* constitutes the three types of wisdom (*trividya*) of the Perfect Teaching;
only through these can one approach the fruit, for they are not the three types of wisdom found in the "dry" or "moist" teachings. △ Fourth, the explanation of "approaching."
Why is this? Because the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all bodhisattvas is entirely contained within this sutra.
This sutra opens the gate of skillful means and reveals the mark of reality. This treasury of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is profound, firm, remote, and deep;
no one has been able to reach it until now. Today, the Buddha teaches and brings bodhisattvas to fulfillment, revealing it for their sake.
All Bodhisattvas point to the provisional causes for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and they point to the provisional fruits;
both these provisional causes and provisional fruits are subsumed within this sutra, just as all soil, whether dry or moist, depends upon water.
"Opening the gate of expedient means and revealing the true aspect" means that what was not previously taught is now all being taught; whereas previously only two contemplations were taught.
As skillful means, these have now all been opened; they are themselves the ultimate reality. How could they still be mere "gates"?
Previously, the Small Vehicle’s skillful means and its fruits were taught; yet if even the fruits of the Small Vehicle are not the true mark of reality, how much more so the minor skillful means?
That which was always a gate has now all been opened as the true mark of reality. What you practice is the Bodhisattva path.
The definitive teaching on the Dharma of the Śrāvakas is the king of all sutras;
even mundane speech and the arts of livelihood—what was previously taught as skillful means is now fully revealed as the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), without contradiction.
This causes all sentient beings to open, reveal, awaken to, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*); in every form and scent, there is nothing that is not [this].
Whether the Buddha-dharma be considered a gate or not a gate, all are opened to reveal the true mark and manifest the water of the Buddha-nature.
Had these not been opened, it would have been deep, firm, obscure, and remote, such that no one could reach it;
now that they are opened, one immediately perceives the water without any dry earth. △ Five: Distinguishing the False.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, if there are bodhisattvas who, upon hearing this Lotus Sūtra, become startled, doubtful, or terrified,

you should know that they are bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds. If there are śrāvakas who, upon hearing this sūtra, become startled, doubtful, or terrified, you should know that they are those possessed of overweening pride.
Bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds and śrāvakas of overweening pride—who, upon hearing this sutra, are all struck with alarm, doubt, and fear—are like dry soil;
they are not even moist soil, let alone able to see water. This concludes the first section: Praising the Dharma of the Sutra.

△ Second, showing the proper method, which has two parts: 1. Directly clarifying the method; 2. Clarifying the five benefits. In the first part (directly clarifying the method), there are three sections; the first is the heading.
Chapter Two: Explanation; Part Three: Encouragement to Practice. Now, for the first [part]:
"Bhaiṣajyarāja, if there be sons or daughters of good family who, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, wish to preach this Lotus Sūtra to the fourfold assembly, how should they preach it?
Those sons or daughters of good family should enter the Tathāgata’s chamber and don the Tathāgata’s robe."
Only when one is clothed in the Tathāgata’s robe and seated upon the Tathāgata’s seat should one extensively expound this sutra for the fourfold assembly.
△ Second, the explanation:
"The Tathāgata’s chamber" is the heart of great compassion toward all sentient beings; "the Tathāgata’s robe" is gentleness.
The seat of the Tathāgata, which is the mind of patience, is the emptiness of all phenomena.
The chamber of great compassion is, when considered from the perspective of the same essence (*samatā*), the Dharmakāya;
when it embraces sentient beings, it is liberation (*vimukti*); and that which enables sentient beings to realize this same essence is Prajñā. As for the garment of gentle patience...
That which is covered is the Dharmakāya; that which covers and adorns the body is Prajñā;
that which harmonizes with light to benefit beings is Vimukti. Regarding the seat of the emptiness of phenomena:
that which sits upon it is Prajñā; that which is sat upon is the Dharmakāya; the profound correspondence between the body and the seat is Vimukti. Furthermore, there is more.

Compassionate peace and bliss are the Provisional and Accomplishing Practices (*sambhāra-mārga*); gentleness that subdues anger and severs delusions are the Contemplation Practice (*vipaśyanā-mārga*);
and sitting upon the seat is the Reality Practice (*tattva-mārga*). These three dharmas are further elaborated within the "Peaceful Practices" (*sukha-vihāra*).

What was previously called "adorned with the Buddha's ornaments" and "covered with robes" refers precisely to these robes; what was previously called "borne upon the shoulders of the Tathāgata" refers to this as well.
Furthermore, it is said that rubbing his head with his hand refers to this very seat; what was said above regarding "dwelling together with the Tathāgata" refers to this very chamber.
△ Third, the exhortation to practice:
Abiding within this, one should thereafter, with a mind free from indolence, extensively expound [the teaching] for the sake of all bodhisattvas and the fourfold assembly.

Since this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* first exhorts one to dwell securely in the three dharmas and then exhorts an untiring mind before extensively explaining [the teaching], we know that this instruction is intended only for beginners in the practice of contemplation;
once one reaches the stage of "semblance," the wondrous sound will spontaneously pervade the three thousandfold world-systems.
There is no need for exhortation. This concludes the initial section clarifying the method. II. Clarifying the Five Benefits.
"O Bhaiṣajyarāja, in other lands I shall dispatch emanated persons to assemble for them a congregation to hear the Dharma (1. Dispatching Emanated Persons).
I shall also dispatch emanated bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās to listen to their preaching of the Dharma. These emanated persons, having heard [the teaching]..."

If one faithfully accepts and follows the Dharma without opposition (2. dispatching transformations of the fourfold assembly), and if the teacher of the Dharma is in a secluded place, I shall at that time extensively dispatch devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, and so forth to listen to their preaching of the Dharma (3. dispatching the eight classes).
Although I am in another land, I will from time to time cause the teacher of the Dharma to behold my own body (4. beholding the Buddha-body). If, regarding this sutra...
If they have forgotten the punctuation or the phrasing of the text, I shall explain it for them so that they may attain completeness (the fifth being the *dhāraṇī*).
If their initial resolve is not yet pure, one may only dispatch emanated beings; one must not yet dispatch the fourfold assembly or the eight classes of supernatural beings.

This is because if devas and nāgas were to see them, they might rely on this to become arrogant, which would obstruct and harm their path; therefore, they must not be allowed to see them. If the mind...
If one is free from attachment, one is capable of seeing the Buddha and attaining *dhāraṇī*, thereby realizing great benefit; how much more so for devas, nāgas, and others?
This concludes the first section, the long prose passage, within the second part: Praising the Sūtra-Dharma and Demonstrating the Proper Method. △ Second, the Verse Recitation, which has three parts:
First, the general exhortation; second, the verse on the long prose passage; third, the concluding exhortation. Now, the first.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Those who wish to abandon all indolence should listen to this sutra; it is difficult to hear, and those who can believe and accept it are likewise rare."

△ Second, the two verses on the long prose section have two parts: first, the verses praising [the Buddha] by way of the fruit; second, the verses on the method. Within the first part, there are two sections:

first, the verses establishing the analogy; second, the verses applying the dharma (the application). The latter is brief and does not include the praise of the proximate fruit, nor does it explain the proximate [fruit], nor does it exclude what is not [the fruit].

First: It is like a person who, thirsty and needing water, digs in a high plateau; seeing only dry soil, they know the water is still far off, but gradually seeing moist soil and mud, they know with certainty that the water is near.
△ Second, the application of the analogy to the Dharma in verse:
"Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know that such persons as these, who have not heard the Lotus Sūtra, are very far from the Buddha's wisdom.
If they hear this profound sūtra—which definitively clarifies the Dharma of the Śrāvakas and is the king of all sūtras—and having heard it, contemplate it with earnest attention..."
One should know that such persons are close to the Buddha’s wisdom.
First, the praise of the fruit through verse is concluded. △ Second, the verses on the method [of practice] consist of two parts: first, the verses that correctly clarify the method;
second, the verses that clarify the five benefits. Now, the first part.
If a person says that one who would preach this sutra should enter the Tathāgata’s chamber, don the Tathāgata’s robes, and sit upon the Tathāgata’s seat—
wherein one is fearless among the assembly and explains it in detail for others— then great compassion is the chamber, gentleness and patience are the robes,
and the emptiness of all phenomena is the seat. When preaching this sutra, if someone should revile them with harsh words:
One should endure being struck by blades, staves, tiles, or stones because one is mindful of the Buddha.
The first half-verse introduces the topic; the next verse provides the explanation; and the final verse offers the exhortation to practice.
△ Second, two verses clarify the five benefits.
"In thousands of millions of billions of lands, I manifest a pure and solid body, preaching the Dharma for sentient beings throughout immeasurable billions of kalpas.
This generally clarifies the Tathāgata’s intention to benefit [beings] through five matters; it is precisely because the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) pervades the ten directions.
Only then can one provide protection for the practitioner through these five matters.
If, after my parinirvāṇa, there are those who can preach this sutra, I shall dispatch emanations of the fourfold assembly—
bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, and pure laymen and women— to make offerings to that Dharma-preacher.
This verse transcends [the previous] and constitutes the second [section], which dispatches the fourfold assembly.

It guides all sentient beings, gathering them to listen to the Dharma; if anyone intends to inflict harm with swords, staves, tiles, or stones, it then dispatches emanated beings to act as their protectors.
This is a verse summarizing the first [instance of] dispatching a transformation-body.

If a person preaching the Dharma is alone in a secluded place, silent and without the sound of human voices, while reading or reciting this sutra, I will at that time manifest a body of pure radiance for them;
if they have forgotten or lost any passages, I will explain them so that they may become fluent and proficient.
This verse transcends the fifth and encompasses the dhāraṇī.
If a person possesses these virtues, or explains the state of emptiness (*ākāśāyatana*) to the fourfold assembly, or recites this sutra, they shall all be able to see my body.
This verse concerns the fourth [point], which is causing one to see the Buddha. To be "endowed with these virtues" refers to the three virtues of the chamber, the robes, and the seat.
If a person dwells in a secluded place, I shall dispatch devas, nāga kings, yakṣas, and spirits to serve as their assembly for listening to the Dharma.
Because such a person delights in preaching the Dharma and distinguishes it without hindrance, and because all Buddhas protect and mind them, they are able to bring joy to the great assembly.
This concludes the third summary verse, which dispatches the eight classes [of spirits]. The two verses of the long prose section are now finished. △ Third, the concluding exhortation:

"If one draws near to the Dharma Master, one will swiftly attain the Bodhisattva path; by following this teacher and learning from him, one shall come to see Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."
