Chapter Eleven: The Appearance of the Jeweled Stūpa. Regarding the stūpa:
it is called *stūpa* or *thūpa*, and in the new terminology, *stūpa*. This is translated as "square mound" (*fangfen*). It is also... [text continues]
It is translated as "spiritual temple" (lingmiao), also as "high and manifest" (gaoxian), and as "stūpa" (futu). That which contains *śarīra* is called a *tā* (tower/stūpa);

that which lacks *śarīra* is called a *caitya* (zhiti). Regarding *śarīra*, they are further discussed in terms of being whole or fragmented; for example, when Śākyamuni fragmented his body, he produced eight *hu* of *śarīra*.
After King Aśoka, eighty-four thousand precious *tā*s were constructed to enshrine them, distributed throughout [the land].
Because the entire-body śarīra of the Buddha Many Treasures has not been dispersed, there is now but a single stūpa for this famous mountain in the world.

Furthermore, according to the Vinaya, stūpas are erected at four locations: the place of the Buddha’s birth, the place where he attained the Way, the place where he turned the wheel of Dharma, and the place where he entered nirvana.
Now, the True Mark of the Lotus Sutra and the three bodies of all Buddhas are all produced from this [mountain]. Regarding all Buddhas...
It is here that the Buddhas sit upon the site of enlightenment; it is here that the Buddhas turn the wheel of the Dharma;
it is here that the Buddhas enter parinirvāṇa. This Lotus Sūtra itself is the four stupas of the Buddhas of the three periods of time:

the Buddhas of the past have already resided here, the Buddhas of the present are all seated here, and the Buddhas of the future shall do likewise. This stupa has appeared to manifest this matter, which all four assemblies behold.
Therefore, it is said in the *Jiànbǎotǎ pǐn* (Chapter on Seeing the Jeweled Stupa) of the *Yíngluò jīng* (Ākāśagarbha Sūtra):

"To build stupas filling the four continents to enshrine the relics of a single Buddha is not as meritorious as making offerings to the Tathāgata’s physical body (*rūpakāya*), for it is from the physical body that relics arise.

Furthermore, to build stupas filling a great trichiliocosm to enshrine the physical body is not as meritorious as making offerings to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), for it is by means of the Dharma-body [that the physical body exists]."
Because he possesses a physical body, one should know that his seeing of forms is inferior to hearing the sutra; for by hearing the sutra, one possesses the Dharma-body.
Since the sutras vary between partial and complete, the Dharma-body is either whole or fragmented, and its merits are unequal. This present sutra exclusively expounds the perfect principle;
as it is the entire Dharma-body, the merit of upholding this sutra is profound, and the power of its wide propagation is great. Thus, the Stupa of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna [emerged from the earth].
The earth split open to manifest this matter, and because the fourfold assembly all witnessed it, it is called the "Chapter on Seeing the Jeweled Stūpa" (for the sake of others).
Having completed the three cycles of preaching the Dharma, those who emerged from the earth raised a great voice, once again praising with "Excellent! to seal the true teaching;

this serves as proof for what was previously done for the purpose of opening the stūpa. Since it was necessary to assemble the emanated bodies in order to open the stūpa, once the stūpa had been opened, they entered.
The stūpa sits side-by-side [with the Buddha] and proclaims in a great voice, summoning his original disciples from the earth;

only after this does the length of his lifespan become clearly manifest. This sequence—first the invitation and subsequently the emergence from the earth—is such that the fourfold assembly all beholds it;

therefore, it is called the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Jeweled Stūpa" (*Ratnakoṭi-parivarta*). (As an antidote: While the Many-Treasures Buddha (*Prabhūtaratna*) demonstrates his parinirvāṇa, his entire body and *śarīra* remain solemnly present.
Yet, as it was not dispersed and one heard his voice, this signifies that extinction is non-extinction, representing the Dharmakāya;
the Tathāgata’s entry into the stupa signifies the symmetry of the two bodies, representing the Sambhogakāya; and the gathering of clouds of emanations represents the Nirmāṇakāya.
Thus, the three Buddhas and their three bodies are neither identical nor different, so that the fourfold assembly may behold them; therefore, it is said that "the jewels were seen."
**Chapter on the Stūpa (The Ultimate Meaning)** There are two intentions regarding the emergence of the stūpa:

First, the emission of sound serves to certify that the merits of the propagation of the Dharma through the three previous turnings of the wheel are all truly real, and are not merely provisional or partial teachings as discussed in the preceding sections;

this is explained according to the meaning of the teaching (*yìjiào*). Second, by opening the stūpa, the subsequent sounds are raised to penetrate the lower realms and summon the original disciples, thereby clarifying [the ultimate truth].
The long-standing doubt that the site of enlightenment was recently established is suddenly shattered; this is the meaning of the "Original and Traced" (honji-suijaku).
Furthermore, the emergence from the earth of the Stupa of Long-Age reveals the power of sovereign spiritual penetration (*ṛddhi*), manifesting the benefit of sentient beings throughout past ages.
The emission of a great sound reveals the power of the lion’s majestic stride, manifesting the opening of the provisional to reveal the real throughout the ten directions.

There is also a great vow: "If future Buddhas preach this sutra, my jeweled stupa shall arrive at each of those places to serve as a witness, manifesting the power of great majesty and ferocity to reveal that the future is eternally abiding and imperishable.

Regarding the interpretation through the contemplation of the mind (*guanxin*): by practicing contemplation based on the sutra, one accords with the *dharmakāya*; thus, the objective realm and wisdom will necessarily converge.
Just as when the stūpa arrives to bear witness, the realms and wisdom of the sūtra have already been realized, and thus the great retribution is fulfilled.
As Śākyamuni and Prabhūtaratna sit together upon a single seat, because the great retribution is perfected, they manifest responses according to the capacities of beings.

Because all the emanation bodies assemble through the emergence of Prabhūtaratna, the three Buddhas become manifest. Through the upholding of this sūtra, one possesses the three bodies of Samantabhadra.
Zhiyun states that the three bodies of the Buddha arise from the Vaipulya [sūtras]; this is precisely the meaning here.

△ Within the second section, the "Circulation of the Trace Gate," the second chapter, "The Appearance of the Jeweled Stupa," is divided into two parts: first, the long prose version; second, the verse recitation.

Within the first part, there are three sections: first, the manifestation of Prabhūtaratna; second, the distant gathering of the emanated Buddhas; third, Śākyamuni’s proclamation of the invitation. Regarding the first:
Sixth: First, the appearance of the stupa; second, the offerings of the devas; third, the praise of Prabhūtaratna; fourth, the astonishment and doubt of the assembly;
fifth, the request for the Great Joyful One to preach; sixth, the Tathāgata’s response. Now, the first [section].
At that time, a stupa made of the seven precious jewels, five hundred yojanas in height and two hundred and fifty yojanas in length and breadth,
emerged from the earth and remained suspended in mid-air. It was adorned with various kinds of precious objects,
featuring five thousand railings and tens of millions of chambers, and was further embellished with countless banners and streamers, hanging jeweled necklaces, and ten thousand precious bells.
A hundred million [banners] were suspended above it, and from all four sides issued the fragrance of *tāmālapatra* sandalwood, pervading the entire world;
these various banners and canopies were composed of the seven treasures— gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, agate, pearl, and ruby—
and reached as high as the palace of the Four Heavenly Kings.
The seven treasures represent the nature-virtues (*prakṛti-guṇa*), which are the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) and the seven riches of the noble ones (*saptāryadhanas*).

The stupa represents the realm of true reality (*dharmatā*), the locus upon which the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) relies. (While each of the four teachings discusses the seven factors of enlightenment and the seven riches, here they pertain only to the Perfect Teaching [Yuanjiao]. Furthermore, while these exist even at the causal stage of the Perfect Teaching, here we refer to those of the ultimate fruit; the seven factors of enlightenment and the seven riches are all attained through cultivation.

Since this clarifies that cultivation arises entirely from nature and nature is fully revealed through cultivation, they are thus unconditioned nature-virtues. Its height of five hundred *yojanas* refers to twenty thousand [leagues].
The vertical pole represents the myriad practices within the cause and the myriad virtues within the fruit;

its height and breadth of two hundred and fifty *yojanas* represent the adornment of the ten thousand virtues. The earth represents the ground of ignorance, while the space represents the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
By having nothing to destroy, one destroys the ground of ignorance; by having nothing to dwell upon, one dwells [in the ultimate].
Because it is the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), it is said that they "emerge from the earth and abide in mid-air. This also serves as a proof for what follows:
the people of the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*) have not yet opened the principle of the *tathāgatagarbha* and remain obscured by ignorance, like a stupa buried in the ground.

Now, having heard the threefold exposition of the revelation, the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*) is opened and the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is manifested, just as the stupa emerges into the air; this is the proof.
The preceding section establishes that the attainment of the Dharmakāya has long been manifest, like a stupa situated in space that no one can open;

it signifies that the original ground was accomplished long ago yet remains unrecognized by the multitude. If one reveals the traces to manifest the original ground and attains realization without doubt, this constitutes the "arising of the subsequent.
If the stupa emerges from the earth, it signifies the manifestation of the Dharmakāya; in this regard, it is both the same as and different from other sutras.
When Sakyamuni manifests the Dharma-body, it is the same as that of the Two Vehicles; when [the Buddha] manifests the Dharma-body, it is different.

If the stupa is in the air and the gate opens to reveal the Buddha, this symbolizes the disclosure of the original trace and the manifestation of the fundamental source, which is forever distinct from other sutras.

If the stupa comes to attest to the preceding events, the matter has already been made manifest, so there is no need for doubt. As for the stupa’s arrival after the events have occurred, it possesses a hidden significance unknown to the multitude.
The various kinds of precious objects symbolize the manifold adornments of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). The railings symbolize the dhāraṇīs;

the gabled chambers symbolize the chamber of immeasurable compassion, and they also symbolize the chamber of immeasurable emptiness (*śūnyatā*). The banners and streamers symbolize the superior marks of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*);
the hanging necklaces symbolize the merits of the forty stages (*bhūmi*), as well as morality (*śīla*), concentration, wisdom, and dhāraṇīs.
Above, it adorns the Dharma-body; below, it reaches out to sentient beings. The jeweled bells represent the eightfold voice and the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
The fragrance emanating from the four sides represents the unconditioned Four Noble Truths; the wind of the Path blows the fragrance of the four virtues.

The seven-jeweled banners and canopies reach as high as the palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings, representing the power of supernatural penetrations and compassion—all of which are inherent virtues (*prakṛti-guṇa*) accomplished through the seven factors of enlightenment and the seven riches.
All [these beings] fully realized the principle of the Four Noble Truths of Unconditioned Action (*anabhisaṃskāra*).
△ Second, the offerings of the devas: The Trāyastriṃśa Heaven rained down *mandārava* flowers as an offering to the precious stūpa;
likewise did all other devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and so forth.
Billions of beings made offerings of all kinds of flowers, incense, necklaces, banners, canopies, and musical performances to the precious stupa, honoring, respecting, and praising it;

the meaning of these matters is clear and requires no further explanation. However, to explain this according to principle: the thirty-three heavens represent the stages of abiding, practicing, and advancing as three.
The ten stages of the *bhūmis* constitute one stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), and Equal Enlightenment constitutes one stage of Sublime Enlightenment (*pravarabodhi*).
Taken together, these form thirty-three stages, all of which equally rely upon the ultimate realm of true reality (*tathatā-paramārtha-viṣaya*). As for the raining down of *māndārava* flowers:
the initial mind already possesses the merits of the forty-two stages, and the final mind is likewise so; both are characterized by the causal flowers belonging to the forty stages.

This signifies turning toward the Dharmakāya. The subsequent mention of the other devas and nāgas indicates that those at the stages of the inner and outer ordinary beings likewise rely on the precious marks to turn toward the fruit and practice the cause. △ Third, the praise by Prabhūtaratna.
At that time, from within the jeweled stupa, a great voice issued forth, praising: "Excellent, excellent!

Śākyamuni, World-Honored One, you have been able to preach for the great assembly the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*—the Dharma for instructing bodhisattvas through the great wisdom of equality, which is protected by the Buddhas.
It is so, it is so! Śākyamuni, World-Honored One, all that has been spoken by you is indeed the truth."
"Truly so.
Excellent, excellent!"—this was an exclamation praising how [the teaching] accords with principle and accords with the capacity [of the audience]. There are two meanings of "equality":
first, the equality of phenomena, which is the principle of the Middle Way; second, the equality of sentient beings, meaning that all sentient beings equally attain the Buddha-wisdom, the Great One.
"Thus, thus" refers to the meaning of height and breadth as previously described: first, it is the suchness of the true principle of the Dharma-nature;

second, it is the suchness of the capacities and natures of all sentient beings. Therefore, both are entirely real. This correctly verifies that the previous revelation of the provisional to manifest the real was not in vain. △ Fourth, the assembly is struck with wonder and doubt.
At that time, the fourfold assembly saw the great jeweled stupa abiding in mid-air and heard the sounds issuing from within it;
all attained the joy of the Dharma and, marveling at this unprecedented occurrence, rose from their seats, joined their palms in reverence, and withdrew to stand to one side.

All attained the joy of the Dharma, clearly realizing and attesting to what they had previously found strange and unprecedented; they rose and stood to one side, secretly assisting in the emergence of what followed.
△ Fifth, the Question of Mahāratnakūṭa:
At that time, there was a bodhisattva-mahāsattva named Mahāratnakūṭa (Great Joyous Eloquence), who knew all the worlds of devas and humans... [text continues]
With minds full of doubt, the asuras and others addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, by what causes and conditions has this jeweled stūpa emerged from the earth, and why does it emit such sounds from within?"
According to the intent of the answer below, the questions are also threefold: first, asking for what reason this stūpa exists; second, asking why the stūpa emerged from the earth;
third, asking why it emits such sounds. △ Sixth, the Tathāgata’s answer is threefold: first, he answers in advance why it surged forth;
second, he subsequently answers for what reason the stūpa exists; third, he answers why [it emerged].
He uttered these words. First:
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāratnakūṭa: "Within this precious stupa is the entire body of a Tathāgata.
In the past, in the east, beyond immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of asaṃkhyeya worlds, there was a land named Ratnaviśuddha. Within it..."
There is a Buddha named Prabhūtaratna who, while practicing the bodhisattva path, made this great vow: "If,
after I have attained Buddhahood and entered parinirvāṇa, there should be a place in the lands of the ten directions where the Lotus Sūtra is being preached,
may my stupa emerge before them for the sake of hearing this sūtra, appearing as a witness and praising it, saying, 'Excellent!'"
This clarifies that the reason this precious stūpa emerges from the earth is to serve as a witness for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Question: Previously it was said that [the bodhisattvas] emerged from the earth, yet now it is said they come from the east; why is this? Answer: The "east" describes their original conditions, while "emerging" expresses the fulfillment of their past vows;
thus, there is no contradiction. If one considers the symbolic significance of the teachings, the east is the foremost among all directions. Therefore...
The preceding section explains the reason for the emergence from the earth through symbolic manifestation. △ Second, it provides a retrospective answer as to why there are stupas:
because that Buddha commanded them to construct these stupas.
After that Buddha had attained enlightenment and was approaching his parinirvāṇa, he addressed the bhikṣus amidst the assembly of devas and humans, saying: "I..."
After my parinirvāṇa, those who wish to make offerings to my entire body should erect a single great stūpa.
△ Third, the answer to why this sound was uttered: it is because of the presence of supernormal powers and fundamental vows.
By the power of his supernatural vows, wherever in the worlds of the ten directions there may be one preaching the Lotus Sūtra, that precious stupa will emerge before them;
the entire body of the Tathāgata remains within the stupa, praising him, saying: "Excellent, excellent, Mahāpratibhāna!
Now, because the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna hears the preaching of the Lotus Sūtra, his stupa has emerged from the earth."
He emerged and uttered words of praise, saying, "Excellent, excellent!
The *Śāstra* explains that the Buddha Prabhūtaratna did not preach the Dharma before entering parinirvāṇa. Master Nanyue said:
"That Buddha told the bhikṣus—those who were people receiving transformation—that he had not preached the Dharma at all. How can this be?"
This is because they have only obtained the three [vehicles] and have not yet attained the revelation of the One; therefore, it is said that they are unable to preach the Dharma.
For this reason, even though they have entered parinirvāṇa, wherever they may be, whenever the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is preached, they all rejoice and bear witness to it.
Question: Is it not the case that in the worlds of the ten directions there are other Buddhas who have not yet revealed [the One]? If they do not reveal it, then [what of them]?
One should formulate this vow: "Why is it that only the Many-Treasures Buddha [is present]? If we do not make this vow, our path to Buddhahood will differ;

if we do make the vow, all shall together be permitted to hear the sutra. Furthermore, since the transformations of all Buddhas are preceded by their foresight of the capacities of beings, how could they wait until after attaining Buddhahood—only then failing to reveal [the truth]—before one begins to make the vow?
The answer is that whether they are the same or different, whether they reveal or do not reveal, and whether there is a vow or no vow, [all are consistent].

Thus, according to conditions, if there are those for whom a vow is appropriate, they shall all come; why worry that they will not assemble? To issue the vow only later would likewise be to fail to discern their capacities.
This concludes the first section: the manifestation of Prabhūtaratna. △ Second, the manifestation of the distant assembly of transformation bodies, in seven parts:
1. Mahāpratibhāna requests to see Prabhūtaratna; 2. The instruction on the gathering of the transformation bodies; 3. Mahāpratibhāna requests [the Buddha to speak].

[This section] comprises seven parts: (1) gathering [the assembly], (2) emitting four rays of light, (3) summoning the five Buddhas from afar, (4) their arrival, (5) the adornment and purification of the realm, (6) the bestowal of the desire [to open the stūpa], and (7) the opening of the stūpa. Now, for the first:
at that time, by the supernatural power of the Tathāgata, the Bodhisattva Mahāpratibhāna addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, we..."
They wished to behold this Buddha-body;

wishing to open the stupa, they assembled the Buddhas, and the Buddhas immediately entrusted [the matter] to them. Having been entrusted, they summoned those from the lower regions, and those from the lower regions emerged.
Thus, the near was opened to reveal the distant—this is the reason for this great matter, for it is the supernatural power of the Tathāgata.
This is the inquiry. △ Second, clarifying the gathering of the manifested bodies.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Pramuditanirdeśa: "The Buddha Prabhūtaratna has a profound and solemn vow:
'If my jeweled stupa emerges before the various Buddhas for the sake of hearing the Lotus Sutra, should anyone wish to [reveal] my body...'"
"To show the fourfold assembly, those Buddhas who are emanations of that Buddha, currently preaching the Dharma in worlds throughout the ten directions, will all return and assemble in one place;
only then will my own body appear. Mahāratnapratibhāna, those Buddhas who are my emanations and are currently preaching the Dharma in worlds throughout the ten directions should now assemble."

It must be that the emanated bodies are gathered together before the stupa can be opened; this is precisely to secretly reveal the merits of the original ground. If the roots are deep, the branches flourish;

if the source is distant, the stream is long. Since it is thus with the emanated bodies, which extend horizontally throughout the ten directions, how could the original ground not transcend the kalpas vertically?
△ Third, the request for the gathering through great eloquence.

Mahāpratibhāna addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, we also wish to see the various Buddhas who are emanations of the World-Honored One, in order to pay them homage and make offerings to them.
△ Fourth, emitting light to summon from afar.

At that time, the Buddha emitted a single ray of light from the tuft of white hair between his eyebrows, and immediately he saw the Buddhas in lands to the east as numerous as the sands of five million billion nayutas of Ganges Rivers. Those lands were all made of crystal, adorned with jewel-trees and precious garments;
they were filled with countless thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattvas, who spread jeweled canopies everywhere.
The lands above are covered with jeweled nets, and there the Buddhas of those realms preach all dharmas with great and wondrous voices;
furthermore, one sees immeasurable thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattvas filling those lands, preaching the Dharma for the sake of the multitudes.
It is likewise in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir—everywhere reached by the light from the white tuft between the eyebrows.
The various Buddhas who manifest their bodies mostly reside in pure lands; this Sahā world alone is an impure land.
That a Buddha is able to preach the Lotus Sūtra within this impure Sahā world is the most difficult of difficulties.

Yet, it is precisely because of this impurity that it is necessary to establish the provisional through the real, and because of the establishment of the provisional, it is necessary to reveal the provisional.
By means of this revelation of reality, the reality revealed is finally able to be fully elucidated;
from its inception to its consummation, the Tathāgata’s wondrous skill in establishing transformation is exhausted without remainder—this may be called "a lotus emerging from the mud.

Furthermore, it should be understood that in this land, Śākyamuni refers to all Buddhas as his own emanations (nirmāṇakāya), while the Buddhas of other lands refer to both those other Buddhas and to Śākyamuni himself.
Since the various Buddhas who have manifested emanations here in this land to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* have all arrived and granted their consent for the opening of the stupa—

and since there are places in each of their respective lands where the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is being preached— the Buddhas of those lands as well as Śākyamuni of this land will certainly go together to grant their consent for the opening of the stupa.
Thus, the pure and the impure interpenetrate, this and that mutually merge, yet the roles of guest and host remain distinct, and the subject and object do not [confuse].
The principle of the true mark of the One Vehicle and the doctrine of the unimpeded Dharma-realm are vividly present within the range of sight and hearing.
△ Fifth, the Arrival of All Buddhas:
At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions each addressed the assembly of Bodhisattvas, saying: "Good sons, we shall now proceed to the Sahā world."
[He] went to the Sahā world to the presence of Śākyamuni Buddha and also made offerings to the precious stupa of the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna.
△ Sixth, Adorning and Purifying the Realm: Part One, Transforming the Sahā World;
Part Two, Transforming each of the eight directions by two hundred *nayuta-koti* [times]; Part Three, Transforming each of the eight directions by two hundred *nayuta-koti* [times]. Now...
First: At that time, the Sahā world was immediately transformed into purity, with lapis lazuli as its ground and adorned with jeweled trees;
golden cords demarcated the eightfold paths, and it was devoid of all villages, hamlets, camps, cities, oceans, rivers, mountains, streams, and forests.
Great precious incense was burned, and *mandārava* flowers were strewn everywhere across the ground;

it was covered above by nets and canopies of jewels, with various jeweled bells suspended from them. Having set aside this assembly and moved the devas and humans to other lands, each of those Buddhas took a great bodhisattva as an attendant and arrived at the Jewel [World] in the Sahā universe.
Beneath each of these trees, which were five hundred yojanas high, the branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits were adorned in successive layers.
At the foot of every precious tree there was a lion throne five yojanas high, likewise embellished with great jewels.
At that time, the various Buddhas each sat cross-legged upon their respective thrones, and in this manner they gradually filled the three [thousandfold worlds].
Even within a thousandfold great trichiliocosm, the emanated bodies of Śākyamuni Buddha in a single direction have not yet come to an end.
△ Second, he transforms each of the eight directions, each by two million *nayuta* of worlds.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha, wishing to provide space for all the Buddhas who had manifested as his emanations,
further transformed two million billion nayutas of lands in each of the eight directions, making them all pure and free from hells, hungry ghosts, animals, and asuras;
he also transferred the devas and humans from those lands to other realms, and the lands thus transformed were likewise made of lapis lazuli.
The ground was made of lapis lazuli and adorned with jewel trees; the trees were five hundred yojanas high, their branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits arrayed in successive order.
Beneath each tree was a precious lion throne five yojanas high, embellished with various kinds of jewels.
Furthermore, there were no great oceans, rivers, Mount Mucilinda, or Mount Mahāmucilinda.
The Cakravāḍa Mountains, the Mahācakravāḍa Mountains, Mount Sumeru, and all other kings of mountains together constitute a single Buddha-field.

The ground is made of jewels, level and even, covered everywhere by jeweled canopies with latticed curtains; banners and parasols are suspended above, great precious incense is burned, and celestial jewel-flowers are strewn across the entire earth.
At the third watch, he transformed eight directions, each consisting of two hundred *koṭi-nayuta* worlds.
Because Śākyamuni Buddha intended for the various Buddhas to sit therein in the future, he further transformed another two hundred *koṭi-nayuta* lands in each of the eight directions,
making them all pure and free from the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals.
The asuras further transported the devas and humans to other lands in the realms they had transformed;
these lands also had floors of lapis lazuli and were adorned with precious trees five hundred yojanas high, whose branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits were arranged in successive layers of splendor.
Beneath each tree stood a precious lion throne five yojanas high, likewise embellished with great jewels.
Furthermore, there were no great oceans, rivers, Mount Mucilinda, Mount Mahāmucilinda,
the Cakravāḍa mountains, the Mahācakravāḍa mountains, or Sumeru and other such kings of mountains; rather, it was a single Buddha-field with a ground of jewels,
level and even, entirely covered by jeweled latticed canopies, with various banners and parasols suspended from them, and great precious incense being burned everywhere.

Celestial jewel flowers were spread everywhere across the ground. At that time, the various Buddhas who had emanated from Śākyamuni Buddha in the east—residing in lands as numerous as the sands of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of Ganges Rivers—each came to this assembly while preaching the Dharma.
In this manner, the Buddhas of the ten directions all arrived and sat in the eight directions.
At that time, in each and every direction, four million *koṭi-nayuta* lands were filled with Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.

They purified the lands through three transformations, precisely by means of *samādhi*. Regarding this *samādhi*, there are three stages: first, they transformed the Sahā world; this was the *pratyāhāra* (withdrawal).

The power capable of transforming the defiled into the pure, followed by transforming each of the eight directions by two million *koṭi-nayuta* [times], is the power of mastery over transformation (*pariṇāma-vaśitā*) as a superior station (*abhibhv-āyatana*).

Then, transforming each of the eight directions again by two million *koṭi-nayuta* [times], is the power of the ten universal bases (*daśa-kṛtsnāyatana*), which is vast, pervasive, and unimpeded. Furthermore, the first transformation represents the purification of views.
The second transformation represents the purification of the sands of dust; the third transformation represents the purification of ignorance. Question:

In the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, when the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas from the ten directions bearing the same names come to witness the Dharma-gate being taught, it only says they "fill the ten directions" and does not say they transform the defiled into the pure. This precisely reveals the equality of the pure and the defiled.

Wu-xing further clarifies that self and other are not separated and the great and small are unimpeded. Now, if one transforms the defiled into the pure, then purity and defilement have not yet been forgotten; if one merely relocates devas and humans, then self and other remain separated. If one wishes to accommodate the emanated bodies while further transforming the land, then the great and the small will both be fully preserved—would this not equal the *Avataṃsaka*? Answer: Regarding the applications found in various sutras: 1. **The *Lotus Sūtra***: It is said that the Buddha’s lifespan is immeasurable, yet it is also said that he attained Buddhahood at the age of eighty. This is because his original vow was to manifest a long life for the sake of beings, yet he also manifested a short life to guide those who require such instruction. Thus, the long and the short are both present; this is the principle of the unimpededness of the great and the small. 2. **The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra***: It is said that the Buddha’s body is eternal, yet it is also said that he entered parinirvāṇa. This is because his original vow was to manifest impermanence to lead those who are attached to permanence. Thus, the eternal and the impermanent are both present; this is the principle of the unimpededness of the great and the small. 3. **The *Vimalakīrti Sūtra***: It is said that the Buddha’s land is pure, yet it is also said that he appeared in the Sahā world. This is because his original vow was to manifest a defiled land to lead those who are attached to purity. Thus, the pure and the defiled are both present; this is the principle of the unimpededness of the great and the small. 4. **The *Śūraṅgama Samādhi Sūtra***: It is said that the Buddha’s body is invisible, yet it is also said that he appears before all beings. This is because his original vow was to manifest invisibility to lead those who are attached to form. Thus, the visible and the invisible are both present; this is the principle of the unimpededness of the great and the small. 5. **The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra***: It is said that the Buddha’s wisdom is inconceivable, yet it is also said that he taught the five aggregates. This is because his original vow was to manifest the five aggregates to lead those who are attached to wisdom. Thus, the inconceivable and the five aggregates are both present; this is the principle of the unimpededness of the great and the small. In these cases, the great and the small are both present without obstruction. Furthermore, regarding the transformation of the land: if one transforms the defiled into the pure, then the defiled and the pure are not yet forgotten. If one merely moves devas and humans, then self and other remain separated. If one wishes to accommodate the emanated bodies while further transforming the land, then the great and the small will both be fully preserved. How could this not be equal to the *Avataṃsaka*? This is because the various sutras each employ their own specific methods to reveal the same ultimate truth.
Regarding supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), whether they are numerous or few, extensive or narrow, what is valued is their ability to manifest the principle according to the capacity of beings.

Since the *Avataṃsaka* alone addresses those of great capacity and directly manifests the perfect principle, although its scope of spiritual power is vast and extensive, it is not yet considered a difficult feat.

In this present sutra, however, the small is opened up to become the great, and the partial is clearly elucidated as the perfect—like breaking a formidable enemy—therefore it is truly rare; how much more so when it concerns the Pure Land?

If defilement truly possessed an intrinsic nature, how could it be transformed into purity? If there were a separation between self and others regarding the fruits [of their actions], how could they be peacefully shifted [to one another]?
If there were obstructions regarding the magnitude of the fruits, how could they be universally unified into a single land?

One should know that the manifestation of principle through the fusion and transcendence of matters such as purity and defilement, self and other, and large and small, is precisely the non-obstruction of phenomena and principle.
The gate does not destroy the phenomena of purity and impurity, this and that, large and small;
rather, it immediately reveals the principle that there is neither purity nor impurity, neither this nor that, neither large nor small.

Although the principle of neither purity nor impurity, neither this nor that, neither large nor small is revealed, the phenomena of purity and impurity, this and that, large and small remain clearly distinct.
This is precisely the gate of the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena (*shishi wuai men*).

Therefore, if one relies upon the great wisdom of equality (*pingdeng dahui*), then the *Avataṃsaka*, *Vaipulya*, *Prajñāpāramitā*, and *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* sūtras should not be recklessly ranked as superior or inferior.

However, if one relies upon the revelation of the provisional to manifest the real (*kaiquan xianshi*) and the revelation of the traces to manifest the fundamental (*kaiti xianben*), then the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* alone possesses this merit. Those who read the scriptures well prize reaching the essence and the central tenet.

If one employs characteristics improperly and merely compares and evaluates based on outward deeds, one will end up either praising or disparaging the Great Dharma taught by the Tathāgata—just as it would be to praise Śakra while disparaging Kauśika. Question: Regarding the three transformations of the land into purity, this should be the power of the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*;
why then do they still employ the mundane meditations (*dhyāna*) of the Hīnayāna? Answer: Small... [text fragment]
Riding upon the *vimokṣas*, one transforms only the small chiliocosm; the *abhibhvāyatanas* transform only the medium chiliocosm; and the ten *kṛtsnāyatanas* transform only the great trichiliocosm.
Now, to reveal the provisional through the real, these minor matters of dhyāna are actually the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*;

thus, while their names are attached to the Small Vehicle, their power and function are Great. Question: If this is so, then why would any single samādhi alone be able to effect these three transformations?
It must be by means of the three samādhis; the answer is that it is precisely because they do not destroy the provisional designations (*prajñapti*) of all phenomena. Question:
If the three types of samādhi of the Hīnayāna cannot universally destroy the three delusions, then the three types of samādhi of the Buddha-fruit should not destroy delusions sequentially.
Answer: Since the Śūraṅgama [samādhi] is itself the phenomenon that is identical to principle, it can spontaneously [accomplish this].

One perfect circle breaks through the three delusions; now, regarding the function of samādhi, we discuss it primarily in terms of its correct efficacy, yet because it also refers to what is manifested, it is said that the function of breaking delusions resides in the Buddha while what is manifested resides in the capacity of the practitioner (*ki*). Although the capacities may be of the three grades, the three delusions have already been broken;
nevertheless, they must still be further broken in the future. This concludes the sixth section: Adorning and Purifying the Realm. △ Seventh: Granting Consent to Open the Stūpa.

Furthermore, regarding the five points: first, the Buddhas of the past inquire after his well-being and express their desire [to meet him]; second, Śākyamuni opens the stūpa; third, the two assemblies both see and hear [the same thing]; fourth, the two Buddhas sit together sharing a single seat; fifth, at the request of the fourfold assembly, they ascend into the air. Now, the first point: The Buddhas of the ten directions, having gathered from the ten directions, each sat upon a lotus throne. At that time, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddhas of the ten directions, and addressed them: "World-Honored Ones, may you all attend to me for a moment. I wish to open this stūpa of the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna. Then, the Buddhas of the ten directions addressed the Buddha Śākyamuni: "World-Honored One, we shall now go together to that place. Having spoken thus, they each emitted a great light from the crown of their heads, illuminating the worlds of the ten directions as far as the limits of space, and caused the various beings within those lands to all perceive the presence of the Buddhas. Then, the Buddhas of the ten directions, together with the Buddha Śākyamuni, arrived at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa in the kingdom of Rājagṛha. At that time, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, entered into a state of meditative concentration called "The Array of the Light of the Tathāgatas," and by the power of that samādhi, he opened the stūpa of the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna. At that moment, the stūpa was opened, and the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna emerged from within it, seated upright upon his lion throne, his body whole and unbroken, as if he had only recently entered parinirvāṇa. Then, the Buddhas of the ten directions, together with the Buddha Śākyamuni, approached the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna and paid homage at his feet. Having paid homage, they withdrew to one side and sat down. At that time, the fourfold assembly saw the Buddhas of the ten directions and heard their voices, and they were all filled with joy and wonder. Then, the Buddhas of the ten directions addressed the Buddha Śākyamuni: "World-Honored One, please allow us to share a seat with the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna. The Buddha Śākyamuni replied: "Virtuous ones, do as you wish. Thereupon, the Buddhas of the ten directions, together with the Buddha Śākyamuni, shared a single seat with the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna and sat down. At that time, the fourfold assembly, seeing the Buddhas of the ten directions and hearing their voices, were all filled with joy and wonder. They then addressed the Buddha Śākyamuni: "World-Honored One, what is the cause and condition for these Buddhas of the ten directions to appear here? The Buddha Śākyamuni told the fourfold assembly: "Good sons, listen attentively. I shall explain it for you. Good sons, there is a samādhi called 'The Array of the Light of the Tathāgatas. Because the Tathāgata has attained this samādhi, he is able to manifest the bodies of all the Buddhas of the ten directions. Good sons, the Tathāgata has attained this samādhi for immeasurable, incalculable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas. Good sons, if there were a man who could grind all the worlds of the ten directions into fine dust, and then take a single grain of that dust to represent one kalpa, even if he exhausted all the grains of dust in this way, the number of kalpas would still not reach the end of the time since the Tathāgata first attained this samādhi. Good sons, the Tathāgata has been abiding in this samādhi for such an immeasurable, incalculable length of time, yet he does not weary of it. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata has long cultivated the practice of great compassion, and because he wishes to cause all sentient beings to attain the bliss of the Dharma. At that time, the fourfold assembly, having heard the Buddha’s words, were all filled with joy and faith, and they praised the Buddha in verse: "The Great Sage, the Honored One of the World, Has long cultivated the practice of great compassion. He manifests the bodies of all the Buddhas, Causing all sentient beings to rejoice. Then, the fourfold assembly addressed the Buddha Śākyamuni: "World-Honored One, we pray that you will permit us to enter this samādhi. The Buddha Śākyamuni said: "Good sons, you may do so according to your wishes. Thereupon, the fourfold assembly all entered the samādhi of the Tathāgatas' array of light. Having entered it, they saw the bodies of all the Buddhas of the ten directions, and they also heard the teachings being expounded by those Buddhas. Having seen and heard this, they were all filled with joy and faith, and they praised the Buddha in verse: "The Great Sage, the Honored One of the World, Is truly the King of the Dharma. Today we have seen the Buddhas of the ten directions, And heard the subtle sounds of the Dharma being preached. At that time, the fourfold assembly, having seen the Buddhas of the ten directions and heard their voices, were all filled with joy and faith. They then addressed the Buddha Śākyamuni: "World-Honored One, we pray that you will permit us to dwell in the air. The Buddha Śākyamuni said: "Good sons, you may do so according to your wishes. Thereupon, the fourfold assembly all ascended into the air. At that time, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, wishing to further clarify this meaning, spoke these verses: "The Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, Whose fame is vast and far-reaching, Has long practiced the path of the Bodhisattva, And has now attained parinirvāṇa. Because he has accomplished the great vow, He appears before the world. The Buddhas of the ten directions, All come to pay homage to him. The fourfold assembly, Seeing and hearing this, Are all filled with joy, And praise the Buddha's virtues. Thus ends the first section.
At that time, each of those Buddhas was seated upon a lion throne beneath a jeweled tree;
they all dispatched their attendants to inquire after the health of Śākyamuni Buddha, each carrying a handful of precious flowers and addressing them thus:
"Good son, go to the Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain to the place where Śākyamuni Buddha resides, and speak these words on my behalf: 'Are you free from illness and affliction? Are you physically strong?'"
The Blessed One, the Bodhisattvas, and the assembly of Śrāvakas were all at ease and secure. Having scattered these precious flowers as an offering to the Buddha, they spoke these words:
"That certain Buddha has granted his consent for this jeweled stūpa to be opened; other Buddhas have likewise dispatched their messengers."
The various Buddhas collectively grant their consent (*chanda*) to open the stupa, just as the procedure for granting consent is performed within the Saṃgha.

The *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* clarifies that several Buddhas grant their consent, and the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* likewise clarifies that a thousand Buddhas together preach the Prajñā;

yet in none of these cases is it stated that they are the emanations (*nirmāṇakāya*) of Śākyamuni. According to the present sutra, they must be his emanations, for he employs skillful means (*upāya*).

It is not explicitly stated [in other sutras], but this present sutra not only mentions a great number, but directly states that these emanated bodies have all arrived and expressed their consent (*chanda*). 2. Śākyamuni Opens the Stūpa.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha saw that the emanated Buddhas had all assembled and were each seated upon their thrones.
Upon the lion thrones, all heard the various Buddhas grant their consent for the joint opening of the precious stupa; immediately, they rose from their seats and remained suspended in mid-air.
All fourfold assemblies stood up, joined their palms, and gazed upon the Buddha with single-minded devotion.
Thereupon, Śākyamuni Buddha opened the door of the seven-jeweled stupa with his right finger, emitting a great sound like that of removing the bolt and opening the gate of a great city.
The gate:
opening it with the right hand signifies the use of provisional means (*upāya*). Opening the stupa signifies the opening of the provisional;

seeing the Buddha signifies the manifestation of the ultimate (*paramārtha*), which both confirms what precedes and introduces what follows. Thus, withdrawing the bolt signifies the removal of obstructions and the opening of the great city.
The "gate" (*mon*) secretly symbolizes the manifestation of the traces. △ Third: The fourfold assembly all saw and heard together.

At that moment, the entire assembly beheld the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna within the jeweled stupa, seated upon a lion throne, his entire body intact and undispersed as if he had entered meditative concentration; they also heard his voice saying, "Excellent, excellent, Śākyamuni!"
"The Buddha has most excellently preached this Lotus Sūtra; it is for the sake of hearing this sūtra that I have come here.

At that time, the fourfold assembly, seeing the past Buddha—who had entered parinirvāṇa immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas ago—utter such words, marveled at this unprecedented event and scattered clusters of celestial jewel-flowers over the Buddha Prabhūtaratna and Śākyamuni Buddha.
△ Fourth: The Two Buddhas Sit Sharing a Seat.
At that time, within the jeweled stupa, the Buddha Prabhūtaratna divided half of his seat with Śākyamuni Buddha and spoke these words:
"Śākyamuni Buddha, you may take this seat. Immediately, Śākyamuni Buddha entered it.
Within the stupa, he sat upon half of that seat, assuming the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*).
△ 5. The Fourfold Assembly Requests an Additional Space in the Void.
At that time, the great assembly saw two Tathāgatas within the seven-jeweled stupa, seated upon lion thrones in the full lotus posture.
As they sat, each thought to themselves: "Our seats are high and far away; we pray that the Tathāgata, by means of his supernormal powers, may cause us all to dwell together in the void.
Immediately, Śākyamuni Buddha, by means of his supernormal powers, received the great assembly, and they were all situated in the void.
Question: Since the assembly is all together in the void, for what reason do the emanations (nirmāṇakāya) still remain on the ground? Answer:

At that time, the assembly has already heard the "Gate of Traces" (jīmen), wherein the provisional was opened and they have entered the *dharmadhātu* of eternal quiescent light (*nitya-śānti-prabhāsvara-kṣetra*). Therefore, the void-dwelling represents this [state].

As for the emanations, they manifest traces each within their own respective lands of transformation; thus, they remain on the ground to represent this. Furthermore, Śākyamuni will soon reveal his original state.
Furthermore, they first dwell in emptiness to manifest this, each having its own underlying principle; there is no need for doubt. This concludes the second section:
Clarifying the Gathering of the Manifested Bodies from Afar. △ Third, Clarifying Śākyamuni’s Call for Recruitment.
With a great voice, he universally addressed the fourfold assembly: "Who among you is able to extensively expound the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* in this Sahā world-system?
Now is the very time; before long, the Tathāgata shall enter parinirvāṇa. The Buddha wishes to entrust this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* to one who may uphold it."
First, he solicits who can explain it extensively, referring to this Sahā world. Second, he clarifies that the time for the entrustment has arrived, meaning that he is about to enter parinirvāṇa.

Third, regarding the entrustment itself, there are two further points: first, to clarify those currently present, which refers to the eighty thousand great beings at the beginning of the "Dharma-Preacher" chapter (*Dharmabhāṇaka-parivarta*), the twenty thousand bodhisattvas at the beginning of the "Upholding" chapter (*Parīndanā-parivarta*), and so forth.
The World-Honored One’s gaze upon the assembly of eighty quadrillion nayutas of bodhisattvas has two purposes: first, to clarify that there is a specific intent behind his presence;

second, to indicate that the original disciples who emerged from the earth have been made to touch upon and circulate throughout all places, and furthermore, to initiate the discourse on the Buddha’s lifespan.
The initial long prose section concludes here. △ Second, the verse summary, in three parts: first, the verse on Prabhūtaratna; second, the verse on the emanated bodies.
The entrustment consists of three verses. Herein is the first.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

"The Holy Lord, the World-Honored One, although he has long since entered parinirvāṇa, still comes for the sake of the Dharma while remaining within the jeweled stūpa; how much more so, then, should all people [heed it]?"
Not being diligent in the Dharma, even though this Buddha has been in parinirvāṇa for incalculable kalpas, he has gone everywhere to listen to the Dharma because it is so difficult to encounter.
This was due to that Buddha’s original vow: "After my parinirvāṇa, wherever I go, I shall always go there to listen to the Dharma."
△ Second, the verse on the emanated bodies:

Furthermore, my emanated bodies—immeasurable Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—have come desiring to hear the Dharma and to behold the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, who has entered parinirvāṇa;
each has relinquished their wondrous lands, their assemblies of disciples, and all offerings from devas, humans, nāgas, and spirits.
In order to cause the Dharma to abide for a long time, they have come here to sit; by the supernatural power of the Buddhas, immeasurable multitudes have been moved so that the lands are purified.
Each Buddha proceeds beneath a jeweled tree, which is adorned like a lotus in a pure pond.
Beneath these jeweled trees are lion thrones, upon which the Buddhas sit, their radiance and adornments appearing as if in the midst of the deep night.

Yet, emitting great torches of fire from their bodies that produce sublime fragrances which pervade the lands of the ten directions, sentient beings who are perfumed by them experience a joy beyond measure;
it is like a great wind blowing against the branches of small trees. By such skillful means, they cause the Dharma to abide for a long time.
The preceding section clarifying the distant gathering of the emanated bodies consists of seven passages; the current verse summary is extremely concise.

The first three stanzas summarize the second point regarding the "gathering of those who should assemble," which includes the initial request to see Prabhūtaratna and the three subsequent requests for the assembly. The next single stanza summarizes the purification of the buddha-field.
The final four and a half stanzas summarize the arrival of all the Buddhas together. △ Third, the summary of the entrustment, in two parts: first, the introduction...

Third, the three Buddhas exhort the circulation [of the sutra], which has two parts: first, citing the difficult-to-maintain dharmas to exhort circulation; second, the initial section has three sub-parts:
first, seeking out the appropriate person; second, the formal citation; third, the three Buddhas exhorting the maintenance of the sutra; fourth, explaining the intent of the exhortation.

First: He addressed the great assembly, saying, "After my parinirvāṇa, who among you is able to protect, uphold, read, and recite this sutra? Now, before the Buddha, you shall each speak your own vow."
△ Second, the formal exhortation by the three Buddhas to uphold the sutra.
Although the Buddha Prabhūtaratna has long since entered parinirvāṇa, he utters this lion’s roar by virtue of his great vow:
"The Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna and my own person—those emanated Buddhas who have gathered here—should understand this intent: 'O sons of the Buddha, who among you is able to protect the Dharma?'"
One should make great vows so that [this teaching] may endure for a long time.
△ Third, the explanation of the intent behind the exhortation:
Whoever is able to protect this sutra and its Dharma is thereby making offerings to me and to this Prabhūtaratna Buddha.
While remaining within this jeweled stupa, you shall travel throughout the ten directions for the sake of this sutra, and furthermore,

you shall make offerings to all the manifested Buddhas who have come to adorn and embellish these worlds; if you preach this sutra, it will be as if you were seeing me, the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, and all those manifested Buddhas.

To be able to protect and uphold this sutra is itself to make offerings to the three Buddhas; to preach this sutra is itself to possess the vision of the three Buddhas. This explains the intent behind the exhortation.
Having first cited the three Buddhas to encourage its circulation, [the section] concludes. II. Citing the Dharma that is difficult to uphold to encourage its circulation.
A. First, the actual citation of the exhortation. B. Second, the explanation of the intent behind the exhortation. Within B, first: [The actual citation of the exhortation].

First, the earnest exhortation; second, the formal presentation of what is difficult to maintain as an exhortation; third, the explanation of the meaning of its difficulty to maintain. Now, for the first:
"O sons of good family, each of you should contemplate this matter of difficulty with careful attention and should resolve to make great vows."
△ Second, the formal presentation of the difficulty of upholding [this teaching] as an encouragement:
Although other sūtras are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, even explaining these does not constitute a difficulty;
nor would it be difficult to take Mount Sumeru and hurl it to countless Buddha-fields in other directions; yet, to move the great trichiliocosm with a single toe—[this is the true difficulty].
To hurl [a person] far away to another land is not yet difficult; nor is it difficult to stand upon the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) and expound immeasurable other sutras for the multitude.
However, to be able to preach this sutra in the evil world after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa—this alone is truly difficult.
Even if someone were to grasp empty space with their hands and travel about, that would not be difficult after my extinction.
To write it oneself or to have another write it is difficult; yet, even to place the entire great earth upon one’s toenails and ascend to the Brahma Heaven is not as difficult as this:
for after the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, to read this sutra even briefly amidst this degenerate age is truly difficult.
Furthermore, even if one were to carry dry grass into the conflagration at the end of a kalpa and enter it without being burned, that would not be as difficult.
After my parinirvāṇa, if one upholds this sutra and expounds it for even a single person, that would be difficult.

If one upholds the eighty-four thousand treasuries of the Dharma and the twelve divisions of the scriptures to preach them for others, enabling all listeners to attain the six supernormal powers—even if one can do so, it is not yet difficult compared to what follows:
after my passing, to hear and receive this sutra and inquire into its meaning and intent.

This would indeed be difficult: if someone were to preach the Dharma so that immeasurable, countless, and incalculable beings as numerous as the sands of ten million billion Ganges Rivers attain arhatship and possess the six supernormal powers, although such a benefit exists, it would still not be considered difficult.
However, after my parinirvāṇa, if one can receive, uphold, and maintain a sūtra such as this, that indeed would be difficult.
The eighty-four thousand dharma-treasuries and the twelve divisions of the scriptures encompass both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna;

because the first four "flavors" of the teachings all carry expedient means, they are relatively easy to uphold and expound. This sutra, however, exclusively elucidates the single reality and is therefore doubly difficult.
△ Third, explaining the reason it is difficult to uphold.
For the sake of the Buddha-way, throughout immeasurable lands from the beginning until now, I have extensively expounded various sutras;
among them, this sutra is the foremost. If there are those who can uphold it, they uphold the body of the Buddha.

Not only has this teaching not been explicitly expounded for over forty years in this land, but even though much has been taught from beginning to end in immeasurable lands, there has never been a discourse as profound as this sutra in its discussion of the Buddha’s intention.
The essence, substance, and function of this sutra—namely, the robes, the seat, and the chamber—are the three bodies (trikāya) of the Buddha; that which can sustain them is the sustaining power.

The Buddha’s intention regarding this body is not easily understood; thus ends the initial formal exhortation. △ Second, the explanation of the intent behind the exhortation has three parts: first, a renewed recruitment of those who uphold the sutra;

second, clarifying that the ability to uphold what is difficult to uphold brings joy and praise from all Buddhas; third, clarifying that this immediately constitutes the supreme practices of self-cultivation and the transformation of others. Now, the first part: The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Universal Worthy: "Good son, you should know that there are places where the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is recited, chanted, copied, or upheld. In those places, one should build a stupa made of the seven treasures, four-sided and five-storied, reaching up to the Brahma-heaven, adorned with various precious jewels, and decorated with banners and canopies. One should offer incense, flowers, necklaces, powdered incense, perfumed paste, burning incense, music, songs, and dances, as well as various offerings of clothing, food, drink, bedding, and medicine. Furthermore, one should provide for the needs of the monks who preach the Dharma, ensuring they have no lack of clothing, food, bedding, or medicine. Good son, if there is a person who, having heard this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, accepts it with faith and joy, copies it, and upholds it, then the merit obtained by that person shall be even greater than the former. (This concludes the first part.)
"O sons of good family, after my parinirvāṇa, who among you is able to receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra? Now, before the Buddha, speak your own vow.
△ Second, it is explained that if one can uphold what is difficult to uphold, all Buddhas will rejoice and praise them.
This sutra is difficult to uphold; if one upholds it even for a moment, I shall rejoice, and all Buddhas will do likewise.

What, then, is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)? It is the performance of all meritorious deeds, as well as the cultivation of the body, the cultivation of the mind, and the cultivation of wisdom.
When one cultivates through the ultimate truth, one quickly fulfills the six pāramitās. Whether walking or sitting, one abandons all grasping.
To have thoughts that take giving as their object of focus is *dāna*; not to transgress is *śīla*; not to produce afflictions within the sense-spheres is *kṣānti*;
not to abandon detachment is *vīrya*; not to be negligent regarding activities is *dhyāna*; and the non-arising of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is *prajñā*.
Furthermore, relinquishing the aggregates (*skandha*) is *dāna*; not to harbor conceptualizations regarding the aggregates is...
To have no notion of self regarding the aggregates (*skandha*) is ethical discipline (*śīla*); to give rise to a sense of enmity toward the aggregates is diligence (*vīrya*);
not being inflamed by the aggregates is meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); to ultimately abandon the aggregates is wisdom (*prajñā*). To relinquish the elements (*dhātu*) is generosity (*dāna*);

to remain unperturbed and unclouded regarding the elements is ethical discipline; to relinquish the causal conditions regarding the elements is patience (*kṣānti*); to relinquish them repeatedly regarding the elements is diligence.
The non-arising of the elements (*dhātu*) is *dhyāna*; that these elements are like illusions is *prajñā*.
Such as these are called the profound essential teachings on skillful means regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), which can fulfill the six *pāramitās*.
Because one practices this Dharma for oneself and for others, all Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time cultivate this Dharma to achieve *bodhi*; it is not [otherwise].
This Dharma can also pacify the suffering of the path of afflictions and the path of cyclic existence for sentient beings, and establish them upon the path to Bodhi.
