When a Bodhisattva in training cultivates the four immeasurables (*catur-apramāṇa*) separately in order to deliver all beings, if they reach the fruition, they are named Great Loving-kindness, Great Compassion, Great Sympathetic Joy, and Great Equanimity.
According to the general teaching, these are cultivated by those of the three vehicles (*triyāna*) together;

yet, while there is a distinction between self-benefit and benefit for others, in the gradual cultivation of the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*), one cultivates them sequentially, whereas in the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya-yāna*), they are fully present within a single mind. This is the fourth aspect of the "one trace and four origins."
The preceding six perfections may be understood as examples.

[He possesses] the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, the purple-golden hue, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four methods of attraction, the eighteen unique qualities, and the power of the divine path;
thus he attains equal and perfect enlightenment and extensively delivers sentient beings.

These thirty-two marks of a clear fruit and perfection are fully present within the *Fajie Cidian Chumen* (The First Gate to the Sequence of the Dharma Realm) and other texts such as the *Fashu* (Enumeration of Dharmas);
their wording has also been briefly excerpted there, so I have not had the leisure to record them here.

Since the Tripiṭaka masters take diligence and the observance of precepts as the foundation of the marks—if one does not maintain the precepts, one cannot even attain the bodies of gods or humans, let alone Buddhahood.

The Shared Teaching (sāmānyayāna) takes emptiness and non-arising as the fundamental characteristic; the Distinct Teaching (bhedayāna) takes the knowledge of the paths and modes (mārgajñatā) as the fundamental characteristic;
and the Perfect Teaching (pūrṇayāna) takes the true reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa) as the fundamental characteristic. Now, hearing the Lotus Sutra causes me to become fully endowed with these;

this is to manifest and attain them in accordance with their true nature, while also being able to practice the preceding three [teachings] as provisional traces. These include the eighty minor marks, the ten powers, and the supernormal knowledges.
As in all such cases according to the Dharma, one must first recognize the distinct characteristics of the four teachings before finally returning to the ultimate Perfect Teaching;
this is entirely due to the spiritual friend Devadatta.
This section concludes the proof by means of the sutra, demonstrating how it benefits those who master it; first, the explanation of the disciples’ fulfillment of the perfect cause is complete.

II. Explaining that the Wondrous Fruit shall be Attained by the Dharma Master. This has three parts: first, explaining the attainment of the primary fruit; second, explaining those who are transformed and saved;
third, explaining the benefits after [the teacher’s] passing. Now, the first part.

He addressed the fourfold assembly: "Devadatta, after the passing of immeasurable kalpas, shall attain Buddhahood, with the name Tathāgata Devendra, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān; his world shall be named Devamārga."
Therefore, the cause is named "Heavenly Heat" (Tianre), the fruit is named "King of Heaven" (Tianwang), and the realm is named "Path of Heaven" (Tian Dao).

This is because the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of the inherent virtue of one's nature is the "Heaven of the First Principle" (*prathama-artha-deva*); it is neither contrary nor compliant, yet it is both contrary and compliant.

It is not contrary, yet it is contrary—this contrariness is inconceivable; because it is contrary while being compliant, it is named "Heavenly Heat. It is not compliant, yet it is compliant—this compliance is... [incomplete].

The inconceivable unifies the inverse to form the compliant; thus it is called the "King of Heaven’s Practice. Because one traverses what is not the Way to penetrate the Buddha-way, it is called the "Way of Heaven.
Question: In the Vinaya Piṭaka, it is clarified that when Devadatta was about to enter hell, he attained rootless faith and uttered "Namo" [Homage];
before he could even say "Buddha," his body fell into the abyss. The Buddha prophesied that this would take three kalpas.
When his retribution was finished and he emerged from prison, he was destined to attain the fruit of a Pratyekabuddha and was named Namu.

Having realized the Way, he held out his alms bowl to receive offerings; just as he had received some food, he used his supernormal power of recollecting past lives to observe his own former existence.
Realizing that this was due to the power of the single utterance of "Namu" made at the time of his death, he felt ashamed to accept the food and subsequently entered parinirvāṇa.
What is so extraordinary about the predictions (*vyākaraṇa*) in this sutra? The answer is:

the great Bodhisattvas sport with supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), manifesting universally through the thirty-two forms of response and possessing bodies that encompass the ten realms throughout the entire Dharma-realm and for all future time.
This is exemplified by the deeds of Aṅgulimāla, Saccaka Nigaṇṭha, Kālodāyin, and others, which were adapted to both the great and small capacities of sentient beings.
The vast differences in what is perceived all arise from having attained a portion of the Tathāgata’s three mysteries; if one understands this meaning,
then one will know that although Śākyamuni Buddha attained Buddhahood long ago, he nevertheless manifested the practice of causal deeds in ages such as Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū and Prabhūtaratna,

continuing down to this present chapter which clarifies how he sought the Dharma and received the prediction of enlightenment from Dīpaṃkara— each and every instance being nothing other than his compassionate descent.

It is for this reason that he earnestly extols skillful means as being excellent for benefiting sentient beings through his manifested traces. △ Second, explaining those who are transformed and delivered:

At that time, the Buddha Tathāgata Devendra remained in the world for twenty intermediate kalpas, extensively expounding the wondrous Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Sands of sentient beings attained the fruit of arhatship; immeasurable sentient beings resolved their minds on pratyekabuddhahood;
and sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges resolved their minds on the unsurpassed path, attained the patience of non-arising, and reached the stage of non-retrogression.
△ III. Benefits after the Extinction of the Three Knowledges.
After the Parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata Devendra, the True Dharma remained in the world for twenty intermediate kalpas.

A stupa made of the seven precious jewels was erected over his entire bodily relics (śarīra), sixty yojanas in height and forty yojanas in length and breadth; all the devas and human beings [honored it].
With various flower powders, incense, burning perfumes, ointments, robes, necklaces, banners, flags, precious parasols, and musical performances and hymns,
they prostrated and made offerings to the wondrous stupa made of the seven treasures; thereby, immeasurable sentient beings attained the fruit of Arhatship,
immeasurable sentient beings realized the state of Pratyekabuddha, and inconceivable numbers of sentient beings gave rise to the Bodhi-mind and reached the stage of non-retrogression.
The second section, concluding the reconciliation of the ancient and the modern, is finished. △ Third, the exhortation to believe.

The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: "In future ages, if there are good men or good women who, upon hearing this 'Devadatta Chapter' of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, develop a pure heart of faith and reverence and do not give rise to doubt or confusion, they shall not fall into hell."
Those born as hungry ghosts or animals will be reborn before the Buddhas of the ten directions; wherever they are born, they shall constantly hear this sutra.
If they are born among humans or devas, they will experience supreme and wondrous bliss; or, they will be born by transformation upon lotus flowers in the presence of the Buddhas.
One whose mind is pure, faithful, and respectful does not give rise to false discrimination regarding the traces of good and evil; this is called a "pure mind.
One who deeply understands that every manifestation of birth is shown as an enemy is precisely one who has perfected the great furnace for becoming a Buddha;
this is called "faith. Toward those who act as enemies and causes of affliction, such a person is able to give rise to the perception of them as true spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).

This is called "venerating and thoroughly understanding": striking a bell to produce sound, whetting a blade for sharpness, refining gold for its purity, and chilling a plum for its fragrance—taking only the benefit without dwelling on the means.
It is like a child drinking milk who does not criticize his mother’s ugliness, or a person gathering fruit who does not disdain the curvature of the branches.
When no doubt arises, this is truly what is meant by "hearing-wisdom" (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).

Only through the wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) and the wisdom derived from cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) can one permanently leave the three miserable realms (*tridurgati*), constantly serve all Buddhas, and eternally hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, thereby attaining birth by transformation (*upapāduka*).
This first section concludes the account of how Sadāprarudita mastered the sutra in the past and Śākyamuni attained enlightenment.
△ Second, the account of how Mañjuśrī masters the sutra today and the Dragon Girl attains Buddhahood. This has two parts: first, the mastery of the sutra; second, the benefits.
Regarding the first five sections of the initial chapter: (1) Jñānākara requests to withdraw; (2) the World-Honored One stops him;
(3) Mañjuśrī arrives shortly thereafter; (4) Jñānākara questions him; (5) Mañjuśrī answers. Now, the first section.

At that time, a bodhisattva named Zhijí (Jñānakūṭa), who had followed the World-Honored One Prabhūtaratna from the region below, addressed the Buddha Prabhūtaratna, saying, "I shall now return to my own land.

Having asked this of Prabhūtaratna, [the assembly] wondered how it could still be said that he had entered parinirvāṇa while there was a bodhisattva following him. [The Buddha] replied, "It is indeed so."
Those who serve and make offerings to the jeweled stupa are able to follow it everywhere to hear the sutras through their supernormal powers and the force of their vows;
this is also because they are drawn in and sustained by the spiritual power of the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna.
△ Second, the World-Honored One stops them.
Śākyamuni Buddha said to Jñānakośa, "Good son, wait but a moment.
Here is a bodhisattva named Mañjuśrī with whom you may meet and discuss the sublime Dharma; you may then return to your own land."
The wisdom-accumulating (Zhijí) thought that the Stūpa of Prabhūtaratna had emerged solely for the purpose of verifying the sutra;

now that the exhortation for its circulation was complete, he requested its return. Śākyamuni did so because, although the Trace Gate (jìmén) was concluded, the Essential Gate (běnmén) had not yet been revealed.
Thus, by entrusting [the matter] to Mañjuśrī, he preserved the secret intent of Prabhūtaratna Buddha, which is beyond the comprehension of ordinary bodhisattvas. △
Then Mañjuśrī arrived. At that time, Mañjuśrī sat upon a thousand-petaled lotus flower as large as a chariot wheel;

the bodhisattvas who had come with him likewise sat upon precious lotus flowers, spontaneously emerging from the palace of the Sāgara Dragon King in the great ocean and remaining suspended in the void.
He proceeded to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, descended from his lotus, and approached the Buddha; he prostrated with his head at the feet of the two World-Honored Ones.
Having completed his salutations, he went to the place of Prajñākūṭa, exchanged greetings with him, and withdrew to sit to one side.
Question: In the introduction [of this scripture], Mañjuśrī was already seated; why has he now come from the ocean? Answer: There are three reasons for this.
First, he does not leave this assembly to transform sentient beings in the ocean; such a sacred realm of hidden and manifest presence cannot be fathomed by ordinary beings.

Second, since his benefit was fully accomplished while he was present in the introduction, why must his departure be announced beforehand? Third, it is when he arrives that great benefit is produced. Therefore, [his coming] is not required.
Regarding the statement that "the assembly comes from the ocean in three ways," the Sanskrit original is extremely extensive while the Chinese translation is very brief;
it may contain passages describing the emergence of assemblies, such as those found in the "Entering the Dharma Realm" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Question:
Outside the three thousandfold world system, there are each four hundred trillion nayutas of lands where there are no longer great oceans; why, then, does Mañjuśrī [act in this way]?
He further said: "The explanation that the events were brought by the sea-spirit (Sāgara) is not incorrect; moreover, this is inconceivable. Now, I shall explain it through three points.
First, since both the devas and humans have been moved and the great ocean has been transformed, the supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) must have come from the very place where they were moved;
thus, there should be no fault regarding distance. Second, even if the multitude in the ocean were moved, the Dragon Palace itself would remain unmoved. As for the dragons, they say..."
If that which moves has already changed its location, and one follows that change yet remains unchanging in its fundamental state, what is there that is not possible? Regarding these three points:

those without karmic conditions have been relocated, while those with conditions have now come here. This inconceivable mountain and sea remain exactly as they were, yet cause the multitude not to see them;
this is merely a transformation of perception, not a change in their essential substance. Since Mañjuśrī did not depart by rising from his seat, [the assembly likewise does not perceive him].
Since the land is both defiled and pure, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states that when it is moved to another land, no one perceives any coming or going.
Here, however, although there is the appearance of coming and going, the land itself does not actually move;

thus we know that for those who possess the karmic capacity (*yōki*), the land transforms and all beings are moved, yet they still perceive themselves as coming. For those who lack such conditions (*muen*), the land appears to come to them from afar.

Yet, because they do not arrive, although the principle remains unmoving, the accomplishment of the transformation follows a fixed pattern; thus, what is perceived differs as the times of coming and going vary.
If even the transformative protocols of a Bodhisattva are such, how could the transformations established by a Buddha be the same as those of ordinary beings? Question:

Since he does not arise before departing, why is it said that he "comes"? Answer: It is shown so that the assemblies on both sides may know the power and efficacy of the sutra, and recognize the benefits derived from receiving its teachings.
Therefore, it must be said that while they do not come from here nor go elsewhere, their coming and going are both for the benefit of sentient beings;
why, then, raise this objection? Thus we know that although it is said they depart from this land, they are not necessarily seen arriving in another land.
That they are not seen arriving there and not seen departing here—this movement, which is neither coming nor going, is as evident as the account in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*.
When he came and pressed the ground with his toes, the great assembly saw themselves sitting upon precious lotus flowers, while the soil remained as filthy as before.
△ Fourth, the Inquiry of Jñānakūṭa:
Bodhisattva Jñānakūṭa asked Mañjuśrī, "O Benevolent One, how many sentient beings were transformed by you when you went to the Dragon Palace?"

What? △ Fifth, Mañjuśrī’s response, which is further divided into four parts: first, the answer that the benefit is exceedingly great; second, the gathering of those who have received the benefit as proof;
third, Mañjuśrī’s summary of the benefits; and fourth, Dharmākara’s praise in verse. Now, the first part.
Mañjuśrī said: "Their number is immeasurable, beyond calculation, not to be proclaimed by mouth nor fathomed by mind;
wait but a moment, and you shall know it for yourself."
△ Second, the assembly of those who have received benefit and attained realization.
Before these words were finished, countless bodhisattvas sat upon precious lotus flowers, emerging from the ocean and proceeding to Vulture Peak Mountain, where they remained suspended in the air.
All these bodhisattvas had been transformed and delivered by Mañjuśrī and were fully endowed with bodhicitta.

They all together discussed the six pāramitās of the bodhisattva practices; the original śrāvakas, while in the midst of the air, expounded the śrāvaka practices to cause them all to cultivate the Mahāyāna meaning of emptiness.
Seated upon jeweled lotus flowers, these innumerable bodhisattvas possess two types of origins: first, those who originally resolved their minds on Great Awakening;
second, those who were originally śrāvakas. Now, having received the Dharma-transformation of Mañjuśrī, they all return to the single reality.
The meaning of emptiness in the Mahāyāna is precisely the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena. △ Third, Mañjuśrī concludes by stating the benefits.
Mañjuśrī said to Zhìjī (Jñānakośa), "Such were the deeds of his teaching and transformation in the ocean.
△ Fourth, the verse praise by Zhìjī:
At that time, the Bodhisattva Zhìjī praised him in verse, saying:
Possessing great wisdom, virtue, and heroic vigor, you have transformed and delivered immeasurable multitudes;

now this entire great assembly and I have all witnessed you expound the meaning of the true mark and reveal the Dharma of the One Vehicle, widely guiding all sentient beings so that they may swiftly achieve Bodhi.

The first section, explaining the general application of the sutra, is concluded. △ Second, explaining the benefits, in nine parts: First, Mañjuśrī’s self-narration; second, Zhijizhang’s questioning; third, Mañjuśrī’s response;
fourth, Zhijizhang’s adherence to the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao) as a source of doubt; fifth, the Dragon Girl’s clarification of the Perfect Teaching (Yuan-jiao) to resolve the doubt;
sixth, Śāriputra’s challenge based on the provisional authority of the Tripiṭaka; seventh, the Dragon Girl’s removal of doubt through the One Reality; eighth, at that time... [text fragment].
The assembly, having heard and seen this, attained benefit; the nine thousand bodhisattvas and Śāriputra accepted it in silence.
First, Mañjuśrī said: "In the midst of the ocean, I have always preached only the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*."
△ Second, the inquiry of Jñānākara.
Jñānākara addressed Mañjuśrī, saying: "This sutra is exceedingly profound and subtle, a treasure among all sutras, rare in the world.
Are there any sentient beings who, by applying themselves with diligent vigor and practicing this sutra, will quickly attain Buddhahood?"
△ Third, Mañjuśrī’s reply. Mañjuśrī said:
"There is a daughter of the Dragon King Sāgara who is eight years of age.

She possesses sharp faculties and wisdom, well understands the faculties, karma, and conduct of sentient beings, has attained dhāraṇīs, and has realized the profound secret treasury taught by all Buddhas."

They are able to receive and uphold [the teachings], enter deeply into meditative concentration, and thoroughly penetrate all dharmas; in a single kṣaṇa, they give rise to the bodhicitta and attain non-retrogression.
Their eloquence is unimpeded, and they regard all sentient beings with compassion as if they were their own infants.

Fully endowed with merit, they express through both thought and speech that which is subtle, wondrous, vast, compassionate, benevolent, and yielding; their will is harmonious and elegant, enabling them to reach the state of Bodhi.
Wisdom that skillfully knows the *dhāraṇīs* of sentient beings and is able to receive the Buddha-treasury is perfect wisdom (*prajñā*).

To enter deeply into meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and thoroughly penetrate all phenomena is perfect concentration (*samādhi*). Because concentration and wisdom are equal, one is able to give rise to the bodhicitta in a single instant (*kṣaṇa*).
That which is called "awakening to non-arising" is precisely seeing that the instant is itself the limit of the instant (*kṣaṇakoti*).
Samādhi is the realization that in this very moment there is neither arising nor intrinsic nature, and thus one suddenly enters the inconceivable Dharma-realm.
That is to say: when the slightest thought arises, the three thousand [realms] are fully present; as these three thousand are empty, one attains non-retrogression in position;

as these three thousand are provisional, one attains non-retrogression in practice; as these three thousand are the Middle Way, one attains non-retrogression in mindfulness. One clearly understands that they are neither sequential nor separate.

Because it does not perversely illuminate both the horizontal and the vertical simultaneously, its eloquence is unimpeded. One realizes for oneself that one's own mind-nature is identical to that of all Buddhas;
because one pities sentient beings who share this same essence yet remain lost in delusion, one regards them with compassion as if they were one's own infants.
Since one can thus harmonize upward with all Buddhas and downward with all sentient beings, one’s merit and virtue are fully perfected, enabling one to reach Bodhi. Thus one reflects in the mind.
The oral exposition of these four lines all praises his perfect practice. △ Fourth, Zhizhi Bodhisattva takes the Separate Teaching as a basis for doubt.

Zhizhi Bodhisattva said: "I have seen that Śākyamuni Tathāgata, throughout immeasurable kalpas, performed difficult and painful practices, accumulating merit and virtue while seeking the path to Bodhi without ever ceasing; he observed the three thousand great thousandfold worlds, and even..."
There is not even a space the size of a mustard seed where this bodhisattva has not sacrificed her body and life for the sake of sentient beings;
only after that did she attain the path of enlightenment. Do not disbelieve that this woman attained perfect awakening in a mere instant.
Jizhi’s retinue followed the precious stupa specifically to verify the Perfect Sūtra; how could they possibly have lacked faith? It was merely to resolve the doubts of sentient beings.
Śākyamuni’s ascetic practices and his manifestation of traces—whether identical or distinct—are the provisional means for transforming others.

The Dragon Girl’s aspiration and her immediate ascent to the stage of non-retrogression are the reality of one's own practice. (This simply contrasts the partial with the provisional and the Perfect with the real. In an instant, she ascended.
What the text refers to as "a single moment" (*kṣaṇa*) is, in fact, the non-duality of the provisional and the ultimate, wherein phenomena and principle are mutually integrated.

Since Śākyamuni manifested his traces and performed difficult deeds while having already long ago realized the perfect principle, it follows that even the Dragon Girl’s manifestation of awakening in a single moment must have been preceded by the long-term accumulation of provisions.
Furthermore, the very source of liberation over immeasurable eons is precisely this single thought-moment; how could it be otherwise? It is but a brief instant.

Recently, it has been established that the ten periods of time—past and present—are inherently complete within a single moment, just as the Rishi Gokhura took Sudhana by the hand and, in the space of one thought-instant, fully traversed kalpas as numerous as the atoms of all lands to serve various Buddhas and practice the path of a Bodhisattva; thus, the Buddha-activities of the nature-realm are manifest and clear.
If one were to claim that the Separate Teaching (Bianjiao) belongs exclusively to phenomena while the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) belongs exclusively to principle, [it would be a misunderstanding].
If phenomena and principle are divided, one still falls into extreme attachments. If phenomena are not principle, how can they establish themselves?
If principle is not phenomena, how can it manifest itself? I pray that those who read this scripture will reflect upon this. △ Fifth: The Dragon Girl’s Clarification of Perfection to Resolve Doubts.
Before his speech had concluded, the Dragon King’s daughter suddenly appeared before him; she prostrated herself in homage and, standing to one side, praised him with these verses:
"You have profoundly realized the nature of sin and merit, Illuminating the ten directions. Your subtle and pure Dharma-body Is endowed with the thirty-two marks."
Adorned with the eighty kinds of excellent marks, my Dharma-body is venerated by devas and humans and revered by dragons and spirits;
among all classes of sentient beings, there are none who do not honor it. Furthermore, I have heard that only a Buddha can personally witness and know the attainment of Bodhi;
may you certify that I am expounding the Mahāyāna teachings to deliver suffering sentient beings across [the sea of existence].

This is because the Dragon Girl attained liberation by upholding this sutra; thus, her spontaneous praise of the Buddha serves both to clarify his perfect enlightenment (*paripūrṇa*) and to resolve doubts.
The first two and a half verses praise the Buddha’s perfect enlightenment, while the final verse cites evidence to resolve doubts.

Regarding the initial statement, "profoundly penetrating the characteristics of sin and merit, universally illuminating the ten directions": the characteristics of sin and merit are simply the ten dharmas.

Regarding the characteristics of the ten realms: the three miserable paths constitute transgression, while the heavenly realms constitute merit; the out-flowing (*sāsrava*) constitutes transgression, while the non-out-flowing (*anāsrava*) constitutes merit;

abiding in solitary emptiness constitutes transgression, while entering into the provisional constitutes merit; the two extremes constitute transgression, while the Middle Way constitutes merit; the "but" Middle Way constitutes transgression, while the Perfect Middle Way constitutes merit.
Since these characteristics of the ten realms have been set forth, there is nothing—from the essential nature (*dharmatā*) down to the retributive fruit—that is not [encompassed].
All ten dharma-realms, including their aspects of sin and merit, are equally phenomena born of causes and conditions;

in their very substance, they are simultaneously empty, provisional, and the Middle. The *Tripiṭaka* (Threefold) Teaching merely penetrates the single phrase "causes and conditions," illuminating six realms but not ten;
though it penetrates, its penetration is not deep, and its illumination is not universal. The *Common* (Shared) Teaching merely penetrates that the causes and conditions of the six realms are empty.

It is neither a profound illumination nor a pervasive discernment; though one may reach understanding and illumination sequentially, this cannot yet be called "profound penetration" or "pervasive illumination.

Only the person of perfect enlightenment (yuanren) understands that the single thought-moment before one’s eyes penetrates vertically to the bottom of the three truths and encompasses horizontally the limits of the ten realms.
Since there is not a single truth that is not the ten realms, there is no verticality that is not vertical.
If it is one realm rather than the three truths, then it is neither horizontal nor vertical; yet it is both horizontal and vertical.

Therefore, it is said that "one profoundly penetrates the characteristics of sin and merit, universally illuminating the ten directions. Furthermore, these horizontal and vertical aspects are collectively termed "inherent virtue" (*prakṛti-guṇa*);
this inherent virtue is neither horizontal nor vertical because all ordinary beings and sages are eternally equal. For now, it is described as such.
In the practice of the nature-inherent cultivation (*xingcheng xiuxi*), one must clarify the six stages of "immediacy" (*liuji*). This practice is neither horizontal nor vertical;

because the unconditioned dharma (*asamskṛta-dharma*) possesses distinctions, it is conventionally described as vertical. The principle is present even within delusion; it is a matter of realization or non-realization, and illumination or non-illumination.

From the stage of "name" (*mingzi*) onward, one attains the names of realization and illumination. Upon reaching the ultimate stage, realization becomes most profound and illumination [becomes most complete].

Because this most comprehensive [text] now praises the ultimate virtues of the Buddha, it says: "Profoundly penetrating the characteristics of sin and merit, universally illuminating the ten directions.

As for the "subtle, wondrous, and pure Dharma-body": the Three Thousand Worlds are provisional (the *jia*); thus they are subtle (*wei*). The Three Thousand Worlds are the Middle Way (*zhong*); thus they are wondrous (*miao*).
The Three Thousand Worlds are empty (*kong*); thus they are pure (*jing*). These three virtues are neither vertical nor horizontal, neither simultaneous nor separate; they are precisely all Buddhas.
The realized *dharmakāya* is without marks (*animitta*) and yet nothing is not manifested within it; its true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) serves as the foundation for the ocean of major and minor marks.
Thus, it possesses the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics. Each and every mark and characteristic is itself the *dharmadhātu*;
being originally possessed by the *dharmakāya*, they are further employed to adorn the *dharmakāya*. This is what is meant by "the entirety of nature (*prakṛti*) becoming cultivation (*bhāvanā*)."
The phrase "the complete cultivation reveals the nature" means that the four lines concerning devas, humans, and so forth may be understood according to the text.
Furthermore, the statement "hearing [this Dharma] achieves Bodhi" reiterates the praise of Mañjuśrī regarding the Dragon Girl’s ability to reach Bodhi in a single kṣaṇa.
The phrase "only a Buddha can bear witness" cites the Buddha as testimony to resolve the doubts of Ratnakūṭa. I shall expound the Great... [text ends].

The intent of the phrase "delivering suffering sentient beings by means of the teachings" is to manifest that he shall before long proceed to the Immaculate World (*Vimalā-loka*) in the south, where he will attain equal and perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and turn the great wheel of Dharma (*mahā-dharmacakra*). △ Sixth, Śāriputra raises a provisional objection based on the Three Piṭakas.
Then Śāriputra said to the dragon girl, "That you will attain the unsurpassed path before long—this is difficult to believe.
Why is this? The female body is defiled and impure; it is not a vessel for the Dharma. How could one possibly attain unsurpassed bodhi?

The Buddha-way is vast and remote; only after passing through immeasurable kalpas, accumulating practices through diligent suffering, and fully cultivating all the pāramitās, can one finally achieve it."
Furthermore, the female body still possesses five obstacles: first, one cannot become a Brahmā King; second, Śakra; third, a Māra King;
fourth, a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin); and fifth, the body of a Buddha. How, then, can a female body swiftly attain Buddhahood?
In the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, Śāriputra once engaged in a dialogue with a celestial maiden and immediately came to understand that there is no fixed characteristic of male or female;
how much more so now, having attained awakening during the first week and ascended to the first stage (*bhūmi*) of the Perfect Teaching, where his realization is identical to that of the dragon girl.
How could such a real objection exist? It is merely a question posed on behalf of sentient beings. △ Seven: The Dragon.
The girl dispelled their doubts with a single jewel.
At that time, the dragon girl took a precious gem worth as much as the three-thousandfold world system and offered it to the Buddha;
the Buddha immediately accepted it. The dragon girl then said to the Bodhisattva Zhijip and the Venerable Śāriputra: "I have presented this jewel..."

The World-Honored One accepted this matter. [The girl] asked quickly, "Is it not so? He replied, "It is very fast. The girl said, "By means of your supernatural power, observe my attainment of Buddhahood;
it shall be even swifter than this.

The precious jewel symbolizes the cultivation and perfection of the causal stage; offering it to the Buddha symbolizes that the cause will achieve its fruition. The Buddha’s acceptance of it symbolizes...
The attainment of the fruit is exceedingly swift. According to the interpretation based on the contemplation of the mind: initial awakening is the jewel and fundamental awakening is the Buddha;
when initial awakening accords with fundamental awakening, it is as if placing the jewel upon the Buddha, and the Buddha immediately accepts it.
At that time, the entire assembly saw the dragon girl suddenly transform into a male and, endowed with the practices of a bodhisattva,
proceed immediately to the Stainless World in the southern quarter. There she sat upon a precious lotus flower and attained perfect enlightenment,
manifesting the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics, and extensively expounding the sublime Dharma for all sentient beings throughout the ten directions.
Question: The *T’ai ching* (Womb Sūtra) states that the daughters of Māra, Brahmā, and Śakra do not discard their bodies nor receive new ones, yet all attain Buddhahood in their present bodies;
it then says they subsequently transform into males before attaining Buddhahood. What is the meaning of this in terms of provisional and ultimate truth? Answer:

The statement in the *T’ai ching* regarding attaining Buddhahood in the present body refers to the realization of one’s own practice (*svayam-mārga*) through the destruction of ignorance and delusion; it is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). This...
The sutra’s explanation of becoming a man refers to the manifestation of the eight phases of attaining enlightenment for the sake of transforming others; it is an expedient means (*upāya*).
One must know that according to the Perfect and Sudden Teaching (*yuan-dun jiao*), one can attain Buddhahood in this very life by practicing the wondrous path.
Therefore, it is said: "The Dharma-nature is like a great ocean; it does not speak of 'this' or 'that. Whether ordinary person or sage, all are equal, without high or low. Only...
When the defilements of the mind are extinguished, realization is attained as easily as turning over one's hand;
because their actual practice was so swift, they manifested through expedient means to bring it to completion, causing people to believe deeply and without doubt. Question:

If a woman transforms into a man and immediately sits at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), lacking such signs as descending from heaven, dwelling in the womb, and leaving home, how can this be called "attaining enlightenment through the eight phases" (aṣṭalakṣaṇābhisambodhi)?

Answer: The distinction between pure and impure lands regarding the eight phases [of a Buddha’s life] does not necessarily require them to be identical in every respect. Furthermore, the manifestations of the Dharma-body are inconceivable;
while this land perceives the transformation from female to male, that land may still perceive the beginning and end of the eight phases—how could this be impossible?
As for Śāriputra and others who have already attained the stage of perfect dwelling (yuan-zhu), they too are capable of manifesting the eight phases to become Buddhas. Why is this so?
The prophecy [of his own enlightenment] still lies beyond vast kalpas; yet, if one answers from the perspective of his own practice according to reality, the principle realized is uniform;
but if one answers from the perspective of transforming others through expedient means, the capacities of sentient beings are unequal.

Furthermore, since all the great disciples are manifestations of the Dharma-body appearing in various places with different traces, how can we know that he has not manifested the attainment of Buddhahood in other realms? Question: Even if that were the case...
Śāriputra and the others have already acted as Buddhas in other realms; why, then, must they again manifest the reception of a prediction here?

The answer is that the prediction is bestowed here so that sentient beings may see and hear it, thereby further binding the conditions for future encounters and enabling them to attain liberation in the future.
Thus, horizontally, it pervades the ten directions; vertically, it continues through successive generations without end, extensively delivering sentient beings.
The realm of this [Dharma] remains inexhaustible; how could it possibly be fathomed by calculating with worldly sentiments or measured by the mind? Such are the great matters of the Dharma-realm.
△ At that time, the assembly witnessed and heard this, and all gained benefit.
Then, the Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings—humans and non-humans alike—all from afar...

Seeing that dragon girl attain Buddhahood and preach the Dharma for the sake of all those in the assembly—both devas and humans—their hearts were filled with great joy, and they all paid homage from afar.

Innumerable sentient beings in that land heard the Dharma, attained realization, and reached the stage of non-retrogression; innumerable sentient beings received the prediction of their future enlightenment.
The Immaculate World shook in six ways, and three thousand sentient beings in the Sahā world established themselves [in the stages of the path].
Three thousand sentient beings on the stage of non-retrogression gave rise to the bodhicitta and received their predictions of enlightenment.

First, it clarifies seeing from afar and hearing from afar, followed by prostrations from afar; next, it clarifies the benefits attained in that land, and finally, it clarifies the benefits attained in this land.

This is because the conditions for the southern region were ripe, making it appropriate for him to manifest as a Buddha through the eight phases of enlightenment, whereas the conditions in this land were thin.

Because the Dragon Girl’s teaching was entirely through the power of the Samādhi of Universally Manifesting the Physical Body, which arises from the essence to manifest function, she was able to manifest a single body as all bodies, appearing in accordance with what is appropriate. △ Ninth:
Jñānakūṭa and Śāriputra silently accepted it in faith.
The Bodhisattva Jñānakūṭa, Śāriputra, and the entire assembly accepted this with silent faith.
The Chapter on Devadatta concludes. Chapter Thirteen:
The Chapter on Upholding.
Because twenty thousand bodhisattvas received the command to propagate the sutra, this is titled the "Chapter on Upholding" (Chih-p'in).

Because eighty quadrillion nayutas were further exhorted to propagate the sutra, it is titled the "Chapter on Exhorting to Uphold" (Kuan-chih-p'in). △ This is the fourth chapter of the circulation section of the Trace Gate (Ji-men).

The text is divided into two parts: first, clarifying the upholding; second, clarifying the exhortation to uphold. Within the first part, there are three sections; the first concerns the twenty thousand bodhisattvas.
1. Śākyamuni entrusts the sutra to this land; 2. the two śrāvakas make a vow to propagate it in other lands;
3. the bhikṣuṇīs request a prediction. First:
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāpratibhāna, together with the two...
Together with their retinues of ten thousand bodhisattvas, they all made this vow before the Buddha: "We pray only that the World-Honored One need not worry;
after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, we shall uphold, recite, and expound this sutra.

In the evil world to come, sentient beings will have diminished roots of goodness, while those of overweening pride will increase, becoming greedy for profit and offerings, increasing unwholesome roots, and becoming estranged from the Dharma."
Although liberation is difficult to attain, we shall rouse the power of great patience to study and recite this sutra, uphold it, explain it, transcribe it,
and offer various kinds of worship, not begrudging even our own bodies or lives.
△ Second, the Śrāvakas vow to propagate [this sutra] in other lands.
At that time, five hundred Arhats among the assembly who had received the prediction of enlightenment addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, we also make this vow to extensively expound this sutra in other lands. Furthermore, there were eight thousand persons, both those still in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Those who had received the prediction of enlightenment rose from their seats, joined their palms toward the Buddha, and made this vow:
"World-Honored One, we too shall widely expound this sutra in other lands. Why is this?

It is because the people in this Sahā world are for the most part depraved and evil, harboring overweening pride, possessing meager merit, and being turbid with anger, deceitful, and insincere in heart."
Question: These śrāvakas have already become mahāsattvas; why, then, are they unable to propagate this sutra in this land? Answer:

It is in order to lead in those bodhisattvas who are beginners and at the start of their practice, who are unable to propagate the sutra through ascetic practices in an evil age, and furthermore, to open the "Chapter on Peaceful Practices" (Anrakugyō-hon).
△ Third, the nuns request a prediction [of their future enlightenment]. Part four: First, the prediction for Mahāprajāpatī and the six [nuns].
1. The Thousand Nuns; 2. The Record of Yaśodharā; 3. The Nuns’ Comprehension; 4. The Nuns’ Aspiration. First, regarding the initial section:
At that time, the Buddha’s maternal aunt, the Bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī, together with bhikṣus, both those in training and those beyond training...
Six thousand bhikṣuṇīs rose from their seats, joined their palms with single-minded devotion, and gazed upon the Honored One’s countenance without averting their eyes for a moment.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Gautamī: "For what reason do you look upon the Tathāgata with a sorrowful expression?
Does it not occur to your mind that I have failed to mention your name when bestowing the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi? Gautamī...
"Dammi, I have previously given a general prediction for all śrāvakas; now you wish to know your own prediction:

in a future age, within the teachings of sixty-eight thousand *koṭis* of Buddhas, you shall become a great Dharma-preacher, and together with six thousand bhikṣuṇīs—both those in training and those beyond training—you shall all be Dharma-preachers. In this manner, you shall gradually fulfill the qualities of a bodhisattva."
"You shall attain Buddhahood with the name Sarvasattvapriyadarśana Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna,
Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. Gautamī,
this prediction of successive succession was granted to the Buddha Sarvasattvapriyadarśana and to six thousand bodhisattvas.
He attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Kautamī is also called Gautamī, which is the same as Gotama; this is merely a difference in the weight of the Sanskrit pronunciation.
This translates as "the most excellent on earth," and because he belonged to the noble Kṣatriya clan, he was addressed by this name. △ Second, the prediction concerning Yaśodharā.
Ānanda, at that time the bhikṣuṇī Yaśodharā, mother of Rāhula, had this thought: "The World-Honored One has not mentioned my name alone among those who receive predictions.
The Buddha said to Yaśodharā: "In a future age, after hundreds of thousands of millions..."
Having cultivated the bodhisattva path within the teachings of billions of Buddhas as a great Dharma teacher,
he will gradually perfect the Buddha-way and shall attain Buddhahood in the land of *Sukhāvatī*, where his name shall be Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna,
Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, named *Sahasraraśmipratimaṇḍita*.
The Buddha’s lifespan is immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
△ Third, the nuns’ understanding.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī, along with the bhikṣuṇī Yaśodharā and...
His retinue was all filled with great joy at having attained what they had never experienced before, and they spoke these verses before the Buddha:
"O World-Honored One, Guide, you bring peace and security to devas and humans; having heard our prediction, our minds are fully satisfied."
△ Fourth, the Vows of the Bhikṣuṇīs.
After the bhikṣuṇīs had spoken these verses, they addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, we too shall be able to widely proclaim this sutra in other lands."

The intention behind his modesty regarding this land is the same as that of the śrāvakas mentioned above; alternatively, it may be because the conditions for the nuns and the śrāvakas have ripened in other lands.

The first section, clarifying the reception and upholding [of the teaching], is complete. △ Second, clarifying the exhortation to uphold [the teaching]. This has two parts: first, the long prose; second, the verse summary.
Within the first part, there are four sections: first, the Buddha gazes with his eye; second, the bodhisattvas request an instruction; third, the Buddha recollects them in silence.
Now, regarding the four vows made in accordance with the Buddha’s intention, this is the first.
At that time, the World-Honored One gazed upon eighty quadrillion nayutas of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

As for those who gaze upon him with silent exhortation rather than verbal instruction: although no specific command has been issued above, the profound depth of the merit of upholding this sutra has been clearly demonstrated through these citations;
furthermore, the fact that Prabhūtaratna and his emanations have come from afar to urge and inspire us is a sufficient demonstration of such earnest intent.

Those who wish to respond to this call should immediately make their vows; there is no need for further words. Moreover, it is also for... [the sake of]... (Note: The final phrase "Moreover, it is also for" indicates a textual ellipsis or transition to another point not fully provided in the source fragment.)
It was not proclaimed because [the Buddha] wished to protect the vows of the śrāvakas from other directions. △ Second, the Bodhisattvas’ request for instruction:
All these bodhisattvas were *avaivartika*, turning the wheel of the non-retrogressive Dharma and having attained various *dhāraṇīs*.
They immediately rose from their seats, went before the Buddha, joined their palms with single-minded devotion, and thought thus: "If the World-Honored One would grant us..."
He commanded us, "Those who uphold and recite this sutra should widely proclaim this Dharma according to the Buddha's teachings.
△ Third, mindfulness of the Buddha in silence:
Again, he thought, "The Buddha is now silent and does not issue a command; what should I do?"
△ Fourth, making a vow in accordance with the Buddha’s intention.

At that time, the bodhisattvas, out of reverence for and compliance with the Buddha’s intention, and desiring to fulfill their own original vows, uttered a lion’s roar before the Buddha and made this vow:
“World-Honored One, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, we shall travel back and forth throughout the ten directions...”
In the worlds of the ten directions, may all sentient beings who write out this sutra, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, explain its meaning,
practice according to the Dharma, and maintain right mindfulness— all these are due to the Buddha’s majestic power; we pray that the World-Honored One, remaining in other lands,
will behold us from afar and protect us.
Second, the exhortation to uphold [the teaching]. The first part, the long prose section, is concluded. △ Second, the verse summary:
these independent verses are requested by various bodhisattvas and others for the purpose of protecting the propagation of the sutra. They describe the methods for propagating the sutra oneself;

this is because the Buddha, having finished explaining the methods in the "Dharma Master" chapter, had the jeweled stupa seek out those who could employ such methods, and Dharmodgata was led forth to serve as such a person.
Regarding "the standard method" (*fang gui*): Śākyamuni is one who received the dharma-method from the assembly; thus it is said that he took his own body as a bed and seat, and so forth.

This present chapter concerns the "standard method for peaceful conduct in the evil age. Since this is the standard method for those at the beginning of their practice, it says, "abiding on the ground of patience," and so forth, as will be explained in detail later.
If it were otherwise, then there would be no standard method for propagating the sutra, like [the case of] Chi.
Entering the ranks with one's own body, one does not fail to fulfill the words of donning the armor; these words were not set forth in vain. Following the text, there are four sections:

first, clarifying the propagation of the sutra while wearing robes; second, clarifying the propagation of the sutra upon entering the chamber; third, clarifying the propagation of the sutra while seated on the seat;

fourth, a summary concluding the request for understanding. Within the first section, there are three parts: first, a general discussion of the timing to clarify the wearing of robes; second, a specific clarification...
First, regarding the intention behind donning the robes for the sake of the objects of patience that have become clearly manifest:
at that moment, all the bodhisattvas together raised their voices and spoke in verse:
"We pray that you do not worry; after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, within the terrors of this evil age, we shall extensively proclaim [the Dharma]."
△ Second, the specific clarification of the objects to be endured, in three parts: First, a general clarification of "false persons," who are the secular masses;
second, the clarification of those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*) within the Gate of the Way; third, the clarification of those with overweening pride who usurp the status of sages.
Within this, the first may still be endured; the second exceeds the former; and the third is most extreme, as each subsequent type becomes increasingly difficult to recognize.
First: We shall endure all instances of ignorant people who revile us with harsh words or attack us with swords and staves.
Second: Clarifying those within the Way who possess overweening pride.

In this degenerate age, there are bhikṣus whose minds are characterized by false wisdom and crookedness; having not attained anything, they claim to have attained it, and their hearts are filled with pride.
△ Third, those who falsely claim sainthood through overweening pride (adhimāna).
There may be some forest-dweller (āraṇyaka) wearing patched robes who dwells in seclusion and claims to practice the true path;

yet he despises those among the people who propagate the Lotus Sutra. Because he is greedily attached to gain and offerings, he deceives laypeople by preaching a counterfeit Dharma, and is thus venerated by the ignorant of the world.
His outward demeanor appears like that of an arhat possessing the six supernormal powers; however, such a person, though dwelling in a forest hermitage, actually harbors [evil intent].
With evil intent, they constantly think of worldly matters such as fame and profit; they merely pretend to be forest-dwellers (*āraṇyaka*).

They take particular pleasure in exposing the faults of us who propagate the Mahāyāna, speaking thus in slander: "These bhikṣus, out of greed for gain and offerings, preach the discourses of external paths and have composed these sūtras themselves to deceive and delude the people of the world, seeking only fame and renown."
Therefore, they constantly dwell among the great assemblies with the intent to destroy us (the Chinese who propagate the Dharma).
For this reason, they slander kings, ministers, brahmins, householders, and other groups of monks, speaking ill of us and saying:
"These people hold wrong views; they preach the doctrines of external paths."
*Āraṇya*, *ārañña*, *araṇa*, and *āraṇika* are translated as "without strife" (*wu zheng*) and also as "a place without clamor or confusion.
One who dwells in an *āraṇya* location does so to subdue the afflictions (*kleśa*); however, if one now exalts oneself and disparages others, this is not the practice of being without strife.
Therefore, such a person is said to be an "āraṇya-dweller in name only. This is stated in the *Vinaya Piṭaka* and...

The *Mahāratnakūṭa-sūtra*, the "Chapter on the Jewel Banner" (*Ratnarāśi-parivarta*), the *Ratnamegha-sūtra*, the *Buddhapiṭaka-sūtra*, and others each extensively clarify the practice of the araṇya-dweller.
If one has not yet attained correspondence with this practice, it is appropriate to seek out a teacher to advance on the Path;

why hastily cling to ignorance and self-righteousness? I pray that all practitioners will reflect deeply upon themselves. This concludes the second section, which clarifies the objects of forbearance. △
The third is the intention regarding wearing robes:
"Out of reverence for the Buddha, we shall endure all these evils. Although we may be slighted by such people who say, 'You yourselves composed this sutra;
it is all the Buddha's work,' we must endure such words of contempt. Furthermore, [we shall do so] during the age of turbidity."
In this evil age, there will be many terrors and malevolent spirits that enter our bodies to revile and insult us.
Out of our reverent faith in the Buddha, we shall don the armor of patience; for the sake of expounding this sutra, we shall endure these various hardships.

We do not cherish our own bodies or lives, but only regret that we might fail to attain the Unsurpassed Way. In future ages, we shall protect and uphold what the World-Honored One has entrusted to us.
One should know for oneself that in this defiled and evil age, bhikṣus will not understand the Buddha’s skillful means and the teachings he gave according to what was appropriate;
they will speak with harsh words, frown, and be repeatedly expelled and kept away from stūpas and monasteries.
Because of such various evils, one should endure these matters by recollecting the Buddha’s injunctions.

"Armor" refers to mail. The "armor of forbearance" means that by being able to endure insults, one may enter an evil world without being wounded, just as one who enters battle wearing armor is not harmed by swords or arrows. One must know that each of the four teachings has its own armor of forbearance;
for instance, in the *Madhyama Āgama*, the bhikṣu Kālakāra addressed the Buddha, saying: "The house..."
When Śāriputra reviled me, saying, "I am a black-toothed monk," the Buddha immediately called Śāriputra and asked him:
"Did you truly revile the bhikṣu Kālakasūtra? Śāriputra replied: "My mind was not settled when I said I reviled you; my mind is now settled. How could I have said I reviled you?
It is like breaking a cow's horn—it does not cause harm to others. It is like a castrated youth; he feels shame but causes no distress."
The mind of that person is like earth, water, fire, and wind; it receives both the pure and the impure, such as excrement, urine, mucus, and saliva, yet it does not revile them.
The mind is like a broom that sweeps away both the pure and the impure alike. It is also like a broken vessel filled with fat placed in the sun, from which drops constantly leak out.
When one observes that the nine orifices of the body are constantly leaking impurities, how can one revile or speak ill [of the body]?
Regarding others, it is as if one were to tie dead snakes, dogs, and the like around the necks of pure youths; yet, out of shame and self-reproach, one does not revile or speak ill of them.
The Buddha asked such evil persons: "How do you view them? Śāriputra replied: "A person has five aspects:
though their body, speech, and mind may be unwholesome, one contemplates only their goodness and not their unwholesomeness, just as one regards a patchwork robe."
A bhikṣu sees a heap of refuse containing tattered rags; grasping them with his left hand and spreading them out with his right, he discards the impure parts and takes only the pure.
He contemplates the purity of that body to regulate his own body; he discards its speech and mind to admonish his own speech and mind.

While the conduct of his two [faculties of] speech is pure, his body and mind are impure; thus he contemplates their speech while discarding their body and mind, like one parched with heat and thirst.

If one encounters a pond with much grass, one should part the grass and scoop up water to cool the body and quench thirst. One should purify the three [faculties]: while the body and speech may not be pure, one should still contemplate the intention;
one should not rely on the body or speech. It is like being hot and thirsty while traveling on a road where there is but a small amount of water in a cow’s footprint;
if one were to scoop it up with the hands, the water would become turbid. Therefore, one should kneel with both knees and rest both hands upon the ground, bringing the mouth close to drink.

Use this to eliminate feverish thirst. Regarding those whose three karmas are all impure, although they have nothing of use, one should contemplate them with deep compassion, as if seeing a sick person on the road and settling them into comfort.

By contemplating this impurity, may they encounter virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) who treat their three karmas so that they do not fall into the three miserable realms (*apāya*). Regarding those whose three karmas are all pure, always maintain mindfulness of this.
A person uses self-instruction as a metaphor for mindfulness and aspiration, being like a cool pond filled with many flowers and grasses where one who is parched with heat enters to find relief.
One should constantly contemplate the objective realm to eliminate one's own evils;
this is the armor of suffering, impermanence, impurity, non-self, and emptiness used within the Tripiṭaka teaching. The Confucianist says: "Upon seeing the virtuous, think of becoming like them."

The passage from the *Zi Jian* stating, "If one sees the unvirtuous, one reflects within oneself," and the saying, "In a group of three walking together, there will surely be someone who can be my teacher;
I shall follow what is good in them and reform what is not good," also carry this same meaning. The *Vibhāṣā* states: "To 'recollect' (nian) is to revile; it is a single word.
The rest are merely sounds of calling. What is the use of calling out such sounds to me all day long? (From the *A-ju*).

"Lu-xie" (盧奢) means "to revile," while "Ku-lu-xie" (拘盧奢) means "a call. I should not now dwell upon that letter *A*. If there is the letter *A*, it is called reviling; if there is no letter *A*, it is simply a call.

Furthermore, what is considered vulgar speech in this region may be words of praise in another land. If I were to dwell upon such vulgar speech, there would be no place for me to find joy. There are many such examples:

for instance, while *śīla* and *kṣānti* are not regarded as elegant terms here, they are in fact two of the *pāramitās* in other lands. Moreover, even within this territory, there are different designations for the north and south, such as [the term for] "Zhejiang" (*zhe*).

What is called "praise" in Min may be called "censure" elsewhere; such instances are too numerous to list. Furthermore, observe that if these words of censure were reversed, they would immediately become praise.

For example, when seeing a guest depart, if one says, "You left too early," it is intended as a request for them to stay; yet if one says, "Go early," it is intended as a dismissal. Dismissal is censure, while staying is praise.

Again, when eating a meal and a guest arrives, if one says, "You came too early," it is censure; if one says, "Come early," it is praise. Worldly people cling to what they perceive, arbitrarily establishing priority and sequence to create praise and censure. These are merely accumulations of deluded sentiments; the nature of speech and sound is empty. Furthermore—
Abusive speech is but a small portion of one element (dhātu), a small portion of one base (āyatana), and a small portion of one aggregate (skandha).

Abusive speech is little, while non-abusive speech is much. (Among the eighteen elements, it is a small portion of the sound-element; among the twelve bases, it is a small portion of the sound-base; among the five aggregates, it is a small portion of the form-aggregate. Even though this small portion constitutes abusive speech, the remainder is not.
Furthermore, who is it that accomplishes abusive speech? Abusive speech is accomplished by me. What does it do to me? (The other person merely grasps the sound themselves...)

To claim that a collection of names constitutes an insult is like saying that because ugliness resides on someone's face, it must interfere with the mirror. Furthermore, an insult is not formed by a single syllable; rather, two syllables together form an insult.
Yet, there is no moment when these two syllables are uttered simultaneously. When the second syllable is uttered, the first has already ceased.
Moreover, both the insulter and the insulted cease at the same moment in a single kṣaṇa; what effect could this have upon me?
These [practitioners] take the emptiness resulting from analytical investigation as their armor. Furthermore, both the one who reviles and the one who is reviled are alike illusory persons;
the words of revilement and the sounds of reviling are alike echoes from a valley. If one observes closely, a real self and real dharmas are utterly unfindable.

How could one not endure this? This very emptiness is the armor. Moreover, ordinary beings, failing to understand that revilement is empty, give rise to various sorrows and afflictions, thereby increasing [their suffering].

Because the three poisons are long-standing, there is the dharma-realm of the three miserable realms (*durgati*); because one forcibly practices patience, there is the dharma-realm of humans and devas;
because the noble ones realize that abuse is empty and sever their own fetters and afflictions (*kleśa*), there is the dharma-realm of the two vehicles (*yāna*).

Furthermore, one gives rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) toward the abuser, thinking to extract them from their suffering, just as a mother would toward a son who, being mad and deluded, reviles her.
Because he constantly feels compassion for you and hopes for your recovery from illness, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-realm observe this sequence in such a manner;
the arising of the ten realms within the midst of abuse, with their various differences in function, is provisionally designated as "armor.
Since this sutra clarifies the instruction of mindfulness of the Buddha, one should endure these matters. "Buddha" refers to the Jewel of the Buddha, and "instruction" refers to the command.
The Dharma Jewel and the Buddha Jewel are non-dual; they are one with the Sangha Jewel. These Three Jewels are equal across both ordinary beings and sages.
While the Buddhas have already awakened, sentient beings remain deluded. For the sake of these sentient beings, I turn back from delusion to awakening and uphold and expound this sutra.
I clearly know that my own mind is equal to the Buddhas above and to sentient beings below. The awakening of the Buddhas is precisely the awakening of my own mind.
The delusion of sentient beings is precisely my own delusion; such armor is the chamber of compassion and the seat of the emptiness of dharmas.
This single armor is all armors; it is the armor of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). The first section, clarifying the donning of the robe to propagate the sutra, is concluded.
△ Second, clarifying the entering of the chamber to propagate the sutra.
In all villages and cities, wherever there are those who seek the Dharma, I shall go to each of their places and preach the teachings entrusted by the Buddha.
Third, [this is] the exposition of the sūtra while seated:
"I am the messenger of the World-Honored One; dwelling among the assembly, I have no fear. I shall skillfully preach the Dharma; may the Buddha dwell in peace."
△ Fourth, the conclusion and request for understanding:
Before the World-Honored One and all the Buddhas who have come from the ten directions, I have made this vow; the Buddhas themselves know my heart.
The "Chapter on Upholding" is finished.
