Composed by the later student Ouyi Zhixu of Ancient Wu.
Chapter Fourteen: On Peaceful Conduct. This is explained in three parts:
first, an explanation based on the facts; second, an explanation following the text; and third, an explanation of the dharma-gate. Each has both concise and detailed versions.
To briefly clarify the explanation based on the facts: because the body is free from danger, it is peaceful; because the mind is free from sorrow and affliction, it is blissful.
Because the body is at ease and the mind is joyful, one is able to advance in the practice of the oral karma of propagating the sūtra. To briefly clarify the commentary attached to the text:
first, regarding the text of the "Chapter on Attaching [to the Three Jewels]," wearing the Tathāgata’s robe brings peace to the *dharmakāya*;

entering the Tathāgata’s chamber brings joy to the mind through liberation; and sitting upon the Tathāgata’s seat brings progress in conduct guided by *prajñā*. Furthermore, this is also attached to the present chapter.

Because he dwells in the stage of patience (*kṣānti-bhūmi*), his body is at ease and not impetuous; because his mind joyfully contemplates the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, he practices progress (*vīrya*).
To briefly explain this dharma-gate: "peace" (*an-*) means immovability; "joy" (*rāma*) means non-reception; "practice" (*caryā*) means non-action.
Immovable means that which cannot be moved by the cycle of birth and death in the six realms or by the nirvana of the two vehicles.
Since one does not take either of the two extremes as an object, the Dharma-body is without movement;
it abides immovably like Mount Sumeru, and is thus called the "Dharma-gate of Constant Abiding and Immovability. As stated in the preceding text:
"The body, along with the hands and feet, is tranquil and unmoving; the mind is always serene and never distracted"—this is precisely that meaning. There is no experiencer.
One does not accept the five types of reception of ordinary beings, nor even the five types of reception of views arising within the Perfect Teaching—all of these are not accepted.

(First, regarding the four propositions of the outsiders and the ineffable, these are termed the five receptions; next, regarding each of the four gates of the Tripitaka, Shared, and Distinct Teachings, as well as their respective ineffables, there are likewise five receptions;

finally, regarding the four gates of the Perfect Teaching and its ineffable, if one has not yet realized the truth and gives rise to attached views, these are also called the five receptions. When the essence and teaching enter into principle, and there is no longer anything to be received within that principle, only then is it called "non-acceptance. Where there is acceptance, there is [bondage].)
If there is no sensation of suffering, then there is no suffering; where there is neither suffering nor pleasure, this is called "Great Bliss.

For one who practices, if there is that which is received, then there is that which is practiced; if there is no receiving, then there is nothing to practice. One does not practice the conduct of ordinary beings, nor does one practice the conduct of noble sages;
therefore, it is said that by practicing non-practice, one practices the Middle Way. For this reason, it is called "practice. Next, [the text] will further elaborate.
Explanation of the Matter: "Peace and Bliss" refers to Great Nirvāṇa, a name established from the perspective of the fruit.

"The Practitioner" refers to the path to Nirvāṇa, a name derived from the perspective of the cause. If those with the view of permanence among non-Buddhists practice asceticism, then both cause and fruit are suffering.
If those with the view of annihilation among non-Buddhists indulge their desires to seek pleasure, then the cause is pleasure while the fruit is suffering. If one analyzes phenomena...
The Two Vehicles attain nirvana through impermanence, clumsy means, and the arrival of suffering after great effort; thus, their cause is suffering while their fruit is bliss.
Now, because this [Mahāyāna] is the skillful means of reality, both cause and fruit are blissful. As the Great Sūtra says: "Those who practice fixed suffering are the ordinary worldlings;
those who practice fixed suffering-and-bliss are the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; those who practice fixed bliss are the bodhisattvas."
Now, among the bodhisattvas, one should further distinguish three types: the bodhisattvas of the Tripitaka, for whom there are teachings but no realization;

the bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching, whose causes and fruits pertain to all three vehicles and are both partial; and the bodhisattvas of the Distinct Teaching, whose causes are partial but whose fruits are perfect.

The bodhisattvas of the Perfect Teaching possess both perfect causes and perfect fruits. It is precisely because of these wondrous causes and wondrous fruits—both perfect and complete—that they are called the "Peaceful and Blissful Practices."

Furthermore, I shall now provide a more extensive textual explanation of the "Peaceful Practices" (*sukhavihāra*), which constitute the path to *nirvāṇa*. There are three meanings of *nirvāṇa*, namely, the secret treasury of the three virtues (*triguṇa-guhya-kośa*).
There are three meanings of the practices: the practice of tranquility (*śamatha*), the practice of insight (*vipaśyanā*), and the practice of compassion (*karuṇā*).

Regarding the practice of tranquility, it means being gentle at all three times, remaining serene whether encountering opposition or compliance; this is precisely the practice of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), as referred to in the aforementioned text.
The robe of the Tathāgata is the light of non-discrimination arising from the practitioner’s wisdom of the single true reality;

this is the essence of the practice of *prajñā*, which corresponds to what was previously called the "Tathāgata’s seat. The practice of compassion consists of the four great vows to universally deliver all beings;
this is the essence of the practice of *vimukti*, which corresponds to what was previously called the "Tathāgata’s chamber. Taken together, these...
The three types of conduct constitute the path to nirvāṇa; collectively, the three virtues serve as the objects of these practices.

These objects are termed "peaceful bliss" (*sukha*), and the path is termed "conduct" (*caryā*). As the *Mahāśāstra* states: "From the first generation of the bodhicitta, the Bodhisattva constantly contemplates the path to nirvāṇa.
During the causal stage, he employs these three dharmas to guide his three karmas as his practice. Because the three karmas are purified, this is precisely the purification of the six [sense bases]."
When the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*) are purified and one awakens to a corresponding understanding, thereby attaining entry into the true fruit, this is called the Buddha-eye, -ear, and so forth.

The causes are termed the practice of tranquility (*śamatha*), and the fruits are termed the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇaguṇa*). The causes are termed the practice of insight (*vipaśyanā*), and the fruits are termed the virtue of wisdom (*jñānaguṇa*).

Furthermore, the causes are termed the practice of compassion (*maitrīkaruṇā*), and the fruits are termed the virtue of grace (*anugrahaguṇa*). Moreover, the causes are termed the three karmas (*trikarma*), and the fruits are termed the three secrets (*triguhyaka*). At that time—
When compassion guides the three karmas toward the fruit of benefiting others, it is called the inconceivable transformation of the three wheels (*trimaṇḍala-acintya-vikurvaṇa*).
When one contemplates in this way, there is no further discrimination; within all phenomena (*dharmas*), there is entirely the nature of peace and bliss.
All sentient beings are themselves Great Nirvāṇa and cannot be extinguished again. Because one practices on what are not paths and thereby penetrates the Buddha-way, it is so named.

This is the practice of peaceful dwelling (*sukha-vihāra*). This practice accords with the meaning of *nirvāṇa*. That sutra states: "Furthermore, there is one practice which is the practice of the Tathāgata.
Here, "Tathāgata" refers to the person, and "peaceful dwelling" refers to the Dharma. The Tathāgata is the person of peaceful dwelling, and peaceful dwelling is the Dharma of the Tathāgata.
In summary, their meanings are not different; they are distinct yet not different. That sutra clarifies this.

The precious trees of gold and silver are analogous to the grove of stainless jewels (*anāsrava-ratna-vana*), which corresponds to the robe of the patience of cessation (*śānti-akṣānti*) in this sutra.

That sutra clarifies the great river of golden sand flowing directly into the Western Sea, which corresponds to the single true wisdom (*eka-tattva-prajñā*) in this sutra; it corresponds to the seat of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā-āsana*).
That sutra clarifies the woman who has attained the Way as being free from flattery and crookedness, which corresponds to the unconditional great compassion (*nirālamba-mahāmaitrī*) in this [sutra].
The *Compassionate Chamber Sūtra* merges with that [other] sūtra; therein it is called the "Meaning Without Remainder," while in this sūtra it is called the "Unsurpassed Path.

Furthermore, the noble conduct (*ārya-caryā*) elucidated in that sūtra is the Tathāgata’s seat, the celestial conduct (*deva-caryā*) is the Tathāgata’s robe, and the Brahma-conduct, infantile conduct, and sickly conduct are the Tathāgata’s chamber.
Question: The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* clarifies the practice of associating with kings and maintaining...
A bow with arrows subdues the wicked; this sutra distances itself from power and influence, being humble, compassionate, and kind.

Since its firmness and flexibility differ so greatly, how can it not be distinct [from other teachings]? Answer: The Great Sutra (the Lotus Sutra) focuses specifically on subjugation while abiding in the stage of regarding all beings as one's only child;
has it ever lacked inclusion? This sutra (the Vajracchedikā) focuses specifically on inclusion, yet what has it ever lacked subjugation—such that one’s head would be split into seven pieces?
I humbly submit that each of these points necessarily encompasses four aspects: "being appropriate to the occasion" corresponds to the world-intent (*loka-artha*);

"acceptance" corresponds to the person-intent (*pudgala-artha*); "subduing" corresponds to the remedial intent (*pratipakṣa-artha*); and "realizing the Way" corresponds to the ultimate intent (*paramārtha-artha*).

Furthermore, I shall explain this more extensively through the gateways of the Dharma, namely: the gateway of immovability, the gateway of non-acceptance, and the gateway of non-practice, as fully detailed in the *Xuan*.
The ten kinds of threefold dharmas can be understood by analogy with this pattern. If these meanings are categorized according to the four *siddhāntas*:
the differentiation of the three dharmas corresponds to the *loka-siddhānta*; liberation corresponds to the *puruṣa-siddhānta*; Prajñā corresponds to the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta*;

and the Dharma-body is the *paramārtha-siddhānta*. Question: What is the sequence of these "Peaceful Practices"? Answer: The perfect practice of the *Lotus Sūtra* is such that a single practice encompasses the infinite.
Regarding the inconceivable practice of which meditative concentration is prior and which is subsequent, for the time being, following the text as it is explained:
in the "Chapter on the Dharma Master," the method of propagating the sutra is briefly shown, taking the benefit of others as the primary principle; therefore, entering the room is clarified first.

In this chapter, the propagation of the sutra in the evil age and the pacification of all afflictions are distinguished; therefore, putting on the robes is clarified first. Thus, the sequence of before and after is merely presented reciprocally. If one were to rely upon...
Regarding the practitioner who explains: all dharmas have from the very beginning been characterized by constant quiescence;

yet, when they arise in opposition to that quiescence, one must first use *prajñā* to dispel these burdens. This is sitting upon the Tathāgata’s seat. Although all dharmas are non-arising, *prajñā* arises;

through its essence of compassion, it takes pity on sentient beings and thus practices the Path. Next, one enters the Tathāgata’s chamber; having already transformed others through compassion, [one now abides therein].

The world inevitably involves opposition; one must certainly practice patience toward it. Next, one dons the robe of the Tathāgata. Although the teaching follows a sequential order, in actual practice it is not sequential.
When entering emptiness, one simultaneously possesses all dharmas; how much more so for loving-kindness and patience? Regarding the four modes of peaceful conduct (*sukha-caryā*):
first, physical action is guided by śamatha, vipaśyanā, loving-kindness, and compassion; second, [verbal and mental actions] are guided by śamatha, vipaśyanā, loving-kindness, and compassion.

The three aspects of verbal karma are guided by *śamatha*, *vipaśyanā*, compassion, and loving-kindness; the four aspects of mental karma are guided by *śamatha*, *vipaśyanā*, compassion, and loving-kindness, as well as by vows.
Because there is *śamatha* in bodily karma, one leaves behind coarse physical actions; because there is *vipaśyanā*, one does not apprehend the body nor bodily karma.
Because there is nothing to be apprehended, one does not fall into the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), for there is compassion and loving-kindness.

Diligently cultivating physical and mental karma for the broad benefit of all, one does not fall into the stages of the two vehicles. Because of the practice of *śamatha*, one wears the robe of the Tathāgata;
because of the practice of *vipaśyanā*, one sits upon the seat of the Tathāgata; and because of great compassion, one enters the chamber of the Tathāgata.

Through the practice of *śamatha* that is free from faults, the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*) is perfected; through the practice of *vipaśyanā* that is free from attachment, the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*) is perfected; and through great compassion, there is the benefiting of others.

Thus, one accomplishes the quality of grace (*anugraha*); this grace serves to perfect the quality of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*), and through the quality of wisdom, one is able to penetrate the quality of cessation (*prahāṇa-guṇa*).
This is called the "peaceful practice of bodily action" (*kāya-karma-śānta-caryā*). The same applies to the vows of speech and mind. Regarding the intent of this chapter:

it concerns those great Bodhisattvas who have received the mandate to propagate this sutra, who deeply understand the provisional and the real, who extensively know the gradual and the sudden, and who furthermore master the capacities of sentient beings.

By virtue of the sovereign power of spiritual transformation (*ṛddhi*), one is no longer subject to obstruction or hindrance by the afflictions of this defiled age; thus, there is no need to further demonstrate specific methods.

However, for those who initially rely on their original resolve to cultivate perfect practice and enter this defiled world to propagate the sutra, yet find themselves afflicted by the turbidity of the age such that their own practice fails to establish itself and they lack the capacity for transformative work—on account of such persons, it is necessary to demonstrate the "Practice of Peaceful Bliss" (*anuvartana-pratipatti*).
This is the fifth chapter on the circulation of the *迹门* (Ji-men). The text is divided into two parts: first, the question; second, the answer.
Within the first part, there are two sections: first, praising the profound practice of the bodhisattvas of the preceding chapter who are able to propagate the sutra according to the Dharma;
second, asking how a beginner bodhisattva should propagate the sutra in an evil age. This is the first [section].
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, these bodhisattvas are truly rare;
out of reverence and obedience toward the Buddha, they have made a great vow to protect, uphold, read, and recite this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* in the future evil age.”
△ Second, the question regarding how a beginner bodhisattva propagates the sutra in an evil age:
"World-Honored One, how can a bodhisattva mahāsattva preach this sutra in the evil age hereafter?"

△ Second, the response is divided into three parts: first, a general presentation of the chapter; second, an explanation of the methods of practice; and third, a general clarification of the characteristics of the perfection of practice.
Now, for the first part: The Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī: "If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, in the future evil age, wishes to expound this sutra..."
One should dwell securely in four dharmas.
△ Second, the explanation of the method of practice, which has four parts: first, the peaceful practice of body; second, the peaceful practice of speech;
third, the peaceful practice of mind; fourth, the peaceful practice of vow. Within the first [the peaceful practice of body], there are two parts: first, the long prose section; second, the verses.
In the long prose commentary on the verse, there are two parts: first, the heading, and second, the explanation. This is the first part.
First, one who abides in the bodhisattva’s sphere of conduct (*caryā-vihāra*) and sphere of association (*sevā-vihāra*) is able to expound this sutra for the sake of sentient beings.
To approach the principle and explain it briefly is called the "place of practice" (*caryā-sthāna*), which refers to the primary practice (*samyak-caryā*) in relation to its essential matters.

To explain it extensively by attaching to specific phenomena is called the "place of intimacy" (*upaniṣad-sthāna*), which refers to the auxiliary practices (*anukūla-caryā*). However, while the explanations may be extensive or brief, there is no difference in depth between their principles, as will be explained in detail below.
Part Two: Explanation of the Two [Places]. First, the explanation of the place of practice; second, the explanation of the place of intimacy. Now, the first.
Mañjuśrī, what is called the sphere of practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the stage of patience, being gentle, compliant, and harmonious, neither impetuous nor startled in mind;

furthermore, if they do not engage in any activity regarding phenomena, yet contemplate all phenomena according to their true nature, and neither engage in practice nor make distinctions—this is called a bodhisattva.
The sphere of activity of the Mahāsattva.

This is explained as threefold: first, with reference to a single dharma, namely the one true reality (*ekābhisaṃbodhi-satya*); second, with reference to two dharmas, namely the two patiences regarding arising and dharmas;
and third, with reference to three dharmas, namely the three inconceivable truths. Regarding the first, the one true reality: it is for...

That which is the refuge of all and the foundation for all, yet is universally non-discriminative, is called the "ground of dwelling in patience" (kṣānti-bhūmi) because all dharmas take refuge therein. Because all manifold practices come to rest, it is named "patience.
This is precisely the practice of non-practice, the robe of the Tathāgata. (Although in principle there is no practice, one acts in reliance upon that principle; thus practice is attained.)

Because the cessation of principle is called non-practice, and practice is itself non-practice, it is said: "to practice the practice of non-practice. Because it serves as the foundation for all things, it is said to be gentle, harmonious, compliant, and so forth;
thus all practices attain their principle and achieve fulfillment. It is like the myriad things that grow by obtaining the earth.
If one attains this fundamental principle, then in hardness one can be soft, in opposition one can be compliant, in violence one can govern, and in agitation one can bring peace—limitlessly so.
Merit arises from the ground of the single reality of the Middle Way; it arises from that which is non-arising, yet it gives rise to merit.

This is the practice of non-practice within practice, the "Tathāgata’s Chamber. Because one does not act [in accordance with] principle, yet acts within practice, and because it is universally free from discrimination, it is said:
"Furthermore, regarding all phenomena, one realizes that the nature and characteristics of practice and non-practice are non-dual, and thus perceives all dharmas."
True names are neither conceptualized nor characterized by non-conceptualization; they can be called "neither practicing nor non-practicing non-conceptualization.

This is the seat of the Tathāgata—the practice that is neither practice nor non-practice (it is called "non-practice" because there is no practice regarding phenomena, and it is called "not non-practice" because there is no non-conceptualization).
Because there are no three practices yet there are three practices, it is called "practice"; it is identical to the single reality.
Because it is based on the truths, it is called the "abode. First, the explanation of the practice-abode (*caryā-vihāra*) by means of a single dharma is complete.

Next, the two types of patience regarding arising and dharmas (*utpatti-dharma-kṣānti*) refer precisely to the two emptinesses of arising and dharmas (*utpatti-śūnyatā* and *dharma-śūnyatā*). This differs from that of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*):

the emptiness of arising in the Two Vehicles merely destroys the attachment to a self within the realm of desire; the emptiness of dharmas in the Two Vehicles merely destroys the attachment to false causes and conditions and to the absence of causes and conditions within the realm of desire.
Now, it is explained that in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), the two kinds of emptiness—concerning the provisional names of the ten realms—are identical to the Middle Way;

therefore, no further provisional names of the ten realms can be obtained, which is why it is called "emptiness of persons" (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). Concerning the real dharmas of the ten realms, they are identical to the Middle Way;

therefore, no further real dharmas of the ten realms can be obtained, which is why it is called "emptiness of phenomena" (*dharma-śūnyatā*). If these are further expanded, they constitute the four types of patience (*kṣānti*), namely:

There are the Patience of Prostration (*adhimukti-kṣānti*), the Patience of Accordance (*anuloma-kṣānti*), the Patience of Non-arising (*anutpāda-kṣānti*), and the Patience of Quiescence (*nirvāṇa-kṣānti*).

Alternatively, they may be categorized as five patiences by adding the Patience of Faith (*śraddhā-kṣānti*); or as six patiences by further adding the Patience of Harmonious Compliance (*anuvartana-kṣānti*).

When correlated with the forty-two stages (*bhūmi*), they constitute forty-two patiences; since a single stage possesses the merits of all forty-two stages, how could a single patience not possess these four?

Regarding the twelve dharmas of patience (*kṣānti*), let us for now interpret the text according to the four patiences, which differ fundamentally from those of the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*).

In the Separate Teaching, the two patiences of "subduing" and "compliance" constitute the stage of patience toward beings (*sattva-kṣānti*); thus they are shallow. The two patiences of "non-arising" and "quiescence" constitute the stage of patience toward phenomena (*dharma-kṣānti*);
thus they are deep. It is not so in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*): these two and four patiences all pervade both the beginning and the end. Why is this? What are they?
The principle of emptiness is itself the Middle Way. Initially, one cultivates the four patiences (*kṣānti*) to enter the Middle Way and perceive the principle of the two kinds of emptiness;

even at the final stage of mind, one merely exhaustively investigates this principle of the two kinds of emptiness. Thus, the Great Sūtra says: "The initial aspiration and the ultimate goal are not two.

If one were to categorize the four patiences based on a lack of distinction between shallow and deep, then from the very first aspiration, one would perfectly subdue the five abodes of delusion (*pañca-vāsa*).
Up to the Vajraśekhara stage, all are called the Patience of Subjugation (*vinaya-kṣānti*), because from beginning to end they do not contradict the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*).

All are called the Patience of Accordance (*anuloma-kṣānti*), because from beginning to end they do not give rise to the mind of the two extremes. All are called the Patience of Non-arising (*anutpāda-kṣānti*), because from beginning to end they bring all conditioned activities to rest.

All are called the Patience of Quiescence (*nirvāṇa-kṣānti*), because from beginning to end they cause all practices to cease. (Ordinary beings, while lost in delusion, [possess] the principle of the two kinds of emptiness; these four patiences are the "patience of names" (*nāma-kṣānti*) produced through understanding upon hearing the sutras.)

The two kinds of emptiness and four kinds of patience (nirvedha-bhāgīya) constitute the perfect subduing of the five abodes (*pañca-vihāra*) during the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*). The two kinds of emptiness and four kinds of patience of the "patience" stage (*kṣānti*) correspond to the purity of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya-pariśuddhi*) during the stage of semblance (*pratirūpaka*). The two kinds of emptiness and four kinds of patience of the forty-one stages constitute the partial realization (*pradeśa-prativedha*). The two kinds of emptiness and four kinds of patience of the sublime enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), the ultimate fruit, constitute the final perfection (*niṣṭhā-gata*) of the two kinds of emptiness and four kinds of patience.

As the Sūtra says: "To abide in the ground of patience is to abide in the ground of the two kinds of emptiness and four kinds of patience. "Gentleness and flexibility" refers to the patience of subduing (*vinaya-kṣānti*); "excellent compliance" and so forth refer to the patience of compliance (*anuloma-kṣānti*);
and "hearing of the suffering of birth and death without being suddenly terrified" refers to the patience of non-retrogression (*avinivartana-kṣānti*).
Because one does not experience alarm or fear regarding the bliss of *nirvāṇa*, nor the sudden seeking of its realization;

nor regarding the Buddha’s permanence versus impermanence, whether the two vehicles will become Buddhas or not, the difference or non-difference between *saṃsāra* and *nirvāṇa*, or the length, brevity, difficulty, or ease of the Buddha-way—neither long nor short, neither difficult nor easy—and so forth, it is called "Accordant Patience" (*anulomikī-kṣānti*). Furthermore, regarding the Dharma...

To observe all phenomena as they truly are without any mental activity is the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); likewise, neither acting nor discriminating is the patience of cessation (*nirodha-kṣānti*).
The former two are called the patience toward beings (*sattva-kṣānti*), and the latter two are called the patience toward phenomena (*dharma-kṣānti*).

From beginning to end, to endure all phenomena through the principle of the two emptinesses (*dvividha-śūnyatā*) is to don the robe of the Tathāgata; to abide securely within the principle of the two emptinesses is to sit.
The Tathāgata’s seat consists in having compassion for all sentient beings; this is entering the Tathāgata’s chamber.

The two emptinesses and the four patiences are called the principle of practice, which is precisely the locus; therefore, it is said that this is the bodhisattva’s sphere of activity (*caryā-viṣaya*).

Having concluded the explanation of the sphere of activity by means of these two dharmas, thirdly, regarding the inconceivable three truths: abiding on the ground of patience provides a general discussion of the three truths as follows.

Only when one has a firm ground to rely upon can one practice patience. One who is gentle, harmonious, and compliant is well-aligned with the True Truth (*paramārtha-satya*), capable of enduring the false views and cravings—both internal and external—as well as cold, heat, and other such conditions. Yet, they are neither impetuous nor startled;

being at ease within the Conventional Truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), they endure the various sensory conditions and respond appropriately to the capacities of others, and thus their physical presence is not impetuous.

"Enduring opposition and following compliance so that the mind is not startled," and "having no practice regarding phenomena," mean that one is able to endure the two extremes within the Middle Truth;
thus it is said there is "no practice. Because one correctly abides in the Middle Way, it is said one "contemplates the true aspect.
Furthermore, because even the Middle reality cannot be attained, it is said one "also does not practice" and "does not differentiate. This is based on the three truths.
The place-name is termed "patience" (*kṣānti*); the five stages of dwelling are termed "conduct" (*caryā*). This conduct is also threefold, namely:

the practice of cessation (*śamatha-caryā*), which is to act while not acting and to be attached to the Tathāgata’s robe; the practice of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-caryā*), which is neither acting nor non-acting and to sit upon the Tathāgata’s seat;
and the practice of compassion (*karuṇā-caryā*), which is to act while not acting and to enter the Tathāgata’s chamber. These are what are called the three dharmas.
The explanation of the Bodhisattva’s sphere of practice clarifies the method for propagating the sutra. △ Second, the explanation of the sphere of intimacy has three parts:

first, discussing intimacy by way of remoteness; second, discussing intimacy by way of proximity; third, discussing intimacy by way of that which is neither remote nor proximate (the characters "remote" and "proximate" are both read with the departing tone, functioning as flexible, provisional terms).
First, discussing intimacy by way of remoteness: this is to rely upon the gateway of precepts to assist in the accomplishment of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
Compassion is also extensively explained as dwelling in the stage of patience (*kṣānti-bhūmi*), whether practicing or not practicing. The text consists of ten points:

first, distancing oneself from powerful influence, up to tenth, distancing oneself from domestic animals and dependents. Among these, nine pertain to *saṃsāra*, while the fifth—referring to the two vehicles (*dviyāna*)—pertains to *nirvāṇa*.
To distance oneself from both is called "approaching the Middle Way. First is distancing oneself from powerful influence.
What is meant by the places a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should frequent and those he should not?

A bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not frequent kings, princes, ministers, or high officials, for fear that beginners might rely upon their power and influence and thereby lose the right path; though such association may seem to offer slight benefit at first, it will ultimately lead to great harm.
Loss. △ Second, distancing oneself from heterodox persons and heterodox teachings:

one does not associate with various non-Buddhist practitioners such as brahmins or Nirgranthas, nor with those who compose secular writings, praise foreign scriptures, or follow the Lokāyatas and Prati-Lokāyatas.
"Brahmin" (*brāhmaṇa*) refers to one of pure lineage who remains at home and serves Brahmā. "Nirgrantha" (translated here as "Freed from Bonds") is the general name for non-Buddhist renunciants.
"Lokāyata" (also called *Veda*) refers to the scriptures of the non-Buddhists of the Western Regions;
it is that which provides explanations based on attachment and false views. "To oppose" (*niḥsaraṇa*) means to pose a challenging question. That is to say:

These are those who raise challenges based on craving and false views; since their correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*) is not yet established, they must be strictly guarded against and severed, for fear that through such habitual attachment they will become deluded regarding the true principle. △ Third, staying far away from violent and dangerous games.
Furthermore, one should not associate with those who engage in violent games such as boxing, wrestling, or various performances by *naṭas* (actors).
*Naṭa* here refers to "strength," meaning games of physical prowess. One does not associate with them for fear of becoming distracted and dissolute. △
Fourth, regarding those from afar who are outcasts (*caṇḍāla*):
furthermore, even if such persons as outcasts, or those who follow the evil disciplines of raising pigs, sheep, chickens, or dogs, or hunting,
fishing, and trapping, should occasionally come to him, he shall preach the Dharma for them without harboring any expectations.
One should not associate with those who resemble *caṇḍālas*, for they cause people to lose their compassion. △ Fifth, one should distance oneself from the assembly of the Two Vehicles.
Furthermore, one should not associate with or even inquire after śrāvaka bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who seek [only] the path of voice-hearers;
nor should one dwell or reside together with them, whether in a private room, on a walking path (*caṅkrama*), or within a lecture hall.
When those who come arrive, he preaches the Dharma according to their needs without seeking anything for himself.

Because he keeps those inclined toward the Two Vehicles at a distance from Bodhi—since in the Western lands the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna each abide separately without intermingling—it is said that "if they have not yet received the Great [Vehicle], do not obstruct their aspiration for the Small. Thus, it is said that he "preaches the Dharma according to what is appropriate."
△ Sixth, the perception of distant desire.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should not take up the signs that give rise to perceptions of desire regarding the bodies of women when preaching the Dharma;
nor should he delight in seeing them. If he enters the homes of others, he should not stay with young girls or virgins.
One should not converse with widows, for the desire they conceive can most effectively destroy the bodhicitta. △ Seventh, regarding eunuchs:
one should likewise not draw near to the five types of eunuchs to form close or intimate bonds.
Those who are not male (*pandaka*) are most capable of corrupting and disturbing the resolve for enlightenment; thus there are five types of those who are not male:

first, the *jāti-pandaka*, meaning one who is deficient in male organs either in the womb or at the time of birth; second, the *cheda-pandaka*, meaning one whose organs have been severed or have rotted away;
third, the *īrṣyā-pandaka*, meaning one in whom the organs temporarily arise due to another's sexual desire, yet lack functional capacity.
The four types of *pandaka* (eunuchs/impotent) who change gender are those who see a man and turn into a woman, or see a woman and turn into a man.

The five types of *ardha-pandaka* (half-eunuchs) are those who possess sexual function for half the month and lack it for the other half. All of these have experienced the retribution of evil karma created in past lives; they are currently undergoing such adverse results that they are incapable of bearing the Path.

Because they are not vessels for the Buddha-Dharma, they are called those with "heavy obstacles" (*guru-antarāya*) and may not leave the household life. Furthermore, one should not grant them the precepts.
Thick. △ Eighth, avoiding harm and danger:
Not only when entering another's home, but even when there is a necessary reason to enter alone, one should simply recite the Buddha’s name with single-minded devotion.
Fearing that entering another's home alone might invite harm, by reciting the Buddha’s name with single-minded devotion, all obstacles and difficulties will be entirely removed. △ Ninth, avoiding...
To avoid being subject to reproach:

when preaching the Dharma to women, one should not show one's teeth while smiling nor expose one's chest; even for the sake of the Dharma, one should not become overly intimate, let alone for other matters.
In the Vinaya, if one preaches the Dharma to a woman, there must be a man present who understands what is wholesome and unwholesome;

if no such man is present, one must not exceed five or six sentences. This is all for the purpose of distancing oneself from suspicion and avoiding doubt, so as not to increase the unwholesome thoughts of others. △ Ten: Distancing Oneself from Keeping Livestock.
One should not take pleasure in keeping young disciples, śrāmaṇeras, or children, nor should one take pleasure in having them as fellow students.

This is because the dispositions of youths have not yet been settled; if one keeps them oneself, it will hinder the cultivation of the primary practice, and if they are fellow students, they will disturb one’s requests for instruction.
The preceding text spoke only of "dwelling on the ground of patience," which directly takes principle as its object; now, regarding the precepts—
The gates are wide open for the conditions that lead to public humiliation; one should practice seclusion.

This is not done by wielding weapons or staffs, nor by abandoning them entirely, but rather by distancing oneself through right wisdom. These ten dharmas are consistent across all teachings; however, there are slight differences in how they exclude the Two Vehicles in various doctrines.
Now, in propagating this sublime scripture, it must belong to those of the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*). Those who provide commentaries based on the contemplation of the mind should proceed as follows:

There are two types: the general and the specific. Regarding the general: there is nothing that is not the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). What is there to be abandoned? What is there not to be abandoned?
It is neither abandoned nor not abandoned, yet one speaks of abandonment. This is just as when one speaks of "nearness" despite being neither far nor near.

Although the beginner realizes from the outset that all things are fundamentally non-existent, they must repeatedly draw near to this state of detachment. Regarding the specific: it refers to detachment from the three [poisons].
The teachings of the Teacher and the two extremes of worldly power are both deviant dharmas; those who adhere to these two extremes are called deviant people.
The two types of supernatural powers are called violent games; the three delusions are the Caṇḍālas who kill the life of the three wisdoms.

Being biased toward emptiness and extinguishing thought is the assembly of the Two Vehicles; being biased in observing the True, the Conventional, or even the Middle Way, and harboring attachment to the Dharma—all these are likewise [deviant].
The cessation of the perception of desire and abiding in emptiness through the form realm is called the "expedient observation of non-masculinity" (*apuṃstva-upāya*).
This wisdom harms and perfects all mundane objects, which are termed "contemptible. The roots of goodness of the three preceding teachings are termed "young children.
Each of these takes that which has been abandoned as its object; they are distant from the three delusions and close to the three contemplations. First, regarding...

The discussion on the distant and the near is concluded. △ Second, discussing the near by way of the near is the "Gate of Attachment to Concentration," which aids the accomplishment of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* and fosters compassion.
This also expands upon the aforementioned qualities of being gentle, harmonious, and compliant, rather than impetuous;

likewise, the mind is not startled, and one does not engage in [unwholesome] conduct. Above, it directly clarified being neither impetuous nor startled; now, it extensively sets forth the mind that cultivates concentration. Cultivation...
Regarding the gate of meditative cultivation in the state of concentration: by the power of concentration, one brings order to what is turbulent and peace to what is agitated.
Always delighting in seated meditation, one dwells in a secluded place to collect and restrain the mind. Mañjuśrī, this is called the first stage of close attendance.

Constantly delighting in sitting meditation is the mind that cultivates concentration (*samādhi*). Taking pleasure in the dhyāna-method of the Middle Way and True Reality (*bhūtatathatā*) corresponds to the desire (*chanda*) among the five factors, while simultaneously encompassing vigor (*vīrya*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), skillful wisdom (*prajñā*), and one-pointedness of mind (*ekāgratā*).

Dwelling in a secluded place is the location for cultivating concentration, corresponding to the "place" (*sthāna*) among the five conditions. Restraining and gathering the mind is the essential gateway for cultivating concentration.

This refers to rebuking the five desires, abandoning the five hindrances, and harmonizing the five matters. Among the twenty-five expedient means, the preceding text belongs to the section on the precepts (*śīla*), where one distances oneself from the ten disturbances;
this constitutes the first [expedient], the purity of ethical discipline (*śīla-viśuddhi*).

The present passage, which speaks of dwelling in a secluded place, corresponds to the third [expedient], the quietude of a solitary abode (*prānta-śayanāsana*). Since one is already in a secluded place, it necessarily encompasses the fourth [expedient] as well.

Cessation of all worldly affairs is mentioned only briefly and not discussed further; second, the sufficiency of clothing and food; and fifth, the attainment of good spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).

If we clarify the sufficiency of these five conditions by means of contemplating the mind, then the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) serve as clothing, the joy of dhyāna and the joy of the Dharma serve as food, and all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) all serve as good spiritual friends.
Furthermore, regarding the five desires (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*): form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch are all thieves that plunder one's merit;
knowing their faults deeply, one must rest from greedy attachment. Regarding the abandonment of the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*):

namely, sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt—because these shroud and cover concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), they must be abandoned urgently, like cutting down a poisonous tree or apprehending a thief. Thus one should practice self-discipline.
The five matters refer to: regulating food so as to avoid both hunger and overeating; regulating sleep so as to avoid both lack of moderation and indulgence;
regulating the body so as to avoid both laxity and tension; regulating the breath so as to avoid both harshness and smoothness; and regulating the mind so as to avoid both sinking and floating.

Each of these twenty factors possesses its own phenomenal characteristics (*sākāra*) and contemplation of principle (*tattvārtha-vipaśyanā*), as fully detailed in the *Mahā-śamatha-vipaśyanā*; those who require them should seek them therein.
Regarding the five factors: to attain the first dhyāna one must likewise employ these five factors, and this remains true for all subsequent dhyānas.
Now, in terms of the perfect contemplation (*yuan guan*), this means that one desires to enter the Middle Way from the two extremes without being mixed with those extremes;

"purity" refers to flowing in spontaneously, "progress" refers to binding the conditions within the Dharma-realm, and "mindfulness" refers to contemplating the Dharma-realm in a single thought-moment. This is the cultivation of the Middle.

Contemplating skillful means is called "skillful wisdom" (*kauśalya-prajñā*); when the mind ceases its movement toward the two extremes, the water of the mind becomes clear and tranquil, enabling one to know the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of worldly phenomena—this is non-duality (*advaya*). When the mind is pure and constantly unified, one is able to perceive *prajñā*.

Taking these two gates of precept (*śīla*) and concentration (*samādhi*) as the preliminary skillful means (*pūrvaprayoga*), it is therefore concluded that this is the "first stage of close approach. △ Three.

Regarding the discussion that [the object] is neither distant nor near, "near" refers to the gateway of wisdom (*prajñā*) which assists in the accomplishment of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, thereby expanding upon the cultivation of compassion.
Furthermore, it means that while there is no practice regarding phenomena, one contemplates all phenomena according to their true nature (*yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa*);

this is neither practicing nor non-practicing, neither differentiating nor non-differentiating, and neither acting nor non-acting. The text is divided into three parts; first, a general presentation of the object and wisdom. Second... [text continues].
The detailed explanation of the three fetters is now commenced.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva contemplates that all phenomena (*dharma*) are empty.
"Contemplation" refers to the wisdom of the Middle Way; "all phenomena" refers to the objects of the ten dharma-realms; and "empty" means...
This refers to contemplating the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). If one were to discuss wisdom alone, there would be nothing for wisdom to observe;

therefore, by citing "all things," it is revealed that they are all empty. This emptiness is the true mark of all phenomena (*dharmāṇāṃ bhūtalakṣaṇam*), which only Buddhas and Buddhas can fully exhaustively realize.
Now, from the very first moment of the Bodhisattva’s resolve, one observes by means of the Middle Way of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. That is to say, from—
From the beginning to the end, all is practiced through the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
therefore, one is able to open, show, awaken, and enter [the truth], with no intermediate complications or devious aspects whatsoever. △ Second, the detailed explanation.
It is according to reality, non-perverted, immovable, non-retrogressive, and non-reversing; like space, it is of a nature of non-existence;
all paths of language are cut off; it is unarisen, unproduced, and unoriginated; nameless and signless, truly non-existent, immeasurable, boundless, unobstructed, and unimpeded.
The phrase "as-it-is reality" (*yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa*) specifically explains the ten dharma-realms that are the objects of contemplation without inversion;

the following section specifically explains the Middle Way wisdom that contemplates them. Because the two extremes and the three truths are neither one nor different, they are called "as-it-is" (*yathā*);

because they are not the seven stages of expedient means, they are called "real" (*bhūta*). Since its characteristic is the real, it is termed "as-it-is reality. (The two extremes are contrasted with the Middle.)

Within this, there must be the Three Truths; though three, they are not three, for their names are non-existent and they are neither one nor different. Because the Three Truths accord with reality (*yathābhūta*) when distinguished from the seven [categories], they are called "real" (*shi*). This reality is itself signless (*animitta*), yet it pervades all signs.

That which is non-perverted lacks the four inversions of ordinary beings—permanence, bliss, self, and purity—and likewise lacks the four inversions of the Two Vehicles—impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity.
It also lacks the four inversions of those who manifest expediently as permanent, blissful, self, and pure; that is precisely what is neither flourishing nor withered.
Illuminating both prosperity and decay simultaneously is the contemplation of the Middle Way. "Immovable" means not being moved by the two types of death.
"Non-retrogressive" means that with each thought-moment entering extinction, one naturally flows into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (omniscience).

"Non-revolving" means not revolving in the cycle of birth and death like ordinary beings, nor transforming from the state of an ordinary being to that of a sage like the followers of the Two Vehicles. It is like space.
"Emptiness" is merely a name, and within that which cannot be apprehended as a name, the wisdom of the Middle Way contemplation is also merely a name, unfindable upon seeking.
"The nature of non-existence" means there is no self-nature, no other-nature, no common nature, and no nature arising without cause.
"All paths of verbal expression are severed" because it is free from the four extremes and transcends the hundred negations; therefore, it is not [an object of conceptualization].
"Unthinkable and non-arising" means that both delusion and wisdom are fundamentally non-arising;
since the object to be negated and the negating subject accord with reality, both are non-arising, and thus the stages of practice, positions, causes, and effects are all non-arising.
"Non-emerging" means that the entirety of what the Tathāgata treats as afflictions is itself [the path], so there is nothing to emerge from; it never arises again. It does not originate.
Because it enters into the principle, all skillful means, principles, and teachings are quiescent.
That which is "nameless" cannot be expressed by any name; it is non-inverted, and even the term "non-arising" is insufficient to name it.
That which is "signless" cannot be characterized by any sign; it is non-inverted, and even [the term] "non-... [is insufficient].
Even "arising" is insufficient to describe it. "Nameless" means that its nature is empty; "signless" means that its characteristics are empty.
"Truly having nothing" is a profound exclamation praising that the essence of contemplation is not the existence of either of the two extremes.
"Immeasurable" means it is not a numerical dharma such as the aggregates, bases, or elements. "Boundless" means it is not the existence of biased or limited [vehicles] and so forth.
The "limiting dharma" (fenxian fa) refers to that which is unimpeded, meaning it universally enters into all dharmas;
"unobstructed" means there is not a single dharma capable of hindering or stopping it.
Although there are many phrases, they simply refer to the wisdom of the observer—which is signless and non-active—in its true correspondence with the observed object. △ Third, the conclusion.
However, because that which exists arises from causes and conditions and from inversion, one should always joyfully contemplate such characteristics of phenomena;
this is called the second station of intimacy for a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
That which exists merely through causes and conditions is bondage. Above, we directly clarified the wisdom of contemplation regarding the Middle Way;
now we clarify the simultaneous illumination of both extremes. The principle-nature is ultimately pure, as previously stated:

it is neither liberation nor delusion, yet from the causes and conditions of delusion arises birth-and-death, and from the causes and conditions of liberation arises nirvana. Birth-and-death and nirvana are like the six dragons.
Because dance arises from inversion, there is birth and death; because of birth and death, there is nirvana. Thus, all arise from inversion.
Because birth, death, and nirvana exist, there are the ten realms and all dharmas that can be spoken of;
yet these ten realms and all dharmas are ultimately empty and are identical to the true mark (*tathatā*). (The above directly clarifies the wisdom of contemplation of the Middle Way.)

This is largely because [the scriptures] mostly employ the "neither-nor" (ubhayānta-vinirmukta) formulation. However, how could there be a Middle Way that does not illuminate both extremes? Here, by re-clarifying the illumination of the two extremes, the various texts are brought together to manifest the inconceivable essence of the Middle Way (*madhyamaka*).
Furthermore, conditioned co-arising exists within *nirvāṇa*, and birth arises from inversion, leading to birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).
Because *nirvāṇa* and *saṃsāra* exist, there is that which can be spoken of; yet the essence of the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) of the Middle Way realizes *nirvāṇa* while being non-*nirvāṇa*.
Because it cannot be said that one is within birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and yet not subject to birth-and-death, the Bodhisattva always contemplates it with joy:

Nirvāṇa is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), while birth-and-death is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). The substance upon which both Nirvāṇa and birth-and-death depend is neither Nirvāṇa nor birth-and-death;

this is the middle truth (*madhyama-satya*). (In this section, by distinguishing between causes and conditions and inversions, the meaning of the two extremes becomes even more evident; birth-and-death properly belongs to the cause.)

The term "condition" (*pratītya*) is provisionally designated as "inversion" (*viparyāsa*) from the perspective of delusion; yet, when one penetrates these conditions, there is *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, the first phrase is determined to pertain to *nirvāṇa*. Furthermore, all three types of *nirvāṇa* involve the contemplation of conditions.
Since both types of birth-and-death arise from the inversions of the three delusions, there is verbal expression to point from delusion toward awakening.

Moreover, the fact that existence arises from inversion through conditions concludes the inconceivable realm of the Three Truths; thus, the teaching is called "inconceivable," characterized by permanence and bliss.

"Contemplation" refers to the three inconceivable contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*). (All phenomena arising from causes and conditions, which are inverted dharmas, are none other than wondrous objects; based on these inherently existing wondrous objects, the aforementioned wondrous Middle Way contemplation is taught;
by receiving this wondrous teaching, one should constantly delight in contemplating such wondrous objects. The above three sections, explaining by way of both object and wisdom, are now concluded.
Now, the text of all three sections shall be explained collectively by way of contemplation alone. The first states: "Contemplate all dharmas as empty according to reality."

"Characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to the essence of the contemplation. True reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is precisely that which is contemplated; it is only because the contemplating subject is manifested through the object of contemplation that it possesses an essence.
"Not inverted" means that all [aspects] below are explained as the characteristics of contemplation, for they are not moved by the two extremes or the eight inversions.
Thus it is said "not inverted. Because one is not moved, one does not fall into the two stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas or ordinary worldlings; thus it is said "not regressing."
Because it does not revolve in the future, it is not born; because it does not revolve in the past, it does not emerge; because it does not revolve in the present, it does not arise.
The *Vyākhyā* (Commentary) states: "Just as space has no entering, no emerging, and no abiding, so too is the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*:

there is no place for entry in the future (because it does not enter the future from the present, it is thus 'not born'), and no place for emergence in the past (because it does not emerge from the present into the past)."
There is no present abiding (non-abiding in the present is precisely non-arising). The rest may be understood as before. Furthermore, there are nineteen phrases in the sutra text:
the first phrase is the general statement, while the subsequent eighteen phrases correspond to the eighteen emptinesses (*aṣṭādaśa-śūnyatā*) of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.

As for the true mark (*yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa*), it is ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*); being non-perverted, it is internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*), wherein the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) and the self (*ātman*) do not exist within.
Because it is not grasped, it is non-erroneous and immovable; that is, external emptiness (*bahirdhā-śūnyatā*), wherein the external is not moved by the six sense objects.
Because it does not regress—that is, internal-and-external emptiness (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā*)—since all twelve bases (*āyatana*) are empty, it is said to be non-regressing and non-turning.

This refers to the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*); emptiness destroys all phenomena (*dharma*). All phenomena are that which is destroyed, while emptiness is that which destroys; thus, there are no longer any phenomena.

Only emptiness exists here, yet this emptiness is also empty; therefore, it is called "emptiness of emptiness" (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*). Since emptiness is already empty, there is nothing further that can be transformed;
therefore, it is called "non-transforming. That which is like space is the "Great Emptiness" (*mahā-śūnyatā*); because attachment to directions is destroyed, it is said to be "like space.
The nature of non-existence is ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), for all phenomena are left without remainder.
It is called ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*); because it is ultimately empty, it has the nature of non-existence.
All paths of linguistic expression are cut off, which means that all things are empty; because all things are empty and cannot be spoken of, the paths of linguistic expression are cut off.
Non-arising is the emptiness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*): since the conditioned is a combination of causes and conditions, and as there is no such combination, it does not arise. Nor...
"Emergence" is the emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*); because the unconditioned is called "emergence," and the dharma of emergence is empty, it is called "non-emergence.
"Non-arising" is the emptiness of the beginningless (*anavarāgra-śūnyatā*); because an original beginning cannot be found, there is no arising.

"Namelessness" is the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*), and "signlessness" is the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*); both are easily understood. "Truly having nothing" is the emptiness of the unapprehendable (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*).
"Immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*) refers to the emptiness of existing phenomena (*bhāva-śūnyatā*); since existing phenomena possess measure, and that measure is empty, it is called "immeasurable.

"Boundless" (*ananta*) refers to the emptiness of non-existing phenomena (*abhāva-śūnyatā*); since non-existing phenomena are the limits of conceptualization, and these are now empty, it is "boundless.
"Unobstructed" (*asanga*) refers to the emptiness of both existing and non-existing phenomena; since neither can be apprehended, it is called "unobstructed. Un...
Obstruction is itself "emptiness through dispersion" (*vibhava-śūnyatā*); because no obstructing agent can be found, it is said to be "without obstruction.
All eighteen emptinesses are the Middle Way and Right Wisdom; they are all termed "emptiness" because they accord with eighteen kinds of objects, and thus are called "eighteen.
As the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "The Tathāgata constantly cultivates the meaning of the eighteen emptinesses. Therefore, the eighteen emptinesses are used to explain the eighteen phrases.
Furthermore, regarding the eighteen kinds of emptiness (*aṣṭādaśa-śūnyatā*), one may say that the former is general while the latter is specific;

or, from the perspective of essence and characteristics, one may say that the former is the general essence while the latter is the specific essence, and the former is the general characteristic while the latter is the specific characteristic. Furthermore, the first [section] explains by taking both object and wisdom together, whereas the subsequent [sections] explain by taking only contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) as the whole;
however, since contemplation must necessarily contemplate an object, it is permissible to explain them solely in terms of the objects of contemplation that can give rise to [insight].
Contemplation may also be explained solely in terms of the object; now I shall further provide a private interpretation based entirely on the object:
namely, that when a bodhisattva contemplates all phenomena, they are all without exception empty; all phenomena are the true mark (yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa); all phenomena are non-erroneous;
all phenomena are immovable, non-retrogressive, and non-revolving; all phenomena are suchness (tathatā).
Space is of the nature of non-existence; it transcends all paths of verbal expression, being neither born, nor emerging, nor arising.
All phenomena are nameless; all phenomena are signless; all phenomena are truly non-existent;
all phenomena are immeasurable; all phenomena are boundless; all phenomena are unimpeded.
This obstructs the manifestation that the myriad phenomena of the ten realms and a thousand suchnesses—each and every one—is none other than the true mark (*dharmatā*);
it is the provisional being identical with the real, and the conventional being identical with the ultimate.

However, because [phenomena] arise from inversion due to causes and conditions, it is said that this manifests the essence of the signless true mark, which, according to defiled or pure conditions, fully constructs all things within the ten realms, the hundred realms, and the thousand suchnesses.
All phenomena are such that the provisional is the real and the conventional is the true; the non-duality of the provisional and the real is precisely the perfect, inconceivable Two Truths.
Their essence and characteristics are mutually identical, which is termed the Single Truth of Reality.
To speak of emptiness, all things are empty; to speak of existence, all things exist; to speak of the Middle, all things are the Middle. Furthermore...
It is called the "perfect fusion of the three truths," which are neither one, two, nor three, yet though they are one, two, and three, the true principle cannot be designated as one, two, or three.
It is further called the "perfectly wondrous absence of truths. One should always joyfully contemplate such characteristics of phenomena;
this is precisely the correct contemplation of the inconceivable realm. Therefore, it concludes: "The second [stage] is intimacy."

[The interlocutor] asks: Previously it was stated that the "place of practice" (*caryā-sthāna*) is the primary practice (*maula-caryā*), while the "place of proximity" (*upaniṣad-sthāna*) is the auxiliary practice (*sahakāri-caryā*). Now, why is this second "place of proximity" called "correct contemplation" (*samyag-darśana*)? Answer: Did we not say previously? Approaching the principle in brief is called the "place of practice," which is briefly termed "the correct. Approaching the phenomena in detail is called the "place of proximity," which is detailedly termed "the auxiliary. Thus, the former is the brief exposition of the principle, while the latter is the detailed exposition of the phenomena. Therefore, although the names differ, their meaning is identical. Furthermore, because the former is the cause and the latter is the fruit, they are distinct; yet because the former is the essence and the latter is its manifestation, they are one. Hence, the place of proximity is designated as "correct contemplation. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the first [place of practice] is the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), and the second is the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*). Since the path of seeing is the direct realization of the principle, it is called "correct contemplation. Because the path of cultivation is the repeated practice of that realization, it is called the "place of practice. Thus, the two are mutually inclusive. It is for this reason that the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* states: "The place of practice is the place of proximity; the place of proximity is the place of practice. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the former is the stage of the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana-bhūmi*), and the latter is the stage of the noble ones (*ārya-bhūmi*). Since the stage of the noble ones is the direct realization of the principle, it is called "correct contemplation. Since the stage of the ordinary person is the repeated practice of that realization, it is called the "place of practice. Thus, the two are mutually inclusive. It is for this reason that the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* states: "The place of practice is the place of proximity; the place of proximity is the place of practice. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the former is the stage of the Bodhisattva, and the latter is the stage of the Buddha. Since the stage of the Buddha is the direct realization of the principle, it is called "correct contemplation. Since the stage of the Bodhisattva is the repeated practice of that realization, it is called the "place of practice. Thus, the two are mutually inclusive.
