There is the principle of expansion and brevity, yet no difference in depth; in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjia*), there are both the primary and the auxiliary, and both are perfect.

That which is direct is neither primary nor auxiliary; it is the wondrous principle of the Perfect Way. Relying on the extensive text, it can supplement contemplation of the principle and is thus called "auxiliary.

This concludes the first long passage within the "Peaceful and Joyful Practice" (*ānle xing*) of the initial body [of the text]. II. Verses in Praise (Three sections): A. Verses praising the heading. B. Verses explaining the exposition.
The three types of practice are now established. First:
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If there is a bodhisattva who, in the evil age to come, desires to preach this sutra with a heart free from fear, they should enter the sphere of practice."
And the places of association.
△ Second, the verse explanation has two parts: first, one verse discussing the near in terms of the distant; second, two verses concerning that which is neither distant nor near.

The prose section analyzes the "places of practice" (*caritapada*) and "places of association" (*sevanāpada*). In these verses, the essential meaning is condensed and combined into stanzas rather than being presented in strict sequential order to reveal the true significance.
The text contains both detailed and abbreviated explanations, yet the underlying principle is neither shallow nor profound. First:
one should always avoid kings, princes, ministers, and high officials; (1) those who engage in violent games; (3) *caṇḍālas*; (2) non-Buddhist *brahmins*;
and one should also not associate with those of overweening pride (*adhimāna*) or those who are greedily attached to the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).
One must not associate with those who study the Tripitaka, with bhikṣus who have broken the precepts, with those called arhats who are merely names,
with bhikṣuṇīs who are fond of frivolous laughter, with those deeply attached to the five desires, or with upāsikās who seek nirvāṇa in the present life.
If such persons should come to the bodhisattva with a sincere heart for the sake of hearing the Buddha-way, the bodhisattva should then treat them with a mind free from fear.
Do not preach the Dharma with expectations of gain (5, also including the tenth).
Do not associate with or form close intimacies with widows, virgins, or those who are neuter (6, 7).

Furthermore, do not associate with butchers, executioners, hunters, fishermen, or those who kill for profit, sell meat for a living, or traffic in women; one should not associate with such people at all (4).
Do not associate with violent wrestlers, various performers, or courtesans (3, 6). Do not preach the Dharma to women in a secluded place;
if you must preach it, do not engage in joking or laughter (9). When entering a village for alms, take a fellow bhikṣu;
if there is no fellow bhikṣu, single-mindedly recollect the Buddha (8). These are called the proper spheres of conduct and the spheres of proximity.
Because these two places allow for the joyful exposition of the Dharma,
those with overweening pride— those who sit in meditation and, having attained a slight degree of pliancy, falsely claim to have realized some attainment—

as well as those attached to the Three Piṭakas of the Hīnayāna— those who focus solely on names and characteristics and refuse to engage in anything beyond oral and intellectual learning— [do not seek them].
Those who observe the mind for cultivation and realization are called "nominal arhats," meaning those who merely bear the provisional name of an *āraṇyaka*.
Those who are deeply attached to the five desires are those who, among the five sensory objects—form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch—possess a partial predilection for one or another.
Those who seek extinction in the present life are those who seek only the fruit of the Hīnayāna and lack great compassion. Attached to the five...
Desire is the extreme of birth and death; seeking extinction is the extreme of nirvana. One should not approach either of these two; rather, one should clearly approach the Middle Way.
These points were all listed under "places to draw near" in the long prose section, yet here they are summarized as "places of practice" and "places to draw near.

Thus we know that the distinction between the primary and auxiliary practices is merely a matter of breadth and brevity, and there is absolutely no difference in depth. 2. Verse on Neither Far Nor Near:
Furthermore, not practicing the superior, middling, or inferior dharmas, nor conditioned or unconditioned dharmas, nor real or unreal dharmas;
not discriminating between male and female, not attaining any dharmas, and neither knowing nor seeing—this is called the sphere of practice of a bodhisattva.

The Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao) is called the "superior dharma," the Shared Teaching (Tong-jiao) is called the "intermediate dharma," and the Tripitaka Teaching (Zang-jiao) is called the "inferior dharma.

Since all are opened up to enter the Perfect Teaching (Yuan), no further dharmas of the Tripitaka, Shared, or Separate teachings can be found; therefore, they do not proceed [independently]. The afflictions, karma, and suffering of the six realms of ordinary beings are called conditioned and out-flowing dharmas (*saṃskṛta-sāsrava-dharma*);
the merit and wisdom of the four realms of the noble ones are called conditioned and non-out-flowing dharmas (*saṃskṛta-anāsrava-dharma*).
The ten realms of phenomena subject to outflows (*āsrava-dharma*) and the nature of the equality of *tathatā* are called unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).

Conditioned form and mind, which possess a temporary essence and function, are called real phenomena (*dravya-dharma*). The formations dissociated from mind (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), which are provisionally established based on the states (*avasthā*) of form and mind, are called unreal phenomena (*adravya-dharma*).
Furthermore, conditioned phenomena are called unreal phenomena because their nature arises and perishes; unconditioned phenomena are [called real].
Because the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is unchanging, that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*) is called "unreal" because it contradicts that nature;

that which is without outflows (*anāsrava*) is called "real" because it accords with that nature. Alternatively, all things are real because both are called "truths" (the conditioned is conventional truth and the unconditioned is ultimate truth).

All things are unreal because they lack both the subjective aspect (*bhāva*) and the objective aspect (*tattva*); for while there is the subjective aspect of sentient beings, there is no objective reality. (The outflowing [phenomena] belong to sentient beings, but lack objective reality.)

That which does not exist because it lacks principle is called unreal; that which exists within the principle of the untainted (anāsrava) but does not exist for sentient beings because they lack that principle is called unreal.

Now, when none of these [distinctions] are applied, it is because one contemplates all dharmas according to their true mark (yathābhūtalakṣaṇa): conditioned phenomena are the true mark and are no longer merely conditioned;
unconditioned phenomena are the true mark and are no longer merely unconditioned; reality itself is the true mark and is no longer merely real or unreal. It is simply reality.
Because signs are no longer unreal, one does not engage with them; this verse means that while there is no engagement with phenomena, one contemplates all dharmas as they truly are.
Furthermore, "not discriminating between male and female" means that male is itself wisdom (*prajñā*) and female is itself concentration (*samādhi*);
since the dharma-nature of concentration and wisdom is fundamentally beyond words, it cannot be discriminated. One does not [attain].

Because all phenomena are eternally characterized by intrinsic quiescence, that which neither knows nor sees is far removed from the conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) of the grasper and the grasped;
thus, this verse also does not proceed and is non-conceptual.
All phenomena are empty and non-existent; they neither abide eternally nor undergo arising and ceasing. This is called the sphere of intimacy for the wise.
This is a summary verse concerning the contemplation of the emptiness of all phenomena and so forth. The phrase "there is no eternal abiding" negates [the notion of] true reality (*tattva*).

Furthermore, there is neither arising nor ceasing; both the conventional truth and the ultimate truth are negated, thereby correctly revealing the Middle Way. These words are concise yet their meaning is complete.
One who dwells in a secluded place should abandon inverted discrimination regarding whether phenomena exist or do not exist, are real or unreal, and are produced or unproduced.
Cultivating the gathering of the mind so that it dwells immovably like Mount Sumeru, observing that all phenomena are non-existent,
like space, lacking solidity, neither arising nor emerging, neither moving nor receding, eternally abiding in a single mark—
this is called "dwelling nearby."
This verse is spoken because it arises from inversion; thus, it is presented as the object of contemplation.
Furthermore, the verse treats what is proximate as a proximate means (*upāya*), and subsequently restates the correct contemplation of the emptiness of all phenomena and so forth.
In the preceding text, morality and concentration were combined to form the first stage of cultivation, while wisdom is named the second stage of cultivation. Now, by...

Combining the verses on meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), this verse on the gate of precepts (*śīla*) simultaneously concludes the practice and explicitly reveals that the three trainings are mutually integrated and that phenomena and principle are non-dual.
Question: Above it was stated that there is no permanent abiding; why now is it said that there is a single mark of permanence?
Answer: If one speaks of "permanent abiding" in contrast to arising and ceasing, that is merely a conceptual construction of the deluded mind; therefore, such conceptualization must be shattered.

Having analyzed and refuted [the notion of arising], one realizes that the principle is fundamentally eternally abiding (*nitya*). Furthermore, when "eternal abiding" is discussed in contrast to "arising and ceasing," it possesses two characteristics.
Now, since all phenomena (*dharma*) are non-existent, there is neither arising nor ceasing; they are eternally abiding in their very essence, and are thus called "one characteristic" (*eka-lakṣaṇa*).
This one characteristic is the true reality (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa*); the true reality is all phenomena, yet it is not all phenomena. All phenomena are...
Because it is non-dharmic, it is called the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). The explanation of the two verses is complete. △ Third, the accomplishment of practice, which has three parts:

first, the heading indicating the accomplishment of practice; second, the explanation of how the accomplishment of practice results in attaining peace and happiness; third, the summary verse. Now, the first part.
If there are bhikṣus who, after my parinirvāṇa, enter this sphere of practice and this sphere of intimacy when preaching this sūtra,
they will be free from timidity.
Because their external demeanor remains unimpaired when the matter is accomplished, and their inner mind remains unhindered when the principle is established, they are without timidity.
△ Second, explaining that through the perfection of practice one attains peace and happiness:
At times, the Bodhisattva enters a quiet chamber and, with right mindfulness, contemplates the Dharma according to its meaning.
Emerging from meditative concentration, he teaches and elucidates this sutra for kings, princes, ministers, subjects, brahmins, and others, transforming and guiding them.
Their minds are peaceful and secure, free from any timidity or weakness.
This explains the cause of peace and happiness: by practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one ceases transgressions and evils and attains the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*);

externally, one is not harmed. By practicing wisdom (*prajñā*), one becomes detached from all grasping and attains the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*); internally, there is no longer any inversion.
Therefore, the mind is neither timid nor weak; this lack of timidity is called peace and bliss. △ Third, the concluding verse:
Mañjuśrī, this is called the Bodhisattva’s dwelling in the first dharma, by which one is able to preach the Lotus Sūtra in future ages.
The first section, "Peaceful Conduct of the Body," is concluded. △ Second, "Peaceful Conduct of the Mouth," which has two parts: first, the long prose version; second, the verse summary.
Within the first part, there are two sections: first, the heading; second, the explanation. Now, the first [the heading]:
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, one who wishes to preach this sūtra during the final dharma age should abide in the Practice of Peaceful Dwelling.

△ Second, the explanation of the practice is divided into two: first, the practice of cessation (śamatha), and second, the practice of contemplation (vipaśyanā). The practice of cessation prevents transgressions; it is the robe of the Tathāgata.

The practice of contemplation and the preaching of the Dharma constitute the Tathāgata’s seat; furthermore, the practice of tranquility that uproots suffering and the practice of contemplation that bestows happiness constitute the Tathāgata’s chamber.

Regarding the initial practice of tranquility, there are four aspects: first, not speaking ill of others; second, not treating others with contempt; third, not praising one's own virtues while disparaging others;
and fourth, not harboring resentment or malice toward others. This is the first [aspect].
Whether speaking aloud or reading the scriptures, one should not delight in speaking of the faults of others or of the sūtras.
Even if another person has faults, what concern is that to me? One should only reflect inwardly; what leisure is there to criticize others?

To take pleasure in discussing the faults of others is like scattering excrement and filth, which defiles both oneself and others. Such harm and affliction are truly grave; it is not the practice of peace and bliss.

Furthermore, all sūtras are spoken by the Tathāgata as skillful means according to what is appropriate; they are like rock honey, sweet both in the center and at the edges—how could there be any fault in them?

To find fault with the sūtras arises entirely from not understanding the subtle principle of provisional and ultimate truth, and it is also not the practice of peaceful dwelling. △ Second, not being contemptuous.
Furthermore, one should not treat other Dharma masters with contempt.
One must not rely on the Perfect [Teaching] to despise the Partial, nor value the Real while disparaging the Expedient.

Since even the Buddha employed various skillful means to assist in manifesting the Ultimate Truth (paramārtha-satya), how could one presume upon one's own status and fail to protect the capacities of sentient beings? △ Third, not praising or disparaging.
One does not speak of the good, evil, long, or short of others; nor does one mention by name to a śrāvaka the faults or evils of another, nor does one mention by name to praise their excellence.
Since all people loathe hearing of their own shortcomings, to speak of another's faults in their face is equivalent to disparaging them directly.
Therefore, people do not praise themselves. The *Lun* (Treatise) says: "One who praises oneself is an arrogant person; one who disparages oneself is a delusive person;
one who praises others is a sycophantic person; and one who disparages others is a slanderous person.

The wise should weigh these matters according to the four *siddhāntas* (the four purposes) and protect both themselves and others. Furthermore, the *Dīrghanakha-parivarta* (*Rìzàng jīng*) states that during the first, middle, and last watches of the night...
Reducing sleep, practicing with diligence through seated meditation, reciting the sutras, and cultivating the Way, one turns away from birth and death toward the path of Nirvana.
One does not speak of the shortcomings of others nor the virtues of oneself; being humble and modest, one is not arrogant or haughty.
Content with simple clothing, one practices without negligence, maintaining mindfulness and reflection so that the mind does not wander among all sentient beings.
To give rise to a mind of compassion is the characteristic of these practices for bringing peace and happiness to all.

Regarding those of the Śrāvaka vehicle and others whose faculties and dispositions are not fixed: if one praises the Two Vehicles, it may cause them to regress from the Great Vehicle and adopt the Small;
if one disparages the Two Vehicles, it may cause them to lose both the Great and the Small, leaving them with nothing to grasp. △ Fourth, not harboring resentment or aversion.
Furthermore, one should not give rise to thoughts of resentment or disdain.
To think that a certain person or a certain teaching obstructs one’s path is a resentful mind; to think that a certain person or a certain teaching is base or inferior is a disdainful mind.
As soon as the mental faculty stirs, speech is immediately set in motion, and the fault of obstruction arises.
Because of this root cause, one does not give rise to a mind of resentment or aversion. The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states:
"In the past, during the Dharma of Kāśyapa Buddha, there was a bhikṣu who resolved upon bodhicitta and recited and upheld eighty-four thousand collections of both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings.
He felt disdain for a dhūta-bhikṣu who did not recite the sūtras, regarding him as being like a stump. Because of this, he fell [into an evil rebirth]."
In hell one undergoes great suffering; upon emerging from hell, one receives the body of a rākṣasa.
It is only at the time of the Buddha Ruci during the Bhadrakalpa that one finally sheds this ghostly form.

If even ordinary people are like this, how much more so for those who practice the Great Dharma in peace and security while protecting their minor practices—how could they not be careful with their thoughts? Resentment, resentment, dislike, and reproach: resentment is deep, while dislike is shallow.

Only by relinquishing both the shallow and the deep does one truly accord with right practice; this is what is meant by "peaceful conduct of speech. As for what is called "the mind," it is intended to govern speech.
This concludes the first section: Practice through Cessation. II. Practice through Contemplation.
Because they have skillfully cultivated such a mind of peace and happiness, all who listen do not oppose their intentions;
when faced with difficult questions, they do not answer with the teachings of the Hīnayāna, but explain them solely through the Mahāyāna, enabling them to attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Observing that all phenomena are empty and devoid of anything to be grasped or attached to, his mind does not cling to them nor does it oppose the inclinations of others;

because he does not contravene the characteristics of dharmas, he does not answer with the teachings of the Hīnayāna. If he perceives that no great capacity exists, he may preach the Lesser Vehicle so that they may obtain the benefit of skillful means;
however, if he perceives that there is no lack of great capacity yet he preaches the Lesser Vehicle, he fears it will obstruct their great conditions.
Therefore, those at the profound stage possess the wisdom to discern the capacities [of beings] and can thus preach the Dharma according to what is appropriate;
beginners lack the ability to examine things and can only preach the Mahāyāna Dharma. This concludes the long prose section on the "Peaceful Practice of Speech.
II. Verses (three parts): 1. Verses on the Introduction; 2. Verses on the Explanation; 3. Verses on the Accomplishment of Practice. Now, the first part.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The Bodhisattva always delights in preaching the Dharma with peace and security; upon a pure ground, he provides seats and couches.
He anoints his body with oil, bathes away dust and impurities, and puts on fresh, clean garments, so that both internally and externally he is pure."

The long passage simply states that one should dwell within this [state], manifesting distinct aspects and preaching the Dharma with tranquility, desiring to enable others to attain the path of tranquility and the fruit of tranquility; this is precisely entering the Tathāgata’s chamber.
Providing seats upon the pure ground is sitting upon the Tathāgata’s throne. The four lines beginning with "anointing the body with oil" refer to donning the Tathāgata’s robe.
This robe is [offered] by means of these three dharmas; guiding one’s verbal karma through them is called "Peaceful Practice.

Part Two: Verse Explanation, which has two sections: first, verses on the practice of cessation (śamatha); second, verses on the practice of insight (vipaśyanā). Within the first section, there are four parts: first, verses on the second [point], not being arrogant;

second, verses on the third, not praising or disparaging; third, verses on the first, not speaking of faults; fourth, verses on the fourth, not harboring resentment or dislike. [These correspond to] the long prose section.
While both [the preceding section and this one] generally concern the excellence of stillness (*śamatha*), the verses here specifically concern the excellence of practice (*pratipatti*). First:
He settles upon the Dharma-seat and explains according to the questions asked;
as for pride, he does not follow [it], and as for haste, he does not treat others with contempt. Second: Verses on the three points of neither praising nor disparaging.

If there are bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas and upāsikās, kings, princes, ministers, officials, or commoners who approach him with a serene countenance to inquire about subtle and profound meanings, he explains them for them; and if they pose difficult questions, he answers them in accordance with the truth.

One should rely solely on the meaning and not discuss the personal merits or faults of individuals. There are two ways of responding according to the meaning: that which may be answered and that which may not be answered.

If questions and answers involve mutual cross-examination, seeking to establish superiority or inferiority, or determining victory and defeat, one knows for oneself that this is the speech of a wise person;
such cases are those where a response may be given. However, if one acts with self-indulgence, then anyone who dares to oppose it shall be punished.
This is the speech of a king; whether long or short, right or wrong, he knows nothing of these, seeking only victory.
This is the speech of a fool—the second [type] that cannot be answered. △ Third, the verse on not speaking of faults at the outset.

By means of causes, conditions, parables, detailed expositions, and analytical distinctions, through these skillful means, they cause all beings to resolve their minds [on enlightenment], gradually increasing their merit until they enter the Buddha-way.

If there are those who delight in speaking of the faults of people or the scriptures, they give rise to poisonous thoughts toward others; because I do not speak of such faults now, I cause them to resolve their minds [on enlightenment].
The mind enters the Buddha-way, for the Buddha-way arises from joy. (4) The fourth verse praises the four ways of not harboring resentment or dislike:
removing the intent of indolence and the thought of laziness, being free from all sorrow and affliction, and preaching the Dharma with a compassionate heart.
When thoughts of resentment and aversion arise, there is indolence, anxiety, and distress; now, preaching the Dharma with a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) brings forth diligence and joy.
The first verse, which concludes the section on the practice of cessation (*śamatha*), is finished. △ Second, the verse on the practice of insight (*vipaśyanā*).

Day and night they constantly preach the unsurpassed Way of the Buddha, using various causes and conditions and immeasurable parables to reveal and instruct sentient beings, causing them all to rejoice.
They provide clothing, bedding, food and drink, and medicine, yet harbor no expectations regarding these things.

With single-minded devotion, they contemplate the causes and conditions of preaching the Dharma, vowing to attain the Buddha-way and to cause all others to do likewise; this is indeed a great benefit.
They provide offerings with peace and joy.
To expound the Unsurpassed Way is to answer by means of verses solely through the Mahāyāna Dharma;

the vow to attain the Buddha-way is to cause all beings to likewise do so, which is to say, to enable them to attain all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*). The explanation of the two verses is complete. △ Third, the accomplishment of practice.
Fourth, first, the heading marks the accomplishment of practice; second, it clarifies that because there are no internal faults, external difficulties do not arise;
third, it clarifies that because there are wholesome dharmas within, practice is accomplished; fourth, it evaluates the merit. Now, the first [section].
After my parinirvāṇa, if there should be a bhikṣu who is able to expound this wondrous Lotus Sūtra.
△ Second, it is explained that if one is internally free of faults, external difficulties will not arise; just as flies will not come if there is no foul-smelling object.

The mind is free from envy, anger, and all afflictive hindrances; it is likewise free from sorrow and those who revile, and it is without fear of being struck with weapons or staves, nor of being expelled, because it abides in patience.
△ Within the three knowledges (*traividyā*), there are wholesome dharmas by which practice is perfected.
A wise person who thus skillfully cultivates the mind can abide in peace and happiness as I have described above.
If there are no internal faults, it is as stated in the long prose section; if there are internal wholesome qualities, it is as stated in the verse. △
Fourth, the merit of these four modes of measurement:
the merit of such a person cannot be exhausted even by calculation, analogy, or parable throughout thousands of millions of billions of kalpas.
The second section on the "Peaceful Practice of Speech" is concluded. △ Third, the "Peaceful Practice of Mind," which has two parts: first, the long prose, and second, the verse summary.
Regarding the first of the three initial sections— the introduction, the explanation, and the conclusion of the practice—
this is the first. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, those who shall receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra during the final age when the Dharma is about to perish:

△ Second, the explanation [of the three analogies]. First, the practice of cessation (*śamatha*); second, the practice of insight (*vipaśyanā*). The practice of cessation is the robe; the practice of insight is the seat;
the extraction of suffering and the bestowal of happiness is the dwelling. Within the first [section], there are four parts: first, not being jealous or deceitful;
second, not slighting or reviling; third, not disturbing or harassing; fourth, not contending or competing. Now, the first.
To harbor no mind of envy, flattery, or deception:
being unable to endure the prosperity and fame of others is called envy; it arises from greed and results in hatred, and among the stains of hatred, it is the most grave.

To be treacherous and crooked in order to deceive others is called flattery; it conceals one's opposition while displaying compliance, refusing to accept instruction. Greed and delusion constitute [the root of] deceit.
Their fundamental nature is directly contrary to the Path. To feign the possession of virtue in order to seek gain and sustenance is called deception;
because of greed and delusion, they fall into the dharma of wrong livelihood. Erroneously receiving honor and respect, they invite endless suffering.
Therefore, these states of mind are all great obstacles to training in the Path; if even one of them exists, one cannot attain the enlightenment of the Two Vehicles.
How much less could one propagate the Great Dharma to seek the Way above and transform those below? A Bodhisattva practicing the "Peaceful Conduct" must urgently abandon such behavior.
△ Second, do not disparage or revile:
Furthermore, do not treat with contempt or revile those who study the Buddha-way, nor seek out their faults or shortcomings.
Once they have resolved their minds to study the Buddha's path, they immediately enter the ranks of future Buddhas.

Even if their afflictions, habitual tendencies, and natures differ such that they possess varying strengths and weaknesses, one should take what is long [in them] to benefit oneself, rather than seeking out their shortcomings to oppose them.
△ Third, not causing distress or confusion.

If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who seek the path of the śrāvaka, the path of the pratyekabuddha, or the bodhisattva path, one must not trouble them or cause them doubt and regret by saying to them:
"You are very far from the Way; you will never be able to attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā). Why is this? Because you are negligent."
Because such people are indolent regarding the Path,
each of the four assemblies has those who seek the three vehicles (*triyāna*). The meaning of what is sought by these three vehicles comprises the three teachings— the *xiang* (provisional),
*tong* (common), and *bie* (distinct)— all of which are the Tathāgata’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) for gradually and skillfully guiding others toward the ultimate reality.
The provisional means of bestowing [the Dharma] allow the fourfold assembly to seek the Way by relying upon them; thus, they may gradually be led back to the Perfect.

If, however, one relies on one's own perfect understanding to disparage others as being far from the Way, or relies on having a slight practice to disparage others as being negligent and indolent, those who are so disparaged will give rise to doubt and regret;
they will be unable to advance toward realizing the Perfect Principle, and will regress.
Failure to observe the three powers is to disturb the practitioner and invite no small transgression;
only one who possesses the wisdom-eye of the faculty of knowledge can grant or withhold as is appropriate. △ Fourth, non-contention.
Furthermore, one should not engage in frivolous conceptualization (*prapañca*) regarding phenomena or enter into disputes.
Those at the stage of the "name" (*nāman*) have but a shallow understanding of the meaning of the texts and are unable to observe the mind moment by moment;

they give rise to disputes whenever they analyze the phrasing or explain the meaning. This very act of disputing is itself called frivolous conceptualization, let alone when one indulges in the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Verbal mockery and derision turbidly disturb the mind and increase negligence; they are not practices conducive to peace and happiness, and must be strictly avoided.
This concludes the first section: Cessation of Conduct. II. Contemplative Practice (Four Parts): 1. The Contemplation of Great Compassion to remedy jealousy and deceit; 2.

The Contemplation of Being a Benevolent Father to remedy contemptuous abuse; 3. The Contemplation of Being a Great Master to remedy provocation and disturbance; 4. The Teaching of Impartiality to remedy disputes.
Section One: On Compassion.
First, one should give rise to the thought of great compassion toward all sentient beings.
Having given rise to great compassion, one vows to uproot their suffering; how could one then bear to harbor envy, flattery, or deception toward them? Section Two: On Loving-kindness.
One should regard those who reprimand or revile one lightly as a father; one should conceive of all Tathāgatas as compassionate fathers.
Having studied the Buddha-way, one realizes that these future Buddhas are none other than our own Great Compassionate Fathers—how could they possibly be treated with contempt?
They revile others, seeking out their faults and shortcomings. △ Third, regarding the perception of teachers and the remedy for affliction and confusion:
one should regard all Bodhisattvas as great teachers; toward the great Bodhisattvas of the ten directions, one should always, with a profound mind, pay reverence and prostrate.
The members of the three vehicles and the fourfold assembly are none other than bodhisattvas; possessing the virtue of transformative instruction, they are all teachers of sentient beings.

One should always pay them deep-hearted homage and respect—how could one provoke them to distress or cause them to harbor doubts? △ Fourth, resolving disputes through the impartial application of the Dharma.

He teaches the Dharma with equanimity toward all sentient beings; because he accords with the Dharma, he speaks neither too much nor too little, and even for those who deeply love the Dharma, he does not speak excessively.
When the phrasing follows the meaning and the meaning follows the phrasing, this is called "perfect equality. Thus, there is no partiality, and no [unwholesome] thoughts arise.

This is for the sake of settling disputes by means of conforming to the Dharma; therefore, one teaches neither too much nor too little, but bestows it according to the vessel, in accordance with the capacity and acuity of the faculties.
To speak excessively would constitute frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*), for such a person would be unable to comprehend and understand it, resulting in a mere waste of words without real benefit.
If, however, one is able to comprehend and understand it, then it is like the Dragon King Sāgara pouring down rain upon the great ocean, where even a speck of dust is saturated.
To speak of *kṣetra* (fields) and to speak of them again is not considered much; the two explanations are concluded.

△ Third, the conclusion on the accomplishment of practice: "Mañjuśrī, when this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, in the future final age when the Dharma is about to perish, accomplishes this third practice of peace and happiness, no one will be able to disturb or confuse him while he is preaching this Dharma."
Because this is accomplished through the practice of *śamatha*, evil cannot prevail against them.

They will find virtuous companions with whom to read and recite this sutra together; they will attract great assemblies who come to hear and receive it. Having heard it, they will be able to retain it; having retained it, they will be able to recite it;
having recited it, they will be able to explain it; and having explained it, they will be able to write it down or cause others to write it, thereby making offerings to the sutra.
[The first fascicle concludes with] respectful veneration and praise.
This is because, through the accomplishment of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), superior persons gather; thus ends the long prose section on the "Practice for Peaceful Abiding.

II. Verse Recitation. This has two parts: A. Verses that explain and interpret [the preceding prose]. B. Verses on the accomplishment of practice (the introductory summary is omitted here). Regarding the first part:
The second part consists of two verses on the practice of tranquility (*śamatha*) and two verses on the practice of insight (*vipaśyanā*). Now, for the first:
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If one wishes to expound this sutra, one should abandon envy, anger, pride, flattery, deceit, and a false mind; one should constantly cultivate straightforward conduct."
Do not treat others with contempt, nor engage in frivolous discourse regarding the Dharma; do not cause others to doubt or regret by saying, "You shall not attain Buddhahood.
The first four lines of the verse address the initial [faults]: the two characters for "envy" (*īrṣyā*) and "deceit" (*māyā*) are the roots of jealousy;

the two characters for "falsehood" (*mithyā*) and "pretense" (*kuhana*) are the footnotes to flattery and deception. To constantly cultivate integrity and practice uprightness is the gateway to the counteractive measures (*pratipakṣa*). First.
The first five lines of the verse praise the two [practices of] not slighting or reviling; the sixth line praises the four [practices of] not engaging in contention;
the final two lines praise the three [practices of] not causing disturbance. △ Second, the verse on contemplative practice.
These sons of the Buddha preach the Dharma with constant gentleness and patience, possessing compassion for all and never giving rise to a mind of indolence.
Because they pity the multitudes, these great Bodhisattvas of the ten directions practice the Path; one should give rise to a heart of reverence toward them.

They are my Great Teachers, and one should regard the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, as one would an unsurpassed father. Having destroyed the mind of arrogance, they preach the Dharma without obstruction.
The first verse praises the first, the thought of great compassion; the second verse praises the three thoughts of the Great Masters;

the next half-verse praises the two thoughts of the compassionate fathers; and the latter half-verse praises the four ways of preaching the Dharma with equality. This concludes the explanation of the first section.
△ Second, the praise for the accomplishment of practice.
The third dharma: A wise person should thus protect their single-mindedness and practice the conduct of peace and bliss, being honored by immeasurable multitudes.

This concludes the third section on the Conduct of Peace and Bliss in Three Intentions. △ Fourth, the Conduct of Peace and Bliss through Vows. This has two parts: first, the long prose; second, the verse summary. Within the first part, there are two sections:

first, clarifying the method of practice; second, praising the sutra. Within the first of these, there are three further divisions: first, the heading; second, the explanation; third, [the conclusion].
The formation of the practice is now begun.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, in the future final age when the Dharma is about to perish,
there will be those who uphold this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
△ Second, the explanation is divided into three parts: first, clarifying the object of the vow; second, clarifying the reason for generating the vow;
third, formally establishing the vow. Now, the first part:
generating great loving-kindness toward those who are householders and renunciants, and generating great compassion toward those who are not bodhisattvas.
Regarding the mind:
those who have already generated the supramundane mind of the three vehicles are called householders and renunciants;

those who have not yet generated the mind at all are called non-Bodhisattvas. Among those who have generated the mind, those who have not yet severed the pervasive afflictions remain within the three realms.
Those whose names are designated as "laypeople" have already severed the pervasive afflictions and emerged from beyond the three realms; those designated as "renunciants" have likewise emerged.
This encompasses all forty stages of mind across the three vehicles without exception. For those who are not Bodhisattvas, it encompasses all six paths and four modes of birth without exception.
Within each of these ten dharma-realms, there are respective sufferings and origins that should be uprooted; one must arise [in response] to them all.
Regarding Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), there are those for whom the Path and Cessation should be bestowed; all such persons should give rise to Great Loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*).

For those who have already resolved [to attain enlightenment], the sprouts of goodness have already emerged; because one must cultivate them to perfection based on that goodness, one gives rise to Great Loving-kindness.

This loving-kindness is able to uproot the suffering of the three delusions. As for those who have not yet resolved [to attain enlightenment], their evil habits are particularly strong; therefore, one must rescue them by means of their very evil.
For this reason, great compassion arises; this compassion is able to bestow the bliss of the three virtues.
This is called "arising the vow of non-action based on the truth of non-action. △ Second, clarifying the reasons for arising the vow.

One should reflect thus: "Such a person has suffered a great loss; they have not heard, do not know, are not aware of, do not inquire about, do not believe in, and do not understand the Tathāgata’s skillful means of teaching the Dharma according to what is appropriate."
When it is said that the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma through skillful means according to what is appropriate,
this refers generally to the teachings of his entire lifetime— whether sudden or gradual, great or small, perfect or partial, manifest or esoteric, fixed or unfixed,
and even whether combined or singular, contrasted or accompanied, opened or revealed, abolished or established; each and every one of these is such.
Each of these inconceivable skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) accords with what is appropriate for sentient beings;
those who are not bodhisattvas do not hear, know, or awaken to these provisional teachings.

As for bodhisattvas, whether lay or ordained, they do not inquire about, believe in, understand, or hear these wondrous teachings; therefore, they lack the wisdom of hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*) pertaining to the Three Vehicles.

Because they do not know, they lack the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) of the Three Vehicles; because they do not awaken, they lack the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) of the Three Vehicles;

because they do not inquire, they lack the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) of the One Vehicle; because they do not believe, they lack the wisdom of reflection of the One Vehicle; and because they do not understand, they lack the wisdom of cultivation of the One Vehicle.
All these are instances of being deluded regarding the fundamental Path and its cessation, thereby giving rise to the various accumulations of suffering within and beyond the realms.
Realizing that the very mass of suffering is the cause for the arising of the Great Vow of Resolve is why it serves as the basis for its manifestation.
△ Third, the formal establishment of the vow:
Although such a person may not inquire about, believe in, or understand this sutra, I shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At the time of awakening, wherever one may be, by means of the power of supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) and the power of wisdom (*prajñā*), one leads [beings] to abide within this Dharma.

While the previous vow was explained by citing both the provisional and the ultimate through the three types of wisdom, here it refers only to the three types of wisdom— provisional, perfect, and ultimate.

This is because those who establish vows are truly able to encompass skillful means; yet, as they still lack perfect wisdom, they remain objects of compassion, let alone those who are utterly deluded, for whom one should feel even greater pity.
The power of supernatural faculties (*ṛddhibala*) is the Tathāgata’s robe and the Tathāgata’s chamber;

by its power, one manifests various majestic deportments without arising from the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). This is first to move through concentration. The power of wisdom (*prajñābala*) is the Tathāgata’s seat.
Regarding the fourth, "Adorned with the Fourfold Eloquence," it is subsequently extracted by means of wisdom.

To lead [beings] so that they may abide within this Dharma, one must first establish the provisional through the real (*shi*), and then reveal the real by opening the provisional (*kai*). This concludes the two interpretations. △ Third, the conclusion on the perfection of practice, which has two parts:
first, clarifying the departure from faults; second, clarifying the benefits. Now, the first part.
Mañjuśrī, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes this fourth dharma after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata,
there will be no fault when they preach this dharma.
To give rise to great compassion is the practice of entering the Tathāgata’s chamber; its fulfillment consists in knowing that all bodhisattvas are neither bodhisattvas nor non-bodhisattvas.

To lose the provisional and the real regarding the three types of wisdom is the practice of sitting upon the Tathāgata’s seat; its fulfillment consists in establishing the mind through vast vows so that one never tires from beginning to end.
Because the practice of the chamber is fulfilled, there is no fault of the stain of anger; because the practice of the seat is fulfilled, there is no fault of [distraction].
Because the practice of conduct (*caryā*) is perfected, there is no fault of flattery or deception; because the practice of clothing (*vastra-caryā*) is perfected, there is no fault of indolence.

Having personally extracted one's own suffering, one universally extracts the suffering of others; this meaning is identical to the perfection of the practice of tranquility (*śamatha*). △ Second, clarifying the benefits, which is further divided into two parts:
first, the actual clarification; second, the concluding explanation. Now, the first part.
He is constantly provided with offerings, respect, honor, and praise by bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, kings, princes, ministers, commoners, brahmins, householders, and others;
even the devas of the void constantly attend upon him to listen to the Dharma. Whether he is in a village, a city, or a secluded forest, whenever anyone comes to him...
For those who wish to pose difficult questions, the devas constantly protect them day and night for the sake of the Dharma, enabling all listeners to attain joy.

Because their conduct in the home has been perfected, they are honored and attended by humans and devas as they follow and listen to the Dharma; because their conduct in clothing has been perfected, the devas provide protection.
Because the practice of the seat of protection—which is beyond reproach—has been accomplished, the listeners rejoice; having themselves attained bliss, they universally bestow bliss upon others.
This meaning is identical to the accomplishment of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*). △ Second, the explanation of the conclusion.
Why is this so? Because this sutra is protected by the spiritual power of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
Since the Buddhas of the three periods of time all equally protect such a wondrous scripture, how could those who preach this sutra not attain peace?
Having attained such great benefit? This concludes the first section, which clarifies the practice of the Dharma. △ Second, praising the sutra, in two parts:
first, a brief praise according to the Dharma; second, an extensive praise by means of analogies. Now, the first part.
Mañjuśrī, in immeasurable lands, even the name of this Lotus Sūtra cannot be heard,
let alone being seen, upheld, maintained, read, or recited.
The appearance of the Buddhas in the world is remote and difficult to encounter; even if a Buddha were to appear, he would long remain silent regarding this essential point.
Therefore, to even hear its name is already unattainable, let alone to see it, let alone to receive and uphold it, let alone to read and recite it.
This implies that to now obtain the opportunity to see, hear, receive, uphold, read, and recite it is an inconceivable causal condition that must be treasured.
This emphasizes the necessity of practicing according to what has been taught. △ Second, the extensive praise by means of analogies, which is divided into two parts:

first, the analogy of not giving the jewel; second, the analogy of giving the jewel. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, establishing the analogy; second, the application to the Dharma. Within the first of these, there are five points:
first, subduing all kingdoms (up to) fifth, only not giving the jewel. Now, the first point.
Mañjuśrī, it is like a powerful Wheel-Turning Sage King who wishes to subdue various kingdoms through his majestic power.
The Wheel-Turning King is like the Tathāgata; the kingdoms of the world are like the aggregates (skandhas), sense bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus)—the various objects of experience.
△ Second, the minor kings do not submit.
Yet the various minor kings do not obey his commands.
The minor kings are like the various afflictions such as views and craving—the demons that are thieves and robbers, namely the so-called "kings of the forest.
Because they have not yet attained the untainted (anāsrava) discipline, they are said not to obey his commands. △ Third, raising an army to wage a punitive expedition.
At that time, the Wheel-Turning King raises various armies and proceeds to wage war.
His precepts are like sturdy armor, his concentration is like a fortified camp, and his wisdom is like a sharp weapon.
Among the seven noble ones, those on the path to the fruit of Srotāpanna and Sakṛdāgāmin serve as the vanguard; those on the path to the fruits of Anāgāmin and Arhat serve as the second army.
That which is broken by the rear army through the methods of the Middle Way refers to the eighty-four thousand bandits consisting of the three poisons and their equal proportions;
that which is able to break them refers to the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates (the eighty-four thousand aggregates of dharma of the Hīnayāna) as the soldiers and officers.
△ Fourth, bestowing rewards for meritorious service.
When the king sees that his troops have achieved merit in battle, he is filled with great joy and grants rewards according to their merit;
he may grant fields, houses, villages, or cities; or he may grant clothing and articles for adorning the body; or he may grant various kinds of rare treasures, gold, and silver.
Lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, agate, coral, amber, elephants, horses, chariots, servants, and subjects;

fields represent meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), houses represent liberation (*vimukti*), villages represent the first and second fruits [of the path], towns represent the third fruit, and cities represent *nirvāṇa*, which is the fourth fruit.
Clothing represents the ornaments for adorning the body with wholesome dharmas such as shame (*hrī*) and patience (*kṣānti*).

All the various wholesome dharmas that assist the path are likened to the seven kinds of precious jewels; the seven categories of the untainted factors of the path (*anāsrava-mārga*) are likened to elephants, horses, and carriages;
the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) of the two vehicles are likened to male and female servants;
and the tainted wholesome dharmas (*sāsrava-kuśala-dharma*) are likened to the common people. △ Fifth, he alone did not give him the jewel.
Only the bright pearl from within his topknot was not given. Why was this? It was because this single pearl alone exists upon the King’s crown;
if it were given away, the King’s entire retinue would surely be greatly shocked and amazed.

When the capacity for transcending the *paricchinna-bheda* (segmented) [rebirth] is activated, it is called a "lesser meritorious achievement"; when the capacity for transcending the *pariṇāma-vikāra* (transformative) [rebirth] is activated, it is called a "great meritorious achievement.
If one were suddenly granted the crest-jewel before having achieved great merit, one's kinsmen would be startled and wonder at it;

likewise, if this sutra were suddenly preached to sentient beings before their great capacity has been activated, not only would those of the Two Vehicles be perplexed, but even Bodhisattvas would be startled and wonder at it.
The initial establishment of the analogy is concluded. △ Second, the application to the Dharma also has five parts: first, the application to the majestic subjugation of all kingdoms;
(up to) fifth, the application to the fact that he alone does not give the jewel. Now, the first.
Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata is likewise; by the power of meditative concentration and wisdom, he has attained the Dharma-realm and reigns as king over the three realms.

Regarding the attainment of the Dharma-realm through the power of meditative concentration and wisdom: meditative concentration consists of the practice of loving-kindness and patience, which accomplishes merit.
The adornment of the virtue of liberation is wisdom; this is the seat of emptiness, and through the perfection of practice, it constitutes the adornment of the virtue of *prajñā*.
By means of these two cultivations, one manifests the single nature. This corresponds to the aforementioned Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*):
although he is a descendant of royalty, it is because he possesses great power that he attains the throne; thus, "attaining the kingdom" refers to the realization [of the Dharma].

The Constant Quiescent Light Land (sada-prabhāsvara-kṣetra) reigns over the three realms, exercising sovereign control over the three lands of True Reward (samyag-vipāka), Expedient Means (upāya), and Common Residence (sahā-vāsa).
This is intended to employ majestic power to subdue the various kingdoms, causing them to sever the three delusions, transcend the two deaths, and accord with the Dharma-nature.
△ Second, the integration of the minor kings who do not comply.
Yet the various Mara kings refuse to submit.
Within the three realms of cohabitation there are the Mara kings of views and attachments; within the three realms of expedient means there are the Mara kings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
and within the three realms of true retribution there are the Mara kings of ignorance—all of whom do not accord with the Dharma-nature. △ Three.
They mobilized their forces to launch an expedition for conquest.
The Tathāgata’s noble and holy generals engaged them in battle;
that is, the seven worthies as the vanguard and the four fruits as the rearguard fought against the afflictions of views and craving within the realm.
This is the battle. △ Fourth, the bestowal of joy upon those who have performed meritorious service:

Those who have performed meritorious service also rejoice in their hearts. Among the fourfold assembly, [the Buddha] preaches various sutras for them to gladden their minds, bestowing upon them the wealth of the dharmas of dhyāna, liberation, the untainted faculties (indriya), powers (bala), and so forth; furthermore, he grants them nirvāṇa.
He speaks of attaining *nirvāṇa* within the city to guide their minds and cause them all to rejoice.
Being able to subdue views and craving is called "having merit"; the rest may be understood accordingly. △ Fifth, combining [the points], he gives them only the jewel.
Yet he did not preach this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for him.

Although the turbid obstructions had been removed, because the great capacity [for understanding] had not yet been aroused, he did not preach it; thus the analogy of the jewel was not initially given.
II. The analogy of giving the jewel also has two parts: first, establishing the analogy; second, the application to the Dharma. Now, the first part.
Mañjuśrī, it is like a wheel-turning monarch who, seeing among his troops those who have performed great deeds, feels profound joy;
he then takes this pearl of rare faith—which has long remained within his topknot—and, no longer withholding it from others, bestows it upon them.

The analogy of the sovereign wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāmaṇi-rāja) that is perfectly luminous represents the essence of the Middle Way’s true wisdom, which inherently possesses the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*).

"Perfect" (*yuan*) refers to the virtue of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); "luminous" (*ming*) refers to the virtue of Prajñā; and "the wish-fulfilling jewel raining jewels" refers to the virtue of liberation (*vimukti*).

Because it is the primary object of veneration for the ultimate fruit, it rests upon the crown of the King, while the ministers remain below. Since this has never before been heard or seen, it is called "difficult to believe"; yet it is truly the basis for all provisional teachings.

Because it was hidden, it is said to have long resided within the topknot; "untying the topknot" signifies the opening of the provisional, and "bestowing the jewel" signifies the manifestation of the real.
△ Second, the analogy with the Dharma:
The Tathāgata is likewise thus; within the triple world, he acts as the Great Dharma King, teaching and transforming all beings through the Dharma.

When sentient beings see the army of the noble ones battle against the Māra of the five aggregates, the Māra of afflictions, and the Māra of death, achieving great merit and virtue by extinguishing the three poisons, escaping the triple world, and breaking the net of Māra—at that time, the Tathāgata also rejoices greatly.
This *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* can cause sentient beings to reach all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*). It is full of enemies in all worlds and difficult to believe in, as was previously [stated].
What was not previously stated is now explained. The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* says:

"Knowing suffering destroys the demon of the aggregates (*skandha-māra*); severing the origin [of suffering] distances one from the demon of afflictions (*kleśa-māra*); realizing cessation distances one from the demon of death (*mṛtyu-māra*);
and cultivating the path destroys the demon of the sons of gods (*devaputra-māra*). This refers to the destruction of the four demons within the realm of the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*). However...
In the Hīnayāna, when cultivating the supramundane path, it is said that one "destroys the celestial Māra" simply because the celestial Māras cannot act as obstacles;

in reality, however, they have not yet truly subdued the celestial Māra. It is only when the Tathāgata manifests the eight phases of attaining enlightenment in his Nirmāṇakāya that he demonstrates the subduing of the celestial Māra.
Now, [the text] states that [this state] coexists with the five aggregates, the afflictions, and the death Māras.
By vanquishing the three poisons in battle and emerging from the triple world, one’s stage-by-stage cultivation reaches completion;

it is also said that by achieving great merit and destroying the net of Māra, the capacity for the Mahāyāna is awakened. Therefore, with great joy, he preached this wondrous sutra so difficult to believe.
Mañjuśrī, this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the foremost teaching of all Tathāgatas; among all dharmas, it is the most profound.
It is bestowed at the very end, just as a powerful king who has long guarded a bright jewel finally grants it to someone.
Mañjuśrī, this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the secret treasury of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas. Among all...
This has been the most supreme within the sutras; having been guarded throughout the long night and not spoken of falsely, it is only today that I shall expound it for you all.

"By constantly practicing patience and showing compassion for all, one is able to expound the sūtras praised by the Buddha."

The preceding section provided a general explanation of the accomplishment of practice; now, this verse specifically clarifies it. The first line of the verse clarifies the accomplishment of the practice of donning robes;

the second line clarifies the accomplishment of the practice of entering the chamber; the subsequent lines expound upon the accomplishment of the practice of sitting on the seat. △ Second, the retrospective verse on the methods of practice has three parts:
first, the verse on the object of the vow; second, the verse on the cause for arising the vow; third, the verse on the formal establishment [of the vow].
The Vow. First, [the vow] itself.
In the future, at the end of the age, those who uphold this sutra—whether householders, renunciants, or even non-Bodhisattvas—should give rise to compassion toward them.
△ Second, the verse on the reason for giving rise to the vow.
If these people do not hear or believe this sutra, it will be a great loss for them.
△ Third, the verse on the formal establishment of the vow:
"When I attain the Way of the Buddha, I shall use various skillful means to preach this Dharma for them, so that they may abide therein."

The first verse concludes the exposition of the practice. △ Second, the verses praising the sutra: these verses praise the extensive praise by means of metaphors, but do not praise the concise praise according to the Dharma.

Furthermore, in the long prose there are two metaphors and two applications; here, first, there is a general verse for the two metaphors and second, a general verse for the two applications. First, the general verse for the two metaphors.
For example, when a powerful Wheel-Turning King has soldiers who have performed meritorious service in battle, he joyfully bestows various rewards:
elephants, horses, chariots, ornaments for the body, fields, houses, villages, and cities; or he grants them clothing, various kinds of rare jewels, male and female slaves, and wealth.
Just as the king, seeing those who are brave and capable of performing difficult deeds, unties his topknot and gives [its contents] to them.
A bright pearl is bestowed upon him.
The first three verses illustrate the analogy of not giving the pearl; the final verse illustrates the analogy of giving the pearl. △ Second, a general summary combining both.
The Tathāgata is likewise the King of all Dharmas; possessing the great power of patience and a treasure-store of wisdom, he transforms the world according to the Dharma through great compassion.
Seeing all people undergoing various sufferings and desiring liberation, he engages in battle with the Māras.
For the sake of these sentient beings, he expounds various teachings and, through great skillful means, preaches these sūtras. Having thus known the sentient beings...
Having gained their strength, I have finally preached this Lotus Sūtra for them, like a king who unties the bright jewel from his topknot to give it away.
This sūtra is the most honored, the supreme among all sūtras; I have constantly guarded it and did not reveal it recklessly. Now is precisely the right time, and I shall preach it for you.
The first three and a half verses summarize the non-bestowal of the jewel, while the latter three verses summarize the bestowal of the jewel;

thus concludes the second section, the explanation of the methods of practice. △ Third, a general clarification of the signs of the completion of practice, which has three parts: first, the summary exhortation regarding the four practices;
second, the citation of the three rewards as an exhortation; third, the final summary. Now, the first part.
After my parinirvāṇa, those who seek the Buddha-way and wish to attain peace and security in expounding this sutra should personally cultivate these four dharmas.
△ Second, citing the three retributions to provide exhortation—also called the purification of the three obstacles—is further divided into three parts; first, the obstacle of retribution.

There are three types of karmic obstacles: first, those that manifest as retribution in the present life; second, those that manifest as retribution in future lives; and third, those that manifest as retribution in subsequent lives. Regarding the first:
one who reads this sutra will always be free from sorrow and affliction, shall have no illness or pain, and their complexion will be bright and pure.

He constantly experiences no sorrow or affliction, thereby transforming the mind that would otherwise manifest as retribution in the present life; furthermore, he experiences no illness or pain, thereby transforming the physical form that would otherwise manifest as retribution in the present life.
△ Second, the transformation of karmic obstructions so that they manifest as retribution in future lives.
One will not be born into poverty, low station, or ugliness.
The cause of evil karma brings about evil results; by upholding this sutra, one does not perform the karma of poverty or lowliness, and thus is not born in a base or ugly place.
△ Third, the transformation of the afflictive hindrances and the subsequent retribution, in two parts: first, a specific explanation of the three [hindrances].

Regarding the transformation of the afflictive hindrances, there are two general explanations concerning the transformation of all afflictive hindrances; the first of these also has three parts: first, the transformation of the hindrance of attachment;
second, the transformation of the hindrance of aversion; and third, the transformation of the hindrance of delusion. Now, the first [of these].
Sentient beings delight in seeing [the Buddha] as they long for sages and saints; celestial youths serve him as attendants.
Those with much greed were previously treated with contempt by others and further obstructed rebirth in the Brahma Heaven;
now that the obstruction of greed has been transformed, sentient beings revere and admire him, and celestial youths serve him as attendants. △ Second, the transformation of the obstruction of anger.
Swords and staves cannot be brought against him, and poisons cannot harm him. If someone reviles him with evil words, his mouth remains closed;
he wanders without fear like a lion king.
By abandoning anger, he eliminates the swords and arrows within, so that when entering battle, the blades from without do not wound him. △ Third, the transformation of the obstacle of delusion.
The light of wisdom shines like the sun.

First, the specific explanation of the transformation of the three afflictive hindrances is concluded. △ Second, the general explanation of the transformation of all afflictive hindrances has four parts:
first, dreaming of entering the stage of semblance, the ten stages of faith; [omitted] fourth, dreaming of entering the ultimate stage of wondrous enlightenment. Covering...
Since peace and bliss are the practice of the Tathāgata, those who propagate the sutra prefigure the attainment of its fruition; one should know that the power of such propagation is no small matter.
Furthermore, the events of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas are all contained within a single thought-moment of a dream, illustrating that the wondrous Dharma is inconceivable:
the infinite is within the one, and the one is within the infinite, with each aspect manifesting before one.

In the future, he shall surely attain the fruit; his merit in propagating the teachings throughout one lifetime will surpass that of many kalpas. Initially, he dreamed that he entered the stage of "semblance" within the ten levels of faith.
Within that dream, he saw only wondrous things: he beheld all the Tathāgatas seated upon lion thrones, surrounded by assemblies of bhikṣus.
Surrounding the preaching of the Dharma, one also sees nāgas, devas, asuras, and others, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, reverently joining their palms;
they perceive themselves as being preached to by the Buddha.
The first two phrases generally encompass all the preceding texts, while the subsequent four phrases—seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma—represent the upward seeking of the Buddha-way.

Furthermore, the final six lines describe preaching the Dharma for dragon deities and others, representing the downward transformation of sentient beings. △ Second, the dream of entering the stage of the first abode (*prathamābhūmi*) and the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).
Again, one sees the physical marks of all Buddhas as golden in color, emitting immeasurable light that illuminates everything, with voices like Brahmā’s.
The Buddha expounded all dharmas, preaching the unsurpassed Dharma for the fourfold assembly. Seeing him standing in their midst, they joined their palms and praised the Buddha;
hearing the Dharma, they rejoiced and made offerings to him. They attained *dhāraṇīs* and realized non-retrogressive wisdom.

The Buddha, knowing that their minds had deeply entered the path of the Buddha, immediately bestowed upon them the prediction of their attainment of supreme perfect enlightenment: "O sons of good family, in a future age..."
He attains the Great Path of the Buddha of Immeasurable Wisdom, whose land is adorned, pure, and vast beyond compare; there, the fourfold assembly also joins their palms to listen to the Dharma.
Seeing his own body situated therein represents the entry into reality; hearing the Dharma with joy represents the realization of the perfect cause and what is to be attained.
Distinct from the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), one simultaneously attains the *dhāraṇī*, which is the realization of the three types of retention (*tri-dhāraṇī*);

realizes non-retrogressive wisdom, which is the threefold non-retrogression; and receives the prediction of Buddhahood, which is the prediction of the manifestation of the unborn (*anutpāda*). △ Third, the dream-like entry into the stages of practice, the paths, the directions, and the stage of cultivating the path.

Furthermore, one sees oneself in mountain forests cultivating wholesome dharmas, realizing the true marks of reality, and entering deeply into meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), thereby beholding the Buddhas of the ten directions.

"Wholesome dharmas" refers to the practice of wisdom arising in accordance with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) as well as the practice of conduct; these constitute the seven categories of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharmas*).

The ten *pāramitās*, the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*), the four means of attraction (*catvāri saṃgrahavastūni*), the samādhis, the dhāraṇīs, and all other factors of the Buddha-way are the true nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

This true nature is precisely the Middle Way; the Middle Way is neither one nor many. Because one realizes the Middle Way through the destruction of the delusions of the forty chapters, there are forty successive stages of partial realization;
therefore, it is called "realizing all true natures. To enter deeply into meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) is...
Because the Śūraṅgama Samādhi does not perceive the Tathāgata through dualistic characteristics, it is said that one "sees the Buddhas of the ten directions.

Furthermore, because Bodhisattvas in their final stage of mind enter the Vajra Samādhi, and all Buddhas appear before them to confer empowerment and bestow office, it is said that they "see the Buddhas of the ten directions.
△ Fourth, dreaming of entering the ultimate stage of Wondrous Enlightenment.
The bodies of all Buddhas are golden in color, adorned with the marks of a hundred blessings. Hearing the Dharma and preaching it for others, one constantly has such auspicious dreams:

furthermore, one dreams of becoming a king, abandoning the palace, the retinue, and the most exquisite five desires, proceeding to the site of enlightenment, sitting upon the lion throne beneath the Bodhi tree, seeking the Way for seven days, and attaining the wisdom of all Buddhas.
Having attained the unsurpassed path, he shall arise and turn the wheel of Dharma, preaching the Dharma for the fourfold assembly throughout thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas;
he will preach the sublime, untainted Dharma to deliver immeasurable sentient beings, and thereafter he shall enter nirvana, like a lamp extinguished when the smoke has ended.

Dreaming of the Buddha in his eight aspects is a metaphorical manifestation of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). From the stage of *srotāpanna* up to that of *pratyekabuddha*, all possess dreams;
only the Buddha does not dream, because he is free from doubt and residual habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).

The *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* clarifies that those about to realize the ten stages (*bhūmi*) are invariably preceded by dreams. Dreams consist of the independent mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) together with the mental factor of sleep (*middha*).
The various realms manifested through illusion that coincide with dreams of past events are shadows of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*);
if they correspond to future events, they are omens of good or ill fortune.
Now, having recited this King of Sutras and obtained such auspicious dreams, they will not be in vain in the future; this is a favorable omen. Second, citing the three types of retribution:
The exhortation is concluded. △ Third, the general summary:
"If, in future evil ages, one preaches this foremost Dharma, that person shall obtain great benefit, including all the merits mentioned above.
This "Chapter on Peaceful Practices" specifically demonstrates the method for a beginner to propagate the Dharma; it fully contains the ten vehicles of contemplation (*daśayāna-vipaśyanā*).

I shall now briefly indicate the Dharma so that the mind may have a focal point for contemplation. First is the contemplation of the true reality (*yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena, which is the contemplation of the inconceivable realm (*acintya-viṣaya*).

Second is the genuine arousal of the bodhicitta: giving rise to great compassion (*mahāmaitrī*) toward those in the household life and those who have left it, and giving rise to great pity (*mahākaruṇā*) toward those who are not yet bodhisattvas.
Regarding the three karmas [of body, speech, and mind], each possesses cessation (*śamatha*), practice (*caryā*), and contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
Practicing the third skillful means is "settling the mind"; contemplating the emptiness of all phenomena and so forth is the fourth, "pervasive destruction of dharmas";
neither acting nor discriminating is the fifth, "discerning the open and the obstructed. The three karmas and the vows constitute the fulfillment of the four foundations of mindfulness;
based on this fulfillment, one cuts off the two evils and gives rise to the two virtues, thereby accomplishing the faculty of "according with reality."
The sixth is the stage of the path of power and awakening, which is the path of appropriate adjustment;
the seventh is the stage of remedial aids for opening [wisdom], which is the departure from the ten afflictions and disturbances; the eighth is the stage of what is manifested in dreams;

the ninth is the ability to practice patience, wherein the mind is neither violent nor startled; and the tenth is the departure from attachment to phenomena, wherein there is no engagement with phenomena whatsoever.
Taken collectively, these four practices and ten dharmas provide a concise yet comprehensive overview; yet, if discussed in detail, each individual practice contains all ten dharmas.
Furthermore, while the ten dharmas constitute the primary elements, the four practices serve as their auxiliaries. Whether considered as four or as ten, they both involve cause and effect.

Moreover, the four practices represent the general framework while the ten contemplations represent the specific details; whether general or specific, they all encompass the ten dharmas both horizontally and vertically.
The guiding principles ensure that nothing fails to reach its ultimate fulfillment; how could the ritual procedures for the four practices be restricted to their commencement?

Since the wondrous practice of the Perfect Way makes no distinction between beginning and end, the meaning of the "six stages" becomes clear, providing a firm footing for progress. The first section, the Gate of Traces, which opens the provisional to reveal the real, is hereby concluded.
