△ The explanation of the "Chapter on Peaceful Conduct" is concluded. Next, the "Chapter on the Emergence from the Earth" is explained.
Regarding the fifteenth chapter, "The Emergence from the Earth":

because the teachers are majestic and the Way is honored, they bow in humble service to the single command of the Tathāgata and spring forth from the four directions; therefore, it is called "Emergence."

The Chapter on the Emergence from the Earth (The Path Resides in the Master; Therefore the Path Honors the Master. Because the Master Possesses the Path, the Master is Revered. Because the Master is Revered, His Command Must Not Be Disobeyed. Because the Path is Honored, When There Is a Command, One Must Certainly Respond). First, regarding the command:

it is first derived from the end of the "Chapter on the Jeweled Stupa," where it says that the Buddha wishes to entrust this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* to those present; thus, the command is still general. Second, it is derived from the beginning of this chapter, where the Bodhisattvas from other lands request to propagate the Buddha’s teaching, but he stops them, saying:

"In my Sahā world, there are already sixty thousand Ganges-sands [of Bodhisattvas]"; this is the specific command, which pertains to the *loka-prasiddha-tantra* (the standpoint of worldly convention) of this world. First, transforming sentient beings throughout the three periods of time, his grace and benefit are boundless. One.
The ten thousand reflections of the moon—who can fathom them? By summoning the past to manifest the present, the propagation of the sutra benefits those of the current age;

thus it is called the "Chapter on the Emergence from the Earth" (the *puruṣapudgalasiddhānta*). Space is serene, without beginning or end; yet those who are deluded cling to its traces and remain dark regarding its source.
By summoning the past to reveal the present, it shatters attachment to the near and manifests the events of the distant; thus it is called "Emerging from the Earth."

The Chapter on the Emergence from the Earth (The Principle of the Parable of Space): The principle is without priority or posteriority; based on this principle, phenomena are established, and thus things have both their fundamental and manifest aspects. Some cling to the near manifest aspect and thereby lose sight of the distant fundamental.

If they are still deluded regarding the relationship between the fundamental and the manifest, how much more so regarding the inconceivable oneness? Originally, the disciple resided below in the space of his own fundamental abode, while the Teacher remained for a long time in the space above. Now, the Teacher and disciple are together in the present space. Although the space of the past, the space of now, the lower space, and the upper space are identical in essence, the original disciple fundamentally understood the near manifest aspect, whereas the present disciple remains deluded regarding the distant fundamental.

To shatter this clinging to the near, the past is summoned to reveal the present. Because the present disciple’s doubt leads to inquiry, upon hearing the teaching, he finally breaks his attachment to the near. This constitutes the complete application of the antidote.
The Youthful Father of the Tranquil Site has long taken the elixir of the wisdom of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), and thus, though old, he appears as young;
the Elder Son of the Tranquil Light has likewise long received the prescription for eternal non-death, and thus, though young, he appears as old.

To demonstrate the power of these medicines so that all may come to know them, it is called the "Chapter on the Emergence from the Earth" (the first section). The text asks: "From where does this [assembly] come?"
Regarding the causes and conditions for their gathering here, one should know that they emerge by virtue of the four *siddhāntas*.

(However, while the first *siddhānta* is explicitly present in this chapter, the second intention encompasses the latter two chapters, and the third and fourth *siddhāntas* are drawn from subsequent chapters; all these serve as aids to establish the distant [reality], to manifest goodness, to eliminate evil, and to shatter views at their root.

Thus, one knows that the "worldly" (*loka*) is the source of the latter three *siddhāntas*, whereas the current "Chapter on the Emergence" (*Sudurjayaparivarta*) is dedicated specifically to the worldly. △ Second, the opening of the near to reveal the distant. Third, first, from this...

1. From "When you yourselves shall hear this" down to the beginning of the *Vibhaṅgaguṇa-parivarta* (Chapter on the Distinction of Merit), where Maitreya speaks the verses, constitutes the Introductory Section. 2.

From "At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva" down to the end of the *Sadāparibhūta-parivarta* (Chapter on Never-Disparaging), comprising three chapters, constitutes the Main Exposition Section. 3. [The third section follows as indicated by the numbering.]

This half-fascicle consists of the section on the dissemination of the teaching. The initial introduction is divided into two parts: first, the emergence [of the bodhisattvas], and second, the questions and doubts. Within the first part, there are three sections:
first, the bodhisattvas from other directions request that the sutra be propagated; second, the Tathāgata does not grant permission; third, the emergence of those from the lower direction.

First: At that time, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas from other lands who had come in numbers exceeding eight *gaṅgā*-sands rose within the great assembly, joined their palms in homage, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if you would permit us [to do so] regarding the Buddha..."
After my parinirvāṇa, those who diligently apply themselves with vigor in this Sahā world to protect, uphold, read, recite, copy,
and make offerings to this sutra should expound it extensively within this land.

On the other hand, the bodhisattvas, having already heard the exposition of the "Trace Gate" (Jikimon) and the conclusion of its dissemination, because they longed for the supreme merit of this universal propagation of the sutra, vowed to remain here to widely proclaim it. △ Second, the Tathāgata’s refusal.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, saying, "Stop, sons of good family! There is no need for you to protect and uphold this sutra.
Why is this? In my Sahā world, there are already bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the sands of sixty thousand Ganges Rivers;
each of these bodhisattvas has retinues as numerous as the sands of sixty thousand Ganges Rivers. All of these..."

Regarding the fact that people such as yourselves will be able to protect, uphold, recite, and widely expound this sutra after my parinirvāṇa, the Tathāgata restrains you for three reasons: first, each of you has your own specific responsibilities;
if you remain in this land, you would neglect the benefit of others there. Second, the bodhisattvas from other regions have shallow karmic connections with this land.

Even if one desires to proclaim and transmit [the teachings], there will certainly be no great benefit; this is the third point. Furthermore, if permission were granted, one would be unable to summon those of the lowest capacity.
If they do not come, one cannot destroy the near in order to manifest the far. Question:

The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas manifest bodies and project shadows that pervade the ten directions to guide and transform all beings. How can you speak of "self" and "others," or of taking responsibility for oneself while neglecting others?
In that regard, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the Yakṣa [Realm] truly have no sense of "self" or "other";

however, because sentient beings possess specific capacities (*karman*), it is the natural law (*dharmatā*) of the beginningless past that they first form karmic connections with these Buddhas and Bodhisattvas and subsequently reach maturity through them.
For this reason, those from the lower direction must be summoned. There are three meanings for summoning those from the lower direction: first, they are my own disciples.

There are two reasons why you should propagate my Dharma: first, because its conditions are profound and vast, it is able to benefit this land universally and extend to all lands of the emanated bodies;

second, it enables the opening of the near and the manifestation of the far. (In cases where one has only their own responsibility and lacks the benefit for the world, the matter of establishing karmic connections is shallow and there is no benefit for others;

where one cannot break through the near, there is no remedial benefit; and where one cannot manifest the far, there is no benefit of the ultimate truth. Because these four benefits are absent, one must cease [the propagation]. If you, son, propagate your father’s Dharma, there will be benefit for the world, the establishment of karmic connections will be profound and vast, and there will be benefit for others.)

It is called thus because it further opens up the proximate antidote, further reveals the remote ultimate meaning, and fully possesses the four benefits. △ Third, the emergence from below the earth, in two parts:
first, the narrative by the sūtra compiler describing the signs; second, the inquiry. In the first part, there are five sections: first, the emergence; second, the physical appearance;
third, the dwelling place; fourth, hearing the command; fifth, the retinue. Now, the first section.
When the Buddha spoke these words, the earth of the three thousandfold great thousandfold world-system of the Sahā universe quaked and split asunder,
and from within it, immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas simultaneously surged forth.
The earth split open to manifest the fundamental [truth] by revealing the traces that had previously concealed it;
thus, the earth was rent asunder to symbolize this. △ Second, the bodily marks:
the bodies of these bodhisattvas are all golden in color, possessing the thirty-two marks and immeasurable radiance.
△ Third, their dwelling places:
they originally all resided beneath this Sahā world, in the void of space within this realm.
Residing beneath this world means they do not belong to this world; residing in the void of space within this realm means...
Not belonging to that lower realm, neither this nor that, it signifies the Middle Way, the eternally quiescent land of light (*nitya-śānta-prabhā-kṣetra*).

"Eternal" (*nitya*) is the virtue of permanence; "quiescent" (*śānta*) is the virtue of bliss; "light" (*prabhā*) is the virtues of purity and self. "Eternal" is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); "quiescent" is liberation (*vimukti*); "light" is wisdom (*prajñā*).

Among these three virtues, there is nothing that is not eternal, blissful, self, and pure. Among these four virtues, there is nothing that is not identical to emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the provisional (*pratītyasamutpāda*), and the middle way.

This is the secret treasury that is neither vertical nor horizontal; because it is neither identical to this realm nor separate from this realm, it is represented by the space beneath the world-realm.
As for "dwelling," it means dwelling in the secret treasury by means of the dharma of non-dwelling.
One should know that there are four fundamental virtues upon which one relies, and through cultivation, one attains these four virtues.

When both the support and the supported exist together—such that the supporting body relies upon the supported land—and these two meanings are equal, only then is this the characteristic of the body and land of Vairocana.

Therefore, when one person attains Buddhahood, the entire dharma-realm becomes the environment and the physical body of this Buddha. Since it is so for one Buddha, it should be known to be so for all.

The Buddhas are likewise thus: they are mutually pervasive in successive layers, mutually inclusive in successive layers, mutually manifest in successive layers, and mutually fused in successive layers.
Since this is so for all Buddhas, one should know that what is partially realized by all Bodhisattvas is also like this.
Furthermore, since this is so for the perfected cultivation of merit by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one should know that it is also so for all sentient beings.
The nature and virtues of all that is born are likewise such that they are universally pervasive, mutually inclusive, mutually manifest, and mutually fused;

yet, because there is a distinction between delusion and awakening, they are "six" while being eternally "one. Nevertheless, because the *dharmatā* is equal, they are "one" while being eternally "six.
Thus, the environment and inhabitants of the Avīci Hell are entirely present within the self-mind of the Ultimate Sage, and the body and land of Vairocana are not... [separate].
This is to depart from even a single thought of the lower ordinary beings. △ Fourth, hearing the command:
These bodhisattvas heard the voice spoken by Śākyamuni Buddha, which had issued forth from below.
That is to say, they have come because they heard the command; they have come to propagate the Dharma; they have come to shatter attachments; and they have come to reveal the fundamental nature.
△ Fifth, the retinue:
each and every bodhisattva is a leader of the great assembly, each bringing with them a retinue of sixty thousand *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* (Ganges-sand) followers.
How much more so for those who have retinues numbering fifty thousand, forty thousand, thirty thousand, twenty thousand, or ten thousand Ganges-sands (their number being even greater);

how much more so for those with retinues numbering even as much as one Ganges-sand, half a Ganges-sand, a quarter, or even down to a ten-millionth, a billionth, or a nayuta-millionth of a Ganges-sand (their number being even greater);
how much more so for those with retinues numbering ten-million-billion-nayutas?

How much more so for those with retinues of ten million (their number being even greater); how much more so for those with retinues of ten million, one hundred million, or even ten thousand (their numbers increasing twofold at each stage);
how much more so for those with one thousand, one hundred, or even ten (their numbers increasing twofold at each stage);

how much more so for those who lead four, five, four, three, two, or one disciple (their numbers increasing twofold at each stage); and how much more so for those who dwell alone, delighting in the practice of seclusion (their number...).
Increasing manifoldly in this way, such examples are immeasurable and boundless, beyond what can be known through calculation or analogy.
Each and every one of these is the virtue of the Guide, capable of leading the multitude to the place of treasure.

One should know that it is not merely the single individual, nor is the retinue of sixty thousand *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* [sands] alone many. If one considers it from the perspective of the Dharma-gate, the "one" is...
1. A single path of purity; 2. That is both merit and wisdom; 3. That is precepts, concentration, and wisdom; 4. That is the Four Noble Truths;
5. That is the Five Eyes; 6. That is the Six Perfections. Each perfection contains the ten dharma-realms, and each realm has ten aspects; thus, ten makes one hundred.
One hundred possesses one thousand, and the ten wholesome actions constitute ten thousand. Each perfection contains ten thousand, and the six perfections contain sixty thousand.
That is to say, the sixty thousand dharma-gates are many yet not many, one yet not one; they are neither many nor one, yet they are both many and one.
This concludes the initial section by the Sūtra compiler describing the characteristics [of the assembly]. △ Second, explaining the inquiry after his well-being, in five parts:

1. Making offerings through the three karmas; 2. Stating the words of the inquiry; 3. The Buddha’s response regarding his peace and happiness; 4. Verses in praise of sympathetic joy; 5. The Tathāgata [speaks further].

The description and praise of the beginning, middle, and end: first, the explicit explanation of the offering; second, the explanation of the duration of time elapsed; third, the explanation of the empowerment of the Buddha’s spiritual power. Now, for the first [section]:
after these bodhisattvas had emerged from the earth, they each proceeded to the exquisite stupa made of the seven treasures in the void where the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna resided.
Wherever Śākyamuni Buddha went, he would approach the two World-Honored Ones and prostrate himself at their feet; likewise,
wherever he went before the Buddhas seated upon lion thrones beneath the various jewel trees, he would also pay homage, circumambulate them three times to the right,
and with palms joined in reverence, praise them with the various modes of praise used by bodhisattvas, then stand to one side, gazing up at them with joyful devotion.
To the two World-Honored Ones, he prostrates and circumambulates them to the right; this is the offering of the body-karma. He offers various praises; this is the offering of the speech-karma.
He gazes upon them with joy and reverence; this is the offering of the mind-karma. By means of these inconceivable three karmas, he makes offerings to the Inconceivable One.

Because the three bodies act as the agents of response, the Buddha employs his supernatural powers to respond to them, causing the great assembly to perceive a long duration as short and a narrow space as vast. △ Second, clarifying the time period traversed.
From the moment these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas first emerged, they praised the Buddha with various kinds of bodhisattva eulogies;
this continued for a period of fifty intermediate kalpas. During this time, Śākyamuni Buddha sat in silence, and the fourfold assembly likewise remained silent.

He praised the Buddha with various kinds of dharmas of praise for a duration of fifty intermediate kalpas; how could it have been limited to verses numbering as many as the sands of hundreds of thousands of Ganges Rivers?
Thus we know that even if the Sanskrit text were to accumulate to eight *li*, it would not be considered excessive. Question:
Śākyamuni dwelt in this world for barely eighty years, preaching the Dharma for forty-nine years; tradition holds that he preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* during the final eight years.
Question: How can there be these fifty minor kalpas [within a short duration]? Answer:
It is as in the case of Vimalakīrti’s room, which could accommodate thirty-two thousand lion thrones, each eight thousand four hundred yojanas high.
Since it was argued horizontally that the small can contain the large, why should it not be possible for the brief to contain the long when considered vertically? Question: If...
If that were so, one would have to say that half a day was extended to become fifty intermediate kalpas;
why then does the text below state, "By the Buddha’s supernatural power, he caused the great assembly to perceive it as being only half a day"?

The answer is that it is not that half a day was extended to become fifty intermediate kalpas, but rather that fifty intermediate kalpas were contained within half a day—just as when one travels a great distance while carrying a lamp-king kingdom.
When one enters the chamber of one *zhang* by means of a great lion throne, it is not that the chamber is transformed into a lion throne.
When asked, [it is said that] there is no real dharma of length or shortness; they are fundamentally empty. How can there be frivolous conceptualization regarding inclusion or exclusion? Answer:
If one refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), then large and small, long and short, are all equal. If one refers to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), then large and small...
For the time being, these remain distinct; yet, if one considers the deluded mind, it does not realize that the conventional is entirely the real.
Thus, when speaking of the conventional, the great excludes the small and the long excludes the short, such that they do not mutually contain or encompass one another.
When speaking of the real, it is a single flavor that sweeps everything away. However, if one relies on the thorough realization of the real and the conventional by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—
For this reason, it is not merely that one principle encompasses all principles, but rather that one phenomenon encompasses all phenomena.
Thus, a single room accommodates a lion throne, yet the lion throne is not small and the single room is not large.
From this, we know that half a day can contain fifty kalpas, and fifty kalpas do not shorten half a day, nor does half a day extend fifty kalpas. Furthermore, if we discuss quiescence...
Regarding the realm of the retribution of light, the Bodhisattvas of the lower direction constantly extol the Tathāgata face-to-face;
the Tathāgata silently accepts their praise throughout the entirety of future time without weariness or cessation.

However, as for the karmic conditions of the impure land of cohabitation, he remains in the world for eighty years and must proclaim his parinirvāṇa, thereby causing the great assembly to perceive him as such.

If we discuss the karmic conditions for the expedient Pure Land for half a day, those who have already shattered the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) of the triple world but have not yet shattered ignorance and the secondary delusions (*pṛthag-moha*) should see the Bodhisattvas for fifty kalpas as praised in the *Sūtra of Praise*.

Thus we know that this very Vulture Peak, when discussed horizontally across the four lands, shows that sentient beings with meager merit perceive the Buddha entering extinction; this is the characteristic of the Land of Common Dwelling (*sahā-loka*).
Praising the Buddha for fifty minor kalpas without dispersing even for a moment is the mark of the Land of Expedient Means (*upāya-kṣetra*).

To remain constantly on Vulture Peak Mountain throughout asaṃkhyeya kalpas while sentient beings perceive the end of the kalpa is the mark of my land of True Reward and Quiescent Light (*śānta-prabhāsa*).
Question: If it is the case that Bodhisattvas in the Land of Expedient Means praise [the Buddha] for fifty minor kalpas...
If it has not yet dispersed even now, from where could these subsequent thirteen chapters of the sutra have come? The answer is that the Buddha’s supernatural power is inconceivable;
for the sake of some he manifests length, and for the sake of others he manifests brevity. The three periods of time interpenetrate one another without a fixed location.
For example, even a single dream of a practitioner of the *Sukhāvatī* path can span thousands of millions of billions of kalpas—how much more so [the reality of this sutra]? Is this not so?
Can future events be gathered and brought into the present, so that the sentient beings of this land may receive the benefits of the continued circulation [of the Dharma] after my parinirvāṇa?
△ Third, explaining the empowerment through the Buddha’s spiritual power.
Due to the Buddha’s spiritual power, although fifty minor kalpas had passed, the great assembly perceived them as being like half a day. At that time,
by the Buddha’s spiritual power, the fourfold assembly also saw bodhisattvas filling the empty space throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of lands.

If one considers it from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), then kalpas are fundamentally empty; however, considering it now from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), these fifty minor kalpas are real.
Therefore, those who have already destroyed ignorance perceive the fifty minor kalpas [as passing quickly], whereas those who have not yet destroyed ignorance are unable to endure them for long.
By the Buddha’s spiritual power, he causes them to perceive [the duration] as being like half a day, so that they do not give rise to weariness. Furthermore...
The bodhisattvas fill the empty space of immeasurable lands; how could it be that only the fleshly eye cannot gaze afar?
Even with the divine eye, how could one behold them all? Yet now, through the Buddha’s spiritual power, the fourfold assembly is able to see them everywhere.
One should know that what is long is called short because the deluded mind has not yet been dispelled; what is narrow is seen as vast because of a wondrous capacity.
When that which is long is manifested as short, it signifies that the fundamental (ben) is concealed within the provisional (ji);

this provisional must be opened. When that which is narrow is seen as broad, it signifies that the provisional contains the fundamental; this fundamental must be revealed. Furthermore, when viewed with the Buddha-eye, length and shortness are equal, and breadth and narrowness are equal.
According to the principle, there is neither fundamental nor provisional. However, when viewed from the perspective of the four eyes, [the distinction between them remains].
The enlightened one sees the long and the broad, as if knowing the distant source; the deluded see the short and the narrow, as if grasping at the immediate traces.

Now, when those who are confused take the long to be short, it is said that this is the Buddha’s supernormal power (*ṛddhi-bala*), which manifests the Buddha’s ability to accord with [the capacities of] sentient beings.

Even when the narrow is seen as broad, it is likewise said to be the Buddha’s supernormal power, which manifests the Buddha’s ability to shatter delusion. Furthermore, regarding the measure of his lifespan...
By speaking of the old as long, one causes the short to appear; by speaking of the submerged as already emerged, one causes the narrow to appear broad.

Just as seeing fierce rain allows one to know the dragon is great, seeing flourishing flowers allows one to know the pond is deep, and seeing such a vast number of those transformed allows one to know the transformer is exceedingly great and has existed for a long time.
Since this has now been revealed and made manifest, how could the multitude remain in doubt forever? Therefore, the following section concerns supernatural power (*ṛddhi*).
Within this chapter, after a full hundred thousand years have passed, he then withdraws his tongue-organ and no longer speaks, as if it were only half a day.
This concludes the first section on the three types of karmic offerings. △ Second, the presentation of words of inquiry.
Within this assembly of bodhisattvas, there were four leaders: first, Superior Conduct; second, Boundless Conduct; third, Pure Conduct;
and fourth, Established Conduct. These four bodhisattvas were the foremost leaders among the multitude;
with palms joined together before the great assembly, they gazed upon Śākyamuni Buddha and offered their greetings.
"Does the World-Honored One have little illness and little affliction? Is he dwelling in peace and happiness? Are those who are to be delivered easy to teach?
Does he not cause the World-Honored One to become weary? At that time, the four great bodhisattvas spoke these verses:
"Is the World-Honored One at ease, free from illness and affliction? In teaching and transforming sentient beings, do you experience no weariness?
Furthermore, are these sentient beings easy to transform, such that they do not cause the World-Honored One any fatigue?"
The initial mention of the four guides is intended to illustrate the forty stages of opening, showing, awakening, and entering;
this is as in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, which cites Dharmamati, Guṇakāra, Vajradhvaja, and Vajragarbha to explain these forty stages.

All four are called "practitioners" because they have accomplished the practice of peace and bliss. The "superior practitioner" opens the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, transcending the nine [stages].
The "boundless practice of the realms" (*dhātu*) demonstrates the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñānadarśana*), wherein a single practice encompasses all practices.

The "pure practice" is the realization of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, wherein phenomena and principle are harmoniously integrated and subtle. The "established practice" is the entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, whereby one establishes oneself and others, like the great earth.
Regarding the interrogative phrases, the long prose, and the repeated verses, each contains two meanings. First:

Question: Regarding the two questions on the Tathāgata’s peace and happiness—that sentient beings are easy to deliver and that he himself is at ease—peace and happiness refers to his own practice, while being easy to deliver refers to transforming others.
Both self-practice and the transformation of others are not outside the three categories of robes, seat, and chamber.

These three—robes, seat, and chamber—constitute the "Peaceful and Happy Practice" (Anrakugyō) from the preceding chapter, which was used to exhort bodhisattvas who have just begun their practice. Now, the question posed by the Bodhisattvas emerging from the earth to the Buddha likewise does not go beyond these.

It is said that this is not merely the practice of peaceful conduct; therefore, one knows that the principle of the perfect practice from beginning to end is identical to that of the Buddha, who represents ultimate peaceful conduct, while the Bodhisattva represents partial realization of peaceful conduct.

The preceding chapter elucidates the peaceful conduct of contemplative practice (*guanxing*), extending even to all sentient beings, for there is none who is not the "principle-as-such" (*liji*) peaceful conduct. △ Third, the Buddha’s response.
"Peaceful and well.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly of bodhisattvas, saying: "It is so, it is so, noble sons!
The Tathāgata is peaceful, free from illness and free from affliction. All sentient beings are easily transformed and can be delivered."
Why is this? It is because these sentient beings have, from lifetime to lifetime since the beginningless past, constantly received my transformation;
they have also, under past Buddhas, paid respectful homage and planted various roots of goodness.

As soon as these sentient beings see my body and hear what I preach, they all immediately believe and accept it, entering the wisdom of the Tathāgata—except for those who previously practiced and studied the Hīnayāna.
I now cause such persons as these to hear this sutra and enter the Buddha-wisdom.

The Buddha’s answer regarding the two matters of "peaceful ease" (*anurakṣa*) and "easy deliverance" (*sukha-vinaya*) is that they are mutually constitutive: because there is peaceful ease, there is easy deliverance; because there is easy deliverance, there is peaceful ease.
Why is this so? The following explains the grounds for easy deliverance: by means of [the teachings] throughout the various lifetimes of sentient beings...

This is because they are to be transformed; however, there are two types. The first are those who plant various roots of goodness, who upon first seeing my body and hearing the preaching of the *Avataṃsaka*, immediately believe and accept it, entering the wisdom of the Tathāgata; or those who hear the *Vaipulya* or *Prajñāpāramitā* and likewise enter the Buddha-wisdom.
The second are those who previously practiced the Lesser Vehicle, who are gradually tamed and brought to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

It causes those who hear the sutras to enter the Buddha-wisdom (though in the Vaipulya, Prajñā, and Hīnayāna teachings there are also those who enter it secretly, they are not manifest; therefore, this is not mentioned here). Thus we know that the Buddha-wisdom in the Avataṃsaka, Vaipulya, Prajñā, and Saddharmapuṇḍarīka is no different and should not be ranked as superior or inferior. Nevertheless, although the Buddha-wisdom is the same, the pedagogical manifestations (*śāsana-lakṣaṇa*) differ slightly. For now, I shall briefly clarify ten points of distinction by comparing the Avataṃsaka and the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka. First: 1. The Avataṃsaka is the teaching of the initial enlightenment (*prathama-bodhi*), while the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka is the teaching of the final enlightenment (*paścima-bodhi*). 2. The Avataṃsaka is the teaching of the initial turning of the wheel (*prathama-cakra-pravartana*), while the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka is the teaching of the final turning of the wheel. 3. The Avataṃsaka is the teaching of the initial realization of the Way (*prathama-mārga-adhigama*), while the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka is the teaching of the final realization of the Way. 4. The Avataṃsaka is the teaching of the initial attainment of Buddhahood (*prathama-buddhatva-prāpti*), while the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka is the teaching of the final attainment of Buddhahood. 5. The Avataṃsaka is the teaching of the initial entry into the ocean of the Dharma (*prathama-dharmasāgara-praveśa*), while the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka is the teaching of the final entry into the ocean of the Dharma. 6. The Avataṃsaka is the teaching of the initial opening of the gate of the Dharma (*prathama-dharmamukha-vivaraṇa*), while the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka is the teaching of the final opening of the gate of the Dharma. 7. The Avataṃsaka is the teaching of the initial manifestation of the Buddha’s body (*prathama-buddhakāya-saṃdarśana*), while the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka is the teaching of the final manifestation of the Buddha’s body. 8. The Avataṃsaka is the teaching of the initial revelation of the Buddha’s land (*prathama-buddhakṣetra-udbhāvana*), while the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka is the teaching of the final revelation of the Buddha’s land. 9. The Avataṃsaka is the teaching of the initial reception of the Dharma (*prathama-dharma-parigraha*), while the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka is the teaching of the final reception of the Dharma. 10. The Avataṃsaka is the teaching of the initial planting of roots of goodness (*prathama-kuśalamūla-avaropaṇa*), while the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka is the teaching of the final planting of roots of goodness. These are the ten distinctions. Second: [The Avataṃsaka] is the teaching for those of sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*), while the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka is the teaching for those of dull faculties (*mṛdvindriya*). Third: The Avataṃsaka is the teaching for those who have already awakened, while the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka is the teaching for those who have not yet awakened. Fourth: The Avataṃsaka is the teaching for those who have already attained the fruit, while the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka is the teaching for those who have not yet attained the fruit. Fifth: The Avataṃsaka is the teaching for those who have already entered the stream, while the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka is the teaching for those who have not yet entered the stream. Sixth: The Avataṃsaka is the teaching for those who have already crossed over, while the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka is the teaching for those who have not yet crossed over. Seventh: The Avataṃsaka is the teaching for those who have already reached the other shore, while the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka is the teaching for those who have not yet reached the other shore. Eighth: The Avataṃsaka is the teaching for those who have already extinguished suffering, while the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka is the teaching for those who have not yet extinguished suffering. Ninth: The Avataṃsaka is the teaching for those who have already realized the Way, while the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka is the teaching for those who have not yet realized the Way. Tenth: The Avataṃsaka is the teaching for those who have already attained liberation, while the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka is the teaching for those who have not yet attained liberation. These are the ten distinctions. Third: [The Avataṃsaka] is the teaching of the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*), while the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka is the teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). Fourth: The Avataṃsaka is the teaching of the Buddha’s own vehicle, while the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka is the teaching of the convergence of all vehicles. Fifth: The Avataṃsaka is the teaching of the ultimate truth, while the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka is the teaching of the provisional truth. Sixth: The Avataṃsaka is the teaching of the unconditioned, while the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka is the teaching of the conditioned. Seventh: The Avataṃsaka is the teaching of the eternal, while the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka is the teaching of the impermanent. Eighth: The Avataṃsaka is the teaching of bliss, while the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka is the teaching of suffering. Ninth: The Avataṃsaka is the teaching of self, while the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka is the teaching of non-self. Tenth: The Avataṃsaka is the teaching of purity, while the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka is the teaching of impurity. These are the ten distinctions. Fourth: [The Avataṃsaka] is the teaching of the primary principle, while the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka is the teaching of the secondary application. Fifth: The Avataṃsaka is the teaching of the root, while the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka is the teaching of the branches. Sixth: The Avataṃsaka is the teaching of the essence, while the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka is the teaching of the function. Seventh: The Avataṃsaka is the teaching of the cause, while the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka is the teaching of the fruit. Eighth: The Avataṃsaka is the teaching of the internal, while the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka is the teaching of the external. Ninth: The Avataṃsaka is the teaching of the hidden, while the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka is the teaching of the manifest. Tenth: The Avataṃsaka is the teaching of the profound, while the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka is the teaching of the shallow. These are the ten distinctions. Fifth: [The Avataṃsaka] is the teaching of the sudden (*tun*), while the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka is the teaching of the gradual (*chien*). Sixth: The Avataṃsaka is the teaching of the direct, while the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka is the teaching of the indirect. Seventh: The Avataṃsaka is the teaching of the absolute, while the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka
First, "seeing at the beginning" refers to seeing [the Buddha] when the *Avataṃsaka* was first realized upon his initial enlightenment;
"seeing now" refers to seeing [him] when the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is preached after a long interval as the ultimate truth. Thus, the Buddha-wisdom seen at the beginning and seen now is no different.

Second, regarding "opening and closing" versus "not opening and not closing": in the *Avataṃsaka*, the sun shines upon high mountains and immediately preaches the Sudden [Dharma]; therefore, there is no need for opening and closing.
For those who do not enter [the gate], the Sudden is opened up to explain the Gradual, so that through successive stages of subduing, they may gradually return to the Sudden;

thus, although the Lotus Sūtra opens what was already attained and unifies the opening and the unifying, though these differ, there is no distinction between the two types of Sudden. Third, regarding the horizontal and vertical, the extensive and the concise:
the Avataṃsaka’s Sudden is a direct vertical entry, entering into the Dharma-realm; therefore it is called "vertical" and "extensive," as it does not pass through expedient means.
To speak of the "horizontal" (transverse) aspect, the *Lotus Sūtra* exhaustively covers the five flavors; this is horizontal breadth. To enter the Buddha-wisdom is also vertical breadth.
Since one has already entered the Dharma-realm, one naturally attains mastery over all skillful means; thus, the two sūtras are not different.

Fourth, regarding the distinction between the fundamental and the manifested: in the *Avataṃsaka*, Vairocana is the fundamental [Buddha], while the thousand billion Śākyamunis are the manifested [forms].
If the Lotus Sūtra is taken as the provisional manifestation (*jia*), then the Avataṃsaka Sūtra is its fundamental reality (*ben*);

if the Avataṃsaka is taken as the provisional manifestation, then the Lotus Sūtra is simply its fundamental reality. Furthermore, although the Avataṃsaka speaks of seeing the Tathāgata either at the moment of his initial enlightenment or after immeasurable kalpas since his enlightenment, its intention is likewise to secretly reveal the fundamental reality, though it does not yet do so with explicit clarity.
To say that the realization of the Way has been so long is to speak in terms of neither the fundamental nor the manifest;

for while the principle of the *dharmadhātu* is identical in its being both eternal and fundamental, the phenomena of the hidden and the manifest differ in their temporal proximity. Fifth, regarding whether the teaching was spoken through empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) or not:

in the *Avataṃsaka*, only the *Aśokakusuma* and *Anuvyañjana* chapters were spoken by the Buddha himself; all others were taught by bodhisattvas under empowerment. In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, [the situation is] the reverse.
The three cycles of the Trace Gate (*jìmén*) and the *Běn mén* (Original Gate) concerning the Life Span (*shòuliàng*) and so forth are all spoken by the Buddha himself.

Although the principle of "adding to what was already spoken" (*jiāshuō zìshuō*) remains eternally equal, there are differences in the ritual modes of transformation (*huàyí*). In the sixth [point], regarding the transformation of the land (*biàntǔ*) versus the non-transformation of the land (*bùbiàntǔ*):

the *Huánghuá* (Avataṃsaka) is pure even while being defiled, manifesting the direct Great Way; therefore, it does not require a transformation. The *Fǎhuá* (Lotus Sūtra), however, transforms the defiled into the pure, manifesting the gradual path.

Since provisional authority must ultimately return to the ultimate reality, three transformations are required; if these were not transformed, the Pure Land would not be destroyed, and thus there would be no distinction [between it and the ultimate realm].

Seventh, regarding many locations versus not many locations: the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra’s seven locations and nine assemblies constitute "many locations," whereas the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* takes Vulture Peak and empty space as its locus, and thus is "not many locations. Although the locations differ in number, the principle remains eternally equal. Seventh...
Eighth, regarding "expulsion" (*pratikṣepa*) and "non-expulsion": because there are no Śrāvakas at all in the first assembly of the *Avataṃsaka*, it lacks expulsion;

because the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* directly refutes the attachments of the Lesser Vehicle, it possesses expulsion. Furthermore, in the "Entering the Dharma Realm" (*Gandavyūha*) chapter, the two vehicles are like the deaf and the mute, and thus there is expulsion;
in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, all are given the prophecy of Buddhahood, and thus there is no expulsion. The *Avataṃsaka* only addresses [the Bodhisattvas].
It is relatively easy to achieve results in treating two types of incurable illnesses—whether light or severe—if one is outside the realm [of the Dharma].
However, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* (Lotus Sūtra) can cure even those śrāvakas of fixed nature; if it can cause withered seeds to sprout anew, its achievement of results is even more marvelous.

Ninth, it directly reveals the opening and manifestation [of the truth]; the *Avataṃsaka* is called the "Direct Manifestation of the Real" because it teaches the great direct path of practice. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the "Direct Manifestation of the Real."

The definitive resolution of the Śrāvaka teachings is called "opening the provisional to reveal the real"; the reality thus revealed is ultimately no different [from that of the Mahāyāna]. Tenth, regarding those of sharp and dull faculties:
those of sharp faculties awaken immediately upon hearing the *Avataṃsaka*, whereas those of dull faculties awaken only through the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

Although their faculties differ, the principle they awaken to is one; yet, because it enables those of dull faculties to awaken, its merit is doubly difficult to achieve. Thus, the sūtras should necessarily differ.

Briefly stated, because the ten kinds of distinct wisdoms and the dharma-realm are equal and without differentiation, it is said that upon first seeing my body and hearing what I preach, they all immediately believe and accept it, entering the wisdom of the Tathāgata.

With the exception of those who have previously practiced and studied the Lesser Vehicle, I now cause them also to hear this sutra and enter the Buddha-wisdom; the clear evidence for this is right here, so there is no need for doubt.

Furthermore, various masters perceive the conditions [of the teachings] as distinct and interpret them according to those differing conditions; thus they are deluded and fail to recognize the way back, drifting further and further from the Way.

If one recognizes that the principle is identical—like a thousand chariots sharing the same ruts—the Buddha-wisdom is no different. Nevertheless, the *Avataṃsaka* clarifies Buddha-wisdom by incorporating the Distinct [Teachings];
the Vaipulya sutras clarify Buddha-wisdom by contrasting it with the Three Vehicles; and the *Prajñāpāramitā* clarifies Buddha-wisdom while retaining the two [vehicles].

Only the Lotus Sūtra opens up for those [teachings] that are supplementary, those that are counterparts, and those that are concomitant—even the three baskets (*tripiṭaka*) consisting solely of dharmas of arising and ceasing—causing them all to attain the wisdom of Buddhahood.
Thus, while the perfect principle (*pariniṣpanna-tattva*) which is the referent is no different between them, the teachings that express it differ in being either pure or mixed;
it is truly not in vain that this alone is called "Wondrous. As the ancients said: "The *Avataṃsaka* is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) and the fulfillment."
The *Lotus Sūtra* is said to be of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*), not ultimate, not complete, and not eternal; yet now this text [of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*] is set alongside it.

If that which was initially entered was of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) while what is entered now is of provisional meaning, then it would follow that what was initially entered was the Buddha’s wisdom while what is entered now is not the Buddha’s wisdom.
Since the Buddha’s wisdom is equal in both cases, the definitive meaning must likewise be equal, and the same applies to completeness and eternity. Furthermore...
The people of the Land [of China] call the *Avataṃsaka* the "Perfect Teaching" (*yuánzōng*) and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* the "Not-True Teaching.
Now, this text shall also be used to treat them as equal. △ Fourth, the verses on rejoicing.
At that time, the great Bodhisattvas spoke these verses:
Excellent, excellent, Great Hero, World-Honored One! It is easy for all sentient beings to be transformed and delivered. You have been able to inquire about the profound wisdom of the Buddhas;
having heard it, we shall believe and practice it, and we rejoice in this.

The "questioner" refers to those bodhisattvas who inquire about the Dharma according to their capacities, as found in the *Avataṃsaka*, *Vaipulya*, and *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras, as well as Śāriputra’s three requests in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
The "subject of inquiry" is profound wisdom, namely the wisdom of the Tathāgata. △ Fifth, the Tathāgata’s description and praise.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the foremost great bodhisattvas, saying: "Excellent, excellent, sons of good family!
You are able to give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy toward the Tathāgata."

When the Bodhisattva rejoices in those who are able to inquire and believe, the Buddha then praises his ability to give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) toward the Tathāgata, revealing that all such inquirers are actually manifestations of past Buddhas.

Thus, while the Bodhisattva rejoices in their manifestations, the Tathāgata praises their fundamental reality; this is also a subtle revelation of the [Buddha’s] lifespan. This concludes the first emergence.

The Introduction is concluded. △ Second, the Section on Questions and Doubts, in two parts: First, the questions and doubts of the bodhisattvas of this land; second, the questions and doubts of the bodhisattvas from other lands.
Within the first part, there are two sections: First, the prose narrative describing their doubts; second, the verses formally posing the questions.
First: At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva and the assembly of bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of eight thousand Ganges Rivers all had this thought:
"From the past until now, we have never seen nor heard of such a great multitude of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas."
Emerging from the earth, they stood before the World-Honored One, joined their palms in worship, and inquired after the Tathāgata’s well-being.
Maitreya and the assembly of bodhisattvas were all filled with doubt for four reasons:

first, that since the time of the *Dharmacakrapravartana* until this present assembly, the great beings of the ten directions have come to gather without ceasing, such that they could not be limited by me.
With the power of the wisdom of one in the final birth before Buddhahood, I see and know all; how could I not recognize even a single person among this assembly?
As I travel and transform throughout the ten directions, paying homage to all Buddhas, I am well-acquainted with every ocean-like gathering;

yet even in the places I have traversed, there is no one I do not recognize. Whether coming or going, I seek them out and find none unrecognized. Where there is no one unrecognized, there is no world.
Furthermore, there must be a reason for this doubt. Those great beings (mahāsattvas) were pioneers who had already advanced ahead; Maitreya was a junior scholar from a later generation.

It is as the text says: the later does not know the former. For example, a woman in a state of meditative absorption is a realm unknown to ordinary women, and the realm of a Bodhisattva who has cast off all hindrances (āvaraṇa) is unknown to those who do not recognize it; because they do not recognize it, they do not know it.
Regarding the third point of doubt: because those Great Beings do not give rise to internal or personal goodness for the benefit of non-human beings, they must be questioned.
Since their true reality is fundamentally the ultimate mark (*dharmatā*), they manifest throughout the ten directions to teach and transform others individually;

thus, all their true and responsive manifestations are not within the realm of Maitreya. If one does not recognize their way of benefiting sentient beings, one likewise does not recognize their [diagnosis of] afflictions.
Because it serves as an antidote and brings benefit, there must be inquiry regarding the four points: First, the Buddha, entrusting the propagation of the sutra, summoned the great bodhisattvas;
the bodhisattvas, out of reverence for their master’s solemn command, came. He secretly revealed the *āyus-pramāṇa* (lifespan), yet this was not known by the assembly at that time.

Since they did not recognize the Tathāgata’s secret intent, they would lack the benefit of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*); therefore, inquiry is necessary. However, as for Maitreya’s manifest traces...
Residing in the stage of the "Place of Rebirth" (Upapadya-bhūmi), one’s original ground should also be profound; why then is it as if one does not recognize it? There are two meanings to this:
if discussed according to reality (*tattva*), it is because being near to the state of the Place of Rebirth, one does not realize the long-standing original ground;

if discussed according to skillful means (*upāya*), it is because the original ground is high while the trace is low, causing doubts to arise among sentient beings. △ Second, the verse praising the formal posing of the question, part four: first, questioning the place of origin.
The section on the four invitations to resolve doubts begins here. At that time,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of eight thousand Ganges Rivers,
and desiring to resolve his own doubts as well, joined his palms toward the Buddha and questioned him in verse:
“O Bhagavān, Supreme among Two-Legged Beings, these immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of great assemblies of bodhisattvas have never before been seen by us.
We pray that you will tell us from where they have come and by what causes and conditions they have gathered. They possess massive bodies and great supernormal powers;
their wisdom is inconceivable, their resolve is firm, and they possess the power of great patience. They are a joy for all sentient beings to behold—whence have they come?”
The first question asks from where he has come; the second asks for what cause and condition he has come.
"A great body with great supernormal powers" praises his entering the Tathāgata’s chamber; "wisdom that is inconceivable" praises his sitting upon the Tathāgata’s seat;

and "his resolve is firm and steadfast, possessing the power of great forbearance" praises his wearing the Tathāgata’s robe. These three are all virtues of his own practice. [End of] Chapter on the Multitude.
"That which is joyfully beheld by all beings" praises his virtue in transforming others. △ Second, the enumeration of the retinue:
Each of these bodhisattvas is accompanied by a retinue of immeasurable numbers, such as those equal to the sands of the Ganges River;
some great bodhisattvas lead retinues as numerous as sixty thousand times the sands of the Ganges. Such a great assembly seeks the Buddha-way with a single mind.
These great masters, numbering as many as sixty thousand Ganges-sands, have all come together to make offerings to the Buddha and to protect and uphold this sutra;
there are also those numbering fifty thousand Ganges-sands, whose count exceeds that [of the former], as well as those numbering forty thousand,

thirty thousand, twenty thousand, down to ten thousand, one thousand, one hundred, and so on, until reaching one Ganges-sand, half a Ganges-sand, or even one part in three, four, or ten million billion.
From ten million nayutas of koṭis of disciples, down to fifty million, their number further exceeding one hundred thousand,
ten thousand, one thousand, one hundred, fifty, ten, and even three, two, or one— those who were solitary, without retinue,
and who delighted in dwelling alone— all came together to where the Buddha was; their number surpassed the former by even more.
If one were to count these great assemblies by tallying sticks, even after more kalpas than the sands of the Ganges River, one could not know them all.
△ Third, asking who the teacher of the Dharma is:
Among this assembly of bodhisattvas of great majesty and vigor, who is it that preaches the Dharma to them, instructs and transforms them, and brings them to fulfillment?
From whom did they first resolve their minds [for enlightenment], what Buddha-dharma did they extol, whose sutras did they uphold and practice, and which Buddha-way did they cultivate?
△ Fourth, the conclusion of the request to resolve doubts, which also has four parts: first, the concluding praise; (extending to) fourth, the collective request of the great assembly.
First: Thus [is described] the great power of wisdom and the supernormal knowledges of these bodhisattvas.
Second: The request for an answer regarding their place of origin.
"The earth in the four directions quaked and split open, and from within it all, the World-Honored One emerged. I have never before seen such a thing in my life;
I pray that you will tell us the name of the land from which he comes. I have constantly traveled through various lands, yet I have never seen this assembly;
among these people, I do not recognize even a single individual."
△ Third, the request for an account of the circumstances of his coming.
He suddenly emerged from the earth, vowing to explain the causes and conditions thereof.
△ Fourth, the description of the great assembly’s collective request.

"In this great assembly today, there are immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of these bodhisattvas who all wish to know the causes and conditions regarding the origins and ends of these bodhisattva hosts.
World-Honored One of Immeasurable Virtue, we pray that you will resolve the doubts of the multitude."
Since it is said that one who wishes to know the causal conditions of the beginning and the end must seek the Buddha’s answer regarding the teacher, the place of origin,
and the circumstances of arrival, this concludes the initial inquiry by the bodhisattvas of this land. △ Second, the inquiry by the bodhisattvas of other lands.

At that time, the various emanations of Śākyamuni Buddha who had come from immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of other lands were seated cross-legged upon lion thrones beneath the precious trees in the eight directions;
each of those Buddhas’ attendants saw this great assembly of bodhisattvas coming from the four quarters of the trichiliocosm.

Emerging from the earth and remaining in the air, each addressed his Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, from where have these immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) assemblies of bodhisattvas come?
At that time, each of those Buddhas spoke to his attendant, saying, "Good sons, wait but a moment; there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Maitreya Śākyamuni."
Regarding the matter you have asked concerning the prediction that the Bhikṣuṇī shall next become a Buddha, the Buddha now answers it;
you yourselves shall hear it through this.
Furthermore, the emanated bodies and their retinues, scattered throughout the ten directions, do not yet know their original ground, as the four benefits have not yet been attained.
That Maitreya shared his doubts with the Buddhas, yet none of them provided an answer—waiting instead for Śākyamuni to respond to Maitreya—is because the matters he inquired about were no light ones;
throughout the entire dispensation of the World-Honored One, they had never been explicitly revealed.

It is for this reason that, through these questions and answers, the long life [of the Buddha] is extensively manifested. This great, profound mystery must await Śākyamuni himself to unveil it; you yourself—

Since the purpose of the emanated bodies gathering here is primarily to serve as witnesses, one should not provide an answer. This concludes the introductory section of the first, the Root Chapter. II. The Section on the Formal Exposition. This has two parts: A. The Exhortation and Permission;

B. The Formal Exposition. Part A has two sections: 1. The Long Prose; 2. The Verses. The long prose further has three parts: 1. Description and Praise; 2. The Exhortation; 3. The Permission. Herein is the first: [The Buddha addressed the assembly: "Good sons, you should know that the Tathāgata has already attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* for immeasurable, incalculable, hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas.

Furthermore, good sons, the lifespan of the Tathāgata is immeasurable and cannot be calculated. Good sons, the duration of the Tathāgata’s life is such that it cannot be measured by the number of kalpas, nor can it be known through calculation or analogy. *Note: The passage above illustrates the "Description and Praise" (述歎) section.*
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva: "Excellent, excellent, Ajita!
You are indeed able to ask the Buddha about such a great matter.
The first 'excellent' describes how your words accord with the Buddha’s own mind; the second 'excellent' describes how they accord with the needs of the multitude."
Contemplating the opening of the provisional traces to reveal the fundamental reality is a discourse not yet explicitly revealed within the temporal teachings of a single lifetime;

therefore, it constitutes the Great Matter of the Buddha. Furthermore, because it must be understood in terms of the profound distance between the stages of cultivation and fruition, rather than the principle of the equality of inherent nature, it is termed "phenomenal" (*shi*). △ Second, the admonition.
"You all should together with one mind don the armor of diligence and resolve upon a firm intention.
With a single mind, admonish yourselves not to be distracted; admonish yourselves to be diligent and not indolent; admonish yourselves to be steadfast and not to retreat.

This is because the Tathāgata’s true wisdom was realized long ago, while his provisional traces have endured for a vast duration, his transformation extending through the three periods of time and his benefit pervading the ten directions—this is no ordinary matter."

This is because [the Buddha] has already awakened to that which is beyond the capacity for conceptual thought; it is also a means of admonishing the great assembly by entrusting [the teaching] to Maitreya.
△ Third, the promise:
"The Tathāgata now wishes to reveal and proclaim the wisdom of all Buddhas and the power of the sovereign spiritual transformations of all Buddhas."
The lion-like prowess of all Buddhas; the majestic and powerful might of all Buddhas.
"Wisdom" is the general designation for the fruit-wisdom (*phala-jñāna*). "Sovereignty" is the virtue of self-mastery; "supernatural power" (*abhijñā*) is the virtue of bliss;
"prowess" (*vikrīḍita*) which removes defilements is the virtue of purity; and "majestic might" is the virtue of permanence. These points perfect the four [virtues].
Because his virtue pervades and benefits sentient beings throughout the three periods of time, it is termed "power" (*bala*).

With respect to the past, his activity over vast and remote eons is termed "sovereign supernormal power" (*vibhūti-ṛddhi*); with respect to the present, his emanations filling the ten directions are termed "lion’s sport" (*siṃhavikrīḍita*);
and with respect to the future, his benefit to sentient beings being eternal and inexhaustible is termed "great majesty and ferocity" (*mahāvega-vikrama*), or alternatively, "exertion."
"Swift" represents the manifestation of the aforementioned state for the sake of the great power to benefit beings in the future;
"shaking the ten directions" signifies that benefiting beings in the present is likewise without impediment. Furthermore, "sovereign supernormal powers" is the ultimate chamber of compassion;
"the lion’s majestic leap" is the ultimate seat of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*); and "fierce great power" is the ultimate perfection of patience (*kṣānti*).
Because this robe realizes these three ultimate virtues, its power pervades the ten directions and the three periods of time, providing inexhaustible benefit.

The initial long prose section concludes. II. The Verse Recitation has three parts: first, the verse on the admonition; second, the verse on the permission to be brief; third, the verse on the praise (which is not explicitly detailed).
Now, the first part.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"You should be diligent and single-minded; I wish to speak of this matter, so do not harbor any doubt or regret."
△ Second, the verse of assent:
"The Buddha’s wisdom is inconceivable; you have now produced the power of faith and abide in the excellence of patience.
Regarding the Dharma never heard before, you shall now hear it all. I now comfort you: do not harbor doubt or fear. The Buddha’s words are never untrue."
Wisdom is immeasurable; the supreme Dharma attained is profound and beyond conceptualization. This shall now be explained; listen with a single mind.
[The initial section on the preliminary exhortation concludes. △ Second, the actual exposition, Part One: From this point until the end of the "Life Span" chapter is the primary opening.

Regarding the two types of distinctions—the manifesting of the near and the distant—in the first part of the "Chapter on the Merits of Distinction," the long prose at the beginning constitutes the general bestowal of the prediction of the Dharmakāya;
the verses spoken by Maitreya constitute the general articulation of the understanding and realization. Within this first section, there are two parts:

the first concludes with this chapter, which briefly reveals and clarifies [the teaching] to shake off attachments and give rise to doubt; the second is the "Chapter on Lifespan," which extensively reveals and clarifies [the teaching] to sever doubts and engender faith. Regarding the first of these:

Second, the initial brief opening of the two doubts and requests for instruction, which itself has two parts: first, the long prose section; second, the verse section. The first [of these] also has two parts: first, the answer regarding the teacher; second, the answer regarding the place of origin. The reason why the cause and condition for the assembly is not answered here is that it will be requested again in the subsequent text. Now, the first part: The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* (The Lotus Sutra), translated by Kumārajīva, Volume One: The Introduction. At that time, the World-Honored One was in the city of Rājagṛha, on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, together with a great assembly of twelve thousand bhikṣus—monks who were all arhats, free from outflows, free from afflictions, having accomplished what was to be done, laid down the heavy burden, attained their own benefit, extinguished the fetters of existence, whose minds were liberated through perfect wisdom, and who had attained mastery over their minds. At that time, the World-Honored One was seated upon a lion throne in the center of a jeweled lotus flower, surrounded by a great assembly of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans. These bodhisattvas all dwell in the space beneath this Sahā world, in the void of this realm, reciting and mastering the various sūtras, contemplating and discerning them with correct mindfulness.
The explanation regarding the space below the realm is roughly as previously interpreted; this answers the question of his place of residence, which is identical to his place of origin.

Regarding the phrase "in all the various scriptures" and so forth, it is a subsequent answer to the questions: what Buddha-dharma is being extolled? who receives and upholds the sutras? and what path of the Buddhas is being practiced and cultivated?
As for "in all the various scriptures," for a person of perfect capacity (yuan-chen), the dharma received is such that there is no dharma that is not perfect.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is a wondrous scripture into which all the sūtras of the ten directions and the three periods of time are entirely subsumed;

therein, the provisional and the real are non-dual, such that one never takes up the one while abandoning the other—this answers the praise [of the sūtra]. To read and recite it with thorough mastery is the answer to "receiving and upholding";

to contemplate and discern it is the answer to "correct mindfulness"; and this is the answer to "cultivation. △ Second, the explanation [of the term "upholding"] has two parts: first, the explanation [of the individual terms].
Regarding the two explanations for the dwelling place—praising and upholding its practice—the first is as follows:
These sons of good family, Ānanda, do not delight in being among the multitude or in much speaking;
they always delight in solitary places, practicing with diligence and vigor without ever resting, nor do they dwell relying upon humans or devas.
"Not delighting in being among the multitude" refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) within and without the realm, which are termed the "multitude.
"Discrimination between the two extremes" is termed "having much to say. "A place of stillness" refers to the Middle Way, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Because the single characteristic of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is beyond all dependence and has no remainder, it is called a "place of stillness. "Diligently practicing with vigor, never resting," refers to the mind.
The flow of the mind proceeds spontaneously in accordance with *sarvajñā* (omniscience). It does not rely on humans or devas;

"humans" represent the extreme of existence (*bhava-anta*) and "devas" represent the extreme of emptiness (*śūnyatā-anta*). Because it does not rely on these two extremes, this realm is symbolized by space;
it is the true abiding in the eternally quiescent light of the *dharmatā-kṣetra* (Dharma-nature land). △ Second, the explanation of praising, receiving and upholding, and practicing.
They always delight in profound wisdom that is free from obstruction, and they also always delight in the teachings of all Buddhas, seeking supreme insight with single-minded diligence.
Because they always delight in profound wisdom that is free from obstruction, they accord with all the sūtras.
He extols [the Bodhisattva] because he constantly delights in the Dharma of all Buddhas;
thus he is able to recite and master it, and through contemplation and discernment, he is able to maintain right mindfulness by means of single-minded diligence in seeking unsurpassed wisdom.

For example, suppose there is a person with a handsome appearance and black hair, twenty-five years of age, who points to a hundred-year-old man and says, "This is my son.
This analogy illustrates clinging to what is near while doubting what is distant; having a handsome appearance and black hair merely indicates that he is young.
A person of a hundred years likewise points to a youth and says, "This is my father; he gave birth to and raised us.
This is like the aforementioned case of clinging to what is distant while doubting what is near.
Such a thing is difficult to believe.
This analogy illustrates the difficulty of believing [the teaching]. △ Third, the application to the Dharma:
The Buddha is likewise; since he attained the Way, the duration has not been long.

they have attained great supernormal powers and long cultivated pure conduct (*brahmacarya*); they are well-able to practice all wholesome dharmas in successive order and are adept at questioning and answering—treasures among men.
It is truly rare for all the world that this man,
who has reached a hundred years of age, should not have been born from one who was only twenty-five years old. Today,
the World-Honored One finally says that when he first attained the Way of the Buddha, he caused them to resolve their minds on enlightenment, teaching and guiding them to turn toward it.
That the World-Honored One, having attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* not long ago, should already be able to perform such a deed of great merit—this is indeed difficult to believe.

The Buddha said to the bodhisattvas: "Suppose there is a man who, For eighty thousand years, Has been wandering through various lands, And has now returned to his own home. His father and mother have long since passed away, Leaving behind only a single son. That son has grown up and become an adult, Yet he remains in another country. His parents, longing for him, Have been searching for him for many years. He wanders through various villages and towns, Seeking his parents everywhere. Meanwhile, his parents, Hearing that their son is alive, Are filled with great joy. They tell everyone: 'Our son is here! They build a large house for him, Providing everything he needs. They give him clothing, food, and drink, As well as bedding and other necessities. They also give him servants and maids, To serve and attend upon him. They provide him with carriages and horses, And employ skilled craftsmen. They constantly bestow upon him Various kinds of treasures. They also give him beautiful women, To serve and attend upon him. They treat him with respect and honor, As if he were their own son. They provide him with all manner of things, Never failing to supply what he needs. This refers to the measurement of the lifespan of the Nirmāṇakāya Tathāgata. To measure the lifespan of the Dharmakāya Tathāgata according to principle means that whether a Buddha appears or not, the nature and characteristics [of reality] are eternally thus.

The realm of the profound is the realm of sensation; since it is immeasurable, boundless, eternally abiding, and indestructible, wisdom is likewise so.

It is like a large box requiring a large lid; thus the text says: "My power of wisdom is such that, attained through long-cultivated practice, the light of its insight illumines the immeasurable, and its lifespan lasts for countless kalpas.
