The Tathāgata’s lifespan is contingent upon conditions: if the conditions are long, it is long; if the conditions are brief, it is brief.
It is like the moon appearing in clear water—the moon does not actually come from anywhere—and the moon vanishing when the water is turbid—the moon does not go anywhere either.

Therefore, the text says: "He manifests birth again and again, and he manifests extinction again and again. Or, he may speak of himself using different names, varying in age and stature; this is merely a conventional designation.
The response-body (nirmāṇakāya) shares the same conditions as life; one should know that what is expressed does not transcend the four propositions:
first, finite; second, infinite; third, both finite and infinite; fourth, neither finite nor infinite. That which is finite is impermanent;
that which is infinite is permanent; that which is both is both permanent and impermanent; and that which is neither is neither [permanent nor impermanent].

Thus, it is neither eternal nor non-eternal. Now, by means of the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), I shall provide two further explanations: one according to the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-śāsana*) and one according to the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-śāsana*).
First, regarding the separate explanation for each: "neither eternal nor non-eternal" represents the ultimate limit of the principle of double negation, which is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

"Eternal" refers to the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*); since the wisdom of the reward body is in profound union with the Dharma, it is also neither eternal nor non-eternal; however, this specifically takes up the correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) that follows the adamantine path (*vajramārga*).

Because it is perfected and no longer subject to arising and ceasing, it is called "permanent. Furthermore, according to the doctrine of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*), the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is neither born nor extinguished, and is therefore called "permanent. Because the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*) is produced by causes and conditions, it is not permanent;

yet because it is perfectly accomplished, it is not impermanent—this is the statement of "neither [one] nor [the other]. Being both permanent and impermanent refers to the Response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
Because its function is inexhaustible, it is also eternal; yet because it repeatedly proclaims extinction, it is also impermanent. Impermanence is precisely the Vajra-mind;
from the advancement of the functions of prior wisdom up to the arising and ceasing, appearing and disappearing of ordinary beings, all are impermanent.
The three Buddhas each have one phrase, while ordinary beings share one phrase; thus, this is the distinct meaning of the two Perfect Teachings.
Regarding the general explanation: each of the three bodies is complete with four propositions. As for the four propositions of the *dharmakāya*:
because it is neither born nor extinguished, it is called "permanent"; because it lacks that false, inverted permanence imagined by ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), it is called "impermanent";

because it is quiescent yet simultaneously illuminates both, it is called "both permanent and impermanent"; and because it simultaneously refutes the eight inversions of both ordinary beings and sages, it is called "neither permanent nor impermanent."

Regarding the four propositions concerning the *sambhogakāya* (recompense body): it is called "constant" because it transcends the two vehicles; it is called "not constant" because it is free from false conceptualizations of constancy;

it is called "both constant and not constant" because its wisdom illuminates both simultaneously; and it is called "neither constant nor not constant" because its wisdom is merged with the realm of ultimate truth (*tattva*).
Regarding the four propositions concerning the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body): it is called "constant" because its responsive applications are uninterrupted.
Because it constantly manifests as identical to arising and ceasing, it is called "impermanent"; because it possesses both meanings simultaneously, it is called "both permanent and impermanent";
and because it is neither a true retribution nor produced by karma, it is called "neither permanent nor impermanent.
Even in ordinary beings, these three types of fourfold propositions (catuṣkoṭi) are present; because the nature of the mind remains unchanging while following conditions, it is called "permanent."
That which is called "from beginningless time until the end of the future, transmigrating through birth and death" is, in reality, neither born nor does it die;
this is the permanence of the intrinsically endowed *dharmakāya*.

Yet, when this very mind-nature remains unchanging while following conditions to flow through the five destinies, its arising and ceasing never ceasing, it is termed impermanence; this is the impermanence of the *dharmakāya*.
Because it is unchanging while following conditions, it is eternal; because it changes while following conditions, it is impermanent—this is the meaning of the Dharmakāya as "both.
Although it is unchanging, it is not static; although it follows conditions, it is not annihilated—this is the meaning of the Dharmakāya as "neither.
Based on the Dharmakāya of inherent nature, these four [aspects] can thus be established.

The first set of four propositions concerns how delusion arises based on the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*): delusion is itself *prajñā*, which is the inherently endowed (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara*) Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*).

This also forms four propositions. The second set of four propositions concerns how karma arises based on delusion and suffering: karma is itself liberation (*vimukti*), which is the inherently endowed Response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*). This also forms four propositions.

These constitute the principle of the "Ordinary Person as the Three Bodies" (*pṛthagjana-tattva-trikāya*), each with its own four propositions; yet, even here, there are ultimately no four propositions.
How much more so regarding names! For those who practice with perfection, they understand according to principle;

thus there are the three bodies (trikāya) in four propositions concerning names, and the three bodies in four propositions concerning contemplative practice (*yogācāra*). When the fruit is perfected, these constitute the ultimate three bodies in four propositions.
From beginning to end, one body is the three bodies, and the three bodies are one body—neither identical nor different.

One should know that the body of a single Buddha is not limited by horizontal or vertical dimensions; it inherently possesses all bodies, and its lifespan and merits appear long or short according to the conditions of those who perceive them.
As the Great Sūtra states: "The lifespan of the Buddha as perceived by ordinary beings and those of the Two Vehicles is like the winter sun;
that perceived by Bodhisattvas is like the spring sun; only when Buddhas perceive the Buddha's lifespan is it truly immeasurable, like [the light of the sun at its zenith]."
The reason it is like this in summer is that ordinary beings on the broad ground are obscured by veils and mists;

even though the practitioners of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles of the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings have severed the four abidings, they do not perceive the Middle Way. If they were to abandon the分段 (fen-duan) body and receive the Dharma-nature body, yet have not yet shattered ignorance, the Buddhas they perceive within the land of skillful means are still merely superior beings. One should know that the two vehicles see only winter.

If various bodhisattvas have not yet ascended to the distinct stages (*viśeṣa-bhūmi*) and abide in the realization shared with ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles, they see [the Buddha] as such;
however, if they have shattered ignorance and attained even a partial realization of the *dharmakāya*, then from the perspective of what they have attained, they see the *saṃbhogakāya*.
Yet, if one considers the limit of their lifespan, it is still called the "excellent response body" (*prabhāsvara-nirmāṇakāya*), for they have not yet exhausted the fullness of the *saṃbhogakāya*.
As long as the source has not been fully exhausted and the ultimate limit of the *dharmatā* has not been reached, the lifespan of the Buddha perceived remains like the spring sun;

only when Buddhas and Buddhas together exhaust the nature and its source do they perceive the lifespan of the *dharmakāya*, which is like the summer sun. Therefore, three analogies are raised to illustrate this:
first, among all that is eternal, empty space is foremost; among all lifespans, those of the Tathāgata are foremost.
This analogy illustrates that the lifespan of the Dharmakāya is without beginning or end, its nature and characteristics being凝湛 (congealed and tranquil).

Second, it is like the four rivers all returning to the great ocean; this illustrates that the lifespan of the Saṃbhogakāya is such that the myriad virtues cultivated are all felt as the Buddha’s recompense, returning to the ocean of lifespan.
Third, the Anavatapta Lake gives rise to the four great rivers; this illustrates the Nirmāṇakāya.

The physical body and life span emerge from the Dharma-body and Reward-body, extending or shortening according to conditions. This chapter’s exposition on measurement clarifies all three bodies in general;
however, from a specific perspective, it focuses primarily on the Reward-body. Why is this? Because the meaning is consistent with the text.

As for "consistency of meaning," the wisdom of the Reward-body is in profound accord with the ultimate above and in harmonious accord with the conventional below, such that the three bodies are perfectly complete. As for "consistency with the text," since my attainment of Buddhahood...
Because it is exceedingly vast and remote, that which is accomplished for the benefit of sentient beings throughout the three periods of time is the Dharmakāya;
that which is capable of being accomplished is the Saṃbhogakāya. Since the Dharmakāya and Saṃbhogakāya are unified, they are able to benefit all things.

Inferring from this, the primary intent of this treatise is to expound the merits of the Saṃbhogakāya Buddha. Thus, the various merits of the three bodies have all existed for an immeasurably long past.

That which was first accomplished beneath the Bodhi tree in the distant past kalpas is called the "Root" (hon), while that which was accomplished today at the site of parinirvāṇa is called the "Trace" (shaku).

It is not without the Root that the Trace is manifested, nor is it without the Trace that the Root is revealed. Although the Root and the Trace differ, they are inconceivably one. As for what is found in various sutras...

Regarding the explanation of the fundamental and the manifested (*honjaku*): the Dharma-body and Reward-body (*dharmakāya* and *sambhogakāya*) accomplished within the state of quiescence are taken as the fundamental;
the two types of response-bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*), superior and inferior, that arise from this fundamental are taken as the manifested.

Now, while all three bodies accomplished within the state of quiescence—even those accomplished throughout the intervening period of immeasurable kalpas—are termed "manifested," [this context] specifically selects only that which was accomplished upon the initial, actual attainment of Bodhi.

The three bodies (trikāya) are designated as the "Fundamental," and thus differ from those in other sutras. II. Extensively revealing and clarifying [the teaching] to sever doubts and engender faith, which is divided into two parts:
A. An exhortation to believe; B. The actual response. In part A, there are four sections: 1. The first exhortation; 2. The first request; 3. The second request; 4. The third request.
Together these constitute four requests and four exhortations, including the three requests from the preceding "Trace Gate" (jibon-mon). [End of section] One.
The admonitions consist of five admonitions and seven requests; they are marvelous, momentous, earnest, and solemn. Now, regarding the first three admonitions:
at that time, the Buddha addressed all the bodhisattvas and the entire great assembly, saying, "O sons of good family, you should have faith."
Having explained the Tathāgata’s words of truth, he further addressed the great assembly: "You all should have faith and understanding in the Tathāgata’s words of truth.
Again, he addressed the great assembly: "You all should have faith and understanding in the Tathāgata’s words of truth."
"Sincerity" means loyalty; "truth" means careful verification and reality. It does not deceive things, for its words reach the ultimate truth.

In the past, because capacities were shallow, one could only speak according to the intentions of others; thus, as a skillful means, provisional authority was exercised to speak of the three vehicles and the near path, without yet revealing the sincere reality.
Now, because this is speaking according to one's own intention, it is called "sincere truth. △ Second and third requests.
At that time, the great assembly of bodhisattvas, with Maitreya at their head, joined their palms and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, we pray that you will explain this;
we shall faithfully accept the words of the Buddha. Having thus petitioned three times, they remained silent.
Since the Bodhisattvas have already embraced these sincere instructions, they dare not harbor any doubts; they will certainly believe and accept what is taught. △ Third Request:
They spoke again, saying, "We only pray that you will explain this; we shall believe and accept the Buddha’s words."
△ The Fourfold Prohibition.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the bodhisattvas would not cease their triple entreaty, addressed them, saying: "Listen attentively. The first prohibition regarding faith is concluded.
△ Second, the direct answer, in two parts: first, the long prose; second, the verse summary. Within the first part, there are two sections: first... [text continues]

Correctly opening [the teaching] to reveal both the near and the distant, and clarifying how the Tathāgata benefits sentient beings throughout the three periods of time, there are two parts: first, exposing the attachment to the near;
second, refuting the near to reveal the distant. Now, for the first:
by the power of the Tathāgata’s secret spiritual penetrations, all in the world—devas, humans, and asuras—all believe that...
Now, Śākyamuni Buddha has departed from the palace of the Śākyas and, not far from the city of Gayā,
sits at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) having attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This passage contains three points. First, "the Tathāgata’s power of secret supernatural penetrations" identifies the Dharma that causes delusion.
Second, "all the world, including devas, humans, and asuras" identifies the multitudes who are subject to delusion.
Third, "all say that [this refers to] Śākyamuni and others now" expresses the sentiment of their long-standing delusion; this refers to what is called "the secret."
That one body is itself the three bodies is called "secret" (bi); that the three bodies are themselves one body is called "mysterious" (mi).
Furthermore, that which was not previously taught is called "secret," while that which is known only by the Buddha himself is called "mysterious.

As for the power of spiritual penetration (abhijñā), it is the function of the three bodies. "Spirit" (shen) is the principle of natural immovability, which is the Dharma-nature body; "penetration" (tong) is [the unimpeded functioning].
The obstruction of inconceivable wisdom is the power of the *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body), which constitutes its essential function; the mastery [of this] is the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body).
The Buddha possesses these three bodies equally throughout the three periods of time; he has truly attained the three bodies for a very long time.
Because they were kept secret within the various teachings, all those in the world—gods, humans, and asuras—all believe that [the Buddha] exists only now.
The Buddha first attained these three bodies at the Tree of Enlightenment; thus, one might take what is proximate to doubt what is remote.
In this fundamental teaching, there is no further mention of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), for once they have opened [to the Mahāyāna], they are all termed Bodhisattvas.

Therefore, it refers only to Bodhisattvas, who are subsumed within the three wholesome realms of existence—devas, humans, and asuras—while the other three evil destinies involve heavy karmic offenses.

Those with dull faculties and little wisdom do not understand this notion of "this-worldly" and "other-worldly. There are three kinds of Bodhisattvas: those of this world, those from other worlds, and those who have long resided here.
Those of this world are those originally transformed [by the Buddha] in this life; therefore, they lack attachment to what is near.
Regarding those from other worlds who have long resided here, there are two types: first, those who manifest from the Dharma-body; second, those who previously attained non-arising in past lives.
Alternatively, some may have previously heard [this teaching] regarding the revelation of the trace and the manifestation of the source;

yet, even if they did not hear it in past lives, when their karmic retribution from those lives is exhausted and they receive the Dharma-nature body, they will naturally be able to hear this long-distant discourse upon reaching the stage of the Dharma-body.

For this reason, one should give rise to the thought that Bodhisattvas are largely free from attachment. "Near" refers to two cases: first, those who have only now attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) in this life.
And those who have not yet attained it all share this same view. △ Second, refuting the near to reveal the far.

The preceding admonition regarding truth and reality was precisely for this purpose. This section is divided into two parts: first, the direct revelation of the far; second, the use of analogies to measure its vast duration.
First: "However,
good son, since I truly attained Buddhahood, it has been immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas."

If the time since attaining Buddhahood is exceedingly long and distant, then Gayā is near; this means that [the distance] is immediately eliminated. △ Second, citing a simile to measure the duration of the remote past, which has three parts:
first, citing the simile and posing the question; second, the answer; third, the application to clarify the duration of the remote past. Now, the first part.
Suppose, for example, there were five hundred thousand koṭis of nayutas of asaṃkhyeyas of trichiliocosms, and someone were to grind them into fine dust.
Having passed five hundred thousand koṭis of nayutas of asaṃkhyeyas of worlds to the east, he were to drop a single grain of that dust;
proceeding thus toward the east until all those grains of dust were exhausted—O sons of good family! In this manner...
"What do you think? Is it possible to conceive of, calculate, or know the number of all these worlds?
Even the worlds where the dust has already fallen cannot be described, let alone those where the dust has not yet fallen;
how could they possibly be described? △ Second, the answer.
Maitreya Bodhisattva and the others together addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, these worlds are immeasurable and boundless;
they cannot be known by calculation, nor can they be reached by the power of the mind.

All Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, with their untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), are unable to contemplate or know their limits. We abide in the stage of *avaivartika* (non-retrogression) regarding this matter."
Furthermore, this is not something that can be fully comprehended; World-Honored One, such worlds are immeasurable and boundless.
First, they are beyond the reach of the power of calculation or the mind; second, they are not what can be contemplated by untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*);

third, they are not what can be realized by those who have attained non-retrogression (*avaivartika*). They are known only through the wisdom of the Buddha. Therefore, the merits of the Buddha are like [the ten...].
That the merit of the ten stages (daśabhūmi) is like the soil of the great earth of Jambudvīpa is no empty word.

Since all who attain Buddhahood necessarily realize the same three bodies, it is said that "the Way of all Buddhas is the same. Since their benefit to sentient beings throughout the three periods of time is necessarily the same, it is said that "this is my expedient means," and that all Buddhas are likewise so.
Furthermore, there are four propositions regarding the fundamental and the manifested: (1) the fundamental is high while the manifested is low;

(2) the fundamental is low while the manifested is high; (3) both the fundamental and the manifested are high; and (4) both the fundamental and the manifested are low. These constitute the opening of the teaching for a single period.

It is revealed that why must [the Buddhas] be entirely identical? If one examines the beginning and traces the end, then the essence realized by all Buddhas is the same in its fulfillment of the three bodies (*trikāya*), and the function arising from those bodies is the same in its pervasion of the three periods of time; therefore, it cannot be said that there is any difference. This concludes the first section:

"Correctly Opening the Near to Reveal the Far. △ Second, clarifying how they benefit sentient beings throughout the three periods of time, taking the initial attainment of enlightenment as the starting point.

The essence (*tattva*) is the fundamental, while the arising of function (*vṛtti*) from that essence constitutes the trace (*liṅga*). Furthermore, the initial actual attainment of essence and function is the fundamental;
all subsequent essence and function throughout the three periods of time are considered traces. The text is divided into two parts: first, the explanation by way of Dharma (*dharmadeśanā*);

second, the explanation by way of analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*). Within the first part, there are two sections: first, the explicit clarification of how [the Buddha] benefits sentient beings throughout the three periods of time; second, the summary of this inexhaustibility.

The first section [of the first part] further has three subsections: first, clarifying the benefit of beings in the past; second, clarifying the benefit of beings in the present; and third, clarifying the benefit of beings in the future.
The first of these [three] also has three parts: first, the locus of benefiting beings in the past; second, dispelling doubts regarding the traces of the past;
and third, clarifying what is appropriate for benefiting beings in the past. This is the first [part].
From that time forth, I have constantly remained in this Sahā world preaching the Dharma and transforming sentient beings,
and I have likewise guided and benefited living beings in hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of nayutas of asaṃkhyeya lands in other places.

Regarding the necessity of clarifying the location: since it was previously explained that the attainment of enlightenment occurred a very long time ago, one might wonder where he has resided ever since;

therefore, it is said that he "always resides in this realm" and preaches the Dharma to benefit sentient beings in other lands as well. This Sahā world is precisely the land where his original response-body (nirmāṇakāya) dwells.
Today, his manifested trace-body (nirmāṇakāya) does not depart from its original site; however, because the times of past and present differ, those who perceive it see it as being consumed by fire.
This means that because those who closely examine the source realize the far-reaching truth, it is said: "My pure land is indestructible and eternally abides on Vulture Peak;
how could one leave Gayā to seek elsewhere for eternal quiescence? Apart from the Light of Quiescence (Jiguang), there is no separate Sahā world.
△ Second, dispelling doubts regarding past traces.
"Good sons, regarding this interval, I have spoken of Dīpaṃkara Buddha and others, and have further said that they entered parinirvāṇa;
all such statements were made through skillful means and distinctions."
An objection is raised: If one has been a Buddha for such a long time, why does the Sūtra state that it was only at the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha that he received his prediction?

Furthermore, if one has already attained Buddhahood and realized the eternally abiding body (*nitya-kāya*), why is it said that the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī (Kumārabhūta) received his prediction during the time of Dīpaṃkara, propagated the Dharma, passed away at the end of his life, entered *nirvāṇa*, and was subsequently reborn in another place? Such instances as these [require explanation].

This is not the only instance; now [the text] refutes [such views], saying that all are skillful means and conceptual distinctions, like the illusory phenomena manifested by a magician which are not real.

It is only at that time that one receives the prediction (vyākaraṇa), and even the physical body born of karmic retribution, subject to birth and death, and its passing away at the end of its lifespan, are all merely traces of transformation emanated from the fundamental source. △ Third, clarifying the past.
Regarding what is appropriate for benefiting sentient beings, there are two parts: first, responding to stimuli; second, manifesting transformation. Now, for the first:

"Good sons, if there are sentient beings who come before me, I observe their various faculties, such as faith and so forth, with my Buddha-eye—whether they are sharp or dull—and according to what is required for their deliverance."
"Those who come to me" refers to the past sentient beings whose gradual and sudden capacities have silently struck against the *dharmakāya*.

"Observing with the Buddha-eye" means that having long since attained Buddhahood, one uses the Buddha-eye to examine and illuminate them without any omission or error, intending to manifest two types of responses—inferior and superior—to benefit them.
There are two powers inherent in these excellent capacities: first, [the power of... (text fragment).

There are two types of responses to the cultivation of goodness: first, the provisional fruits of the three vehicles and the flowery rewards for humans and devas; second, the actual fruit of the Buddha-way.

If one observes with the Dharma-eye, one knows that the myriad virtues, according to their relative weight, each receive flowery rewards and provisional fruits, yet one cannot ultimately know that they will eventually attain the fruit of the All-Knowing Wisdom (*sarvajñā-jñāna*). However, if one illuminates the myriad virtues with the Buddha-eye, then...

To be able to fully know the beginning and end of the flowers and fruits means that this sutra exclusively clarifies how the Buddha’s eye observes and knows all the myriad virtues of sentient beings, ultimately attaining the fruit of the Buddha’s seed-wisdom (*buddha-jñāna*). The various faculties such as faith are the five faculties;

the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) is the "revealing cause" (*vyañjanahetu*), while the four faculties of faith, diligence, mindfulness, and concentration all belong to the "contributing cause" (*pratyayahetu*). These two types of goodness—[the revealing cause and the contributing cause]—are [the means].

The faculties (*indriya*) are each categorized as either sharp or dull, encompassing both sudden and gradual capacities. Within this, the sharp and dull faculties of the sudden capacity correspond to the *Vimalakīrti* (Round) and *Śrīmālā* (Distinct) teachings;

the sharp and dull faculties of the gradual capacity correspond to the *Vaipulya* (Shared) and *Āgama* (Treasury) teachings. Furthermore, Mahayana faculties are termed "sharp," while Hinayana faculties are termed "dull.
Moreover, Hinayana faculties are termed "sharp," while those of the Human and Celestial vehicles are termed "dull. This extends even to the four teachings and down to the human level.

The various faculties (*indriya*) of the devas each differ in their sharpness or dullness; the Tathāgata fully illuminates the sharpness or dullness of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) of all sentient beings within the ten dharma realms as their respective capacities (*tūn*), without any omission or error. He manifests forms and sounds according to what is required for their deliverance to benefit them.
△ Second, the bestowing of transformation (*pariṇāmanā*); this has two parts: first, clarifying the dual benefits of form and sound; second, clarifying the attainment of these benefits.
With joy, he now first speaks of his own name differently in various places; he likewise manifests himself as being of different ages, and further declares that he shall enter parinirvāṇa,
while using various skillful means to preach the subtle and wondrous Dharma.
The differences in names and the variations in age—whether manifesting birth where there was no prior birth, or entering nirvana where there was no prior death—are all benefits through form.
Teaching the Dharma through skillful means is the benefit through sound. Regarding "everywhere": vertically, it spans the number of kalpas as numerous as atoms;
horizontally, it pervades the oceans of lands in the ten directions; and within each single kalpa, it is omnipresent throughout the ten directions.
In each and every land, throughout kalpas as numerous as atoms, there is no place or time that is not one where the Tathāgata has manifested his traces.

As for the differences in their names, some manifest as superior responses (victorious emanations), some manifest as inferior responses, and some manifest as the body of a Buddha, or the bodies of bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and so forth.
Since these bodies are not the same, their names are likewise different. Their ages are great...
Since those of lesser capacity have been shown to possess a physical body, they necessarily have a lifespan that varies in length.
Those who are to be delivered by means of manifest birth must appear to be born in various places despite not being born;

likewise, those who are to be delivered by means of manifest extinction must also appear to be extinguished in various places despite not being extinguished. Therefore, it is said that he will again manifest entering into *nirvāṇa*.
Furthermore, those who preach the subtle and wondrous Dharma through various skillful means—
whether by sudden or gradual, manifest or secret, fixed or unfixed, combined or singular, direct or indirect, bestowed or opened, abolished or established—
all these are the Tathāgata’s skillful expedients, intended solely to cause sentient beings to ultimately achieve all-encompassing enlightenment.
Because it is wisdom, it is subtle and profound. △ Second, clarifying the joy of attaining benefit:
It can cause sentient beings to give rise to a heart of joy.

Because it employs both physical form and voice to transform others, they obtain the four benefits of the provisional and the real; yet, by mentioning only "joy," one is raised as a representative example.
This concludes the first section, clarifying how [the Buddha] benefited sentient beings in the past. △ Second, clarifying how he benefits sentient beings in the present, which has two parts:
first, the response and resonance; second, the bestowal of transformation. Now, for the first:
"Good sons, when the Tathāgata sees that various sentient beings delight in inferior teachings, having meager virtue and heavy defilements..."

"The Tathāgata who sees" refers to the illumination of the Buddha-eye. Those sentient beings who delight in inferior teachings (*hīna-dharma*) are the specific capacities (*indriya*) perceived [by the Buddha].
Those who crave the twenty-five states of existence are those with the capacity for humans and devas, termed "delighting in inferior teachings.

Those who seek their own extinction in the present life are those with the capacity for the two vehicles (*dvaya-yāna*), termed "delighting in inferior teachings. Those who delight in the gradual, circuitous path to the Buddha-way are those with the capacity for the third [vehicle].
The capacity of those bodhisattvas to be taught is also termed "delighting in inferior dharmas," and even those who delight in proximate teachings are termed "delighting in inferior dharmas.
Because the functional efficacy of their two virtues—the expedient and the real—is weak and inferior, they are called "of meager merit.

Because the three delusions—view-delusion, thought-delusion, and the dust-sand-like and ignorance-delusions—are dense and heavy, they are called "of heavy defilement. Question: Is it not the case that for those who have not yet been born [into this world] but manifest birth, both sudden and gradual methods are fully provided?

Question: The two types of transformation and the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*) are for those who delight in the Lesser Dharma (*hīnayāna*), while the Perfect and Sudden teaching is intended for those who delight in the Great Dharma (*mahāyāna*).
How, then, can they both be collectively termed "delighting in the Lesser Dharma"? Answer: There are four reasons for this. First, regarding the past:

although they may have resolved upon the Great Mind (*mahācitta*), they were unable to apply themselves with single-minded diligence; being deeply attached to base desires, they failed to attain transcendence from the world. Therefore—

First, regarding the designation "those who desire inferior things" as those who practice the Lesser Dharma (*hīnayāna*): this refers to the present, such as gods and humans before the Buddha has appeared in the world;
although they possess great spiritual capacity (*mahāyāna-śakti*), their minds are defiled by worldly pleasures or attached to false views, and thus they are said to "delight in the Lesser Dharma.
These two meanings are identical to the sense of "rolling about on the ground" in the following parable. Third, regarding the point of cultivation...

Although one's practice does not delight in the three realms, attachment to views, or minor dharmas, yet one delights in the three vehicles and the extinction of ashes—this is also called "delighting in minor dharmas.
Although one does not delight in the proximate fruits of the three vehicles, one delights in practicing the One Vehicle through successive stages;

because one cannot practice it with a single mind in a perfect and sudden manner, this is called "delighting in the minor. These three meanings clarify "delighting in minor dharmas" from the perspective of the causal gate.

Fourth, regarding the gate of the fruit: because they delight in hearing of a small attainment achieved in the near term—starting from their departure from the palace of the Śākyas until they first attained Bodhi—they do not delight in hearing the long-term, great path of many eons; therefore, it is said they "delight in the small. Such a small mind is not something that begins only today;
if they had previously delighted in the Great [Vehicle], the Buddha would not have spoken of his initial attainment. That he speaks of his initial attainment is entirely for their sake.

This is merely for those who delight in the small [vehicle]. △ Second, the manifestation of transformation has two parts: first, clarifying the manifestation of form; second, clarifying the preaching of the Dharma. Now, the first:
For these people, he says, "I left home at a young age and attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. However, I...

In truth, the time since his realization of Buddhahood has been as long as this; however, by means of skillful means (*upāya*), he teaches and transforms sentient beings, causing them to enter the Buddha-way, and thus makes such a statement.
This clarifies that for the sake of sentient beings, he manifests birth within the present, yet although he manifests birth, in reality he is not born. The preceding [section]...
This clarifies that when beings of both sudden and gradual capacities come to respond to the Dharmakāya, it immediately manifests two types of response—superior and inferior.

The inferior response accords with those of gradual capacity, while the superior response accords with those of sudden capacity. Both of these responses possess both the birth-body (*janman-kāya*) and the dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*).

Regarding the manifestation of the signs of birth for the two bodies of the inferior response: the body of true wisdom enters the womb and is born from the right side, immediately proceeding to practice.

Taking seven steps, pointing with one finger to heaven and with one finger to earth, he declared himself "solely honored above and below in heaven and on earth"—this is the manifestation of the birth of the *rūpakāya* (physical body).

Sitting upon auspicious grass, severing the fetters and habitual tendencies through thirty-four moments of mind, and realizing the fivefold Dharma-body—this is the manifestation of the birth of the *dharmakāya*.
As for the manifestations of the birth of the *sambhogakāya* and the *nirmāṇakāya*:
Riding in a sandalwood palace together with the various bodhisattvas, he dwells within the womb of Māyā, constantly preaching the Mahāyāna and performing great Buddha-works.
He emerges from her right side and traverses the ten directions, taking seven steps in each direction and uttering the lion’s roar; this is the manifestation of his birth-body.
Then, sitting upon the Bodhi seat at the field of tranquil extinction, at the final moment of the diamond-like mind, he severs ignorance.

Exhausting wondrous enlightenment, one shines radiantly, thoroughly illuminating the *dharmatā*; the *sarvākārajñatā* is perfectly luminous, and the myriad virtues are universally complete—this is the characteristic of the arising of the *dharmakāya*.
As for "those who leave home," the inferior response involves leaving the realm of *pariccheda-vedanīya-karma*, while the superior response involves leaving the two types of death.

As for "attaining *bodhi*," the inferior response involves attaining the untainted (*anāsrava*) knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising, which is elicited by the four noble truths of birth and cessation.

That which is named Bodhi is the supreme path that should illuminate the three truths as one reality; it is the ultimate attainment of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*) that constitutes Bodhi.

(Regarding the two types of birth—superior and inferior—the physical body and its characteristics are merely a single instance of entrusting the womb and being born; however, because the perceptions of the two capacities, great and small, differ, it is necessary to distinguish them clearly.

It is not that there are two separate instances of entrusting the womb and being born. This applies equally to the two types of renunciation, the two types of attaining enlightenment, and the two types of the Dharma-body’s manifestation of birth; thus it is said that “the two forms are doubly manifested, and the two beginnings are simultaneous”). Now, I...
The passage following "truly attaining Buddhahood" clarifies that, in reality, [the Buddha] was originally unborn.
Although those gods, humans, asuras, and others now see these two kinds of birth-phenomena—the two bodies—and say he has only just been born, this is not actually the case.
Indeed, I truly attained the Way of the Buddha a very long time ago, as described above; even the analogy of the atoms within a world-system falls short of it, for it exceeds even that. Now...
The manifestation of birth is not a real birth. One might wonder: "If it is not a real birth, why does he manifest birth? The explanation is:
It is solely for the sake of skillful means to teach and transform sentient beings of meager virtue and heavy defilements, leading them into the Buddha-way;
therefore, he speaks thus: "I left home at a young age and attained Bodhi. Other Mahāyāna sūtras merely refute the notion of the inferior response-body (*hīna-nirmāṇakāya*).
Regarding the two bodies—the birth-body and the dharma-body—while their arising is in fact not arising, this does not contradict the supreme response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

As for the dharma-body, it has long since attained Buddhahood; it is precisely this that contradicts the notion that the supreme response-body and dharma-body began to arise at the site of enlightenment (Vajrāsana), and thus it is forever distinct from other sutras.
II. Explaining the Teaching of the Dharma, which is twofold: first, the actual explanation of what was taught throughout the one lifetime; second, the interpretive exposition.
Regarding the reason for this skillful exposition:
first, sons of good family, all the sūtras expounded by the Tathāgata are for the purpose of liberating sentient beings; some speak of his own body, others speak of the bodies of others;
some manifest his own body, others manifest the bodies of others; some manifest his own affairs, others manifest the affairs of others.
All that is spoken is true and not false.
The various scriptures he expounded throughout his entire life—comprising the five flavors and eight teachings—are all intended for the liberation of sentient beings.

Taken as a whole, they explain the sudden and gradual, the manifest and esoteric, the determinate and indeterminate; there is nothing that does not administer medicine according to the ailment, so that all may attain deliverance.

It is because they are liberated. Alternatively, it is said that "one's own body" (*svadeha*) and so forth briefly enumerate all the various manifestations found within the teachings of a single lifetime.
To speak of one's own past causes and conditions is called "speaking of one's own body" (*svadeha-nirdeśa*);

to speak of the various causes and conditions of other Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and disciples is called "speaking of another's body" (*paradeha-nirdeśa*); and to manifest the image of a Buddha-realm is called... [the manifestation of a Buddha-realm].

Manifesting one’s own body appearing as the forms of the nine realms is called "manifesting another's body"; alternatively, manifesting a superior response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is called "manifesting one's own body," while manifesting an inferior response-body is called "manifesting another's body.
Manifesting the affairs of the Buddha-realm is called "manifesting one's own affairs," while manifesting the affairs of the nine realms is called "manifesting another's affairs.

Alternatively, manifesting the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) is called "manifesting one's own affairs," while manifesting the abandonment of limited knowledge is called [manifesting another's affairs].

Manifesting great mastery through his own affairs is called "showing one's own matters"; manifesting the nine afflictions and so forth through the affairs of others is called "showing the matters of others.
That all his spoken words are real and not false clarifies that they differ from the metaphorical tales of the world.
For the sake of sentient beings, he manifests each and every thing; each has its cause and its fruit, and each has its beginning and its end.

In whatever he teaches regarding his own person or the persons of others, concerning his own affairs or the affairs of others, there is not the slightest trace of false or deceptive speech; therefore, he is able to deliver all sentient beings.

It is like a master illusionist who, at a crossroads, conjures various things such as elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep; what appears as an elephant is indeed an elephant, and what appears as a horse is indeed a horse.
It was a horse, not a single detail of which failed to resemble it exactly, yet it was able to bring joy to those who were foolish and small-minded.
The Buddha likewise, through the Great Illusion Samādhi of the Dharma-nature, manifests throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time as his own body and the bodies of others,
and as his own deeds and the deeds of others, teaching and showing them to people so that all sentient beings may behold them.
To hear [this] and yet find not a single fact therein, but merely to construct empty words, would cause sentient beings to believe and accept them only to fail in attaining liberation.

△ Second, explaining the reason for the skillful teaching, which has two parts: first, clarifying that it arises from illuminating the principle of the provisional and the real, which is the very basis of the teaching;
second, clarifying that it arises from responding to the capacities of those who follow the gradual and the sudden, which is the actual teaching itself.
The Conditions. Now, for the first time: Why is this so?
Because the Tathāgata knows and perceives the characteristics of the three realms as they truly are: there is no birth-and-death, neither retreating nor emerging;
there is no one remaining in the world, nor anyone who has entered parinirvāṇa; it is neither real nor unreal, neither suchness nor different from suchness. It is not as [it appears].
The Tathāgata clearly perceives such matters within the three realms as they truly are, without any error.

Indeed, in the true nature of reality (*tathatā-dharmatā*) of this present single thought-moment, there is originally not a single dharma to be obtained, yet there is no dharma that is not fully present and no dharma that is not created.
All ordinary beings and sages are equal and without distinction; yet, [this is obscured by] ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles.
Ordinary people are hindered by the two types of death and cannot liberate themselves;

even the great Bodhisattvas of the causal stages are limited by numerical constraints and cannot pervade horizontally or exhaustively vertically—all of this is due to their failure to fully and thoroughly realize the *dharmatā* of true suchness (*tathatā*).
Only the Tathāgata has, over the course of kalpas as long as eternity, attained full and thorough realization.

Because this is the true *dharmatā*, one is able to know and see, through the wisdom of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) and the Buddha-eye, the characteristics of the two kinds of triple world—those of segmented birth-and-death (*paricchinna-saṃsāra*) and those of transformation (*pariṇāma-saṃsāra*)—as being, in their very essence, true suchness (*tathatā*) and the ultimate reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). One thoroughly understands that these two kinds of birth-and-death are not actually birth-and-death;
thus, there is no "retrogression" for those who remain in the world. Since there is no birth-and-death from which to retrogress, [there is no falling back].
Since there is no birth-and-death from which to emerge, there is no one who emerges and attains extinction (*nirvāṇa*). There is neither birth-and-death nor emerging or retreating;
these ten realms of reality are all empty, and there is neither one abiding in the world nor one who has attained extinction.
These ten realms of provisional names are all empty, for birth-and-death and *nirvāṇa* are like a dream from yesterday; thus, they are not real delusions.
Because the dependent origination that serves as the condition for awakening to and realizing nirvāṇa within birth and death is perfectly manifest, it is not non-existent;

because there are distinctions among the ten realms, it is not a state where identity and distinction are indistinguishable; because the single nature is harmoniously integrated despite its distinctions, it is not a state where difference and non-difference are contradictory.
Thus, people within the two types of threefold realms may either perceive the three realms as existent or perceive the three realms as empty.
"It is not as those within the three realms perceive the three realms. Such matters refer back to the aforementioned sublime truth of the ultimate and the conventional:

that birth-and-death is without birth-and-death, that decline is without decline, that emergence is without emergence, that being in the world is without one who is in the world, and that extinction is without one who is extinguished. Thus it is said:
Reality is not reality; unreality is not unreality; suchness is not suchness; difference is not difference—this is called the matter of the conventional being identical with the ultimate.
The Tathāgata perceives this clearly through the wisdom of suchness, without error;

therefore, he can speak according to his wisdom, employing speech that accords with the individual's own disposition, revealing the provisional to manifest the real, and revealing the traces to manifest the source. There is no doubt of this.
There is no birth-and-death, yet one falsely perceives birth-and-death; there is no emergence from it, yet one falsely perceives emergence from it;
there is no abiding in the world, yet one falsely perceives abiding in the world; there is no parinirvāṇa, yet one falsely perceives parinirvāṇa;

it is not real, yet one falsely perceives it as real; it is not empty, yet one falsely perceives it as empty; it is not suchness, yet one falsely perceives it as suchness; it is not different, yet one falsely perceives it as different.
This refers to the fact that while the ultimate truth and the conventional are one, the Tathāgata perceives them clearly through his wisdom of suchness (*yathābhūtajñāna*) without error;

thus, he is able to speak according to [beings'] dispositions, employing speech that accords with their intentions, establishing provisional means for the sake of the ultimate, and manifesting traces from the fundamental reality.
△ Second, it clarifies that because [the teaching] accords with capacities for the gradual and the sudden, this constitutes the conditions for its exposition.
Because sentient beings possess various natures, various desires, various conducts, and various thoughts and discriminations, he—
wishing to cause them to give rise to roots of goodness— performs the work of a Buddha by preaching the Dharma in various ways through diverse causes,
conditions, parables, and expressions, never for a moment ceasing his activity.

"Various kinds" refers to the myriad distinctions between sudden and gradual, sharp and dull faculties. "Nature" (*prakṛti*) refers to the seeds of past faculties as indicated by habitual inclinations.
"Desire" (*chanda*) is the longing that arises from those seeds, manifesting as active conduct.

"Conduct" (*caryā*) refers to the performance of wholesome or unwholesome karmic actions according to those various desires, extending even to the supramundane practices of the Three Vehicles or the One Vehicle.
Regarding "practice" and "recollection-discrimination": according to the actions performed, an understanding arises; this is precisely "similar wisdom.

For various dispositions, one should employ the *puruṣakāra-siddhānta* (the established truth for individuals); for various desires, one should employ the *lokasaṃvṛti-siddhānta* (the established truth for the world);
and for various practices, one should employ the *puruṣakāra-pratipakṣa* (the remedial measures for individuals).
Both [types of practitioners] employ various conceptualizations and discriminations as appropriate; yet, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is entirely [beyond them]. Why is this?
Because as they follow their respective understandings of conceptualization and provide further explanations of the Dharma, they immediately attain a clear realization of the ultimate truth.
Thus, even when one who desires to practice in the first stage (*bhūmi*) wishes to enter the second stage, they must likewise rely upon conceptualization regarding these two.
The realm of the stages (*bhūmi*) is precisely conceptualization (*saṃjñā*). If one gives rise to true understanding in the second stage, this is the contemplation of conceptualization;

by eliminating the dharma of verbal expression and extinguishing it until reaching the stage of Buddhahood, one finally attains ultimate liberation from recollection and conceptualization, obtaining eternal, quiescent illumination.
Therefore, through various causes, conditions, parables, and figurative expressions, the Dharma is taught in manifold ways so that [beings] may give rise [to this understanding].
The Buddha-activities performed by all roots of goodness have never been suspended for even a moment.

Because the roots of goodness of the provisional and the ultimate differ according to the categories of three, five, seven, and nine, they are called "all. Since they ultimately all converge upon the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), they are termed "Buddha-activities.
Through inconceivable transformations of the three wheels, they constantly expound the Dharma day and night to cause others to obtain benefit without interruption.
Because it has ceased, it is said that it has never for a moment been abandoned; this concludes the second section, clarifying the benefit of beings in the present.

△ Third, clarifying the benefit of beings in the future, in two parts: first, the actual clarification that [the Buddha] does not enter extinction yet proclaims extinction to benefit those of the future;

second, explaining the purpose for proclaiming extinction. The first part further divides into two: first, clarifying that the fundamental reality does not undergo extinction; second, clarifying the expedient proclamation of extinction. Now, the first:
In this way, since I attained Buddhahood, an exceedingly long time has passed; my lifespan is immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, and I abide eternally without extinction.
O sons of good family, the lifespan I achieved while originally practicing the bodhisattva path is still not exhausted, and it is twice as much as the number mentioned above.
"His lifespan is exceedingly great and immeasurable for incalculable *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*": this cites past events. "He abides eternally and is never extinguished":
this clearly elucidates his future permanence and his eternal benefit to all beings. "As for my original practice... and so forth:

this cites the cause to illustrate the fruit, thereby clarifying his eternal abiding; it refers to the time before he had originally attained Buddhahood, when he first realized the perfect cause (*pariniṣpanna-hetu*).

Having ascended to the stage of "Perfect Abiding" (*samyak-sthiti*), the lifespan of the partially realized *dharmakāya* is already inexhaustible, being many times greater than the number of atoms mentioned above;
how much more so, then, is the lifespan of the fruition, which is not merely long-lasting but eternally abiding?

For example, when a crown prince’s stipend is already inexhaustible, how could his provisions ever be exhausted once he has ascended to the supreme sovereignty? One should know that such is the case with the lifespan of the *dharmakāya*.

The lifespan of the *saṃbhogakāya* (recompense body) is without beginning and without end; the lifespan of the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) is long or short according to conditions, manifesting as having both beginning and end.
Here, we are specifically clarifying the lifespan attained through cultivation by the *saṃbhogakāya*.

Therefore, although the past was illustrated by using the atoms of lands as a metaphor—thus implying it has a beginning—the future is described directly as eternally abiding and indestructible, which signifies it is without end.

In the end, it is thus: the three bodies are fundamentally neither one nor different. Those of dull faculties see only the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) and do not know that it is identical to the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body) and the *dharmakāya* (dharma body);
therefore, they falsely calculate them to be impermanent. Those of sharp faculties, however, realize the dharma and reward bodies within the emanation body itself;
this is why they are able to know its permanence. △ Second, clarifying the expedient manifestation of extinction.

However, although I am not actually entering parinirvāṇa at this time, I proclaim that I shall enter parinirvāṇa; it is by such skillful means that the Tathāgata teaches and transforms sentient beings.
When sentient beings of the present see the Buddha, hear the Dharma, or even upon first seeing my body and hearing what I say, they all immediately—

Those who, with faith and acceptance, enter the wisdom of the Tathāgata, or those who previously practiced and studied the Hīnayāna—I now cause them all to hear this sutra so that they may enter the Buddha-wisdom.
Once they have entered the Buddha-wisdom, they will know that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and does not perish;
for such people, I do not proclaim my passing into extinction. Furthermore, there are those among the vast multitude who have formed karmic connections over time, even down to five [people].

Those who have receded from the assembly by the thousands, those who have been transferred to other realms, and those sentient beings who, though currently present, have not yet attained the ripening and liberation of their seeds—because these beings have conditions that will arise in the future, they are taught through the skillful means of proclaiming extinction.

One should know that all three bodies possess the meaning of proclaiming extinction despite being non-extinguished. Regarding the non-extinction and proclamation of extinction of the *dharmakāya*, it is as follows:
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Phenomena are fundamentally unborn and thus now non-extinguished; this is precisely the Dharmakāya, which is non-extinguishing.

It further states: "This is the meaning of quiescent extinction (nirvāṇa); this is the Dharmakāya. Why does it proclaim extinction? If one has already fully realized [this truth], one does not proclaim quiescent extinction;
it is proclaimed only for those who have not yet realized it. Furthermore, if one says that "illumination is quiescence," this is the proclamation of extinction. If one says "quiescence..."
Illumination is precisely the manifestation of the Dharmakāya. Although the Dharmakāya is neither born nor extinguished, it nevertheless possesses birth and extinction:
if the deluded mind clings with attachment, afflictions arise and wisdom is extinguished; if the liberated mind is free from defilement, wisdom arises and afflictions are extinguished.
This extinction of delusion and arising of liberation is the extinction of impermanence; yet, if one understands this arising...
The extinction of delusion is itself quiescent cessation; this arising and ceasing is entirely distinguished in reference to the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*).

If the two conditions of delusion and awakening did not exist, one would not proclaim that such arising and ceasing exists. As for the reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*), it is not subject to extinction; who then proclaims its extinction?
Who possesses wisdom and who possesses afflictions such that one says wisdom can destroy afflictions? This is precisely the distinction between light and darkness.
The meaning of "not mutually excluding" is that the *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body) is imperishable.

If sentient beings do not understand this and, upon hearing it, claim that they are themselves Buddhas, they will become arrogant and indolent, no longer practicing the Path. Therefore, it is further proclaimed that the Path can extinguish delusions:
when afflictions exist, there is no wisdom; when wisdom exists, there are no afflictions. Is it not the case, then, that wisdom is able to extinguish [afflictions]?

The afflictions are extinguished; the response body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is not extinguished, yet it proclaims its extinction. This proclaimer must be the function of the reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and the dharma body (*dharmakāya*).
Since their essence is without extinction, how could their function have an end? Thus, the response body is indeed non-extinguishing;

however, for the sake of sentient beings—if they were to see the Buddha constantly—they would give rise to arrogance and self-indulgence. Therefore, [the Buddha] proclaims: "Tonight, I shall enter parinirvāṇa. Furthermore, as for the dharma body...

The essence is neither born nor extinguished; the Reward Body (Sambhogakāya) fully realizes that there is nothing capable of being born or extinguished; and the Response Body (Nirmāṇakāya), though appearing in succession, is itself neither born nor extinguished.
Therefore, all three bodies are equally non-extinguishing. Now, as a skillful means to teach and transform sentient beings, the Response Body proclaims its extinction;
this event is identical to the proclamation of extinction by all three bodies. First, the primary clarification is that they are not extinguished, yet they proclaim their extinction.
This concludes the section on benefiting the future. △ Second, explaining the purpose for proclaiming his extinction; this also has two parts: first, the harm in not passing into extinction;
second, the benefit in proclaiming extinction. Now, the first: Why is this so?
If the Buddha were to remain long in the world, those of meager virtue would fail to plant roots of goodness and would remain impoverished.
Those of low station who are greedily attached to the five desires fall into the net of discursive thought and false views; if they see the Tathāgata as eternally present and imperishable,

they will instead give rise to arrogance and self-indulgence, harboring weariness and indolence, and will be unable to conceive the thought that such an encounter is difficult to find, nor will they develop a heart of reverence.
If one does not plant roots of goodness, then the two types of goodness—ultimate and conventional—will not arise; this is what is meant by being "unbeneficial.

When afflictions of thought (sahakleśa) involve craving and attachment to the five desires, and afflictions of view (dṛṣṭikleśa) enter into discursive conceptualization, then views and thoughts arise, yet one does not sever them.

When ignorance is layered and thick, and one remains ignorant of it, then one does not sever the two types of evil—the pervasive and the specific; this is what is meant by being "detrimental. Furthermore, when arrogance and self-indulgence arise, then...
If one increases views-afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), one harbors aversion and indolence, which immediately increases thought-afflictions (*vitarka-kleśa*); thus there is the difficulty of impairment.

If one does not give rise to the thought that [the Buddha] is difficult to encounter, one cannot produce the understanding of the Truths (*satyadarśana*). If one does not produce a mind of reverence, one cannot produce the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*); therefore, it is of no benefit.
If one sees or hears of the three Buddhas without them ceasing, there is the sense of pride and self-indulgence; if one hears of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*)... [it does not cease].
Upon cessation, they claim that sentient beings are like Maitreya—identical, non-dual, and equal—and that this very equality is the truth.
From this, arrogance arises in their hearts; they think, "All afflictions are fundamentally unborn from the beginning and now likewise do not cease;
what need is there to cultivate the path? Thus, they indulge in sensual pleasures and negligence, proclaiming, "This is the meaning of quiescence. Furthermore:
Hearing that all sentient beings are the very mark of Bodhi, and that the mark of Bodhi is the very mark of afflictions, they fail to realize that light and darkness do not exclude one another;
instead, they manifest the Buddha’s Bodhi and immediately give rise to arrogance and self-indulgence. No longer cultivating goodness, they become indolent and heedless, proclaiming:
"The wisdom of the Sambhogakāya is able to extinguish afflictions and ignorance; its power is great, for it is the Buddha’s Bodhi."

That which can be extinguished by wisdom is not extinguished in the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body), for arrogance and self-indulgence are easily dissolved. △ Second, the proclamation of extinction is beneficial.
Therefore, the Tathāgata speaks through skillful means, saying: "Bhikṣus, you should know that the appearance of the Buddhas in the world is difficult to encounter.
Why is this? Because those of meager merit may, after the passing of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas, perhaps see a Buddha.
Or, for those who do not see [the Tathāgata], it is for this reason that I say: "O monks, the Tathāgata is difficult to encounter.
When these sentient beings hear such words, they will certainly conceive the thought that he is hard to meet;
with hearts full of longing and yearning for the Buddha, they will plant roots of goodness. Therefore, although the Tathāgata does not truly pass into extinction, he speaks of extinction.

[The Buddha] said: "Therefore, it is proclaimed that although the Dharma is fundamentally unborn and does not perish now, one must extinguish delusions before attaining quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*).

While this Dharma-body is difficult to perceive, its meaning is such that although wisdom is said not to extinguish afflictions (*kleśa*), when there is clarity [of mind], [afflictions are extinguished]."
"O Ananda, you are currently possessed of afflictions; how could you have wisdom? You should know that wisdom is able to extinguish obstructing delusions.
This meaning—that the *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body) is difficult to see and the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) is difficult to see but easy to understand—should be known.

When sentient beings hear this proclamation of extinction, they conceive the thought that the Three Buddhas are difficult to encounter; they feel longing, yearning, and thirst [for them]. Thus, evil is extinguished and good arises. Therefore, the three..."

Although the body is not substantial, it proclaims its own extinction upon its passing. This concludes the initial section clarifying how the Buddhas benefit sentient beings throughout the three periods of time.
II. Summary of Non-falsity:
Furthermore, good sons, the dharmas of all Buddha-Tathāgatas are thus; for the sake of delivering sentient beings, they are entirely real and not false.
Having already attained Buddhahood, he has truly realized the three bodies (*trikāya*), all of which are neither born nor extinguished;

yet for the sake of all sentient beings until the end of the future, he manifests birth and extinction. That he has truly realized the three bodies is indeed not false, and that he manifests birth and extinction is likewise not false;
therefore, it is also not false that sentient beings of the three periods of time each receive their respective benefits. If...
If one discusses only principle and not phenomena, or discusses only nature and not cultivation, how can it be called non-illusory? It would be no different from worldly parables.
Furthermore, if one discusses only phenomena without attaining principle, or discusses only cultivation without awakening to nature, how can it be called non-illusory?
It would be no different from the realm of birth and death of the provisional and the Small Vehicle. Therefore, all are truly non-illusory.
This is because the provisional and the real, the origin and the trace, are all without exception true and authentic. The initial explanation by means of the Dharma is concluded.

Composed by the later scholar of Ancient Wu, Ouyi Zhixu. △ Second Section:
Clarifying the Benefit of Sentient Beings Across the Three Periods within the Root Chapter; this section has two parts: the illustrative parable and the application to the Dharma.

The first part (the parable) has two sub-sections: first, the parable of the skilled physician treating his children, which illustrates the benefit of sentient beings across the three periods mentioned above; second, the treatment of the children.

This section on "The Analogy of Actual Benefit" serves as a summary of the preceding [section] to show that [the teaching] is not in vain; it is further divided into three parts: first, the analogy of traveling far, which illustrates the benefit of beings in the past;
second, the analogy of returning, which illustrates the benefit of beings in the present; and third, the analogy of departing again, which illustrates the benefit of beings in the future.
This is the first part.
For example, suppose there is a skilled physician, wise, discerning, and proficient in medicinal formulas, who excels at treating various ailments.
He has many sons—perhaps ten, twenty, or even a hundred—and on account of some business, he travels far away to another country.

In the previous section on the teaching of the Dharma, there were three points: first, benefiting sentient beings; second, clearing away traces of doubt; and third, what is appropriate for benefiting sentient beings.

Now, we shall provide an analogy specifically for what is appropriate for benefiting sentient beings. Within that appropriateness, there is both the response of the recipient and the application of transformation;

here, we provide a complete analogy for this. For example, it is like a skilled physician who excels at treating all manner of illnesses—this immediately serves as an analogy for my observing with the Buddha-eye.

There is the wisdom capable of responding to them; these people are many, numbering even up to a hundred, which is analogous to sentient beings coming to my presence with the karmic capacity to be moved.
Within the process of bestowing transformation, there are two kinds of benefit—those of form and voice—and the joy derived from receiving such benefit.
Here, for brevity, I do not provide an analogy for the joy, nor do I provide an analogy for the benefit of the voice, as it pertains to the physical form.

Furthermore, within this [passage], there is a brief omission of the analogy for "that which is not arising appearing as arising," but only the analogy for "that which is not ceasing appearing as ceasing.
This single point is precisely the matter of a person traveling far to another country due to external conditions. As for the "skilled physician," there are ten types of physicians:

the first is one who treats a disease such that it increases and is not relieved, or even sometimes causes death; this is like the non-Buddhist practitioners of the view of emptiness (*śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi*) who act according to their own whims.
First, teaching others to give rise to wrong views and sever their roots of goodness causes the Dharma-body to perish and the life of wisdom to die.

Second, treating illness without either increasing or decreasing [the afflictions] is like seeing those non-Buddhist ascetics who practice austerities by throwing themselves from cliffs or leaping into fire;

though they perform such good deeds, they do not attain meditative concentration and cannot sever the fetters. Therefore, it does not diminish [the afflictions], yet because they do not sever the fetters, it does not [increase them].

Third, increasing [the afflictions]: this refers to treating a disease by reducing it without increasing its resistance; once cured, it recurs again—this is like the non-Buddhists who practice meditative concentration to sever the fetters.
Fourth, treating a disease such that it does not recur after being cured, yet the treatment is not universal:
this is like those of the Two Vehicles who treat only one or two types of beings with whom they have a karmic connection, unable to treat all universally.

Fifth, although one may be capable of universal and comprehensive treatment, lacking skillful techniques for curing pain—this is likened to the Bodhisattvas of the Six Perfections whose compassion broadly treats others through difficult practices and asceticism; the *Śāstra* calls these "clumsy perfections" (*dullakṣaṇa-pāramitā*).

Sixth, skillful medical treatment cures those without pain or affliction, yet cannot cure those destined to die; this is likened to the realization of the Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching (*sāmānya-śāsana*).

7. The skillful means of the Dharma treat only those ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who possess the capacity for repentance and reform, but do not treat those who are like "spoiled seeds" or the followers of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*).

8. Although one may be able to treat diseases that are difficult to cure, one cannot treat all diseases simultaneously; this is analogous to the Bodhisattvas prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) according to the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyākhyāna*).
9. Although one can treat all diseases simultaneously, one cannot restore them to their original state as they were before.

This is like the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) in the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya*): the first nine can universally treat all ailments and restore them to their original state, yet they cannot cause them to surpass that original state; this is like the forty stages (*bhūmi*) of the Perfect Teaching.

The tenth stage treats all ailments simultaneously, is able to restore them, and furthermore causes them to surpass the original state—this is the Tathāgata. (Regarding the "ten kinds of physicians," this comprehensively includes both heterodox and orthodox, encompassing those partial [teachings].)

The first three types of physicians mentioned previously are also called "healers," because before the Buddha appeared in the world, all non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) claimed for themselves to have left the household life and each led their own followers. Regarding the third type of healer, it is said that "even after being cured, the illness recurs.

Although they have severed the afflictions of phenomena (*dharma-kleśa*), they still fall back into the three miserable realms because the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) have not been severed; thus, after being reborn through the power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they continue to undergo saṃsāra. As the *Āgama* states: "A skilled physician has four qualities: first, he well knows the symptoms of the disease;

second, he knows the origin of the disease; third, he well knows the methods of treatment; fourth, the disease never recurs. Why is this? Because the symptoms of the disease known [by the first two] do not transcend the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), and the origin of the disease known [by the third] does not transcend...

Regarding the methods for treating the primary and secondary [afflictions], they do not exceed the categories of arising-and-ceasing, impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, and impurity. What is called "not producing" [the aspiration for enlightenment] merely refers to abiding in the two types of *nirvāṇa*.

If these four names and meanings are applied universally across all teachings, then each teaching is distinct according to its specific meaning; this does not contradict the principle of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). However, if one were to directly cite those [teachings] to prove this sutra, it would still not accord with the skillful pacification of the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*), nor with the analogy of the "Original Gate" (*benmen*) where there is repeated arising-and-ceasing—this is profoundly unacceptable.

Eighth, regarding "being unable to restore to health": this refers to when one has not yet entered deeply oneself and is thus unable to cause others to see the Original Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). The meaning of the Dharma-body being shrouded by ignorance is like a physical injury; only when it is made visible again is it called "restoration."

Regarding the tenth [category], "surpassing the original" (*guòběn*): the Dharma-body is originally present, and now one is made to realize that original state; thus it is called "returning" (*fù*). This is contrasted with the nature-endowments (*xìngdé*), which are effortless (*wúgōngyòng*); therefore, cultivation is termed "surpassing.

However, from the first stage (*chūzhù*) upward, these may also be termed "partially surpassing" (*fēnguò*), as residual delusions still remain and they are thus termed "returning. Furthermore, yielding to the ultimate stage of perfection is termed "surpassing. The first three types of physicians are the "old physicians" mentioned in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, who use milk as medicine.
The latter seven are all "guest physicians" who lack skillful means and merely employ the teaching of impermanence.
The Dharma of suffering and non-self is like using bitter, sour, or salty medicine with skillful means; having been brought far away [from it], one is led back to drink milk.

This refers to the ultimate and excellent physician. "Excellent" (*liang*) means "skillful"; being fully conversant with the eight arts is analogous to possessing the three types of penetration (*trividya*) and the five eyes.
"Wisdom" (*hui*) refers to the two wisdoms of provisional and ultimate, which deeply understand the two truths. "Sagacity" (*congda*) refers to discerning with the five eyes.

The distinction between sudden and gradual capacities is no different from this. One who is skilled and practiced in prescriptions and medicines is like the twelve divisions of the teachings, whose literary principles are profoundly deep.

The ability to explain the texts is like the prescriptions, and the principles explained therein are like the medicines. While medicines generally apply to all ailments, here we shall speak for now of the principles;
these principles encompass practice. One who is adept at treating various illnesses is like one who can observe and know the sharpness or dullness of the various faculties.

Skillfully employing the four *siddhāntas*, [the Buddha] has many "sons. Regarding the meaning of "son," there are three types: First, the "Son of the Buddha by way of the True Cause" (*hetu-buddhaputra*).

This refers to all sentient beings, who possess the three kinds of nature-virtues (*prakṛti-guṇa*) of Buddha-nature; because they are thus sons of the Buddha, it is said: "The sentient beings therein are all my sons.
Second, the "Son of the Buddha by way of the Contributory Cause" (*pratyaya-buddhaputra*). This refers to those who have previously heard [the Dharma].
Receiving and expounding even a single phrase or a single verse, the subtle understanding thereby produced is the nature of the *li-yin* (revealing cause);

the subtle practice thereby cultivated is the nature of the *yuan-yin* (conditioning cause). With the true nature as the foundation, these three natures are collectively termed the *yuan-yin*, because they are able to assist and trigger the realization of the one reality. Therefore it is said: "The elder’s sons, whether ten, twenty, or even thirty..."
10. First, by means of play, he entered the burning house. 3. The "enabling cause" (了因) refers to the Buddha-sons who awaken to the Way upon hearing the Dharma.
These three causes bring forth development: when the *dharmatā*-mind (*正因*) arises, it is the virtue of the *dharmakāya*; when the wisdom-mind (*了因*) arises, it is the virtue of *prajñā*;
when the wholesome mind (*緣因*) arises, it is the virtue of liberation (*vimukti*). Collectively, these three natures are termed "development" (*了*).
