Because they are able to thoroughly comprehend the meaning of the Middle Way, it is said that they are "born from the Buddha’s mouth" and "transformed by birth from the Dharma," attaining a portion of the Buddha-Dharma and being true children of the Buddha.
If one understands through the causal factor (*hetu*), one constantly sees the Father;

the Father does not travel far away. If one relies on the conditional factor (*pratyaya*), the faculties (*indriya*) have not yet matured, and thus the Father travels far away, such that one may even drink the poison of others.

Regarding the meaning of "medicine" (*bhaiṣajya*), what is now called "having many sons" precisely refers to the universal gathering of those who possess the causal capacity for enlightenment (*gotra*).
"Ten" refers to the capacities within the Buddha-realm among the ten realms. "Twenty" refers to the capacities within both the Buddha and Bodhisattva realms among the ten realms.
Even up to the number "one hundred," because each of the ten realms mutually contains all ten realms, they constitute one hundred; thus it is "one hundred."
Because the three causes within the realms all possess the nature of virtue, and because they all have the significance of generating goodness, they are all called "offspring.
The phrase "having affairs and conditions" is a metaphor for this land having shallow capacities while that region has mature conditions.

"Traveling far to another country" is a metaphor for not entering extinction now, but rather manifesting extinction—this is what is meant by the statement that he will also manifest entry into *nirvāṇa*. △ Second.
The return [to the world] is illustrated by two analogies: first, benefiting beings in the present; second, the manifestation of transformation.
Regarding the first: later, the sons drank the poison of others; when the drug took effect, they became dazed and disordered, rolling about on the ground.

This analogy refers to the preceding passage concerning the correspondence between the capacity of the recipient and the response of the teacher, showing that sentient beings delight in inferior teachings and possess meager virtue while their defilements are heavy.
When the Buddha was in the world, not only did those who heard the Dharma possess some understanding and practice, but even those who neither saw nor heard him still received benefit;
they were like those born blind who, though unable to see the sun’s orb, nonetheless rely upon the sun for their existence.
Since the arising of the aspiration to attain Buddhahood is not itself extinction, yet [the Buddha] manifests extinction, it is not merely that the great earth falls into profound darkness;

even for those who have previously formed karmic connections with him, their pervasive delusions remain unsevered as they gradually become attached to the three realms. Because the poisons of view and thought afflict them, it is said:
"They drink the poison of others and do not know the way out. Because they are distressed and confused, wandering through the six paths of rebirth, it is said: "They wallow upon the ground."
...Thus it is. △ Second, the analogy for the transformation through teaching, in two parts: first, the analogy for manifesting forms; second, the analogy for preaching the Dharma.
Now, the first: At that time, the father returned home. Among his sons who had drunk the poison, some had lost their original minds while others had not.
Seeing their father from afar, they all rejoiced greatly, prostrating themselves, kneeling, and inquiring after his well-being, saying, "We have returned safely and in peace! We were foolish..."
"May those who have mistakenly consumed poison be granted healing and further longevity;
may they return home. This is like explaining to such people that I left home at a young age and attained *sambodhi*, which is not a manifestation of birth but transcends it.
"Or those who have lost their original mind" is like being greedily attached to the three realms and losing what was previously planted.
Whether sudden or gradual, the various roots of goodness may not be lost; this is analogous to one who, though attached to the five desires, does not lose the roots of goodness of the Three Vehicles.

"Seeing his father from afar" is analogous to when the Buddha appears and sentient beings likewise see his physical body (rūpakāya), yet because they are obstructed by the hindrances of views and afflictions, they cannot personally attend upon the Dharma-body (dharmakāya); thus it is called "seeing from afar."
Seeing or hearing of a Buddha’s appearance always brings joy and reverence, as well as the matter of seeking salvation, all of which is clearly explained in various sutras.

△ Second, the analogy for the teaching of the Dharma. The preceding section extensively clarified what was taught throughout the Buddha’s entire lifetime and explained the reasons for his skillful preaching—namely, that he illuminates the principle while conforming to the capacities of beings.
Now, we shall briefly clarify three points, beginning with the first analogy: the Buddha accepting the invitation to turn the wheel of the sudden and gradual teachings.
The turning of the Wheel of Dharma is illustrated by two parables, and the exhortation and benefit by three parables.

This is the first [of the two]. Seeing his son suffering in such a manner, the father sought excellent medicinal herbs according to various medical treatises—herbs that were fully endowed with color, fragrance, and flavor—and having ground, sifted, and blended them together, he gave them to his son to take.
The medicinal prescriptions in the sūtras are likened to all the scriptural teachings, both sudden and gradual; the medicinal herbs are likened to all the Dharma-gates, both sudden and gradual.

Since these are all the supramundane True Dharma, they are called "fine colors. The precepts of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna are likened to the physical manifestations of the activities of guarding body and speech;
the fragrances are likened to the merits of the various meditations on phenomena and principles, which universally permeate.
Furthermore, "taste" is a metaphor for the flavor of the various wisdoms that can realize the principle of emptiness.
That "all are fully possessed" means that regardless of whether one follows the sudden or gradual, the Great or Small Vehicle, or the partial or perfect teachings, all possess these three trainings.

Moreover, form (*rūpa*) is the meaning of the essential substance of the *dharmakāya*; fragrance is the meaning of liberation, which is free from foul odors; and taste is the meaning of the realization of *prajñā*.
Therefore, all dharma-gates—whether Great or Small, partial or perfect—take these three virtues as their essential substance. *Dǎo* (pounding) is a metaphor for the samādhi of emptiness;
*shāi* (sifting) is a metaphor for the samādhi of signlessness; and *héhé* (blending) is a metaphor for the samādhi of wishlessness.
All vehicles, whether Great or Small, partial or perfect, possess these three kinds of samādhi, and each individual samādhi is fully endowed with morality, concentration, and wisdom.
All three [contemplations] likewise take the three virtues as their essential nature, differing only in degree of clarity and obscurity.
Furthermore, the contemplation of emptiness is like pounding, the contemplation of the conventional is like sifting, and the contemplation of the Middle Way is like blending;

these three contemplations do not depart from the precepts, concentration, and wisdom, nor do they transcend the essential nature of the three virtues. One should employ this Dharma for sentient beings of both sudden and gradual capacities.
That practice is called "causing one to take [the medicine]. △ Second, the parable of exhortation and admonition:
He spoke these words: "This great excellent medicine is fully endowed with color, fragrance, and delicious flavor. You all should take it;
it will swiftly eliminate suffering and affliction, so that you shall no longer have any further ailments."
"You all should take [this medicine]; this is the exhortation. Quickly eliminate suffering and affliction; this is the admonition. He exhorts them to take it early and admonishes them not to delay.
All the various scriptures contain both exhortations and admonitions. △ Third, the analogy for the benefit obtained.
Among those sons, those who had not lost their minds saw that this excellent medicine was both fine in color and fragrance, and they immediately took it;
thus their illnesses were entirely cured.
Because the sons have already gathered [the benefits] throughout the ten realms, only those who did not lose their minds are singled out as being able to obtain present benefit.
From the initial attainment of enlightenment until the final liberation at nirvana, all [attainments] arise solely from not losing the roots of goodness of the Three Vehicles.

Just as one sees a color and fragrance and immediately consumes it, and upon consuming it obtains its flavor, and by obtaining the flavor the illness is cured—this is an analogy for how concentration arises from precepts, wisdom is generated from concentration, and one is able to sever the three delusions. This is the second analogy for returning.
The benefit of beings in the present has now been concluded. △ Third, again using an analogy to illustrate the future benefit of beings. The preceding section has two parts:

first, [showing that] although there is no extinction, one proclaims extinction; second, explaining why it is necessary to proclaim extinction. Regarding the first part, there are again two sections: first, clarifying that the fundamental reality does not undergo extinction;

second, clarifying the skillful means of proclaiming extinction. The subsequent section also has two parts: first, clarifying that even though there is no extinction, there is still harm [if one does not proclaim it]; second, clarifying...
The proclamation of extinction being beneficial is now fully illustrated by four analogies: first, an analogy for the case where non-extinction results in harm;

second, an analogy for the skillful means of proclaiming extinction; third, an analogy for the benefit of proclaiming extinction; and fourth, a retrospective analogy for the fundamental reality that there is no extinction.
First, as for this initial case:

although other persons whose minds have been lost likewise feel joy upon seeing their father arrive, inquire after him, and seek treatment for their illness, they will not consent to take the medicine he provides.
Why is this? Because the toxic vapors have penetrated deeply and caused them to lose their original mind; such is the case here.
To find exquisite colors, fragrances, and medicines and yet claim they are not beautiful is like those who have lost their minds;

it refers to those with whom one’s karmic connection was shallow in the past, as well as those with whom no connection was established at all, who cannot attain liberation during the present age of the Buddha but must wait until after his parinirvāṇa for them to gradually ripen and be delivered. This is what that means.
This refers to future potentialities. When the toxic vapors penetrate deeply, it is like being greedily attached to the five desires and entering the net of discursive thought and false views;

regarding fine colors and fragrant medicines as unpalatable is precisely the inability to maintain precepts and practice meditative concentration, which is why one ultimately fails to attain the flavor of the Principle.
This is like the aforementioned arising of arrogance and self-indulgence while harboring weariness and indolence.
△ Second, the analogy of employing skillful means to announce his own extinction.
The father thought to himself: "This son is pitiable; his heart has been pierced by poison and his mind is completely inverted.
Although he sees me and rejoices, seeking a cure, he is unwilling to take such excellent medicine as this. I must now devise a skillful means to cause him to take it."
The physician then spoke these words: "You should know that I am now old and infirm, and the time of my death has arrived.
This excellent medicine remains here; you may take it and drink it, and do not worry that you will not be cured.
Having given this instruction, he went to another country and sent a messenger back to announce: "Your father is already dead."
The arrival of the time of death is like entering *nirvāṇa*. Leaving behind excellent medicine is like leaving behind the various sūtras, teachings, and dharma-gates.
Furthermore, going to another country is like manifesting extinction in this realm while manifesting birth in another realm; thus, the preceding passage says:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One, remaining in another land, will behold us from afar and provide protection. Sending a messenger refers to either taking [the medicine] oneself or...
In the Great Nirvana, he proclaimed aloud to all, employing either supernatural powers, or relics, or the teachings of the sutras to inspire beings.
Now, by means of the words of the Bodhisattvas of the Four Reliances, he tells sentient beings: "The Buddha has already entered parinirvāṇa;
he has left behind only this Dharma. I now proclaim and propagate it; you should receive and practice it. If, in the future, there were none [to uphold it]...
Regarding the transmission of the sutras and the Dharma through the four reliances, how could sentient beings know for themselves that the Buddha has already entered parinirvāṇa?
Therefore, the four reliances are employed as messengers to convey this. △ Third, the analogy of the proclamation of extinction being beneficial.
At that time, the sons, hearing that their father had passed away, were filled with great sorrow and distress, and they thought to themselves:

"If our father were still alive, he would have compassion for us and been able to protect us. Now he has abandoned us and died far away in another land; we find ourselves orphaned and exposed, with no one left to rely upon.
Constantly harboring such grief, their minds finally became clear, and they realized that this medicine possessed a fine color, fragrance, and flavor.
He immediately took it and consumed it, and his toxic illness was entirely cured.
△ Fourth, the analogy follows that the original reality is not extinguished:
Upon hearing that his son had fully recovered, the father immediately returned home and caused him to see him.
This is truly because after my parinirvāṇa, sentient beings awaken, take up the medicine of practice, and create the causal conditions that can evoke the manifestation of future response-bodies.
As the *Śālistamba-sūtra* (Teachings Left Behind) says: "Those who have not yet been delivered have also already created the causal conditions for their deliverance.
Furthermore, there are those who, through diligent effort and reaching the limit of suffering, immediately perceive the Buddhas at the site of enlightenment, such as [the case of] Tiantai.
The Great Master personally beheld that the single assembly on Vulture Peak remains solemnly without dispersal; this is the verification of the efficacy of taking medicine and being cured of illness.

Thus we know that although extinction is real, it is not truly extinguished, and its benefits pervade all future times. The first analogy, the skilled physician treating his son, concludes the section on benefiting sentient beings throughout the three periods of time.
II. The analogy of the physician’s actual benefit for his son illustrates the conclusion above regarding the non-falsity [of the teaching].
"What do you think, sons of good family? Is there anyone who could say that this excellent physician has committed a falsehood?
"No, World-Honored One.
This concludes the first section, the establishment of the analogy. 2. The Application to the Dharma.

The Buddha said, "I am also like this: since my attainment of Buddhahood, for immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of asamkhyeya kalpas, I have used the power of skillful means for the sake of sentient beings to say that I shall enter parinirvāṇa;
yet there is no one who can truly say that I have committed the fault of falsehood."

The fact that he has attained Buddhahood since immeasurable kalpas past corresponds to the analogy of benefiting beings in the past; the statement that he "will enter parinirvāṇa" corresponds to the analogy of benefiting beings in the future.

Because the present is easy to understand, it is not explicitly correlated. Furthermore, there is no one capable of explaining a false correlation to match the reality of the true benefit for his sons.
Having already fully revealed the vast distance of the past, the intent of this current correlation is precisely [to clarify this].
The long prose section concludes, having demonstrated that the meaning of "abiding eternally in the future" is identical to that of *Mahāparinirvāṇa* and the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*.
△ Second, the verse recitation has two parts: first, verses on the primary manifestation of the distant [future]; second, verses on benefiting sentient beings throughout the three periods of time.
First: At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Since I attained Buddhahood, the number of kalpas that have passed is immeasurable—hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of asaṃkhyeya kalpas."
This does not praise the attachment to what is near, but praises the manifestation of what is far-reaching; "hundreds of millions of years" (*koṭi-varṣa*) is a designation for a number.

△ Second, the verse on benefiting sentient beings throughout the three periods of time, which has two parts: first, the verse on the Dharma-explanation; second, the verse on the parable-explanation. Within the first [part], there are two sections:

first, the verse correctly clarifying the benefit of sentient beings throughout the three periods of time; second, the verse summarizing that it is not in vain. Within the first [of these two], there are three parts; first, the verse on the past.

The verses on the present consist of three; the first three of the future; and the first three of the past. First, the initial verse transcends [the sequence] to praise the suitability of benefiting sentient beings in the past.
Second, the subsequent verses praise the locations where he benefited sentient beings in the past. Third, the verses clear away doubts regarding his traces in the past. Now, for the first:
He constantly preaches the Dharma, teaching and transforming countless billions of sentient beings, causing them to enter the Buddha-way;
for immeasurable kalpas since then, for the sake of delivering sentient beings, he has skillfully manifested nirvana.
The verse on "teaching the Dharma and transforming through instruction" refers to the benefit of speech; the verse on "causing entry into the Buddha-way" refers to the benefit of mind;
and the verse on "expedient nirvana" refers to the benefit of body—within this, non-extinction appearing as extinction simultaneously encompasses non-arising appearing as arising.
△ Second, the subsequent verses on the places where he benefited sentient beings in the past.
In reality, I do not enter parinirvāṇa, but dwell eternally here preaching the Dharma.
△ Third, the verse dispels doubts regarding past traces:
"I dwell eternally here; by means of various supernormal powers, I cause deluded sentient beings not to see me, even though I am near."

Although he was nearby, because [the Buddha] did not see him, he saw only the prediction of enlightenment for the Youth (Mañjuśrī) and his passing away, etc. The first verse, concluding the section on the past, is finished.
△ Second, the verses on the present, divided into two parts: first, the verses on the response and transformation; second, the verses on the manifestation of teaching. Now, the first part:
When the multitude saw my parinirvāṇa and made extensive offerings to my relics, they all harbored deep longing and gave rise to hearts of yearning and devotion.
Having gained faith and submission, their natures became upright and their minds supple; with single-minded intent to see the Buddha, they held no regard for their own bodies or lives.
In the section on "Long-Civilized Responsive Resonance," it says: "One delights in the Lesser Dharma, possessing meager virtue and heavy defilements.

Now, regarding the verse that clarifies "making offerings, yearning with thirst, and so forth," the former was spoken from the perspective of not knowing the meaning of long-term accomplishment, whereas the latter is spoken from the perspective of being able to respond to the manifested traces of transformation.
Furthermore, even though one cherishes and yearns with thirst, to the point of not sparing one's own body or life, [one does so] by means of the Buddha-eye.
This observation is merely for those who delight in the immediate accomplishment of minor dharmas. II. Verse on the Transformation of Teaching:
"At that time, I and the assembly of monks together emerged from Vulture Peak Mountain. I then said to sentient beings: 'I am always here and do not perish;
yet, by the power of skillful means, I manifest both extinction and non-extinction.'"
"Simultaneously emerging from Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa" is the verse on manifesting forms. "At that time, I spoke to sentient beings" is the verse on preaching the Dharma.

Within the long prose section on preaching the Dharma, there is first a direct clarification of all that was taught throughout the generations, followed by an explanation of the reasons for the skillful manner of that teaching;
as that text is extremely extensive, the present verses are very concise. The phrase "always remaining here without extinction" merely serves as a verse to reveal the ultimate reality (*dharmatā*).

The two lines on the power of skillful means briefly praise [the Buddha] according to the capacities of beings; this concludes the two verses on the present. △ Third, the verses on the future in long prose have two parts:
first, the direct clarification that he does not pass into extinction while proclaiming his extinction; second, the explanation of the intent behind the necessity of proclaiming his extinction.

Regarding the first part, there are again two sections: first, clarifying that the fundamental reality does not undergo extinction; second, clarifying the proclamation of extinction through skillful means. The current verse does not follow the original sequence.
First, the initial verse provides the skillful means for chanting "extinction" (*nirvāṇa*) while simultaneously explaining the purpose of chanting "extinction.
The two subsequent verses clarify that, in reality, there is no extinction, and they extensively explain the reasons why one fails to see what should be seen. Now, the first [section].
"In other lands where there are sentient beings who revere, believe in, and delight in [the Dharma], I further preach the unsurpassed Dharma among them.

You have not heard this, and thus you merely say that I have entered parinirvāṇa. Because I see sentient beings submerged in suffering and affliction, I do not manifest my body before them to cause them to feel longing and yearning;
rather, it is because their hearts cherish and long for me that I appear and preach the Dharma for them."
The first verse first clarifies that [the Buddha] does not perish; the subsequent half-verse correctly recites the proclamation of his passing;

the next verse recites the explanation for why it is necessary to proclaim his passing; and the final two lines are a verse on how the proclamation of his passing is beneficial, enabling the fulfillment of future capacities and responses.
△ Second, this verse praises the fundamental reality that he does not perish, while extensively explaining the reasons why the unseen is seen.
By such supernormal powers, throughout incalculable eons, I have always remained on Vulture Peak and other dwelling places.
When sentient beings see the world being consumed by the great fires at the end of an eon, my land remains peaceful and secure, constantly filled with devas and humans.
Its gardens, groves, halls, and pavilions are adorned with various jewels; its jewel-trees abound with many flowers and fruits, providing a place of joy and recreation for all sentient beings.
The various devas beat celestial drums and constantly performed manifold musical offerings, raining down *māndārava* flowers upon the Buddha and the great assembly.
This verse indicates that the Dharmakāya (the fundamental body) is indeed imperishable and eternally resides on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa;
it also indicates that the Nirmāṇakāya (the responsive body) at the time of the fundamental body likewise dwells throughout this land and all other abodes, pervading the ten directions.

Whether pure or defiled, all these realms have their origin here; though the traces of these various places do not shift from this source, sentient beings perceive them through deluded vision as being subject to the exhaustion of kalpas.

Yet, the Buddha-lands are fundamentally without birth or extinction. This very realm of cohabitation (*sahā-loka*) is itself the land of expedient means, the land of true reward, and the land of wondrous light and tranquility (*prabhāsvara*). Why is this so? Because this land of mine is peaceful and secure; it is that which the Buddha has realized.
The Dharma of peace and security is precisely the Land of Constant Quiescent Light; because it is realized by the Buddha, it is the Land of Self-Enjoyment Reward.
That gods and humans are constantly filled therein refers to the ten stages as "gods" and the thirty minds as "humans," which is the Land of Other-Enjoyment Reward.
That sentient beings roam and delight therein is the Land of Expedient Means with Remainder, consisting of nine types of directions.

This is the dwelling place of sentient beings; the celestial drums, music, heavenly flowers, and so forth are the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) of the conventional truth within the Land of True Reward, and the five sensory objects of the dharma-nature within the Land of Expedient Means.
My pure land is not destroyed, yet the multitudes perceive it as being utterly consumed by flames, filled with all manner of grief, fear, and suffering.
These sentient beings of sinful karma, due to the conditions of their evil deeds, shall not hear the names of the Triple Gem for incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).

This explanation for why they are not seen is due to the transgressions of their evil karma. Although the three kinds of pure lands—the *sambhogakāya* (recompense), *nirmāṇakāya* (expedient means), and *dharmadhātu* (tranquil light)—are all entirely indestructible, they appear as if incinerated to those sentient beings because of the causal conditions of their evil karma.

From the perspective of those sentient beings, this is a collective deluded vision (*sabhāga-viparyāsa*), yet from the perspective of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, it is still merely an individual deluded vision (*bhinnakarma-viparyāsa*).
Thus it is said.
All those who cultivate merit and are gentle, upright, and sincere shall all see my body here preaching the Dharma.
This explains the reason for being able to see [the Buddha]: it depends upon cultivating the two causes of conditions and realization. "All" refers universally to the three [vehicles].
This refers to cultivation based on the provisional and the real, as well as true cultivation. Merit is the Tathāgata’s chamber;

gentleness is the Tathāgata’s robe; and straightforwardness is the Tathāgata’s seat. When these three analogous dharmas are practiced and perfected, one sees the Tathāgata through the provisional response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
When the three dharmas of realization are perfected, one sees the Tathāgata through the ultimate reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*) of the true retribution.
When the three modes of practice are perfected, one perceives the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body of quiescent light.
At times, for this assembly, he speaks of the Buddha’s immeasurable lifespan; yet for those who see the Buddha only after a long interval, he speaks of the difficulty of encountering a Buddha.
This is a summary based on the fact that sentient beings either see or do not see [the Buddha], which causes what the Tathāgata has taught to appear inconsistent;
yet while the explicit explanations differ, they are all truly not false. The first verse concludes the section correctly clarifying how he benefits beings throughout the three periods of time.
△ Second, the verse summarizes the non-falsity [of the teaching].
Such is my power of wisdom; the light of my insight shines immeasurably, and my lifespan spans countless eons, attained through long-cultivated practice.
You who possess wisdom, do not harbor doubts regarding this; you should sever them so they are forever exhausted. The Buddha’s words are true and not false.

The first verse praises the Dharma of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas as being thus; the long prose cites various Buddhas to corroborate what I have now versified, and I cite myself to corroborate the Buddhas.
What is attained through long-cultivated practice is precisely what this chapter elucidates: the lifespan of the Tathāgata.
This refers to that which is attained through cultivation, not that which is attained by nature (*dharmatā-pratilambhika*); attainment by nature is without beginning and without end.
The essence of sentient beings and Buddhas is identical; through cultivation, one attains it. Buddhas and their paths are the same, having a beginning but no end.

Because they have a beginning, the past is truly accomplished, with some being long-established and others being newly attained. Because they have no end, they abide eternally without extinction throughout all future time.
The next verse concludes by praising that [the path] for the sake of delivering sentient beings is entirely real and not false, exhorting [practitioners] to sever [delusions].

This is the doubt regarding what is perceived as near. First, the verse on the teaching by way of the Dharma is concluded. △ Second, the verse on the teaching by way of analogy has two parts: first, the verse establishing the analogy;
second, the verse applying it to the Dharma. Now, for the first:
"Just as a physician, through skillful means, speaks of his death in order to cure a mad son—though he is actually alive—and no one can say that he speaks falsely."
The first three lines merely praise the single intent that what is not extinguished is the very extinction of manifestation;

this simultaneously reveals the skillful means for benefiting sentient beings throughout the three periods of time, and further demonstrates that extinction is truly not extinction—that which has long passed and that which will eternally abide in the future are both real and not false.
The fourth line praises the concluding summary of their non-falsity. △ Second, the praise of the application to the Dharma.

I, too, am the Father of the World who rescues those afflicted by suffering; yet for the sake of ordinary beings who are deluded and perceive me as truly existing, I speak of my passing into extinction.
Because they hold the view of permanence and see me as such, they give rise to arrogance and self-indulgence, becoming heedless and attached to the five desires, thereby falling into the evil realms.

This verse also summarizes the teaching that there is no extinction, while simultaneously addressing the single intent of manifesting extinction; it further includes the non-extinction and the presence of decline to demonstrate that the proclamation of extinction is a skillful means.
I always know whether sentient beings practice the Path or do not practice the Path, and according to what is appropriate for their deliverance, I preach various dharmas for them.
Every time he forms this thought, "By what means can I cause sentient beings to enter unsurpassed wisdom and swiftly achieve the Buddha-body?
This verse serves as a summary, showing that [the teaching] is not in vain, just like the skillful means of a skilled physician treating his son's illness.
This concludes the initial section on "Correctly Opening the Near to Reveal the Far."
△ The explanation of the "Chapter on the Lifespan of the Tathāgata" is concluded. Next, the "Chapter on the Distinction of Merit" is explained.

This seventeenth chapter contains the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*), the understanding of the teaching (*anujñāna*), and the dissemination (*pariṇāmana*); within these sections of prediction and dissemination, there are each...

Because their capacities differ in depth, it is said that the Buddha’s teaching on the two aspects of his lifespan—the provisional (迹) and the fundamental (本)—provides various benefits to his disciples.

This includes those who attain benefit through the four faiths during the present age, as well as those who attain benefit through the five grades of practice after his parinirvāṇa; therefore, these are called "merits.

(The fundamental disciples are the multitude emerging from the earth; the provisional disciples are the multitude on Vulture Peak. △ Second, the general bestowal of the prediction of the Dharma-body. Part three: The first scripture.

The general summary of the chapter consists of two parts: the distinction between the two Tathāgatas and the manifestation of the three auspicious omens signifying perfect benefit. Now, for the first part:

At that time, the great assembly heard the Buddha speak of the length of his lifespan and the number of kalpas as being thus immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*), whereby countless sentient beings obtained great benefit.
△ Second, the Tathāgata’s analysis:
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ajita:

"When I speak of the long duration of this Tathāgata’s lifespan, six hundred and eighty *nayuta* of *koṭi* of sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, shall attain [the stage of non-retrogression]."
The *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena). In the Trace Gate, during the three cycles of preaching, those of the three faculties received their predictions;

these were all at the stage of the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*) within the first dwelling of the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*. Now, hearing this from the Root Gate, we see that there are likewise so many sentient beings who have entered the Perfect Dwelling (*pariniṣpanna-vihāra*); therefore, we know [this].
The supreme teaching of this one lifetime brings inconceivable benefit.
Furthermore, there are thousands of times more bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have attained the dhāraṇī-door of hearing and retaining;

those who had previously realized non-arising now hear this supreme proclamation of the Fundamental Gate and enter further into the path of cultivation, increasing and perfecting its subtle excellence.

The path of diminishing and transformation gives rise to the realization of the ten stages of perfect abiding; one attains great *dhāraṇī* and is able to receive and uphold the wondrous Dharma of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching, just as the great ocean universally receives and holds the rain from the dragon kings.
Furthermore, there were bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in another world-system who attained the unimpeded eloquence of joyful exposition.
This is because they have increased their path and diminished their births, realizing the ten inconceivable practices of the perfected stage;
thus, by horizontally and vertically penetrating the Buddha-dharma—which is as vast as the sands of the Ganges—they are able to expound freely with unimpeded eloquence.
Furthermore, there were Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in another world-system who attained hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of immeasurable *āvartanī-dhāraṇīs*.

This is the stage of the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) where the path increases and birth is diminished; it is the dharma in which principle and phenomenon are perfectly interfused, and the ultimate and conventional truths are non-dual.
Within one there are immeasurables, and within the immeasurable there is one; they revolve in layers upon layers, mutually encompassing and mutually supporting one another.
Furthermore, there were Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, as numerous as the atoms in a trichiliocosm, who were able to turn the irreversible wheel of Dharma.

This is the increase of the path and the reduction of births that realizes the first bhūmi; it is the continuous flow of mind-moments into the ocean of sarvajñā, the perfect revolution of the three non-retrogressive wheels.
Furthermore, there were bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as numerous as the atoms in two thousand intermediate lands, who were able to turn the wheel of the pure Dharma.
The wheel.

This refers to the two stages of "increasing the path and diminishing birth" and "realizing perfection," wherein one personally leaves behind the defilements of the three delusions and causes others to leave behind the defilements of the three delusions;
hence it is called "turning the pure wheel of Dharma."
Furthermore, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as numerous as the atoms in a small chiliocosm, who will attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* after eight more births.
This is because they have increased their path and diminished their births, having realized the fourth stage (*bhūmi*) and remaining with only eight grades of subtle ignorance.

It is said that one shall attain Bodhi after eight births: by severing the first grade [of delusion], one enters the fifth stage (bhūmi); by severing the second grade, one enters the sixth stage; by severing the third grade, one enters the seventh stage;
by severing the fourth grade, one enters the eighth stage; by severing the fifth grade, one enters the ninth stage; by severing the sixth grade, one enters the tenth stage;
by severing the seventh grade, one enters the Stage of Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi); and by exhausting the eighth grade, one enters the Stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (miao-jue).
With each severance of a grade of ignorance, one diminishes a transformation-rebirth and increases a portion of the Middle Way of clarity.
Furthermore, there are Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as numerous as the atoms in four sets of four continents,
who shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi after four more births.

This refers to the stage of increasing the Path and diminishing birth, wherein one realizes the perfection of the eighth bhūmi while remaining with four grades of subtle ignorance yet to be eliminated.

By diminishing one birth, one enters the ninth bhūmi; by diminishing two births, one enters the tenth bhūmi; by diminishing three births, one enters the Stage of Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi);
and when the four births are fully exhausted, one immediately attains Wondrous Enlightenment (miao-jue).
Furthermore, there were bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as numerous as the atoms in three or four *cāturdvīpaka* worlds, who were destined to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* after three more births.
This refers to those who, having increased their path and diminished their remaining births, had realized the nine stages of perfection; thus, they required only three more births.
Furthermore, there were bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in two sets of four continents who were to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* after two more births.
This was because they had increased their path and diminished their births, thereby realizing the perfection of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), and thus remained with only two births remaining.
Furthermore, there were Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, as numerous as the atoms in a four-continent world-system,
who were destined to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in one more lifetime.
This refers to those who have increased their path and diminished their births, having realized perfect equal enlightenment and thus remaining with only one life remaining.
Furthermore, there were sentient beings as numerous as the atoms in eight worlds who all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

This refers to ordinary worldlings at the level of the "broad ground" (*pṛthagjana*) who, through the power of hearing this sutra, realize the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) and give rise to a semblance of the Bodhicitta.

That so many have attained the Way through this *Honmon* (the Essential Gate) is something that no other sutras can equal. This is truly because the Original Source manifested its traces, opening and guiding beings everywhere;
having encountered these teachings repeatedly throughout the intermediate stages, they have now been brought to maturity.

In this present age, they are tamed through the various flavors of the Dharma, gathered together and condensed, finally converging in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. It is like a farming family where growth begins in spring and continues through summer.

From plowing and sowing through weeding and tending, to the autumn harvest and winter storage—all is gathered at once. After this, even those who subsequently attain the Way are like those who merely gather leftover grains.
Question: Why is there no mention of those in the fifth, sixth, or seventh stages when bestowing the prediction of the Dharma-body?
Answer: This cannot be known through conceptual thought; only a Tathāgata can discern it, and only one in the position of the "Successor" (Bodhisattva of the Final Stage) can.
Question: Why must one necessarily raise doubts regarding this point? Furthermore, how do the *dhāraṇīs* for hearing and retaining, etc., differ from their counterparts in the older texts?
Answer: Names such as "patience in the non-arising of dharmas" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) apply equally to the partial and the perfect, the provisional and the real;

they have no fixed status. One need only provide an exegesis that brings them into accord with the perfect principle. Now, for the sake of convenience in explaining the meaning, I have made this classification.

If one wishes to correlate these [categories] so that they mutually integrate, what is there that is not possible? One should know that only the eight births, the four births, and so forth possess a fixed sequence;
all others are merely correlations and explanations based on their respective meanings. This concludes the second section: The Distinctions of the Tathāgata. △ Third:
The Auspicious Omens Signifying Perfect Benefit.
When the Buddha spoke these words on how these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas had attained great benefit from the Dharma, mandārava flowers and mahāmandārava flowers rained down from the void,
scattering over the Buddhas seated upon lion thrones beneath the immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of jewel trees,
as well as scattering over Śākyamuni seated upon the lion throne within the stupa made of the seven precious gems.
The Buddha, as well as the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna who has long since entered parinirvāṇa, also scattered [flowers] over all the great bodhisattvas and the fourfold assembly;
furthermore, they rained down fine powdered sandalwood and aloeswood incense, while in the midst of space celestial drums resounded of their own accord with profound and far-reaching sounds,
and there fell thousands of kinds of celestial garments, hanging necklaces, pearl necklaces, and maṇi-jewels.

Necklaces and wish-fulfilling jewel necklaces pervaded the nine directions, while various precious incense burners burned priceless incense that naturally reached everywhere to make offerings to the great assembly.
Above each Buddha, there were bodhisattvas holding banners and canopies, ascending in succession up to the Brahma Heaven; these bodhisattvas, with wondrous voices, sang immeasurable verses of praise.
Praising the Buddhas:

herein there are likewise six auspicious omens—first, the omen of the rain of flowers; second, the omen of the rain of incense, which symbolizes the virtue of one's own practice through perfect and wondrous wisdom;
third, the omen of the celestial drums; and fourth, the omen of celestial robes and necklaces, which symbolize the perfect and wondrous teaching and practice.
This is the virtue of transforming others. Fifth, the auspicious sign of offering incense; sixth, the auspicious sign of praising with banners and canopies.

These manifest that one’s own practice and the transformation of others both converge in the ultimate fruit of perfect subtlety. First, regarding the rain of flowers from space: "space" symbolizes the equal Dharma-nature;
from this Dharma-nature arise the flowers of the perfectly subtle wisdom of the forty stages of true reality. As for the preceding...

The text uses the emanated bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) to represent the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), Śākyamuni to represent the reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*), and Prabhūtaratna to represent the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

Now, first the emanated Buddhas are scattered, followed by Śākyamuni and Prabhūtaratna; this intends to reveal that although the three bodies are neither identical nor different, it is only through seeing the response-body that one comes to know the cultivated virtues of the reward-body and the inherent virtues of the dharma-body. Furthermore, [the text] scatters one [of the bodies].

The four assemblies of all bodhisattvas represent that the entire great assembly has attained the wondrous wisdom of the perfect cause and has realized the wondrous fruit of the three bodies (trikāya) without distinction.

The fine powder of sandalwood, aloeswood, and various meritorious incenses also arise from the dharma-nature (dharmatā), and are likewise offered as worship to the three bodies and extended to the four assemblies; this is merely an abbreviated expression of the text. The celestial drum...

The self-sounding [drum] symbolizes the manifestation of the perfect voice that expounds the profound and wondrous teachings. The thousand kinds of celestial robes symbolize the robe of the patience of cessation (*śānti-kṣānti*), which universally covers all things.
The hanging necklaces symbolize the four kinds of necklaces—precepts, concentration, wisdom, and *dhāraṇī*—which gather and transform sentient beings, causing them to give rise to joy.
*Maṇi* is translated here as "as one wishes" (*yathā-icchita*), and is also called "wish-fulfilling."
Regarding the term "jewels" (*maṇi*): it may be a case of intentional repetition (*punarukta*), raising both the Sanskrit and Chinese terms together;

or, the four characters for "necklaces" (*hāra*) may be used as a metaphor for the four types of "ornaments" (*hāra*), such as the precepts. As for "pervading the nine directions," this refers to the rain originally falling from above, pervading the eight directions as well as the space below.
Question: Why is this not like the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, which says they "fill the ten directions"?
Answer: The *Avataṃsaka* uses ten to signify inexhaustibility, while this sutra uses one to signify that all return to the same source. Now, it is said to pervade the nine directions;
this precisely signifies that the principle of the single Buddha-realm universally encompasses the nine realms, such that there are no nine realms that are not the single Buddha-realm.
As for the various precious incense burners burning priceless incense that naturally reaches everywhere to make offerings to the great assembly—this is...
This represents the wondrous virtue of one’s own practice as it universally leads to the ultimate fruit.

Since the preceding [offering] involved raining down flowers and incense to symbolize merit and wisdom, the present burning of incense uses the act of burning to represent wisdom and the fragrance itself to represent merit.

By making offerings to the Buddhas of the three bodies in this great assembly, as well as to the Bodhisattvas, the fourfold assembly, and all future Buddhas, it is said that one "leads to the ultimate fruit."
"Spontaneous" means that it does not depend on human effort, but rather manifests from the dharma-nature and empty space.
As for the various bodhisattvas, they are likewise spontaneously manifested as the forms of bodhisattvas, and they too are born from the dharma-nature and empty space.
"Banner" has the meaning of turning; it signifies the increase of the Path and the diminution of birth. "Canopy" has the meaning of covering; it signifies...
The manifestation of compassion and the sequential progression toward benefiting sentient beings signifies the ascent from cause to fruit.
Reaching as far as the Brahma Heaven—where "Brahma" carries the meaning of purity—signifies the ultimate four virtues (*caturguṇa*).
The singing and praising of the Buddhas with sublime sounds signifies making the voice of the Buddha-way heard by all. Above this, the celestial drum symbolizes the transformation of others.

The teaching on robes and necklaces represents the practice of transforming others; now, the use of banners and canopies represents "practice" (caryā), while the singing of hymns of praise represents "teaching" (deśanā).
These two modes of marvelous virtue for transforming others lead to the same ultimate fruit. Since the perfect benefit is profound, an auspicious omen is manifested to represent it.
In various sutras such as the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Buddhāvataṃsaka*, whenever the Great Dharma was concluded, miraculous wonders were always manifested. Why is this so?
Only Maitreya is not so; thus concludes the general bestowal of the prediction of the Dharma-body for the two [groups]. △ Third, Maitreya’s general expression of understanding and realization.
In the preceding Trace Gate, the bodhisattvas also attained awakening, yet their great task was not yet complete; therefore, they did not present this [realization].

Now that the present Essential Gate has concluded, he entrusts it to the Regent (Maitreya) to express it collectively. The text is divided into three parts; first, the verse on the assembly receiving [the teaching].
The two verses explain the Tathāgata’s discernment, while the three verses signify the auspicious manifestation of perfect benefit. First, at that time,
Maitreya Bodhisattva rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these verses:

The partial realization of the emptiness of phenomena by all Bodhisattvas is termed a "seat. Rising from this seat now symbolizes not dwelling in what has been realized, but rather progressing ever further.
Their fundamental reality is the trace of provisional means; previously they had not revealed their true identity, as if covering their right shoulder.
Now that it has been fully disclosed, they bare their shoulder to signify this. Although the fundamental and the trace differ, they are inconceivably one.
Therefore, they join their palms to signify this; because it increases the Path and diminishes birth, leading swiftly to the ultimate fruit, they face the Buddha to signify this.
The Buddha has preached a rare Dharma never heard before: the World-Honored One possesses great power and an immeasurable lifespan.
When countless sons of the Buddha heard the World-Honored One’s detailed explanation of those who have attained the benefit of the Dharma, joy pervaded their entire bodies.
II. Verses on the Tathāgata’s Detailed Explanation:
Some abide in the stage of non-retrogression; some have attained dhāraṇīs; some possess unimpeded eloquence; and others have mastered the *koṭi-nayuta* *parivarta-dhāraṇī*.

The stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika-bhūmi*) refers to the initial dwelling in the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); the stage of non-retrogression in mindfulness (*smṛty-avaivartika-pada*) is as previously explained, and the rest may be understood accordingly.
Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas, numbering as many as the atoms in a great trichiliocosm, each of whom is able to turn the wheel of the Dharma of non-retrogression;
there are also bodhisattvas, numbering as many as the atoms in a medium chiliocosm, each of whom is able to turn the wheel of the pure Dharma.
Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas, equal in number to the atoms of a small chiliocosm, who each have eight births remaining before they shall attain the path of Buddhahood.
There are also bodhisattvas, equal in number to the atoms of four, three, or two such four-continent worlds, who shall attain Buddhahood after a corresponding number of births.
Or there are bodhisattvas, equal in number to the atoms of a single four-continent world, who have only one birth remaining before they shall attain all-knowledge.
When sentient beings such as these hear that the Buddha’s lifespan is long and far-reaching, they attain the immeasurable, outflow-free (*anāsrava*), and pure fruit of retribution.
"Immeasurable" and "outflow-free" distinguish this from the limited [lifespan] of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). It is called "pure" because it is evoked by sublime causes;
it is called "fruit of retribution" because it is an unobstructed land.
Furthermore, sentient beings as numerous as the atoms in eight worlds, upon hearing the Buddha’s discourse on his lifespan, all resolved their minds upon the Unsurpassed [Enlightenment].
The two verses regarding the Tathāgata’s analysis are concluded. △ Third, the verses on the auspicious signs indicating universal benefit.
The World-Honored One has taught immeasurable and inconceivable dharmas that bring great benefit,
like the boundless sky raining down *māndārava* and *mahāmāndārava* flowers. From as many Buddha-fields as there are sands in the Ganges, Śakras, Brahmās,
and others have come to rain down sandalwood and aloeswood in profusion, falling in a swirling cascade like birds flying through the air to descend and scatter as offerings before the Buddhas.
This verse describes the two auspicious omens of the raining down of flowers and the raining down of incense, which together constitute an offering scattered before all Buddhas.
The additional two lines concerning Brahmā and Śakra signify that the spiritual capacity [of sentient beings] pervades the ten directions.
From the void of space, celestial drums spontaneously produce wondrous sounds, and tens of millions of varieties of heavenly robes swirl and descend.
This verse briefly mentions the two auspicious omens of the celestial drum and the celestial robes, omitting the jeweled necklaces;
yet the celestial robes extend for ten thousand *li*, clearly indicating that those covered by them must be numerous.
Precious incense burners of exquisite fragrance burned priceless incense, which spontaneously pervaded everywhere to make offerings to all the World-Honored Ones.

This verse describes the auspicious signs accompanying the offering of incense. While the long prose version speaks of a "great assembly," this verse states, "World-Honored One, you should know that this great assembly consists entirely of Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Among them, the host of great bodhisattvas holds banners and canopies made of the seven treasures, of ten thousand myriad billions of exquisite varieties, reaching as high as the Brahma Heaven.
Before each of the Buddhas, precious banners were suspended with excellent streamers, and they also sang praises to the Tathāgatas in ten million gāthās.
These verses extolled the auspiciousness of the banners and canopies.
Such various matters as these had never before been heard; hearing that the Buddha’s lifespan was immeasurable, everyone rejoiced.
The Buddha’s name resounded throughout the ten directions, extensively benefiting all sentient beings, so that all were endowed with roots of goodness to assist their unsurpassed resolve.
This verse of summary concludes the auspicious signs indicating a perfect benefit that differs from ordinary portents; therefore, it is said, "never before seen.
This concludes the second section: the Main Exposition.
△ Third, the Section on Circulation: From here below, there are eleven and a half chapters of scripture entirely belonging to the circulation section. Now...
Furthermore, regarding the fact that the three grades and half-grades are used as the basis for the circulation of the Final Teaching (Honmon), there are generally two intentions:
first, the four levels of faith and the five grades are all spoken of in terms of hearing [the teaching] over a long duration;
the two chapters on "Merit of Rejoicing" and "Merit of the Dharma Master" merely clarify the causal merit of the first grade, while the chapter on "Not Disparaging" clarifies its resultant merit.
One should know that these three chapters and a half are specifically for the purpose of circulating the *Benmen* (Original Gate);
for example, from the "Dharma Master" chapter up to the "Peaceful Practices" (*Anle Xing*) constitutes the circulation of the *Jimen* (Traces Gate).
Since both [gates] take the first chapter as the separate introduction (*bie xu*) for the *Jimen*, and the *Jimen* itself inherently possesses the three sections, therefore—

These three chapters and a half constitute the *Honmon* (Original Gate) section of the circulation; this *Honmon* also possesses three stages, with both the *Hon* (Original) and *Jaku* (Trace) each having three parts, which together form the main exposition.
Thus, by means of the five matters of the general introduction (*tsūjō*), the two gates are introduced, and through the eight chapters of the entrustment (*shurui*), the two gates are circulated.
The structural framework is complete and correct, and its outline is distinct and clear. Now, regarding these three chapters and a half:
This is divided into three sections of meaning. First, the first one and a half chapters clarify the causal merits of the initial chapter to encourage its circulation.
Second, the "Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma Master" clarifies the resultant merits of the initial chapter to encourage its circulation.

Third, the "Chapter on the One Who Is Not Disparaged" cites the blessings and transgressions resulting from faith and slander as evidence to encourage its circulation. Within the first of these, there are two parts: first, the clarification of the four kinds of faith in the present; second...

After the section on "Illumination," there are five grades; the first grade further has four parts. The first consists of: (1) faith and understanding in a single thought-moment; (2) comprehending the meaning of the words; (3) hearing, retaining, and making offerings;

and (4) the accomplishment of profound faith and contemplation. This first part [of the fourth] further has two sections: first, the long prose text; second, the verse summary. The first [of these] further has three parts:
first, manifesting the characteristics; second, clarifying the merits; third, clarifying the non-retrogression of the stage and practice. Now, the first [part].

At that time, the Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ajita: "Ajita, if there are sentient beings who, upon hearing that the lifespan of the Buddha is thus long and far-reaching, are able to give rise to even a single thought of faith and understanding..."

Having already distinguished how hearing of the Buddha’s long life brings about profound and vast benefits, those who have not yet entered or abided in the stages awaken to the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*);
those who have already entered or abide in the stages increase their path and diminish their births, standing near the rank of the ultimate sages;

and those who have not yet resolved their minds generate the unsurpassed resolve and enter the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*). All these are cases where past seeds were already deep, so that they now attain liberation through maturation and give rise to the realization of non-arising.

The two stages of the mind both belong to those who are ready for the teaching (*yathābhavyatā*), involving the increase of the Path and the diminution of birth, and they pertain to the influence that initiates the three assemblies of those ready for the teaching;

therefore, they belong to the section on the "Prophecy of the True Teaching. Now, at the beginning of the circulation [of this sutra], it concerns those who first formed a karmic connection—those who have not yet attained the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā-bhūmi*), or who have heard [the teaching] briefly from this assembly, or from the various bodhisattvas currently present.
Thus, through successive transmission, one hears that the Buddha’s lifespan is long and far-reaching;
yet, as time is already extremely brief and what one hears is not much, it is said: "even to the point of being able to give rise to a single thought of faith and understanding.
This expresses the extreme brevity of the time and the shallowness of the benefit obtained. Now, "a single thought" refers precisely to this present, momentary, and subtle mind.
Furthermore, those who possess faith and understanding believe that the principle realized by the Buddha in his original ground is the wondrous principle of the *dharmadhātu*.

This principle is neither real nor provisional, yet it can be both real and provisional: when he personally realizes the principle, it is called "real"; when he employs various skillful means to transform others, it is called "provisional.
This principle is neither fundamental nor derivative, yet it can be both fundamental and derivative; thus, the initial realization of the provisional and the real is established.
The essence and function are termed the "original realization" (honshō) subsequently manifested; the provisional and the real are termed the "traces" (shaku).

Since this principle is both that which the World-Honored One realized long ago and that which sentient beings have been deluded about for a long time, and furthermore that which is equally possessed within every present, infinitesimal thought-moment, it is said: "As is the mind, so is the Buddha; as is the Buddha, so are the multitudes."
The arising of the enlightened mind in Buddhas and sentient beings—these three are without distinction. Thus, wherever one hears this, one is suddenly and brilliantly enlightened;
entering through the words, there is no obstruction. One believes that all dharmas are the Buddha-dharma (the inconceivable True, which is the provisional yet real).
Furthermore, one believes that the Buddha-dharma is not separate from any dharma (the inconceivable Conventional, which is the real yet provisional). This cannot be attained [by conceptualization].
The Buddha-dharma does not grasp any phenomena (double negation), yet it perceives all phenomena and also perceives the Buddha-dharma (double affirmation;

these two phrases belong to the inconceivable). It is three within one (whichever single truth is cited, it inherently contains the three truths); it is one within three (though the three truths are distinguished, they are but the single mind).

This is also "practicing on non-paths while penetrating the Buddha-path" (the nine realms of non-paths are entirely the function of the wondrous path of the Buddha-realm; this explains that all phenomena are [the Buddha-dharma]).
This is the Buddha-dharma. To practice the Buddha-way is to penetrate all ways (explaining that the aforementioned Buddha-dharma is not separated from any dharma).
Not attaining the Buddha-way or any other way (explaining the simultaneous negation), yet penetrating the Buddha-way and all ways (explaining the simultaneous illumination).
Non-existent yet existent (the three truths are all existent); existent yet non-existent (the three truths are all non-existent); neither existent nor non-existent (the three truths...).

All are neither existent nor non-existent. Just as the road before a gate leads everywhere to the east, west, south, and north without any obstruction, so it is with the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind:

whatever they encounter is likewise thus. (The substance of the six sense objects is the Dharma-realm; from antiquity to the present, there is nothing that is not the perfect and wondrous Three Truths.
To be without doubt is called faith (*śraddhā*); to be clear and lucid is called understanding (*adhimukti*). This is the mind of faith and understanding in a single thought-moment.

(Furthermore, hearing the Dharma and attaining faith and understanding is what constitutes "faith-practice. If, while sitting in contemplation, one suddenly attains awakening and penetrates the Three Truths according to one's reflections, it is likewise so (this refers to "dharma-practice" arising from contemplation through the production of a single thought of faith and understanding).
Such faith and understanding belong to the initial stage of the Ten Faiths; one has not yet attained the purity of the six sense organs nor entered the true position of the Iron Wheel. △ Two.
Clarifying the Merits, Part Two: First, a general discussion of the immeasurables; second, a comparative evaluation to manifest their abundance.
Now, the first [section]: the merits obtained are without limit.

△ Second, the comparative evaluation to manifest their abundance, which is further divided into two parts: first, citing the five perfections as the basis for comparison; second, the actual comparison.
The merit of faith and understanding is exceedingly great. First:

if there are good sons or good daughters who, for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, practice the five *pāramitās*—namely, the *dāna-pāramitā* (perfection of giving) and the *śīla-pāramitā* (perfection of ethical discipline)—for eighty million *nayuta* *koṭi* eons...
The *dānapāramitā*, *kṣāntipāramitā*, *vīryapāramitā*, and *dhyānapāramitā*—excluding the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Since *prajñā* is precisely the right wisdom (*samyak-prajñā*) of the present, it is said that the *prajñā* is excluded. Question: Since [the other perfections] are already separated from *prajñā*, why is it said here to exclude it?

If that is so, why should the first five [perfections] not be called *pāramitās*? Answer: This is because, according to the Separate Teaching (*bhedavyavahāra*), practitioners who seek unexcelled bodhi each exhaust the limits of these five [perfections] individually;

thus they may also be termed "crossing over" (*tīrṇa*). This is because, in the Separate Teaching, the final mind of the ten stages of dedication (*daśabhūmi-pratipatti*) is designated as the "conventional limit" (*prajñapti-paryanta*).
Question: Does the sequential *prajñā* of the Separate Teaching not likewise accord with what has been discussed above?
Question: Why is this eliminated? Answer: This is because the discussion of emptiness and the provisional nature [of phenomena] can serve as the object of comparison;

since the realization of the Middle Way is not distinct from them—being equal in name and equal in essence—it must be eliminated. △ Second, the correct refutation shows that the merit of faith and understanding is exceedingly great.

Compared to these merits of the [five perfections], the merit of the former [single moment of faithful understanding] does not equal even one hundredth, one thousandth, one hundred-thousandth, nor one hundred-thousand-millionth part;
it is beyond reach even by calculation, number, or analogy.
△ Third, the stage of non-retrogression in practice:
If a son or daughter of good family possesses such merit, it is impossible for them to regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
While six other minds may still regress and seven minds do not regress, the initial mind of the Perfect [Vehicle] is immediately non-regressive.
This is because, upon hearing the merit of the lifespan, one is aided from without by the Perfect [Vehicle], while being internally perfumed by compliant faith and understanding;
thus, it does not regress. The long prose section concludes. II. Verse Recitation (in three parts): 1. Verses on the Merit (skipping ahead); 2. Verses on the Practices of the Stages.

Regarding the first part of the section on the characteristics of the verses that follow the three [preceding] sections, it is further divided into two: first, the transposed verses that employ comparison to reveal the vastness;
second, the verses that provide a general discussion of the immeasurability. The first of these is further divided into two: first, the verse citing the five perfections as the basis for comparison;
second, the verse formally comparing the merit of faith and understanding to show its great abundance. Now, the first:
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If a person seeks the Buddha's wisdom, for eighty million *nayuta* kalpas they practice the five *pāramitās*.
Throughout these kalpas, they give alms and make offerings to Buddhas, pratyekabuddhas and their disciples, as well as to the assemblies of bodhisattvas."
If one gives various kinds of exquisite food and drink, superior garments, bedding, and dwellings adorned with sandalwood and gardens—
such diverse and subtle offerings as these throughout the duration of all these kalpas— and dedicates them toward the Buddha-way;
or if one further maintains the precepts purely and without flaw, seeking the unsurpassed path, this is praised by all Buddhas.
Furthermore, if one practices patience and dwells in the stage of gentleness, such that even when various evils are inflicted upon them, their mind does not waver;
and if they are able to endure being slighted or troubled by those who have attained some dharma and harbor overweening pride;

and if they further apply themselves with diligence and vigor, their resolve and mindfulness always remaining firm and steadfast for immeasurable billions of kalpas without a single moment of indolence—this is called the perfection of patience.
Furthermore, throughout countless kalpas, dwelling in secluded places—whether sitting or walking—to dispel drowsiness and constantly collect the mind;
by these causes and conditions, one is able to give rise to various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*). For eighty billion *koṭis* of kalpas, one dwells with an undisturbed mind.
Sustaining the merit and vows of this single-mindedness, one seeks the unsurpassed path so that I may attain all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) and exhaust the wisdom of all meditative concentrations.
This person practices all these merits as described above throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas.
△ Second, a verse on the vastness of the merit of correct conviction and understanding.
If there are sons or daughters of good family who, upon hearing my teaching on the lifespan, believe it for even a single thought-moment, their merit shall exceed that [of the former].
This concludes the initial section, which uses a verse of comparison to demonstrate its vastness. II. A subsequent verse summarizing the discussion of the immeasurable.
If a person is entirely free from all doubts and regrets and believes with a profound mind for even a moment, their merit shall be as such.

"A moment" refers to a single thought-instant (*ekakṣaṇa*). This concludes the initial verse praising the merit of transcending [the stages]. II. Verse on the Non-retrogression of Practice and Stages. This has two parts:

first, clarifying that faith and understanding are not easily attained; second, clarifying that because one possesses faith and understanding, one will necessarily make vows, and thus attain [non-retrogression].
[This concludes] the previous section.
Now, for the first [point]: there are certain bodhisattvas who, having practiced the path for immeasurable kalpas, are able to believe and accept my teaching on the lifespan when they hear it.
The phrase "certain bodhisattvas" refers to those of dull faculties; they have practiced the path for immeasurable kalpas.
Only when one's roots of goodness have fully matured can one believe and accept [this teaching]. If the faculties are not yet mature, the Buddha will not preach it for them;

even if they were to hear it, they would certainly harbor doubts and confusion. Thus, faith and understanding are truly not easy to attain. Now, if one possesses sharp faculties, upon first hearing it, they can immediately believe and understand it in a single thought-moment;
such a person may then equal those bodhisattvas who have practiced for a long time, and may even surpass them.
△ Second, because those with clear understanding and faith will necessarily make vows, they shall attain non-retrogression.

Such persons as these receive this sutra upon their heads and vow: "May I, in the future, possess long life to deliver sentient beings, just as the World-Honored One, the King among the Śākyas, now delivers them;
may I preach the Dharma at the site of enlightenment with a lion’s roar, free from all fear."
"In all future ages, when we sit at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and are honored by all, our discourse on the lifespan shall likewise be so.

This refers to those who possess both the sharp and dull faculties; having heard this and attained faith and understanding, they will surely receive it upon their heads and make a vow, whereby they are certain not to regress.
One might ask: for those who have recently attained realization, there is no further growth to speak of.
Question: Why do you say that all cases are likewise? Answer: To say "likewise" refers to the attainment of eternal life.

If one attains eternal life that lasts until the end of the future, it will necessarily exceed this [limit]. Why then do you say it is merely "likewise"? It is because we are speaking from the time of actual accomplishment;
thus, we have cited only this many kalpas of dust. The two verses on the non-retrogression of practice and stages are concluded. △ Third, the Retrospective [Examination].
The verse describes the characteristics:
"If there are those with profound resolve who are pure, upright, and learned, capable of retaining [the teachings] and understanding the Buddha’s words according to their meaning—
such persons as these have no doubt regarding this."
From the direct clarification of this long passage, it is shown that even the arising of a single thought of faith and understanding immediately reveals its merit;
now, I shall specifically explain its characteristics to demonstrate the difficulty of attaining such a single thought of faith and understanding.

If one wishes to be free from doubt regarding the long duration of this Buddha’s lifespan, whether one has practiced for a long time or is a beginner, one must possess a profound mind (*gambhīra-citta*). Furthermore—
One must be pure and upright, as well as possessed of great learning and dhāraṇī, able to understand according to the meaning rather than following the literal text;
only when these three qualities are present can one achieve faith and understanding in a single thought-moment.
Since achieving faith and understanding in a single thought-moment is not easy, the merit resulting from it cannot but be vast. As for "the profound mind," it is [described] above.
The mind that seeks to transform those below realizes that the essence of the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings is fundamentally non-dual;
arising from this realization, one gives rise to the four great vows of effortless action, which is called the "profound mind" (*adhyāśaya*)—this is the Tathāgata’s chamber.

To be pure and upright means not being defiled by the five hindrances; maintaining right mindfulness of True Suchness (*tathatā*) is the Tathāgata’s robe. To have heard much is to be able to synthesize.

One who maintains an understanding of the Buddha’s words according to their meaning is able, upon hearing anything, to grasp all phenomena and comprehend all meanings because they understand the Tathāgata’s speech according to wisdom and according to intention;

thus, even if one has heard little, being able to understand many meanings is called "having heard much," and this is the seat of the Tathāgata. When these three dharmas of contemplative practice are present, [one attains it].

Being able to believe and understand the ultimate three dharmas—once one has believed in the principle of the ultimate three dharmas, there will likewise be no doubt regarding the matters of the original and the manifested (honji-suijaku) within that ultimate state. This concludes the first section: Belief and Understanding through a Single Thought-moment.
△ Second: Explaining the Meaning of the Words.
Furthermore, Ajita, if there are those who hear that the Buddha’s lifespan is long and far-reaching and understand the meaning of these words,
the merit they obtain will be limitless, and they shall be able to give rise to the unsurpassed wisdom of the Tathāgata.
Previously, there was merely a single thought of faith and understanding, like a person drinking water who knows its coldness or warmth for themselves;

now, by understanding the intent of these words, one can briefly cite examples to others, thereby being able to give rise to the unsurpassed wisdom of both self and others. △ Third, making offerings through hearing and retaining [the Dharma].
How much more so for one who extensively hears this sutra—whether by teaching others to hear it, or upholding it oneself, or teaching others to uphold it;

whether by copying it oneself, or teaching others to copy it; or by making offerings to the scroll with flowers, incense, necklaces, banners, pennants, silk canopies, fragrant oils, and ghee lamps—the merit of such a person is immeasurable and boundless, and is able to give rise to all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā).

Through extensive hearing, extensive retention, extensive transcription, and extensive cultivation of offerings, the external resources of one's own practice and the transformation of others cause internal wisdom to enter swiftly;
thus, it is able to give rise to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). △ Fourth, the accomplishment of profound faith through contemplation.
Ajita, if good sons or good daughters, upon hearing me speak of the long duration of my lifespan, believe and understand it with a profound mind,
they shall see the Buddha always dwelling on Vulture Peak, surrounded by a great assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas,
preaching the Dharma; and they shall also see this Sahā world, its ground made of lapis lazuli, level and smooth as a palm, [extending throughout] Jambudvīpa.
The eightfold path is demarcated by gold dust, and rows of jewel trees stand before the various terraces and towers, all of which are composed entirely of jewels;
the assembly of bodhisattvas all dwell therein. If there is anyone who can contemplate in this manner, you should know that this is the mark of profound faith and understanding.
To see the Buddha constantly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa preaching the Dharma together with the great bodhisattvas and the assembly of śrāvakas is the mark of the Land of Skillful Means with Surplus.
Furthermore, to see the Sahā world where the ground is made of lapis lazuli and even the bodhisattvas all dwell therein is the mark of the Land Adorned by True Retribution.
These marks are inherently complete within principle; now, one relies upon this principle to cultivate contemplation.
