Rejoicing in the Merit of Others: A Direct Explanation of the Merit of Those Who Listen from Without. This section has five parts:
first, citing the final person to illustrate the beginning of the initial resolve through successive instruction;
second, comparing the original [merit]; third, the question; fourth, the answer; fifth, the formal comparison. Now, the first part.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ajita:

"Ajita, after the Tathāgata has passed into extinction, if there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās, as well as other wise ones—whether old or young (the 'other wise ones' refers to those who have not yet received the precepts of the fourfold assembly and thus cannot be called bhikṣus or upāsakas, etc., but who possess the latent seeds of Great Vehicle wisdom and, upon hearing this, are able to believe and understand)—they may then expound it according to their capacity, regardless of whether they are old or young. Upon hearing this...
Having rejoiced in this sutra, they depart from the assembly and go elsewhere— whether to a monastery,
a secluded place, a city, a street, a village, or a field— and according to what they have heard (the words and meaning being unerring),
they expound it to their parents, kinsmen, good friends, and spiritual mentors to the best of their ability. Having heard this, these people likewise rejoice and further propagate it.
When other people have heard it and likewise rejoice and pass it on, and so it continues in succession until the fiftieth person—
Ānanda, I shall now describe the merit of that fiftieth son or daughter of good family who rejoices;
you should listen well.
This succession continues up to the fiftieth person, which demonstrates that each subsequent individual is gradually inferior to the one preceding them. Why is this?

Those who rely on the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*) to propagate the Dharma must necessarily possess eloquence (*pratibhāna*), and those who hear it and rejoice in it will surely find the flavor of the Dharma profound.

When such a listener leaves the Dharma assembly and expounds the teaching according to their capacity, although they say they have explained it exactly as they heard it, the principle is certainly not without error.
One who is adorned with eloquent exposition may not necessarily be able to equal the Dharma Master, much less surpass him.

Thus, as this process continues through the second, third, tenth, or twentieth person, they gradually become inferior; how much more so when reaching the fiftieth person—would they not be even more deficient?
Furthermore, while each of the preceding forty-nine people possesses the merit of transmitting the teaching, now [the fiftieth]...

The fifty [verses] discuss only the single thought-moment of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) and do not discuss further transmission; one should know that this is precisely the very beginning of the first chapter.
Now, by clarifying the merit based on this initial single thought-moment of sympathetic joy, it can be understood that subsequent stages need not be explicitly stated.
As for the statement that it is transmitted successively up to the fiftieth, this is merely intended to reveal the gradual deepening of the flavor of the Dharma.
Since their meager merit is gradually inferior, it need not be explained by means of the manifest dharma. △ Second, the comparative evaluation of the source:
Suppose there were sentient beings of the six destinies and four modes of birth in four million *asamkhyeya* worlds—whether born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture, or by transformation;
whether with form or without form; with perception, without perception, or neither with nor without perception—none of them...
Regarding those with two feet, four feet, many feet, and others such as these who are counted among the class of sentient beings,
if there is someone seeking merit who provides them with whatever articles of entertainment they desire, giving to each and every sentient being as much gold,
silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, agate, coral, amber, and various exquisite treasures, as well as elephants, horses, and chariots, filling the entirety of Jambudvīpa.
Riding upon palaces and towers made of the seven precious gems, this great donor thus practiced such giving for a full eighty years.
Having done so, he then thought: "I have already bestowed upon sentient beings all manner of articles for their enjoyment, according to their every desire.
Yet these sentient beings are all in decline; they are over eighty years old, with white hair and wrinkled faces, and death will soon come."

"I shall instruct and guide them with the Buddha-dharma. Thereupon, he gathered these sentient beings, proclaimed the transformative teachings of the Dharma, and instructed, exhorted, benefited, and gladdened them, so that at one and the same time they all attained the stage of Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, and Arhat;
they exhausted all outflows (āsrava) and attained mastery in profound meditative concentration (dhyāna), being endowed with the eight liberations (vimokṣa).
The six destinies—devas, humans, asuras, hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals—possess four modes of birth (*yoni*):
those born from eggs (*aṇḍaja*), those born from wombs (*jarāyuja*), those born from moisture (*saṃsvedaja*), and those born by transformation (*upapāduka*). Devas are born only by transformation;
humans possess all four modes of birth, though they mostly give birth from wombs; asuras possess four modes of birth; and hell-beings are born by transformation.
The "ghosts and beasts" possess four types of form: those with form refer to the desire realm and the form realm; those without form refer to the formless realm;
those with perception refer to the sphere of infinite space and the sphere of infinite consciousness; those without perception refer to the sphere of nothingness;
and those who are neither with nor without perception refer to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. △ Third, the question.
"What do you think? Is the merit obtained by this great donor much?
△ Fourth, the response.
Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the merit of this person is exceedingly great, immeasurable and boundless. If it were such a donor...
The Master merely bestows upon sentient beings all the requisites for happiness, and his merit is immeasurable; how much more so when he causes them to attain the fruit of Arhatship!
△ Fifth, the formal comparison.

The Buddha told Maitreya: "I shall now speak to you clearly. Suppose a person were to bestow all manner of articles of pleasure upon the sentient beings of the six realms throughout four million billion *asaṃkhyeya* worlds, and furthermore cause them to attain the fruit of Arhatship;
the merit thereby acquired would not equal the merit of this fiftieth person who, upon hearing even a single verse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, rejoices with sympathetic joy."
"Ānanda, even a hundredth part, a thousandth part, a hundred-thousand-millionth part, or any fraction reached by calculation or analogy cannot equal it;
it is beyond all knowledge. Such is the merit of the fiftieth person who hears the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* through successive transmission and rejoices in it;
how much more so for those who hear it at the very beginning of the assembly and rejoice?"
The merit of one who rejoices is even more supreme, immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (asaṃkhyeya), beyond all comparison.
Indeed, the recipient of such a gift has received no small amount, filling four hundred trillion asaṃkhyeya world-systems.
First, they are granted worldly happiness for a full eighty years; subsequently, they are granted the bliss of the Dharma, realizing the fruits of the Four Noble Ones. This is not insignificant.
Though great, it does not compare to the initial single thought of universal sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*).
One who fulfills this single thought will surely, throughout the entirety of space and until the end of time, universally deliver all beings and cause them all to attain Buddhahood;
for the ultimate merit does not depart from that initial single thought. This is further explained according to the intent of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* regarding its comparative analysis.
The merit of all the people filling Jambudvīpa does not equal the merit of a single person in Aparagoyānī;

the merit of all the people filling the western continent does not equal the merit of a single person in Pūrvavideha; the merit of all the people filling these three continents does not equal the merit of a single person in Uttarakuru;
and the merit of all the people filling the four continents does not equal one-fourth of the merit of a Cāturmahārājika deva.
The merit of a Heavenly King is not equal to that of a single Śakra; even up to the sixth heaven, it is not equal to the merit of a single Brahmā.
Furthermore, the first dhyāna is not equal to the second dhyāna; the second dhyāna is not equal to the third dhyāna; the third dhyāna is not equal to the fourth dhyāna;

and so on, until the sphere of nothingness is not equal to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. That which is the most venerable within the triple world, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, is not equal to [the merit of] the Unsurpassed [Nirvāṇa].
The merit of a *srotāpanna* is not equal to that of one who has attained the second fruit; the second fruit is not equal to the third fruit; the third fruit is not equal to the fourth fruit;

the fourth fruit is not equal to the *pratyekabuddha* of the Tripitaka Teaching; the *śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha* of the Tripitaka Teaching are not equal to the *śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha* of the Shared Teaching who realize the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*);

the *śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha* of the Shared Teaching who realize the nature of phenomena are not equal to the Bodhisattvas who have emerged into the provisional [world] (*niryāṇa-kuśala*); and the Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching are not equal to [the Bodhisattvas of the Distinct Teaching].

Because those at the initial stage of the Separate Teaching (biejiao) hear of the Middle Way, their final mind of the ten stages of Dedication (shihuixiang) cannot equal the initial mind of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao), which arises from hearing the Perfect [Teaching].
Thus, one should know that the comparison of the merit of generating the resolve for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is not yet considered extraordinary;
it is this sūtra’s comparison of the merit of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) that is most difficult to believe. Yet, even a single thought of sympathetic joy...

Joy is the fulfillment of the ten vehicles; if one understands these ten vehicles, then one’s merit has a basis. Please allow me to briefly clarify them: "Following" means following phenomena and following principle;
phenomenon and principle are the inconceivable realm. "Joy" means rejoicing in oneself and rejoicing in others; this is the bodhicitta.
To follow with joy for even a single thought-moment without distraction is *śamatha* (stopping); to be without delusion is *vipaśyanā* (contemplation). This is wholesome.

Skillfully settling the mind is to harmonize with principle and perfectly subdue ignorance (*avidyā*), as well as the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). Harmonizing with phenomena is to perfectly subdue the ignorance regarding the dust-like [objects] (*rajas-jñāna*).
This is "pervasive penetration of the Dharma. Thoroughly realizing that the provisional and the real are non-dual is "discerning the obstacles and the openings.

Merely within a single thought-moment, to have faith and understanding in the inconceivable Buddha-Dharma is itself the perfect *smṛtyupasthāna* (foundations of mindfulness), which is naturally endowed with all qualities.
The seven categories of the path-factors (*mārgāṅga*) are for the sake of harmonious adjustment. Having already rejoiced [in others' merits], one must take pity on oneself and others;

thus, one must surely cultivate the five repentances (*pañca-pratikramaṇa*), which serve as an aid to opening [the way]. Being able to believe in and accord with both phenomena and principle, as well as their fundamental and manifest aspects, one will certainly not use the ordinary or the deluded to compare oneself with the supreme sages.
This is knowing the stages (*bhūmi*). When one accords with phenomena and accords with principle, neither the forceful nor the gentle demons can prevail.

Movement is the ability to practice patience (*kṣānti*). When the true mind is bound to the true object and true conditions, arising in succession with each true moment mutually infusing the next, this is the departure from attachment to dharmas (*dharmatṛṣṇā*).
How could such merit be reached by the small fruits of worldly material giving or even the dharma-giving? How could such perfect contemplation be reached by those who practice through gradual stages?
The first response, concerning the merit of those who inwardly rejoice, is concluded. △ Second, directly clarifying the merit of those who externally listen to the Dharma, in four parts:
first, going oneself; second, sharing a seat; third, exhorting others; fourth, listening with full attention and practicing accordingly. Now, the first part.
Furthermore, Ajita, if a person, for the sake of this sutra, goes to a monastery and listens or receives it for even a brief moment—
whether sitting or standing— by virtue of this merit, in their next rebirth they will obtain excellent and sublime elephant and horse carriages,
precious palanquins, and celestial palaces.
△ Second, sharing one's seat:
If there is someone sitting at a place where the Dharma is being taught, and another person comes and encourages them to sit and listen by offering to share their seat,
the merit of this person will cause them to obtain the seat of Śakra, the seat of Brahmā, or the seat of a Cakravartin in their next rebirth.
The place where a Wheel-Turning Sage King sits.
△ Third, exhorting others:
"Ajita, if there should be another person who says to someone else, 'There is a sutra named the Lotus Sutra; we should go together to hear it.'"
Having received these instructions, even for a mere moment, one hears of this person’s merit and, upon changing bodies, will be reborn in the same place as a *dhāraṇī*-possessing Bodhisattva:
(1) possessing sharp faculties; (2) possessing wisdom; (3) never being mute throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of lifetimes;
(4) having no foul breath; (5) having a tongue that is always free from disease; (6) having a mouth that is also free from disease; (7) having teeth that do not...
(89) Not soiled or black; (90) not yellow; (91) not sparse; (92) nor are they missing; (93) not uneven; (94) not crooked; (95) the lips do not hang down;
(96) nor are they drawn back or shriveled; (97) not coarse or rough; (98) not scarred or cracked (*dantura* refers here to mouth sores);
(99–100) nor are they damaged or broken; (101–102) nor are they askew or slanted; (103) not thick; (104) not large.
4) Nor is he dark-complexioned (25); he is free from all loathsome features (26); his nose is not flat or sunken (27), nor is it crooked or distorted (28);
his facial complexion is not black (29), nor is it excessively long (30–31); nor is it hunched or curved (32).
He is entirely devoid of any single unpleasing mark (34). His lips, tongue, and teeth are all...
Majestic and excellent (35, 6, 7, 8); the nose is long, high, and straight (39, 44, 11); the facial features are perfectly rounded (42); the eyebrows are high and long (43, 4);
the forehead is broad, level, and even (45, 6, 7); endowed with all the marks of a superior person (48);
in every birth throughout successive lives, they behold the Buddhas (49); and having heard the Dharma, they faithfully accept the teachings (50).
This passage also contains six kinds of faculties and their merits: having sharp faculties is the merit of the six faculties;
having sharp wisdom is the merit of the mind-faculty; not being mute is the merit of the tongue-faculty; having a well-developed, high, and straight nose is the merit of the nose-faculty;

seeing the Buddha is the merit of the eye-faculty; hearing the Dharma is the merit of the ear-faculty; and the remainder are the merits of the body-faculty. Subsequently, the purity of the six faculties is explained.
Purity refers to the merits of the stage of semblance (*sādṛśāvasthā*); what is now discussed, however, are the merits prior to that stage of semblance.
Furthermore, these fifty merits may be complete or incomplete, or obtained one by one; according to their respective capacities, they cannot be treated as identical.

Moreover, while rejoicing (*anumodanā*) pertains to the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-bhāvanā*), what is clarified here is the act of personally proceeding to share the seat and exhort others.
Regarding his three kinds of [attainments], the principle and contemplation have not yet been discussed;

even at the stage of names, the merit of these names is already such as this—how much more so for the stage of contemplative practice, how much more so for the stages of semblance, partial realization, and ultimate realization! △ Fourth, possessing both hearing and practice.
Ajita, you should observe that if the merit of merely exhorting a single person to go and listen to the Dharma is such as this,

how much more so for one who listens with a single-minded focus, hears it, reads it, recites it, explains it in detail for others in the great assembly, and practices according to what has been taught?
The long prose section concludes. △ Second, the verse summary has two parts: first, the verse on the merit of inward sympathetic joy;
second, the verse on the merit of those who outwardly listen to the Dharma. Now, the first part.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "If a person,
having heard this sutra at a Dharma assembly— even so much as a single verse— rejoices and explains it to others,
and if it is thus transmitted in succession until it reaches the fiftieth person, the merit obtained by that final person shall now be analyzed."
Suppose there were a great benefactor who provided immeasurable necessities for eighty years, fulfilling every desire at will.
Seeing his signs of old age—the hair turned white, the face wrinkled, the teeth sparse, and the body withered—he thought, "His death is not far off;
I should now instruct him so that he may attain the fruits of the Path. He then employed skillful means to preach the true Dharma of Nirvana.
"The world is entirely unstable, like foam, bubbles, or a flame; you all should swiftly give rise to a mind of weary detachment.
When the people heard this Dharma, they all attained arhatship, being fully endowed with the six supernormal powers, the three knowledges, and the eight liberations.
Finally, the fiftieth person, upon hearing a single verse, rejoiced with sympathetic joy; the merit of this person surpasses that of the others beyond all comparison.
Thus, by successive transmission, the merit of such a person is already immeasurable; how much more so for those who hear it at the beginning of the Dharma assembly and rejoice accordingly.
II. Verses on the Merit of Those Who Hear from Others (4 parts): 1. Verses exhorting others (transcending the sequence);
2. Verses on going oneself; 3. Verses on sharing one's seat; 4. Verses on listening fully and practicing. Now, the first.
If there is someone who exhorts another person, leading them to listen to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, saying, "This sutra is profound and subtle;

it is difficult to encounter even in ten million kalpas," and that person follows this instruction and goes to listen for even a brief moment—the merit and reward of such a person I shall now explain in detail:

in every successive life they shall have no afflictions of the mouth; their teeth shall not be sparse, yellow, or black; their lips shall not be thick, curled, or cleft; and they shall possess no loathsome features.
His tongue was not dry, black, or short; his nose was high, long, and straight; his forehead was broad and even; his countenance was entirely dignified and handsome, pleasing to all who beheld him;
his breath was free from foul odors, and the fragrance of the *utpala* lotus constantly issued from his mouth.
△ Second, the verse on going oneself:
"If one intentionally goes to a monastic dwelling desiring to hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, and upon hearing it for even a moment feels joy, I shall now describe its merit:
in future lives among gods and humans, one will obtain exquisite elephants, horses, chariots, precious jeweled palanquins, and vehicles in the form of celestial palaces."
△ Third, three verses on sharing one’s seat:

If, at a place where the Dharma is being taught, one encourages others to sit and listen to the sutras, this is a causal condition for merit through which one attains the seats of Śakra, Brahmā, or a Cakravartin king.
△ Fourth, four verses on listening fully and practicing accordingly.
How much more so for one who listens with a single-minded focus, explains its meaning and intent, and practices according to those teachings; the merit of such a person is beyond measure.
This concludes the initial section clarifying the merits of the primary cause, intended to encourage its widespread circulation.
*The Collected Meanings of the Tiantai School on the Lotus Sutra*, Fascicle Six, Part One;
*The Collected Meanings of the Tiantai School on the Lotus Sutra*, Fascicle Six, Part Two.
Composed by the later scholar of Ancient Wu, Ouyi Zhixu.
△ The commentary on the "Chapter on the Merit of Rejoicing" is concluded. Next, the "Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma Master," the nineteenth chapter, is explained.
Regarding the "Dharma Master," there are five types, such as those who receive, uphold, read, and recite the teachings, as explained extensively above in the "Chapter on the Dharma Master."
These five types of practice begin with the stage of names and extend through the stage of partial realization; each may be undertaken according to any one of the practices.
Each of these practices is purified through five grades, yet these five grades pertain to contemplation while the five types pertain to actual phenomena.
Therefore, "reciting" mentioned here does not necessarily refer to those at the second grade, nor does "explaining" necessarily [refer to them].

This refers to the third category of persons. While the preceding "Chapter on Rejoicing" already clarified the merits of the initial resolve in the first chapter, the present section broadly addresses the five matters;
by practicing even a single one of these, one attains purification of the six sense faculties.
Since it states "one shall attain," this is an exhortation by citing the result, namely the merit obtained by those who serve as the five kinds of Dharma-preachers.
However, to purify the six sense organs, one must practice the tenfold method of contemplation (*daśa-yāna-dhyāna*).
One may practice these ten contemplations through reading, or through recitation, or through exposition, or through transcription.
Those of superior faculties will purify the six sense organs upon contemplating the objects; those of middling faculties will attain purification from the second through the sixth contemplations.
Regarding the six sense organs, when one possesses the ten dharmas of the lower grade, the six organs are purified and one attains the stage of partial realization (*pratisamvid*).
The purification of the five sense organs is called "external adornment," while the purification of the mental organ (*manas*) is called "internal adornment.

Furthermore, because all forms and images from the hells up to those of the Buddhas appear within one's own body, it is called "internal adornment," as one universally manifests the form-body (*rūpakāya*).

The samādhi manifests images of the ten realms to transform and deliver all beings; this is called the external adornment of the body. As it is with the body, so it is with the other five sense organs.
As it is with the act of receiving and upholding [the Dharma], so it is with the other four matters. As it is with the Chapter on Rejoicing, so it is twofold for each of the remaining four chapters.
As it is with the semblance stage, so it is twofold for the stage of partial realization; therefore, it is called the "Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma Master."
This is the intention of the world: when practitioners hear this exposition of meritorious benefits, they experience such joy that they cannot contain themselves;
they seek it with tireless diligence, and their faith and progress increase manifold. Therefore, it is called the "Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma Master. This is for the sake of people's minds:
having heard this teaching, they deeply recognize that the Mahāyāna possesses great power, and thus they decisively sever the net of doubt. Therefore, it is called the "Dharma Master."

The "Chapter on Meritorious Virtues" (Guǐdé pǐn) is intended as an antidote to the initial stage of semblance-understanding, which is surpassed by the ultimate limit of the Two Vehicles by hundreds of thousands of millions of times;
it points to the beginning to reveal the end, providing a transcendent understanding of the First Noble Truth (Paramārtha-satya), which is inconceivable.
Therefore, it is called the "Chapter on the Meritorious Virtues of the Dharma Master. This is the intent of entering into the principle. △ Second, clarifying the fruit and merit of the first chapter.
To encourage the circulation [of this teaching] through virtue, there are two parts: first, a general enumeration of the numbers; second, a detailed explanation.
Now, for the first part: At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Constant Diligence:
"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives, maintains, reads, recites, explains, or copies this Lotus Sūtra, such a person shall obtain eight [qualities]."
With one hundred merits of the eyes, twelve hundred merits of the ears, eight hundred merits of the nose, twelve hundred merits of the tongue,
eight hundred merits of the body, and twelve hundred merits of the mind— adorned with these merits,
the six sense faculties are all rendered pure.

The five grades of contemplative practice (*guanxing*) are arranged vertically in terms of a single individual’s five types of Dharma masters, yet they are arranged horizontally in terms of five distinct persons.
However, since each individual contemplation can also completely purify the six sense faculties, it is vertical yet not vertical;

and since any one person may simultaneously perform all five tasks, it is horizontal yet not horizontal. Here, we borrow this "horizontal yet not horizontal" to correspond with the "vertical yet not vertical."
To faithfully accept it is "receiving" (*pratigraha*); to take up its name is "undertaking" (*adhivāsanā*); to bear and receive it is "retaining" (*dhāraṇā*).

Because this is "rejoicing" (*anumodanā*), one should interpret "receiving and retaining" according to the Chapter on Rejoicing (Chapter Two). Reciting and chanting it corresponds to the second chapter;
explaining it corresponds to the third chapter; and copying and making offerings to it can correspond to both the fourth and fifth chapters, as they share a single essence.
In each chapter, one must necessarily correspond with the ten modes of contemplation; therefore, one shall attain the retribution of the purification of the six sense faculties.

Regarding the "eight hundred thousand" and so forth, if one explains the characteristics based solely on the *Great Buddha-Topknot Sūtra*, then both the meaning of inherent virtue (*xingde*) and that of attainment through cultivation (*xiude*) are established.
This is because the present single thought-moment of the mind-nature is fundamentally vertical.

The vertical dimension is exhausted by means of horizontal pervasion; thus, through vertical exhaustion, the three periods of time are manifested as illusions. Through horizontal pervasion, the four directions are manifested as illusions.
If one calculates by period, each period possesses the four directions; three sets of four likewise constitute twelve.

If one calculates by direction, each direction possesses the three periods; four sets of three likewise constitute twelve. Therefore, it is said that "three and four, four and three, revolving to make twelve. This follows accordingly.
In each direction and in each world-system, there must necessarily be ten realms; thus, there are one hundred and twenty.

Within each of these realms, there must necessarily be ten suchnesses (*tathatā*); thus, there are one thousand two hundred. Therefore, it is said that the threefold transformation of the flow results in one, ten, and a hundred thousand:

(originally there is only the One Mind; the first transformation results in the three worlds and four modes of being, totaling twelve; the second transformation results in the hundred realms; the third transformation results in the one thousand two hundred suchnesses).

(One hundred: If one summarizes all ten realms throughout the ten directions and three periods of time, they are likewise comprised solely of these twelve hundred numbers, which are sufficient to exhaustively encompass them.
If one summarizes each and every sentient being, each also possesses these twelve hundred numbers, neither more nor less.
Since each single sentient being fully possesses these twelve hundred numbers, so too does each and every sense faculty.
Possessing these twelve hundred qualities, this inconceivable nature of reality (dharmatā) is such that the entirely real constitutes the delusory, and the entirely delusory is itself the real.
It does not increase in sages nor decrease in ordinary beings; it is no more when in the six sense-faculties and no less when in a single faculty.
Therefore, it is called "intrinsic virtue" (xingde). Sentient beings are deluded regarding this intrinsic virtue and act in opposition to it.
Through cultivation, the functions of the six sense organs become either more or less extensive. The eye perceives clearly what is before it but not what is behind;

since its range is deficient by half in the four intermediate directions, it possesses only eight hundred [units of power]. The ear, however, hears all-pervasively throughout the ten directions, and thus possesses one thousand two hundred.
The nose exhales and inhales, perceiving fragrance at the juncture where the two breaths intersect; because it lacks superior power at that point of transition, it possesses only...
The eight hundred tongues proclaim [the Dharma] without end; the twelve hundred bodies collectively perceive both the contrary and the compliant, yet remain unaware of the departure from them;
and the eight hundred minds silently accommodate all mundane and supramundane dharmas to their ultimate limits.
These twelve hundred are spoken of specifically in terms of deluded sentiment; the person of perfect realization relies upon these inherent virtues to arise.

In accordance with cultivation, the six sense-faculties function interchangeably without further distinction of superior or inferior; a single faculty universally illumines all objects, and a single object universally confronts all faculties.
Thus, every faculty and every object fully manifests the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). This description is made primarily from the perspective of awakening.
Now, as it follows upward toward awakening, it is said that "merit is adorned and purified"; as it follows downward toward deluded sentiment, [the text continues].

Therefore, although the text mentions "eight hundred thousand two" as being different, it further states, "Though one has not yet attained the divine eye," which follows the deluded sentiments of those at a lower level;
and it also states, "The power of the fleshly eye is thus," which follows the enlightened understanding of those at a higher level.
When one faculty is thus, all others may be known accordingly. II. Specific Explanations, divided into six parts: first, the eye-faculty (up to) sixth, the mind-faculty.
First: these sons and daughters of good family, with the pure fleshly eye born of their parents, see all that exists within and without the trichiliocosm—
mountains, forests, rivers, and seas— reaching downward as far as the Avīci Hell and upward as far as the [Heaven of] Ultimate Existence.

From the crown of his head, he also saw all sentient beings therein, as well as their karmic causes and conditions and the places where they were born as retributions—all of which he saw and knew completely.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
If one preaches this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* amidst the great assembly with a mind free from fear, listen to its merits:

such a person shall obtain eight hundred kinds of superior eyes; because they are adorned by these, their vision is exceedingly pure, and with the eyes born of their parents, they see the entirety of the three thousandfold world system, including the inner and outer Mount Merus, Mount Sumeru, and the Iron Ring Mountains.

Furthermore, all sentient beings within the various mountains, forests, great oceans, rivers, and waters—from the Avīci Hell below up to the Peak of Existence above—will all see them, even though they have not yet attained the divine eye; such is the power of their physical eyes.
Now, regarding these five eyes in their successive order: the flesh eye sees manifest forms directly before it; the divine eye sees forms beyond obstructions; the wisdom eye contemplates emptiness;
the dharma eye contemplates the conventional; and the Buddha eye contemplates both. Within the category of the divine eye, those above can see those below, but those below cannot see those above.
For instance, the divine eye obtained as a karmic reward by the Brahma King allows him to see everywhere within the realm he governs, yet he is unable to see beyond it.
When observing other realms with the divine eye of the two vehicles, one can see a great trichiliocosm if one applies mental attention, but cannot see it if one does not apply attention.

Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana was able to see eight thousand worlds through eight thousand samādhis, while Śāriputra could see ten thousand worlds through ten thousand samādhis; these were all achieved by entering meditative absorption.

Only upon emerging from meditative concentration does one see; thus, one does not see now. It is clear that what the parents have given birth to—the physical eye—sees the great trichiliocosm, including its interior and exterior, above and below, and is not something expounded by other teachings. One should know that this is precisely the perfectly interfused physical eye:
in a single eye there are all eyes, and within the physical eye itself it possesses the function of the five eyes. Seeing the great trichiliocosm is itself seeing the heavens.
The function of the eye, as the karmic cause and fruit of seeing, is the purification of the *dharma-cakṣus*;

because it is free from the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava* and *kleśa-āsrava*), it is the purification of the *prajñā-cakṣus*; because it subdues the delusion of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*), it is the function of the *buddha-cakṣus*.
As the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "Though this is the fleshly eye, it is called the Buddha-eye. Because it is the Buddha-eye, it is called pure; for it possesses all five eyes.
That which is called "adornment" is the semblance of the Buddha-eye, and it is also the semblance of the Buddha’s five eyes.

Because it is still a body of segmented existence (*paricchinna-deha*), it is called the "fleshly eye born of one's parents. Thus, in accordance with deluded sentiments, it is said to be "eight hundred";

yet because one has realized a semblance of understanding, it resembles the Tathāgata’s five eyes that accord with the nature (*dharmatā*). Therefore, it is described as "opening" in accordance with [the truth].
Regarding the statement "Awakening and speaking of merit," according to the subsequent text, one should also fully perceive Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the assembly of Śrāvakas;
one should likewise fully perceive sounds, fragrances, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects (dharmas).

Since one has attained the five eyes that are similarly perfect and interfused, one must necessarily attain the six faculties that function interchangeably (*ṣaḍindriya-samprayoga*); however, this is merely omitted from the text. This is the first [verse] within the gāthā.
The three phrases fully manifest the three tracks: being among the great assembly is the Tathāgata’s chamber;
having a mind free from fear is the Tathāgata’s robe; and preaching this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is the Tathāgata’s seat.
Because these three tracks expand the sūtra and the ten vehicles are complete, one attains the purity of the six sense faculties—how could this be in vain? "Mīlū" (Meru) means "light."
It is one of the seven golden mountains. △ Second, the faculty of hearing.

Furthermore, Constantly Diligent, if a good man or a good woman receives, upholds, reads, recites, explains, or transcribes this sutra, they shall obtain twelve hundred merits of the ear. By means of these purified ears, they shall hear the three [realms].

From the great trichiliocosm below, reaching down to the Avīci Hell and up to the Peak of Existence (Bhavāgra), all the various internal and external sounds therein—the voices of elephants, horses, oxen, and chariots; the sounds of weeping, lamentation, and sighing;
the sounds of conchs, drums, bells, and gongs; the sounds of laughter, speech, men, women, boys, and girls—[all these were heard].
The sound of Dharma and the sound of non-Dharma; the sound of suffering and the sound of happiness; the sound of ordinary beings and the sound of noble ones;
the sound of joy and the sound of lack of joy; the sounds of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas;
the sounds of fire, water, wind; and the sounds of hell-beings and animals.
The sounds of hungry ghosts, the sounds of bhikṣus, the sounds of bhikṣuṇīs, the sounds of śrāvakas, the sounds of pratyekabuddhas,
the sounds of bodhisattvas, and the sounds of buddhas— in short, all internal and external sounds whatsoever within the trichiliocosm,
though he has not yet attained the divine ear, he hears them all with the pure, ordinary (fleshly) ears born of his parents.
Hearing and knowing such various discriminated sounds without impairing the faculty of the ear— at that time, the World-Honored One,
wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"With the ears born of one's parents, pure and free from turbidity or defilement, with these constant ears, one hears the sounds of the three thousandfold world-system."
They hear the sounds of elephants, horses, chariots, oxen, bells, gongs, conchs, and drums; the sounds of lutes, harps, and *konghou* zithers; the sounds of flutes and pipes;
the pure and beautiful voices of songs, which they hear without attachment; and they can fully comprehend and understand the countless varieties of human voices.
Furthermore, they hear the subtle and wondrous singing of the devas, as well as the voices of men and women, and the voices of boys and girls.
In the midst of mountains, rivers, and perilous valleys, the cries of the kalaviṅka, the jīvajīvaka, and all other such birds are heard;
the sounds of various agonies and manifold torments from the denizens of hell; the sounds of hungry ghosts, oppressed by hunger and thirst, crying out for food and drink;
and the great sounds produced when the asuras dwelling on the shores of the great ocean converse among themselves.
Thus, the one who preaches the Dharma dwells here and hears these various sounds from afar without his faculty of hearing being impaired;
he hears all the cries of birds and beasts calling to one another throughout the worlds of the ten directions,
as well as the voices and speech of the Brahma heavens— the Ābhāsvara, Śubhakṛtsna, and up to the Akaniṣṭha heavens.

While the Dharma Master dwells here, he hears everything: whether the assembly of bhikṣus or the bhikṣuṇīs are reciting the sūtras or preaching the Dharma to others, while the Dharma Master dwells here, he hears it all.
Furthermore, he hears various bodhisattvas reciting the scriptures and the Dharma, or preaching them to others, or composing and explaining their meanings.
Thus, all these sounds are heard: those of the Great Holy Buddhas who teach and transform sentient beings as they expound the subtle and wondrous Dharma within great assemblies;

and those who uphold this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* shall hear them all—the various sounds throughout the internal and external realms of the trichiliocosm, from the Avīci Hell below up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) above.
All hear their voices without any impairment of the faculty of hearing; because their ears are keen and sharp, they are all able to discern and comprehend them.
Thus, those who uphold this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*—even though they have not yet attained the divine ear—the merit of the ears with which they were born is already such as this.
Pervasively hearing the sounds of the ten dharma-realms within and without the trichiliocosm: hearing the six paths and the two vehicles is the flesh-ear; hearing the two vehicles is the wisdom-ear;
hearing the bodhisattvas is the dharma-ear; hearing the Buddhas is the Buddha-ear. Furthermore, that which is produced by one's parents is the flesh-ear;
being able to hear both the internal and external is the deva-ear; hearing them without attachment is the wisdom-ear.
The ear that is able to discern and know all things is the Dharma-ear; the ear that hears all simultaneously and inconceivably is the Buddha-ear.
△ Third, the faculty of the nose.
Furthermore, Constant Diligence, if a good man or a good woman receives and upholds this sutra, whether reading it or reciting it...
Whether explaining or writing it down, one accomplishes eight hundred merits of the nose; with this purified faculty of the nose,
one perceives the various fragrances throughout the trichiliocosm— above, below, and within and without— such as the fragrance of *sumana* flowers,
*jāti* flowers, *mallikā* flowers, *campaka* flowers, *pāṭala* flowers, and red lotuses.
The fragrance of blue lotuses, the fragrance of white lotuses, the fragrance of flowering trees, the fragrance of fruit-bearing trees,

the fragrance of sandalwood, the fragrance of aloeswood, the fragrance of *tāmālapatra*, the fragrance of *tagara*, and tens of millions of kinds of blended perfumes— whether in powder, pill, or ointment form—
all those who uphold this sutra, while dwelling here in this world, are able to distinguish them all; furthermore, they know the various [fragrances] individually.
Whether it be the fragrance of elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, and goats; the fragrance of men, women, boys, and girls;
or the fragrance of grasses, trees, thickets, and forests—whether near or far—all such fragrances are perceived without error by one who upholds this sutra.
Although remaining here, they also smell the various celestial fragrances of the devas in the heavens.
The fragrance of the *tṛcchattra-kovidāra* tree, the scent of *māndārava* flowers, the scent of *mahāmāndārava* flowers,
the scent of *mañjūṣaka* flowers, the scent of *mahāmañjūṣaka* flowers, various powdered incenses such as sandalwood and aloeswood,
and the scents of diverse mixed flowers— all such celestial fragrances produced by their combination were without exception...
Furthermore, they hear and know the fragrances of the bodies of the devas: when Śakra-devānām-indra is enjoying the pleasures of the five desires and sporting in the Palace of Victory;
when he is in the Hall of the Sublime Dharma preaching the Dharma to the Trāyastriṃśa devas; when he is sporting in the various gardens;
and the fragrances of the bodies of the male and female devas of other realms—all these they smell from afar, just as [the Buddha does].
Thus, they successively perceive the fragrances of the bodies of all the devas, from the Brahma-world up to the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra), as well as the incense burned by those devas;
they likewise perceive from afar the fragrance of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and the fragrance of the bodies of the Buddhas, knowing their locations.
Although they perceive these fragrances, their faculty of the nose remains unimpaired.
It is so; if one wishes to discern and explain it to others, one will remember it without error. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The nose of this person is purified; within this world, whether it be fragrant or foul things, he perceives all varieties completely."
Whether it be the fragrance of *sumana*, *jāti*, *tamāla*, sandalwood, aloeswood, or cinnamon; the scents of various flowers and fruits;
the scents of all sentient beings; or the scents of men and women—the Dharma-preacher, though dwelling at a distance, perceives their locations by smelling these fragrances.
Likewise, the powerful universal monarch (*cakravartin*), the minor wheel-turning kings, their sons, ministers, and palace attendants—he perceives their locations by smelling their fragrances.
By smelling the fragrance, one knows the location of the precious jewels worn upon the body, the treasures hidden in the earth, and the precious women of the wheel-turning monarch;
by smelling the fragrance, one knows the ornaments, garments, and necklaces with which people adorn themselves, as well as the various types of unguents they apply.
By smelling the fragrance, one can fully know whether the devas are walking, sitting, sporting, or performing miracles—all this is known by one who upholds this Lotus Sūtra.
The fragrances of the flowers, fruits, and kernels of all trees, as well as the scent of clarified butter—those who uphold this sutra dwelling here shall know their locations entirely.
In deep and perilous mountain recesses where sandalwood trees are in bloom and sentient beings dwell therein, they shall be able to know them all by smelling the fragrance.
Within the Iron Ring Mountains and the great oceans upon the earth, those who uphold this sutra shall smell the fragrance and know the whereabouts of all sentient beings therein.
When the male and female asuras and their various retinues are engaged in fighting, quarreling, or sporting, they can know [all] by smelling the fragrance.

In wildernesses and perilous narrow passes, they can smell the scent of lions, elephants, tigers, wolves, wild oxen, water buffaloes, and the like, and by smelling the fragrance, they know their locations.
If there are those who are pregnant, they can know whether it is male or female; they can also smell and fully discern those without sexual organs and non-humans.
By the power of smelling fragrances, one knows whether a woman has recently conceived, whether she will bring it to term or not, and whether she will give birth in comfort with a son of merit;
by the power of smelling fragrances, one knows the thoughts of men and women—whether they are stained by desire, delusion, or anger—and likewise knows those who practice virtue.
One can also know all the various treasures hidden underground, such as gold, silver, precious gems, and copper vessels, simply by smelling their fragrance.
Regarding various kinds of necklaces and ornaments, none can recognize their value; yet by smelling their fragrance, one knows their worth, their origin, and where they are located.
Regarding the various celestial flowers—such as the *māndārava*, *mañjūṣaka*, and *pāriyātraka* trees—one can know them all by smelling their fragrance.
Regarding the various celestial palaces, distinguished as superior, middling, or inferior, and adorned with many precious flowers, one can know them all by smelling their fragrance.

In the midst of the celestial gardens, excellent palaces, and various pavilions, there is a Hall of Wondrous Dharma where they take their pleasure; by smelling the fragrance, he is able to know all the devas—
whether they are listening to the Dharma or experiencing the five desires, whether they are coming and going, walking, sitting, or lying down— and by smelling the fragrance,
he is able to know everything regarding the celestial maidens’ garments, their fine flower-fragrances and ornaments, and their movements as they roam and play.
In this manner, proceeding upward through successive stages, he is able to know by the scent all those who enter and emerge from dhyāna up to the Brahma-world;
he is able to know by the scent all those born for the first time or passing away from the Ābhāsvara, Śubhakṛtsna, and even up to the Peak of Existence (Bhavāgra).
Furthermore, among the assembly of bhikṣus who are always diligent in the Dharma—whether sitting, walking, or reciting the sūtras—he is able to know them all by their scent.
Or those who, beneath forest trees, sit with single-minded devotion in meditation or uphold the sūtras—their locations are all known by the scent.
Whether Bodhisattvas of firm resolve are sitting in meditation, reciting and chanting, or preaching the Dharma for others, their presence in every direction is fully known by the scent.
The World-Honored One, revered by all, out of compassion for the multitudes, preaches the Dharma; his location is likewise fully known by the scent.
When sentient beings hear this sutra before the Buddha, they all rejoice and practice according to the Dharma; by smelling the fragrance, they are able to know [all things].
Although they have not yet attained the bodhisattva’s untainted dharma, those who uphold this sutra first attain this mark of the nose.
That which is born of one's parents is the fleshly nose; that which encompasses the interior and exterior of the great trichiliocosm is the celestial nose;
being unstained and unattached is the wisdom nose; discerning without error is the Dharma nose; the simultaneous and mutual functioning of these is the Buddha nose.

This chapter clarifies that the mutual functioning of these noses is most prominent, whereby one thoroughly knows the good and the evil, distinguishes the noble from the base, and discerns the adornments of the celestial palaces.
The nose having the function of the eye: when reading scriptures or preaching the Dharma, one is able to know [the words] by smelling their fragrance. The nose having the function of the ear:
[one perceives] the fragrances of the flowers, fruits, and seeds of various trees, as well as the scent of ghee and oil. The nose having the function of the tongue: entering and emerging from dhyāna;
the eight tactile sensations within dhyāna and the play of the five desires are also objects of touch. The nose having the function of the body: [it perceives] the defilement of desire.

One who possesses a mind of delusion or anger also knows how to cultivate goodness; this is because the nose has the function of consciousness. Generally speaking, if one examines the attachments of deluded sentiments, the nose alone is the most inferior in its functioning;
therefore, the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) of the Hīnayāna are limited to the eyes, ears, body, and mind, and do not clarify the two powers of the nose and tongue.
Nevertheless, the tongue is still somewhat superior as it can preach the Dharma, whereas the nose merely passes through the breath and possesses nothing more.

That he specifically elucidates these superior functions extensively in this chapter is precisely to reveal that the wondrous nature of perfect penetration is truly without superiority or inferiority;
it is merely to conform to the deluded sentiments of beings that he speaks of "eight hundred" as being similar to the Buddha's nose and "one thousand and two" as being perfectly distinct.
△ Fourth, the faculty of the tongue.
Furthermore, Constantly Diligent, if a son or daughter of good family receives, upholds, reads, recites, explains, or transcribes this sutra, they will obtain twelve hundred merits of the tongue;
whether [the food] is pleasant or unpleasant, delicious or not, [they shall perceive it as such].

Whether it be delicious foods or various bitter and astringent things, when they reach his tongue-root, they all transform into supreme flavors, like celestial nectar (*amṛta*), such that there is nothing that is not delicious.

Furthermore, if he uses his tongue-root to deliver discourses within a great assembly, he produces a profound and wondrous sound that can penetrate their hearts, causing them all to rejoice and experience happiness.
Moreover, when the sons of gods, daughters of gods, Śakra, Brahmā, and the various deities hear him, [they likewise find joy].
When this profound and wondrous voice delivers its discourse, the sequence of its teachings is heard by all who come to listen:

the nāgas and nāga daughters, yakṣas and yakṣī daughters, gandharvas and gandharvī daughters, asuras and asurī daughters, garuḍas and garuḍī daughters, kiṃnaras and kiṃnarī daughters, mahoragas and... [mahoragīs].
The *hūlaga* women all came to approach, pay homage, and make offerings for the sake of hearing the Dharma; likewise, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs,

upāsakas, upāsikās, kings, princes, ministers, and their retinues, as well as minor universal monarchs (*kṣudra-cakravartin*) and great universal monarchs (*mahā-cakravartin*) with their seven treasures,
a thousand sons, and their inner and outer attendants, all came together upon their palaces to hear the Dharma.
Because this bodhisattva skillfully expounds the Dharma, brahmins, householders, and all the people within the kingdom attend upon and make offerings to him for as long as they live.
Furthermore, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas always delight in seeing him.
In whichever direction this person may be, all the buddhas turn toward that place and preach the Dharma to him, and he is able to receive and uphold it all.
The Buddha-dharma can also produce the sounds of profound and wondrous Dharma. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The tongue-faculty of such a person is pure, and they shall never again experience foul flavors; whatever they eat or consume shall all become nectar."

Using a profound, pure, and wondrous voice, he preaches the Dharma to the great assembly; through various causes, conditions, and parables, he guides the minds of sentient beings so that all who hear it rejoice.

They provide all manner of supreme offerings, and the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, and others all come together with reverent hearts to listen to this Dharma. If this speaker of the Dharma wishes to use a wondrous voice—

Pervading the trichiliocosm, he can reach it at will; the great and small universal monarchs (*cakravartin*), together with their retinues of a thousand sons, constantly approach with palms joined in reverence to hear and receive the Dharma.
The devas, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas also constantly and joyfully come to make offerings. So too do Brahmā, the Māra King, Īśvara, and Maheśvara.

Thus, the hosts of devas constantly come to his dwelling; the Buddhas and their disciples, hearing the sound of his preaching the Dharma, always keep him in mind and protect him, and at times they manifest themselves before him.
That which is born of one's parents is the fleshly tongue; its ability to produce the speech of the ten dharma-realms clarifies the meaning of the five tongues.
Furthermore, its ability to produce the speech of the ten realms is the celestial tongue; its indestructibility is the wisdom tongue; its lack of error is the Dharma tongue;
and its simultaneous mutual functioning is the Buddha tongue. Question: If harsh or foul flavors reach the tongue, they all transform into superior [flavors].
If various tastes reach the eye, why do they not transform it into a beautiful color? The previous answer was not analogous: tastes have both harmful and beneficial effects;

that which is harmful transforms [the sense organ], while that which is not harmful does not. Various visible forms do not damage the eye, and thus the case is not analogous. The present explanation is not so:
all visible forms are identical to the Buddha’s form, all sounds are identical to the Buddha’s voice, and so on, up to all phenomena being identical [to the Buddha’s phenomena].
If the Buddha-dharma and all such things are equally pure, what hindrance is there to universally knowing all forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects without confusion or error?
Furthermore, what hindrance is there to making distinctions? Though free from attachment, one is still able to discern;

how could this be the same as the emptiness-contemplation of the two vehicles? Though one makes distinctions, the various faculties are not impaired; how could this be the same as the stagnation of ordinary beings?
One who possesses the faculty of mastery may instead form a conception of it as something rigid and obstructive. △ Five: The Body Faculty.

Furthermore, Constantly Diligent, if a son or daughter of good family receives, upholds, reads, recites, explains, or transcribes this sutra, they shall obtain eight hundred merits of the body and attain a pure body like clear lapis lazuli.
Because the body of the sentient being *Sarvasattvapriyadarśana* was pure, the births and deaths of all beings in the trichiliocosm—
whether superior or inferior, beautiful or ugly, born in good or evil realms— all appeared within it; likewise, the Cakravāḍa Mountains,
Mahācakravāḍa Mountains, Sumeru Mountains, and Mahāsumeru Mountains, as well as all the sentient beings dwelling upon them, were all manifested therein.
From the Avīci Hell below to the Peak of Existence above, all things and all sentient beings appear within it;
even the sounds of the Dharma preached by śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas all manifest as their physical forms and images within his body.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If one upholds the Lotus Sutra, their body will be exceedingly pure, like that of clear lapis lazuli, which all sentient beings joyfully behold;
it is also like a bright, clean mirror that reflects all forms and images. Upon such a pure body, the Bodhisattva perceives everything that exists in the world."

He alone clearly perceives this while others do not see it: all the various forms of the multitudes of beings within the trichiliocosm—gods, humans, asuras, hell-dwellers, hungry ghosts, and animals—all appear within his own body;
likewise, the palaces of the devas up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), as well as the Iron Ring Mountains (*cakravāḍa*) and Mount Meru and Mahāmeru.
The waters of all great oceans appear within his body; likewise, all Buddhas, śrāvakas, and bodhisattvas—whether teaching the Dharma alone or in assembly—all appear therein.
Although he has not yet attained the wondrous body of the untainted dharma-nature, everything appears within this pure, ordinary body born of parents.

All that exists in the world manifests within the body as the function of the physical body; reaching upward to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), it manifests within the body as the function of the celestial body;
for the followers of the Two Vehicles, it manifests within the body as the function of the wisdom-body (*prajñā-kāya*);

for Bodhisattvas, it manifests within the body as the function of the dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*); and for Buddhas, it manifests within the body as the function of the Buddha-body. All are perfected simultaneously.

Manifesting at one time the mutual functioning [of the Buddha-body], at one time being without error [the Dharma-body], and at one time being without attachment [the Wisdom-body]. △ Sixth, the faculty of mind.
Furthermore, Constant Vigor, if a son or daughter of good family, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata,
receives, upholds, reads, recites, explains, or transcribes this sutra, they will attain twelve hundred merits of the mental faculty (*manas*).
By means of this purified mental faculty, even upon hearing a single verse or a single phrase, they will penetrate immeasurable and boundless meanings and understand them.

Having already been able to expound upon a single phrase or a single verse for as long as one month, four months, or even up to a year, all the teachings he proclaims accord with their underlying meaning and never contradict the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
Whether he speaks of secular scriptures, worldly discourse, or the arts of livelihood, all are in harmony with the True Dharma. Within this three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system...
He fully knows the movements of the minds of sentient beings, their mental activities, and their conceptual proliferations;
although he has not yet attained untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), his faculty of mind is thus purified.
Whatever this person contemplates or deliberates upon is entirely the Buddha-dharma, none of which is not true, and it is all that was spoken in the sūtras of previous Buddhas. At that time—
The World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The mind of such a person is pure, clear, sharp, and free from turbidity or defilement. With this wondrous faculty of the mind, they know the superior, middling, and inferior dharmas;
even upon hearing a single verse, they penetrate immeasurable meanings and explain them in sequence according to the Dharma—from one month, four months, to a year."

All sentient beings within and without this world—whether devas, nāgas, humans, yakṣas, ghosts, spirits, or others—who dwell within the six realms of existence, shall at once come to know all their various thoughts;

they shall hear and be able to receive and uphold the teachings on the hundred blessings that adorn the marks of the countless Buddhas of the ten directions as those Buddhas preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings. This is the retribution for upholding the Lotus Sūtra.
Contemplating immeasurable meanings, they preach the Dharma in immeasurable ways; from beginning to end, they never forget or err because they uphold the Lotus Sūtra.
Thus they fully know the characteristics of all dharmas, recognize their sequence according to their meaning, and penetrate names and language.
What they preach is exactly as they have realized it; because they expound this Dharma, they possess no fear among the assembly.

The faculty of mind of one who upholds the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is purified in this way; although they have not yet attained the outflows-free state (*anāsrava*), they already possess such signs.

Such a person, upholding this sūtra, dwells in a rare and sublime stage, being joyful toward and cherished by all sentient beings, and is able to expound the Dharma through the analysis of ten million kinds of skillful speech, because they uphold the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
That all worldly livelihoods and industries accord with the True Dharma is the purity of the human mind;

that one fully knows the actions and movements of devas is the purity of the celestial mind. The four months represent the Four Noble Truths, and the twelve months of a year represent the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination;
that these do not contradict the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*) is the purity of the wisdom-mind. One.
The first Mahāyāna within the *Moon Manifestation*—that is, the purity of the Dharma-intent—is such that whatever one contemplates is all that was taught in the sūtras of the former Buddhas;
it is the purity of the Buddha-intent, perfectly luminous at once, mutually perfect at once, untainted at once, and unerring at once.
This concludes the second section: explaining the meritorious virtues of the fruit of the first chapter to encourage its circulation.
△ The explanation of the "Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma-Master" is completed. Next, the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging" is explained.

In this twentieth chapter, "The Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging," he harbors within the understanding that none are to be disparaged, while externally he respects those who are not to be disparaged (the world); thus, he establishes the practice of never-disparaging through his very person.

(As for people,) he orally proclaims the teaching of "Not Disparaging" (*adhimāna*); (as an antidote,) he causes people to adopt the title "Not Disparaging. Regarding (the ultimate meaning) of the interpretation of "Not Disparaging," the *Fahua lun* states:
"This bodhisattva knows that sentient beings possess Buddha-nature and therefore does not dare to disparage them. There are five kinds of Buddha-nature:

the Nature as Direct Cause (*hetu-buddhadhātu*), which pervades both the fundamental and the actual (pervading delusion and awakening, as well as cause and effect); and the Nature as Condition (*pratyaya*) and the Nature as Fulfillment (*pariniṣpanna*).

The seeds are inherently present and not merely acquired now (this refers back to the nature-endowment to clarify the two causes, as they correspond to the newly perfumed causes that result in cultivated attainment).

The nature of the fruit (*bodhi*) and the nature of the fruit of fruits (*nirvāṇa*) are certain to be attained; it will never be in vain. (When the *vijñapti*-cause reaches fruition, it is termed *bodhi*; when the *pratyaya*-cause reaches fruition, it is termed *nirvāṇa*.

Furthermore, when the three causal natures reach fruition, the *vijñapti*-causes are termed the three kinds of *bodhi*, and the *pratyaya*-causes are termed the three kinds of *nirvāṇa*). This is called the understanding of the "Not-Light" (Avalokita); one should understand it thus.
Because all people are likewise so, this is called the "object of reverence and non-contempt. Because one reveres this object, it is called the "practice of non-contempt";

because one proclaims these words, it is called the "teaching of non-contempt. That which was formerly used by detractors to label people is now used by the compilers of the sutra to title this chapter;
this is the explanation based on causes and conditions (*nidāna*). Regarding the explanation according to the teachings (*yāna*), there are two: the *piṭaka* (Treasury) and the *āgama* (Tradition).

The teaching does not explicitly expound the Middle Way; it distinguishes between the Buddha-nature of those who enter through the Universal (P’an-chiao) and those who enter through the Particular (Chiao-men), clarifying two types of people who possess Buddha-nature and three types of people who lack it.

While the Particular Teaching speaks only of the *pratyaya-hetu* (causal) Buddha-nature and does not mention the *ālambana-hetu* (conditional) or *nirvāṇa-hetu* (resultant) natures—let alone the nature of the fruit (*phala-bhāva*) or the nature beyond the fruit (*phalaphala-bhāva*)—the present text states: "You shall all become Buddhas," thereby fully [establishing the universal presence of Buddha-nature].
Because there are five Buddha-natures, this is precisely the revelation of the Perfect [Teaching]. Thus, the *Jian shi sanmei jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Seeing Reality) states:
"The Buddha spoke to his father, the King, saying that all are Buddhas. The King asked, "Are all sentient beings Buddhas?
The Buddha replied, "If one sees sentient beings according to reality, for them they are indeed Buddhas. Now, if we apply this statement to the present case...
To see the Buddha as he truly is, is precisely not to regard him as a "sage" (ārya). It is like a beginner at archery who misses the mark more often than hitting it;

by taking the ground itself as the target, there is nowhere he does not hit. If one discriminates between the worthy and the noble, asking who is right and who is wrong, and observes them according to reality, that very observation is the Buddha.
Regarding "original" and "traced" (honji-suijaku): the original [Buddha] has already attained Buddhahood long ago, long ago, in the midst of the vast eons.

Manifesting his traces once again in the era of King Majestic Sound (Vaiśvānara-rāja), he was known as Never-Disparaging (Sadāparibhūta) to propagate the teachings of the fourfold and onefold reality (shishikyō ichijikyō) and to deliver sentient beings;

now, manifesting his traces yet again, he demonstrates the attainment of perfect enlightenment. This succession of manifestations is inexhaustible, a manifestation of the power of Great Might (Mahāsthāmaprāpta).

As for the contemplation of the mind: suffering is the Buddha-nature of the direct cause (samyak-hetu); delusion is the Buddha-nature of the understanding cause (parijñāna-hetu); and karma is [the Buddha-nature of the producing cause].

The *pratyaya-hetu-buddha-nature* is the *jñāna-hetu-buddha-nature* (the cause as realization), which is the *phala-buddha-nature* (the fruit); the *pratyaya-hetu* itself is the *phala-phala-buddha-nature* (the fruit of the fruit).
Furthermore, when these three causes reach fruition, they are renamed the "three *bodhi*s" and the "three *nirvāṇa*s.

Thus, the three causes of the nature-merit (*prakṛti-guṇa*) constitute the causal nature (*hetu-svabhāva*), the resultant nature (*phala-svabhāva*), and the nature of the fruit of the fruit (*phala-phala-svabhāva*). These three causes and five natures are fully present in a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*), neither sequential nor disjointed.
To universally regard all sentient beings as neither identical nor different, and to always maintain this understanding—that is precisely what is meant by "Never-Disparaging.

thus we know this is a manifestation of the causal practices following the attainment of fruition. Question:

they are all the power of sovereign supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*), the power of the lion’s boundless stride (*siṃhavikrīḍita*), and the power of fierce and great majesty. [Question: What is the fruit?
Later, because he manifested the practice of "Not Disdaining," he merely circulated the single phrase "attaining Buddhahood" and was thereby able to purify his six sense organs.
If one were a genuine beginner, it might not necessarily be so. Answer: Generally speaking, all that is called "provisional" (upāya) is intended to lead toward the "real.
If the real practice were not effective, then provisional practice would be rendered in vain; moreover, the understanding of "Not Disdaining" is precisely the single thought-moment (ekacitta-kṣaṇa).

Rejoicing in the initial resolve and its merit is already inconceivable; since practice is established based on understanding, one will surely purify the six sense organs—why then need one harbor doubt?
It is simply that the practice of "Not Disparaging" is not limited to prostration alone, as is clearly explained in the following text. △ Second, the Name and Title.
There was a Buddha named King of Majestic Sound (Vaiśvānara-rāja), a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Well-Gone, Knower of the World,

the kalpa is named Free from Decline, and the land is named Great Achievement.

for those seeking the state of a pratyekabuddha, he taught the Dharma corresponding to the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination; and for all bodhisattvas, [he taught] based on anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi...
The teaching on the three types of enlightenment (trividha-bodhi) explains that one should ultimately attain the Buddha-wisdom through the six pāramitās.
First, there are the three [types of enlightenment] as skillful means; subsequently, the ultimate attainment of Buddha-wisdom reveals that they are entirely identical to the present Buddha.
