Mahāsthāmaprāpta, the lifespan of the Buddha King of Awesome Sound (Vaiśvānara-rāja), was forty thousand *koṭi-nayuta* Ganges-sand kalpas.
△ 6. The True and Semblance Dharma Periods.

The number of kalpas for which the True Dharma remains in the world is equal to the number of atoms in one Jambudvīpa; the number of kalpas for which the Semblance Dharma remains in the world is equal to the number of atoms in the four continents.
After that Buddha has extensively benefited sentient beings, he will then enter parinirvāṇa.
The first section, explaining the very first Buddha, is concluded. II. Explaining the subsequent twenty thousand koṭis of Buddhas:

After the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma had completely vanished, another Buddha appeared in this land, also named King of Awesome Sound Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men...
The World-Honored Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and Teachers of Gods and Humans, appeared in succession in this manner—twenty trillion Buddhas all bearing the same name.

Following the periods of the True Dharma, the Semblance Dharma, and the Extinction of the Dharma, the Buddhas subsequently appeared; it was the natural law that the conditions for the maturation and liberation of sentient beings were thus brought about.

Therefore, the first section, which clarifies the origin of the matter, is concluded. △ Second, the clarification of the fundamental matter (*mūlavastu*) specifically concerns the events during the time of the original Buddha Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja, namely the story of the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging.
This is the matter of our World-Honored One manifesting his traces and once again demonstrating his past practice of the bodhisattva path.
The text is divided into three parts; first, regarding that original time, both names are presented together.
The second pair clarifies the characteristics of praise and disparagement; the third pair clarifies the retributions for praise and disparagement. Now, regarding the first:

after the Tathāgata King of Majestic Sound had already entered parinirvāṇa and the True Dharma had ceased, during the period of the Semblance Dharma, there were monks of overweening pride who possessed great power. At that time, there was a bodhisattva monk named Never-Disparaging.
"Original time" refers to the period of the Semblance Dharma of the Buddha King of Majestic Sound at the very beginning.
"Those who disparage" were called those of overweening pride (*adhimāna*) during that original time; "those who believe" were called Constantly-Not-Light during that original time.

As for those of overweening pride, because they upheld provisional teachings and practiced provisional conduct, they attained slight realizations but did not know the relative depth of the successive stages; they mistakenly identified the stage of "warmth" (*uṣmagata*) with the four *dhyānas*.
Thinking that they have attained the four fruits of the path, they falsely conceive a sense of self-satisfaction;
these are precisely the kind of "unlearned bhikṣus" who, even if they do not openly disparage others, will surely fall due to their own fierce and poisonous nature.

Since all such people are destined for downfall, it is appropriate to establish them as the seed for the lower Perfect and Sudden teaching; therefore, through prostration and the bestowing of predictions, the conditions for their deliverance are created. △ Second, the Pair.

The second section clarifies the characteristics of those who revile [the teaching]; it has two parts: first, clarifying what the believer attains; second, clarifying the loss incurred by the reviler.
Now, for the first part:
regarding the attainment of great power, by what causes and conditions was that bhikṣu named "Never-Disparaging"? Whenever he saw anyone—whether a bhikṣu...
The bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās all paid homage and praised him, saying:
"We deeply revere you and do not dare to treat you with contempt. Why is this? You all practice the bodhisattva path and shall surely attain Buddhahood.
Yet this bhikṣu does not focus on reading or reciting the sūtras, but instead practices only prostrations, and so forth...
Seeing the fourfold assembly from afar, he likewise went to them to pay homage and offer praise, saying these words:
"I do not dare to treat you with contempt; you shall all become Buddhas."

The name "Never-Disparaging" (*Sadāparibhūta*) refers to the person (the one who realizes the principle). That upon seeing anyone, one prostrates to them all, refers to the practice (the one who acts according to the principle).
To speak these words refers to the teaching (the one who instructs according to the principle). These constitute the fourfold unity of self-cultivation. "All of you" refers to the person;
"all practicing the bodhisattva path" refers to the practice; and "you shall surely attain Buddhahood" refers to the realization of the principle. This explains [the meaning].
The three unities constitute the unity of the teaching; this is by means of the four unities that one transforms others.

This is truly because at that time, the fourfold assembly was numerous and had given rise to overweening pride (*adhimāna*), clinging to the "expedient of expedients" and the "smallness of the small" (the *Āgama* teachings were already expedients, the *uṣmagata* stage was an expedient within those teachings, and the four fruits were already "small," while the four *dhyānas* were the "smallest of the small"). Therefore, [the Buddha] opened [the path] by means of the true meaning of the Mahāyāna.
Xiao [the Master] did not dare to treat [the disciples] with negligence, thereby remedying the fault of *adhimāna* (overweening pride). He said: "You all practice the Bodhisattva path;
these four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are the *uṣmagata* (heat) stage of the Mahāyāna. The four dhyānas together support the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
If you know that what you practice is the Bodhisattva path, then from beginning to end the principle is equal, yet the successive stages (*krama-pada*) are clearly distinct. Ultimately, he never...

Those who give rise to overweening pride and do not specialize in recitation and chanting, but instead practice only prostrations, manifest the characteristics of the first stage, the Chapter on Rejoicing:
rejoicing that all phenomena possess the nature of peace and bliss, which is the single true reality;
and rejoicing that all persons possess the three Buddha-natures, such that those with a mind shall all attain Buddhahood—this is the nature of the direct cause (*samyak-hetu*).
To read and recite the provisional vehicle’s bequeathed Dharma of King Majestic Sound is the nature of the *liàoyīn* (the cause of realization);

the *nuǎnfǎ* (warmth) and the four *dhyānas* are all the path of the bodhisattva, as they constitute the nature of the *yuán yīn* (the causal condition). Therefore, one must not treat them with contempt but should instead revere them deeply.

To revere both persons and the Dharma without giving rise to contention is the meaning of "rejoicing" (*suíxǐ*). Furthermore, the phrase "even seeing the fourfold assembly from afar" serves as an illustration.
The fourfold "one" of the origin signifies the one person; seeing the four assemblies from afar represents the one person of the origin; going to pay homage represents the one practice of the origin;
speaking these words represents the one teaching of the origin; and the statement that "all shall become Buddhas" represents the one principle of the origin.

By means of these fourfold "ones" of origin and trace, those who are stubbornly afflicted by overweening pride are caused to develop the wondrous seeds of the Perfect and Sudden teaching—this may be called attaining [the goal].
This is the grand tenet of the True Teaching: to not treat others lightly and to deeply respect them is the seat of the Tathāgata;
to endure being struck and reviled is the robe of the Tathāgata; and to constantly practice with a mind of compassion without ceasing is the hall of the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, this deep respect is the mental action (*manas-karma*), this teaching of not treating others lightly is the verbal action (*vāk-karma*), and going to pay homage is the physical action (*kāya-karma*); these are the three.
To practice the vow of peaceful conduct together with compassion and mercy can be called attaining the sublime benefit of its circulation.
Question: Since both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna Vinayas prohibit bhikṣus from bowing to laypeople, how can it be said that [this practice] is universally applicable to the fourfold assembly?

Answer: It is for the sake of transforming those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*), so as to enable them to obtain both immediate and ultimate benefits (for among the fourfold assembly, there are those who accept [the teaching] and those who do not).

One receives immediate benefits rather than merely distant ones. Great skillful means and knowledge of the opportune moment do not obstruct the breaking of formal rules; the four practices for peaceful dwelling must rely upon the Vinaya texts. Question:
Regarding the "Great Sūtra" (Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra), what is the difference between the veneration of those who know the Dharma and the veneration of a *Vimalakīrti*-like bhikṣu toward laypeople?
Answer: They are not the same. The "Great Sūtra" manifests the resolve to revere the Dharma, as it seeks instruction from that [layperson].

In the practice of "forgetting emotions" (*wangqing*), one forgets transgressions while offering reverence, as the grace of Vimalakīrti’s attainment of *dharmakṣānti* does not abide by constant worldly rules.

therefore, when contrasted with the four modes of peaceful conduct (*catur-śukla-vihāra*), although the underlying principle is not different, there are seven distinctions in their ritual procedures:

first, whereas that [practice] involves sitting securely upon the Dharma-seat and preaching according to questions, this [practice] involves going to pay homage because one sees the fourfold assembly from afar; second, whereas that... [text continues].

First, those who have developed faith through the minor scriptures (*kṣudra-śāstra*) do not yet possess the cause for Buddhahood; yet, even if they now disparage this sutra, it shall still become a wondrous seed.

△ Second, explaining the faults of those who disparage it:
Among the fourfold assembly, there are those who give rise to a mind of anger and impurity, using foul language and abuse to say, "This is ignorant."
"From where has this bhikṣu come that he says, 'I do not slight you, but I bestow upon you the prediction that you shall become Buddhas,' when we have no need for such a false prediction?"
This clarifies that those with overweening pride do not believe in the four "ones" and instead slander and revile [the teaching].
First, they do not believe in the teaching because they reject such false prophecies;

since they regard the prophecy as false, they do not know that their own practice is the bodhisattva path—this is the first lack of faith in practice. Furthermore, they do not know that they themselves shall attain Buddhahood.
That is to say, there was one person who lacked faith and one who [lacked faith] in principle.
Having experienced this for many years, he was constantly reviled, yet he never gave rise to anger and always spoke these words:
"You shall become a Buddha. When he said these words, the crowd sometimes struck and pelted him with sticks, wood, tiles, and stones, but he would avoid them and flee.
Even while dwelling at a distance, he would still cry out in a loud voice, "I do not dare to slight you; you shall all become Buddhas.
Because he constantly spoke these words, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās who were possessed of overweening pride (adhimāna) called him "Never-Disparaging" (Sadāparibhūta).
Not becoming angry when reviled, but constantly saying these words, constitutes the mark of forming deep faith and non-retrogression.
Being struck with staves and the like, yet remaining unyielding, constitutes the first of the four [stages] for opening up the provisional to reveal the real.

Fleeing to stay at a distance while still shouting out loudly because of being slandered, constitutes the first of the four [stages] for opening up the near to reveal the distant, and is thus called "Never-Disparaging."
He also asked: "Why was it that for forty-odd years Śākyamuni did not strive to preach quickly, yet did not disparage those who spoke rashly whenever they saw something?
He answered: "Those who already possessed goodness were protected by Śākyamuni through minor [teachings];

△ Section Three: Clarifying the Retribution for Faith and Slander (in two parts). First, clarifying the retribution for those who have faith; second, clarifying the retribution for those who slander. Within the first part, there are two sub-sections: first, clarifying the retribution; second, correlating the ancient and the modern. Now, the first [sub-section]: The Buddha told Ānanda: "In the past, during the time of the Tathāgata Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja, there was a king named *Vimaladatta*. He had a son named *Ratnacchattra*, who was handsome, possessed of a pleasing countenance, and endowed with all excellent marks. At that time, the King’s younger brother was named *Vimalanetra*. He was wise, intelligent, and possessed great eloquence. He served as the King’s minister and was deeply trusted by the sovereign. At that time, the World-Honored One Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja appeared in the world and turned the wheel of the Dharma. The King, having heard of this, went to the Buddha’s dwelling with his ministers and retinue to pay homage and listen to the teaching. Having heard the Dharma, he attained the stage of non-retrogression. His son, Prince Ratnacchattra, also followed him to hear the Dharma and attained the stage of non-retrogression. However, the King’s younger brother, Vimalanetra, did not go to the Buddha to hear the teaching. Subsequently, the King passed away and was reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven, while his son, Prince Ratnacchattra, became the Universal Monarch of Jambudvīpa. Because he had planted roots of goodness under the Buddha Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja, he now rules over the four continents, possesses the seven treasures, and enjoys immeasurable bliss. Furthermore, because he had attained the stage of non-retrogression, he will never again fall back. As for the King’s younger brother, Vimalanetra, because he failed to go to the Buddha to hear the Dharma, he fell into the Avīci Hell after his death. After exhausting the retribution of that hell, he was reborn as a hungry ghost, suffering from hunger and thirst. After exhausting the retribution of the hungry ghosts, he was reborn as a beast, specifically a large fish in the great ocean. Because he had previously been a human, he could speak human language. Whenever merchants traveling by sea encountered wind and waves and were about to perish, they would recite the names of the Buddhas of the ten directions. That fish, hearing these names, would leap out of the water onto the shore, where it would die and be reborn as a human. Yet, because of the residual karma of its previous lives, it would always be born into lowly families, such as those of hunters or fishermen, and would suffer various afflictions. Ānanda, you should know that the King of that time was none other than myself. My son, Prince Ratnacchattra, was Śākyamuni Buddha. The King’s younger brother, Vimalanetra, was Devadatta. Because Devadatta slandered me, he suffered the retribution of the Avīci Hell for one small kalpa. After exhausting that retribution, he was reborn as a hungry ghost for five hundred years. After exhausting that retribution, he was reborn as a large fish in the great ocean for five hundred years. After exhausting that retribution, he was reborn as a human for five hundred years, yet always in lowly families and constantly afflicted by various sufferings. Ānanda, you should know that if one slanders the Tathāgata, the retribution is even more severe than this. Therefore, Ānanda, you should protect and uphold this sutra, and do not allow others to slander it. [End of] the first part: Clarifying the retribution. [End of] the first section. When this bhikṣu was about to pass away, he heard in the midst of the void all twenty quadrillion verses of the Lotus Sūtra previously preached by the Buddha King of Majestic Voice;

After his life came to an end, he encountered two thousand koṭis of Buddhas, all named Candrasūryapradīpa (Sun-Moon-Lamp), and within their Dharma he preached this Lotus Sūtra. By these causes and conditions, he again encountered two...

He preached the Dharma among the fourfold assembly with a mind free from fear and attained great power; thus, he was named Constantly Fearless (*Sadāparibhūta*).
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Light made offerings to this many Buddhas, honoring, respecting,
and praising them while planting various roots of goodness; subsequently, he encountered ten million billion more Buddhas,

Question: Since Adhimātra-asaṃkucita (Never-Disparaging) was a manifestation of Śākyamuni, it is beyond doubt that he appeared in the body of a bodhisattva bhikṣu to preach the Dharma for those who were to be saved by such a form;
furthermore, as one who does not arise yet manifests arising and does not cease yet manifests cessation, this is certainly so.
However, regarding his hearing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* preached by Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja at the time of his death—how is this to be understood?

Question: Having attained the purity of the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya-viśuddhi*), how can it be said that the Buddha of the fruition stage manifests his body and yet still awaits hearing [the Dharma] from another Buddha, as if his organs were not yet pure and only become pure through hearing and upholding? Answer: Since this belongs to a manifestation subsequent to the fruition stage, what is there that is improper?

Prior to this, when the six organs were not yet pure, this was the practice of the Perfect Illness (*yuanbingxing*); now, at the end of life, hearing and upholding the sutra constitutes the Perfect [Practice].
The practice of an infant is the great power of spiritual penetration; the power of eloquence in joyful exposition is the Tathāgata’s seat;

and the power of great, sublime tranquility is the Tathāgata’s robe. Adorned with these three dharmas, one can cause the six sense faculties of the fourfold assembly to transform their destruction into faith.
Furthermore, it was asked: "Since you have already attained Buddhahood in the past, why do you say that you must now plant various roots of goodness?"
"From the perfection of the faculties up to the perfection of the qualities, one shall attain Buddhahood. The answer is:

"For example, it is like the potter Zhu Gong, who was skilled in the extraordinary arts of becoming wealthy. He resided in one place and accumulated goods worth ten billion, yet he abandoned them and departed without taking a single coin.
He went to another place and built a fortune from bare hands, accumulating wealth worth ten billion, and again abandoned it and departed. Furthermore,"

Just as one who accumulates wealth in other places leaves behind billions of buddhas, so too does he set aside his original ground merits and instead manifest the practice of causes and the attainment of fruits throughout the ten directions and across the three periods of time, continuing ceaselessly and inconceivably;
therefore it is said: "The lifespan I achieved when I originally practiced the bodhisattva path remains even now."
When one has not yet exhausted [the cycle] and attains Buddhahood, one does not employ the lifespan accomplished by a bodhisattva;
likewise, when manifesting traces in this world, one does not employ all the merits possessed in one’s original ground. Furthermore, the Brahmajāla Sūtra states:
"I have now come to this world eight thousand times for the sake of this Sahā world, sitting upon the Vajra-flower Radiance King throne. Since [this is so] in the Sahā world...

It should also be understood by analogy that since the Bhagavān has manifested his attainment of Buddhahood eight thousand times, the places where his emanations have pervaded other regions are likewise to be known.

Among these, regarding those who possess faith, there are three types of retribution: first, the purification of the six sense faculties and the extension of their lifespan, which is the "present retribution";
second, encountering a Buddha at the end of life, which is the "retribution of the next birth"; and third, again encountering various Buddhas until they eventually attain Buddhahood themselves.
This is the retribution for that [past life]. △ Second, the reconciliation of the ancient and the modern:
"What do you think, Mahāsthāmaprāpta? Was the Bodhisattva Constantly-Not-Light at that time someone else?
It was none other than myself. Had I not, in past lives, upheld, recited, and explained this sutra for others..."
"One can swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; because I received, upheld, recited, and expounded this sutra for others under previous Buddhas, I have swiftly attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
First, the formal conclusion and reconciliation; next, from "If I, in past lives... onwards, this is the exhortation for those who possess faith to follow accordingly.
It is like the merchant Tao Zhu-gong, who returned empty-handed to another place and yet achieved great wealth;
if one does not employ extraordinary methods, one cannot swiftly attain a fortune of billions. One should know that the *Lotus Sūtra* is the extraordinary method for swiftly attaining Buddhahood.

The first section, explaining the retribution for those who believe, is concluded. △ Second, explaining the retribution for those who disparage [the teaching], in two parts: first, explaining the retribution;
second, correlating the past with the present. Now, for the first part:
Mahāsthāmaprāpta, at that time the fourfold assembly—bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—out of anger...
"Because you harbored a mind of malice and treated me with contempt, for two hundred billion kalpas you shall never encounter a Buddha, hear the Dharma, or see the Sangha.

For a thousand kalpas you shall undergo great suffering in the Avīci Hell. Once this retribution is exhausted, you will again meet the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging, who will teach and transform you toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

Because of their slanders, they fell into suffering; yet, because they heard the prediction of their future Buddhahood, established the conditions for the Perfect and Sudden [teachings], and were further sustained by the power of the great vows of the Bodhisattva Viśeṣacintin, they were able to meet once more and receive his instruction and transformation.
Question: At that time, since the fourfold assembly had already all believed, submitted, and followed him, why did they still fall into suffering for so long? Answer: This...
There are two intentions [behind this]: first, that since the physical act of striking and the verbal act of reviling have already constituted grave karma, one must logically undergo retribution;
this first point is intended to warn practitioners that they must not rashly give rise to anger or commit transgressions.

Second, as a long period of time has passed, among the fourfold assembly there are both those who remain and those who have died; those who remain may have faith and submission, but those who have died have not yet repented. Furthermore—
Among those who have faith and follow [the teachings], there are differences in the depth of their remorse and the diligence of their practice; these matters are not uniform.
Those whose remorse is deep and whose practice is diligent may avoid falling; even if they do fall, they easily emerge.

If one's remorse is shallow and one's practice is lax, one will naturally fall first and only later gain benefit. As for those who have not yet repented, their fall into suffering will be long-lasting—this is solely due to the Bodhisattva.

"Through the gathering-in of compassion, one will ultimately attain liberation. Question: "If one falls into suffering due to slandering [the Dharma], why does a Bodhisattva act as a cause for that suffering?
Answer: "Since such a person harbors overweening pride (*adhimāna*), they would certainly fall into suffering even if they did not slander.

Now, by falling into suffering because of their slander, it serves as a remote cause (*viprakṛṣṭa-hetu*)—just as when a person falls to the ground, they must rise from the ground. Therefore, [it is] by means of the correct..."

[Question: Since slander leads one toward the heterodox and causes one to fall into the realms of questioning, why not employ the power of supernatural faculties (*ṛddhibala*) to cause them all to immediately believe, submit, and follow?

[Answer: It is not that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not wish to do so; rather, because the capacities and dispositions (*indriya*) of sentient beings differ individually, there are those who have already reached the hells and would absolutely refuse to resolve their minds [toward awakening]. This is like a skilled physician treating a malignant disease.
One cannot help but employ acupuncture, moxibustion, and bitter medicines. △ Second, the reconciliation of past and present:
"As for those who gained great power—what do you think? Were the four assemblies who constantly disparaged this bodhisattva at that time anyone else?
They were none other than the five hundred bodhisattvas such as Bhadrapāla and the five [bodhisattvas] such as Siṃhacandra in this assembly today."
The one hundred bhikṣuṇīs and the five hundred upāsakas, such as Si-fu (Siddhārtha) and others, were all those who had become non-retrogressive regarding anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This concludes the second pair of sections clarifying the retributions for faith and slander in former lives. △ Third, the exhortation to uphold [the Dharma].
Mahāsthāmaprāpta, you should know that this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* brings great benefit to all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas,
enabling them to reach *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Therefore, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata,
all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should constantly receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, and transcribe this sūtra.
As clarified above, this not only enables those who believe to quickly attain Buddhahood, but also ensures that even those who disparage it will ultimately achieve non-retrogression;
therefore, one should diligently practice the five kinds of deeds, namely: receiving and upholding, reading and reciting, explaining, and transcribing.
This concludes the initial section on the long prose. II. Verse Recitation (consists of two parts): A. Verses on the karmic retribution for belief and disparagement. B. Verses on exhortation.
Omitting the verses on the two fingers, this section consists of two parts: first, the verses on the fundamental matter; second, the verses on the primary narrative.
Now, for the first part:
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
In the past, there was a Buddha named King of Majestic Sound (Vaiśvānara-rāja), whose divine wisdom was immeasurable and who led all devas, humans, nāgas, and spirits, being honored by them all.
△ Second, the verses on the original events (pūrvayoga) have three parts: first, verses that jointly designate the two names; second, verses that jointly clarify faith and slander; third...
The verse clarifies both the retribution and the fruit;

this is the first part. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, when the Dharma was about to perish, there was a bodhisattva named Sadāparibhūta, at which time the fourfold assembly was attached to the dharmas.
To be conceptually attached to dharmas is itself an expression of overweening pride (*adhimāna*). This dharma cannot be demonstrated; its verbal characteristics are quiescent.
To definitively assert that it exists is attachment to dharmas; to definitively assert that it does not exist is also attachment to dharmas;
to definitively assert that it both exists and does not exist is also attachment to dharmas; and to definitively assert that it neither exists nor does not exist is also attachment to dharmas.
"Samādhi" refers to that which cannot be described because it is free from the four extremes; furthermore, since even this [description] is a clinging to dharmas, the *Buddhapiṭaka Sūtra* states:
"The sin of using a wheel of swords to slaughter the people of Jambudvīpa is still slight compared to the sin of one who preaches the Mahāyāna with a mind of attainment.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "From disputing over existence and non-existence, even up to disputing over neither existence nor non-existence..."
There is the "Non-contention" (araṇā), which is like a cowhide or a dragon-rope—neither can avoid the affliction [of being caught]. The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* says:
"The Buddhas teach the Dharma of emptiness primarily to transform those attached to existence. If there are those who become attached to emptiness, they cannot be transformed even by the Buddhas.

If one definitively asserts that all phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent, this is called the discourse of the deluded. One should know that if one attains the four *siddhāntas*, [one is liberated].

If one acts for oneself and transforms others while being able to remain unattached in both cases, one is free from fault; however, if one loses the intent of the four *siddhāntas*, then acting for oneself and transforming others will both result in attachment to dharmas.

Because of this attachment to dharmas, there arises a mind that seeks attainment, and by giving rise to arrogance regarding inferior and minor realizations, this is called "overweening pride" (*adhimāna*).
△ Second, the verse on the dual clarification of praise and blame.
The Bodhisattva Never Disparaging went to where they were and said to them, "I do not disparage you;
all of you who practice the Way shall surely become Buddhas. When those people heard this, they reviled and abused him, yet the Bodhisattva Never Disparaging was able to endure it all.

△ Three verses clarify the retributive fruits for both [the believer and the slanderer]. Part one: One verse clarifies the fruit for the believer; two verses clarify the fruit for the slanderer. Now, the first:
When their offenses have been exhausted and they approach the end of life, they shall hear this sutra, and by the power of their six sense organs being purified, [they attain supernatural faculties].
He increased their lifespans and further expounded this sutra extensively for all those attached to dharmas;

through the Bodhisattva’s teaching and transformation, they were all brought to fulfillment and established in the Buddha-way. Because Mañjuśrī did not disparage others at the end of his life, he encountered countless Buddhas;
by virtue of preaching this sutra, he obtained immeasurable merit, gradually perfected his virtues, and swiftly attained the Buddha-way. At that time, "Not Disparaging" was none other than myself.

Regarding those whose offenses have been completed: since they manifest traces in the world for the sake of those whose six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*) are not yet purified, they must demonstrate the karmic retribution of those with similar ailments.
Because of these offenses, they frequently encounter beatings and insults; yet, through their ability to endure them, their offenses are exhausted and their faculties become pure.
△ Second, the verse on the retribution for those who disparage.
At that time, those among the fourfold assembly who were devoted to the Dharma heard the words of the Bodhisattva Never Disparaging: "You shall become Buddhas;

by this causal condition, you shall encounter countless Buddhas. Furthermore, the five hundred bodhisattvas in this assembly, as well as the faithful laymen and laywomen of the fourfold assembly who are now listening to the Dharma before me—these are all people whom I exhorted in previous lives to listen to and receive this sutra.
The foremost Dharma is revealed and taught to people so that they may abide in *nirvāṇa* and uphold such a sutra from lifetime to lifetime.
This concludes the first verse concerning the karmic retribution for faith and slander. II. The second verse encourages upholding [the sutra].
Only after billions of billions of kalpas, reaching an inconceivable time, shall one hear this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.

For billions of billions of kalpas, reaching an inconceivable time, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have preached this sūtra. Therefore, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, those who practice should not give rise to doubt upon hearing such a sūtra as this;
they should single-mindedly propagate this sūtra, so that in life after life they may encounter the Buddhas.

"One will swiftly attain the Buddha-way. [Question: Since it is clear that this sutra brings great benefit even to those who revile it, resulting in their ultimate gain, why is it that the Buddhas only preach this sutra at times after billions upon billions of kalpas, until they reach the inconceivable? [Answer: The answer is as follows: This sutra is the supreme Dharma-treasure of all the Buddhas of the three periods of time. It is the most profound and subtle teaching, difficult to encounter and difficult to believe. Because sentient beings have long been steeped in afflictions, their faculties are dull and weak; they are attached to worldly pleasures and find it difficult to abandon them. Therefore, the Buddhas wait for the right time and opportunity to preach this sutra. Furthermore, the power of the Buddhas' original vows is such that they do not preach this sutra lightly. Only when the conditions are fully matured—when there are many sentient beings who can receive and uphold it, and when the obstacles to its propagation have been removed—do the Buddhas preach it. Moreover, because this sutra is so profound and subtle, it is difficult to understand and difficult to practice. If preached prematurely, it would lead to confusion and slander. For these reasons, the Buddhas preach this sutra only at rare intervals throughout immeasurable kalpas. This is why it is said that one attains the fruit of Buddhahood swiftly through this sutra, yet it is only preached by the Buddhas after an inconceivable number of eons.
When there are the four *siddhārtha* (universal benefits), one may preach; without the four *siddhārtha*, the Buddhas never speak the Dharma falsely.

Therefore, if one wishes to propagate the Great Dharma, one must first clearly understand the causes and conditions of the four *siddhārtha*. This concludes the separate explanation of the two gates of the Trace and the Origin.
△ Third, the section on the circulation of the text and its original; these two gates together comprise eight chapters, which are divided into three thematic sections:

first, the two chapters on "Supernatural Power" and "Entrustment" clarify the entrustment and circulation; second, the five chapters beginning with "Bhaiṣajyarāja" encourage circulation by means of exhorting others;
third, the "Samantabhadra’s Exhortation" chapter encourages circulation by means of one's own practice. Within the first of these, there are two parts, the first of which is "Supernatural Power."
Chapter on the Bodhisattva Receiving the Mandate to Propagate the Sūtra: Part Two, the Chapter on Entrustment, clarifies the Tathāgata’s entrustment by placing his hand upon [the bodhisattva’s] head.
△ The explanation of the Chapter on the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging is completed; next, the explanation of the Chapter on the Tathāgata’s Supernatural Powers begins.
Chapter Twenty-one: The Tathāgata’s Supernatural Powers.
The Tathāgata has already finished explaining above; "supernatural" (*ṛddhi*) refers to that which cannot be fathomed, and "power" (*bala*) refers to its functional efficacy.

That which cannot be fathomed is the profound, natural essence; that which is functionally efficacious is the great power of transformation. Herein, for the sake of entrusting the profound Dharma, he manifests [these powers].

Because there are ten kinds of great power, it is called the "Chapter on Spiritual Power" (*Ṛddhibala-parivarta*). "Spiritual" (*ṛddhi*) resides within and is the essence and substance; "power" (*bala*) is named for its function as the trunk and activity, which manifests the utility of the sūtra.

The Buddha’s exposition of the primary and secondary aspects (*honjaku*) through the power and function of the wheel of speech has already concluded previously; now, furthermore, the wheel of body manifests this supreme function to cause the masses to circulate the teaching of the primary and secondary aspects. Therefore, it is said: "The substance is profound and the power is great.

△ First, clarifying that the bodhisattvas receive the mandate to propagate the sūtra. This has two parts: first, the long prose; second, the verse recitation. Within the first part, there are three sections. First, the bodhisattvas receive [the mandate].
[The Buddha] commands the two Buddhas to manifest their supernatural powers and summarizes the three points to exhort them to uphold [the teaching]. First:

At that time, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as numerous as the atoms in a thousand worlds, who had emerged from the earth, all stood before the Buddha with single-minded palms joined, gazing up at his honored countenance and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, regarding us, the disciples of the Buddha..."
After the Parinirvāṇa of the World-Honored One, in whatever lands and places his emanations have entered extinction, this sutra should be extensively proclaimed.
Why is this? Because we ourselves also desire to obtain this truly pure Great Dharma, to receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, copy, and make offerings to it.
The vow to propagate the sutra is threefold: first, clarifying the time, which is after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa; second, clarifying the location, which is the lands of the emanation bodies;
and third, clarifying the benefit, which is not only to benefit others but also to personally attain the True and Pure Great Dharma, thereby providing salvation for both self and others.
"True" refers to the substantial essence, while "Pure" refers to provisional function; the non-duality of the provisional and the real is termed [the True-Pure].
Furthermore, being neither provisional nor real is called "True"; being able to be both provisional and real is called "Pure"; and the non-duality of cessation and illumination is called "Great.

△ Second, the Buddha manifests his spiritual powers, which has two parts: first, a general indication based on those addressed; second, the actual manifestation based on what is symbolized. Now, the first part.

At that time, the World-Honored One [addressed] Mañjuśrī and countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who had long resided in the Sahā world, as well as the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās,
devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas.
Before all the assemblies, including humans and non-humans, he manifested great supernatural powers.
Mañjuśrī and others were those who had come as transformed manifestations to convert the assembly; the "original residents" were those who had been fundamentally converted from the lower realms;
and the "various bhikṣus and other assemblies" were those who had come from other directions or arrived from the various emanation-bodies of the Buddha. △

Second, regarding the ten manifestations of the actual presence as indicated [by the preceding]: first, the protrusion of the tongue; second, the emission of light from the pores; third, the clearing of the throat;

fourth, the snapping of the fingers; fifth, the shaking of the earth; sixth, the universal vision of the great assembly; seventh, the proclamation from mid-air; eighth, the distant taking of refuge; ninth, the distant making of offerings;
tenth, the universal penetration of the ten directions as if they were a single buddha-field. First, the protrusion of the tongue.
From his two pores he emitted light,
and from his broad and long tongue it extended upward as far as the Brahma-world; from all his pores he emitted immeasurable and innumerable rays of light of various colors,
which completely illuminated the worlds of the ten directions, as did the Buddhas seated upon lion-thrones beneath the jeweled trees.
When Śākyamuni Buddha and the Buddhas beneath the jewel trees thus extend their broad and long tongues and emit immeasurable light,
manifesting such supernatural powers for a full hundred thousand years, they subsequently withdraw their tongue-marks.
The protrusion of the broad and long tongue manifests truthful speech. The tongues of those with merit reach their noses;

the tongues of the Buddhas of the Three Treasuries reach the hairline; now it reaches the Brahma Heaven. This manifestation transcends the characteristics of both ordinary beings and sages. Since its appearance is extraordinary, what is taught is all the more trustworthy.
One should know that the opening of the three to reveal the one, and the opening of the near to reveal the far, are all real and not false. [The] pores...

The emission of light that shines everywhere signifies that the principle of the two gates is one. In the introduction, the white tuft of hair shining toward the east signified the initial vision of the single principle by those on the seven stages of expedient means.

Now that the present Gate of the Essential Teaching has concluded, the emission of all-encompassing light that illuminates all lands enables the ultimate Buddha-wisdom and the realm of knowledge to be fully realized even for those at the stage of the first thought of enlightenment. This is the transformative path of the various Buddhas who have manifested their bodies.

Because they are identical, it is likewise so for another hundred thousand years. The mind horizontally encompasses the ten realms and the thousand suchnesses, and vertically reaches the extremes of past and present throughout the ten periods of time.
Within these eight years, there are again a full hundred thousand years, as explained above regarding the fifty minor kalpas.
Now, since this great assembly has simultaneously shattered ignorance, there is no need to rely on supernatural powers.
By his power, he caused them to perceive it as being like half a day. △ Third, [he] coughed and fourth, snapped his fingers.
Simultaneously coughing and snapping their fingers together, these two sounds reached throughout the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions.
Coughing is a sign of unobstructed flow and also the manner of being about to speak. For over forty years, I have not been able to speak the truth;
now that I have attained this expansion and there is no longer any obstruction, the Great Matter is fully realized.
Therefore, I cough, wishing to entrust this Dharma to the Bodhisattvas so that they may guide and benefit sentient beings in future generations, speaking of this very matter.

Therefore, a cough signifies the teaching of the One Vehicle; a single snap of the fingers signifies rejoicing. Rejoicing that the seven stages of expedient means enter together into the Perfect Path;
rejoicing that within the Perfect Stage one increases the Path and diminishes birth; rejoicing that all Bodhisattvas uphold the Great Dharma of True Purity;
and rejoicing that future generations shall obtain the Unsurpassed Treasure—this snap of the fingers signifies that these are the persons [who attain] this. Thus ends the snap of the fingers.
As well as his coughing and clearing of the throat, which penetrate vertically through the three periods of time and extend horizontally throughout the ten directions.
△ Fifth, the earth shakes and the great assembly is universally seen. The earth shook in six ways, and within it were sentient beings—devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and asuras.
By the Buddha’s supernatural power, the garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans,
and others all beheld the Buddhas beneath the countless, boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of jewel trees upon lion thrones in this Sahā world;
they also saw Śākyamuni Buddha together with the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna within the jeweled stupa.

Seated upon the lion throne, they also saw immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and the fourfold assembly respectfully surrounding Śākyamuni Buddha; having seen this, they were all filled with great joy,
experiencing what they had never known before.
The fact that the earth in the worlds of the ten directions all shook in six ways signifies the movement of the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) of all sentient beings to bring them to purity;
it also signifies the six successive stages of breaking through ignorance throughout the beginning and end of the Perfect Path, representing the first [of the ten] practices.
That everyone here beholds this great assembly signifies that the Way of all Buddhas is the same, and from now on, it shall likewise be so.
It is thus. Previously, five thousand [monks] rose and departed; three transformations were performed to relocate them back to their original abodes.

Furthermore, those among the humans and non-humans of the ten directions whose spiritual faculties (*indriya*) were not yet mature and who could not gather here at this Dharma assembly—now, by means of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), they are all made to see [the scene] from afar, thereby forming bonds of joy. This is the general auspicious omen for their future deliverance.
...and so forth. △ Seventh, the proclamation from the void:
immediately, the devas in the midst of the void raised their voices and proclaimed:
"Beyond these immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of asaṃkhyeya worlds, there is a land named Sahā; therein dwells a Buddha named Śākyamuni."
“Nirgrantha, I now preach for you Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas a Mahāyāna sūtra titled ‘The Lotus of the Wondrous Dharma,’ which teaches the Dharma for Bodhisattvas and is protected by the Buddhas.
You all should, with deep resolve, rejoice in it, and you should also pay homage to and make offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha.”
Although they were enabled by the Buddha’s power to see the great assembly from afar, they still did not know the name of the Buddha or for what purpose the assembly had gathered.
Now, the devas in the void proclaim this so that they may hear and know it, enabling them to rejoice and make offerings of the sublime Dharma to the World-Honored One;
this immediately signifies that there will be teaching in the future—this is the first [point]. △ Eighth, the remote taking of refuge.
Having heard the voice from the midst of space, those sentient beings joined their palms toward the Sahā world and spoke these words:
"Homage to Śākyamuni Buddha! Homage to Śākyamuni Buddha!"
With palms joined, one pays homage, saying "Namo," as a disciple of the Buddha; this signifies that there will be such persons in the future. △ Ninth, remote offering:
with various flowers, incense, necklaces, banners, canopies, and all manner of ornaments for the body, as well as rare jewels and exquisite objects—these are all...

They scattered various offerings from afar toward the Sahā world; these objects came from the ten directions like a gathering of clouds, transforming into a precious canopy that completely covered all the Buddhas therein.
The various objects scattered [as offerings] transform into jeweled canopies that cover all the Buddhas above;

this signifies that all myriad virtues converge and are fully imbued with the fruit of Buddhahood—this is the first instance of future practice. △ Tenth: Universal penetration throughout the ten directions as if they were a single Buddha-land.
At that time, the worlds of the ten directions were unimpededly interpenetrated as if they were a single buddha-land.

This signifies that, in principle, the future is one. Having realized this principle, the provisional and the real, the fundamental and the trace, and the inconceivable unity of their differences, are non-different.
Second, the Buddhas have finished manifesting their spiritual powers. △ Third, the summary of the essentials and the exhortation to uphold [the teaching].

Fourth, there are four sections: first, the praise and entrustment; second, the summary of the essential points and entrustment; third, the encouragement and entrustment; fourth, the explanation of the entrustment. Now, for the first:
At that time, the Buddha addressed the great assembly of Bodhisattvas, such as Upward-Going (*Urdhvagama*) and others, saying: "The spiritual power of all Buddhas is thus immeasurable and boundless."

The limit is inconceivable; even if I were to use such supernormal powers to expound the merits of this sutra for the sake of entrustment throughout immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, I would still be unable to exhaust them.
△ Second, the summary and entrustment.

To state it briefly: all the dharmas possessed by the Tathāgata, all the sovereign spiritual powers of the Tathāgata, all the secret and essential treasuries of the Tathāgata, and all the most profound matters of the Tathāgata are contained within this sutra.
To proclaim and manifest:
"all dharmas" refers to the fact that all phenomena whatsoever are the Buddha-dharma; this is the summary of the name "All-Wondrous.
"Mastery of spiritual power" refers to penetrating without obstruction and possessing the eight masteries; this is the summary of the "wondrous function."
That which is the treasury of secret essentials pervades all places; it is the wondrous substance that binds together the true aspect (*dharmatā*).
That which is the matter of profound depth is that all causes and effects constitute this single great matter; it is the wondrous thesis that binds them together.

That these are all proclaimed and clearly expounded within this sutra is the summary of the entire scripture, which consists of only four [sections]. Having grasped its pivotal handle, it is hereby bestowed.
I entrust this to you. △ Third, the exhortation and entrustment:
"Therefore, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, you should with one mind receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, copy, and practice according to the teaching.
In whatever land there may be those who receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, copy, and practice according to the teaching..."
Wherever this sūtra on the practice of cultivation may be situated— whether in a garden, in a grove, beneath a tree, in a monastery,
in a layperson’s house, in a hall, or in a mountain valley or wilderness— one should erect a stūpa at each such place and make offerings to it.
△ Fourth, the explanation of the entrustment.
Why is this so? One should know that this place is the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*);
it is here that all Buddhas attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, it is here that all Buddhas turn the wheel of the Dharma, and it is here that all Buddhas enter *parinirvāṇa*.
Nirvāṇa. Why is it that one should erect a stūpa wherever a sūtra scroll is located? It is because such a place is a site of the Way (bodhimaṇḍa).
Any place where the Way is attained, where the Wheel of Dharma is turned, or where Nirvāṇa is entered is called a site of the Way. This is the site of the Way.
This collectively explains that all things are wondrous; "attaining bodhi" refers to the realization of the secret and essential treasury, which explains the wondrous essence (*miao-ti*).

"Turning the wheel of the Dharma" refers to the teaching and demonstration of the profound matters of the causes and effects of one's own practice regarding its original and manifest traces, which explains the wondrous purpose (*miao-zong*).
"Parinirvāṇa" is not extinction; it proclaims extinction while possessing sovereign spiritual power, which explains [the wondrous function].
The wondrous function is the attainment of Bodhi, which is the Dharmakāya; the turning of the wheel of Dharma is Prajñā; and entry into Nirvāṇa is Vimukti.
These three dharmas constitute the Secret Treasury (Guhyakośa). Because the Buddha abides therein, it is the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and has the meaning of a stūpa;
therefore, one should erect a stūpa to manifest this. The initial long prose section concludes. △ Second, the verse summary, in two parts: first—
Two verses on supernatural power summarize the essential points and exhort one to uphold them. First:
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The Buddhas, the saviors of the world, abide in great supernormal powers; for the sake of gladdening sentient beings, they manifest immeasurable displays of supernatural power."
The mark of his tongue reaches the Brahma-heaven, and from his body he emits countless rays of light; for those who seek the Buddha-way, he manifests this rare event.
The sound of the Buddhas’ clearing their throats and the snapping of their fingers resounds throughout the lands of the ten directions, and the earth shakes in six ways.
Because they are able to uphold this sutra after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, all the Buddhas rejoice and manifest immeasurable supernatural powers.
The ten kinds of supernatural powers are only praised in the first five verses; the latter five are omitted because they all manifest through the vibration of two sounds.
Furthermore, the first five and the latter five do not differ in their expressed meaning, differing only in that the former refers to the present and the latter to the future;
thus, by citing the present as an example for the future, they are omitted. △ Second, the verse concluding the essentials and exhorting to uphold them, part three: the initial verse.
The two verses of praise and summary also encompass the intent of the entrustment; the three subsequent verses provide encouragement.
First, because this sutra is being entrusted, the praises for those who uphold it cannot be exhausted even throughout immeasurable eons.
The merit of such a person is boundless and inexhaustible, like the ten directions of empty space, whose limits cannot be found.
The long prose states that even if one were to speak of the merits of this sutra, they could not be fully exhausted. Now, the verse says: "The merits of such a person are boundless and inexhaustible.
Because the Dharma is wondrous, the person is wondrous; because the person is wondrous, the Dharma is wondrous. Thus, they manifest one another.
△ Second, the verse summary of the essentials, which also explains four points: first, the verse on all dharmas; second, the verse on sovereign spiritual powers.
The three verses on the power [of the teaching] are the treasury of essential secrets; the four verses on the profound matters are as follows. First:
"Whoever upholds this sutra has already seen me, and has also seen the Buddha Prabhūtaratna and all his emanations, as well as my teaching of the bodhisattvas today."
All dharmas do not transcend the transformer, the realized one, and the transformed;

because there is no second vehicle and nothing is brought along [from elsewhere], these dharmas are pure and wondrous, and thus constitute the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), which serves as the general heading for the three. △ Second, the verse on sovereign spiritual power.
Those who are able to uphold this sutra will cause me, as well as my emanations, the Buddha Prabhūtaratna who has entered parinirvāṇa, and all others to rejoice;
they shall also see and make offerings to the Buddhas currently present in the ten directions, as well as those of the past and future, causing them all to attain joy.
Joy is itself the manifestation of spiritual power, and it is also the most peaceful state of nirvana.
△ Third, the verse on the treasury of secret essentials:
"The secret and essential Dharma attained by all Buddhas when sitting at the site of enlightenment—those who can uphold this sutra shall also attain it before long."
This is identical to the Buddhas attaining *samyak-saṃbodhi* and realizing the wondrous essence of the secret treasury.
△ Fourth, the verse on the profound matter:
"One who can uphold this sutra will possess inexhaustible eloquence in explaining the meanings, names, and phrases of all dharmas."

Like the wind in the sky, they encounter no obstacles; after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, they will understand the causes, conditions, and sequence of the sūtras spoken by the Buddha, and explain them according to their meaning as it truly is.

Just as the light of the sun and moon can dispel all darkness, these people, moving through the world, can extinguish the darkness of sentient beings and teach immeasurable bodhisattvas to ultimately abide in the One Vehicle.
To transform and guide bodhisattvas through the religious teachings of the cause and fruit of the One Vehicle is precisely what constitutes the turning of the wheel of Dharma.
This concludes the summary and simultaneous explanation of the two verses. △ Third, the verse on exhortation and encouragement.
Therefore, those who possess wisdom, having heard these merits and benefits, should uphold this sutra after my parinirvāṇa;
such persons will have no doubt whatsoever regarding the Buddha-way.
The text omits verses on the construction of stupas and offerings, stating only that one should have no doubt regarding the Buddha-way;
this is because it is deeply believed that this very place is a *bodhimaṇḍa*, where all Buddhas attain *bodhi*, turn the wheel of the Dharma, and enter *nirvāṇa*.
This concludes the initial clarification of how the Bodhisattva received his mandate to propagate the sutra.
△ The explanation of the "Chapter on the Tathāgata’s Supernatural Power" is concluded. Next, the "Chapter on the Entrustment" (Parīndanā-parivarta) is explained.
Chapter Twenty-two: "Entrustment.

"Entrustment" (*parīndanā*) refers to that which the Buddha has committed to others; "entrustment" (*parīndanā*) means that you must propagate this with diligence. This is obtained from the holy decree of the Tathāgata.

"Entrusting" (*niyojana*) refers to receiving what has been entrusted upon the crown of one's head; "being entrusted with" (*parindana*) refers to this being sweet and not laborious. This is designated as "entrusting" based on the Bodhisattva’s respectful compliance.

"Being entrusted by" refers to that which is entrusted by the golden mouth of the Tathāgata; "receiving upon the crown of the head" refers to the Bodhisattva’s sincere heart bearing this responsibility.

This is discussed in terms of both the bestowal and the reception. Therefore, the Tathāgata rose from his seat in person, extended his hand, rubbed [the Bodhisattva’s] head, and bestowed [this entrustment].

Because this dharma is difficult to encounter, the great assembly bows their bodies and joins their palms; as commanded by the World-Honored One, they shall practice it with full devotion. Because they receive it with such earnestness, it is called the "Chapter on Entrustment.

△ Second, explaining the Tathāgata’s entrustment by stroking the heads [of the assembly]. This has two parts: first, the entrustment; second, the rejoicing. Within the first part, there are three sections:

first, the Tathāgata’s entrustment; second, the Bodhisattvas’ acceptance. Within the first section (the Tathāgata’s entrustment), there are three parts: first, the Tathāgata’s entrustment; second, the Bodhisattvas’ acceptance. (The second part of the second section follows.)

The three matters are concluded; this is the first of the three sections concerning the proclamation of the dispersal. First, the formal entrustment; second, the explanation of the entrustment; third, the admonition regarding the entrustment. Now, for the first:
at that time, Śākyamuni Buddha rose from his Dharma seat within the jeweled stupa and, manifesting great supernatural power, used his right hand...
The Buddha rubbed the crowns of the heads of immeasurable bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and spoke these words:
"I have cultivated this Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, so difficult to attain, throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
I now entrust it to you; you should single-mindedly propagate this Dharma and cause it to flourish and increase extensively."
Thus, [the Buddha] placed his hand upon the crowns of the heads of all these Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas and spoke these words:
"I have cultivated this Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, so difficult to attain, for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of asaṃkhyeya kalpas;
I now entrust it to you. You should receive, uphold, read, and recite it, and widely proclaim this Dharma."
All sentient beings universally hear and know this.

Because the Tathāgata, with the skillful hand of his single expedient wisdom, simultaneously and universally strokes the crowns of the heads of immeasurable bodhisattvas who possess true wisdom, he is called the Tathāgata Who Manifests Great Supernatural Power; and because the Tathāgata bestows the Way to transform others, he uses his right hand.
Because the Bodhisattva Biaoquan (Manifesting Expedient Means) himself practices and receives the Way, he uses his crown to symbolize the ultimate reality (*tattva*).
By extending his hand to stroke the crown, he entrusts the body; by the presence of ultimate wisdom, he entrusts the mind; and by speaking these words, he entrusts the speech.
He makes this threefold, earnest, and sincere entrustment so that all may practice for themselves and transform others, thereby fulfilling the four *siddhāntas*.
It is forever and eternally inexhaustible. △ Second, the explanation of the entrustment.
Why is this so? Because the Tathāgata possesses great compassion, is free from all stinginess, and has no fear;
he is able to bestow upon sentient beings the Buddha’s wisdom, the Tathāgata’s wisdom, and spontaneous wisdom. The Tathāgata is [the father] of all sentient beings.
O great donors among living beings, you too should follow and learn the Dharma of the Tathāgata, and do not give rise to stinginess.
Great compassion is the ultimate chamber; being free from all stinginess is the ultimate robe;
and being without fear is the ultimate seat. The wisdom of the Buddha is the awakening to the true nature of all phenomena.
The wisdom of the Tathāgata arises from nature through cultivation, proceeding from cause to fruit; it is the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*).
Natural wisdom is its innate essence, which simultaneously illuminates both [aspects] without duality; it is the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Regarding the three—garment, seat, and chamber—each possesses these three wisdoms. The triad of one and three is mutually identical, and the one and three are mutually integrated; by means of this, he transforms others.

To have a name as a great donor but no seat in the chamber of clothing signifies that one’s great vows are not universal; to have a seat in the chamber of clothing but no chamber of the Dharma-body signifies that the Dharma-body is incomplete;
to have a chamber of the Dharma-body but no seat in the chamber of clothing signifies that the destruction of delusions is not comprehensive. Do not give rise to stinginess;
this is the exhortation to practice the realization of a donor who should study to become a supreme great donor. If there is stinginess, then there is no compassion.
Furthermore, because there is fear, raising a single phrase is itself an exhortation to propagate the sutra according to the three modes of conduct. △ Third, the entrustment with a warning:
"In future ages, if there are good men or good women who believe in the Tathāgata’s wisdom, you should for them..."
"Preach this Lotus Sūtra so that they may hear and know it, for the purpose of enabling those people to attain the wisdom of a Buddha.
If there are sentient beings who do not believe or accept it, you should instruct, benefit, and gladden them by pointing toward other profound dharmas of the Tathāgata.
If you are able to act in this way, you will have repaid the kindness of all Buddhas."

Except for the wisdom of the Buddha, all else is termed "the remainder. Because the provisional is established for the sake of the real, and because the provisional contains the real, all are termed "profound.
Thus we know that praising only the Buddha Vehicle cannot universally encompass the teachings of the preceding three vehicles;
it would not yet constitute the transmission of the Dharma to repay the Buddha’s kindness. The first section, on the Tathāgata’s entrustment, is concluded. △ Second, the Bodhisattvas’ reception.
At that time, having heard these words spoken by the Buddha, all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas were filled with great joy that pervaded their entire bodies;
they increased their reverence, bowing their heads with palms joined toward the Buddha, and together they cried out in one voice:
"As the World-Honored One has commanded, we shall carry it out completely. Indeed, World-Honored One, may you have no further concern; we, the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, [will do so]."

Thus, repeating this three times, they all raised their voices and said, "As the World-Honored One has commanded, we shall respectfully carry it out. Indeed, World-Honored One, may you have no further concern.
To receive with joy and reverence is to accept it with the mind; to bow the body with a bent head is to accept it with the person. Thus they all raised their voices together.
"Orally receiving" means to accept with one's own mouth; it refers to the "entrustment of correct transmission" as commanded by the World-Honored One, which one should practice and uphold.
"Fully practicing" refers to the "entrustment of the three dharmas," meaning to receive, explain, and transmit them. "May you have no worries" refers to the "entrustment of admonition.

These three entrustments from the Tathāgata and the three receptions by the Bodhisattva are performed with such profound earnestness and gravity as have never before occurred in the course of a single lifetime. △ When these three matters are concluded, the assembly is dismissed.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha commanded the various emanated Buddhas who had come from the ten directions to each return to their own lands, saying:
"May the Buddhas each abide as they please, and let the stupa of Prabhūtaratna return to its former state."
The emanated bodies have assembled for the purpose of opening the stupa; having completed the task of opening the stupa, they are now permitted to return each to their respective native lands.

Because the jeweled stupa has come as a witness to the sutra, and because the two gates of the manifest and the fundamental have already been concluded, I respectfully request that it be closed again as it was before.
Since the stupa is not to be opened again, the emanated bodies depart and do not appear, yet the stupa remains audible.
Because it concerns the Dharma, the text below closes [the hall] yet he remains; if one asks why the stupa is closed even when listening to the Dharma, the answer is:

because he has already realized the truth, he closes it, whereas for the purpose of circulating [the teaching], he remains at the beginning. Once the entrustment is complete, [there follows] the second section: Rejoicing.
When these words were spoken, the immeasurable Buddhas of the ten directions who were seated beneath jeweled trees on lion thrones,
as well as the Buddha Prabhūtaratna, the boundless assembly of asaṃkhyeya bodhisattvas such as Uṣṇīṣaśiraskalokadhātupratibhāsavairocana,
the śrāvaka fourfold assembly including Śāriputra, and all the devas, humans, asuras, and others in the world, heard what the Buddha had said.
It is said that all rejoice.
The Buddhas rejoice because they have accomplished the task of transforming others; the Bodhisattvas rejoice because they have attained the Dharma for their own practice.
Furthermore, it is said that one rejoices because people are pure—this refers to the Buddha. One rejoices because one has heard the pure Dharma—this refers to the sublime sutra.
Because they have attained realization of purity, they rejoice in those who benefit others in the present and future; this concludes the first section clarifying the entrustment and circulation.
△ Second, from the chapter on Bhaiṣajyarāja downward, five chapters concern exhorting others to circulate [the teaching], which is further divided into four parts. First, Bhaiṣajyarāja...
In the "Chapter on the King," it exhorts the masters who propagate the Dharma that they should be like the Medicine King, exhausting their spiritual powers and their very lives;
it is only by wishing for the Great Dharma to be widely propagated and for sentient beings to obtain benefit that disciples may have a standard to follow.
In the two chapters on "Wonderful Sound" and "Avalokiteśvara," it exhorts the disciples who receive the Dharma not to give rise to contempt for those who propagate the Dharma.
Why is this? It is because the Great Beings from other directions who have received the mandate to propagate this sutra universally manifest in physical forms that lack fixed standards;
they cannot be viewed with the eyes of cattle or sheep, nor can they be measured by the intellectual capacity of ordinary people.

The "Chapter on the Three Dhāraṇīs" clarifies the protective power of mantras; the "Chapter on the Four Sublime Adornments" clarifies the person who attains them; furthermore, it concerns the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja.
The ascetic practices ride upon this One Vehicle through the wondrous voice of Avalokiteśvara;
the samādhis ride upon this One Vehicle through the dhāraṇī of total retention; the wondrous adornments ride upon this One Vehicle through the power of vows;
and Samantabhadra rides upon this One Vehicle through supernatural powers. Suchness and the true mark are the essence of that which is ridden—the Buddha-realm.
Cause and effect are that which is mounted; ascetic practices and the like are the vehicle and the conditions for mounting it.
Because these are adapted to the capacities of sentient beings, the propagators manifest different conditions, yet the essence of what is mounted remains the wondrous Dharma.
Since all causes and effects rely upon the One Reality to benefit living beings, it is called the "vehicle of vehicles" (yānānu-yāna).
△ The commentary on the "Chapter on Entrustment" concludes. Next, the commentary on the "Chapter on the Past Deeds of Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja.

Regarding the twenty-third chapter, the "Past Deeds of Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja," the *Bhaiṣajyarāja-bhaiṣajyasamudgata-sūtra* states: "In the past, he was named Jyotīrasa, and from the Venerable Sūryagarbha, he heard [the Dharma]."
It is said that by offering medicinal herbs from the Snowy Mountains to the Sangha, one makes the vow:

"May I, in the future, be able to cure the dual ailments of body and mind for all sentient beings. The entire world rejoices, and he is hailed as the Great Medicine King Buddha. The *Uṣṇīṣa Sūtra* states:
"Throughout beginningless kalpas, I have been a skilled physician for the world; with my own mouth, I have tasted every medicinal flavor within the Sahā world, serving [all beings]."

The Tathāgata distinguished the causes of flavors, and from this [distinction], he attained awakening. The Tathāgata confirmed the names of my two brothers, the Bodhisattvas Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata.
This passage clarifies that the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana suddenly cast away his body and further burned both his arms;
he regarded life lightly and the Dharma as weighty, so that while his life perished, the Way remained. By citing the past, he reveals the present; hence these words.
This is the "Chapter on Past Deeds. It is said that these various chapters are all intended to enable sentient beings to obtain the benefits of the four *siddhāntas*;

one need not be strictly bound by their specific allocation. Part One: Exhorting the Masters Who Propagate the Dharma. This section consists of four parts: first, the question; second, the answer; third, the benefits;
and fourth, the praise of the Many-Jeweled Stūpa. Now, the first part.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how does the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja roam throughout the Sahā world?
World-Honored One, this Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja has performed hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, billions, and nayutas of difficult and painful practices.
Excellent, World-Honored One! We pray that you will briefly explain this for the sake of the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans."
The gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others,
as well as the bodhisattvas who had come from other lands and this assembly of śrāvakas, all heard [this] and rejoiced.
First, "The World-Honored One" and below is the general inquiry regarding his travels and conversions; second, "The World-Honored One" and below is the specific inquiry regarding ascetic practices.

Third, "Excellent! and below is the request for a response. Traveling and converting others is altruism (*parārtha*); ascetic practice is self-benefit (*svārtha*). Traveling and converting is also a form of ascetic practice, and ascetic practice is also altruistic.
From "Having already [attained]" and below, the passages concerning Subhūti’s wondrous voice and so forth do not, in total, go beyond these two benefits of self and others.
In practice, these do not go beyond wisdom (*jñāna*) and severance (*prahāṇa*); in benefit for others, they do not go beyond concentration (*samādhi*) and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Generally speaking, those who travel must be fully endowed with the bodies of the ten dharma-realms, just like the Bodhisattvas Miaoyin (Wonderful Sound) and Guanyin (Avalokiteśvara).
However, because he specifically cites ascetic practices (*duḥkha-caryā*) to suit the needs of his audience, the intent of his question lies in ascetic practice. △ Second, the answer has two parts.

Initially, the response regarding his practicing asceticism and wandering to transform beings either refers to the *Sarvarūpasaṃdarśana-samādhi* (the Samādhi of Universally Manifesting Physical Forms) or to the following two chapters.

In the first section of the second part, which praises the sutra, there are two sub-sections: first, clarifying the basis of the events; second, clarifying the primary events. This is the first [sub-section].
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña:

"In the past, immeasurable kalpas ago, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there was a Buddha named Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsasirī Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat. That Buddha had eighty..."
There were a billion great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and a great assembly of voice-hearers (*śrāvaka*) as numerous as seventy-two Ganges sands;
the Buddha’s lifespan was forty-two thousand kalpas, and the lifespans of the bodhisattvas were equal to that.

That land has no women, nor do there exist hells, hungry ghosts, animals, or asuras, nor any of the various difficulties. The ground is as level as the palm of a hand and is composed of lapis lazuli, with precious trees made of *vaiḍūrya*.
Adorned with jeweled canopies covering them above and hanging banners of precious flowers, jeweled vases, and incense burners pervaded the entire realm.
Jeweled pedestals were made of the seven treasures; for every tree there was a pedestal, and each tree stood at a distance of one arrow-shot from its pedestal.
Beneath all these jeweled trees sat bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, and upon each jeweled pedestal were ten billion devas performing divine rites.
They offered musical performances and songs of praise to the Buddha as an act of worship.
△ Second, explaining the past events (pūrvayoga), which has three parts: first, the Buddha preaching the Dharma; second, performing acts of worship; third, correlating the past with the present.
First: At that time,
that Buddha was preaching the Lotus Sūtra for the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana, as well as for the assembly of bodhisattvas and the assembly of śrāvakas.
This is also like the present Buddha’s instruction to Śāriputra regarding how the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa [instructed] through the medium of Prabhāsa.
△ Second, the cultivation of offerings, which has two parts: first, offerings made during the present life; second, offerings made in future lives. Within the first part, there are two sections:
first, practicing to attain the Dharma; second, forming the thought of repaying kindness. Now, the first section.
This Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana delighted in practicing asceticism; within the Dharma of the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsaśrī,
he practiced walking meditation with diligence and single-mindedly sought Buddhahood for twelve thousand years, after which he attained the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Forms.
△ Second, the reflection on repaying the debt of gratitude, which also has two parts: first, making offerings through the power of samādhi; second, making offerings by burning the body.
Now, the first part:
Having attained this samādhi, his heart was filled with great joy, and he immediately thought: "I have attained the manifestation of all physical forms."
"All these samādhis are obtained through the power of having heard the Lotus Sūtra; I shall now make offerings to the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsaśrī and the Lotus Sūtra.
Immediately, he entered this samādhi, and from the midst of space there fell rain-like clouds of *māndārava* flowers, *mahāmāndārava* flowers, and fine powders of black sandalwood, filling the void.

Furthermore, he rained down the fragrance of *candana* sandalwood from this side of the ocean; six *zhu* of this incense were worth as much as the entire Sahā world, and it was used to make offerings to the Buddha.
Because the principle of the Samādhi of Universal Manifestation has no entering or exiting, yet its functional application is the power of samādhi, it is said that he "entered. △
Second, the offering by burning the body, which has three parts: first, the burning of the body; second, the Buddha’s praise; and third, the timing. Now, for the first part:

Having made this offering, he arose from samādhi and thought to himself, "Although I have made offerings to the Buddha through supernatural powers, it is not as good as making an offering with my own body.
He then consumed various fragrances, such as sandalwood, *kunkuma*, *turuṣka*, and *turuppa*.
Having drunk the fragrant oils of *kālānusāri*, agallochum, and *campaka* flowers for twelve hundred years,
he anointed his body with these fragrant oils before the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsaśrī. Wrapping himself in celestial jewel robes and pouring over himself the fragrant oils,
