he used his supernatural powers and vows so that the radiance of his own body spontaneously shone forth, illuminating eighty billion worlds.

In worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, those with supernatural powers and vows clarify that they do not employ worldly fire; rather, relying on the samādhis they have attained, they give rise to vows for the benefit of others.
Because they burn inconceivable realms with the fire of contemplative wisdom, their radiance shines universally throughout many lands.
The two Buddhas praised him.
All the Buddhas within those eighty billion Ganges-sand worlds simultaneously praised him, saying: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
This is true diligence; this is called the true Dharma-offering to the Tathāgata. If one were to offer flowers, incense, necklaces, burning incense, or powdered incense..."
It cannot be equaled by offerings of such various things as incense, unguents, celestial silken banners and canopies, or the sandalwood from this side of the sea;
nor even by the giving of kingdoms, cities, wives, or children.
Noble son, this is called the foremost gift; it is the most honored and supreme among all gifts, for it is the offering of the Dharma.
Having spoken these words to nourish all the Tathāgatas, they each became silent.

As for what constitutes the true offering of Dharma: it is the internal application of contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*) to contemplate the causes and effects of afflictions, using the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatā-prajñā*) to dissolve them;
therefore, it is called the "True Dharma. Furthermore, one contemplates that whether it be the body or the fire—the offerer, the object offered, or the act of offering—all are [empty].
In the true reality (*dharmatā*), who is it that burns, who is it that is ignited, who makes the offering, and who receives it? It is for this reason that it is called the "True Dharma.
When one contemplates in this manner, suffering becomes the *dharmadhātu*; because one gains benefit through seeing and hearing [the Dharma], it is called "riding upon the vehicle" (*yāna-yāna*).
If it were otherwise, it would become a fruitless ascetic practice. △ Third, the seasonal timing.
His body burned for twelve hundred years, and only after this period did his body perish. Previously, he consumed fragrant oil for twelve hundred years;
this represents the use of the path of skillful means to first purify the accumulation of all sufferings within the realm of the twelve links of dependent origination.
Now, the burning of his body likewise lasts for twelve hundred years, representing the same.
By means of the fire of true wisdom, one eternally exhausts the accumulation of all sufferings of the twelve links of dependent origination beyond the realms.

First, the section on the completion of the offering through the practice of austerities at birth. △ Second, the fivefold offering of the subsequent life: 1. Birth into the royal family; 2. Relating past events; 3.
Going to the Buddha’s presence; 4. The Tathāgata’s entrustment; 5. Receiving the command to uphold the teaching. Now, the first [section].
After the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana had performed such a Dharma-offering,
at the end of his life he was reborn by transformation in the land of the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsaśrī, within the household of King Viśuddhaguṇa, sitting cross-legged.
△ Second, the narration of past events (*itivṛttaka*).
He spoke these verses for his father, saying: "Great King, you should now know that as I was walking there, I immediately attained the Samādhi of Manifesting All Bodies;
through diligent great exertion, I sacrificed my beloved body. Thus he spoke.
Having finished the verses, he addressed his father, saying: "The Buddha Sun-Moon Pure Brightness Virtue is still currently present.
Having first made offerings to that Buddha, I attained the *dhāraṇī* of understanding the languages of all sentient beings.
Furthermore, I have heard these verses of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, numbering eight hundred thousand million billion nayutas, *khangkara*, *vimvara*, and *akṣobhya*."
I shall now return to make offerings to this Buddha.
By burning my body as an offering to the Buddha, I have attained the *dhāraṇī* and heard the verses of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*;

this is because I have attained the Dharma-nature body (*dharmatākāya*) and am forever not separated from the Buddha. If one considers this according to the sequence of events, it means that I attained the hearing [of the Dharma] while in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

If even the Wondrous Dharma, like the Buddha himself, enters the intermediate state (antarābhava) to teach and transform beings therein, how much more so must Bodhisattvas possess bodies in the intermediate state?
△ Third, approaching the Buddha’s presence:
Having made his announcement, he immediately sat upon a seven-jeweled platform, ascended into the void to a height of seven *tāla* trees, and proceeded to where the Buddha was.
He bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet, joined his palms with ten fingers together, and praised the Buddha in verse: “Your countenance is most wondrous and sublime;
Your radiance illuminates the ten directions. I have previously made offerings to you, And now I come again to behold you in person.
At that time, after the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana had spoken this verse, he addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, World-Honored One, you still remain in the world.”
△ 4. The Entrustment of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsa addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana: "Son of good family, the time for my parinirvāṇa has arrived;
the moment of my final extinction has come. You should prepare a seat, for tonight I shall [enter parinirvāṇa]."
At the time of his parinirvāṇa, he further commanded the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana:
"Good son, I entrust my Buddha-dharma to you, as well as to all the bodhisattvas, great disciples, and the Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
I also entrust to you this trichiliocosm of seven-jeweled worlds, including its jeweled trees, jeweled terraces, and attendants."
"All the devas are entrusted to you; after my parinirvāṇa, all my śarīra relics are also entrusted to you.
You must cause them to be widely distributed and extensively honored, and you should erect several thousands of stūpas.
Thus did the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsa instruct the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana, who subsequently entered nirvāṇa during the final watch of the night.
The term "Buddha-dharma" refers generally to all the teachings of the One Vehicle, while "Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi dharma" specifically refers to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.

△ Fifth, Entrusted with the Mandate to Maintain [the Dharma], which has four parts: first, erecting a stupa; second, burning an arm; third, benefiting others; fourth, manifesting retribution in this life. Now, the first part.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana, seeing the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, was moved by grief and remorse, longing for the Buddha.
He immediately used *candana* from this side of the ocean to construct a pyre as an offering for the Buddha’s body and cremated him.
After the fire had been extinguished, he collected the relics and fashioned eighty-four thousand precious jars to enshrine them.
The stupa was three worlds high, adorned with a banner-pole and decorated with hanging pennants and canopies, from which various jeweled bells were suspended.
△ Second, the burning of the arm.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana again thought to himself: "Although I have made this offering..."
"My mind is still not yet satisfied; I shall now further make offerings to the relics. He then addressed the assembly of all bodhisattvas, great disciples, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and others:
"You all should concentrate your minds as I now make offerings to the relics of the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsa.
Having spoken these words, he proceeded before the eighty-four thousand stūpas.
However, he made offerings for seventy-two thousand years with arms adorned by a hundred merits. [The interlocutor] asks:
"If burning the body lasts only one thousand two hundred years, why is the time for burning the arm so long? [The answer is:

Previously, it was for his own practice, so that his body would be exhausted and enter extinction; now, it is for the sake of propagating the Dharma so that sentient beings may realize the Three Vehicles, which is why it is said to last for "innumerable" years and so forth.

Since it has already been stated that countless śrāvakas have resolved their minds upon bodhicitta, we know that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, [the Buddha] did not allow these individuals to abide in the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle; this applies equally to this land. △ Third, the benefits.
He caused countless seekers of the śrāvaka vehicle— immeasurable asaṃkhyeya persons—
to resolve upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and enabled them all to abide in the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Bodies.
△ Fourth, the present retribution.
At that time, the bodhisattvas, devas, humans, asuras, and others, seeing that he was without arms, were distressed and filled with sorrow, and spoke these words:
"This Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana is our teacher and the one who instructs us."
Now, having burned his arms so that his body was no longer complete, at that time the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana stood amidst the great assembly and made this vow:
"If I have truly abandoned these two arms and shall certainly attain the golden-colored body of a Buddha, and if this is not false, may my two arms be restored as they were before.
Having made this vow, they were naturally restored once again by virtue of this.
This was brought about by the profound and thick accumulation of the Bodhisattva’s merit and wisdom;
at that moment, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and the heavens rained down precious flowers, such that all humans and devas experienced what they had never known before.
"The golden-hued body" refers to the ultimate, eternal form of the fruit of wondrous enlightenment; this concludes the second section on the cultivation of offerings.
△ Third, the conclusion and correlation of the ancient and the modern, which has two parts: first, the correlation, and second, the exhortation to practice. Now, the first part.
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva宿王華 (Śrīkūṭarāja): "What do you think? Is the Bodhisattva一切眾生喜見 (Sarvasattvapriyadarśana) someone else?

He is none other than the present Bodhisattva藥王 (Bhaiṣajyarāja). The number of times he has sacrificed his body as an act of giving is thus immeasurable—hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas."
△ Second, the exhortation to practice:
"O Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña, if there should be one who resolves to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and is able to burn a finger,
or even a single toe, as an offering to a Buddha-stūpa, this is superior to [offering] kingdoms, cities, wives, children, and the three [jewels]."

Even if one were to offer the mountains, forests, rivers, ponds, and all manner of precious treasures within a thousand great trichiliocosm worlds as an offering, it would not equal the merit of offering a single finger—whether a single joint, two joints, or a full finger.

This is because causing even a single finger to exhaust the *satkāyadṛṣṭi* (the view of a self-identity) in sentient beings is the most difficult task to accomplish; thus, the merit of offering a finger far surpasses external gifts such as one's wife and children.
Question: Are external things such as the body, kingdoms, and cities considered external wealth? Question: In the Vinaya, it is prohibited to burn the body or fingers;

yet here there is an exhortation to burn the finger. How should this matter be understood? Answer: There are distinctions between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna precepts, and their underlying pedagogical intent differs.

The Hīnayāna prohibitions establish offenses for such acts, whereas the Mahāyāna prohibitions permit burning [the body] for a specific purpose. Thus, the Brahmajāla Sūtra states: "If one does not burn the body, arms, or fingers to make offerings to the Buddhas..."
The *Buddha-naishkramya-bodhisattva-mahā-uṣṇīṣa-sūtra* states:

"If one can light a single lamp before an image of the Tathāgata, burn a finger-joint, or offer a single incense stick upon one's body, all karmic debts from beginningless time will be repaid at once.
Indeed, it is easy to follow minor practices; what difficulty is there in not burning [one's body]? Yet, to follow the Great Way is truly difficult; only by burning [oneself] is it not so.

If one considers the transition between generations to be of great significance when failing to uphold the precepts, then both the Great and Small Vehicles will collapse. One should know that the conditions and capacities of those in this land are entirely deluded;

they do not understand the sequence of the Great and Small, nor the order of the summer retreats (*varṣā*). (One should permit the "Small Summer" in order to establish the "Great Summer. When the Great comes first and the Small follows, with what intention does one receive it?

(Is it because one knows the *bhikṣu* precepts are what must be studied within the Mahāyāna? Or is it because one admires the high status of a *bhikṣu* and merely hangs on to the empty name? Or is it...)

[Is it that one] retreats from the Great [Vehicle], seeks the Small, and instead studies the Small Dharma? First the Small and later the Great opens the way for the Śrāvaka; prohibiting first the Great and later the Small prohibits the Bodhisattva.

The rules of opening and prohibition are fully contained in the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*. If one first takes the Great and later the Small, one is still called a "Bodhisattva Bhikṣu. How can there be two assemblies within a single boundary (*sīmā*)?

In the case of the Great [Vehicle], one relies on the Great Precepts first, followed by the Small in reliance on the Small [Vehicle]. Within a single body, how are the two natures—identity and difference—related? [The answer is: the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*) of the Mahāyāna...

The essence of the precepts culminates in the Buddha-body; for a bhikṣu, the unmanifest restraint (*avijñapti-saṃvara*) lasts only as long as one’s life. When the great is upheld through the small, from what source does the benefit arise?

(It is because the bhikṣu serves as a model for gods and humans, and his rules of conduct must not be deficient in even a single instance. When the small is recited for the sake of the great, who can fathom the resulting harm?

(One who has not received the full ordination should not eavesdrop, let alone recite it themselves. One should diligently distinguish [the two] to serve as seeds for future generations; for the vehicle upon which one rides consists entirely of the sublime Dharma, and thus one relies upon it.

Because the One Reality establishes cause and effect, and because one employs the vehicle to benefit sentient beings, one should merely examine one’s own virtue, observe the mind through various circumstances, and ensure that one's actions accord with the mind.
Regarding what should be followed and what should be restrained, the first answer concludes the section on ascetic practices.
II. Praising the Sūtra: A. First, praising those who uphold it; B. Second, praising the Dharma upheld; C. Third, clarifying the profound merit of upholding the sūtra.
First: Suppose there were another person who, having filled a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures, offered them as alms to the Buddha, the great Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Arhats;
the merit obtained by that person would not equal that of one who upholds this Dharma.
In the *Lotus Sūtra*, even a single four-line verse brings the greatest merit.
Offering the seven treasures to the Four Noble Ones is not equal to upholding a single verse of the Dharma.

Among all things, there is nothing that can give birth to, nourish, perfect, or bring glory to the noble ones more than the Dharma. △ Second, praising the Dharma that is upheld, which has two parts; first, praising the Dharma.

The second part: Praising the Dharma through its essence and function (*tǐ-yòng*). (The "essence" here does not refer to the essence of the specific thesis, but rather indicates the entire treatise as the essence;

the "function" does not refer to the function of the specific thesis alone, but points to the common functions—such as those indicated by the characters [打-丁+(改-己)] and 等—that are shared by the essence, the thesis, and the function within the treatise. Now, for the first [of these]:
Ratnākara, it is just as the ocean is the foremost among all streams, rivers, and torrents;
so too is this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* the most profound and vast among all the sūtras spoken by the Tathāgatas.

The flowing streams and great rivers are metaphors for the four flavors of milk, curd, cream, and butter—the provisional teachings. The ocean is a metaphor for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the "Ultimate Cream";
it is the deepest because it fully reveals the original ground, and the greatest because it universally opens up all things.
Furthermore, just as among all mountains— the Earth Mountains, the Black Mountains, the Lesser Iron Ring Mountains,
the Greater Iron Ring Mountains, and the Ten Treasure Mountains— Mount Sumeru is the foremost, so too is this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* the most supreme among all sūtras.
The ten jewel-mountains are named in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, and Mount Sumeru is one of them. Because the earth is made of black iron and the Cakravāḍa mountains, they are not composed of jewels.
Although the other nine are made of jewels, they are inhabited by various gods and nāgas either individually or in pairs;

only this Mount Sumeru is composed of the four jewels and is the exclusive dwelling place of devas. This is analogous to the forty stages of mind (*citta*) that serve as the basis for what is expounded in other teachings.
The principles upon which the ten stages—whether pertaining to ordinary beings, sages, or saints—are based, whether conventional, ultimate, or middle, are considered inferior.
This sutra, however, elucidates that which is supported by them: it is the basis for the devas of opening, showing, awakening, and entering;
it is the treasure of permanence, bliss, self, and purity. Therefore, it is the foremost and most supreme.
Furthermore, just as among the many stars the Moon Deity is the most preeminent, so too is this Lotus Sūtra;
it is the most illuminating among the hundreds of thousands of millions of kinds of sūtras and dharmas.
The stars and the moon both appear at night, which may be used as a metaphor for provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*). The stars are numerous yet small, and they neither wax nor wane;

this illustrates how the meanings expounded in various sutras are expedient means according to individual dispositions, each catering to a single capacity without mastery. The moon appears alone yet is large, and it can both wax and wane;
this illustrates how the meaning expounded in this sutra is an expedient that accords with ultimate reality (*tattva*), illuminating through the union of the real and the provisional.
It is the most clear and luminous among all dharmas.
Furthermore, just as the Sun Deva is able to dispel all darkness, so too this sutra is able to destroy the darkness of all that is unwholesome.
The rising of the sun is called "day," which can be used as an analogy for ultimate wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*).

Since other sutras do not reveal the provisional (*upāya*) to manifest the single ultimate reality, they cannot eliminate the darkness of clinging to the three [vehicles], nor can they eliminate the darkness of clinging to the near [vehicle].
If even this sutra breaks through the darkness of the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samayakabodhi*), how much more so must it break through all other forms of darkness?

Furthermore, just as among all minor kings, the Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin) is the most supreme, so too is this sutra the most honored among all scriptures. The Tripitaka teaching is like the minor kings;
the three vehicles of the distinct teachings are like the Iron-Wheel-Turning Kings; and the three vehicles of the common teaching...
The "identical yet distinct" teaching (*tongwei bie jiao*) is like a copper wheel-turning king (*tāmra-cakra-vartin*), which sequentially explains the two principles of the True and the Middle.

The "separated from the partial" Perfect teaching (*ge pian zhi yuan*) is like a silver wheel-turning king (*rūpya-cakra-vartin*), which instantaneously explains the three truths but does not include those of the fixed nature among the two vehicles (*niyata-dvaya-yāna*).

This sutra’s Perfect teaching of revelation (*kai xian zhi yuan*) is like a golden wheel-turning king (*suvarṇa-cakra-vartin*); even those in the northern continent who cling to ice and hold to non-self are [included].
It returns to the sovereign control.
Furthermore, just as Śakra is the king among the gods of the Thirty-three Heavens, so too is this sutra the king among all sutras.
The thirty-two heavens, with eight in each of the four directions, may be compared to the four teachings, each having four gates for self-cultivation and the transformation of others;
this sutra governs them all, and thus it is like Śakra, the king of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
Furthermore, just as Mahābrahmā is the father of all sentient beings, so too is this sutra the father of all noble ones—
both those in training and those beyond training— as well as those who have resolved their minds upon awakening as bodhisattvas.

When the kalpa is about to end, it is the natural law for all sentient beings of the world to be reborn above in the Second Dhyāna Heaven of Light (the heavens of Limited Light, Immeasurable Light, and Light-Sound are collectively termed the Heavens of Light). Only when the kalpa-fire arises and has destroyed the world does it become empty.

Once it has become empty and the world is formed again, those among the beings of the Heaven of Light whose life-span has expired are born through transformation by the power of their merit and virtue at the beginning of the new world.
Dhyāna is Mahābrahmādeva. Originally there was but one person who thought to himself, "Why is it that there is no companion here?
Subsequently, those from the Ābhāsvara Heaven whose life-spans had ended also came to be born through transformation in the First Dhyāna;
these are the Brahma-purohitas and the Brahma-kāyikas. Therefore, the Great Brahmā King claimed of himself, "I am all."
Sentient beings call the Brahmā King their father, yet this is a false conceptualization and not the ultimate truth;
it is merely spoken in accordance with the sentiments of sentient beings by borrowing this analogy. This sutra correctly elucidates the wondrous principle of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*);
the true mark is universally able to give birth to all dharmas, and all worthy ones and sages study it.
Those who are beyond training (aśaikṣa) and those bodhisattvas who have resolved their minds toward the four teachings both achieve accomplishment by relying upon the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa);
therefore, [the Buddha] is their father.
Furthermore, among all ordinary persons, there are those who are stream-enterers (srotāpanna), once-returners (sakṛdāgāmin), non-returners (anāgāmin), and arhats.
The Pratyekabuddha is the foremost; this sutra is likewise so. Among all the sūtras spoken by all Tathāgatas, or spoken by Bodhisattvas, or spoken by Śrāvakas, it is the most supreme.
Any who are able to receive and uphold this sutra shall likewise be the foremost among all sentient beings.
Vimalakīrti emerged from the world without a Buddha present, attaining solitary transcendence and awakening without relying on hearing the Dharma;

therefore, his field of merit is superior to that of those in the four fruits. What is taught in other sutras involves expedient means, such as when those in the four fruits attain awakening only through hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
What this sutra elucidates purely clarifies the principle of the unconditioned and the single reality; it concerns only the realization of that reality.
It is characterized by spontaneous entry, like a pratyekabuddha who does not rely on external conditions.
Among all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, the bodhisattva is foremost; this sutra is likewise the foremost among all sūtras and dharmas.

The three vehicles all belong to the stage of causes; only the Bodhisattva is the foremost. Other sutras clarify the seven stages of expedient means as causes, which are comparable to the two vehicles.
This sutra clarifies the perfect cause as unsurpassed, which is comparable to the Bodhisattva—this is precisely what it means for the cause to be foremost.
Just as the Buddha is the King of all Dharmas, so too is this sutra the king among all sutras.

While other sutras clarify that the Buddha attained enlightenment recently at the Seat of Enlightenment (Bodhimaṇḍa), this sutra clarifies that the Buddha attained enlightenment long ago, in the distant past.
Thus, this wondrous sutra encompasses all that was taught throughout his entire life; it is the foremost of fruits, like the great ocean, Mount Sumeru, or the moon.
The ten similes—of the sun, the wheel-turning king, Śakra, Mahābrahmā, the pratyekabuddha, the bodhisattva, and the Buddha—reveal its supreme excellence.
This concludes the first section: Praising the Essence of the Dharma. △ Second, praising the Function of the Dharma.
O Rājanvatsa, this sutra can save all sentient beings (general indication of bestowing and rescuing);

this sutra can cause all sentient beings to be free from all suffering and affliction (specifically clarifying the extraction of suffering); this sutra can greatly benefit all sentient beings and fulfill their aspirations (specifically clarifying the bestowal of happiness).
It is like a cool pond that can satisfy all who are parched and exhausted; it is like one who is cold finding [warmth].
Like a naked person obtaining clothing, like a merchant obtaining his master, like a child obtaining its mother, like one crossing water obtaining a boat, like a sick person obtaining a physician,
like one in darkness obtaining a lamp, like a poor person obtaining treasure, like a subject obtaining a king, like a trader obtaining the sea, and like a torch dispelling darkness—
using these twelve similes to illustrate the perfection and extraction— this Lotus Sūtra is likewise able to cause sentient beings [to attain liberation].
[The Bodhisattva] is freed from all suffering and all illness, and is able to untie all the bonds of birth and death (concluding the summary and the extraction).

Second, the praise of the Dharma upheld is finished. △ Third, clarifying that the merit of upholding the sutra is profound; this has two parts: first, clarifying the merit of upholding the entire sutra;
second, clarifying the merit of upholding this chapter. Now, the first part.

If a person hears this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, whether writing it themselves or having others write it, the merit they obtain is such that even if one were to use the wisdom of a Buddha to measure its extent,
one could not reach its limit. If one writes this scripture with flowers, incense, necklaces, burning incense, powdered incense,
ointment incense, banners, canopies, robes, and various kinds of lamps— such as ghee lamps, oil lamps, and other fragrant lamps— [the merit is likewise immeasurable].
The merit obtained from making offerings of oil lamps— whether of *campaka* oil,
*sumana* oil, *pāṭala* oil, *bāliśika* oil, or *navamālikā* oil— is likewise immeasurable.
△ Second, explaining the merit of upholding this chapter. This section has two parts: first, the comparative evaluation; second, the entrustment. Now, for the first:
"O Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña, if there be anyone who hears this 'Chapter on the Past Deeds of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja,' they shall likewise attain immeasurable and boundless merit.
If there be women who hear this 'Chapter on the Past Deeds of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja' and are able to receive and uphold it..."
All these women shall hereafter no longer receive a female body. If, during the final five hundred years after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata,
there is a woman who hears this sutra and practices according to its teaching, she will, at the end of her life here, go directly to the Land of Peace and Bliss—
the dwelling place surrounded by Amitābha Buddha and the great bodhisattvas— and be born within a lotus flower upon a jeweled throne.
He was no longer troubled by greed, nor troubled by anger or delusion, nor troubled by the defilements of pride, envy, and the like.
He attained the bodhisattva’s supernormal powers and the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Having attained this patience, his faculty of sight became pure; with this purified faculty of sight, he beheld seven million two thousand *koṭis*.
At that time, as many Buddhas, Tathāgatas, as there are grains of sand in ten billion Ganges Rivers, will all together praise you from afar, saying:

"Excellent, excellent, son of good family! That you are able, within the Dharma of Śākyamuni Buddha, to receive, uphold, read, recite, contemplate, and explain this sutra for others— the merit you thereby obtain is immeasurable and boundless; even fire cannot burn it."
Water cannot wash away your merit; even if a thousand Buddhas were to speak together, they could not exhaust it.
You have now been able to destroy all the mara-enemies, shatter the army of birth and death, and utterly annihilate all other adversaries.
Son of good family, hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, through their supernormal powers, protect you among all the devas and humans in every world.
There is no one like you, except for the Tathāgata; among all the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and even bodhisattvas, there is none whose wisdom and meditative concentration equals yours.
Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña, this bodhisattva has accomplished such power of merit and wisdom.
If anyone hears this "Chapter on the Past Deeds of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja" and can rejoice in it with sympathetic joy...

One who praises the good will have the fragrance of blue lotuses constantly issue from their mouth in this present life, and the fragrance of ox-head sandalwood constantly issue from the pores of their body; the merit they obtain is as described above.

Those who receive and uphold this chapter shall not take on a female body; for women, the view of their own female form is particularly heavy, yet the merit of this ascetic practice of renouncing the body can uproot it.
If one practices according to the teaching, they will be able to be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss;
thus, this sutra serves as the cause for the Pure Land, alongside the *Sutra of the Sixteen Contemplations* and the *Larger and Smaller Amitābha Sutras*.
They are equal, non-dual, and without distinction, as this sutra explains regarding the practice of the three tracks and the four modes of peaceful conduct (*catur-āśvāsa-caryā*).

If one subdues the five stages of dwelling (*pañca-vihāra*), one is born in the Pure Land of Shared Residence (*sahā-loka-purī*); if one purifies the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*), one is born in the Pure Land of Expedient Means (*upāya-purī*);

and if one shatters ignorance (*avidyā*), one is born in the Pure Land of True Reward (*bhoga-purī*), which is also a partial realization of the Land of Tranquil Light (*prabhāsvara-purī*). Question: Regarding purity...

Question: Since the earth is so vast, how can it be peaceful and blissful? Answer: It is because all beings are gathered through the vows of the Tathāgata; because the karmic conditions of their past affinities are profound;

because they fix their minds upon a single point to achieve concentration; and because "one is all" due to the inconceivable nature of reality. For these reasons, many sutras praise and describe this extensively.
Within the text, the fact that fragrance issues from the body and mouth is the immediate retribution (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karman*); the rest follows accordingly.
[This includes] retribution in this life and retribution in future lives. △ Second, the entrustment:
"Therefore, Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña, I entrust this 'Chapter on the Past Deeds of Bhaiṣajyarāja Bodhisattva' to you.
After my parinirvāṇa, during the final five hundred years, you must widely proclaim and disseminate it throughout Jambudvīpa so that it shall not be severed."
Māras, Mārakāyikas, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, kumbhāṇḍas, and others will find an opportunity [to cause harm].
Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña, you should protect this sūtra by means of your supernormal powers. Why is this?
This sūtra is the excellent medicine for the illnesses of the people of Jambudvīpa. If anyone who is ill hears this sūtra, their illness will immediately be extinguished, and they will not grow old.
"Amitāyus, King of Constellations, if you see anyone who upholds this sutra, you should take blue lotuses filled with powdered incense and scatter them over that person.
Having scattered them, you should form this thought: 'This person will, before long, surely take grass and sit at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) to shatter the armies of Māra;
they shall blow the Dharma conch and beat the great Dharma drum to deliver and liberate all beings.'"

All sentient beings are in the ocean of old age, sickness, and death; therefore, those who seek the Buddha-way, upon seeing anyone who receives and upholds this sutra, should give rise to a mind of reverence toward them in this way.

Not aging is bliss; not dying is permanence. Hearing the sutra, one attains the understanding of permanence and bliss, becoming serene and fearless as the diseases of the three delusions are extinguished.

Chapter Twenty-four: The Past Deeds of Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara. Regarding the title "Past Deeds" (*pūrvayoga*) for this chapter:
when the Bodhisattva Padmaśrī asked about the signs of the emission of light and the subsequent invitation [of the Buddha], it was revealed that he had appeared from the east.

This chapter fully elucidates the causes and conditions, as well as the karmic fruits and retributions, of his past offerings of music and precious bowls to the Buddhas; it further clarifies his present manifestation.
It is called the "Chapter on Original Deeds" because it concerns the function of the Samādhi of All Physical Bodies (*sarva-rūpa-kāya-samādhi*).

Furthermore, while the "Chapter on the Medicine King" explains only original practices and does not clarify the universal transformation of wandering [throughout the world], and the "Universal Gate Chapter" explains only the wandering transformation and does not clarify original practices, this present chapter elucidates both.
Moreover, whereas the two chapters on the Medicine King and the Universal Gate were taught in response to questions, these are now taught by means of light.
The summoning and the preaching mutually manifest and reveal the perfect practice; it is not meant that there is any superiority or inferiority between them.

The text of this chapter is divided into six sections: first, emitting light to summon from the east; second, receiving the command and coming from the west; third, propagating the sutra in the ten directions;
fourth, the two lands obtaining benefit; fifth, returning to one's original country; sixth, hearing this chapter and advancing on the Path. First, emitting light to summon from the east.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha emitted the light from the *uṣṇīṣa*— the mark of a Great Man— and emitted the light from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows,
illuminating all the Buddhas in the eastern direction, as numerous as the sands of one hundred and eight million *nayuta* Ganges Rivers.
Beyond this number of worlds, there is a world named Pure Light Adornment (*Vimalaprabhā-vyūha*). In that land dwells a Buddha named Pure Flower Constellation King Wisdom Tathāgata,
Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men,
Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One, who [is surrounded] by immeasurable and boundless bodhisattvas.
Surrounded by a multitude who paid him respectful homage, Śākyamuni Buddha preached the Dharma for them; the radiance from the white tuft of hair between his brows illuminated that land everywhere.
Because the Buddha is the ultimate person, he is called the Great Being (Mahāpuruṣa), possessing the subtle and pure Dharma-body endowed with the thirty-two marks.

Since every mark is the Dharma-realm, they are called the marks of a Great Being (*mahāpuruṣa*). The *uṣṇīṣa* (crown-protrusion) and the *ūrṇā-kośa* (white tuft of hair between the brows) are two such marks of a Great Being.
The *uṣṇīṣa* symbolizes the perfectly consummate fruit of the wondrous result, while the *ūrṇā* symbolizes the wondrous cause of the Middle Way.

This intends to reveal that after attaining the fruit, the Bodhisattva Wondrous Sound (*Ghoṣeśvara*) practices the cause, just like Mañjuśrī, Maitreya, Bhaiṣajyarāja, Avalokiteśvara, and Samantabhadra.

the sentient beings of this land are better suited to obtain the four benefits through Dharma-megha, and for this reason, he is summoned. Question: The bodhisattvas of the ten directions are capable...
