The common person does not know this; it is like a master of physiognomy who skillfully recognizes that the single mind of a sentient being is fully endowed with the nature and characteristics of the hundred realms and thousand suchnesses.
The situation for ordinary beings is likewise: though the principle is inherently complete, they are deluded by their emotions.

The sage awakens to this consciousness, just as that master of physiognomy knows that these thousand kinds of natures and characteristics are all phenomena produced by causes and conditions—whether produced by evil causes and conditions or otherwise.

Since phenomena possess the nature of suffering from its characteristics to its very root and end, and one has not yet attained liberation from it, one contemplates this suffering and gives rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

Since phenomena produced by wholesome causes and conditions possess the nature of happiness from its characteristics to its very root and end, and one has not yet realized it, one contemplates this and gives rise to great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*). This is explained in detail in the first fascicle of the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning).

The realms and their characteristics are equal. When a Bodhisattva deeply contemplates that the ten dharma-realms and the thousandfold varieties of sentient beings' characteristics are all fully present within a single mind, and traces them back to their source, they perceive that both the evil and the good inherent in their nature are already perfectly clear and distinct;
how much more so when one cultivates and realizes these good and evil qualities through practice? It is like seeing that even on the Snowy Mountains there exists the King of Medicines.

Furthermore, regarding poisonous weeds: by contemplating their inherent nature, one gives rise to a heart of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) through the feeling of pity and sorrow for their evil poison, desiring to uproot their suffering;

and by contemplating their inherent nature, one gives rise to a heart of great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*) through the feeling of joy, affection, and fondness for their goodness, desiring to bestow happiness upon them.
These ten dharma-realms encompass all sentient beings without exception; it is for the sake of these sentient beings that [the practice is undertaken].
If one cultivates loving-kindness and compassion through provisional names, is this not the universal compassion based on sentient beings? Question:

Since the heavy sufferings of the hell realm have not yet been uprooted, how can one bestow happiness upon them? Answer: When sentient beings enter the hells, they frequently give rise to three thoughts;

the Bodhisattva, seizing this opportunity, immediately provides the causes for their happiness—therefore, it is said that he bestows happiness. Furthermore, the Bodhisattva is capable of great compassion.
To undergo suffering on their behalf so that they may find rest, and to lighten the remaining nine types of suffering while bestowing happiness—the meaning of this is readily understood.

Next, to clarify the universal compassion that takes phenomena as its object (*dharmālambana-maitrī-karuṇā*): one contemplates the nature and characteristics of the ten dharma-realms (*daśa-dharmadhātu*), seeing that all good and evil are entirely empty.

The ten dharma-realms are merely provisional designations (*prajñapti*), and these provisional designations are themselves empty. Within the ten dharma-realms, there are form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; [the same applies to] form, sensation, and so forth.

Perception, mental formations, and consciousness are all empty; the ten dharma realms and their respective locations are all empty. Being without self and without what belongs to a self, they are unattainable.
Like illusions and transformations, they lack true reality and possess the mark of eternal quiescence, ultimately returning to emptiness.
Why do sentient beings insist on calculating them as real? Unaware and unknowing, they undergo suffering and affliction, finding no liberation.

The bliss of unconditioned quiescence is now sought; wishing to uproot this suffering, one gives rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), and wishing to bestow this bliss, one gives rise to great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*).
Thus, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states: "To be able to preach such a Dharma for the sake of sentient beings is true loving-kindness.

If one were to give rise to compassion and loving-kindness by taking only a single dharma-realm as an object, could it truly be called universal? Now, [the bodhisattva] takes the ten... as the object.
Is the Dharma-realm not universal? Regarding the universality of the three types of objectless compassion (*anālambana-karuṇā*):

if one were to take as objects the characteristics, natures, and distinctions of the provisional designations of the ten dharma-realms, then these designations would not be provisional. Since the ten dharma-realms are like illusions and transformations, they are empty;

yet this emptiness is neither non-empty nor provisional. Therefore, it does not take the characteristics and natures of the ten dharma-realms as its object, for they are not non-empty. Thus, it does not take them as its object.
When the reality of the ten dharma realms negates these two extremes, being without abiding and without attachment, it is called the Middle Way;

yet even this middle is not an object to be grasped, for it is ultimately pure. When contemplating in this manner, although one does not deliberately grasp at emptiness or the provisional, one spontaneously illuminates both extremes, giving rise to non-referential compassion that uproots the suffering of the two deaths and bestows the bliss of the Middle Way.

Just as a magnet attracts iron without anyone instructing it, through natural resonance; so too does unconditioned great compassion (*nirālamba-mahākaruṇā*) attract those with the capacity for the Three Truths, without error and without the need for deliberate thought.
When a practitioner first cultivates this compassion at the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), they immediately enter the five grades of the stage of contemplative practice (*kuan-hsing*).
Through unconditioned great compassion, they advance into the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*), reaching the stage of semblance (*sādṛśya*).
Based on compassion, one subsequently enters the Ten Abodes (*daśavihāra*), where one partially realizes (*pradeśa-prativedha*) non-referential compassion (*anālambana-karuṇā*).

This continues up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samalaṃbuddhatva*), where the neighboring ultimate compassion universally permeates sentient beings. Responding without movement, it is like a clear mirror manifesting images or a magnet attracting iron.
Because it is fully endowed with the Three Truths (*trisatya*), it is called "Universal Pervasion" (*pǔtōng*); because it leads to the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*), it is termed a "Gate."
Furthermore, regarding the "Four Great Vows": "Great" (*hong*) refers to breadth; "Vow" (*shi*) refers to restraint; and "Vow" (*yuan*) refers to seeking.
It means to extensively seek the supreme Dharma by restraining the mind. Therefore, they are called the Four Great Vows. The foundation of the Great Vows is compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā*).

Since compassion takes suffering and happiness as its objects, the Great Vows likewise rely upon the Four Noble Truths. If one perceives the Noble Truth of Suffering as oppressive, agonizing, and bitter...
Because he gives rise to this vow based on the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), it is said: "Those who have not crossed over, may I cause them to cross.

Because he sees the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*) as a source of inversion, delusion, and bondage, and gives rise to this vow based upon it, it is said: "Those who are not liberated, may I cause them to be liberated.

Because sentient beings do not recognize the pure path that can bring one out of birth and death to the ground of peace and happiness, and because he wishes to show sentient beings and establish them upon this path, it is said: [“May I cause them to attain nirvana”].
To bring those who are not yet at peace to peace, and to sever the bonds of the fetters at the stage where afflictions are extinguished, is called *nirvāṇa*.
Because one makes a vow based on this [realization] for the sake of sentient beings who have not yet realized it, it is said that those who have not attained *nirvāṇa* shall attain it.

Since the causes of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) are difficult to recognize while their suffering fruits are easy to know, the fruit is mentioned first and the cause later. Furthermore, because the principle of *nirvāṇa* is subtle, skillful means are required.
Cause precedes effect; these Four Noble Truths do not transcend the single mind. Deluded in mind, one gives rise to karma; karma then brings about its fruit.
If one wishes to know the source of the fruit, the fruit arises solely from the accumulation [of causes]. By restraining the mind and ceasing karma, the wheel of birth and death is destroyed.
The subduing of afflictions is called the Path (*mārga*). Through unremitting cultivation, the patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*) is manifested, and both cause and fruit are extinguished.
The cessation of [defilements] is termed "extinction" (*nirodha*); although there are four distinctions, they ultimately constitute a single moment of thought and are not separate dharmas.

Since this is the case for the Four Truths, it is likewise for the Great Vows (*mahāpraṇidhāna*). However, when ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) weary of the lower realms and grasp for the higher, they establish their vows based on this;

yet, as they have not yet realized the Four Truths, these are not called the Universal (*sarvaga*) or Shared (*sādhāraṇa*) Teachings. Furthermore, seeing only the Four Truths of the limited [birth-and-death] (*paricchinna*) is also not so called.

In the Universal and Distinctive Teachings (*pǔbiéjiào*), one first addresses the *duànfēn* (segmented) death and rebirth, and subsequently addresses the *biànyì* (transformational) death and rebirth; this is not yet the Universal-Round Teaching (*pǔyuánjiào*).
In the Universal-Round Teaching, a Bodhisattva, within a single mind, universally knows all suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. Regarding the universal knowledge of the origin (*jí*):

the "afflictions of view and craving" (*jiàn'ài*) of ordinary beings constitute the "active" (*yòuzuò*) origin, while the "attachment to emptiness" (*zhùkōng*) of the Two Vehicles constitutes the "non-active" (*wúzuò*) origin. Therefore, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* says:
The Dharma is called "untainted"; if one is tainted by the Dharma, it is called a "tainted dharma" and is not the seeking of the Dharma.

Furthermore, it is said that as long as the fetters and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are not yet exhausted, flowers will cling to the body; this means that the delusion of transformation (*pariṇāma-vaśitā*) has not been removed at all.

The *Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "O Bhikṣus, regarding this Mahāyāna, you have not yet attained the True Dharma; until the various fetters and afflictions are eliminated, [the Dharma] will be absent."

That which constitutes "active accumulation" (*kriyā-samudaya*)—up to and including the arising of craving for the Dharma that accords with the Path (*anuloma-dharmatṛṣṇā*)—is also "non-active accumulation" (*akriyā-samudaya*).

One who thoroughly knows suffering does so because of the existence of accumulation; for while active accumulation invites the suffering of the fragmented [birth-and-death] (*paricchinna-duḥkha*), non-active accumulation invites the suffering of transformation (*pariṇāma-duḥkha*).
Thus, the Truth of the Path within the realms (*dhātu*) is itself the Truth of Accumulation beyond the realms; it is the Truth of Cessation within the realms.

This refers to the Truth of Suffering outside the realms (*dhātu*). The Truth of Cessation, which is the path for fully knowing the antidote to the Truth of Origination, consists of the five precepts and ten wholesome paths for humans and devas, as well as the four dhyānas and four concentrations;

these lead to the two types of *nirvāṇa*—with and without remainder—through both the Shared and the Distinct teachings. The Separate Teaching proceeds through distinct stages to reach the eternally abiding truth.
The inability to have immeasurable paths within a single path is not called the Universal Path. In the Perfect Teaching, the Middle Way is itself the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*).
The *Sutra on the Contemplation of Samantabhadra* states that the cause of the Mahayana is the true reality of all phenomena;
practicing this path is called the "Perfect Cause," and for this reason it is termed the "Universal Path. The Nirvana attained therein is ultimate, eternally abiding, and encompasses all things.
Afflictions are forever eliminated without remainder, just as the fire at the end of an eon leaves no embers behind. The *Samantabhadra-dhyāna-sūtra* states:

"The fruit of the Mahāyāna is the realization of the true nature of all phenomena; such extinction is called the 'perfect fruit' (*pariniṣpanna-phala*), and thus it is termed 'universal extinction' (*sarva-nirodha*).

Since the Four Noble Truths that are the objects of contemplation are already exhaustive, how could the vows arising from the contemplation of those truths not be universal? Therefore, they are called "vast and universal vows."
Furthermore, the practitioner’s sequential five practices are not yet the universal single mind; only when these five practices are universal and complete is it called "universal.

As explained in the "Excellence of Practice" section of the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning), regarding the severance of delusions: if one enters emptiness from the conventional, one merely severs the four abidings (*catur-vāsa*), yet the flowers still cling to the body.
This is not yet the true Dharma for removing all fetters (*saṃyojana*); one has merely departed from falsehood but has not yet attained the One Mind.

Because it liberates all, it is not called "universal. If one enters the provisional from emptiness merely to eliminate the "dust-like" delusions without relying on the fundamental [Middle Way], this is also not called "universal.
If emptiness and the provisional are non-dual and the Middle Way—the fundamental—is correctly contemplated, then once the root is toppled, the branches and twigs naturally fall away.
It is like overturning the great earth, where grasses and trees are all crushed; therefore, it is called the "universality" of severing delusions.
Regarding those who enter the Dharma-gate: if those of the Two Vehicles can enter one Dharma-gate but cannot enter two, how much less so many?
Furthermore, if one cultivates distinct practices with shallow and deep gradations, this is not called "universal.
If one enters the King Samādhi, all samādhis are included within it; it is like a king’s arrival, which must be accompanied by his retinue, and that retinue in turn...

The King’s Samādhi that has a retinue is also like this: the samādhi of one truth is the samādhi of the three truths, and each of these samādhis of the three truths further has immeasurable dharma-gates as its retinue;
because they all enter into the King’s Samādhi, it is called "Entering Universally into Dharma-Gates. As for "supernatural powers," when an Arhat first perceives the great trichiliocosm...

The first stage of the Grounds (bhūmi) seeing a hundred worlds, the second stage seeing a thousand worlds, and so forth, are all called "limited" supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) because they are restricted in scope. Why is this?

Since the objects they take as conditions are narrow, the supernatural powers they manifest are likewise small. Now, the Bodhisattvas of the Perfect Teaching universally take the ten dharma-realms as their objects;
the supernatural powers they manifest see throughout the ten dharma-realms without limit or exhaustion. Even the practitioners of the Three Vehicles cannot [attain such power].
If one knows its name, how much more so its realm? Since this is the case for what is seen by the eye, other instances may be known by analogy.
Regarding the "skillful means" (upāya), there are those of progressive practice, which are the skillful means of self-cultivation prior to the Path;

and there are those of initiating activity, which are the skillful means of transforming others subsequent to the Path. Here, we are specifically clarifying the skillful means subsequent to the Path. As for the Two Vehicles and those of provisional [capacity]...

A Bodhisattva at this stage, through the skillful means of their own practice, is only able to enter a single dharma-gate; thus, when they arise to transform others, they can only match what they themselves have attained.
Both before and after attaining this path, they are not yet universal. Now, a Bodhisattva of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) takes the two truths as skillful means;
having gathered all skillful means and entered the Middle Way, they simultaneously illumine both truths.
The spiritual transformations of the two truths pervade the ten dharma-realms, yet within them the Middle Way suffers no diminution;
thus, both before and after the path, they are called "universal. As for those who preach the Dharma:

those of the Two Vehicles and Bodhisattvas of provisional stages cannot simultaneously answer the voices of all beings, nor can they cause those from different regions and diverse customs to understand at once. Now, in the Perfect Teaching...
When a person expounds the Dharma at one time, beings of various types each attain understanding according to their kind; with a single wondrous voice, it pervades the ten directions.

Just as a *tūṇa* lute produces sound according to the mind’s intent, it is therefore called "universal" (*puya*) in the preaching of the Dharma. Regarding the making of offerings to the Buddhas, there are two kinds:

first, the offering of things (*vastu*), and second, the offering of principle (*dharma*). As for the offering of things, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "It is not merely for the sake of making offerings to a single [Buddha]..."
The Buddha does not do so merely to make offerings to as many Buddhas as there are atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields; rather,
it is because he desires to universally make offerings to all Buddhas throughout the entire Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space,

that he does not arise from the samādhi of cessation yet manifests various dignified demeanors, remains in meditative concentration with palms joined to praise the Kings of the Dharma, and offers his body, life, and wealth to them all.
The ritual implements extend throughout the ten directions, as described in the *Vow-King of Samantabhadra*.

As for the offering of principle, the mind of perfect wisdom and correct contemplation is termed "awakening" (*jue*); awakening is itself the Buddha. To cultivate this wisdom through the perfuming of myriad practices is to make offerings to the Buddhas;
therefore, it is said that making offerings to all Buddhas is universal, thereby accomplishing the benefit of sentient beings.
For example, the light of a firefly, a lamp, a candle, a star, or the moon provides only slight benefit;
however, when the sunlight illuminates the world, it causes all grasses, trees, thickets, and forests to grow everywhere, bringing flowers and fruits to full maturity.

In this analogy, the non-Buddhists are like fireflies, the followers of the Two Vehicles are like lamps and candles, the bodhisattvas of the Distinct Teaching are like stars, and the bodhisattvas of the Separate Teaching are like the moon. Now, as for the bodhisattvas of the Perfect Teaching...

Like the sun’s orb or a great cloud, which at once pours down rain equally upon the four quarters so that the three types of grass and two types of trees each attain growth, it is said that [the Buddha] “accomplishes sentient beings universally. How can the meaning of the Universal Gate (Pumen) be fully exhausted?
I have briefly cited ten meanings merely to show its beginning. One should simply contemplate the dharma of the mind-nature of the present single thought.

When you are fully endowed with the three thousand nature-and-characteristics—which are simultaneously empty, provisionally existent, and the Middle—this is precisely the wondrous realm of the unconditioned Four Noble Truths.
Taking this wondrous realm as an object, one gives rise to compassion; through compassion, one universally establishes great vows;
and through these great vows, one universally relies upon this to practice every single practice within a single practice. Thus, in relying upon this for practice, one cuts off [all delusions].

Because the delusions are severed once and for all, the severing of delusions universally relies upon this; because one dharma-gate is all dharma-gates, entering the dharma-gate universally relies upon this.
From this, supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) arise—namely, the transformation of the unmanifested (*avyākṛta-nirmāṇa*)—and thus the arising of supernatural powers universally relies upon this.
From this, skillful means (*upāya*) arise, universally accommodating the ten realms through provisional and real, sudden and gradual teachings.

Because of various capacities and conditions, skillful means universally rely on this to preach the Dharma; because a single voice universally responds to all sounds, preaching the Dharma universally relies on this;
because all Buddhas of the three periods of time accept their offerings, making offerings universally relies on this;
and because the myriad capacities within the dharma-realm all obtain the four benefits, the accomplishment [of sentient beings] universally relies on this.
The principle that the nature of the minds of all sentient beings is universally undiminished is the *prajñapti* (name) stage of the Universal Gate;

the thorough subduing of the five abodes [of ignorance] is the *nāman* (name) stage of the Universal Gate; the purification of the six sense organs is the *ābhāsagata* (similarity) stage of the Universal Gate;

the opening, showing, awakening, and entering [into the Dharma] is the *prativedha* (partial realization) stage of the Universal Gate; and the penetrating [realization] of the Dharma-realm is the *praveśa* (full realization) stage of the Universal Gate.
To thoroughly exhaust the source and fully realize the nature is the ultimate meaning of the Universal Gate (*Pumen*). The explanation of the title of this chapter is complete.
This chapter was recited by the Dharma Master Dharmakṣema for the King of Hexi, Juqu Mengxun, which cured his illness;
thus it has been circulated separately. This is truly because the Great Being Avalokiteśvara has a particularly deep affinity with this region. Wisdom.
The Great Master also separately expounded the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) and the *Yishu* (Commentary), each consisting of two fascicles. The *Xuanyi* is also structured in five stages:
taking "humanity, dharma, and so forth" as the name, as already explained previously; taking the union of numinous wisdom with the Dharma-body as the essence (*ti*);

taking responsive resonance as the school (*zong*); taking compassion for benefiting sentient beings as the function (*yong*); and taking the circulation of the *tendoku* (clarified butter) flavor as the teaching-appearance (*jiaoxiang*).
*The Collected Meanings of the Tiantai School on the Lotus Sutra*, Volume Seven, Part One;
*The Collected Meanings of the Tiantai School on the Lotus Sutra*, Volume Seven, Part Two.
Compiled by the later scholar of Ancient Wu, Ouyi Zhixu.
△ Entering the text of the "Universal Gate" (Samantamukha-parivarta) is divided into two parts: first, the questions and answers; second, the merits of hearing this chapter.

The first part [the questions and answers] is further divided into two: first, the long prose; second, the verses. The long prose contains two rounds of questions and answers. The first round is divided into two: first, the question; second, the answer. This is the first [the question].
At that time, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed him in this way:
"World-Honored One, for what causes and conditions is the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara named 'Avalokiteśvara'?"
"At that time" means that the exposition on the Bodhisattvas of the East is finished, and it is now the time to speak of the Bodhisattvas of the West.
(World) Having finished explaining the arising of goodness in the East, it is now the time to explain the arising of goodness in the West.

(For the sake of men) Having finished explaining the severing of doubt in the East, it is now the time to explain the severing of doubt in the West. (As an antidote) Having finished explaining the attainment of the Way in the East, it is now... [the time to explain the attainment of the Way in the West].

The statement that attaining the Way in the West is inexhaustible refers to the realm of the *paramārtha* (the ultimate truth). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* clarifies that emptiness is inexhaustible, which refers to the *tathatā* (the true nature).

The *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra* clarifies the eighty gates of inexhaustibility, and the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* clarifies ten kinds of inexhaustibility; these refer to the *saṃvṛti* (conventional truth). The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:
"That which is inexhaustible is neither exhausted nor non-exhausted, and is therefore called 'inexhaustible'"; this refers to the *madhyamā-pratipad* (the middle way). This is the intended meaning.
Wisdom is precisely the threefold wisdom of the one mind. When wisdom accords with its object and the object follows wisdom into emptiness, this is called "Inexhaustible Intention" (Emptiness).

Furthermore, "intention" is the foundation of both the mundane and the supramundane. When wisdom follows the object and the objects are manifold, such that wisdom is manifold, this is called "Inexhaustible Intention" (Provisionality).
Furthermore, "intention" is the dharma-realm; because everything is the dharma-realm, it is said to be capable [of encompassing all].
Contemplating the nature of the mind is called the supreme concentration (the middle). One who speaks these words is able to inquire because they possess the two adornments.
As for the causes and conditions: if one considers sentient beings, the two capacities for good and evil serve as the cause, while the sage’s numinous wisdom and compassion serve as the condition.
If one considers the bodhisattva, contemplative wisdom and compassion serve as [the cause].
This is due to the conditions created by the karmic resonance of sentient beings. △ Second, the response in three parts: first, the general response; second, the specific response;
third, the exhortation to uphold the name. This last part corresponds to the fourteen fearlessnesses elucidated in the *Mahā-śūraṅgama Sūtra*. Now, the first part.
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati: "Good son, if there are immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of sentient beings who undergo various sufferings and afflictions,
and they hear of this Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara and single-mindedly call upon his name,
the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara will immediately behold their voices, and they shall all attain liberation."
"Immeasurable hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands, millions, and billions of sentient beings" indicates the various capacities within the ten dharma realms.
"Undergo all manner of suffering and affliction" clarifies that the retributive fruits induced by individual karmic actions (*bieye*) differ from one another:

there are those who alone undergo a single suffering, those who alone undergo manifold sufferings, those for whom many undergo a single suffering, and those for whom many undergo manifold sufferings; here, the emphasis is placed on the latter case.
Suffering is abundant and constitutes the realm from which Bodhisattvas deliver others. Encountering suffering arises from the evil of two lifetimes;
hearing the Name is itself the goodness of two lifetimes. To single-mindedly recite the Name involves both the phenomenal (the event) and the noumenal (the principle).

Thus, this union of good and evil constitutes the dynamic resonance between the seeker and the response. "To immediately contemplate their voices" means that the response is swift; all shall attain [liberation].
Liberation responds to this through universality. There are four meanings of "hearing": hearing what is heard, hearing what is not heard, not hearing what is heard, and not hearing what is not heard.
To penetrate any one of these according to one's capacity is precisely the hearing-wisdom (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) of the four teachings.

To single-mindedly recite the name is the contemplative-wisdom (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) and the cultivational-wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) of the four teachings. "Single-mindedness in practice" means that thoughts succeed one another in continuity, without giving rise to distraction.

"Single-mindedness in principle through contemplation" means realizing that this mind is neither self, other, nor both, nor is it without cause; that the essence of both the one who invokes and that which is invoked is the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
"Single-mindedness in phenomena" refers to liberation through the difficulty of phenomena; "single-mindedness in principle" refers to liberation through the difficulty of principle.
Their response according to one's invocation is as certain as the simultaneous act of pecking and hatching. Yet, if one continues the invocation for years without [attaining] it—

That those who receive even a slight benefit do so solely because they have not yet attained the state of single-mindedness is true; nevertheless, it can still serve as a causal condition for attaining liberation in the future.
Thus, although the merit of reciting the Name even with a distracted mind is never in vain, the efficacy may simply be slower or faster.
△ Second, the specific answers in three parts: 1. Clarifying the response based on the capacity of vocal karma; 2. [Clarifying the response] based on the capacity of mental karma.

The third section, "Manifesting Response," clarifies the response according to the three types of karmic capacity. Regarding the first two [subsections], the first clarifies the seven calamities, and the second provides a concluding eulogy.
Within the first [section on the seven calamities], there are seven parts, beginning with the calamity of fire and ending with the seventh, the calamity of hostile bandits. Now, the first [calamity].
If there are those who hold the name of this Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, even if they enter a great fire, the fire shall not burn them.
This is due to the majestic spiritual power of this Bodhisattva.
Holding the name is good; entering the fire is evil. Through the convergence of good and evil as a karmic stimulus, the majestic spiritual power [is manifested], and thus the fire [cannot harm them].

That which cannot be burned is the "response" (ying). Regarding the fire of karmic retribution: from the hells below up to the First Dhyāna above, all are discussed in terms of the capacity for response (ji-ying). Regarding the fire of evil karma:
from the hells below up to the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-perception (Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana) above, all are discussed in terms of the capacity for response.

Regarding the fire of afflictions (kleśa): from the hells below up to the Stage of Equal Enlightenment (Samyak-saṃbodhi) above, all are discussed in terms of the capacity for response. △ Second, the calamity of water.
If one is being swept away by a great flood and invokes his name, one immediately finds shallow ground.
Being swept away by water represents evil; invoking the name represents good. This constitutes the catalyst (*ki*), and finding shallow ground is the response (*ō*).
Regarding retribution: the waters of hell flow from below up to the Second Dhyāna heaven; the waters of evil karma pervade the three realms; and the waters of affliction pervade [all states].
The nine realms are discussed together regarding the resonance between the capacity and the stimulus. △ Third, the peril of the rākṣasas:

Suppose there are hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of sentient beings who, seeking treasures such as gold, silver, lapis lazuli, tridacna, agate, coral, amber, and pearls, enter the great ocean; even if a black wind should blow their ship and cast it adrift—

If there should be even a single person within that rākṣasa realm who invokes the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, all those people shall attain liberation from the perils of the rākṣasas; for this reason, he is named Avalokiteśvara.
This rākṣasa calamity is also a retribution for the calamity of wind. The rākṣasas of karmic retribution reside in the Desire Realm; the rākṣasas of evil karma pervade the Three Realms;
and the rākṣasas of afflictions extend throughout the Nine Realms. Furthermore, the winds of karmic retribution reach up to the Third Dhyāna;

the winds of evil karma pervade the Three Realms; and the winds of afflictions extend throughout the Nine Realms. When discussing these individually in terms of their capacity and response, they may all be understood by analogy. △
Fourth is the peril of blades and staves.
If there is anyone who, when about to be harmed, calls upon the name of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara,
the blades and staves held by their assailants will immediately break into pieces, and they shall obtain liberation.
The swords and staves of karmic retribution are restricted to the realm of those who dwell on earth; the swords and staves of evil karma pervade the three realms;
and the swords and staves of affliction extend throughout the nine realms. △ Fifth, the calamity of ghosts:
If yakṣas and rākṣasas fill the lands of the trichiliocosm and come to harass people, upon hearing them recite [the name], they shall depart.
As for the name of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, even these evil ghosts cannot even look upon him with an evil eye, much less inflict harm.

The difficulty regarding the ghosts may be understood by analogy with the preceding discussion on the rākṣasas. As for the phrase "filling the great trichiliocosm," this is merely a figurative expression.
It is revealed that when the evil ghosts of afflictions fill [the world], merely reciting the name can subdue them. △ Sixth, the difficulty of shackles and fetters:
Suppose there is a person, whether guilty or innocent, whose body is bound and constrained by cangues, manacles, and shackles;
if they recite the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, all these shall be broken and destroyed, and they will immediately attain liberation.

To have offenses is evil in the present life; to be without offenses is evil from the past. That which is upon the hands is called *cangue*; that upon the feet is called *shackles*; that upon the head is called *collar*;
that which binds the entire body is called *chains*. A "seal" (*jian*) refers to confinement; a "bond" (*xi*) refers to fetters.

The chains of karmic retribution exist within the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*); the chains of evil karma pervade the three realms; the chains of affliction (*kleśa*) extend throughout the nine realms.
...and so forth. △ Seventh, the peril of hostile robbers:

Suppose the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system were filled with hostile robbers, and a certain merchant leader, leading a caravan of merchants carrying heavy treasures, was passing through a dangerous road. Among them, one person raised this cry: "O virtuous sons, do not..."
"If you encounter fear, you should with one mind invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
This Bodhisattva is able to bestow fearlessness upon sentient beings; if you invoke his name, you shall be liberated from these hostile bandits.
Upon hearing this, all the merchants raised their voices together and said, "Namo Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva," thus invoking his name.
Therefore, one immediately attains liberation.
The phrase "filling the great trichiliocosm" is also a figurative expression. To deprive one of their name is called an "enemy"; to seize one's wealth is called a "robber.
The retribution of these enemies and robbers exists within the realm of desire; the enemies of evil karma exist throughout the three realms; and the enemies of afflictions pervade all nine realms.

Regarding the interpretation through the contemplation of the mind: the great trichiliocosm filled with enemies and bandits represents the seeds of afflictions accumulated since beginningless time within the eighth storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*).

The caravan leader represents the sixth consciousness. The merchants represent the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), the particular mental factors (*viniyata*), and all other wholesome mental concomitants (*kuśala-caitta*).
The precious treasures represent the Dharma of the Three Vehicles that transcends the world. Passing through the perilous road represents the journey through the realms of existence.
When the various remedial dharmas encounter the various afflictions, one among them— whether it be resolute conviction (*adhimukti*),

wholesome wisdom (*kuśala-prajñā*), or faith (*śraddhā*)— single-mindedly recites the name. When the four teachings and the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation all arise as a single sound,
the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) necessarily corresponds with all wholesome mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), whereby liberation is immediately attained.

This refers to the realization of the principles elucidated by the four teachings. Furthermore, these seven perils represent that within the bodies of sentient beings there are the six great elements:
fire corresponds to the fire element, water to the water element, wind to the wind element, and swords, staves, shackles, and fetters all correspond to the earth element.
The three thousandfold world system represents the space element, while rākṣasas and vengeful thieves represent the consciousness element.
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva contemplates these six great elements as all being the Tathāgatagarbha—each being identical to emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.

Because he himself is liberated, he is able to liberate others. Sentient beings are deluded regarding the nature of these six great elements and thus undergo the retribution of evil karma and afflictions, as well as various hardships;
yet even while they are in a state of delusion, their inherent nature and virtues remain unchanged, fundamentally identical to that of a Buddha.

Because the essence of the *sattva* is identical, although there are distinctions in the four teachings and four benefits obtained—according to whether their hearing of the name, mindfulness, and understanding are partial or complete, and their practice is shallow or deep—in the ultimate attainment of the *sarvākārajñatā*, there is no difference.
This concludes the first section, clarifying the seven calamities. △ Second, the concluding praise.
Such is the majestic and sublime power of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the Inexhaustible One.
"Sublime" means lofty and manifest; his merit transcends the nine realms and thus he is lofty, while his name is proclaimed throughout the three lands and thus he is manifest.

First, the response was clarified through the faculty of speech; this concludes that section. △ Second, clarifying the response through the faculty of mind, in two parts: first, clarifying the three [aspects].
This is the second section on the "poisons," consisting of two parts.
This is the first: If there are sentient beings who abound in lustful desire, by constantly mindfuly revering Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, they shall immediately become free from desire;
if they abound in anger, by constantly mindfuly revering Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, they shall immediately become free from anger; if they abound in...
If the ignorant constantly contemplate and pay homage to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, they shall immediately be freed from delusion.
Greed, anger, and delusion are evil; constant contemplation and homage are good. These two constitute the "stimulus" (the capacity for response), and being freed from them is the "response.
As for the phenomena of greed and anger, they are restricted to the Desire Realm; as for the phenomenon of delusion, it pervades all three realms. This is the principle.

Regarding "poisons": those of the Two Vehicles take their attachment to the Truth as desire, their fear of the mundane as hatred, and their failure to understand that birth-and-death and Nirvana are like illusions as ignorance.

Bodhisattvas who have emerged into the provisional [provisional] realm take their playful exercise of supernatural powers as desire, their reviling and loathing of the Two Vehicles as hatred, and their failure to penetrate the Middle Way as ignorance.
Bodhisattvas prior to the stages take their semblance of attachment to the Middle Way as desire.
Abandoning both extremes constitutes the removal of hatred; failing to break through ignorance constitutes delusion.
This continues even until the final moment of the mind of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), where because subtle ignorance remains unbroke, subtle desire and anger remain unremoved.

Now, by means of great compassion, the Bodhisattva, from the first generation of the mind of enlightenment, contemplates that these afflictions—greed, hatred, and delusion—are all produced through causes and conditions.
Each and every phenomenon is itself emptiness, the provisional, and the middle. Because it is emptiness, one is free from the three poisons of ordinary beings;
because it is the provisional, one is free from the three poisons of the two vehicles; because it is the middle, one is free from the three poisons of bodhisattvas.
Thus, one accomplishes the three kinds of inconceivable roots of goodness, which is also the dharma-gate of accomplishing inconceivable great greed, great anger, and great delusion.

Therefore, for those who constantly maintain mindfulness and reverence, there are various distinctions according to their understanding of the partial and the perfect, and according to their practice of the shallow and the deep;
yet ultimately, they all return to non-differentiation. △ Second, the concluding praise.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, Immeasurable Intent, possesses such great and majestic spiritual powers that he brings benefit to many;
therefore, sentient beings should always keep him in mind.

This concludes the second section: clarifying the response by way of the faculty of mental action (*manas-karman*). △ Third, clarifying the response by way of the faculty of physical action (*kāya-karman*), in two parts: first, the explanation...
Second, the two types of seeking and the praise of the resulting bonds. First:
If there is a woman who wishes to seek a son, by bowing to and making offerings to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, she shall give birth to a son endowed with merit and wisdom;
if she wishes to seek a daughter, she shall give birth to a daughter who is upright, beautiful, and possesses auspicious marks, having planted roots of virtue in previous lives.
Originally, she was beloved and respected by all.
When seeking sons or daughters, she singled out the woman because women suffer from childlessness;
they are abandoned by their husbands, despised by their co-wives, and ridiculed by those around them. Thus, through her prostrations and offerings, this karmic resonance occurred.

The birth of sons and daughters is the Dharma-gate of Universal Response. Regarding its interpretation: within the Four Teachings, those who have not yet realized the ultimate principle are all termed "women.

Each of the Four Teachings distinguishes between "wisdom-men" and "concentration-women. This is because the Great Being (the Buddha) first realized both the provisional and the real aspects of male and female;
thus, he is able to act as a sovereign condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) that enables all practitioners to achieve their respective accomplishments in concentration and wisdom.
Furthermore, those in the desire realm who possess wisdom but lack concentration are like madmen; those in the formless realms who possess concentration but lack wisdom are like foolish women.
Those in the four dhyānas, where wisdom and concentration are balanced, are like virtuous men or beautiful women.

Yet, these men lack the power to shatter delusions, and these women lack the strength to give birth to the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state; thus, they too are useless. This refers to both the "male" and "female" categories within the *zang* (Treasury) and *tong* (Pervasive) teachings.
The wisdom of the two vehicles can sever the delusions of views and thought; this is like a man capable of performing the work of the household.

Samādhi can certainly give rise to the outflow-free state (anāsrava); this is like a woman capable of bearing offspring. However, if wisdom cannot shatter ignorance and perceive the Buddha-nature, it is a man who is not truly a man.
If samādhi cannot conceive the child of the Middle Way, it is a woman who is like a barren woman. Thus, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra says: "Two..."
Bodhisattvas who rely on samādhi while wisdom is deficient do not perceive the Buddha-nature; likewise, those with abundant wisdom but deficient samādhi also do not perceive the Buddha-nature.

Only when the true illumination of wisdom arises at the first stage (*bhūmi*) of the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-yāna*), and non-referential compassion (*apratisthita-maitrī*) is perfected, is one called a "true man" or "true woman.

At the first dwelling (*vihāra*) of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), when the Middle Way is perceived, concentration and wisdom are fully possessed, and thus the characteristics of both male and female are complete.
The name "Virtue" (Puṇya) for the man refers to concentration accompanied by wisdom; the name "Uprightness" (Ārjava) for the woman refers to wisdom accompanied by concentration.
△ Second, the concluding praise:
"O Akṣayamati, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara possesses such power. If there are sentient beings who pay homage and prostrate to him..."
The merit of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva is never in vain.
"In vain" (*tángjuān*) means to discard or waste; this phrase also serves to resolve doubts. There are those who perform prostrations yet do not obtain sons or daughters;
this is solely because their spiritual capacity (*jī*) is shallow, such that what they seek is not yet fulfilled. Nevertheless, the merit of their prostrations is ultimately never lost.
The two specific answers are concluded. △ Third, the answer by way of exhorting others to uphold the name has three parts: first, the exhortation to uphold; second, the comparative evaluation;
third, the concluding praise. Now, for the first:
"For this reason, all sentient beings should receive and uphold the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva."

The preceding section explained the causes and conditions for Avalokiteśvara’s acquisition of his name; since his power is so vast that it cannot be fully discerned through physical form or substance, this text merely recounts the names and discusses the virtues.
Because those who wish to take refuge and revere him should accept and uphold his name, the text concludes with an exhortation to uphold the name.

This is because the great and magnificent title of his myriad virtues truly accords with reality; this single name and single character inherently possess all qualities by the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
The three thousand nature-and-characteristics and the wondrous principle of the three truths are naturally and perfectly encompassed;

sudden and gradual, partial and perfect, provisional and real—these wondrous wisdoms are naturally such that the fundamental reality and wisdom are inherently non-dual. While non-dual, they are dual, and thus reality and wisdom remain distinct.
To raise up a single provisional name, all provisional names, all real dharmas, and all lands are thereby subsumed.
Since these are merely provisional names for that [reality], the merit of hearing the name is already inconceivable; the merit of upholding it is even more inconceivable.
If this is so for upholding the name, it is likewise for visualizing his primary reward (the Buddha) and his secondary rewards (the pure land).
Therefore, one should know that the *Amitābha Sūtra*, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, and this wondrous sūtra are one and the same.
This profound and rare Dharma-gate of the Perfect and Sudden is without superior or inferior. △ Second, the comparative evaluation:

"Ajita, suppose there were a person who received and upheld the names of sixty-two billion Ganges-sands of Bodhisattvas, and furthermore, throughout their entire life, provided them with food and drink, clothing, bedding, and medicine. What do you think? Would this good man..."
“Good son, daughter of good family, are the merits of this person many? Ajita said, “Very many, World-Honored One.

The Buddha said, “If there were another person who, for even a single moment, upholds the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and pays him homage and makes offerings, the merit of these two persons would be exactly equal and no different;
it could not be exhausted even in hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas.”

The text contains four meanings: first, the basis for evaluation; second, the question; third, the answer; and fourth, the actual evaluation. Within the section on the basis for evaluation, four "many" factors are presented:
first, the many fields of merit, numbering sixty-two billion times the sands of the Ganges; second, the many instances of upholding, which refers to the many instances of maintaining the name;
third, the many durations of time, which refers to throughout one's entire life; and fourth, the many seeds, which refers to the offerings of the four requisites such as food and drink.
These four "many" [factors] are generally taken as the basis for comparison. The question and answer can be understood from this.
Within the actual process of comparison, one again cites the four "few" [factors] to compare with the four "many. Specifically, regarding Avalokiteśvara, the field of merit is small;

the holding of the name is also small; even "for a time" indicates that the duration is small; and regarding prostration and making offerings, if one does not mention the four items, then the seeds are small.

That the merits of the few and the many are perfectly equal and without distinction arises precisely because true suchness (*tathatā*) and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) are, by their very nature, devoid of oneness or multiplicity and are fundamentally equal.
Because Avalokiteśvara has realized this limit of reality, his oneness is not one; he is perfectly equal to the many.
Because sixty-two billion have realized this limit of reality, their multiplicity is not many; they are perfectly equal to the one. Thus, one is one.

Because the middle [level] of liberation is immeasurable, it is said that there are six billion two hundred million [beings] liberated in the middle; because the middle [level] of liberation is one, it is said that Avalokiteśvara hears [them].
The *Ear-Examination Sūtra* (*Ērzhànchá jīng*) states: "Those who are able to hear my name shall likewise hear the names of the Buddhas of the ten directions.
This is also the same meaning. △ Third, the concluding praise.
When Akṣayamati upholds the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, he obtains such immeasurable and boundless benefits of merit.
This first round of question and answer clarifies that the three karmas of sentient beings manifest as the objective field, while the numinous wisdom of the Dharmakāya responds in profound stillness.
The section on the names of the objects and wisdom as causes and conditions for Avalokiteśvara is concluded. △ Next, this section also has two parts: first, the question; second, the answer.
Now, the first part:
Bodhisattva Akṣayamati addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, how does the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara traverse this Sahā world?"
Regarding the world of Saha, how does he employ the power of skillful means to preach the Dharma for sentient beings? What are the details of these matters? There are three points of inquiry:
first, "how does he travel," which asks about his physical activity (kāyakarma); second, "how does he speak," which asks about his verbal activity (vākkarma);
and third, "what are his skillful means," which asks about his mental activity (manaskarma). This is precisely the inconceivable transformation of the three wheels.
These are called the three ways in which [the Buddha] needs no protection and the three absences of error. Regarding inconceivable transformation:
he may manifest the body of a Buddha, and likewise manifest the speech and mind of a Buddha; he may even manifest as a Vajrapāṇi deity, and likewise manifest the vajra-mind and vajra-speech.
Although these manifestations employ skillful means to benefit sentient beings, they do not diminish the wisdom of the Dharmakāya.
The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states: "One who is skillfully able to discern the characteristics of all phenomena remains unmoved within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

To be unmoved yet to act is called inconceivable transformation. Question: How can the mental karma (*manas-karma*) be transformed? Answer: The noble mind (*ārya-citta*) is beyond the capacity of measurement;

yet, if one wishes to demonstrate it, even insects can be made to understand it. Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* says: [...]* *Note: The ellipsis indicates the continuation of the passage from the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* as required by the context.*
The spiritual power of the Unsurpassed Enlightened One is inconceivable; he transforms immeasurable beings, causing them all to possess a mind.
As for non-protection, he dwells in the inconceivable Dharma-gate of universal perfection; truly, he does not engage in mental application, calculation, deliberation, or sequential management.
It is like a bright mirror that reflects whatever is set before it immediately, without discrimination and without sequence.
Regarding "no failure": the faculties and capacities of sentient beings differ, and there are variations in depth;

although Avalokiteśvara does not form a deliberate thought to adapt to these capacities, his adaptation never fails, as he mysteriously accords with each individual, harmonizing both phenomena and principle.
△ Second, the answer, which has three parts: first, the specific answer; second, the general answer; third, the exhortation to make offerings. Now, the first part.

The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati: "Good son, if there are sentient beings in any land who should be delivered by means of a Buddha-body, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva immediately manifests a Buddha-body and preaches the Dharma for them.

If they should be delivered by means of a Pratyekabuddha-body, he immediately manifests a Pratyekabuddha-body and preaches the Dharma for them. If they should be delivered by means of a Śrāvaka-body..."
To those who are to be saved by appearing in the form of a śrāvaka, he manifests in the body of a śrāvaka and preaches the Dharma to them.
To those who are to be saved by appearing in the body of a Brahmā king, he manifests in the body of a Brahmā king and preaches the Dharma to them.

To those who are to be saved by appearing in the body of Śakra, he manifests in the body of Śakra and preaches the Dharma to them. To those who are to be saved by appearing in the body of Maheśvara, he manifests in the body of Maheśvara.
When manifesting in a body to preach the Dharma, he manifests in the body of Maheśvara for those who are to be delivered by the body of Maheśvara and preaches the Dharma;
he manifests in the body of a Heavenly General for those who are to be delivered by the body of a Heavenly General and preaches the Dharma;
he manifests in the body of Vaiśravaṇa for those who are to be delivered by the body of Vaiśravaṇa.

Entering through the gates of their bodies, he preaches the Dharma to them. To those who should be liberated by appearing in the body of a minor king, he manifests as a minor king and preaches the Dharma to them.
To those who should be liberated by appearing in the body of an elder, he manifests as an elder and preaches the Dharma to them.

To those who should be liberated by appearing in the body of a householder, he manifests as a householder and preaches the Dharma to them. To those who should be liberated by appearing in the body of a minister...
To those who are to be saved by means of the body of a government official, he manifests as a government official and preaches the Dharma for them.
To those who are to be saved by means of the body of a Brahmin, he manifests as a Brahmin and preaches the Dharma for them.
To those who are to be saved by means of the bodies of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās, he manifests as a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, upāsaka, or [upāsikā].
If she should appear in the form of a laywoman (*upāsikā*) to teach the Dharma, she manifests as a laywoman to teach the Dharma to those who are to be saved by such a form.
If they are to be saved by the forms of elders, householders, officials, or Brahmin women, she manifests as a woman to teach them the Dharma.
If they are to be saved by the forms of boys or girls, she manifests as a boy or a girl to teach them the Dharma. If they are to be saved by the forms of devas, nāgas, or yakṣas...
To those who are to be delivered through the bodies of yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and so forth,
he manifests all these forms and preaches the Dharma to them. To those who are to be delivered by means of the Vajrapāṇi deity,
he manifests as the Vajrapāṇi deity and preaches the Dharma to them.
One should respond with words to the expedient means of mental karma (*manas-karman*) to know the appropriate capacity; respond by manifesting the body to the physical karma (*kāya-karman*);
and respond by preaching the Dharma to the verbal karma (*vāk-karman*). These three karmas are fundamentally inseparable. Herein, the thirty-three bodies are specifically clarified;
if humans and non-humans are included, they constitute thirty-five bodies. The *Mahābuddhatoṣaṇī-sūtra* clarifies thirty.
Second, one should separately distinguish the Pratyekabuddhas to make four [categories], while grouping the four types of women into one;

though the text omits mention of the Garuḍas, this is due to the principle of inclusion and exclusion rather than any increase or decrease in number. In summary, these are simply the bodies of the ten dharma-realms.
As for the failure to mention the Bodhisattva body, it is because the Bodhisattva dharma-realm is being explained in detail, while the manifestation of the others is merely indicated in brief.
The images of the nine dharma-realms are used to manifest the meaning of the ten realms being mutually inclusive in a重重 (repeatedly layered) and inexhaustible manner.

The reason the hell realm is not mentioned separately is that it is subsumed within the category of non-human beings. As for "sentient beings in various lands," this refers to the capacities of the ten dharma-realms across the three types of lands:
the Land of True Reward, the Land of Expedient Means, and the Land of Shared Residence. Within the Land of True Reward, [the teachings] are purely...

The Bodhisattva, for the sake of sentient beings, possesses only the capacity for the Buddha-realm (*buddhadhātu*). Within the land of skillful means (*upāyabhūmi*), there are nine kinds of sentient beings:

namely, those of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*) who have attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) according to the Tripitaka Teaching; those of the Three Vehicles who have severed the delusions common to all according to the Shared Teaching;

and those of the Separate [Teaching] at the thirty minds and those of the Perfect Teaching at the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*). There are two kinds of capacities: first, the capacity for the Buddha-realm; second, the capacity for the Bodhisattva-realm.

The *sattva*-dhātu is the capacity [of the audience]. Within the *sāmbhogika-kṣetra* (land of communal enjoyment), there are fully present sentient beings of the nine realms and the capacities of the ten realms;

in response to these capacities, the appropriate response is established, which must necessarily include the Buddha-bodies of the ten realms. Furthermore, there are distinctions between the four teachings:

the *pratyekabuddha* has both those who rely on conditions (*saṃyoga-pratyeka*) and those who are solitary (*viveka-pratyeka*), differing from the *śrāvaka*. Moreover, there are the four stages and four fruits of the analytical dharma (*vikalpa-dharma*) and the dharma of the essence (*svabhāva-dharma*), as well as the manifestations that accord with [the needs of others].

Since the five flavors are manifested through successive transformations and subduing in different ways, it stands to reason that after manifesting as the Brahma King, he should also manifest as the two kings of Ābhāsvara and Śubhakṛtsna.
After manifesting as Śakra, it stands to reason that he should also manifest as the three kings of Yāma, Tuṣita, and Nirmāṇarati.
Maheśvara is the lord of the desire realm, while Mahāmaheśvara is the lord of the fourth dhyāna. Furthermore, regarding what is called Vaiśravaṇa...
Since he must manifest as the other three heavens, the *Buddhoṣṇīṣa* simply refers to them as the Four Heavenly Kings (*catur-mahārāja*).

Since they are called "lesser kings," they must also manifest as the four kinds of Wheel-Turning Kings (*cakravartin*). Furthermore, regarding the mention of "humans and non-humans" (*manuṣya-amanuṣya*):

if one speaks of "humans," what is not included among the young and old, the noble and the lowly? If one speaks of "non-humans," what is not included among those in the hells, ghosts, and animals? Therefore, below...
The text states: "He wanders through various lands in manifold forms; this can only be known through the mind, for how could it ever be fully described?

As a teacher of the Dharma, he accords with their capacities—whether by means of expedient or real teachings, sudden or gradual methods, or manifest or secret modes—thereby enabling them to attain the four benefits of both the provisional and the real, ultimately leading them all back to the single benefit of the ultimate reality. △ Second, the general response.
Akṣayamati, it is because the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara has accomplished such merit that he travels through various lands in manifold forms to deliver sentient beings.
The previous detailed response concerning the thirty-five bodies was extensive in its wording but narrow in its scope; this present response summarizes these merits.

The text is concise while its meaning is vast; it is evident that by means of various forms, he does not limit himself to thirty-five bodies, and in traveling through all lands, he is not confined to the Sahā world.
△ Third, the exhortation to make offerings, in two parts: first, the exhortation;
second, receiving the instruction. Now, the first.
Therefore, you all should with one mind make offerings to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is able to bestow fearlessness amidst terrors and urgent perils;
for this reason, throughout this Sahā world, he is universally called the "Bestower of Fearlessness."
Since he is named Avalokiteśvara and also named Abhayamdada (Bestower of Fearlessness), he receives his names from his virtues; as the virtues are inexhaustible, the names are likewise inexhaustible.
△ Second, receiving the command, in six parts: first, accepting the mission; second, not accepting it; third, re-accepting it; fourth, the Buddha’s exhortation;
fifth, having accepted, turning it over to others; sixth, the concluding praise. Now, the first part.
The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I shall now make an offering to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
He then untied from his neck a necklace of various precious jewels worth hundreds of thousands of taels of gold and presented it to him, saying:
"Virtuous One, please accept this precious jewel necklace as a gift of Dharma."
"Various precious jewel necklaces" refers to ornaments composed of various jewels interspersed with beads.

As for the "necklace of Akṣayamati’s high station," how could it merely be worth hundreds of thousands of taels? It is like saying that the common people and the myriad subjects do not merely number one hundred ten thousand.
Furthermore, the neck represents the principle of the single reality within the Middle Way, through which numerous and inexhaustible Dharma-gates [are manifested].

Adorning the true reality (*dharmatā*) is like wearing a necklace; "untying" it signifies that because the Bodhisattva practices constant relinquishment, they do not dwell upon, cling to, rely on, or depend upon any merit from vows and practices, nor even upon the Buddha-wisdom, bodhi, or nirvāṇa—hence it is called "untying.
The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states that precept, concentration, wisdom, and dhāraṇī serve as...
The adornment of the Dharma-body with necklaces numbering one hundred thousand signifies that each of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) possesses ten thousand virtues.

As for "Dharma-giving" (*dharmadāna*), "wealth" here refers to the wealth of the Dharma; it is the teaching that all phenomena born of causes and conditions are simultaneously empty, provisional, and the Middle—thus the three truths are fully present within a single mind.
Being equal toward the Dharma, one is likewise equal toward material wealth; such is the nature of this giving.
This is precisely the gift of Dharma. △ Second, not accepting it:
At that time, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva was unwilling to accept it.

In terms of the facts, although Akṣayamati had offered it as an act of worship by imperial command, Avalokiteśvara had not yet received such a command; therefore, he was unwilling to accept the offering.
One should practice humility; because the vast function of the samādhi that briefly manifests the Dharma-principles is such that nothing is received, there is no grasping.
△ Third, the offering of respect:
Ajita further addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying, "Virtuous One, out of compassion for us, please accept this necklace."
[Adornment.
Or he may request that those above take pity on those below; or, even if their status is equal, they may likewise take pity on one another.

Or, thinking "I shall bestow benevolence and compassion upon the fourfold assembly," he accepts [offerings] out of compassion for the fourfold assembly, yet he accepts all these receptions with a state of non-reception. △ Four.
The Buddha exhorted him.

At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara: "You should take pity upon this Bodhisattva Akṣayamati, as well as the fourfold assembly, the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas."
Because they are human or non-human beings, they accept these necklaces;
since the Bodhisattva gives them for the sake of sentient beings, they should likewise accept them for the sake of sentient beings. △ Fifth, having accepted them, they are offered in turn.
Thereupon, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, out of compassion for the fourfold assembly and for the devas,
nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans,
took the necklace and divided it into two parts; he offered one part to Śākyamuni Buddha and the other part to the stupa of Prabhūtaratna Buddha.

Taking this single *dharmadāna* necklace and dividing it into two parts symbolizes that the one true reality (*ekasatyalakṣaṇa*) manifests throughout its entirety as both principle and phenomena—the two causes.
Offering these to the two Buddhas symbolizes approaching the two fruits by means of the two causes.

The perfection of principle corresponds to the Dharma-Buddha (*dharmabuddha*), and the perfection of phenomena corresponds to the Reward-Buddha (*saṃbhogabuddha*); thus, the two Buddhas again represent the two fruits. △ Sixth, the concluding praise.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, whose intention is inexhaustible, possesses such sovereign spiritual powers that he wanders throughout the Sahā world.
This concludes the initial long prose section. II. Verse Recitation: Because Master Kumārajīva did not translate it, the older editions all lack these verses.

The *Yishu* (Commentary on the Meaning) likewise does not explain [this section]. The *Xu gaoseng zhuan* (Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks) states that these verses were translated by Jñānagupta;
since they have now been added throughout the current circulating editions, I have provided an exegesis based on the topical divisions established by Master Ciyun.
The major sections are three: first, the paired verses on the two questions; second, the paired verses on the two answers.
The third section consists of two pairs of verses offering exhortations. Herein is the first.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati addressed the Buddha in verse, asking:
"World-Honored One, you are endowed with wondrous marks; I now ask again: for what causes and conditions is this Son of the Buddha named Avalokiteśvara?"
The first line praises the Buddha’s virtues; the second line contains both questions; and the final two lines separately versify the first question.
△ Second, the double versification of the two answers: first, a supplementary verse summarizing the praise of practice and vows; second, the separate versification of the two answers.
First: The Honored One with Perfectly Endowed Sublime Marks replied in verse to Akṣayamati: "Listen to the practice of Avalokiteśvara; he responds skillfully to all places.
His great vows are as deep as the ocean, spanning inconceivable kalpas. He has attended upon many thousands of billions of Buddhas and made vast, pure aspirations."
The first two lines are the words of the Sūtra’s narrator; the following six lines are the Buddha’s direct response. “Listen well” is an exhortation to generate the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*).
The practitioner of Avalokiteśvara contemplates the sounds of the ten realms with the threefold wisdom of a single mind, causing immeasurable sufferings to be liberated all at once;
this is already the accomplishment of the practice of benefiting others. “Skillfully responding to all places” means that...
"Moving the true mind to manifest forms in the three lands through thirty-two transformations, appearing everywhere—this is the power of the universal gate’s spiritual penetrations.
These two phrases collectively praise the two bodies—the true and the responsive—that have been realized.

"The profound vow is as deep as the ocean" clarifies that at the time of first generating the bodhicitta, one takes the unconditioned Four Noble Truths as the object; thus, it horizontally encompasses the ten realms.

"Vertically penetrating the three truths" means that [the Dharma-body] is both vast and profound. "Throughout kalpas," etc., clarifies that during this interval, he fulfilled his vows through practice;
because the time elapsed was long, the Buddhas he served were many, and the vows he made were great, he has now attained the two bodies of Truth and Response (dharmakāya and nirmāṇakāya).
This is like a boat rising when the water swells, or a Buddha appearing great when the mud is thick. △ Second, the separate verses on the two answers.

The second part [of the previous section] consists of two verses: the first verse answers the preceding question, and the second verse answers the subsequent question. Within the first of these, there are two parts: the first verse provides a general answer, and the second verse provides a detailed answer. Now, for the first:
"I shall briefly explain for you that hearing my name and seeing my body and mind are not in vain; they are capable of extinguishing all suffering within the realms of existence."

"A brief explanation" means to state the essentials. Hearing the name refers to the vocal karma of the responsive capacity; seeing the body refers to the bodily karma of the responsive capacity; mental recollection refers to the mental karma of the responsive capacity.
