The first verse concerns the first peril of fire, continuing through the twelfth verse which adds the perils of thunder and rain. Herein is the first:
"Even if one should harbor a malicious intent and push another into a great pit of fire, by the power of mindfulness of Avalokiteśvara, the fiery pit shall be transformed into a pool."

Regarding "one who contemplates that Avalokiteśvara": if this is spoken from the perspective of the Buddha, saying "Avalokiteśvara is for him," then "self" and "other" are provisionally distinguished based on the relationship between teacher and disciple.

If it is from the perspective of sentient beings "contemplating that Avalokiteśvara," then "self" and "other" are momentarily distinguished based on the principle of resonance and response (*ganying*).

Yet, both teacher and disciple, and resonance and response, are nothing other than the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); while the subject and object appear distinct, they are ultimately transcended. Sentient beings contemplate their own [nature].
The Avalokiteśvara within one's own mind and the sentient being within one's own mind respond to one another through the inconceivable power of resonance.
△ Second, a verse on the second peril of water.
Or if drifting upon the vast ocean, amidst the perils of dragons, fish, and various ghosts, by contemplating the power of Avalokiteśvara, one cannot be submerged by the waves.
△ Third, an added verse on the peril of falling from Mount Sumeru.
Or if one were on the peak of Mount Sumeru and was pushed over by someone, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, one would abide in the sky like the sun.
In terms of the phenomenal aspect (*vastu*), this is a figurative expression; even if one were to fall from Mount Sumeru, one would not be harmed, let alone from other mountains.

In terms of contemplative understanding (*vipaśyanā*), it means that one is fundamentally within the Middle Way, the true reality (*dharmatā*), the nature-virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*) of the King of Mountains, Sumeru.

When ignorant and wicked people push one into the sea of the two deaths, by recollecting Avalokiteśvara, the three wisdoms and three virtues immediately become identical to those of all Buddhas, abiding in non-abiding.
△ Fourth, adding a verse: "Falling into the perilous mountain of diamond is as difficult to escape as Mount Sumeru."
Or if pursued by wicked men and cast down from Mount Vajra, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, not even a single hair can be harmed.
△ Fifth, this verse anticipates the seventh peril: the danger of hostile bandits.

Or if one encounters hostile bandits surrounding them, each wielding a blade to inflict harm, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, they will all immediately give rise to a compassionate heart.
(△ Six: A summary verse on the fourth peril, that of blades and staves.)
Or if one encounters the suffering of royal punishment and faces execution at the point of death, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, the blade shall instantly break into pieces.
(7) This is a retrospective verse on the sixth [peril], that of shackles and fetters.
Or if one is imprisoned and shackled, with hands and feet bound by cangues and fetters, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, one shall be released and attain liberation.
△ Eighth: An added verse on the perils of curses and poisonous drugs.
Regarding curses, various poisons, and those who wish to harm one’s body, through the power of recollecting Avalokiteśvara, they shall return to the person who originated them.

If a sorcerer dispatches ghosts and spirits to kill another, yet that person is protected by various merits and virtues such that they cannot be killed, the law dictates that [the curse] must return to the person themselves;
this is explained in great detail in the Secret Section (Guhyatantra), and it should be understood that it returns.

I, too, possess the benefits of the four *siddhāntas*. Su Shi’s revision, stating that "both families will have no trouble," reflects a narrow and shallow understanding, as it fails to recognize the subtle art of *saṃgraha* (gathering) and *vinaya* (subduing). △ Ninth: A retrospective verse on the fifth difficulty, that of ghosts.
Or if one encounters evil rākṣasas, venomous dragons, various ghosts, and the like, when they call upon the power of Avalokiteśvara, none dare to harm them.
△ Tenth, the verse on the peril of ferocious beasts:
If one is surrounded by ferocious beasts with fearsome sharp teeth and claws, by calling upon the power of Avalokiteśvara, they will flee swiftly to boundless directions.
△11. Added Verse on the Perils of Snakes and Scorpions:

Vipers, serpents, vipers, and scorpions—whose poisonous vapors blaze like smoke and fire—upon recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, shall turn back of their own accord at the mere sound of his name.
△ Twelfth, the verse on the calamity of thunder and rain:
When clouds and thunder roll, lightning flashes, and hail falls with torrential rain, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, they shall be dispersed and vanish at that very moment.

The seven difficulties in the main verses and the five added verses together total twelve; each must be fully explained in relation to retribution, evil karma, afflictions, the six destinies, and the four teachings.
If one summarizes what they represent, they do not go beyond the six great elements: Mount Sumeru and the vajra are the earth element;
thunder and lightning are the fire element; hail and rain are the water element; and beasts, snakes, and incantations are the wind element.
The incantations all identify that the Great Bodhisattva, while in the stage of causes, contemplated these six great elements as being emptiness, the provisional, and the middle;
now, abiding at the juncture of the six kinds of reality-as-it-is (*yathābhūta*), he universally rescues all from suffering and affliction throughout the Dharma-realm. To state the essential point:
all things, both the environment and its inhabitants, are the wondrous form and wondrous mind of Avalokiteśvara; all sentient beings are, in turn, within the sage’s wondrous form and mind.
Yet one creates difficulties for oneself, like touching a treasure in the dark and injuring one's own body; seeking salvation through the three karmas is none other than Avalokiteśvara.
Therefore, when the conditions are met, the response is immediate. One should contemplate this principle in every thought-moment;

what concern is there that it would not be identical to Avalokiteśvara’s benefiting of sentient beings? The first verse, concluding the section on the seven calamities, is finished. II. The second part: Verses on the three poisons and the two requests.
Sentient beings are beset by calamities and oppressed by immeasurable suffering; through the wondrous power of wisdom, Avalokiteśvara can rescue the world from its pain.
Within and beyond the realms, there are the sufferings of the three poisons, as well as the sufferings of being neither male nor female;

thus, they are immeasurable. This concludes the first verse, which answers the preceding question. △ Second, the verse answering the subsequent question has two parts: first, the actual verse showing the manifestation.

Second, the added verses clarify the capacity [of the audience] and the response [of the Buddha]. First, the main verses demonstrate the manifestations; there are both specific and general aspects. Specifically, they clarify the thirty-two responses;

generally, they clarify the multiplicity of bodies and the multiplicity of objects. Now, without distinguishing between the specific and the general, we shall explain the inconceivable transformation of the three wheels collectively, which is divided into three parts:
first, clarifying how the body universally responds through physical action (*kāyakarman*); second, clarifying the mental [action]...
The universal contemplation of karma and the universal exposition of verbal karma through the three types of supernormal knowledge (trividyā). First:

Endowed with the power of supernatural faculties (ṛddhibala) and having extensively cultivated the skillful means of wisdom, there is no land among the worlds of the ten directions where he does not manifest his body.
Through various evil destinies—namely, birth as hell-beings, hungry ghosts, or animals, and the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death—he causes them all to be gradually extinguished.
"Being fully endowed with the power of spiritual penetrations (*abhijñā*)" refers to the wondrous functioning of the entire body of the hundred realms and thousand suchnesses.
"Extensively cultivating wisdom and skillful means" refers to the two wisdoms of provisional and ultimate reality illuminating the nature to give rise to penetration.

In the preceding passage, the three evil destinies were implicitly contained within the two characters "non-human" (*amanuṣya*); now that they are explicitly set forth, we know that he possesses bodies of the ten dharma-realms. (Section)

The various forms of suffering associated with the transformation of the aggregates each possess four characteristics; by gradually causing them all to be extinguished, one returns to the eternal, quiescent light.

Whether employing provisional or ultimate teachings, he guides others step by step with skillful means, applying remedies according to what is appropriate. It is clear that he does not cling to fixed methods.
△ Second, explaining the mental karma of universal contemplation.
Directly perceiving purity, contemplating vast wisdom, and contemplating compassion and loving-kindness, one should always aspire and gaze upon the stainless,
pure light— the sun of wisdom that shatters all darkness, subdues the winds and fires of calamity, and universally illuminates the world.
The first verse clarifies the essence of what is realized; the second verse clarifies the function that arises therefrom.
"True Contemplation" refers to realizing inconceivable emptiness (*śūnyatā*). "Pure Contemplation" refers to realizing inconceivable provisionality (*prajñapti*).
"Vast Wisdom Contemplation" refers to realizing inconceivable centrality (*madhyama*). "Compassionate Contemplation" [refers to] employing these three inconceivable contemplations for all...

Sentient beings share the same compassionate longing; those who practice the contemplation of compassion possess the inconceivable threefold contemplation and share the same power of compassion as the Buddha-Tathāgata.
Because they share this power of compassion, it is said that they "constantly vow to share the same compassionate longing";

because they constantly gaze upward [in reverence], and because they have deeply realized this single mind and threefold contemplation, they emit stainless, pure light, which is called [the Light of Wisdom].

The Sun of Wisdom can shatter the darkness of the Truth of Accumulation—the three delusions within the ten realms—and subdue the suffering of the Truth of Suffering—the calamities of the winds and fires of the two deaths within the ten realms;
it can bestow the Path and Cessation upon the ten realms, universally illuminating the world.
△ Third, the universal preaching of the karma of speech.

The thunderous roar of the precepts as the essence of compassion, and the wondrous great cloud of a benevolent mind, pour down the nectar-like rain of the Dharma to extinguish the flames of affliction.
To preach the Great Dharma, one must necessarily rely upon body and mind as the foundation for bestowing the teaching;

because he manifests his physical form to preach the Dharma in order to deliver sentient beings, the manifested body is called the "Essence of Great Compassion," while the "benevolent mind" mentioned below serves as its counterpart.

This is merely a concise illustration of the single character’s imagery. First, one uses the virtue of the precepts to awaken people, just as when the thunder of heaven shakes, there is nothing that is not solemnized;
therefore, it is said: "The compassionate essence is the thundering of the precepts. To extract suffering and bestow happiness is called Great Compassion;
because the mind acts without conditions, it is termed "wondrous," and because there is nothing it does not cover, it is like a great cloud; therefore, it is called "Loving-kindness."
The mind is like a wondrous great cloud; the nectar of the devas, when consumed, prevents death. The Dharma rain it pours down is likewise:
those who hear it awaken to the Way and realize the life of eternal abiding. The three delusions, afflictions, and the flames of suffering are extinguished and eradicated simultaneously;
all ten realms attain deliverance. The initial section on the "Manifestation of the Verses" concludes. △ Second, the "Supplementary Verses."
Manifesting the capacity and manifesting the response:
when caught in legal disputes before government officials or amidst the terrors of battle, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, all enemies shall retreat and disperse.

Regarding the thirty-two manifestations in the long prose section, although these responses pertain to manifest capacities, they may be either hidden or manifest and cannot be fixed as one way or another.

Judging from the current verse, which states, "If one calls upon that Avalokiteśvara," it is clearly manifesting the capacity of the practitioner (*karman*). Regarding "fear of litigation and disputes," there are three interpretations:
[1] it refers to the retribution of past karma; [2] it refers to afflictions (*kleśa*); or [3] this may also be an added verse where the seven calamities were mistakenly transposed.
However, if it simply says "the multitude of enemies retreat and disperse," this may still refer to a response in the unseen realm (*adṛṣṭa*). Second, the two paired verses.
The two responses are concluded. △ Third, the double verse on the two exhortations. Part one: the first verse on the previous exhortation to hold the name;

part two: the verse on the subsequent exhortation to make offerings. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, clarifying the profundity and subtlety of the object and wisdom to exhort constant mindfulness;
second, clarifying the unfathomability of response and resonance to exhort against doubt. Now, the first section.
The wondrous voice, the Avalokiteśvara voice, the Brahma voice, the ocean-tide voice—these surpass all worldly sounds; therefore, one should always keep them in mind.
This clarifies that the Bodhisattva possesses manifold virtues and bears manifold names;
because each and every name expounds the inconceivable virtue of the perfectly interfused Dharmadhātu, one must keep them in mind. That which is provisional yet real is called the "Wondrous Voice."

Because the provisional is identical to the real, it is called the "Avalokiteśvara" (Contemplator of the World’s Sounds); because it accords with the fundamentally pure nature, it is called the "Brahma-sound";

and because it accords with the capacities of the ten realms, it is called the "Ocean-tide Sound. Since the provisional and the real are non-dual, and self and other are non-dual, it surpasses the sounds of the ten dharma-realms of the mundane world.
Because the provisional is itself the real, and the other is itself the self, it surpasses the nine [realms] expounded by the Separate Teaching.

Because delusion regarding the realms arises from the awakening to principle, and because the real is itself the provisional, and the self is itself the other, this [teaching] surpasses the Buddha-realm expounded in the Separate Teaching, which relies on principle to sever the nine grades of afflictions. Therefore, the single name "Avalokiteśvara" is equal in merit to sixty-two billion names.
△ Second, clarifying that response and resonance are unfathomable to encourage one not to harbor doubts.
Do not give rise to doubt in every thought-moment; Avalokiteśvara, the Pure and Holy One, can act as a refuge in the face of suffering and the perils of death.
When doubt is removed, mindfulness is perfected; when mindfulness is perfected, one may be liberated from the two deaths. Therefore, he exhorts you not to doubt.
The first verse concludes the previous section on the exhortation to hold his name. II. The second verse is the exhortation to make offerings.
Possessing all merits, he gazes upon sentient beings with eyes of compassion; his ocean-like mass of blessings is immeasurable, and for this reason, he should be venerated.

Veneration is the offering of the three karmas. The first section, consisting of the question and answer, is concluded. II. The Merit of Hearing This Chapter. This has two parts: first, the Earth Deity’s praise and testimony;
second, the narrative of the benefits by the Sūtra compiler. Now, the first part.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sustaining the Earth rose from his seat, approached the Buddha, and addressed him, saying: "World-Honored One,
if there are sentient beings who hear this chapter on the Sovereign Acts of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and the Universal Gate Manifestation of Supernatural Powers,
you should know that the merit of such persons is not small."
Mastery of action refers to attaining great sovereignty over the seven calamities, the three poisons, and the two types of seeking.

Manifestation through the Universal Gate refers to manifesting bodies corresponding to the ten dharma realms and preaching the Dharma through skillful means. The merit of those who merely hear it is already not small;
how much more so for those who receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, copy, and practice according to the teaching! Thus it is said.
The title is explained neither generically nor specifically, yet it is established so that those who hear it may obtain great merit;
thus, the Bodhisattva Susthiti (Earth-Holding) must praise and certify it. The *Mahābuddhoṣṇīṣa Sūtra* states:

"Vipaśyin Buddha placed his hand upon my head and said, 'If you level the ground of your mind, then the ground of the world will all become level. Thereupon, my mind was opened, and I saw the subtle dust of my own body and—"

Having realized the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) as being no different from all the atoms constituting the world-systems, and having heard the Tathāgatas proclaim the ground of the Buddhas' wondrous Lotus-like knowledge and vision, I first acted as their witness and leader.

Since I have realized that the Great Ground is fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, I have realized that the seven elements (*sapta-dhātu*) are all the Tathāgata-garbha; since I have realized that the seven elements are all [the Tathāgata-garbha]...

The Tathāgatagarbha is precisely the realization that the five aggregates (skandhas), the six sense bases (āyatanas), the twelve bases (āyatanas), and the eighteen elements (dhātus) are all the Tathāgatagarbha.

Having realized that the aggregates, bases, and elements are all the Tathāgatagarbha, one then realizes that the seven calamities, the three poisons, and even the bodies of the ten dharma-realms are all the Tathāgatagarbha;
therefore, one is able to realize the merit of this "Chapter on Hearing. △ Second, the Sūtra text.
The family account is further elaborated.
When the Buddha spoke this "Universal Gate" chapter, eighty-four thousand sentient beings among the assembly all gave rise to the mind of peerless,
unsurpassed, right, and full enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
The "Peerless One" (asama-sama) refers to unsurpassed Bodhi; having attained this principle, one becomes equal to all dharmas and thus achieves the Unsurpassed.

It is like a world-transcending elixir that has no peer: while it transforms other substances into elixirs themselves, this refers to the Perfect [Teaching] of Manifestation, which horizontally encompasses all things and brings them back to the Single Reality. Furthermore, if one investigates...

At the moment of first generating the bodhicitta, one is already equal to the Buddha-fruit, which has no peer; this is like a universal monarch (cakravartin), who is equal to his father at the very moment of birth.
This is discussed in terms of the vertical sequence of cause and effect regarding the essence of the true reality (*dharmatā*), wherein the beginning and end are perfectly distinct.
Furthermore, mind is itself principle, and principle is itself mind; there is no principle apart from mind.
Outside of principle there is no mind; mind and principle exist only as names. Since the nature of names is empty, both are ineffable.
What thing could be equal to what other thing, such that one speaks of "the unequally equal"? Though ineffable, it is spoken of; this mind is equated with this principle.
Therefore, it is called "unequally equal. This refers to the simultaneous negation and illumination of both, not to a horizontal [superficial] relation.

It is not vertical but horizontal, yet it is vertical; there are three ways of generating the aspiration for enlightenment: first, generating the aspiration through contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*);

second, generating the aspiration through semblance realization; and third, generating the aspiration through partial realization. Here, it must be the latter, partial realization. Regarding the exhortation to circulate [the teaching] for the sake of others, this concludes the two sections on encouraging the disciples who receive the Dharma.
△ The explanation of the "Universal Gate" (Pumen-pin) is completed; next, the "Dhāraṇī" (Tuoluoni-pin) is explained.
Chapter Twenty-six: Dhāraṇī. *Dhāraṇī* is translated here as "Total Retention" (Zongchi):
it retains evil so that it does not arise, and it retains good so that it is not lost. (In the world) it is also translated as "Obstruction" (Zhe).
Holding that which can hold the good (for people), one can obstruct evil (as an antidote); obstructing extreme evil, one holds the goodness of the middle (the ultimate truth).
The methods used in various sutras differ: some specialize in treating illnesses, such as the treatment of hemorrhoids; some specialize in protecting the Dharma, as in this text;

some specialize in extinguishing transgressions, such as the Vaipulya sutras; and some are universally applicable for treating illness, extinguishing transgressions, and protecting the scriptures, such as the *Qing Guanshiyin* (Invoking Avalokiteśvara).

The sounds and so forth, or the great divine mantra, the great illuminating mantra, the unsurpassed mantra, and the peerless mantra, do not treat illness, do not extinguish transgressions, and do not protect the sutras.
Furthermore, the Secret Division (Guhyatantra) generally comprises three categories:

first, the Buddha Family, which itself consists of five sub-families spoken by the five Buddhas; second, the Bodhisattva Family; and third, the Spirit Family. Each of these families [is further divided].
Within each [of these], there are three categories of dharmas—superior, middling, and inferior. Accomplishing increase (*puṣṭi*) is called the superior dharma;
averting calamities (*śāntika*) and summoning (*vaśīkaraṇa*) are called the middling dharma; and subjugation (*abhicāruka*) is called the inferior dharma.

Within the superior dharma, one further distinguishes three grades, each with its own ritual procedures, its own visualization methods, and its own strict prohibitions; yet all are universally governed by the unsurpassed bodhicitta as their primary principle.
If one lacks the transmission of a teacher, it is called "stealing the Dharma. If one violates the rules of conduct, one will incur an evil retribution.
If one transgresses the strict prohibitions or rashly speaks of one's spiritual efficacy to others, one will invite extraordinary calamities.

All of these are the Tathāgata’s inconceivable four *siddhi* methods for benefiting sentient beings; one must strictly rely on the sūtras and fortunately not deviate from the teachings. What was formerly called "incantation" (*dhāraṇī*) is now [referred to as]... [new term].

It is translated as *mantra* (true word) or *vidyā* (knowledge/incantation). Alternatively, because it is the name of a king of spirits (*bhūta-rāja*), it is able to subjugate spirits and deities (*bhūta-loka*).
Or, it is like a secret signal used within an army to ensure coordination among the troops. Or, it is like a secret method for subduing the wicked (as an antidote).
Or, it is the secret speech of the Tathāgata; for example, when a king says "Saindhava," his subjects do not understand [the specific meaning].
Only a wise minister can understand this: when washing, he offers water; when drinking, he offers a vessel; when eating, he offers salt;
when traveling, he offers a horse. It is the same with *dhāraṇī*: it is but a single dharma that possesses all powers universally.

Because it heals illness, eliminates transgressions, gives rise to goodness, and accords with the Path (the Ultimate Truth), its original sound is preserved without translation. △ Third: The Incantation.
In this evil age, those who protect and propagate this sutra frequently encounter many afflictions and difficulties; therefore, it is protected by means of mantras so that the Way may flow forth.

The text consists of four sections: first, the question regarding the merit of upholding the sutra; second, the answer that it is exceedingly great; third, the request for protection by means of dharanis;
and fourth, the benefits gained upon hearing this chapter. Now, the first section.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha,
and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if there are good men or good women who are able to receive and uphold the Lotus Sutra,
or read and recite it until they have mastered it, or copy its scrolls— how much merit will they obtain?"
[The Bodhisattva] replied: "Very much.

The Buddha said to Bhaiṣajyarāja: "If there were a son or daughter of good family who made offerings to as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in eight hundred million nayutas of Ganges Rivers, what do you think? Would the merit they obtain be great?"

"It is very much so, World-Honored One. The Buddha said, "If a son of good family or a daughter of good family is able to receive and uphold even a single four-line verse from this sutra, reading and reciting it, understanding its meaning, and practicing according to the teaching, their merit will be very great."
△ Third, the request for protection by means of mantras. This has five parts: first, Bhaiṣajyarāja; second, Śūradatta; third, Vaiśravaṇa; fourth, Dhṛtarāṣṭra; fifth, the rākṣasī.
Within the first part, there are four sections: first, the request; second, the teaching; third, the praise; fourth, the seal. Now, the first section.

World-Honored One, this dhāraṇī divine mantra has been spoken by as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in sixty-two billion Ganges Rivers;
if anyone should injure or defame this Dharma-preacher, they would thereby injure and defame all those Buddhas.
△ Four Seals.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha praised the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja, saying: "Excellent, excellent, Bhaiṣajyarāja!
Because you have compassionately protected this Dharma-preacher, you have spoken this dhāraṇī, which will bring great benefit to all sentient beings."
△ Second, the section on Vīradatta. Part one: the request; part two: the teaching; part three: the praise. Now, the first:

At that time, the Bodhisattva Vīradatta addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, I too shall preach a dhāraṇī for the protection of those who read, recite, receive, and uphold the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. If this Dharma-master obtains this dhāraṇī, even if yakṣas..."
Whether it be rākṣasas, pūtanas, kimpuruṣas, kumbhāṇḍas, or pretas, none shall be able to find an opportunity to exploit his weaknesses.

the tuft of hair between his eyebrows is as white as a conch or the moon; his teeth are white, even, and closely set, constantly emitting radiance; and his lips—"

His complexion was a beautiful red, like the *bimba* fruit. At that time, King Subhavyūha, having praised the Buddha for such immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of virtues, joined his palms with single-minded devotion before the Tathāgata and addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"World-Honored One, it is unprecedented! The Dharma of the Tathāgata is fully accomplished and inconceivably subtle."
"By virtue of these meritorious teachings and precepts, my conduct shall be secure, pleasant, and wholesome. From this day forward, I shall no longer act according to my own whims;
I shall not give rise to false views, arrogance, anger, or any other evil thoughts. Having spoken these words, he prostrated before the Buddha and departed.
Because he profoundly penetrates the true reality (*dharmatā*), he externally admires the Buddha’s virtues while internally transforming his own mind;

it is like realizing that ice and water share the same nature of moisture—once the ice is melted by hot water, it will never congeal again. This concludes the section on the benefits obtained by those transformed by Siming.
△ Fifth, the conclusion correlating the ancient and the modern.
The Buddha addressed the great assembly: "What do you think? Is King Subhavyūha anyone else? He is none other than the present Bodhisattva Flower Virtue (Puṣpaśrī).
And who was his Queen Pure Virtue (Viśuddhaguṇā)? She is the present Bodhisattva Adorned with Radiant Marks (Prabhāsa-vyūha-lakṣaṇa), who now stands before the Buddha.
Because he felt compassion for King Subhavyūha and his retinue, he was born in that Land of Radiant Adornment."
Those two sons are now the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja and the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyasamudgata.

Having accomplished such great merits as these, these two Bodhisattvas, Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata, have planted the roots of all virtues under immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas;
they have accomplished inconceivable and manifold wholesome merits. If there is anyone who recognizes these two—
Even all the devas and people of the world should pay homage to the name of a bodhisattva.
△ Sixth, awakening to the Way upon hearing this chapter.
When the Buddha preached this "Chapter on the Past Deeds of King Subhavyūha," eighty-four thousand people became free from dust and removed from defilement.
Within all phenomena, one attains the purity of the Dharma-eye.

Having attained the purity of the Dharma-eye within all phenomena, one universally illumines the three thousand [worlds] and thoroughly penetrates the nature of all phenomena—whether provisional or real—without obstruction or defiled attachment.
This is either a partial realization (*pradeśa-sākṣātkriyā*) or a semblance realization (*pratirūpa-sākṣātkriyā*), occurring in the second moment of mind.
The exhortation to propagate [the teaching] by means of benefiting others is concluded.
△ Third, the exhortation to propagate [the teaching] by means of one's own practice.
Chapter Twenty-Eight: Samantabhadra Bodhisattva’s Exhortation to Resolve.
The *Brahma-voice Viśvabhū Mahā-śāstra* and the *Viśvabhū Sūtra* both translate [the name] as Bianji (遍吉, "Pervasive Auspiciousness"). This sūtra translates it as Puxian (普賢, "Universal Worthy").

"Pu" (普) carries the meaning of "pervasive," and "xian" (賢) carries the meaning of "auspicious. Because he dwells at the summit of the assembly of those who have attained Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) and has subdued all paths, he is named "Pu" (Universal).
Because the path of severance is nearly exhausted and he is adjacent to the ultimate limit of the final stage, he is so named.
To be virtuous is like the moon on the fourteenth night; it is nearly like the moon on the fifteenth night. The *Buddha-uṣṇīṣa Sūtra* says:

"If I employ my mind-hearing to distinguish all the knowledge and views of sentient beings, and if there is even a single sentient being beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges who illuminates the practice of Samantabhadra within their own mind, I shall mount a six-tusked elephant and [go to them]."

My hundred thousand bodies all arrive at that place; even if their obstructions are so deep that they do not yet see me, I will, in the midst of darkness, touch the crowns of those people’s heads, protect them, and comfort them, causing them to achieve success. What is now called "exhortation" is a term for longing for the Dharma.
Having heard the beginning and end of this sutra in its entirety while staying far away in that land, [the Bodhisattvas] desire to personally practice it and transform others.
Because he is eternal and inexhaustible, he comes from the East once more to request the correct teaching, exhorting [the Buddha] to practice for himself;
he further requests the circulation of the Dharma, exhorting him to transform others. He then exhorts him collectively through vows, fully embodying the intent of the four *siddhāntas*.
"For the sake of making offerings to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, I shall manifest my own body. If you see my body..."
In the world-system Mahāpramudita, all beings, upon seeing me, further intensify their diligence and immediately attain samādhi and dhāraṇī.
They are such that no non-human being can destroy them, nor are they ever deluded by women;
this is the universal remedy (pratipakṣa). Bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms of a buddha-field possess the foremost path of Samantabhadra.

The meaning is complete; for these reasons of the four *siddhāntas*, [the Buddha] comes to exhort and inspire. The preceding judgment divides the text on the circulation of the teaching into three parts:
first, the three spiritual powers; second, the entrustment which clearly elucidates the transmission;

and third, from the chapter on Bhaiṣajyarāja downward through five chapters, which cite the great power of the Bodhisattvas’ transformative path to exhort the circulation of the teaching. Now, in this present chapter, the vows of Samantabhadra are cited.
The power of the vow is great for the purpose of encouraging its circulation. The text is divided into four parts: first, the arrival;

second, the exhortation to practice; third, the description of the practice; and fourth, the benefits of the practice. △ First, the arrival, which has three sections: first, making offerings to those above; second, transforming those below; and third, practicing reverence.

First: At that time, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, by means of his sovereign supernormal powers, majestic virtue, and renown, arrived from the east together with immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable great bodhisattvas; all the lands through which they passed were universally shaken.
It rains precious lotus flowers and performs immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of various kinds of music.
Sovereignty is the principle; supernatural power is the practice; majesty is the person; renown is the teaching.
Furthermore, sovereignty is permanence; supernatural power is bliss; majesty is the self; renown is purity—thus it is said.
To speak thus, these four virtues are all fully present: through majestic power, he causes the earth to tremble; through renown, flowers rain down;

through supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), music is played; and through mastery, movement, raining, and playing occur simultaneously. This is like a great dragon flying through the air, causing clouds to gather and rain to flow forth;
this is the power of the mind, the power of the Dharma, the power of sentient beings, and the power of responsive transformation (*nirmāṇa*).
This has been brought about by the inconceivable power of his strength; through these four virtues of wondrous power, he has come from afar to exhort and inspire us.
Regarding the four matters and the places he has visited, his own practice of making supreme offerings was as described above. Question:

In the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, it is clarified that Samantabhadra Bodhisattva dwells in accordance with the Truth (*tathatā*) and not within a land. Why, then, is it said here that he comes from the East? Answer: That sūtra...
This sutra reveals the nature of that which is realized; it is based here upon the traces of the Responsive Manifestation (nirmāṇakāya).

Since even those starting from the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) can partially realize the *tathatā* dharma-nature, how much more so for the traces followed by Samantabhadra? Furthermore, as for the traces followed by Prabhūtaratna, he is said to be in the East;
how much more so for Samantabhadra? If one knows that there are no lands outside of true nature (*dharmatā*), then one truly knows lands.
Beyond this, there is nothing else that can truly be dwelt upon. △ Second, the downward transformation:

Furthermore, he was surrounded by a great assembly of countless devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, each manifesting their majestic virtue and supernatural powers.
Power. According to what is appropriate for others, he manifests the forms of the eight classes of beings, complete with both principal and retinue, and endowed with the four virtues;

because two [of the virtues] are subsumed by each, it is said that "each manifests the power of majestic virtue and supernormal faculties. One should know that those followed are all the Dharma-body. Furthermore, together with...
The Great Bodhisattvas manifest their ultimate merit, while the eight classes of beings manifest their provisional merit;
both the provisional and the ultimate possess the four virtues and carry the dual intent of making offerings to those above and transforming those below. △ Third, the cultivation of reverence.
Upon arriving at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa in the Sahā world, he prostrated with his head at the feet of Śākyamuni Buddha and circumambulated him seven times to the right.
This concludes the section on his initial arrival. II. Encouraging the Aspiration (Dvaya): A. Encouraging the Aspiration through Inquiry; B. Encouraging the Aspiration through Vows.
The first of the two initial sections consists of a question and an answer. Now, for the first:

he addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, from afar in the land of the Buddha Ratnatejobhyudgatarāja, I have heard that in this Sahā world the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is being preached, and I have come together with immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of bodhisattvas."
We wish to hear and receive it; we pray that the World-Honored One will explain it for us:
how can good sons and good daughters, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, obtain this Lotus Sūtra?
I shall now explain this for you; please further clarify the essential points for the correct exposition and circulation [of this teaching].

How can one obtain this sutra? It means obtaining the sublime understanding of the correct exposition and circulation. "Please clarify the correct exposition" is an exhortation to develop one's own practice (*sva-pratipatti*);

"please circulate it" is an exhortation to develop the transformation of others (*parārtha*). This desire to cause the wondrous Dharma to flow forth infinitely is what is meant by "craving for the Dharma."
This is not the result of extreme contemplation. △ Second, the answer.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra: "If good sons or good daughters accomplish four dharmas, they shall obtain this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata.
First, they are protected and remembered by all Buddhas; second, they plant a multitude of virtues."
First, they enter the stage of right determination; second, they give rise to the mind that seeks to rescue all sentient beings.
Son of good family, son of good family, if a man or woman of good family accomplishes these four dharmas, they will certainly obtain this sutra after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata.
Since Samantabhadra Bodhisattva has requested both the correct exposition and the propagation of the teaching, the Buddha now answers with four dharmas to address both;
first, he answers regarding the correct exposition, which involves opening up the provisional to reveal the ultimate.

Although the Buddha possesses great compassion that is equal toward all sentient beings and seeks to deliver them universally, these beings are deluded and turn their backs on the Dharma-nature, like those living beneath overturned basins who cannot see the light themselves.

If, by means of the light of the sun [of wisdom], one can distance oneself from evil [worlds] and follow what is good [as a human], turn back from delusion [as the remedy] and return to awakening [the ultimate truth], opening the knowledge and vision of sentient beings to reveal the knowledge and vision of the Buddha, then this accords with the Sage’s mind;

this is being protected and mindful of by all Buddhas [the Dharma-body]. If the knowledge and vision of the Buddha is opened, then Prajñā illuminates; this is planting the roots of all virtues. Furthermore—
That which is neither distracted, nor savoring, nor grasping, nor abandoning is the entry into the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) (Prajñā).
Furthermore, that which above accords with the power of loving-kindness and below accords with the longing of compassion is the arousal of the mind to rescue sentient beings (Vimukti).

One should know that these four dharmas are nothing other than the opening of the provisional to reveal the real, and the realization of the three perfect virtues (*tri-dharmadhātu*). Moreover, "being protected and remembered by all Buddhas" is the opening [of the provisional].

Planting the roots of myriad virtues through the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is the manifestation of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; entering the stage of right determination is the entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;

giving rise to the mind that saves living beings is the awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. These four points encompass the essentials of the Gate of Traces. Furthermore, traces have their source:
because there are the three virtues of the Source, there are the three virtues within the traces. It is from the Source that these are revealed and manifested.
Because there is awakening and entry, there is the manifestation of awakening and entry within the traces (*jia*). Now, by revealing the traces, the fundamental reality (*ben*) is manifested;

since the fundamental and the trace are neither two nor distinct, he answers their request with these four dharmas as the formal teaching. Next, regarding the answer concerning the propagation [of the Dharma]:

the essentials of propagation consist of only three or four points. Now, being protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas and entering the stage of the right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), one is immediately established in suchness.
To plant the roots of all virtues is the practice of physical ease; to sit upon the Tathāgata’s seat is the practice of verbal ease;

to enter the Tathāgata’s chamber by giving rise to the mind that saves living beings is the practice of mental ease; and to be protected and remembered by all Buddhas is the practice of the vow of ease.

Because he practices, he answers his request with four dharmas for the purpose of circulating [the teaching]. First, in response to his two requests, he cites four [dharmas] as a canopy covering the entire sutra;
the meaning of his coming from afar to exhort and inspire is such that if one can practice these four dharmas, one will certainly understand the essence of the sutra.
Therefore, it says, "one will certainly obtain this sutra. This concludes the formal request for the exposition. One who can transport this understanding...
If one transmits this to others and they attain this faith and understanding, they become the first type of person who serves as a support;
if they attain true understanding, they become the second, third, and fourth types of persons who serve as supports. This constitutes the request for the circulation [of the teaching].
The first section, the exhortation through inquiry, is concluded. △ Second, the exhortation through vows, which has two parts: 1. The vow to protect people; 2. The vow to protect [the Dharma].

Regarding the six sections of the beginning of the Dharma: first, warding off external obstacles; second, teaching the internal Dharma; third, covering [the assembly] with supernormal powers; fourth, showing the proximate cause; fifth, showing the proximate fruit; and sixth, the concluding summary and exhortation. Now, the first section: The Buddha was dwelling at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, in Śrāvastī, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "Bhikṣus, you should know that there are four kinds of persons in the world. The Buddha spoke thus: "What are the four? First, the person who is like a broken water jar; second, the person who is like a leaking water jar; third, the person who is like a well-sealed water jar; and fourth, the person who is like a full water jar. What is meant by 'a person like a broken water jar'? It refers to one who has not yet heard the Dharma and Vinaya taught by the Tathāgata, nor has he practiced them. Upon hearing the Dharma and Vinaya taught by the Tathāgata, he does not believe or accept it, and consequently loses what he has previously gained. This is called a person like a broken water jar. What is meant by 'a person like a leaking water jar'? It refers to one who has heard the Dharma and Vinaya taught by the Tathāgata and has practiced them. Upon hearing the Dharma and Vinaya taught by the Tathāgata, he believes and accepts it, yet he loses what he has previously gained. This is called a person like a leaking water jar. What is meant by 'a person like a well-sealed water jar'? It refers to one who has heard the Dharma and Vinaya taught by the Tathāgata and has practiced them. Upon hearing the Dharma and Vinaya taught by the Tathāgata, he believes and accepts it, and does not lose what he has previously gained. This is called a person like a well-sealed water jar. What is meant by 'a person like a full water jar'? It refers to one who has heard the Dharma and Vinaya taught by the Tathāgata and has practiced them. Upon hearing the Dharma and Vinaya taught by the Tathāgata, he believes and accepts it, and having attained what he had not previously attained, he increases what he had previously attained. This is called a person like a full water jar. Bhikṣus, these are the four kinds of persons in the world. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to further explain this meaning, spoke in verse: "A person like a broken jar Does not hear the Dharma; Having heard it, they do not believe, And thus lose what they have gained. A person like a leaking jar Hears the Dharma and practices it; Having heard it, they believe, Yet lose what they have gained. A person like a sealed jar Hears the Dharma and practices it; Having heard it, they believe, And do not lose what they have gained. A person like a full jar Hears the Dharma and practices it; Having heard it, they believe, Increasing what they have gained. At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and faithfully practiced it. (Note: The above constitutes the first section, "Warding Off External Obstacles," within the six-part introduction.)

At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, in the final five hundred years of the defiled and evil age, for those who receive, uphold, and recite this sutra, I shall provide protection and remove their misfortunes and afflictions, causing them to attain peace and security.
I shall ensure that no one seeking to find an opportunity against them succeeds—whether it be Māras, sons of Māra, daughters of Māra, or the subjects of Māra."
Those possessed by Māra— whether yakṣas, rākṣasas, kumbhāṇḍas, piśācas, kiṃnaras, pūtanas, vetālas,
or other such beings who afflict people— shall find no opportunity to harm them.

Vedala is the lord of spirits who perform rites of suppression and incantation; this is translated as "Excellence" (Shanmiao). △ Second, teaching by means of internal dharmas, which is further divided into three parts:
first, practicing while standing and reciting; second, reflecting while seated; third, diligent practice for twenty-one days. Now, the first part.
Whether this person is walking or standing while reading and reciting this sutra, at that time I shall mount the white six-tusked elephant king and,
together with a great assembly of bodhisattvas, go to their place and manifest my own body to make offerings, provide protection, and comfort their hearts;
this is also for the sake of making offerings to the Lotus Sutra.
△ Second, if they sit in contemplation:
if this person sits in contemplation of this sutra, at that time I shall again mount the king of white elephants and appear before that person.
If there be any single phrase or verse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* that they have forgotten, I shall instruct them and restore it to them.
They shall read and recite it together until they have mastered it. At that time, those who uphold, read, and recite the Lotus Sūtra will behold my body and experience great joy;

they will become even more diligent in their practice. Because they behold me, they will immediately attain samādhis and dhāraṇīs, namely the *Sūryagati* (Turning) Dhāraṇī, the hundreds of thousands of millions of *Sūryagati* Dhāraṇīs, and the *Dharmasvara-upāya* (Skillful Means of the Sound of the Dharma) Dhāraṇī.
Luo-ni (Lakṣaṇī) attains such dhāraṇīs as these.
"Revolution" (xuan) means revolving from the provisional to enter emptiness; "hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, and billions" means revolving from emptiness to enter the provisional.
"Dharma-sound skillful means" (fayin fangbian) means that these two serve as skillful means for attaining entry into the Middle Way, the primary truth. △ Three, Thirty-seven.
Vigorous effort. World-Honored One, if in a future age, during the final five hundred years of the defiled and evil world, there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas,
or upāsikās who seek it, uphold it, recite it, transcribe it, and desire to cultivate it—
During the twenty-one days [of my preaching] of the Lotus Sutra, you should practice with single-minded diligence until the twenty-one days are complete.

At that time, I shall mount a six-tusked white elephant and, surrounded by immeasurable bodhisattvas, manifest before that person in a body pleasing to all sentient beings, preaching the Dharma to instruct, benefit, and gladden them; furthermore, I shall bestow upon them the *dhāraṇī*.
"Because one has obtained this dhāraṇī-mantra, no non-human being can destroy them, nor shall they be deluded or disturbed by women;
my own body shall also constantly protect such a person. I only pray that the World-Honored One will grant me leave to speak this dhāraṇī-mantra.
Thereupon, before the Buddha, he spoke the mantra, saying:
Atandati (1), tandatavati (2), tandatavadi (3), tandat-kuśale (4),
tandatuśale (5), tuśale (6), tuśaravati (7), buddhaprasanne (8), sarvadhāraṇī-āvartani (9), sarvavaśa-āvartani.
(10) Ābhojanī; (11) Saṃghāvaśeṣanī; (12) Saṃghanairgaṭanī; (13) Asaṃkhyeya; (14) Saṃghabheda; (15) Tiri-ā-saṃgha-tūlya-arāti-parāti; (16) Sarvasaṃghati-samādhi-garandi; (17) [End].
*Sarvadharma-supratiṣṭhita* (18); *Sarvasattvarutakauśalyānugata* (19); *Syanabhigītā* (20).
Having thus completed the instruction on the internal Dharma, he thirdly covered [the assembly] with his supernatural power (*ṛddhibala*).
World-Honored One, if there are bodhisattvas who hear this dhāraṇī, they should know it is the power of Samantabhadra’s spiritual penetrations;
if the Lotus Sūtra circulates in Jambudvīpa and there are those who receive and uphold it, they should form this thought:
"All of this is due to the majestic spiritual power of Samantabhadra."
△ Fourth, showing the superior causes: If there are those who receive,
uphold, read, recite, correctly contemplate, and understand the meaning and intent [of this teaching], and practice according to what is taught,

you should know that such persons perform the conduct of Samantabhadra, have deeply planted roots of goodness in the presence of immeasurable and boundless Buddhas, and are [protected] by all Tathāgatas...
The Buddha comes and strokes their head with his hand.

This signifies that by practicing the conduct of Samantabhadra, they will attain liberation like the Buddhas of the future; that they have deeply planted roots of goodness under the Buddhas of the past;
and that they are being matured by the Buddhas of the present as he strokes their head. △ Fifth, showing the proximate fruit.
If one merely transcribes this, at the end of their life they shall be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; at that time,

eighty-four thousand celestial maidens will perform various musical entertainments to welcome them, and the person will immediately don a crown of the seven treasures and enjoy themselves in pleasure among the handmaidens—
how much more so for those who receive, uphold, read, recite, correctly contemplate, and understand its meaning and intent as it was taught!

Regarding this practice, if there is anyone who upholds, recites, and understands its meaning and intent, at the end of that person's life, a thousand Buddhas will extend their hands to them, ensuring they are not terrified and do not fall into the evil realms. They will immediately proceed to the Tuṣita Heaven to the abode of Maitreya Bodhisattva.
Maitreya Bodhisattva possesses the thirty-two marks of a Great Being and is surrounded by a multitude of great bodhisattvas numbering one hundred [thousand].
Among those born there, one gains such merits and benefits as these, accompanied by a retinue of hundreds of thousands of millions of celestial maidens.

Merely by being able to transcribe [this text], one is born near the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; if one possesses the five qualities of a Dharma-master, one is born in Tuṣita and becomes a member of the retinue of the Future Buddha (Upapadyaka).
Question: Why is one not born in the Land of Peace and Bliss (Sukhāvatī)? Answer: If one makes pure vows, then according to them—
According to the depth of their contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), four kinds of blissful lands are produced;
if one does not resolve to attain the Pure Land, then according to the completion of the five grades of merit, one will be reborn in Tuṣita. △ Sixth, the summary and exhortation.

Therefore, the wise person should single-mindedly write this themselves or have others write it, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, maintain right mindfulness of it, and practice according to its teachings.
This concludes the section on the initial vow to protect persons. 2. The Vow to Protect the Dharma.

“World-Honored One, by means of my supernormal powers, I shall now protect this sutra and cause it to be widely circulated within Jambudvīpa after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, so that it shall not be interrupted.”

The second section on exhortation is concluded. △ Third, the description of the two types of arousal [of the resolve]: first, the description of protecting the Dharma; second, the description of protecting persons. Now, the first:
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha praised him, saying: "Excellent, excellent! Samantabhadra, you are able to protect and assist this..."
The Sūtra has already brought peace, happiness, and benefit to many sentient beings;

you have accomplished inconceivable merit and profound great compassion, and having long ago resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, you are able to make such vows of supernatural power to protect this Sūtra. I, too, shall protect it with my own supernatural powers.
Those who uphold the name of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, and uphold the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*—all these are through the supernatural power of Samantabhadra.

Hearing the name of Samantabhadra and upholding his name are all through the supernatural power of the Tathāgata. This passage simultaneously describes the third type of person protected [by the sūtra].

This is covered by the power of spiritual transformations (*ṛddhi*). △ Second, the description of the protectors, in five parts: first, the description of the second teaching which uses internal dharmas;

second, the description of the fourth which shows the superior causes; third, the description of the fifth which shows the proximate fruits; fourth, the description of the first which wards off external difficulties;
fifth, the description of the summary conclusion and exhortation. Now, the first part.

Samantabhadra, you should know that if there are those who receive, uphold, read, recite, correctly contemplate, practice, and transcribe this Lotus Sūtra, such persons shall see Śākyamuni Buddha as if hearing this sūtra directly from the Buddha’s own mouth;
you should know that such persons have made offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha; you should know that such persons are praised by the Buddha with the words, "Excellent! You should know.
One should know that such a person has had their head stroked by the hand of Śākyamuni Buddha and is covered by the robe of Śākyamuni Buddha.
To see Śākyamuni Buddha is not merely to see the white elephant with six tusks, the body of Samantabhadra; it is to hear [the Dharma] from the mouth of the Buddha.
Not only was Samantabhadra reciting together with him; the Buddha praised him, saying "Excellent," and stroked him while covering him with his robe.

Not only was Samantabhadra providing protection through mantras; the praise "Excellent" signifies the accomplishment of the practice of the empty seat, the stroking of the body signifies the accomplishment of the practice of the compassionate chamber, and the covering with the robe signifies the accomplishment of the practice of the robe of patience.
△ Second, the description of the fourth [section], showing the superior causes.

Such a person no longer craves worldly pleasures, does not take delight in the scriptures or writings of non-Buddhists, nor does he enjoy associating with such people or with those who are evil—whether they be butchers, those who raise pigs, sheep, chickens, or dogs, hunters, or those who traffic in female beauty.
This person’s mind is upright and honest; he possesses right mindfulness and merit.
By this power, such a person is not afflicted by the three poisons, nor are they afflicted by envy, self-conceit, false pride, or overweening pride;
such a person has few desires and is content, and is able to cultivate the conduct of Samantabhadra.
△ Third, the fifth section describes the near fruit.

If, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, during the final five hundred years, there is anyone who sees one who receives, upholds, reads, or recites the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, they should form this thought:
"This person shall before long proceed to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), destroy the hosts of Māra, and attain [enlightenment]."
One shall turn the wheel of the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, beat the drum of the Dharma, blow the conch of the Dharma, and rain down the rain of the Dharma;
one shall sit upon the lion Dharma-seat amidst the great assembly of devas and humans.
Samantabhadra, if anyone in a future age upholds, receives, reads, or recites this sutra, that person shall no longer be greedily attached to clothing, bedding, food, drink, or life’s necessities.
The aspirations of living beings shall not be in vain, and they shall obtain their karmic rewards even in this present life.
When one proceeds to the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), one will surely achieve the ultimate fruit; how could it stop at the proximate fruits of the Trāyastriṃśa or Tuṣita heavens?
Although one does not crave the four requisites of life, one still obtains their karmic rewards in this present life; how could it stop until after death, when one is reborn [in a higher realm]?
"Is it Heaven? △ Fourth, describing the first [aspect]: warding off external difficulties.

If there are those who speak with contempt and disparagement, saying, "You are merely a madman; practicing such deeds in vain, you shall ultimately gain nothing," and that as a retribution for such sins, one shall be blind life after life;
whereas if there are those who offer worship and praise, one shall [reap the benefits] in this very life.
If one sees someone who receives and upholds this sutra and exposes their faults—
whether real or unreal— that person will suffer from leprosy in this present life. Furthermore, those who mock them lightly shall, in every successive lifetime,
have teeth that are sparse and missing, ugly lips, flat noses, contorted hands and feet, squinting eyes, and bodies foul with stench, suffering from malignant sores and pus.

Regarding blood, water, abdominal ailments, shortness of breath, and various other grave illnesses, the Buddha extensively demonstrated the offenses of those who disparage [this teaching] so that they might recognize their transgressions and reform them, rather than causing mutual affliction and disorder.

It is not only that those who uphold the sutra find it difficult to extinguish [their karmic obstacles], but even for those who wish to disparage it, merit arises; when there is neither disparagement nor difficulty, both parties shall enjoy peace and happiness.
To provide vast salvation without partiality is the height of compassion. △ Fifth, the concluding summary and exhortation:
Therefore, Samantabhadra, if you see one who receives and upholds this sutra, you should go out to welcome them from afar, treating them with the same reverence as you would the Buddha.

The third section, describing the arousal [of the aspiration], is concluded. △ Fourth, the benefits of the arousal, in two parts: first, the benefits of hearing this chapter; second, the benefits of hearing the sutra. Now, the first:
When this "Chapter on the Exhortation of Samantabhadra" was being spoken, bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, immeasurable and boundless, attained the hundred [samādhis].
Bodhisattvas equal in number to the atoms of a trichiliocosm, possessing ten million billion *āvartana-dhāraṇīs* and fully endowed with the path of Samantabhadra—
these ten million billion *āvartana-dhāraṇīs* are nothing other than the wisdom of the differentiation of the Dharma-realm, fully endowed with Samantabhadra.
The Way is the fulfillment of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), bordering upon the ultimate state of the Holy Ones. △ Second, the benefits of hearing the sutra:

When the Buddha spoke this sutra, the entire great assembly—including Samantabhadra and other bodhisattvas, Śāriputra and other śrāvakas, as well as devas, nāgas, humans, and non-humans—were all greatly rejoiced; they received and upheld the Buddha’s words and paid homage.
And they departed.
Regarding the three matters of joy, as previously explained, why here is he still called a *śrāvaka*? This is merely because the compiler of the sutra has preserved his original status.
Furthermore, the compiler refers to him as a "Mahāyāna *śrāvaka*" so that, by means of the sound of the Buddha-way, he may... [lead others].
All have heard it.

Postscript.
Alas! This wondrous Dharma of the Perfect and Sudden is difficult to encounter even over vast eons;

that I, a foolish and ignorant person, have by fortunate circumstance met with it—each time I open and read it, it is as if I had heard it in a former life—is this not due to the majestic spiritual power of Samantabhadra and the protective merit of Śākyamuni?
Since the Great Master Zhiyi can no longer appear, later worthies stubbornly cling to their views, causing strife and contention to proliferate.
This dharma-gate of perfect interfusion and absolute transcendence was nearly lost to the prejudices of "this" and "that," or right and wrong;

yet those who propagate it have made its defensive walls ever higher and deeper, while those who look upon it grow increasingly suspicious and fearful day by day. Hearing of it and witnessing it with my own eyes, I feel a sense of frustration and heartache.
Undaunted by my own mediocrity, I have ventured to introduce this teaching, taking up my brush on the eleventh month of the year Jichu (1949).
On the fifth day of the first month, I had just finished composing the preface, but lay ill for half a month until the nineteenth, when I was finally able to exert myself in the task.
Day and night I applied myself with diligence, my hand never ceasing from writing and my eyes never ceasing from reading.

On the twenty-sixth day of the twelfth month, I completed three fascicles of the sutra text; calculating the total, there are eight fascicles of the *Huìyì* (Compendium of Meanings). After a three-day break, on the day of Gengyin:
I began drafting this on New Year’s Day, and it was only after a full month that it was completed.
In total, the collected commentaries comprise sixteen volumes, requiring sixty-eight days of dedicated mental and physical effort. Alas!
I have heard that in ancient times, some were able to recite the entire Avataṃsaka Sūtra in the time of a single incense stick; yet I, Xù, am of dull faculties and have had to labor so strenuously.

This may well be ridiculed; yet, by using this to guide and receive beginners so that they may gradually awaken to the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the *Lotus Sūtra*, neither pressing the sword to its hilt nor gazing out at the vast ocean, Śākyamuni, Samantabhadra, and the Venerable Zhiyi will surely witness the earnest toil of Xu.
This colophon was written with the brush laid down at the hour of Si on the first day of the second month of the Gengyin year.
